In which one of the Virginians returns to England

It was a fine autumn morning in 1759, and the air hung heavy with the scent of woodsmoke and damp earth. At Oakhurst, the great estate nestled in the rolling hills of Surrey, the leaves had begun to turn—crimson, gold, and russet—drifting down like embers from the trees. The house stood quiet, its stone walls weathered by time and memory, its windows reflecting the pale blue sky. Within, the servants moved with hushed precision, preparing for the arrival of a guest whose name had long been whispered across the drawing-rooms of London and the plantations of Virginia.

He came not by coach but on horseback, riding through mist-laden lanes, his cloak flapping behind him like a banner. His face, though still young, bore the marks of distant lands—the sun-kissed skin, the sharpness of purpose in his eyes. He was Harry Esmond, son of a planter and a lady of English blood, raised among tobacco fields and Indian trails, yet now returning to the soil of his ancestors.

As he dismounted before the portico, the old butler stepped forward, bowing low. “Mr. Harry Esmond?” he asked, voice trembling slightly.

“Aye,” replied Harry, stepping down with ease. “And you are Mr. Warrington’s man?”

The butler nodded. “I am. And if you’ll follow me, sir, your rooms have been prepared.”

Harry smiled faintly. “Then let us be about it. After six years abroad, I’ve no desire to linger in the cold.”

Inside, the house breathed history. Portraits lined the hallways—men in powdered wigs, women in silk gowns, their eyes fixed as if watching every step he took. One painting caught his attention: a woman with dark hair and a look of quiet strength, her hand resting on a child’s shoulder. Below it read: *Lady Hester Esmond, née Warrington.*

He paused. “She was my mother,” he murmured, more to himself than anyone else.

That evening, at dinner, the family gathered around the long oak table. There were cousins, uncles, aunts—all speaking in voices that seemed both familiar and strange. The talk turned to politics, war, and the colonies. America, they said, was restless. The French were still in Canada. And the King, though far away, was always near in conversation.

But Harry listened only half-heartedly. His thoughts wandered—not to the wars or the land, but to the woman who had died giving birth to him, and to the father he had never known. He remembered the stories told in Virginia: how his father had left England under scandal, how his mother had followed him across the sea, only to die in childbirth.

Now, standing beneath the chandeliers of Oakhurst, he felt both welcome and out of place. He was home—but not truly. He was a Virginian, yes, but also an Englishman. A gentleman, perhaps, but one shaped by forests and frontier life.

Later, alone in his room, he lit a pipe and stared out the window. The moon rose over the garden, casting silver light upon the sleeping grounds. Somewhere, a dog barked. Then silence.

He sighed. “Well,” he said aloud, “here I am. Let the world begin again.”

On the wall of a study in Boston, once occupied by one of America’s most celebrated writers, hang two crossed swords—each worn by a relative during the War of Independence. One belonged to a loyalist who fought for the Crown; the other, to a patriot who stood firm for liberty. Though their blades faced opposite causes, both were carried with courage and honor. The man who now owns these relics has earned a name respected on both sides of the Atlantic—where intellect and character are welcomed without question. This tale echoes those swords: it tells of two brothers born in Virginia, sons of the Old Dominion, who found themselves on opposing sides during the great conflict, yet reunited at its end not as enemies, but as kin, their bond unbroken by war.

In an English parlor adorned with polished wood and ancestral portraits, I once saw the likenesses of these two men—the one in scarlet, the other in blue and buff—hanging side by side. Their descendant showed me letters they wrote, books they read, papers they kept. These relics had long been treasured by a woman whose memory was as strong as her love for her children: Madam Esmond Warrington. To distinguish them from others bearing the same noble name, she called them “The Virginians”—a name that would come to define their legacy.

They lived at the edge of the old world, just before it faded into history. They knew kings and generals, courtiers and outlaws, soldiers and scholars. Through their letters, we glimpse figures who once walked the earth—men whose voices seem to rise from yellowed pages stained with ink, tears, and even blood. One letter bears a bullet hole; another is smeared with the blood of its writer. Such documents might have vanished if not for the care of one devoted woman—Madam Esmond—who saved every word her sons ever sent, from the first note of a boyish affection to the final message delivered hours before her death.

Among them was a letter from Henry, the younger twin, writing to his brother George, then recovering from a sprain at Castlewood, Virginia, thanking their grandfather for a horse he rode with his tutor. And later, a final missive: “From my beloved son,” received moments before she passed. She never journeyed to Europe except once, in the reign of King George II, with her parents. When Castlewood burned during the war, she fled to Richmond and became known thereafter as Madam Esmond—no longer concerned with the Warrington name, which she held in low regard compared to her own lineage.

These letters are sparse—not full narratives, but sketches, hints, glimpses of lives lived across continents. Perhaps I have misread their tone or imagined too much. Yet as I studied them, I tried to place myself in their shoes—to feel where they stood, whom they spoke to, what stirred beneath their words. I’ve drawn their characters as I believed them to be, shaped their conversations as I thought they might have sounded, and sought to breathe life into a past that feels almost within reach. Whether I succeeded, dear reader, you must judge.

It was a summer morning in 1756, under the reign of King George II, when the *Young Rachel*, a Virginia-bound ship under Captain Edward Franks, sailed up the Avon River after its annual voyage to the Potomac. With the tide, it glided toward Bristol and moored near Trail’s wharf, where Mr. Trail, part-owner of the vessel, watched from his counting house. Seeing the ship arrive, he rowed over and climbed aboard.

Mr. Trail, a solemn man with thick hair and a serious face, greeted Captain Franks warmly, congratulating him on a safe return. After offering thanks to Heaven, he turned to business: cargo, passengers, profits.

Franks, a cheerful fellow with a ready laugh, replied, “We’ve only one passenger—a young gentleman who took the state cabin—and this ugly negro boy fetching the trunks.”

“Confound your luck!” said Trail, frowning. “The *Duke William* brought fourteen passengers last week—half our size!”

“And this gentleman,” continued Franks, “doesn’t pay a penny. Swear now, it’ll do you good, Mr. Trail—it’s the best medicine I know.”

“A passenger taking the whole cabin and not paying? Good heavens, Captain Franks—are you mad?”

“Ask him yourself—he’s coming.”

And indeed, a young man stepped onto the deck. He was about nineteen, dressed in deep mourning, carrying a cloak and a sword. He called out cheerfully, “Gumbo, you fool—why aren’t you getting the baggage out? Well, shipmate, our journey ends today. You’ll see all the little ones tonight—Polly, Betty, Little Tommy. Give my love to Mrs. Franks. Yesterday I thought the voyage would never end. Now I’m almost sorry it’s over. That little berth in my cabin looks so cozy now I’m leaving it.”

Trail scowled at the free rider. He barely nodded as Franks introduced him. “This is Mr. Trail, sir—name you’ve heard of.”

“It’s well known in Bristol,” said Trail, stiffly.

“And this is Mr. Warrington—son of Madam Esmond Warrington of Castlewood,” added Franks.

At once, Trail removed his hat and bowed deeply, as if before royalty. “Gracious powers, Mr. Warrington! What a delight! How fortunate your voyage has been! Let me welcome you to England—my boat awaits. As the son of my benefactress, Mrs. Esmond Warrington, whose name is honored on Bristol Exchange, I’m honored to greet you. Isn’t it, Franks?”

“There’s no better tobacco than from Virginia,” said Franks, pulling out a brass box and stuffing a plug into his mouth. “You’ll take to it, sir—I promise. Won’t you, Mr. Trail? I wish you had ten shiploads instead of one. I’ve told Madam Esmond that—I’ve ridden through her plantation. She treats me like a lord. No waiting in the counting room like some folks do.” (He glanced pointedly at Trail.)

“She’s a true lady,” he added. “Could have a thousand hogsheads as easily as her hundreds—if only there were hands enough.”

“I’ve recently entered the Guinea trade,” said Trail, eager to impress. “I could supply her ladyship with any number of healthy young negroes by next fall.”

“We do not buy or sell people from Africa,” said the young man coldly. “My grandfather and mother opposed it. I cannot bear the thought of trading in human suffering.”

“But it’s for their good!” cried Trail. “Their temporal and spiritual salvation! Let me speak with you further at my home. I can offer you a Christian household, honest fare, and a warm welcome. Can’t I, Captain Franks?”

“Can’t say,” growled Franks. “Never invited me to dinner. Only once to psalm-singing and a sermon by Mr. Ward. Not my kind of entertainment.”

Ignoring the jab, Trail pressed on. “Business is business, young sir. As heir to Lady Esmond’s estate—do I speak to the rightful heir?”

The young man bowed slightly. “Yes.”

“And I urge you, at once, to expand your fortune. As your factor, I’d be remiss not to advise it. As a prudent man, should I hesitate to speak of profit? No, my dear Mr. George.”

“My name is not George,” said the youth, turning away. His eyes filled with tears. “It’s Henry.”

“Gracious powers!” cried Trail. “But you’re the heir—George Esmond Warrington, Esq.—”

“Hold your tongue, you fool!” roared Franks, striking Trail hard on the ribs. “Don’t you see the lad is weeping? Look at his black clothes!”

“What do you mean?” demanded Trail. “Mr. George is the heir—I know Colonel Esmond’s will.”

“Mr. George is there,” said Franks, pointing upward. “Up there. On the topmast—or beyond.”

“Where?”

“Mr. George is there,” repeated Franks, raising his finger to the sky. “He died a year ago, July 9th. He went with General Braddock to the Belle Riviere. A thousand men—every one—were killed. Cut down like wheat. You know how the Indians fight, Mr. Trail?” He ran a hand around his head.

“Horrible,” said Trail. “Truly horrible. He was a fine young man—just like this one, only with black hair—now lying in some Indian wigwam. He used to come aboard the *Young Rachel*. Always had his books opened on deck before landing. Shy, quiet—unlike this one, who was full of songs and laughter. When he heard the news, he collapsed. Took ill—fever from the Potomac swamps—but he’s recovered on this voyage. The sea does wonders. And now, the young gentleman can’t mourn forever. Since we sighted Ireland, he’s been happy again—though sometimes, when he laughs, he says, ‘I wish my dearest Georgy could share this with me.’ Mention the name, and he breaks down.”

And the captain himself blinked back tears.

Trail assumed a solemn air, prepared to offer condolences. But Henry Warrington refused his hospitality, stayed only long enough to drink wine and collect money, and left quickly. But he parted warmly with Captain Franks, and the crew cheered as he stepped ashore.

Harry Warrington and his brother had often studied maps of England, planning their return. Every American raised with love for the mother country—especially those of Anglo-Saxon descent—dreams of such a journey. They imagine the places their parents described, the lands whispered in stories. The word *Home*, as used by Americans toward Britain, carries a weight of longing few can understand.

Harry had mapped his route carefully: from Bristol to Bath, to Salisbury, Winchester, Hexton, and finally, Castlewood. He had planned every mile. Before London’s grand churches, the Tower, Whitehall, Shakespeare’s grave, and the battlefields of Derby, Falkirk, and Culloden—before all these sacred sites—there was one destination more sacred than any: Castlewood House, the family seat in Hampshire, where his parents’ stories had always led him.

As he traveled, the landscape unfolded like a dream. From the inn hall, the plump landlady watched him pass, surrounded by punch bowls and silver flagons. The chamberlain bowed him upstairs. The chambermaid curtsied. Gumbo, in the kitchen, boasted of his master’s wealth and grand estate.

The postchaise raced through scenery more beautiful than Harry had ever seen. For modern Americans, England’s woods and villages may seem idyllic. But for Harry, accustomed to swamps and log cabins, this was paradise. The roads were alive—wagons clattered, coaches flew, packhorses straggled, lords galloped past in gilt carriages. Farmers trotted to market, parsons jolted along on donkeys, children waved, milkmaids curtseyed. Church spires gleamed, cottages sparkled, elms rustled in the breeze.

To be nineteen, healthy, wealthy, traveling at nine miles an hour—what joy! But Harry had eyes only for home.

Finally, the chaise stopped at the rustic inn on Castlewood Green. The sign bore the Three Castles—the crest of the Esmond family. Above the gate of Castlewood House hung the same emblem—the hatchment of Francis, Lord Castlewood, now dead, his son ruling in his place.

Harry had heard much of Lord Francis. It was for Frank’s sake that Colonel Esmond gave up his claim to English titles and retired to Virginia. The late earl had been a wild youth, fought under Marlborough, married a foreign wife, embraced Catholicism, then returned to the Church of England. He had supported the Crown, earned a peerage from King George II, and died in peace.

Though Colonel Esmond loved him, Madam Esmond disliked her half-brother—finding him dull unless drunk, boisterous, and vulgar. The boys admired their grandfather more than their kinsman.

With a pounding heart, Harry approached the house where his grandsire had grown up. The village green sloped down to the river, spanned by an ancient stone bridge. Beyond rose the gray stone mansion, gabled and buttressed, backed by dark woods.

At the gate sat an old man on a stone bench. A dog curled at his feet. Above, a window framed with flowers revealed curious faces—girls watching the stranger in black and his ebony servant, also in mourning.

To Harry’s surprise, the old man greeted him by name.

“You’ve had a nice ride to Hextonth, Master Harry. The sorrel carried you well.”

“I think you’re Lockwood,” said Harry, voice trembling, extending his hand.

His grandfather had spoken often of Lockwood, who had served Colonel Esmond and Viscount Francis in Marlborough’s wars.

The old man blinked. “They say I forget things—but not that. Just now, my daughter asked, ‘Father, why are you in black?’ ‘Because my lord is dead,’ I said. ‘A foul blow. Master Frank is my lord now. And Master Harry—why, you’ve grown taller, changed your hair—but I know you.’”

A girl stepped out, curtseying. “Grandfather doesn’t remember well,” she said, pointing to her head.

“You’ve heard of Lockwood?” asked Harry.

“And you—have you heard of Colonel Francis Esmond?”

“Captain and Major in Webb’s Foot,” said Lockwood proudly. “Served him in two campaigns. Wasn’t I, Ponto?”

“The Colonel who married Viscountess Rachel—my late lord’s mother? Who went to live among the Indians? We’ve heard of him. We’ve his portrait in the gallery—he painted it himself.”

“He went to Virginia, died seven years ago. I am his grandson.”

“Lord, your honour!” cried Molly. “Your skin’s as white as mine! Grandfather, hear this? He’s Colonel Esmond’s grandson—sent us tobacco, came all the way from Virginia!”

“To see you, Lockwood,” said Harry. “And the family. I set foot in England yesterday. My first visit is to home. May I see the house—even if the family is away?”

Molly ventured, “Mrs. Barker will let your honour in.”

And so Harry Warrington crossed the courtyard, moving with ease as if he had been born there—while Molly followed, and Gumbo bowed profusely, whispering compliments.

Colonel Esmond’s grandson rang the bell of Castlewood, the ancestral home, but for a long while no one seemed to heed his call. When at last a servant emerged, he showed little interest in the fact that the visitor was a relation. The family was away, and John, the servant, cared little for distant kin—his only concern was returning to his card game with Thomas in the window seat. The housekeeper was busy preparing for the arrival of my lord and my lady, expected that evening. Only after persistent pleading did Harry gain permission to view my lady’s sitting room and the gallery of portraits. There, sure enough, hung a likeness of his grandfather—dressed in periwig and breastplate, identical to the portrait in Virginia—and a painting of his grandmother as Lady Castlewood, clothed in the fashion of Charles II’s reign: bare-necked, her golden hair falling in ringlets over her shoulders, the same curls Harry remembered once silvered by age. But before he could linger long, the housekeeper curtly dismissed him. Her own family was arriving soon—the Countess, my lord and his brother, the young ladies, and the Baroness Bernstein, who would occupy the state bedroom.

Who was the Baroness? She was the aunt of the young ladies, and Harry jotted down her name on a slip of paper from his pocketbook and placed it on a table in the hall: “Henry Esmond Warrington, of Castlewood, Virginia, arrived yesterday—staying at the Three Castles.” The lackeys rose hastily from their cards to open the door, eager for their “wails” (tips), and Gumbo left his bench at the gate, where he’d been chatting with old Lockwood, the porter, who took Harry’s guinea without understanding its significance.

During his brief visit to the ancestral seat, Harry had seen only little Polly’s face as showing any warmth or kindness. He walked away, hiding his disappointment, wounded by the coldness of the place. They ought to have known him. Had any of them ridden to his house in Virginia—whether the master were present or not—they would have been welcomed with open arms. Yet here, beneath the shadow of his ancestors’ hall, he found himself begging for a simple meal of bacon and eggs at a country alehouse.

After dinner, he went to the bridge and sat upon it, gazing toward the old house, where the sun was sinking behind the trees and rooks flew home to their nests in the elms. His imagination conjured visions of the past—knights crossing the ford, cavaliers from King Charles’s time, my Lord Castlewood, his grandmother’s first husband, riding forth with hawk and hound. Memories of his beloved brother stirred within him, bringing a wave of tenderness so sharp it made him lower his head, sorrow renewed for the companion with whom he had shared every joy and grief until recently.

Lost in thought, punctuated by the clink of the blacksmith’s forge nearby, the cawing of rooks, and birds calling through the twilight, two young men on horseback thundered across the bridge. One cursed loudly, calling him a fool and ordering him out of the way. The other, perhaps fearing he’d knocked the foot traveler off balance, spurred ahead, shouting to his companion, “Come on, Tom!” Before Harry could recover from the shock or anger at their rudeness, they were already climbing the hill toward Castlewood.

Moments later, two liveried servants on horseback followed, scowling at the stranger on the bridge—a true British welcome: “Curse you, who are you?” Then came a coach-and-six, a heavy vehicle drawn by six horses, carrying three ladies, two maids, and an armed man seated behind. Three pale, handsome faces peered out at Harry as the carriage passed. He recognized the family crest and offered a salute, but none returned it. The gentleman behind glared at him haughtily. Harry felt utterly alone. He longed to return to Captain Franks. The Rachel, with her small, restless cabin, seemed suddenly more inviting than this cold, indifferent world.

The landlord of the Three Castles had shown Harry a chamber, but he refused to unpack his trunk, certain the family would invite him to stay. Hour after hour passed—no invitation came. Finally, he allowed his luggage to be opened and called for slippers and gown. Just before dark, a second carriage with four horses crossed the bridge, and a stout, high-cheeked woman with dark eyes stared sharply at Mr. Warrington. That was the Baroness Bernstein, the landlord said—my lord’s aunt. Harry recalled that the first Lady Castlewood had been of German descent.

Earl, countess, baroness, postillions, gentlemen, and horses all vanished into the castle gates. Harry, defeated and lonely, finally retired to bed, his heart heavy with neglect. He could not sleep, and soon the sounds of revelry erupted from the inn’s bar—shouts, curses, giggles, screams—enough to keep any man awake.

Then came Gumbo’s voice outside: “You cannot go in, sar—my master asleep, sar!” But a shrill, oath-filled voice—Harry recognized it immediately—screamed back, calling Gumbo a “stupid negro woolly-pate,” and shoved him aside. A flood of oaths poured into the room, followed by a young man.

“Beg your pardon, Cousin Warrington,” the young man cried, “are you asleep? I beg your pardon for nearly riding you into the river. Didn’t know you—course shouldn’t have done it—thought it was a lawyer with a writ—dressed in black, you know. Gad! Thought it was Nathan come to nab me.” Mr. William laughed wildly. Clearly, he was drunk.

“You did me great honor to mistake me for a sheriff’s officer, cousin,” Harry replied gravely, sitting up in his nightcap.

“Gad! I thought it was Nathan, and was going to send you souse into the river. But I ask your pardon. You see, I’d been drinking at the Bell at Hexton, and the punch is good there. Hullo! You, Davis! A bowl of punch; d’you hear?”

“I’ve had my share for tonight, cousin, and I should think you have,” Harry continued, maintaining his dignity.

“You want me to go, Cousin What’s-your-name, I see,” Mr. William said, sobering slightly. “You want me to go, and they want me to come, and I didn’t want to come. I said, I’d see him hanged first—that’s what I said. Why should I trouble myself to come down all alone of an evening, and look after a fellow I don’t care a pin for? Zackly what I said. Zackly what Castlewood said. Why the devil should he go down? Castlewood says, and so said my lady, but the Baroness would have you. It’s all the Baroness’s doing, and if she says a thing, it must be done; so you must just get up and come.”

Mr. Esmond spoke with rapid, indistinct energy, pacing the room. But Harry was furious. “I tell you what, cousin,” he exclaimed, “I won’t move for the Countess, or for the Baroness, or for all the cousins in Castlewood.”

When the landlord entered with the punch, the young man in bed bellowed at him to turn the “sot” out.

“Sot, you little tobacconist! Sot, you Cherokee!” shrieked Mr. William. “Jump out of bed, and I’ll drive my sword through your body. Why didn’t I do it today when I took you for a bailiff—a confounded pettifogging bum-bailiff!” He ranted on in drunken frenzy until the landlord, drawer, hostler, and kitchen staff arrived to drag him away. Afterward, Harry pulled the covers tightly around him, seething with anger, and likely fell into a deep, bitter sleep.

The next morning, the landlord was far more attentive, now knowing Harry’s name and status. Messengers had come from Castlewood during the night to fetch both young gentlemen home. Poor Mr. William, it turned out, had returned in a wheelbarrow—something he was not unfamiliar with. “He never remembers nothing about it the next day,” the landlord assured Harry. “He’s of a real kind nature, Mr. William. The men get crowns and half-crowns from him by saying he beat them overnight when he was in liquor. He’s the devil when he’s tipsy, Mr. William, but when he’s sober, he’s the very kindest of young gentlemen.”

As nothing is unknown to biographers of such tales, it may be well to reveal what transpired inside Castlewood House while Harry waited outside, hoping for some sign of recognition.

Upon arrival, the family discovered the note Harry had left. His appearance sparked a brief domestic debate. My Lord Castlewood believed it must have been the young man seen on the bridge. Since they hadn’t drowned him, they ought to invite him. A servant should carry a message. Lady Fanny suggested it would be more courteous for one of the brothers to go. Lord Castlewood had no objection—William should go.

But Mr. William declared (with even greater force) that he’d rather be hanged than go. Lady Maria remarked the young man at the bridge was quite attractive. “Castlewood is dreadfully dull,” she said. “Neither of my brothers does anything to make it amusing. He may be vulgar—no doubt he is—but let us see the American.”

Lady Castlewood remained neutral, favoring delay. “Wait till your aunt arrives,” she advised. “Perhaps the Baroness won’t like to see the young man. At least, let us consult her before we invite him.”

So the hospitality due to poor Harry Warrington remained suspended.

At length, the Baroness Bernstein’s carriage appeared. Though uncertain about the Virginian’s reception, the family greeted her with fervent enthusiasm. The state chamber had been readied. The cook had arrived the day before with instructions to prepare a supper exactly to her taste. The dining room sparkled with silver, set amid family portraits: the late Viscount, his parents, his sister—two exquisite paintings. There was Vandyck’s portrait of the former Viscount and his wife. And Colonel Esmond, the Virginia relative, whose grandson drew only mild interest from the household.

The supper was excellent, and the Baroness enjoyed it thoroughly. For an hour or two, the entire family hovered around her, attentive and respectful. The Countess pressed the best dishes upon her, partaking freely herself. The butler refilled her champagne glass the moment it was empty. The younger members listened more than they spoke, awaiting her amusement. She was lively, witty, and seemingly acquainted with everyone in Europe—and knew scandalous stories about each. Even the usually severe Countess smiled at the most outrageous tales. The girls exchanged glances and laughed at their mother’s cue. The boys giggled and roared, delighted by their sisters’ embarrassment. Wine flowed freely, and later, a smoking bowl of punch was brought to the table.

The Baroness reminisced about many nights spent at this very table beside her father. “That was his place,” she pointed to where the Countess now sat. “I saw none of the old plate. It was all melted to pay his gambling debts.” She raised her voice. “Young gentlemen, I hope you don’t play.”

“Never, on my word,” said Castlewood.

“Never, ’pon honour,” said Will, winking at his brother.

The Baroness was pleased. “Good boys,” she declared. Her cheeks flushed with punch, she grew animated, perhaps coarse—but times were different, and her audience inclined to leniency.

She spoke to the boys about their father, grandfather, and others in the family. “The only man of the family was that one,” she said, pointing with a still-graceful arm toward the portrait of the military man in red coat and cuirass. “The Virginian? What is he good for? I always thought he was good for nothing but cultivating tobacco and my grandmother,” my lord chuckled.

She struck the table so hard the glasses danced. “I say he was the best of you all. There never was one of the male Esmonds with more brains than a goose—except him. He wasn’t fit for this wicked, selfish world, and he was right to leave it. Where would your father have been, young people, but for him?”

“Was he particularly kind to our papa?” asked Lady Maria.

“Old stories, my dear Maria!” the Countess snapped. “I’m sure my dear Earl was very kind to him in giving him that great estate in Virginia.”

“Since his brother’s death, the lad who was here today is heir to that property,” said the Baroness. “Mr. Draper told me so! Peste! I don’t know why my father gave up such a property.”

“Who has been here today?” the Baroness asked, alarmed.

“Harry Esmond Warrington, of Virginia,” my lord replied. “A lad whom Will nearly pitched into the river, and whom I pressed my lady to invite.”

“You mean that one of the Virginian boys has been to Castlewood and hasn’t been asked to stay?”

“There is but one of them, my dear creature,” the Earl interjected. “The other—you know—has just been…”

“For shame, for shame!”

“Oh! It ain’t pleasant, I confess, to be se——”

“Do you mean that a grandson of Henry Esmond, the master of this house, has been here, and none of you have offered him hospitality?”

“Since we didn’t know it, and he is staying at the Inn?” Will added.

“That he is staying at the Inn, and you are sitting there!” the Baroness cried. “This is too bad—call somebody to me. Get me my hood—I’ll go to the boy myself. Come with me this instant, my Lord Castlewood.”

The young man rose, clearly angered. “Madame the Baroness of Bernstein,” he said, “your ladyship is welcome to go. But as for me, I don’t choose to have such words as ‘shameful’ applied to my conduct. I won’t go fetch the young gentleman from Virginia, and I propose to sit here and finish this bowl of punch. Eugene! Don’t Eugene me, madam. I know her ladyship has a great deal of money, which you are desirous should remain in our amiable family. You want it more than I do. Cringe for it—I won’t.” He sank back into his chair.

The Baroness looked at the family, heads lowered, then at my lord, but without malice. She leaned close and whispered rapidly in German: “I was wrong when I said the Colonel was the only man of the family. Thou canst, if thou willest, Eugene.”

To which my lord merely bowed.

“If you do not wish an old woman to go out at this hour, let William, at least, go and fetch his cousin,” she said.

“The very thing I proposed to him.”

“And so did we—and so did we!” the daughters chimed in.

“I am sure I only wanted the dear Baroness’s consent!” their mother added. “And shall be charmed to welcome our young relative.”

“Will! Put on thy pattens and get a lantern, and go fetch the Virginian,” my lord ordered.

“And we will have another bowl of punch when he comes,” William said, already overindulged. And he went forth—how we have seen; how he drank more punch; how ill he succeeded.

The noble lady of Castlewood, catching sight of young Harry by the riverside, must have seen a handsome, engaging youth—perhaps with reasons of her own for wanting him absent from her household. Not all mothers welcome interesting young men of nineteen when virgins of twenty are present. If Harry’s lands had lain in Norfolk or Devon instead of Virginia, the Countess might have been more eager. Had she desired him, she would have given him her hand willingly. Our fashionable folk may be selfish, but at least they show it plainly. Cold-hearted, yes—but not hypocritical.

Why should Lady Castlewood go to any trouble to welcome the young stranger? Because he was friendless? Only a fool would believe that. People of fashion are friendly to those with many friends. A poor lad, alone, from a distant land, with modest means not yet his own, uncouth manners, provincial ways—should a great lady go out of her way for such a youth? Allons donc! He was better off at the alehouse than at the castle.

This, no doubt, was her opinion—and the Baroness Bernstein, who knew her perfectly, understood it well. The Baroness was also a woman of the world, capable of selfishness like any other. She understood precisely why the Castlewood family deferred to her—mother, daughters, sons alike—and amused herself with their greed, their humiliations, their artless reverence for her purse. They were not rich; Lady Castlewood’s fortune was settled on her children. The elder siblings had inherited only flaxen hair from their German mother and a pedigree of immense distinction. But rich or poor, all craved the Baroness’s wealth. In this, the wealthy are no less greedy than the poor.

So when Madam Bernstein struck the table, making glasses and people tremble, it was not from genuine fury, but from the warmth of punch and champagne, and a generous impulse stirred by wine and pity for the lonely youth waiting outside his ancestors’ door. She was not truly angry with her relatives—she knew they would act exactly as they had.

Their selfishness and humility alike amused her, as did Castlewood’s defiance. He was selfish like the rest, but not as petty. And as he frankly admitted, he could afford a little independence, having a decent estate to fall back upon.

Madam Bernstein was an energetic woman, restless, resolute, extraordinarily active for her age. She rose long before the languid Castlewood ladies (just returned from London’s balls) had left their feather beds, or jolly Will had slept off his punch. She paced the dew-dappled terraces, where flowers bloomed in neat parterres, box hedges stood crisp and dark, marble fauns and dryads cooled beneath them, birds sang, fountains splashed, and rooks called from the great wood.

Did the familiar scene stir memories? Did it recall childhood days of innocence, or awaken remorse? Her manner was unusually gentle when, after half an hour, the young Virginian appeared—sent by a morning billet from one of the Lockwoods. The note, signed B. Bernstein, informed Mr. Esmond Warrington that his relatives at Castlewood, including a dear friend of his grandfather, were anxious for him to come to “Colonel Esmond’s house in England.”

Now, accordingly, Harry approached, passing under the Gothic archway, stepping down from terrace to terrace, hat in hand, fair hair fluttering, slim figure clad in mourning. The Baroness found him handsome and modest. He bowed low—a gesture worthy of Versailles. She held out her hand, and when his closed over it, she laid her other gently on his ruffle. She gazed warmly into his honest, blushing face.

“I knew your grandfather very well, Harry,” she said. “So you came yesterday to see his portrait, and they turned you away—though you know the house was his by right?”

Harry blushed deeply. “The servants did not know me. A young gentleman came to me last night,” he said, “when I was peevish, and he, I fear, was tipsy. I spoke rudely to my cousin and would ask his pardon. Your ladyship knows that in Virginia, our manners toward strangers are different. I had expected another kind of welcome. Was it you, madam, who sent my cousin to me last night?”

“I sent him. But you will find your cousins most friendly today. You must stay here. Lord Castlewood would have come to you this morning, but I was so eager to see you. Breakfast in an hour. Meantime, talk to me. We will send for your servant and baggage. Give me your arm. Stop—I dropped my cane when you came. You shall be my cane.”

“My grandfather used to call us his crutches,” said Harry.

“You are like him, though you are fair.”

Henry Esmond, Esq., a man who had served as Colonel during the wars of Queen Anne’s reign, found himself at the close of that era entangled in efforts to restore the Stuart line to the English throne. Though the nation ultimately chose a different dynasty, several loyalists fled beyond the seas, and among them was Colonel Esmond, advised by friends to seek refuge abroad. Yet his regrets over past actions were sincere, and when the new sovereign—renowned for his mildness—ascended the throne, reconciliation proved swift. Through the influence of trusted allies, Esmond’s name was cleared, and he was once again welcomed into the fold.

He belonged to an ancient English family whose ancestral seat stood at Castlewood, in Hampshire. It was widely known that both King James II and his son had offered the title of Marquis to Colonel Esmond and his father. Indeed, the elder Esmond might have claimed an Irish peerage passed down through generations, had not a technicality prevented it—a matter he never sought to correct. Wearied by political strife and burdened by personal matters across Europe, Henry Esmond turned his gaze toward the New World. He settled in Virginia, where his ancestor had been granted vast lands by King Charles I. There, on this distant shore, his daughter and grandsons were born, and his wife passed away.

She had been the widow of the Colonel’s cousin, Viscount Castlewood, who died in a duel with Lord Mohun near the end of William III’s reign. When she married Henry Esmond, she brought with her not only grief but a legacy of noble blood. In honor of his homeland, Esmond named his Virginia estate Castlewood, mirroring the ancestral home left behind. Life here mirrored English customs in nearly every way. The colony remained steadfastly loyal to the Crown. Virginians proudly claimed that King Charles II had reigned in their midst long before he ruled in England. The Church of England was upheld with reverence, and the gentry prided themselves on their ties to aristocratic families across the sea.

They looked down upon the Dutch merchants of New York and the Puritan settlers of Pennsylvania and New England, who pursued wealth with little regard for tradition or grace. Nowhere in the colonies was there less inclination toward republicanism than in Virginia—the very province that would one day lead the charge against British rule. Yet in those days, the land was governed by a patriarchal order. Plantation owners lived in a manner almost feudal, their great estates worked by scores of servants—some indentured, others enslaved—who labored under the authority of their masters. The soil yielded food, livestock, and game; rivers teemed with fish; and ships carried tobacco from private wharves along the Potomac and James Rivers to London and Bristol, returning with English goods and manufactured wares.

Hospitality was a sacred duty. No guest was ever turned away. The gentry visited one another freely, traveling between mansions as if bound by ancient custom. Slavery, though deeply entrenched, was not yet debated as a moral issue. To own black servants was considered natural and proper. The treatment of enslaved people, while far from humane by modern standards, was often less harsh than elsewhere—food was abundant, labor was grueling but not always cruel, and many slaves seemed content enough in their lot. To suggest emancipation to Madam Esmond of Castlewood would have been as absurd as asking her to release her horses from their stables. She believed firmly in discipline and order—both for men and beasts.

Her father, however, harbored doubts. A man of skeptical mind, he questioned many things, yet never acted on his misgivings. Something in his past had cast a shadow over his spirit—a quiet melancholy that lingered even in his later years. He was kind, affectionate, and deferential, especially to women, whom he rarely contradicted. But there was a sense of resignation about him, as though life had been a duty rather than a joy. He submitted to its course without complaint, and perhaps found peace only in his final hours.

After losing his wife, he entrusted the management of his household and affairs to his daughter. He accepted her guidance without resistance. As long as he had books and solitude, he desired nothing more. Guests were received with warmth and wit—he enjoyed their company, yet felt no sorrow when they departed. “My love,” he once told his daughter, “I shall not be sorry to go myself. And you, though the most devoted of daughters, will console yourself in time. Why should I, so old, be romantic? You may still be young enough for such fancies.” He spoke lightly, though not entirely truthfully—for his daughter was a practical woman, lacking any trace of sentimentality.

Fifteen years passed in Virginia, and prosperity flourished on the Esmond estate. At last, the Colonel agreed to his daughter’s plan to build a grander mansion than the modest wooden house he had lived in. Several neighbors had already erected fine homes, and perhaps ambition stirred within her. While the Colonel cared little for architecture or heraldry, his daughter took pride in her lineage. She believed fiercely in the nobility and antiquity of her bloodline, and her father, now mellowed by age, indulged her whims with gentle humor.

He even assisted her, using his knowledge of genealogy and his skill in painting. Heraldry was once a vital part of noble education, and during her travels in Europe, Miss Esmond had studied her family's history with fervor. She returned to Virginia armed with documents, pedigrees, and learned treatises on nobility. These convinced her beyond doubt that the Esmonds descended not only from Norman warriors who followed William the Conqueror but also from native English royalty. Two magnificent family trees, painted by her father’s hand, illustrated this dual origin: one branch reached back to Emperor Charlemagne, depicted in full armor with imperial mantle and crown; the other to Queen Boadicea, portrayed in flowing robes, adorned with a golden crown and blue-tinted tattoos—her image crafted with care and imagination.

From these illustrious roots, the family tree rose until it converged in the thirteenth century upon a fortunate ancestor who claimed descent from both lines.

Of the Warringtons, her husband’s family, she held little regard. Though she styled herself Esmond Warrington, she was universally known as Madam Esmond of Castlewood after her father’s death. It is possible that disputes over rank occasionally disturbed her temper. Though her father had once possessed a marquisate patent from King James—only to burn it and disown it—she often behaved as if the title were valid. She considered the English Esmonds inferior to her own branch, and among colonial society, she made no secret of her superiority.

This led to quarrels, sharp words, and even minor scuffles at Governor’s assemblies in Jamestown. But why dwell on such trifles? The individuals involved are long gone, and the Republic has swept away the old hierarchies. Before independence, Virginia was arguably the most aristocratic region in the world. Its people were raised to revere English institutions and remain loyal to the Crown. The twin sons of Castlewood, George and Harry, were no exception—they were taught from childhood to honor the king and uphold their family’s dignity.

When their grandfather died, their mother, in solemn ceremony, declared George, the elder by half an hour, her heir and successor. Harry was instructed to show obedience to his brother. The entire household, including the numerous enslaved people and indentured servants, was ordered to recognize George’s authority. Only two figures in the family resisted: Madam Mountain, a loyal friend of Mrs. Esmond, and Harry’s foster-mother, a devoted Black woman who could not understand why her child should not be first—especially since, in her view, he was handsomer, stronger, and cleverer than his brother. In truth, the twins were nearly identical in appearance, differing only in hair color. When wrapped in nightcaps, they were indistinguishable even to strangers.

Yet in temperament, they were worlds apart. George was calm, thoughtful, and quiet. Harry was bold, energetic, and loud. He learned quickly once engaged, but resisted study until provoked. Threats of punishment failed to move him, while George often helped him with lessons. Harry had a military bent—he drilled the younger slaves like soldiers, caned them playfully, and fought spirited boxing matches with them, never holding grudges when defeated. George, by contrast, avoided conflict and treated all with gentleness.

Each boy had a personal servant assigned to him. Once, George found his young black servant asleep on his bed and sat beside him, brushing flies from the child’s face with a feather fan. Old Gumbo, the servant’s father, discovered the scene and cried out in horror. Madam Esmond, furious, ordered the child whipped. George pleaded desperately, wept openly, and begged for mercy—but his mother refused. The boy was taken away, begging his master not to cry.

A fierce argument erupted between mother and son. George insisted the punishment was unjust—“a shame,” he said—and declared that as master of the boy, no one—not even his mother—had the right to touch him. He vowed, shouting an oath that shocked everyone present, that on the day he came of age, he would free young Gumbo. That night, he visited the slave quarters and gave the boy one of his toys.

The child was indeed impudent and lazy, but no worse for the beating, as the Colonel likely thought. He quietly approved of the punishment when his daughter insisted, then laughed good-naturedly when Harry exclaimed, “You let mamma rule you in everything, grandpapa.”

“Why, so I do,” replied the old man. “Rachel, my love, the way I am petticoat-ridden is so evident that even this baby has noticed it.”

“Then why don’t you stand up like a man?” demanded little Harry, always ready to support his brother.

Grandpapa blinked. “Because I like sitting down best, my dear. I’m an old gentleman, and standing fatigues me.”

Harry, with his playful nature and affinity for his grandfather’s interests, became his favorite companion. He would chatter endlessly, laughing and storytelling, while George remained silent and reserved. George thrived in the library, where he read books long before he could comprehend them. Harry, meanwhile, was alive in the stables, woods, and fields—eager for hunts and fishing trips, showing early promise as a sportsman.

Once, when the Colonel’s ship sailed for Europe, the boys were asked what gifts Captain Franks should bring them. George hesitated between books and a fiddle. Harry instantly demanded a small gun. Madam Warrington (as she then was) was dismayed that her eldest son showed such low tastes, but praised Harry’s choice as fitting for a gentleman of noble birth.

“Books, papa, I can see are a reasonable choice,” she said to her father, who tried to defend George’s preference. “Though I suppose you already possess every book in existence. But I cannot imagine—though I may be wrong—I cannot imagine—that my son, grandson of a Marquis, should become a fiddler.”

“Should be a fiddlestick, my dear,” the Colonel replied gently. “Remember, Heaven’s ways are not ours. Each soul has its own realm of thought, and it is a sin to intrude. Suppose George loves music? You cannot stop him any more than you can command a rose not to bloom or a bird not to sing.”

“A bird sings by instinct,” Mrs. Warrington retorted. “George did not come into the world with a fiddle in his hand. I hated the harpsichord as a girl at Kensington School, and only learned it to please my mother. Say what you will, dear sir, I simply cannot believe fiddling is suitable for a person of fashion.”

“And King David played the harp, my dear?”

“I wish my papa would read him more, and not speak of him in that manner,” Mrs. Warrington interrupted.

“Nay, my dear,” the father replied softly, “it was only by way of illustration.”

It was true, as the Colonel confessed in his memoirs, that he was always guided by women. With his wife gone, he doted on his daughter—laughing at her quirks, indulging her prejudices, making jokes of her opinions while allowing them full sway. He nurtured her imperious nature, though he believed strongly that one could not reshape character through force, and that excessive control bred hypocrisy.

At last, the time came for Mr. Esmond to leave this world. He laid down his burdens as if relieved. We need not open our story with tolling bells or mournful sermons. Those who heard Parson Broadbent’s eulogy in Jamestown wondered at his eloquence and Latin fluency. Perhaps Mr. Dempster, the boys’ Scottish tutor, knew the truth—he had corrected the proofs of the speech, which was printed at Benjamin Franklin’s press in Philadelphia at the request of the Governor and many distinguished citizens.

No funeral in the colony had ever matched the splendor arranged by Madam Esmond for her father—one who would have smiled at such extravagance. The young boys, draped in mourning black, led the procession, followed by Lord Fairfax of Greenway Court, the Governor of Virginia in his coach, the Randolphs, Careys, Harrisons, Washingtons, and others. All respected the departed man—for his kindness, intellect, generosity, and quiet dignity.

Upon hearing of his passing, the family of Colonel Esmond’s stepson, Lord Castlewood of Hampshire, offered to pay for the marble slab commemorating his mother and husband. After due preparation, the monument was erected, bearing the Esmond arms and coronet, flanked by cherubic figures in mourning, and inscribed with an epitaph that, for once, spoke only truth.

Kind friends, generous neighbours, a name respected through generations, a vast estate, and enough wealth to live comfortably—these are the marks of a fortunate life. Add to them a well-kept home filled with all that is needed and much that is desired, servants both white and black eager to serve, good health, loving children, and—let us be honest—a fine cook, a well-stocked cellar, and a library full of books: should not such a person be considered blessed? Madam Esmond Warrington had all these gifts. She counted them each day in her morning and evening prayers. She was devout, charitable to the poor, and never knowingly wronged another soul.

Imagine her seated in her domain, Castlewood, in Westmorland County, Virginia—a true queen in her own right. The local gentry came to pay their respects; her sons were dutiful; her servants vied to obey her every word; the poor whites were grateful for her kindness and trusted her remedies when sick; even the lesser landowners gave way to her opinions, especially at backgammon, where she always won. With all this power and comfort, one might think the little Princess Pocahontas, as she was fondly called, lived in perfect contentment. But perhaps her husband’s early death was a mercy. Had he lived longer, they would have quarrelled bitterly—or he would have become a henpecked husband, a fate not uncommon in those days. For truth be told, Madam Esmond ruled over everyone she met. If people submitted, she was kind and generous; if they resisted, she fought until either they or she gave in.

We all carry our sins, as we confess every Sunday—and no one declared this more plainly than she. As a mortal woman, she may have been mistaken, but she rarely admitted it to herself, and never to others. Her father, in his later years, watched her with amusement as she displayed her stubbornness and pride. He saw her flaws, and his quiet humour unsettled her. But after the Colonel passed away, no one remained who could tame her will. And so I must confess, I am glad I did not live at Castlewood a hundred years ago. I suspect life there would not have been very pleasant.

Who among us is truly happy? Even in Eden, there was a serpent. Would Eve have listened to him if she had been perfectly content? Perhaps not.

The management of Castlewood had long rested in the capable hands of the energetic Madam Esmond, even before her husband died. Now she oversaw everything with strict care: she dismissed the Colonel’s English factor and appointed a new one; built and improved buildings; planted crops; grew tobacco; hired a new overseer; and brought in a fresh tutor. Though she loved her father deeply, she did not follow all his ways. Had she not obeyed her parents throughout their lives, as any dutiful daughter should? So, too, ought all children to obey their parents, that their days might be long in the land.

This little queen ruled her little kingdom with an iron hand, and her sons were merely her first subjects. Soon after her husband’s death, she dropped the name Warrington and began calling herself Madam Esmond in public. Her family lineage was known throughout the colony. She took pride in speaking of the Marquis title granted by King James to her father and grandfather. Though her father had shown great generosity by giving up his titles to the younger branch—the half-brother, Lord Castlewood, and his heirs—she and her sons belonged to the elder line of Esmonds. They deserved proper recognition.

Lord Fairfax was the only man in Virginia whom she allowed precedence over herself. She insisted on being addressed first at gatherings, ahead of Lieutenant-Governors’ wives and judges’ ladies. Only before the Governor’s wife—representative of the Crown—would she yield. Records from family letters reveal fierce disputes between her and other colonial ladies over such matters of etiquette.

As for her husband’s family, the Warringtons of England, she regarded them as insignificant. She had married the younger son of an English baronet from Norfolk—not out of love, but to please her parents, whom she always obeyed. At such a young age—fresh from boarding school—she would have jumped into the sea if her father had commanded it. “And that,” she once said, “is always the way with the Esmonds.”

The English Warringtons were not pleased with how she treated them or spoke of them. Once a year, she sent formal letters to her relatives in England, including the noble Esmonds of Hampshire. But when a Judge’s wife returning to England met Lady Warrington in London, she repeated some of the things Madam Esmond had said about her English kin. Lady Warrington likely shared the story with Lady Castlewood, and from then on, the letters from Virginia went unanswered. This angered Madam Esmond deeply, and she soon stopped writing altogether.

Thus, the good lady fell out with her neighbours, her relatives—and, as it must be admitted, with her sons as well.

An early conflict arose when she dismissed Mr. Dempster, the boys’ tutor and her late husband’s secretary. During her father’s lifetime, she had barely tolerated him—and he had found her hard to bear. She distrusted scholars, believing bookworms dangerous, prone to spread subversive ideas. She heard whispers that Dempster was a Jesuit in disguise, and so he was forced to leave Castlewood, build a cabin in the woods, and teach school while practising medicine among the scattered settlers.

Master George vowed never to abandon his old tutor—and kept his promise. Harry, however, preferred fishing and hunting to books, and had never grown close to the poor scholar.

Another dispute followed. Upon the death of an aunt and then her husband, George Warrington became heir to six thousand pounds, with Madam Esmond named as one of the trustees. Yet she refused to accept that she was only a trustee, not the owner. When the London lawyer—the other trustee—refused to send the money at her command, she flew into a rage.

“Is not all I possess my sons’?” she demanded. “Would I not cut myself into pieces to help them? With that money, I could have bought Mr. Boulter’s estate and slaves—adding a thousand pounds a year to our income, and securing a proper future for my Harry!”

Her neighbour, Mr. Washington of Mount Vernon, tried to explain that the agent had a duty to act only for the rightful beneficiaries. But Madam Esmond would not listen. She accused the lawyer of insolence, calling him a pettifogger who doubted the honour of a mother and an Esmond.

It must be acknowledged—this Virginian princess had a fiery spirit.

When George, her eldest son, was asked to decide, he sided with Mr. Washington and the lawyer. He said he could not take the money—it wasn’t his to claim. He wished he could give it to his mother, but he had no authority. Yet Madam Esmond would hear none of it. Her feelings were her law.

Here was a chance to secure Harry’s future—dear Harry, left with only a meagre inheritance as the younger brother. And the London men refused to help! Her own son, who inherited her father’s estate, refused to assist. To think a child of hers could be so ungenerous at fourteen!

She wept, scorned, hinted, and raged—then withdrew, only to erupt again in passionate appeals to Heaven. It was a familiar scene, still seen today: women whose logic is drenched in tears, and justice in their hearts forever aflame.

This clash hardened her resolve. She began saving strictly for Harry, determined to provide him with a proper fortune. Work on the grand buildings Colonel Esmond had begun at Castlewood ceased. Ships from New York had brought Dutch bricks; mantelpieces, carved woodwork, glass, carpets, and fine furnishings had been shipped from England—all now abandoned. No more books were purchased. Wine shipments were halted.

Madam Esmond regretted deeply the cost of a fine carriage from England. On Sundays, she rode only to church, groaning inwardly as she looked at her sons beside her.

“Harry, Harry!” she whispered. “I wish I had saved that money for you, my poor, portionless child—three hundred and eighty guineas to Messieurs Hatchett!”

“You’ll give me plenty while you live,” Harry replied cheerfully. “And George will give me plenty when you’re gone.”

“Not unless he changes his heart,” she replied grimly, casting a glance at her elder son. “Not unless Heaven softens him and teaches him charity—of which I pray night and day. As Mountain knows, do you not, Mountain?”

Mrs. Mountain, widow of Ensign Mountain and Madam Esmond’s companion and housekeeper, sat beside her. She took the fourth seat in the family coach on Sundays.

“Humph,” Mrs. Mountain muttered. “I’ve seen you fretting over this legacy long enough. I don’t see why you need to.”

“Oh no! No need!” the widow cried, rustling in her silks. “Of course I have no need to worry—because my eldest son is disobedient and unkind—because he has an estate, and poor Harry, bless him, has nothing but a mess of pottage!”

George stared at her, eyes filling with tears. “I wish you’d bless me too, O my mother!” he sobbed, breaking down completely.

In an instant, Harry had his arms around his brother’s neck, kissing him again and again.

“Never mind, George,” he said softly. “I know whether you’re a good brother or not. Don’t listen to what she says. She doesn’t mean it.”

“I do mean it, child,” the mother snapped. “Would to Heaven—”

“HOLD YOUR TONGUE, I SAY!” Harry roared.

“It’s a shame to speak like that to him, ma'am,” said Mrs. Mountain, shaking his hand.

“And so it is, Harry,” she agreed. “You’ve never spoken truer words.”

“Mrs. Mountain, do you dare set my children against me?” the widow demanded.

“From this very day, madam—” Mrs. Mountain began.

“Turn me and my child into the street? Do,” she replied. “That will be a fine revenge for the English lawyer refusing your boy’s money. Find another companion who’ll tell you black is white and flatter you. That’s not my way, madam. When shall I go? I shan’t be long packing. I brought little into Castlewood, and I’ll take little out.”

“Hush! The bells are ringing for church, Mountain. Let us try, if you please, to compose ourselves,” said the widow. And she looked at her children with eyes full of affection—perhaps at one, perhaps at both.

George kept his head bowed. Harry, sitting near, slipped his arm around his brother’s shoulders during the sermon, holding him close.

Harry had been telling his story in his own lively way, punctuated by youthful exclamations, answering questions as they came. The elderly lady seemed never tired of listening. Her hostess and daughters came several times, inviting her to ride, walk, drink tea, or play cards—but she declined each time, saying she found endless pleasure in Harry’s talk.

Especially when members of the Castlewood family were present, she grew more attentive, insisting Harry speak close to her ear, and calling out, “Hush, my dears! I can’t hear our cousin speak.” The others would leave, trying to appear cheerful.

“Are you my cousin, too?” Harry asked honestly. “You seem kinder than my other cousins.”

They were in the wainscoted parlour, where the family had eaten meals for two centuries. Portraits of ancestors lined the walls. Above the old lady’s chair hung a Kneller painting—one of the finest in the gallery—depicting a young woman of twenty-four or twenty-five, dressed in the flowing garments of Queen Anne’s reign, her auburn hair parted across a fair forehead, falling over pearly shoulders and a graceful neck.

When Harry asked if she was his cousin, she replied, “That portrait is by Sir Godfrey, who thought himself the greatest painter in the world. But he was not as good as Lely, who painted your grandmother—my Lady Castlewood, Colonel Esmond’s wife. Nor as good as Van Dyck, who painted your great-grandfather—yonder. And he looks, Harry, like a much finer gentleman than he really was. Some of us are painted darker than we are. Did you recognise your grandmother in that picture? She had the most beautiful fair hair and figure of any woman of her time.”

“I thought I knew it instinctively,” Harry said. “A certain likeness to my mother.”

“Did Mrs. Warrington—excuse me, I believe she calls herself Madam or my Lady Esmond now—ever tell you about another daughter her mother had in England before marrying your grandfather?”

“She never mentioned one.”

“Nor your grandfather?”

“Never. But in his picture-books—he made them for us children—he often drew a face very like the one above you. That, and Viscount Francis, and King James III., he drew dozens of times.”

“And the picture above me—does it remind you of anyone, Harry?”

“No, indeed.”

“Ah! Here is a sermon!” the lady sighed. “Harry, that was my face once—yes, it was. And I was called Beatrix Esmond. And your mother is my half-sister, child. And she has never even mentioned my name!”

As Harry Warrington recounted the simple tale of his adventures at home, Madam Bernstein—sharp-witted, worldly, and deeply amused by human nature—no doubt formed her own judgments about the people and events he described. If her opinion was not entirely favorable, what wonder? For all men and women are flawed, and life, however grand or humble, is rarely without its trials and disappointments. The city-born lady recoiled at the very thought of her American sister’s rural existence—a life that would seem dull and unrefined to most urbanites. Yet little Madam Warrington knew no other way, and found contentment in it, as she did in herself. Just because we consider ourselves connoisseurs of fine things does not mean others suffer in their simpler fare. To Hodge, a plain meal of bread and bacon is not misery—it is sustenance.

Madam Warrington lived a life full of duties, perhaps monotonous to some, but deeply satisfying to her. She was a brisk, capable woman, managing every aspect of Castlewood’s vast estate. No pie was baked without her oversight; she saw to the maids’ spinning, supervised the kitchen staff, rode out on her pony to inspect the fields, and watched over the overseers and enslaved laborers working in tobacco and corn. When one of the slaves fell ill, she would visit him in the quarters regardless of weather, treating him with firm resolve. Her closet held ancient remedies, distilled waters, and potions—her medicine chest struck fear into her neighbors, who trembled at the prospect of illness, lest she descend upon them with her decoctions and pills.

A century before, Virginia had few towns; the estates of the gentry were self-contained villages, each ruled like a small kingdom. Rachel Esmond reigned over Castlewood like a minor queen, while her neighbors governed their lands as petty princes. Many of these landowners lived lavishly, though in rough comfort—clothes for servants often frayed, houses open to strangers, proud and idle, devoted to hunting and field sports befitting gentlemen of noble birth. Madam Warrington matched their hospitality, yet surpassed them in prudence. More than one man would have gladly shared her life interest in the estate and stepped into the role of father to her boys. But where was the man worthy of such a woman—of noble blood, high breeding, and exalted spirit? There was talk of appointing the Duke of Cumberland as viceroy—or even king—over America. Madam Warrington’s friends laughed, saying she waited for him. She replied gravely, “Men of higher rank than His Royal Highness have sought alliance with the Esmonds.”

Under her, she had an officer’s widow—Mrs. Mountain—who had once been her companion at school, just as her late husband had served alongside Mr. Warrington. At the Kensington Academy, when English girls tormented the young American girl, mocking her lofty airs from childhood, Fanny Parker defended her. They both married ensigns in King’s Regiment, forming a close bond—“my Fanny,” “my Rachel,” they wrote to each other. Then Fanny’s husband died in poverty, leaving no means for her or her infant child. Captain Franks brought her across the Atlantic aboard the *Young Rachel*.

Castlewood had ample room, and Mrs. Mountain brought warmth and liveliness to the household. She played cards with the mistress, taught music to the eldest boy, welcomed guests with cheer, arranged chambers for visitors, and managed the linen and presses. A kind, lively widow, she attracted many unmarried gentlemen in the colony, who asked her to marry them. But she chose to keep her name—Mountain—though it had brought her no fortune. One marriage was enough, she said. Her husband had spent both their fortunes with gentle charm, and her last trinkets went toward his funeral. As long as Madam Warrington kept her at Castlewood, she preferred a home without a husband to any offered in Virginia.

The two women quarreled often—bitterly sometimes—but always made up. When either boy fell ill, they competed in care and tenderness. In Colonel Esmond’s final days, Mrs. Mountain’s cheerful presence had been greatly valued. Madam Warrington cherished his memory above all others. So year after year, when Captain Franks asked, in jest, whether she’d return with him, she declined—she would stay another year.

When suitors came to Madam Warrington, as they inevitably did, she received them politely, sometimes teasing them: “Is it Mrs. Mountain you’ve come for?” She would urge them to court Fanny—she was of good English stock, kind-hearted, and would make any gentleman happy. If the suitor insisted he meant only her, she would curtsey gravely, say she had misunderstood, and declare that the daughter of the Marquis of Esmond lived for her people and sons, and would never change her condition.

Like Queen Elizabeth, she ruled with a mixture of authority and charm—inspiring affection, awe, and occasional cruelty, depending on her mood. No compliment was too grand for her to accept. Her vanity was well known, and the witty among them took pleasure in flattering her. Rattling Jack Firebrace of Henrico County stayed months at Castlewood, a favorite, because he recited verses he stole from pocket-books. Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania wagered fifty hogsheads against five that he could get her to establish a new order of knighthood—and won.

The elder son, George, observed these quirks with growing unease. From childhood, he resented flattery aimed at his mother, and mocked it with biting satire. “The Esmonds have always been jealous,” she would say gravely, “and my poor boy takes after his grandfather.” George loathed Jack Firebrace and Tom Humbold. Harry, meanwhile, enjoyed their company—hunting, fishing, cockfighting, and revelry.

One winter, after their first tutor left, Madam Esmond took the boys to Williamsburg for schooling. There, they heard the famed preacher Mr. Whitfield, whose arrival stirred the colony. Unlike neighboring provinces, Virginia was officially Church of England—clergymen were state-paid, with glebes granted to them. Without a bishop in America, ministers were imported from England—often second-rate men, parsons in disgrace, or noblemen’s dependents seeking refuge. It was no surprise that Whitfield’s powerful voice moved souls that Mr. Broadbent, the local chaplain, could not touch.

At first, the boys were captivated. They sang hymns, listened with fervor, and eagerly awaited the “call” of salvation—a spiritual awakening sweeping Protestant England. Had Whitfield stayed longer, both might have worn black coats instead of military epaulettes.

But Whitfield could not remain. His mission was to awaken the entire American church. He left behind letters of encouragement and promised to send a tutor who would teach not only secular knowledge, but also deepen their faith.

Soon, a young clergyman arrived from England—Mr. Ward. He had a voice as loud as Whitfield’s and could preach endlessly. Night and evening, the hall echoed with his sermons. The enslaved domestic workers crept to the doors to listen; servants crowded the porch windows. The black sheep of Castlewood—its enslaved population—were especially moved. When he led a hymn, a mighty chorus rose from the house, heard across the Potomac—something unheard in the Colonel’s time, for he distrusted clergymen and once said he’d argue with none except over backgammon.

Ward was handsome, and Madam Esmond admired his preaching. Women of the era, less educated and more impressionable, were prone to idolize such men. For weeks, she listened raptly, insisting her neighbors attend and convert. She particularly wished to influence young Mr. Washington, urging him repeatedly to stay at Castlewood and benefit from the spiritual instruction. But he always had pressing business elsewhere, and invariably rode off just before services began.

The boys, however, grew restless under Ward. They found him a poor scholar, dull, and ill-mannered. George knew more Latin and Greek than his tutor and caught him in constant errors. Harry, bolder, mimicked Ward’s eating and speaking, making the household laugh—Mrs. Mountain crowing with delight. Madam Esmond might have seen through Ward’s pretensions, but her sons’ resistance hardened her resolve. “What matters if he lacks learning?” she declared. “In what is truly precious, he can instruct us all. His manners may be coarse, but Heaven chooses not from the wealthy. I wish you knew one book as well as he does. It is your pride—the pride of all Esmonds—that blinds you.”

That evening, Ward preached on Naaman the Syrian, who refused to wash in Jordan’s waters, preferring his own rivers. The lesson: pride leads to ruin, and obedience to God’s appointed teacher is essential. Ward, clearly, saw himself as the guardian of divine truth.

George responded with sarcasm—perhaps inherited from his grandfather—using it to unsettle the household. He twisted Ward’s pompous phrases into jokes, making the young preacher flush with anger. He provoked Madam Esmond, especially when he sent Harry into fits of laughter. Her authority was challenged; her chosen minister scorned; her youngest son corrupted by rebellion. She resolved to restore order.

The boys were fourteen—Harry taller, more mature; George delicate, still boyish in appearance. Cane punishment was common then—used by sergeants, masters, overseers. The boys had been whipped by their Scotch tutor, Mr. Dempster, in their grandfather’s day. Harry, in particular, had grown accustomed to it. But after the Colonel’s death, discipline had relaxed. Now, with both mother and Mrs. Mountain defied, Madam Esmond turned to coercion.

She consulted Mr. Ward, who found scriptural justification for corporal punishment—no argument needed. He had begun by flattering the boys, hoping to stay at Castlewood permanently. But they mocked his flattery, scorned his manners, yawned at his sermons. The more their mother favored him, the more they despised him. Tutor and pupils hated each other.

Mrs. Mountain, loyal to the boys—especially George—warned them. “Ward is more obsequious than ever to your mother. It sickens me to hear him flatter, to see him gobble! You must be careful. Your mother was talking about you to Major Washington the other day. I don’t trust him—he’s too old for me. But he’s handsome, yes. And I know how much wild oats your father sowed, and my poor Mountain too. Show me Washington’s wild oats—I’ll bet there isn’t a grain!”

“You’re right, Mounty,” Harry said. “He told me exactly the same thing—‘Discipline must be preserved. There can be only one command in a house.’”

“Let him run his own house,” George retorted haughtily. The warning only made him more defiant.

The next day, the storm broke. During morning lessons, George argued with Ward—insubordinate, unjust. Even Harry admitted he was wrong. Ward kept his temper—suppressed rage, as one does when restraining fury. He said he would speak to Madam Esmond.

At dinner, Ward requested her to stay and calmly presented the dispute. He asked Harry to confirm his account. Harry reluctantly agreed.

Standing beneath the Colonel’s portrait, George said coldly, “What Mr. Ward said is correct.”

“To be tutor to such a pupil is absurd,” Ward declared, launching into a long speech filled with Scripture. At each phrase, George smiled mockingly, pished scornfully. Finally, Ward asked permission to retire.

“Not until you punish this disobedient child,” Madam Esmond snapped, anger rising. “If love fails, stronger measures must be taken. I punish you now, rebellious boy, to spare you greater punishment later. Discipline must be upheld. There can be only one command in a house, and I am its mistress. Mr. Ward, you will punish him—as we agreed. If he resists, my overseer and servants will assist you.”

She spoke with fire, citing scripture constantly—invoking God’s law in family affairs. This was the education she’d received from her fiery young spiritual guide. Was it comforting? Perhaps not.

Midway through her tirade, George felt guilt. “There can be only one command,” he said slowly, pale. “And I know who said those words before you. Mother… I have been wrong to Mr. Ward.”

“He confesses! He asks pardon!” Harry exclaimed. “That’s enough, George!”

“No!” the mother cried. “The penalty must be paid. When I was headstrong, my mother punished me, and I submitted. So must you. Mr. Ward, do your duty.”

“Stop, mother—you don’t know what you’re doing!” George pleaded.

“I know that he who spares the rod spoils the child!” she thundered, quoting Scripture again.

On the mantelpiece stood a china cup—precious to her, once used by her father. George suddenly picked it up. A strange smile crossed his face.

“Stay one minute. Don’t go yet,” he said. “You value this cup, mother?”

Harry stared.

“If I break it,” George continued, “it can never be mended. All the tinker’s rivets couldn’t make it whole again. My dear old grandpapa’s cup. I have been wrong. Mr. Ward, I ask your pardon. I will try to amend.”

The widow looked at him with contempt. “I thought,” she said, “I thought an Esmond had more courage than to be afraid…”

Then—Harry gasped. George raised the cup and dropped it onto the marble slab.

It shattered.

“It’s too late, Hal,” George said. “You’ll never mend it. Now, mother, I am ready. Will you come and see if I’m afraid? Mr. Ward, I am your servant. Your servant? Your slave! And the next time I meet Mr. Washington, madam, I’ll thank him for his advice.”

“I say, do your duty, sir!” she shrieked, stamping her foot. George bowed low and walked toward the study.

“Stop! For God’s sake, mother, stop!” Harry begged.

But passion consumed her. “You only encourage him!” she shouted. “If I had to do it myself, I would!”

Harry, heartbroken and furious, left the room as Mr. Ward and George entered.

The widow sat down, staring at the broken cup. Silence. Then—shrieks from the study.

Mr. Ward emerged bleeding, wounded on the head. Behind him, Harry, eyes blazing, brandishing his grandfather’s hunting knife, which hung among the Colonel’s weapons in the library.

“I don’t care. I did it,” Harry said. “I couldn’t stand seeing him strike my brother. When he lifted his hand, I threw the ruler. I couldn’t help it. I won’t bear it. If anyone lifts a hand to me or my brother, I’ll take his life!”

After the departure of her spiritual adviser and chaplain, Madam Esmond found herself once more at peace with her son. Though George never spoke of their quarrel, it lingered in his thoughts like a shadow, heavy and unspoken. Soon after, he fell ill—fever took hold of him swiftly, and during the worst of it, delirium seized his mind. In the hush of midnight, as he tossed upon his bed, he would cry out in anguish: “Broken! Broken! It never, never can be mended!” His mother sat by his side, silent and trembling, her heart pierced by the sound of her child’s torment.

Her remedies proved useless. The medicines she kept in her cabinet—her trusted nostrums—failed to bring relief. At last, she was forced to seek help from a man she had long resented. One winter morning, little Mr. Dempster saw her arrive on horseback, her face pale, her breath fogging in the cold air. She had ridden through snow and wind to beg for his aid. “I shall bury my resentment, madam,” he said gently, “as you buried your pride. Please God, I may have time enough to help my dear young pupil.”

He packed his instruments, called his servant, shut the door of his lonely hut, and returned to Castlewood. That night, death seemed near. For days, George hovered between life and darkness. But under Mr. Dempster’s care, the fever broke. The chills lessened, and slowly, steadily, the boy regained strength.

A change of air was advised—perhaps even a journey to England. But Madam Esmond admitted, with regret, that she had been too quick to turn away from her children’s kin across the sea. Instead, they decided upon a northern and eastern tour. With Mr. Dempster as tutor and two servants in attendance, the two young gentlemen set out for New York. From there, they traveled up the winding Hudson River to Albany, where they were welcomed into the homes of the province’s finest families. Then, guided by letters of introduction, they crossed into the French territories, where they were received with warmth and curiosity by the local gentry.

Harry thrived in the wilderness. He joined Indian camps, hunted bears, and traded furs. But George, whose health remained fragile and whose interests lay elsewhere, became a favorite among the French ladies. They admired his fluency in their language, his elegant manner, and his grace in dance. He perfected his accent so thoroughly that some believed him to be a native-born Frenchman. He played the violin with charm, sang the latest French songs—though his voice began to crack as it changed from boyish treble to deep bass—and even engaged in a duel with a young ensign of the Auvergne regiment, the Chevalier de la Jabotière. He wounded the officer in the shoulder, not from malice, but from honor. Afterward, they swore eternal friendship.

Madame de Mouchy, the superintendent’s wife, wrote to Madam Esmond praising George’s conduct. “What a son you must be blessed with!” she declared. Had Mr. Whitfield heard such news, he might have frowned—yet Madam Esmond rejoiced, proud of her son’s accomplishments.

When the brothers returned home after ten months abroad, their mother was astonished by their transformation. George had grown tall and strong, nearly matching Harry in height. Now, when powdered, the boys looked so much alike that one could scarcely tell them apart. But in daily life, they wore their hair naturally—George’s dark and raven-black, Harry’s light and tied with a ribbon.
