Those who have read earlier pages of this tale will recall that George Esmond was a youth of sharp sensibility, generous yet deeply jealous, noble in spirit, and unable to forgive an injury—even if he refused to take revenge. He left Castlewood with no affection for a certain gentleman whose name would one day echo throughout history. And he returned no less firm in his opinion.

Mr. Washington, though barely twenty-one, carried himself with the gravity of a man twice his age. He had managed his family’s affairs since childhood and was trusted by all—more than many older men. Mrs. Mountain, Madam Esmond’s companion and friend, adored both boys and their patroness, despite frequent quarrels. She was also a gifted letter-writer, full of wit and mischief. Her imagination often ran wild, especially when it came to matchmaking.

She was convinced that every unmarried man who visited Castlewood had designs on the widow. She insisted that Mr. Ward meant to court her, and that Madam Esmond secretly favored him. She knew Mr. Washington wanted to marry—after all, such a clever young man would surely seek a wealthy wife. As for age differences? Why, the Major was fifteen years younger than Madam Esmond. But what did that matter? Their family had seen such unions before. “My lady’s mother was how many years older than the Colonel?” she would muse. “And she was so jealous she wouldn’t let him out of her sight!” Poor Colonel, indeed—he’d been henpecked by his daughter too. And she would follow her mother’s example, Mrs. Mountain predicted, marrying again without a doubt.

Madam Esmond stood only five feet tall, even in her highest heels and headdress. Mr. Washington, meanwhile, towered at six feet two. Great men always married small women, Mrs. Mountain argued. “Therefore,” she concluded, “he must be looking after the widow.” What could be clearer?

She shared these theories with George, whom she called “my boy.” “For Heaven’s sake, Mountain,” he begged, “please keep quiet about this.”
“I’ll try,” she replied, “but I can’t close my eyes forever.” And then she recounted a hundred incidents—the way Mr. Washington walked into the house, the way Madam Esmond greeted him, the way she consulted him about every matter, great or small. She pointed out the room at Castlewood now known as “Mr. Washington’s room”—where he left his clothes and portmanteau when he left. “Ah, George, George,” she sighed, “one day he won’t go away.”

George listened, stiffening with each word. Toward his mother’s favorite, he adopted a cold politeness that irritated the honest gentleman, though he never complained. Or worse—sharp sarcasm, which he delivered like a blade through brambles, just as he once cut through thorny thickets while hunting with Harry Warrington. When the others rode off, George retreated to his study, lost in books—mathematics, Latin, French—growing more solitary with each passing day.

Harry was away on a hunting expedition when Mr. Washington arrived at Castlewood. The visit was tender, intimate, marked by a warmth that made George’s jealousy flare almost to bursting. But it was not a stay—it was a farewell. Major Washington was setting off on a dangerous journey to the western frontier, beyond the reach of civilization.

The French had begun to encroach upon British lands. Settlers in Virginia and Pennsylvania had been driven from their farms by armed Frenchmen. The governors of the colonies grew alarmed. Britain claimed all territory inland from its coastal charters, stretching westward to the Pacific. France, meanwhile, aimed to connect its northern and southern colonies through the Mississippi and St. Lawrence rivers, laying claim to the vast interior.

Though peace had been signed in 1748 between the European powers, the colonial dispute simmered. By 1753, it erupted along the Ohio River, where British and French settlers met. Yet neither side acknowledged the true owners of the land—the Native tribes who had lived there for generations. The courts of London and Paris chose to ignore them, treating the conflict as a European affair—while using the Indians’ weapons and alliances as tools of war.

The Ohio Company, granted land by Virginia, found its settlements invaded by French soldiers, who expelled the English settlers. They turned to Lieutenant-Governor Dinwiddie for protection. He decided to send a message to the French commander, demanding they cease their incursions.

Young Mr. Washington volunteered eagerly. With a guide, interpreter, and a few men, he journeyed through forests and frozen rivers in the fall of 1753, traveling from Williamsburg nearly to Lake Erie. He reached Fort le Boeuf and delivered his message. The reply was curt: “We are ordered to hold this place and drive all English from it. We intend to take possession of the Ohio.”

With that, he returned through perilous terrain, navigating by compass, camping in the snow. Harry Warrington cursed his luck—had he been home, he might have joined such a noble adventure. When Washington returned, victorious in purpose if not in outcome, he was more beloved than ever by Madam Esmond. She held him up as a model for her sons. “Ah, Harry,” she would say, “you with your cockfights and races—while the Major is out there in the wilderness, facing the French and the frozen rivers!” To George, she added, “Learning is good, but I wish my eldest son were doing something for his country.”

“I desire nothing more than to serve,” George replied. “But I will not serve under Mr. Washington, nor ask a commission from Mr. Dinwiddie.”

“An Esmond serves only with the king’s commission,” Madam said firmly. “And I would rather beg my bread than ask favors from that man.”

At the time, Washington was raising a regiment with the limited resources of Virginia. He hoped to establish a stronger presence against the French. A smaller force under Colonel Trent had already been sent west, tasked with fortifying a position near what is now Pittsburgh. But outnumbered and outgunned, they were forced to retreat. The French seized the fort, strengthened it, and named it Fort Du Quesne.

No shots had yet been fired—yet war loomed. Then, in 1754, a young Virginian officer, eager to defend his homeland, fired the first shot. It was a simple act, born of duty—not ambition. Yet it sparked a war that would rage for sixty years, sweep across continents, shatter empires, and birth a new nation.

That officer was George Washington. He led a small force to confront the French, met their advance guard, and opened fire—killing their leader. Outnumbered and surrounded, he was forced to surrender. On July 4, 1754, he marched out of Fort Necessity, gave up the fort, and returned home—his command ended, his regiment disbanded.

Defeated and humbled, he returned to Castlewood. He was still young, perhaps too young to bear such a burden. He spoke to George Warrington, holding out his hand. “I was angry when we parted,” he said. “You seemed to scorn me and my regiment. I thought you laughed at us.”

George took his hand. “Nay, you have done your best,” he said. “One hundred fifty starving men, half-starved and low on ammunition, cannot stand against five times their number, fully armed. And everyone knows you would do your duty.”

Harry and I saw the French in Canada last year,” George added. “They obey one will. In our colonies, each governor rules alone. The troops they sent were royal soldiers…”

“Oh, but some of ours should be here!” Madam Esmond interrupted, tossing her head. “A few good English regiments would make those white-coats run!”

“You think little of provincials,” the Colonel said grimly. “And I must admit, we’ve been unlucky. You praised me so highly when I was here before—remember your predictions of victory? Your wine flowed freely. All those dreams are over now. I’m grateful you receive a beaten man so kindly.”

He bowed his head, ashamed.

George, sensitive and moved by the other’s sorrow, was about to speak comfortingly—when his mother stepped in.

“Kind of us to receive you, Colonel Washington?” she said. “I never heard that when men are down, our sex are less their friends.” And she gave him a graceful curtsey.

George watched, his heart tightening. More than ever, he felt the weight of rivalry—of love, of admiration, of belonging—pulled away from him.

Few men could claim more sympathy than one who is brave, young, handsome, and unfortunate. Madam Esmond might have had twenty sons, yet she still found reason to admire her youngest—the soldier boy whose name was spoken with such pride in every corner of Castlewood. Mr. Washington’s room had never felt more like his own; it was as if he had taken root in the very heart of their home. She spoke of him everywhere, praising him before all guests, pointing out his virtues to her sons with a warmth that left no doubt of her regard. She contrasted his steadfast character with Harry’s restless love of pleasure—“the wild boy!”—and George’s quiet absorption in books, which she deemed too much of a retreat from duty.

But George did not share her admiration. His jealousy grew with each compliment, until it became a constant shadow over his thoughts. He turned bitter jokes into barbs so sharp they cut through the air, though his mother remained oblivious, confused by his sarcasm and baffled by his dark moods. To her, he was still the thoughtful son; to him, the world had grown colder, and he saw only the weight of expectation pressing down upon him.

Meanwhile, the wider world stirred with events that would soon reshape the lives of this modest family. The conflict between French and English settlers in North America had ceased to be merely local—it had become a war of nations. Reinforcements from France had arrived in Canada, and now English troops were expected in Virginia. It was a time of rising tension, when peace could no longer be taken for granted.

From Quebec came a letter addressed to George Warrington, written by Madame la Présidente de Mouchy, a lady of noble bearing and deep affection for the young Virginian. “Alas, my dear friend,” she wrote, “how cruelly fate has divided us! I see you leaving your beloved mother to rush into the arms of Bellona. I imagine you wounded after fierce battles. I hesitate even to wish victory to our lilies, knowing you stand beneath the banners of the Leopard. There are enmities the heart does not recognize—ours surely are at peace amidst the storm. All here send their love and greetings, especially Monsieur le Chasseur d’Ours, your brother (that cool Hippolyte, who preferred the hunt to the gentle talk of our ladies!). Your friend, your enemy, the Chevalier de la Jabotière, burns to meet you on the field of Mars. Last night, M. Du Quesne spoke of you at dinner. And I, your husband, send warm remembrances to your young friend, joined always with those of your sincere Présidente de Mouchy.”

The “banner of the Leopard” mentioned in her letter was indeed unfurled across the colonies. The king’s forces were being mustered, determined to reclaim the territories seized by the French. Two regiments were raised and funded by the Crown in America, while another fleet carried two additional regiments from England under a seasoned commander.

In February 1755, Commodore Keppel anchored his ship, the *Centurion*—once commanded by Anson on his famous circumnavigation—in Hampton Roads. With him came two warships, General Braddock, his staff, and part of the army. Braddock had been appointed by the Duke of Cumberland, a man known then as “The Duke par excellence.” Though not without controversy, he was a figure of great influence in England, and his presence signaled serious intent.

Soon after, a fleet of transports followed, bringing supplies, soldiers, and funds. Braddock landed his troops at Alexandria on the Potomac and journeyed to Annapolis, Maryland, where he summoned colonial governors to a council. He urged them to mobilize their provinces in support of the common cause, warning that the moment for action had come.

His arrival sent waves of excitement through the colonies, none greater than at Castlewood. Harry, ever eager for adventure, rode immediately to Alexandria to see the encamped soldiers. He marveled at their orderly lines, the crisp music of fifes and drums, and the disciplined bearing of the officers. He quickly made friends among them, longing to join their mission. They welcomed him at their mess, and he returned home full of stories and dreams.

Madam Esmond approved. She believed these English gentlemen offered her sons a chance to mingle with men of true breeding—unlike the horse-racing, cock-fighting squires of Virginia or the petty lawyers and flatterers at the lieutenant-governor’s table. She had an eye for sycophants and mocked the petty rivalries of Williamsburg’s courtiers. But while she praised the officers’ manners, neither Harry nor George fully shared her enthusiasm. If she had known the truth—heard their drunken songs, seen their disorder, witnessed how many of them staggered home after nights of revelry—she might have thought twice about recommending them to her sons.

Yet the soldiers’ behavior grew worse. They swaggered through the countryside, frightening farmers and villagers alike. Braddock raged against their lack of discipline and accused the colonists of cowardly reluctance to aid the Crown. The troops began to act like conquerors, mocking the locals and even insulting the wives of Indian allies who had joined the English ranks. In outrage, the chiefs withdrew their support—and within months, Braddock lost the vital help he would have needed most.

Some whispers reached Madam Esmond, but she dismissed them. Soldiers were soldiers, she said. Those who visited Castlewood were polite, well-mannered men, and so they were. She received them graciously, offering them the best hunting and hospitality the land could provide.

Then came word from General Braddock himself. He sent courteous messages to Castlewood, recalling that his father had once served alongside Colonel Esmond under the famed Marlborough. The name of Colonel Esmond was still respected in England, and Braddock wished to pay his respects to the daughter of such a distinguished officer. He asked permission to visit Castlewood.

Had she known why he sought her favor, perhaps Madam Esmond would not have been so touched. But she did not know. Instead, she accepted with dignity, writing back in elegant script, thanking him and asking when he might honor her home with his presence.

At Alexandria, Braddock held levees, and among those who paid homage were the twin sons of Castlewood. Dressed in their finest London suits, mounted on their best horses, and attended by their two servants in smart liveries, they rode in procession to meet the general.

Braddock was in a sour mood. He barely acknowledged the young men, asking only casually of his aide-de-camp, “Who are those young Squire Gawkeys in blue and gold and red waistcoats?”

Mr. Dinwiddie, the Lieutenant-Governor of Virginia, replied, “Those are the sons of the Princess Pocahontas.”

With a furious oath, Braddock demanded, “Who the deuce was she?”

Dinwiddie, who had little respect for Madam Esmond—having endured her sharp tongue and lofty airs—gave a mocking account of her, ridiculing her pretensions and telling tales that amused the general so thoroughly that he fell asleep.

When he awoke, Dinwiddie was gone, but a gentleman from Philadelphia remained, engaged in conversation with the officers. Braddock resumed the discussion, speaking harshly of Madam Esmond, calling her an old fool and expressing contempt for the colonial gentry.

But Benjamin Franklin of Philadelphia stepped in. He corrected the general’s impression, explaining that Madam Esmond owned vast lands, cattle, and stores—all of which could prove invaluable. He advised Braddock to treat her with care and respect.

Impressed by Franklin’s intelligence, Braddock ordered an aide to invite the two young Virginians to dinner the next day. When they arrived, he was far more cordial, and the officers treated them with warmth. They conducted themselves with grace and humility, returning home pleased with the experience—and their mother delighted by the general’s civility.

She replied to Braddock’s message with a letter of equal elegance, accepting his invitation and requesting a date for his visit.

In Castlewood, talk of war and the coming campaign filled every hour. For Harry, it was the dream of a lifetime. He lived for battle, spent his days with the officers in Williamsburg, polished every gun and sword in the house, and revived childhood games—ordering the negroes into mock formations. He was ready, eager, and burning to serve.

His mother, though proud, felt a deep sorrow. She knew one of her sons would have to go. She admired George, but loved Harry with all her heart. Yet Harry, though desperate to leave, dared not speak openly. When he brought up the subject with George, his elder brother’s face darkened.

Harry, loyal to the core, looked up to George as his natural leader. He feared what George might say—and dreaded what he might decide.

And indeed, George was not untouched by the call of duty. He studied the campaigns of Eugene and Marlborough, read his grandfather’s military texts, and re-read Plutarch’s biographies of the greatest warriors. He and Dempster, the old Scotchman, resumed fencing lessons—though Dempster never revealed where he’d learned his skill.

When Braddock’s offer came—would one of the young gentlemen care to join the campaign?—Harry’s eyes lit up. He cried out, “I would go with all my heart!”

But George looked at him steadily and said, “One of us will be proud to serve his Excellency. But the other must stay—to care for our mother.”

Harry remained silent. He trusted George’s judgment. Even in his deepest desire, he would not speak until George had decided.

They rode home in silence, each thinking the same thoughts, afraid to voice them. Only when they returned did they tell their mother.

“I knew it would come,” she said softly. “At such a time, our family must do its duty. Have you decided… which of you will leave me?”

“Of course I should go, Mother,” Harry blurted, turning crimson. “The youngest ought to go.”

Mrs. Mountain, present in the room, nodded firmly. “There! Mountain says so. I told you so!”

“But the head of the family ought to go,” George said quietly. “No—you’re ill. You haven’t recovered from your fever. Should he go, Mountain?”

“You would make the better soldier, I know it, dear Hal,” Mrs. Mountain replied. “You and Mr. Washington are great friends. You could travel together. And he doesn’t care for me—nor I for him, though he is admired. But it is the law of honour, my Harry.”

She turned to George with extraordinary tenderness. “The grief I feel is that I must refuse you. I must go. Had Fate given you just half an hour more life than I had, it would have been your turn—and you would have claimed your right to go first.”

“Yes, George,” Harry whispered. “I would.”

“You will stay,” George said, “and take care of Castlewood and our mother. If anything happens to me, you are here to fill my place. I would give way—I know you would lay down your life for me. But we must each do our duty. What would our grandfather say if he were here?”

Their mother looked at them proudly. “My papa would say his boys were gentlemen,” she murmured, then left the room, unable to hide her emotion.

Word spread quickly through the household. Dinah, George’s foster-mother, wept bitterly at losing him. Phillis, Harry’s nurse, grumbled that Master George was favored again. Sady, George’s servant, boasted of the feats he would perform. Gumbo, Harry’s boy, pretended to mourn—but at home, he was no warrior.

Yet none was angrier than Mrs. Mountain. She insisted George stay. “You don’t know what you’re doing!” she exclaimed. “You’ll bring nothing but trouble.”

George was surprised by her persistence. “I know Harry would make the better soldier,” he said. “But duty calls me.”

“To stay is your duty!” she shouted, stamping her foot.

“Why didn’t Mother say so earlier?” George asked.

“Your mother?” Mrs. Mountain laughed grimly. “Your mother, my poor child?”

“What do you mean?” George asked, blood rushing to his face.

“She wants you away, George,” she continued, wagging her head. “It may be that when you return, you’ll find a father-in-law waiting.”

George stared. “What in heaven do you mean?”

“I see everything,” she said. “Colonel Washington wants a rich wife. When you’re gone, he’ll ask your mother to marry him. And you’ll come back to find him master here.”

“But he’s going on the campaign too,” George protested.

“He’s going on the marrying campaign, child!” she insisted. “General Braddock told me he accepted the post of aide-de-camp.”

“An artifice!” she snapped. “A trick to blind you! He’ll be wounded and return—just wait and see. I have proof—look!”

She pulled from her pocket a sheet of paper in Washington’s handwriting.

“How did you get this?” George asked, pale.

“I found it in the Major’s chamber,” she admitted, embarrassed.

“You read private letters of a guest?” George shouted. “For shame! I won’t look at it!”

He threw it into the fire.

“I couldn’t help it,” she said. “By chance—pure chance. Governor Dinwiddie is taking the Major’s room, and I was moving things. This paper fell out. I just glanced—only to see what it was. Then I knew I had to read it.”

“Oh, you are a martyr to duty, Mountain,” George said coldly.

“Don’t mock me,” she pleaded. “I’ve watched you, nursed you, carried you when you were sick. I’m your mother in every way—your real mother, perhaps.”

“Stop!” George said sharply. “Don’t speak like that.”

But she did not stop. “You are ungrateful,” she said. “All of you. My Mr. Mountain was a wretch—and you are no better.”

The fire burned low. The paper lay in ashes, safe from harm—or so she thought.

George sat in silence, consumed by jealousy and dread. When his mother asked him at dinner why he looked so pale, he replied, “Do you suppose, madam, that leaving a mother like you does not cause me great pain?”

She could not understand his words, his strange laughter, his sudden bursts of anger. He drank heavily, joked wildly, called to the servants, laughed at them. Each time the door opened, he turned toward it—just as Mrs. Mountain did, fearing Mr. Washington would appear.

On the day set for Madam Esmond’s reception of General Braddock, Castlewood was transformed into a scene of opulent festivity. The great house stood resplendent in its best attire—flags fluttered above the portico, fresh flowers adorned every window ledge, and the gardens were swept clean and trimmed with care. Madam Esmond herself appeared in a gown of deep crimson silk, embroidered with silver thread and edged with lace that shimmered like moonlight on water. It was a dress far more grand than she usually wore, but she had chosen it deliberately, to honor her guest and to lend dignity to an occasion that weighed heavily upon her heart.

The first arrival was the General’s new aide-de-camp, Mr. Washington, who rode up under a clear blue sky, his horse sleek and well-groomed, his uniform polished to a mirror shine. He dismounted at the steps, bowing low as he handed the reins to the waiting negro servants, who led the animal away to its familiar stall. No young man in the colony rode better or carried himself with greater grace than this one, and Madam Esmond greeted him warmly in the covered gallery before the house.

For several moments, while Major Washington removed his riding boots, he and the widow walked slowly along the gallery, speaking in quiet tones. She had much to say—about the General’s impending visit, about the news of her son’s departure, and about the strange turn of events that brought such men as Franklin of Pennsylvania into the company of the Commander-in-Chief. She spoke with a mixture of pride and unease, for though she admired the General’s rank and power, she could not help but wonder at the world that now surrounded them.

“Mr. Franklin,” she remarked, “was once a printer’s boy, I understand. And yet here he is, traveling in the coach of our most noble commander.”

Mr. Washington smiled gently. “Madam, I have seen many men rise from humble beginnings. But none, I assure you, with such wit, industry, and sense as Mr. Franklin. He may not wear the trappings of nobility, but he carries within him a mind that would command respect in any court.”

Madam Esmond shook her head slightly. “I only hope my son does not find himself among such common folk when he goes off to war. I trust he will be with gentlemen—true gentlemen—of fashion and breeding.”

The Major paused, then said quietly, “There are no perfect companions, madam. Young men must learn from all sorts—the good and the bad. They must hear both wisdom and folly, and judge for themselves.”

“And yet,” she insisted, “he will be with veterans of the finest army in Europe, officers bred in the courts of kings, friends of His Royal Highness the Duke…”

She trailed off, and Washington merely inclined his head. He did not wish to speak too freely of matters that might wound her feelings.

“And with you, dear Colonel,” she added, turning to him with a soft smile, “whom my father always held in highest esteem. You will take care of him, sir? Though you are but five years older, I trust you more than any other officer. My father often told us children to look up to you. I have always done so myself.”

“I would have given anything to win Colonel Esmond’s favor,” replied Washington, bowing with courteous gravity. “And if I could earn your regard, madam, I should consider myself the happiest man alive.”

The widow blushed deeply, and dropped into a curtsey so low and graceful that it was said no woman in the province could match it. “Then I shall always count you among my dearest friends,” she said softly, offering her hand. He kissed it with profound respect.

They walked back into the house together, where George Warrington soon joined them—dressed in his finest clothes, powdered wig neatly arranged, sword at his side, and bearing himself with all the stiff formality of a gentleman just come of age.

He bowed deeply to his mother and again to the Colonel, but there was no warmth in his eyes. A polite smile touched his lips, yet his gaze flickered with something sharper—anger, perhaps, or disappointment. What had passed between them? Nothing overt, nothing improper. Yet both the widow and the Colonel seemed strangely flushed, their expressions strained.

“Have you had good sport today, Mr. George?” asked Washington, trying to ease the tension.

“No,” George replied sharply. “Have you?”

The Colonel, never one for idle talk, began at once to describe his morning’s hunt—a long and detailed account of how he and the king’s officers had pursued birds through the woods, how they had shot game, and how General Braddock, despite his bulk and clumsy boots, had managed to flounder through the forest with a pack of dogs and negroes barking wildly beside him.

“He actually shot a deer,” Washington laughed, “with a fowling-piece in hand, while the dogs were still chasing it!”

“Great God, sir!” cried Braddock, puffing and blowing, “what would Sir Robert Walpole have said to see such a sight in Norfolk?”

Madam Esmond chuckled delicately. “Indeed, Colonel, you are vastly comical this afternoon!”

But George remained silent, his face darkening further.

“You mean Sir Robert Walpole, the Prime Minister?” asked Harry, who had just entered the room, dressed identically to his brother—gold-braided coat, silver-hilted sword, solitaire ring gleaming on his finger.

“Yes,” said Washington. “The General has spoken of visiting him, of the great hunts at Houghton, the palace, the paintings. I confess, I’d give much to see a proper fox-chase in England.”

George sneered. “And yet here we are, hunting elephants and buffaloes, I suppose. Or is it rock-fish and roe-deer? I know not what you call it. But I am no sportsman.”

“You’re a milksop,” said Washington, unable to hide his irritation.

“Indeed,” said George, drawing out a pink ribbon from his apron strings—his mother’s favorite color—and holding it up. “Look at these lovely ties! Who wouldn’t want to be bound by them? See how charming they are! I remember when they were black—for my grandfather.”

“And who would not mourn such a gentleman?” asked Washington, puzzled.

“Ah, Harry!” burst out Madam Esmond, tears filling her eyes as her younger son stepped forward. “Oh, Harry, Harry!”

“What is it, mother?” asked Harry, embracing her.

“I don’t know,” said Washington, biting his lip. “A mere question about ribbons, I believe.”

“Sir,” snapped George, “will you please to speak for yourself?”

The Colonel straightened, then lowered his voice. “He speaks too much for himself,” sighed the widow.

George turned to her. “I protest I do not know the source of these tears any more than the source of the Nile. And if the portrait of my father were to begin to cry, I should wonder at paternal sorrow as much as at maternal.”

He twirled on his scarlet heels with a flourish.

“George Warrington!” exclaimed Harry, “what devil’s dance is that?”

“I do not dance,” said George, “but I can sing.” And without another word, he sat down at the harpsichord and began to play and sing:

The melody echoed through the hall, and Washington, stepping from the balcony, paused to listen.

“I am playing *God save the King*,” said George, smirking, “in compliment to the new expedition.”

“You never know whether you are laughing or serious,” said Washington, “but surely that is not the tune.”

George played a series of rapid trills and quavers, showing off his skill. The Colonel watched, uncertain—was this a man of war or a delicate musician?

At last, Washington checked his watch. “His Excellency’s coach will be here shortly. If you’ll excuse me, I shall retire to prepare.”

“Colonel Washington knows the way to his room,” said George, still at the harpsichord, glancing over his shoulder but making no move to assist.

“Let me show him,” said Madam Esmond, her voice sharp with anger. And with that, she swept from the room, followed by the bewildered Colonel.

George continued to pound the keys, lost in thought.

Harry stepped forward. “For heaven’s sake, George, what does this mean?”

“Why shouldn’t he kiss her hand?” George retorted, pulling out a folded paper from his pocket. “I told you—he did.”

“It was only kindness,” said Harry.

“Kindness!” George shrieked. “Look at this!”

He unfolded the note. It read:

*...is older than myself, but I, again, am older than my years; and you know, dear brother, have ever been considered a sober person. All children are better for a father's superintendence, and her two, I trust, will find in me a tender friend and guardian.*

“Friend and guardian!” George spat, clenching his fists. “Curse him!”

Harry read on:

*...The flattering offer which General Braddock hath made me, will, of course, oblige me to postpone this matter until after the campaign. When we have given the French a sufficient drubbing, I shall return to repose under my own vine and fig-tree.*

“Under my own vine and fig-tree,” George repeated bitterly, pointing to the creeping vines climbing the wall. “That’s Castlewood. That’s home.”

And then came the final line:

And the letter ended.

“Rachel,” George whispered. “Rachel is not weeping for her children. She wants to be comforted.”

He looked at his brother. “Now, Harry. Let us go upstairs at once. Kneel down, as becomes us, and pray: ‘Dear papa, welcome to your house of Castlewood.’”

His Excellency, the Commander-in-Chief, set out to visit Madam Esmond with all the grandeur befitting the most distinguished figure in His Majesty’s North American colonies. A troop of dragoons led the procession from Williamsburg, their horses clattering through the dusty streets amid cheers and shouts from a loyal crowd—mostly enslaved people who lined the road to witness the spectacle. The General rode in his own ornate coach, flanked by Captain Talmadge, his Master of the Horse, who remained at the carriage door before riding alongside during the journey. Major Danvers, aide-de-camp, sat in the front seat beside Mr. Benjamin Franklin, the postmaster from Philadelphia—a man once a printer’s apprentice but now renowned for his sharp wit and wide-ranging knowledge of both the colonies and England, where he had traveled more than once.

“Truly remarkable,” the General remarked, tipping his hat with a gracious bow, “how a man of such modest beginnings could acquire so much learning—and yet carry himself with such refined manners. Mr. Franklin, you surprise me!”

The postmaster bowed low. “It has been my fortune,” he replied, “to meet gentlemen like yourself, and I’ve done my best to learn from them. My father was poor, and schooling in New England was scarce. But I’ve gathered what I could—though nothing, I assure you, compares to what one finds in England.”

General Braddock laughed heartily. “Ah, education! There are officers in the army, by George, who can’t tell whether to spell *bull* with one or two *b’s*. I’ve heard the Duke of Marlborough wasn’t much of a penman either. I never served under him—he was before my time—but he gave the French a sound beating, scholar or not.”

Mr. Franklin nodded. “I’m aware of that.”

“And my Duke?” Braddock continued, eyes twinkling. “No scholar, eh? Aha, Mr. Postmaster—I see your wink says it all.”

Franklin immediately dropped his expression, turning his gaze to the General’s jolly, round face with an innocence as pure as a child’s. “He may not be a scholar,” he said, “but no French general ever matched him. He saved the crown for the finest king in Christendom—our beloved King George.”

Off came Franklin’s hat, and from beneath his powdered wig, a halo of white dust floated into the air.

“He is the soldier’s true friend,” Braddock declared. “And the fiercest foe to those beggarly red-coated Scots rebels and scheming Jesuits who’d steal our liberty and religion. His Royal Highness—the Prince of Wales—is no scholar either, but he’s one of the noblest gentlemen alive.”

“I’ve seen him on horseback,” said Franklin, “at a review in Hyde Park. The Duke is indeed a magnificent rider.”

“You’ll drink to him tonight,” Braddock announced. “He’s the best master, the best friend, the best son any king could have—and the finest gentleman who ever wore an epaulet.”

“Epaulets are quite beyond my calling,” Franklin chuckled. “You know I live in a Quaker city.”

“Of course they are,” Braddock replied, good-naturedly. “To each his trade. You, sir, to your books—we welcome that. We, to fight and govern. Hey, gentlemen? Look at these roads! This cursed coach bounces like a buck!” He spotted a rider ahead, accompanied by two negro boys in livery. “Who’s that on the fine gelding?”

“Mr. Washington,” said the aide-de-camp.

“I’d take him for a corporal in the Horse Grenadiers,” Braddock declared. “He carries himself well. Knows this country, too, Mr. Franklin.”

“Yes, indeed.”

“And a remarkably polished young man—considering his upbringing. I’d have thought he’d have the grace of Europe about him.”

“He does his best,” Franklin said, glancing at the General—this towering embodiment of English elegance, swaying side to side in the carriage, face flushed as crimson as his coat, swearing at nearly every word, ignorant of everything outside military matters—except perhaps wine and women. Not born to nobility, yet fiercely proud of his lack of pedigree; brave as a bulldog, fierce, lustful, generous, prodigal, gentle in mood, quick to laugh, dull of wit, utterly unlearned, yet certain his country was the greatest in the world—and himself as noble a gentleman as any in it.

“Yes,” Franklin added, “he’s quite impressive for a provincial. He was beaten at Fort What-d’ye-call-um last year, near the Thingamy River. What was its name again, Talmadge?”

“The Lord knows, sir,” Talmadge answered, grinning. “And I dare say the Postmaster does too—judging by that wink.”

“Oh, Captain!”

“It was a trap,” said the General. “Only militia and Indians with him. Good day, Mr. Washington. Fine horse, sir. That was your first action?”

“That at Fort Necessity?” Washington replied, saluting gravely as he approached, followed by two smartly dressed negro grooms. “Yes, sir. I began poorly—never having faced battle until that unfortunate day.”

“You were raw levies,” Braddock said. “You should have seen our militia flee from the Scotch—curse them! You needed regular troops.”

“It is my deepest wish,” Washington said, “to serve with such men.”

“By George, we shall try to grant you that,” Braddock declared, letting loose another thunderous oath. The heavy coach rolled onward toward Castlewood, while Washington asked permission to ride ahead and inform Madam Esmond of the General’s imminent arrival.

The Commander-in-Chief moved so slowly that several lesser guests, invited to meet him, overtook the procession. Unwilling to pass the great man, they formed a long, dusty train behind the carriage. First came Mr. Dinwiddie, the Lieutenant-Governor, attended by his servants and accompanied by Parson Broadbent, the jovial chaplain of Williamsburg. Soon after came little Mr. Dempster, the schoolmaster, wearing his grand Ramillies wig reserved for formal occasions. Then appeared Mr. Laws, the judge, with his wife seated behind him on a pillion, and their negro servant carrying a box with her cap, mounted on a mule. The sight was so absurd that Major Danvers and Mr. Franklin burst into laughter—though quietly, so as not to disturb the General, who by now was fast asleep. Braddock, roused only slightly, ordered the odd rearguard to move forward, leaving him and his dragoons to proceed at their own pace. There would be room for all at Castlewood when they arrived.

There was food, drink, and tobacco for the soldiers of His Majesty; laughter and music for the enslaved; and a warm, generous welcome for their masters.

The General required constant help at table, holding out his glass repeatedly, demanding more wine, more meat, more ale. Nathan’s sangaree, a sweetened rum punch, he declared excellent, and drank deeply of it even before dinner. Cider, brandy, ale, and fine Bordeaux wine flowed freely—some of it brought personally by Colonel Esmond from England, which little Mr. Dempster claimed was fit for the Pope’s table, winking slyly at Parson Broadbent. The clergyman returned the wink, though he didn’t understand Latin—nor did he care. Broadbent was a roistering divine, fond of gambling, cockfighting, and drinking, who had spent time in Fleet Prison and frequented Newmarket and Hockley-in-the-Hole. Sent to Virginia by Lord Cingbars—whose mother, incidentally, was Broadbent’s own mother—his reputation was mixed. He had hunted birds, fish, and game with young George Esmond, and fought cocks with him. Some whispered that Broadbent was the poacher whom Washington once caught and caned by the river at Mount Vernon. He escaped into the dark, but bore the marks of a black eye and a torn collar when he returned weeks later. The boys had played cards, hunted, fished, and shared many adventures together—though Harry, the younger brother, often stayed behind to study with other tutors, while George read his own books, keeping his secrets close.

At the feast, every bird that flew and every fish that swam in Virginia waters found its way to Madam Esmond’s table. The gumbo was praised as perfection—so much so that young George’s black servant, discovered eating from a bowl behind the door by the late Colonel, was humorously christened “Gumbo” on the spot. The shad were rich and fresh, the stewed terrapins worthy of London aldermen—so good, in fact, that Braddock offered them to the Duke himself. Stewed terrapin, indeed, was fit for any duke—or emperor. The enslaved cooks at Castlewood were masterful, trained under the watchful eyes of both the late and present Madam Esmond. Certain dishes—especially the sweets and flans—Madam Esmond prepared herself, carving with dexterity, rolling up her lace-trimmed sleeves to reveal delicate arms and small hands, performing the ancient ritual of hospitality with grace and charm.

In those days, it was customary for the mistress of the house to preside over the meal with warmth and attention—encouraging guests, knowing how to carve, offering new courses, and cheering others on. She leaned toward Braddock: “I’ve kept the jowl of this salmon for you, Excellency—no refusal, please.” To Franklin: “You drink only water, sir—yet our cellar holds wines that give no headache.” To Judge Laws: “You love woodcock pie?”

“Because I know who makes the pastry,” the judge replied, bowing deeply. “I wish my wife had Madam Esmond’s skill. I often say to her, ‘My dear, I wish you had Madam Esmond’s hand.’”

“It is a very pretty hand,” said Franklin, “and I suspect others might admire it too.”

Mr. Esmond glanced uneasily at the remark.

“A lovely hand for light pie-crust,” the judge continued, “and my compliments, madam.” He believed such praise would please her. She simply replied that she had learned cooking in England, under her mother’s tutelage, and made dishes her father and sons enjoyed. If they liked them, she was glad.

More conversation followed, more dishes, ten times more meat than needed. Washington spoke little, but he, Talmadge, Danvers, and Franklin discussed roads, rivers, supply trains, artillery, and the challenges of colonial militias. On the table, Washington placed bits of bread to mark key points—then a servant wiped the Potomac away with a napkin and swept the Ohio into a spoon.

After dinner, Parson Broadbent rose and walked behind the Lieutenant-Governor’s chair to say grace, then resumed his place. Then came the desserts—puddings, cakes, custards, and preserves—so numerous and elaborate that few modern readers would care to list them. But Madam Esmond had prepared them all with care and pride.

When the table was cleared, Nathan, her chief steward, placed a glass before each guest and filled his mistress’s. Bowing to the company, she raised her glass. “I offer only one toast,” she said, “but I know you will join me heartily.” Then, she called out, “His Majesty!” Braddock and the others echoed the name with loyalty. After a toast and a salute, she withdrew between rows of enslaved servants, curtsying deeply at the door.

Madam Esmond carried herself with admirable spirit throughout the evening—gay, elegant, and full of cheer. The few ladies present admired her grace and the splendor of the feast. But scarcely had they entered the drawing-room when her composure cracked. Seated beside Mrs. Laws, she suddenly broke down, weeping into her handkerchief mid-compliment. “Ah, madam,” she sobbed, “it may be an honor to host the King’s representative—our family has welcomed greater men than Mr. Braddock. But he comes to take one of my sons away. Who knows if he’ll return? Last night, I dreamed he lay wounded, pale, blood streaming from his side. I wouldn’t let my grief show before the gentlemen—but you, Mrs. Justice, who’ve lost children, who know a mother’s heart—wouldn’t think less of me if I wept tonight.”

The ladies offered comfort. She tried to regain control, remembering her duties. “It will be time enough to grieve when he’s gone,” she said. “My boy must not see me weak. Our parting must not be made worse by my sorrow. It is right for men of his rank to answer their country’s call. That has always been the Esmond way. The same Power that preserved my father through twenty battles in Queen Anne’s time—may it now protect my son.”

Then, instead of mourning, she joined her friends at a card game and a cup of coffee, while the gentlemen lingered in the next room, drinking and toasting.

When one lady suggested they were staying too long, Madam Esmond replied: “Let them stay. It’s rare for young men here to be in such company. Though their talk may be bold, gentlemen of fashion will respect youth and speak nothing unsuitable.”

Clearly, the English visitors enjoyed the feast. As the ladies played, Nathan slipped into the room and whispered to Mrs. Mountain. “No more!” she cried at first. “They can have the common Bordeaux, but not the Colonel’s special claret—already drunk, along with ale, cider, Burgundy, Lisbon, and Madeira!”

But Madam Esmond insisted on generosity. Mrs. Mountain reluctantly fetched the keys and hurried to the vault where the Colonel’s prized Bordeaux still rested—surviving its owner, who had long since passed into the earth.

On the way, she asked if anyone had overindulged. Nathan said Mister Broadbent was tipsy—as usual. The General, too, seemed affected. And Master George? “A lilly drunk,” Nathan insisted.

“Master George?” Mrs. Mountain exclaimed. “He hasn’t touched a drop in days!”

Yet Nathan stood firm. George had been filling his glass, talking, singing, making jokes—especially at Mr. Washington’s expense, which had angered the young colonel.

“Well,” Mrs. Mountain said, “a gentleman ought to enjoy himself among friends. Let him pass the bottle.”

She trotted off to the cellar with renewed speed.

Young George Esmond’s recent behavior—his teasing, his mockery—had deeply offended Mr. Washington. Though only a few years older than the Castlewood twins, Washington was known for his maturity and restraint. The boys had long looked up to him as mentor, guide, and friend—almost everyone did. He demanded seriousness from others, and his presence silenced frivolity. To him, jests seemed misplaced. He understood them slowly, and they faded in his presence.

“He always seemed great to me,” wrote Harry Warrington years later. “Like a hero. When he taught us surveying, or rode to hounds—it felt like leading an army. If he fired, the bird fell. If he cast a net, the largest fish were caught. His words were few, but wise—never idle, always grave, strong, ready to do duty. Even my brother, who disliked him, respected him—more than any man alive.”

Mr. Washington was the first to leave the gathering. Young George had spoken freely, taunting him with remarks he couldn’t answer. Angered beyond endurance, he walked out through the open windows onto the broad veranda.

Madam Esmond saw him pacing there, and, the evening being warm, she left her cards and joined him.

“I see the gentlemen linger over their wine,” she said gently.

“Drinking makes good soldiers,” he replied. “Some here are doing their duty.”

“And the General leads?”

“No doubt,” Washington said softly. “But he is the General. I cannot comment on his conduct. Perhaps British officers are different from us. Our sun is hot—we don’t need wine to heat our blood. Toasts seem a matter of honor to them. Talmadge told me just now that an officer cannot refuse a toast any more than a challenge. He hated it at first, but learned to endure it—with great resolve.”

“What do you talk about for so long?” she asked.

“I cannot tell you all,” he said. “We discussed the war, Contrecoeur’s forces, how we might reach him. The General plans to command from his coach—lightly dismissing the enemy. But if we meet them, I trust we’ll prevail.”

“How can there be doubt?” she asked—her father had served under Marlborough.

“Mr. Franklin,” Washington continued, “spoke wisely. He would have said more, but the English gentlemen dismissed him as a raw provincial. They insist we don’t know what disciplined troops can do. Why not build turnpikes and inns for his Excellency? ‘There are some inns,’ says Danvers, ‘not as comfortable as ours.’ ‘No,’ says Franklin, ‘you can’t expect that.’ He drinks water, laughs at them—but I wonder if it’s fair for a water-drinker to sit and judge men over their wine.”

“And my boys?” she asked, laying a hand on his arm. “Harry promised me—when he gives his word, I trust him. George is always moderate. Why do you look so grave?”

He hesitated, unable to explain.

With General Braddock and the other guests of Castlewood comfortably settled in their rooms, the two young Warringtons retired to their own chamber, eager to share their thoughts on the day’s most momentous event. The idea of their mother marrying the younger son of a colonial family—once trained as a land surveyor—was unthinkable. Could the heir of the noble Marquises of Esmond truly unite with such a man? And what of Castlewood itself, now under the care of a stepfather barely twenty-three years old? It was an outrage! Harry, fired by indignation, declared he would rush straight to his mother’s bedroom—where her black maids were gently removing the jewels and finery she had worn for the feast—and protest with all his might. If the match went forward, he vowed they would leave at once, return to their modest estate in Virginia, and never speak to her again.

George, however, had another plan—one far more daring. “Mother,” he said, “cannot marry a man who has wounded or killed one of us—or whom we have wounded or killed. We must challenge him, Harry.”

Harry saw the wisdom in this instantly. “You’re right, George,” he agreed. “She wouldn’t marry our murderer. And if we wound him, the matter is settled. *Cadit quaestio*, as Mr. Dempster used to say. Shall I send my boy to deliver a challenge to Colonel Washington now?”

“My dear Harry,” replied George, recalling with pride his own duel at Quebec, “you’re not yet accustomed to matters of honour.”

“No,” admitted Harry, sighing as he looked up at his elder brother with admiration and envy.

“We cannot insult a gentleman in our own home,” George continued, speaking with quiet dignity. “The laws of honour forbid it. But we may ride out with him, and once beyond the park gates, we can make our feelings known.”

“That we will!” exclaimed Harry, gripping his brother’s hand. “And that we shall. I say, Georgy…” His face flushed red, and George asked what he wanted.

“This is my turn,” Harry pleaded. “If you go on the campaign, I should be allowed the other affair. Truly, I ought to.”

“Again, the head of the house must lead,” George said with regal composure. “If I fall, Harry, you shall avenge me. But I must fight Colonel Washington. He is mine especially. Was it not he who advised my mother to order that wretch Ward to lay hands on me?”

“Ah, George,” interjected the more gentle Harry, “you ought to forgive and forget.”

“Forgive?” George retorted sharply. “Never, while I live. One cannot command a man to forget. A wrong today remains a wrong tomorrow. I’ve never done harm to another, and I won’t suffer it, if I can help it. I despise Mr. Ward, but I don’t think he’ll ever forgive you for that blow with the ruler. Colonel Washington is our enemy—mine above all. He has already advised one injustice against me, and now plots a greater. We must punish him.”

The old Bordeaux wine had set George’s usually pale face aflame. Harry, ever devoted to his brother, admired his boldness and eloquence, and quietly prepared to follow his lead. They retired to bed, George giving strict instructions to Harry to remain courteous to all guests still under their mother’s roof the next day.

Courtesy and discretion prevent us from revealing which of Madam Esmond’s guests succumbed first to the generous hospitality of Castlewood. The descendants of Messrs. Talmadge and Danvers, aides-de-camp to the General, might prefer not to hear how their ancestors were once overcome by drink; yet the men themselves took no shame in it, and likely indulged just as freely in their own time. Let us imagine them staggering to their beds, supported by sympathetic servants; and the General himself, too robust a drinker to yield to mere bottles of wine, escorted by the young gentlemen to his room, soon asleep under Bacchus’s tender care. Madam Esmond observed the state of her guests without surprise or dismay. She rose early, preparing cooling drinks for their parched throats, which her servants delivered to each chamber.

At breakfast, one English officer teased Mr. Franklin, who refused both wine and the morning toddy, saying he missed two pleasures: the drink and the remedy. The young man laughed and proposed continuing both. Colonel Washington, the General’s new American aide, remained sober and composed. The British officers insisted they must teach him the ways of the English army, but the Virginian replied gravely that he had no desire to learn that part of military education.

Busy with the aftermath of the grand dinner and breakfast, Madam Esmond had little time to observe her sons closely—but she noticed that George was exceptionally polite to Colonel Washington, as to every guest.

Before departing, General Braddock held a private audience with Madam Esmond, formally offering to take her son into his household. When arrangements for George’s departure were finalized between mother and future commander, Madam Esmond showed no signs of fear, though she surely felt the risks her son faced. She knew he must enter the world and meet its trials. “Mr. Braddock is a fine gentleman in the morning,” she told her aide-de-camp, Mrs. Mountain, “and though my father did not drink, many of England’s finest do.” The cheerful General shook hands with George after the interview, welcoming him and instructing him to report to Frederick in three days—shortly before the expedition began.

Now the great coach was summoned again. The General’s escort pranced around it, and the other guests mounted their horses. Madam Esmond saw the General to the steps of the veranda, followed by her sons, who stood beside the coach door. The guard trumpeter blew a sharp note, the negroes shouted “Huzzay, and God save the King,” and General Braddock, graciously thanking his hosts, rolled away toward headquarters.

As the boys ascended the steps, Colonel Washington was once more taking leave of their mother. No doubt she had urged him to protect George. “With my life,” the Colonel assured her. “You may depend on me.” Then, turning to the lads, he said, “Farewell, my dear Harry. With you, George, it is no adieu—we shall meet again in three days at the camp.”

Both young men were headed into danger—perhaps death. Colonel Washington was leaving, and she would see him no more before the war began. It was no wonder the widow was deeply moved.

George Warrington watched his mother’s emotion and interpreted it with a cold, bitter scorn. “Stay yet a moment,” he said steadily, “to comfort our mother. Only time to get booted, and my brother and I will ride with you a short way, George.” His horses had already been saddled. Soon the three young men were riding together, their negro grooms following behind. Mrs. Mountain, knowing she had stirred trouble between them and fearing the outcome, felt relieved that Mr. Washington left without a quarrel—without even a declaration of love to the widow.

No man could appear more courteous than George Warrington to his namesake, the Colonel. The latter was surprised and pleased by the change in his young friend. The shared peril, the necessity of future alliance, the long-standing bond between the Colonel and the Esmond family, and the tender farewells exchanged with the mistress of Castlewood all softened his heart. He chose to overlook past grievances and grew more friendly than ever. George was bright and cheerful; it was Harry who seemed melancholy, riding silently beside his brother, keeping his distance from Colonel Washington, who had once drawn him close.

They discussed the war and the likely outcome—none doubted its success. Two thousand seasoned British troops, led by their commander, could not fail against any force the French could muster, so long as they moved promptly. The passionate young Virginian held deep respect for the discipline and courage of regular soldiers. King George II had no more loyal subject than the General’s new aide-de-camp.

They rode amicably until reaching Benson’s, a rough log tavern where, by custom, guests paid for food and shelter. Here was also a recruiting station, and several officers and men of Halkett’s regiment were gathered. Colonel Washington assumed his young friends would bid him farewell here.

While their horses were watered, they entered the common room, where a simple meal awaited those who wished to eat. George Warrington entered with a particularly lively air, while Harry looked pale and distressed.

“One would think, Squire Harry,” remarked Benson, “that you were the one leaving home to fight the French and Indians, not Mr. George.”

“I may fear for my brother’s safety,” Harry replied, “though I could bear my own well enough. It’s not my fault I stay behind.”

“No indeed, brother,” George added.

“Harry Warrington’s courage needs no proof!” declared Colonel Washington.

“You do the family honor by speaking so well of us, Colonel,” said George, bowing low. “I dare say we can hold our own, if need be.”

Yet as George boasted, Harry looked far from brave. When their eyes met, he read in George’s gaze a terrible certainty. “You’re not going to do it now?” he whispered.

“Yes, now,” George answered, steady as stone.

“For God’s sake, let me have the chance. You’re going to the campaign—you shouldn’t have everything. There might be a misunderstanding, George. We may be wrong.”

“Psha,” George scoffed. “How can we be? It must be done now. Don’t worry. No names will be mentioned—I’ll find a suitable excuse.”

Two officers of Halkett’s regiment, known to the brothers, sat beneath the porch, the Virginian toddy-bowl before them.

“What are you plotting, gentlemen?” called one. “Is it a drink?”

Their voices were thick, their faces flushed—clearly they had already drunk heavily.

“The very thing,” George said cheerfully. “Fresh glasses, Mr. Benson! What, no glasses? Then we’ll drink from the bowl.”

“Many a good man has drunk from it,” Benson said. One by one, the boys bowed to their military acquaintances and touched the bowl with their lips. The liquor seemed undiminished, though George, in particular, acted like a seasoned drinker, declaring it delicious after their ride. He called to Colonel Washington, who stood at the porch, inviting him to join.

The tone was disrespectful—echoing the manner George had lately adopted, which had irritated the Colonel. The Colonel bowed and said he was not thirsty.

“Nay, the liquor is paid for,” George insisted. “Don’t fear, Colonel.”

“I said I wasn’t thirsty,” the Colonel replied, drumming his foot. “I didn’t say the liquor was paid for.”

“When the King’s health is proposed,” George cried, “an officer cannot refuse. I drink to His Majesty, gentlemen. Colonel Washington, you may drink or not. The King!”

This was a point of military honor. Captain Grace and Mr. Waring of Halkett’s both drank “The King.” Harry Warrington drank “The King.” Colonel Washington, eyes blazing, took a small sip from the bowl.

Then Captain Grace proposed “The Duke and the Army”—a toast no one could ignore. The Colonel had to swallow it.

“You don’t seem to enjoy the toast, Colonel,” George remarked.

“I tell you again,” the Colonel replied, “I don’t want to drink. It seems to me the Duke and the Army would serve better if their healths weren’t toasted so often.”

“You’re not yet familiar with regular troops’ customs,” Captain Grace said, voice slurred.

“Perhaps not, sir.”

“A British officer,” Grace continued, “never neglects such a toast. A man who refuses to drink the Duke’s health—hang me, such a man should be tried by court-martial!”

“What means this language to me?” roared Colonel Washington, slamming his fist on the table. “You are drunk, sir!”

“A cursed provincial officer says I’m drunk!” shrieked Captain Grace. “Waring, do you hear that?”

“I heard it, sir!” George Warrington cried. “We all heard it. He came at my invitation—the liquor was mine, the table was mine—and I am shocked to hear such language directed at my esteemed guest, Captain Waring.”

“Confound your impudence, you infernal young jackanapes!” bellowed the Colonel. “You dare insult me before British officers and criticize my words? For months I’ve borne your insolence—if I hadn’t loved your mother—yes, sir, and your grandfather and your brother—I would—”

His words failed him. The Colonel stood speechless, face purple, limbs trembling with rage.

“You would what, sir?” George asked calmly. “If you didn’t love my grandfather, my brother, or my mother? You’re using her affection as an excuse for your behavior. What would you do, sir, may I ask again?”

“I would put you across my knee and whip you, you snarling little puppy!” the Colonel shouted, regaining breath. “That’s what I’d do!”

“Because you’ve known us all our lives and made our home your own,” Harry burst out, rising, “is no reason to insult either of us! What you said, George Washington, is an insult to both of us. You will apologize, sir!”

“Apologize?”

“Or give us the reparation due to gentlemen,” Harry continued.

The Colonel’s heart sank. He realized he might be forced to draw blood from one of the boys he cherished. As Harry stood before him—fair-haired, flushed, voice quivering—a wave of tenderness swept over him. “I—I am bewildered,” he said. “My words may have been hasty. What has George been meaning these past months? Tell me, and perhaps—”

But evil stirred within young George Warrington. His dark eyes burned with hatred. “You’re avoiding the question, sir,” he said, “just as you avoided the toast. I am not a child to endure your arrogance. You publicly insulted me in public, and I demand satisfaction.”

“In Heaven’s name, be it!” the Colonel said, grief etched on his face.

“And you insulted me!” Captain Grace cried, swaying toward him. “What did he say? Confound the militia captain—colonel, what is he? You insulted me! Oh, Waring! To think I should be insulted by a militia captain!” Tears welled in the Captain’s eyes.

“I insult you, you hog!” the Colonel roared, unmoved by humor.

And then a fourth adversary appeared.

“Great Powers, sir!” Captain Waring exclaimed. “Are three affairs not enough? Must I join in too? You have a quarrel with these two young gentlemen.”

“Hasty words, sir!” Harry repeated.

“Hasty words, sir!” Waring echoed. “A gentleman tells another he’ll put him across his knees and whip him, and you call that hasty? If anyone said to me, ‘Charles Waring,’ or ‘Captain Waring, I’ll put you across my knees and whip you,’ I’d drive my cheese-toaster through his body, even if he were as big as Goliath. That’s one affair with young Mr. George Warrington. Mr. Harry, of course, will stand by his brother—that’s two. Between Grace and the Colonel, apology is impossible. And now—run me through the body—you call an officer of my regiment—of Halkett’s, sir—a hog before my face! Great heavens, sir! Mr. Washington, are you all like this in Virginia? Excuse me, I mean no offense, but by Gad, Colonel! I must tell you—you are the most quarrelsome man I’ve ever seen. Call a disabled officer of my regiment—disabled, ain’t you, Grace?—call him a hog before me! You withdraw it, sir—withdraw it!”

“Is this some conspiracy against me?” the Colonel thundered. “It seems I’m drunk, and not you, as you all are. I withdraw nothing. I apologize for nothing. By heavens! I will meet one or half a dozen of you—young or old, drunk or sober!”

“I do not wish to hear more insults,” George Warrington said coldly. “This affair can proceed without further offense from you. When will you give me the meeting?”

“The sooner the better, sir!” the Colonel snapped.

“The sooner the better!” hiccupped Captain Grace, swearing profusely—oaths being the natural seasoning of gentlemanly talk in those days. He staggered to his feet, reached for his sword, and fell as he grasped it. “The sooner the better!” he yelled from the ground, waving his weapon and knocking his hat over his eyes.

“At least this gentleman’s business will wait till tomorrow,” the militia Colonel said, turning to the other officer. “You won’t bring your man out today, Captain Waring?”

“I confess neither his hand nor mine is steady,” Waring admitted.

“Mine is!” George Warrington declared, glaring at his enemy.

The Colonel, equally fierce, replied, “Be it so—what weapon, sir?”

“Not small-swords, Colonel. We can beat you with them. You know that from our old bouts. Pistols had better be the word.”

“As you please, George Warrington—and God forgive you, George! God pardon you, Harry! for dragging me into this quarrel,” the Colonel said, face heavy with sorrow.

Harry hung his head, but George remained calm. “I, sir? It was not I who called names, who spoke of a cane, who insulted a gentleman in public before army officers. This is not the first time you’ve treated me like a slave, talked of the whip for me.”

The Colonel recoiled, face crimson, struck by sudden memory.

“Great heavens, George! Is it that boyish quarrel you still remember?”

“Who made you the overseer of Castlewood?” George spat, grinding his teeth. “I am not your slave, George Washington, and I never will be. I hated you then, and I hate you now. You insulted me, and I am a gentleman, as you are. Is that not enough?”

“Too much, only too much,” the Colonel said, grief written on his face. “Do you bear malice too, Harry? I never thought this of you!”

“I stand by my brother,” Harry said, turning away from the Colonel’s gaze, clasping George’s hand.

The sadness in their adversary’s face did not fade. “Heaven be good to us!” he muttered. “It’s all clear now.” He turned to George. “I’ll write a few letters, and I am at your service, Mr. Warrington.”

“You have your pistols at your saddle. I rode without any, but I’ll send Sady back for mine. That gives you enough time, Colonel Washington?”

“Plenty of time, sir.” Each bowed deeply. George linked arms with his brother and walked away. The Colonel looked at the two helpless captains, one propped by Captain Benson, the tavern keeper.

“It’s not entirely their fault, Colonel,” Benson said grimly. “Jack Firebrace and Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania were here this morning, trading horses with them. Jack and Tom got them to play cards—and they lost. Then Jack and Tom challenged them to drink for Old England’s honor—and they lost that, too. They’re kind-hearted when sober, but they’re a pair of fools now.”

“Captain Benson,” the Colonel said, “you’re an old frontier man, once an officer of ours. Will you help me in this matter with the young gentlemen?”

“I’ll stand by and see fair play, Colonel. I won’t interfere, but I’ll see justice done. Madam Esmond has helped me many times—tended my wife in childbirth, cured our Betty in the fever. You won’t be too hard on those boys, will you? Though I’ve seen both of them shoot—the fair one hunts well, as you know, but the older one’s a wonder at an ace of spades.”

The Virginian Colonel sat in silence within one chamber of the tavern, his thoughts heavy and his preparations grim. Across the hall, his adversary occupied himself with matters of a more solemn kind—writing a farewell letter to his mother, dictated by his younger brother and secretary, Harry Warrington. The words flowed with a grandeur that belied the trembling hand beneath them.

“…I scarcely suppose you will carry out the intentions you have at present in view,” George read aloud, emphasizing each syllable as if it were a judgment. “After this morning’s event, should I fall—as probably will be the case—your plans may well be abandoned.”

“Don’t say that, Georgy!” cried Harry, his voice cracking. “You’ll not fall! You can’t mean it!”

“‘As probably will be the case,’” George repeated, his tone unyielding. “You know what a good shot Colonel Washington is. And though I myself am no novice with a pistol, ‘tis likely one or both of us will fall.”

He paused, then added with cold irony: “I scarcely suppose you will carry out the intentions you have at present in view.” The bitterness in his voice was sharper than any blade.

Harry wept openly as he scribbled down the words. His fingers shook, and the ink blurred across the page. He had written “in view” as “in vew,” and a tear, salt and hot, smudged the line beneath.

“I can’t think about spelling now,” he whispered, burying his face in his hands. “I’m too miserable. Perhaps—perhaps it’s all nonsense. Maybe Colonel Washington never meant to take Castlewood. Never pretended to be our superior there. Never told Mother to have me flogged. Never intended to marry her. Never insulted me before the king’s officers. Never wrote to his brother saying we’d be better off under his rule?”

George snapped his fingers sharply. “The paper is here!” he said, slapping his breast-pocket. “If anything happens to me, Harry Warrington, you’ll find it on my corpse!”

“Write it yourself,” Harry begged, wiping his eyes with his elbows, ruining the entire draft. “I can’t do it anymore.”

So George took up a fresh sheet and began again. This time, he poured into the letter every ounce of learning and feeling he possessed—the long Latin phrases, the lofty sentiments, the quiet satire that only a young man with a scholar’s mind could muster. He asked that his trusted negro servant, Sady, be freed. That his copy of Horace be preserved. That his tutor, Mr. Dempster, receive a modest provision. That his silver fruit-knife, music books, and harpsichord go to little Fanny Mountain. And that Harry keep a lock of his hair—“as a token of my ever fond and faithfully attached George.”

With a flourish, he sealed it with the family crest—his grandfather’s seal—and placed it aside.

Then he pulled out his grandfather’s gold watch. “Two hours and a half gone,” he murmured. “Sady should be back with the pistols.”

“Take the watch,” he said softly. “It’s yours.”

“No good!” Harry cried, throwing his arms around him. “If he fights you, I’ll fight him too. If he kills you, I’ll kill him! Let him have a shot at me!”

The words spilled from his lips like curses—words so raw, so full of passion, that even the angels above might have winced as they recorded them in their celestial ledgers.

Meanwhile, General Braddock’s new aide-de-camp had already penned five letters in his bold, decisive hand. One to his mother at Mount Vernon. One to his brother. One addressed simply “M. C.” One to Major-General Braddock. And the fifth—delivered by a boy who overheard—was for Madam Esmond.

At this, Harry let out another cry of rage, and the recording angel once more fled across the heavens.

It was the tavern keeper who relayed these tidings. The Captain, dressed in his old militia uniform for the occasion, informed the boys that the Colonel was pacing in the garden, awaiting them. The regulars, he added, were nearly sober now.

A small plot near the log cabin had been fenced with shingles and cleared for a kitchen garden. There, beneath the pale afternoon sun, stood Colonel Washington—hands behind his back, head bowed, his face grave and sorrowful. Negro servants crowded at the palings, watching. Officers under the porch stirred from their sleep, waking to the gravity of the moment.

Captain Waring walked slowly beneath the sloping roof, while Captain Grace leaned over the railing, eyes wide but unfocused. Benson’s Tavern was no stranger to violence—cockfights, horse races, boxing matches—all drew the Virginia countryside together. Many a man had left there with broken ribs or blinded eyes. Gentlemen, farmers, slaves—they all came to witness the spectacle.

Now, the Colonel paced alone, lost in thought. There was no escape. No way out but through the duel—the brutal, accepted path of honor. He had spoken harshly to a young man, provoked by youthful insolence. The boy had demanded reparation. And though the Colonel regretted the heat of his words, he knew he must answer.

He did not wish to believe that George Warrington’s jealousy had festered so long. But the wrong was his, and the price must be paid.

Suddenly, a roar erupted from the distance—a cacophony of voices, loud and joyous. The negroes, always lovers of noise, especially when riding, shrieked and howled. Then came the clatter of hooves.

Mr. Sady burst into the courtyard on a steaming horse, firing a pistol into the air. Another shot rang out. The horse, familiar with such displays, remained calm. Sady rode in amid flapping chickens, squealing pigs, and bellowing comrades. He grinned, pulled the pistols from their holsters, snapped the locks, and pointed them at a fleeing pig.

“Comin’, mas’r,” he called. “Everybody a-comin’.”

And indeed, they were.

Horsemen approached rapidly. Little Mr. Dempster spurred his pony forward, digging his heels in. Behind him rode a woman in riding habit—on Madam Esmond’s grey mare. Could it be Madam Esmond? No—she was too stout. It was Mrs. Mountain.

“O Lor! O Golly! Hoop! Here dey come! Hurray!” the negroes cried.

Dr. Dempster and Mrs. Mountain clattered into the yard, dismounted, pushed through the crowd, and rushed into the house. They tore through the rooms, burst onto the porch, where the British officers stared in dazed confusion, and hurried down the steps into the garden.

There stood George and Harry, facing their tall opponent. Before George could speak, Mrs. Mountain threw her arms around him.

“Oh, George, my darling! It’s a mistake! A terrible mistake—and it’s all my fault!”

“What mistake?” George asked, stepping back.

“That paper—I found it in his portfolio. The one where he says he’s marrying a widow with two children. Who else could it be but your mother? But it’s not! It’s not your mother at all! It’s Miss Custis—the wealthy widow the Colonel intends to wed. He always chooses rich ones. I knew he would. And he told Madam Esmond just before he left—said the marriage would happen after the campaign. And your mother—she’s furious, boys! When Sady came for the pistols and told the whole house you were going to fight, I told him to fire them off. I galloped after him, nearly broke my bones getting here!”

“I’ve a mind to break Sady’s,” George growled. “I ordered him not to say a word.”

“Thank God he didn’t,” Harry whispered.

“Thank God he didn’t,” echoed George.

“But what will Colonel Washington think?” George muttered, still angry. “That my servant told my mother I was going to duel?”

“You’ve shown your proof,” Harry said gently. “And thank Heaven, you’re not going to fight our old friend—our grandfather’s old friend. It was a mistake. There’s no quarrel now, is there? You acted under a false impression.”

“I certainly did,” George admitted. “But—”

“George! George Washington!” Harry suddenly shouted, springing across the cabbage patch toward the bowling green, where the Colonel stood.

We cannot hear his words, but we see them—the boy’s hands outstretched, his face alight with urgency and love. We imagine the tale spilling forth—of mistaken papers, jealous hearts, and a misunderstanding that could have ended in blood.

And when he finished, something rare happened. In those days, such gestures were common, but they are forgotten now. The Colonel stepped forward, took Harry in his arms, and held him tightly. His voice trembled. “Thank God, thank God for this!”

“Oh, George,” Harry said, tears in his eyes, “how I wish I could go with you on the campaign!”

The Colonel squeezed his hands, a bond forged in trust and shared history. Then he turned to George Warrington, extended his hand, and offered a formal greeting—no embrace, no warmth, only dignity.

“I find I have done you a wrong, Colonel Washington,” George said. “I must apologize—not for the error, but for my behavior since.”

“The error was mine,” Mrs. Mountain interjected. “I found the paper and showed it to George. All women are jealous.”

“Tis a pity you could not have kept your eyes off my private paper, madam,” Washington replied coolly. “A great deal of harm has come because I chose to keep secrets that concerned only myself and another. For a long time, George Warrington’s heart has been black with anger toward me. My feelings toward him have not been much kinder. All this pain might have been avoided had my papers stayed where they belonged.”

He paused. “I shall say no more, lest my emotions betray me again.”

Then, turning to Harry, he said, “Heaven bless thee, Harry.”

To George, he added, “Farewell. And take a true friend’s advice—try not to assume evil in those you call friends.”

“We shall meet again at the camp,” he continued. “And we’ll save our weapons for the enemy.”

With a stately bow to the English officers, the Colonel turned and rode away—swift, silent, and free of burden.

Behind him, the world breathed again.

Let us suppose that the farewell between the brothers has passed, and George now takes his place within Mr. Braddock’s household, while Harry returns to Castlewood, where duty and quiet life await him. Yet though he is home, his heart remains with the army—his true calling, his passion. The tasks of country life offer no joy; they feel like idle shadows compared to the grand purpose of war. He does not admit how deeply he grieves at being bound to this peaceful, homely roof—now heavier with silence than ever since George departed.

Harry walks past his brother’s empty chamber without looking in, avoids the door as if it might betray a wound. At meals, he sits at the head of the table, once occupied by George, and sips his drink from the silver tankard, his eyes distant, his breath slow. Each day, Madam Warrington raises her voice in firm salute: “The King!” And on Sundays, when Harry reads the service aloud, she joins in prayer for all travelers—by land and sea—with an extra weight of solemnity. She speaks of George constantly, cheerfully, confidently—as if his return were certain. She enters his room with her head high, untouched by outward sorrow. His books are arranged neatly, his linen folded with care. She talks of him with reverence, asking the old servants what must be done “when Mr. George comes home,” as though he were already returning through the garden gate.

Mrs. Mountain weeps whenever George’s name is mentioned. Harry’s face grows pale, almost grim, as if he fears some unseen blow. But his mother? She remains calm, composed. She makes more mistakes at piquet and backgammon than one would expect from her, and the servants find her awake and dressed before dawn. She has asked Mr. Dempster to return to live at Castlewood, and though she was once known for her sharpness and pride, she now speaks gently, listens quietly, and responds with soft authority. She often recalls her father—his campaigns, his scars, his survival—and says, “He came out of every battle unbroken, and so I trust my eldest son will.”

George writes frequently. Once the army began its march, he began keeping a rough journal, sending it home when possible. These letters are read with great eagerness by Harry, and more than once, on long summer evenings, the whole household gathers around the tea-table as Harry reads aloud. Madam Esmond sits upright—never leaning back, never yielding to comfort—as little Fanny Mountain sews beside her, and Mr. Dempster and Mrs. Mountain sit over their cards. The old servants move softly in the dim light, listening intently.

Hear now Harry Warrington reading his brother’s words:

“It must be said that the provinces are behaving shamefully toward His Majesty King George II., and his representative here is furious. Virginia is bad enough, Maryland worse, but Pennsylvania is the worst of all. We beg them to send troops from England, promising to support them once they arrive. Yet not only do they fail to keep their word, but they charge exorbitant prices for cattle and supplies—some even cheat the soldiers who have come to defend them. No wonder the General swears, and the men grow restless. Delays have been endless.
