Because the colonies failed to deliver promised provisions or transport, weeks and months have passed—time during which, no doubt, the French have strengthened their positions on our frontier and in the forts they seized from us.

Though I’ve never liked Colonel Washington, I must acknowledge that your favorite (I’m not jealous, Hal) is a brave man and a capable officer. The family respects him greatly, and the General often seeks his counsel. Indeed, he’s nearly the only one who has seen the Indians in full war paint, and I confess I think he was right to fire upon Monsieur Jumonville last year.

There will be no further trouble over that brawl at Benson’s Tavern—not any more than there was over the proposed duel between Colonel W. and a certain young gentleman whose name I’ll omit. Captain Waring wanted to renew the quarrel when he arrived in camp, bringing a message from Captain Grace, whom your friend—brave as Hector—is eager to confront. He even called upon Colonel Wingfield, another aide-de-camp, to stand by him. But when Wingfield learned the truth—that the quarrel began because Grace was drunk, fanned by Waring’s own tipsiness, and that two officers from the 44th had insulted a militia man—he swore Colonel Washington would not fight them. He threatened to report them directly to His Excellency, who would bring both captains before a court-martial for drunkenness, disorderly conduct, and disrespect. They had no choice but to drop their swords and swallow their anger. Out of their cups, they were civil enough, and ate humble pie with good appetites at a reconciliation dinner hosted by Colonel W., where he was as perfectly correct and stiff as Prince Prettyman himself. Hang him! He has no faults—and that’s why I dislike him. When he marries that widow—ah me! What a dreary life she will lead.”

“Now, I wonder at the taste of some men—and the boldness of some women,” says Madam Esmond, setting down her teacup. “What woman, once married, could forget herself so completely as to marry again? Don’t you agree, Mountain?”

“Monstrous!” replies Mrs. Mountain, with a peculiar expression.

Mr. Dempster stares into his glass of punch, silent.

Harry looks as though he is choking—either with laughter or something deeper—but his mother says, “Go on, Harry. Continue with your brother’s journal. He writes well—but ah, will he ever write like my father?”

Harry resumes:

“We maintain strict order in camp. Orders against drunkenness and misconduct are strictly enforced. Rolls are taken three times daily—morning, noon, and night—and reports of absentees or offenders are submitted to the regimental commander, who ensures punishment. Men are disciplined, and the drums are always beating. Oh, Harry, it made me sick to see the first blood drawn from a strong white back, and to hear the pitiful cry of the poor fellow.”

“Oh, dreadful!” cries Madam Esmond. “I’d have killed Ward if he’d flogged me. Thank Heaven I escaped with only a crack of the ruler! The men are cared for well enough. I wish the officers were too. The Indians just broke camp and withdrew in anger—because the young officers were constantly drinking with the squaws—and—well—hum—ha.”

Here Harry pauses, perhaps unwilling to continue in front of little Fanny, who sits primly by her mother’s side, stitching her sampler.

“Skip that part about the disgusting drunkards,” says Madam Esmond. Harry clears his throat and continues, louder now:

“Each regiment holds Divine Service every Sunday under its colors. The General does everything in his power to prevent looting and to encourage locals to bring in supplies. He has declared that any soldier who molests market traders shall be shot. He raised the price of provisions by a penny per pound and lent money from his own pocket to supply the camp. All in all, this General is a strange mix. He flogs his men without mercy, yet gives freely. He swears frightful oaths and tells stories that would shock Mountain—”

“Why me?” asks Mountain. “What do I have to do with the General’s foolish tales?”

“Never mind the stories,” says the mistress of the house. “Just go on, Harry.”

“He tells stories that would shock Mountain after dinner—but never misses church. He adores his Great Duke, and speaks his name constantly. Our two regiments served in Scotland—where I imagine Mr. Dempster knew the color of their facings.”

“We saw the tails of their coats, as well as their facings,” grumbles the Jacobite tutor.

“Colonel Washington has suffered a severe fever and has barely been able to keep up with the march. Shouldn’t he return home and be cared for by his widow? When either of us falls ill, we’re soon friends again. But I can’t forgive him for having wronged him. Good heavens! How I’ve hated him these past months! Oh, Harry, I was furious at the tavern the other day when Mountain interrupted us so quickly. We should have fired a bit of powder between us and cleared the air. But though I don’t love him as you do, I know he’s a good soldier, a decent officer, and a brave, honest man. And I’ll respect him no less for not wanting to be our stepfather.”

“A stepfather indeed!” cries Harry’s mother. “Jealousy and prejudice have driven the poor child mad! Do you truly believe the Marquis of Esmond’s daughter and heiress could not find better stepfathers for her sons than a mere provincial surveyor? If there are any more such remarks in George’s journal, Harry, I beg you skip them.”

“‘Tis a fine sight,” Harry continues, reading from the journal, “to see a long line of redcoats winding through the woods or taking position after the march. Our vigilance against surprise is constant. We dare the Indians to attack us unawares, and our advance scouts and native allies have actually encountered the enemy, taking scalps. These French and their painted allies are cruel villains—we give them no mercy. Just yesterday, we found a small boy scalped but still alive in a lone house, where his parents had been murdered by savage foes. So angry is our General at their brutality that he has offered five pounds for every Indian scalp brought in.”

“When the march ends, you should see our camp—the care taken in its layout. Our baggage and the General’s tents are placed at the center. Outlying sentries are posted in pairs, threes, tens, even entire companies. In case of surprise, they are ordered to rush to the main body and rally around the tents and baggage, which are arranged to form a strong fortress. Sady and I are now marching on foot—my horses carry supplies. The Pennsylvanians sent such poor animals that they quickly gave out. The best horses were given up, and Roxana now carries packs instead of her young master. She knows me well, whinnies when she sees me, and I walk beside her, talking as we go.”

“July 4. To guard against surprise, we are warned to pay close attention to the drumbeat—halting at the long roll, marching at the long march. We are more alert now. Our advanced pickets are doubled, two sentries at each post. Men on picket duty remain armed with fixed bayonets all night, relieved every two hours. Those relieved lie down near their arms but may not leave their posts. It’s clear we are nearing the enemy. This packet goes with the General’s orders to Colonel Dunbar’s camp, thirty miles behind us, then to Frederick, then to my honored mother’s house at Castlewood. I send my duty and kindest regards to all friends there, and much love to my dearest brother—from his affectionate—GEORGE E. WARRINGTON.”

By July, the land lay scorched under the sun. Ten days had passed without news from the army advancing on the Ohio. Though progress through the forest was slow, the troops—led by seasoned officers—were now accustomed to the wilderness and feared no ambush. Precautions were thorough. Scouts and skirmishers had already discovered and destroyed enemy outposts. The latest intelligence said the army had moved far beyond the site of Washington’s defeat the previous year, and within two days would be within a day’s march of the French fort. No one doubted they would take it. The number of French reinforcements from Montreal was known. With two veteran British regiments, plus allies from Virginia and Pennsylvania, Braddock’s force was clearly superior.

This was the talk in the scattered towns of Virginia—at gentlemen’s homes, roadside taverns, wherever people gathered to discuss the war. Messengers sent back by the General reported well. It was believed the enemy would not resist. Had they meant to attack, they could have struck at dozens of points where the British had passed unchallenged.

And George—had he really given up his beloved mare, Roxana, and marched on foot? Madam Esmond vowed he should have the finest horse in Virginia or Carolina. Horses were plentiful, and for money, they could be had. Only for the King’s service were they withheld.

At Castlewood, the family spoke cheerfully at meals, never admitting fear, never doubting victory. Yet privately, they were restless, constantly leaving the house, riding from neighbor to neighbor in search of news. Rumors spread fast. When Colonel Jack, a famed border warrior, offered his hunters to the General—only to be refused—the news of his defection lit a thousand tongues.

The enslaved men, galloping through the countryside at night for pleasure or love, carried whispers across vast distances. They knew the army’s movements for at least two weeks after departure. They laughed at the tricks played on the troops—overcharging for horses, food, and supplies. A bargain over a foreigner was common among New Yorkers, Pennsylvanians, and Marylanders—though in later times, Americans became innocent, fair, and free from greed.

For three weeks, all news was hopeful. At supper, the Castlewood circle spoke with confidence. But on July 10th, darkness fell over the province. Fear touched every face. Negroes looked at their masters with wide eyes, then whispered among themselves. The fiddles stopped. Songs ceased. Servants rode off in haste, seeking news.

Taverns were packed with riders, drinking, cursing, shouting their grim tales. The army had been ambushed. Cut down almost to the last man. Officers were picked off by French marksmen and savages. The General was wounded, carried from the field in his sash. Four days later, the report came: the General was dead—scalped by a French Indian.

Ah! Poor Mrs. Mountain screamed when Gumbo brought the news from across the James River, and little Fanny leapt into her mother’s arms, crying.

“Lord God Almighty, watch over us, and defend my boy!” cried Mrs. Esmond, falling to her knees, hands lifted to heaven.

The gentlemen were away when the rumor reached them, but returned within hours, each from his own hunt for truth. The Scots tutor dared not meet the widow’s agonized gaze. Harry Warrington was as pale as his mother. The manner of the General’s death might be false—but he was dead. The army had been surprised, fled, slaughtered without seeing the enemy.

An express had arrived from Dunbar’s camp. Fugitives were streaming in. Should Harry go? He must go. He and stout little Dempster armed themselves and mounted, taking two servants with them. They followed the trail the expedition had carved through the woods. With every mile, the horror of the battle grew greater.

The day after the defeat, survivors had reached Dunbar’s camp, fifty miles from the battlefield. There, Harry and his companions rode, stopping stragglers, asking for news, giving coin, hearing again and again the same terrible tale: a thousand men slain, two-thirds of the officers dead, all the General’s aides-de-camp hit. Hit? But were they killed? Those who fell did not rise. The tomahawk had done its work.

O brother, brother!

All the memories of youth flooded back—the laughter, the vows, the tender bonds of childhood. Harry’s grief was unbearable. Wounded men looked up and softened at his sorrow. Rough women wept at the sight of his grief. Even the hardened old tutor could scarcely look at him, overwhelmed with tears—for he mourned not only the pupil he loved, but the noble young man who now lay dead beneath the savage blade.

With every mile Harry Warrington traveled toward Pennsylvania, the tales of the British disaster grew darker and more certain. The two famed regiments—veterans of battles in Scotland and across Europe—had fled before an enemy they scarcely saw. Their vaunted discipline and courage had failed them against a scattered force of French soldiers and Native warriors hidden among the trees. The commander of the expedition, though grievously wounded four times and shot from his horse three times, had fought with unyielding bravery. He died three days after the battle, his final wound proving mortal.

Harry heard these stories from various travelers, each adding grim detail to the tale. They spoke of the river crossing, the long march through dense wilderness, the sudden gunfire ahead, the futile attempts to advance, and the artillery’s struggle to clear a path. Then came the ambush—the deadly shots from behind every tree and bush, the relentless fusillade that felled at least half the army. But not all were lost. One of the General’s aides-de-camp, a Virginian gentleman, was said to be ill at Dunbar’s camp. A survivor—though which one?—was all Harry could think.

He rode on without delay, reaching the encampment at last. There, beneath a canvas tent, he found George Washington, pale and weakened by fever. It was not his brother.

A deeper sorrow than illness seized Harry when he saw the officer. “Ah, George!” he cried, voice breaking. “If you truly loved him, you would have brought him back—alive or dead!”

But Washington could not speak of it fully. For three days after the battle, he had been at the General’s side, tending to him as he lay dying. On July 9th, he had seen young George Warrington ride forward with orders from Braddock—orders that sent him into the thick of the fight. He never returned.

After Braddock’s death, Washington had made his way back to the battlefield. The bodies left behind were stripped, mutilated, and ravaged by wild beasts. Among them, he buried one he believed to be George Warrington’s. The grief of that search had worsened his own illness.

“Why did you not bring him back?” Harry demanded again, refusing to accept the silence.

Nothing would satisfy him but to go himself. With money and resolve, he hired guides and crossed the river where the army had passed. He walked the entire length of the battlefield—once a forest now haunted only by carrion birds and decay. The corpses, still under the trees, were festering, torn apart by time and scavengers. Harry had never seen death so brutally revealed. Only once before—when he had seen his grandfather pass peacefully, a soft smile upon his lips—had he witnessed such stillness. Now, this horror turned his stomach and chilled his blood.

What could the empty woods or the rotting remains tell him?

He resolved to go to the French fort, where the victors had retreated. Perhaps they held news. But his guides refused. “The French might spare us,” one warned, “but the Indians will not. Keep your hair for your mother, young sir. She’s already lost one son. Don’t let her lose another.”

So Harry returned to Dunbar’s camp, only to fall ill himself. Fever seized him, followed by delirium. He lay in the same bed where Washington had recovered, watched over by Dempster, who had nursed him through many sicknesses. For days, Harry knew not who stood beside him. Dempster feared the widow would lose both sons. Yet, slowly, the fever broke. Harry regained strength enough to mount his horse.

Mr. Washington and Dempster escorted him home.

It was with heavy hearts that they approached Castlewood. A servant had gone ahead to warn of their arrival. First to meet them was Mrs. Mountain and her daughter, Fanny. She wept and embraced Harry, but barely acknowledged Washington. Then little Fanny stepped forward, hands behind her back, and asked, “Why haven’t you brought George back too?”

Harry did not hear. The sobs and embraces of his nurse drowned out the child’s words.

Dempster was welcomed warmly. “We know you would do anything for us, Mr. Dempster,” Mrs. Mountain said, offering her hand. “Make a curtsey to Mr. Dempster, Fanny. And remember to be grateful to those who helped our family.”

Then she turned to Washington. “Will you take refreshment before you ride, Colonel?”

He declined. “Only water for myself, and a moment to rest my horse. I’ll trouble Castlewood no further.”

“You have your room here, George,” Harry insisted. “Mother is getting it ready!”

“Hush,” Mrs. Mountain whispered. “She won’t see him.”

“Not see George? But he’s like a son of the house!”

“She won’t see him,” the woman repeated firmly. “When the Colonel’s man arrived, Madam Esmond left this room—where she’d been reading Drelincourt—and said she could not face him. Will you go to her?”

Harry took Washington’s arm and excused himself. “I’ll return in a moment.” He hurried up the stairs, avoiding the door to his brother’s room—until Madam Esmond emerged from it, arms around him, leading him inside.

The room was untouched. A settee sat near the bed. A book of psalms lay open on the coverlet. Everything was exactly as George had left it.

“My poor child,” she said, eyes glistening. “How thin you’ve grown! How haggard you look. Never mind. A mother’s care will restore you. You went bravely to find your brother. If others had shown such loyalty, he might still be here. But don’t despair. Our hero will return. I know he is not dead.”

(Perhaps Harry thought to himself that his mother had never spoken of George so tenderly before.)

“Dry your tears, my dear. He will come back. I know it.”

When Harry pressed for proof, she said, “Two nights running, I’ve seen my father in dreams. He told me George is alive—held captive by the Indians.”

Her grief had not broken her; it had hardened her. Her eyes burned with anger, her spirit stirred. Harry was startled by her intensity.

When he begged her to greet Washington, she recoiled. “I cannot touch his hand,” she declared. “He took my son from me. I cannot sleep under the same roof with him.”

“But he gave me his bed when I was sick,” Harry protested. “He was ill himself, thinking only of his friend. Would any other man have done the same?”

“A friend? A fine friend!” she sneered. “Of all the General’s aides, he alone returns unharmed. The brave fall, but he lives. I entrusted my son—my pride—to him, and he leaves him in the woods while he comes home safe! What welcome should I give such a man?”

“No gentleman,” Harry said fiercely, “has ever been refused shelter under my grandfather’s roof.”

“Oh, no—no gentleman!” she retorted. “Come, son. Let us pay our respects to this one.”

And so, with trembling arms, she descended the stairs, entered the parlor, and offered Washington a formal curtsey. She extended her hand—only briefly—then withdrew it.

“I wish our meeting had been happier, Colonel,” she said coldly.

“You grieve no more than I do, madam,” he replied quietly.

“I might have wished this meeting spared,” she continued. “That my boy’s illness hadn’t delayed you. Home, good nursing, and your mother and Doctor Dempster will heal him soon.”

“It was my duty to ride with him,” Washington murmured.

“You’ve endured the campaign with remarkable endurance,” she said, bowing again. “I wish someone else had returned in your place.”

“Your son’s safety is more important than mine,” he said gently.

“And yet,” she insisted, “you must leave soon. My spirits are not fit for company. But your friends may stay. I will nurse Harry upstairs. Mountain, prepare the cedar room for Mr. Washington. Anything in the house is his.”

She turned sharply. “Farewell, sir. Please send my compliments to your mother and to young Martha Custis. Come, my son.”

And with another icy bow, she left, her eyes fixed on Washington as if daring him to speak.

Though Madam Esmond clung to belief, Castlewood remained shrouded in sorrow. She forbade mourning, but her heart wore black. To seek her son was to hope against hope. No confirmed report of his death had come. No one had seen him fall. Yet hundreds had perished unseen, their last moments known only to enemies and dying comrades.

Twelve days after the defeat, Sady, George’s servant, limped back to Castlewood—wounded, disfigured. He could not recount the battle clearly, only that he had fled from the baggage train. He had no news of his master since the morning of the fight. For days, he hid in the slave quarters, afraid to face Madam Esmond’s wrath.

Neighbors whispered she was deluded. Yet her conviction was so strong that even Harry sometimes began to believe. It seemed natural to her that her father, now in the next world, should appear to her in dreams and promise her son’s survival. She believed her instincts had never failed her. When her boys fell ill or faced danger, she always sensed it—before word arrived. She listed half a dozen such instances, all confirmed by her household.

George was not dead. He was a prisoner. He would return. As surely as King George would send reinforcements to reclaim British honor, so would her son return to rule Castlewood.

As for Washington—he would never enter her presence willingly. He had sworn to protect George with his life. Why was her son gone, and he alive? How dared he stand before her?

She claimed she bore no ill will—but as an Esmond, she demanded honor. Washington had forfeited hers. Orders, some argued, bound him. “Psha!” she scoffed. “A promise is a promise. He swore to guard George’s life. Where is my boy? And why is he whole, while George lies lost?”

She mocked the idea that bullets had pierced his coat. “Can’t I fire two shots through this skirt right now?” she laughed. “Would I die? Ha! Death is nothing to me.”

Her laughter was sharp, cruel—a weapon born of grief and pride.

So Harry met Washington in secret—taverns, court-houses, provincial gatherings. No man of honor, she vowed, could meet him after his betrayal.

She raged when she learned they had met. “What heart must you have, Harry, to shake hands with the man I consider George’s murderer?”

“For shame!” she cried. “To forget your noble brother for that tall, awkward colonel with his foul oaths!”

“How can he be George’s murderer?” Harry asked. “You say George is alive.”

“Because my instinct never fails,” she replied. “Because I see him now—though not as noble as he once was. Because my father appeared to me twice in dreams.”

“You doubt that?” she challenged. “It’s because you’ve never loved anyone deeply enough. Only those who love truly can see their loved ones in dreams.”

“I think I loved George,” Harry said softly. “I’ve prayed for dreams of him. But I’ve seen none.”

“How can you talk of loving him, and then meet Washington at horse races?” she snapped. “Can you, Mountain?”

“We understand that our boy is unhappy,” Mrs. Mountain grumbled. “He grows weaker, spends his days at taverns with idle men. This place is not healing him.”

She was right. Grief had turned to division.

“Since that day in July,” Harry confessed later to Madame de Bernstein, “my mother has not been herself. She praised George constantly, yet never seemed to enjoy his presence. She buried herself in books of devotion—books that only deepen sorrow. A darkness fell over Castlewood. We all grew ill, pale as ghosts. Mountain told me she stayed awake for nights. I’ve seen her at my bedside, so gaunt I thought I saw a specter.”

She had driven herself into a state bordering on madness. Harry fell ill again and again. No medicine could cure him. They moved to Richmond, where they hoped for better air. He improved slightly, but not enough. Doctors advised a sea voyage.

At first, she considered joining him. But—

(Here the lad blushed and lowered his head.)

“They did not agree,” he said. “Though we loved each other dearly, we parted ways. So I sailed from the James River, landed at Bristol. And it was only on July 9th this year, at sea, as we had agreed, that I put on mourning for my brother.”

Thus, the mistress of Castlewood, though respected and wealthy, had the gift of making those around her miserable. She quarreled with those she loved most, ruled with jealous pride, until they were glad to leave.

Money, status, a grand house—yet Harry Warrington was glad to escape it all.

Who is truly happy? What good is a feast of roasted ox if one finds no joy in it? Is it better to be loved and tormented, or to live in quiet indifference? To follow one’s desires, undisturbed, and die without sorrow?

When her sons were gone, Madam Esmond forgot their faults. Speaking of them, she painted them as perfect saints—never flawed, never troublesome.

Without them, she turned to Mrs. Mountain and little Fanny, tormenting them in turn. But women endure more easily than men. They forgive—or pretend to. Let us hope the servants found peace, that they returned kindness for cruelty, that quarrels ended with tea and cards.

But without the boys, Castlewood was a hollow shell. She left an overseer to manage the land, visiting only occasionally. In Richmond, she built a new home, expanded it, filled it with guests and preachers, and set herself upon a throne of social influence. The slaves, fond of society, rejoiced in the change.

And so, as Harry Warrington sails onward to Europe, we leave Madam Esmond in her bright city, ruling her little kingdom, surrounded by the comfort she could not find in the solitude of her great house.

When the legendary Trojan wanderer told Queen Dido of his perils and escapes, her heart was captivated by his eloquence and the sorrowful grace with which he recounted his trials. So moved was she that a tale more poignant than any before unfolded—one that would leave her mourning the moment she first listened to that persuasive voice. Harry Warrington lacked Aeneas’s rhetorical power, and his aunt, Madame Bernstein, was far from the sentimental nature of Dido. Yet as the young man spoke—his words simple but sincere, his tone warm and unassuming—she found herself stirred in ways she had long believed impossible. There were few moments of joy in her solitary life, few places where tenderness could take root. But now, with this boy’s presence, something unfamiliar stirred within her: a softness, a longing, an almost painful warmth.

She grew fond of him—not merely for his charm, but for the gentle affection he inspired. It was a feeling she had not known since childhood, and it both startled and delighted her. She watched him closely, her pulse quickening when he entered a room, her cheeks warming at his nearness. Her eyes followed him with quiet admiration. “Ah,” she thought, “if only I had had a son like this—I would have loved him beyond all measure.”

But a voice within her whispered caution. “Wait, Beatrix Esmond. You know better. These feelings will pass. The boy may fade from your memory; he may speak too much, or too little. And you—you will be alone again. That is your fate.”

Yet what if life were indeed a desert? Then even brief oases mattered. Let one enjoy the shade, the water, the fleeting comfort—today. Tomorrow would bring its own burdens, its own march forward. For now, she allowed herself to feel.

As Harry spoke of his mother, Madame Bernstein noticed familiar traits—her manner, her speech, the way she looked upon things. He spoke of his mother’s pride, her jealousy—something she admitted with a touch of shame. “Yes,” he said, “she was jealous. Of Colonel Washington?” “She liked him,” Harry insisted, “but only as a friend. She swore a hundred times she felt nothing else.” And then, with a blush, he confessed, “I once… I was absurdly jealous myself.”

“Then you’ll see,” Madame Bernstein replied softly, “that my half-sister will never forgive him.”

“And don’t be surprised,” she added, “if women are drawn to men younger than themselves. Do I not dote on you? And aren’t these Castlewood folk positively consumed with envy?”

Though there might be murmurs behind closed doors, no ill will showed in the household’s behavior toward their young guest. Within days, Harry Warrington had become “Cousin Harry” to all—youth and adults alike. Especially in Madame Bernstein’s presence, the Countess of Castlewood treated him with particular kindness. In private, she often praised him to the Baroness, marveling at his poise and elegance. “How could such a child from so distant a land learn to carry himself so well?” she would ask.

The Baroness took these compliments with quiet pleasure. (And here, let me pause—though I am but a humble chronicler, I cannot help admiring the subtle art of ladies in conversation. How they praise while they wound! How they smile while they stab! With what delicate precision they drop poison into the cup, hand it around with a grin, and watch the family drink it down—unaware, perhaps, that the sweetness hides a bitter sting.)

“I wonder,” Madame de Bernstein once remarked, “how the boy came to be so refined.”

“His mother,” the Countess replied, “was raised by two truly noble people. Colonel Esmond had a dignified courtesy, a manner rare today.”

“Ah, but we all praise our own time!” countered the Countess. “My grandmother used to say there was nothing like Charles the Second’s court.”

“My mother saw King James the Second’s court briefly,” Madame Bernstein said. “She was not born to it—her father was a country clergyman—but she was exquisitely bred. Colonel Esmond, her second husband, traveled widely, knew the best society in Europe. They did not leave their manners behind in the wilderness. Our boy inherited them naturally.”

“Nay,” the Countess replied gently, “I do not think you’re being fair to your mother. No woman can be perfect who turns cold toward her daughter—as you’ve admitted she did. A complete woman must have a heart. Manners matter, yes, but without affection, all is vanity. I live only for my children—for Willy, though he’s stubborn, and Fanny, though she’s willful. My sweet, dear ones!”

She kissed the bracelets on each arm—miniatures of her children—and sighed. “If they were to die,” she whispered, “I would die too.”

Two Italian greyhounds, Mimi and Fanchon, leapt into her arms, nuzzling her hands but avoiding her rouged cheeks.

“You have a good heart,” said Madame Bernstein. “That is what matters most.”

“Indeed,” the Countess agreed. “And you must share some of it with our American nephew—our cousin—though I’m not sure how he fits into the family.”

“I am but a guest here,” Madame Bernstein replied. “Castlewood belongs to Lord Castlewood. What can I do for the young Virginian that hasn’t already been done? He is charming. Are we jealous of him for it? And though we see how deeply I care for him, do your nephews and nieces protest? Poor children—they may feel slighted. In just hours, this boy has won more favor than they’ve earned in years. But do they resent him? Willy took him riding. This morning, Maria played the harpsichord while Fanny taught him the minuet. Such a lovely scene—it brought tears to my eyes.”

Madame Bernstein, however, had overheard what truly happened during that moment. Lady Castlewood entered the room, boots still dusty from the kennels, her son William beside her.

“Bravi! Bravi!” she exclaimed, clapping. “Charming!” She smiled warmly at Harry, then shot a glance at Fanny that the girl understood perfectly. Maria at the harpsichord played with renewed vigor, nodding her curls over the keys.

“Infernal young Choctaw!” William muttered. “Is he teaching Fanny the war-dance? Is Fan going to show him her tricks now?”

That was what his mother’s look meant.

Fanny made Harry a low curtsey. He blushed, and they stopped dancing, flustered.

“Don’t stop!” the Countess said, sitting at the instrument. “Let me play for you.”

“I don’t know how to dance,” Harry admitted, hanging his head.

“And Fanny was teaching you? Go on, dearest Fanny!”

“Go on!” William growled.

“I’d rather not,” Harry said, regaining composure. “I’d rather not embarrass myself.”

“When you know how,” he added, “I’ll ask my cousin to dance with me.”

“That will be soon, dear Cousin Warrington,” the Countess said, smiling.

“What game is she playing now?” William wondered, unable to fathom his mother’s schemes.

As the Countess called Fanny to her side and left the room, her tone changed completely.

“You booby!” she snapped. “You double idiot! What are you doing with that Huron? You don’t want to marry a creature like that and end up a squaw in a wigwam!”

“Don’t, mamma!” Fanny gasped, as her mother pinched her arm until it turned blue.

“I’m sure he’s very well,” Fanny whimpered. “You said so yourself.”

“Very well? Yes! But heir to a swamp, a negro, a log cabin, and a barrel of tobacco! My Lady Frances Esmond, remember your rank, your name, your mother! At three days’ acquaintance, you’re dancing—with this brat from Virginia?”

“He’s our cousin,” Fanny pleaded.

“A creature from nowhere isn’t your cousin! How do we know he is? He might be a valet who stole his master’s coat and ran off in his carriage.”

“But Madame de Bernstein says he is,” Fanny insisted. “And he looks exactly like the Esmonds.”

“Madame de Bernstein has her favorites. She likes him today—why should she tomorrow? Before company, be civil. But in private, I forbid you to see him or encourage him.”

“I don’t care if you forbid me!” Fanny cried, rising in rebellion.

“Very well,” her mother said coldly. “Then I speak to your father. If I can’t reason with you, your brother will.”

At that point, the conversation ended—or at least, Madame Bernstein’s informant could hear no more. Later, she would tell Harry only part of what she knew. For now, he saw only kindness. Lady Castlewood was polite. The young ladies welcomed him. Lord Castlewood, though reserved, treated him no differently than others. William invited him to ride, race, drink, and play cards. When Harry mentioned leaving, they all urged him to stay.

He did not know that his presence stirred hidden currents—jealousies, ambitions, secrets. He believed he was welcomed because he was kin. He did not suspect that the very people whose hands he shook, whose cups he drank from, might one day turn against him.

The second day after Harry Warrington’s arrival at Castlewood was a Sunday, and the quiet of the estate was broken only by the distant chime of the chapel bell. The chapel, attached to the castle, served as the village church, and a door from the great hall led directly into the family’s private pew—a stately box with carved woodwork and velvet cushions where the Esmonds had sat for generations. As the hour approached, the household gathered in order: my lord at the head, followed by his sister, Madame de Bernstein, the ladies of the house, and the young Virginian cousin, who watched with curiosity as the family took their places.

Below, the villagers filled the pews—men in smockfrocks, women in wide-brimmed hats, children peering over shoulders. A few ancient banners hung from the rafters, dusty and faded, bearing crests long forgotten by all but the most attentive eye. Harry found himself imagining that these had once flown over battlefields during the Civil Wars, carried by loyal retainers of the Esmond name, whose history he had read with pride in the letters of his ancestors.

At the altar rails stood the effigy of Sir Francis Esmond, who had lived in the time of King James I—the common forefather of every person present in the family pew. He knelt eternally on his stone hassock, hands folded upon a prayer book carved from marble, beneath an emblazoned shield of arms. It was a silent sentinel of memory, watching over the living as they knelt.

Madame de Bernstein, widow of a bishop, never missed a service. She conducted her devotions with solemn dignity, her posture and expression so composed that she seemed almost a match for the stone ancestor beside her. The clergyman, Mr. Sampson, was a tall, handsome man with a high colour and a voice full of life. He read the service with such animation that even the Scripture passages sounded like scenes from a play. His tone rose and fell with dramatic effect, and when he reached the psalm, the organ began to swell—played by one of the younger ladies of the house, her fingers dancing lightly over the keys.

But then came a sudden disturbance. From the servants’ pew, a deep, rich voice broke through the harmony—not in tune, yet so powerful and clear that it silenced the choir. It was Gumbo, Mr. Warrington’s African servant, who had recognized the melody and begun to sing it with astonishing volume and sweetness. The whole congregation turned. Even the parson covered his mouth with his handkerchief, and the London gentlemen blinked in astonishment. Gumbo, unaware of the commotion, sang on—his eyes fixed on the book before him, though he could not read a single word. He sang by ear, and with such passion that the clerk’s voice faded into silence. When the music ended, there was a moment of hushed awe, then a ripple of laughter from the back.

After the hymn, the sermon began. Mr. Sampson spoke plainly, without the stiff phrasing Harry had grown used to from the Calvinistic preachers in Virginia. Instead, he told a story—one he had witnessed just the week before: the execution of a horse-stealer at Assizes. He described the man’s life—the decent farmer, the loving wife, the children clinging to him at the cart. He painted the agony of separation, the walk to the gallows, the final moments under the noose. He did not quote scripture; he spoke as a man to men, warning them of the dangers of vice—drinking, gambling, cockfighting, poaching—and how easily a good man might fall.

He made the law seem alive: watching in the dark woods, setting traps, chasing the thief across highways and fields. He galloped the stolen horse through counties, but always behind came Retribution—swift, relentless, unyielding. He acted out the scene: whispering to the criminal, dropping a handkerchief on the clerk’s head. Harry started as if struck.

Twenty minutes passed, but to him it felt like five. The sermon was gripping, vivid, and real. The gentry in the great pew leaned forward, captivated. Harry noticed that the servants, especially Gumbo, sat rigid with attention, as if afraid to breathe. But the villagers paid little mind. Gaffer Brown and Gammer Jones accepted the tale as part of life. The red-cloaked girls under their broad hats remained untouched.

When the sermon ended, my lord nodded slowly to the pulpit. “Sampson has been strong today,” he said. “He has assaulted the Philistines in great force.”

“Beautiful, beautiful!” murmured Harry.

“Bet five to four it was his Assize sermon,” said William. “He’s been over to Winton to preach, and to see those dogs.”

As the organ played the last notes and the congregation filed out into the golden afternoon light, only Sir Francis Esmond remained—still kneeling, still praying, in stone.

Mr. Sampson stepped from his vestry in his cassock and greeted the gentlemen lingering near the pew. “Come up,” called William, “and tell us about those dogs.”

The chaplain smiled and nodded. They moved into the gallery connecting the church to the house, where they joined my lord and Harry. Mr. Sampson was introduced to the Virginian cousin. He bowed deeply, expressing hope that Harry would take inspiration from his English kin.

“Are you related to Sir Miles Warrington of Norfolk?” he asked.

“Yes,” replied Harry. “He was my father’s elder brother.”

“A pity he has a son,” said the chaplain. “A fine estate, and Mr. Warrington looks well suited to inherit it.”

“Tell me about my uncle,” Harry urged.

“Two more jolly dogs, two more drunken dogs, saving your presence, Mr. Warrington, than Sir Miles and his son, I never saw,” said the parson. “Sir Miles was a staunch friend of Sir Robert’s. He can drink down any man in the county—except his own son and a few others.”

“And the other dogs?” asked William, grinning. “For Heaven hath made him a prey to dogs and all kinds of birds, like the Greeks in the Iliad—”

“I know that line,” Harry interrupted, blushing. “I only know five more, but I know that one.” He looked down, thinking: *Ah, my dear brother George knew all the Iliad and the Odyssey—and nearly every book ever written.*

“What on earth are you talking about now?” asked William.

The chaplain returned to the dogs. Then, naturally, they turned to horses.

William was eager about the Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon. “Have you brought any news of it, Parson?”

“The odds are five to four on Brilliant against the field,” said the parson gravely, “but mind you, Jason is a good horse.”

“Whose horse?” asked my lord.

“Duke of Ancaster’s. By Cartouche out of Miss Langley,” replied the divine.

“Do you have horse races in Virginia?” asked the chaplain.

“Haven’t we!” cried Harry. “But oh! I long to see a good English race!”

“Do you… bet a little?” continued the parson.

“I have done such a thing,” Harry replied with a smile.

“I’ll take Brilliant even against the field, for ponies with you, cousin!” shouted William.

“I’ll give or take three to one against Jason!” said the clergyman.

“I don’t bet on horses I don’t know,” said Harry, surprised to hear the parson speak so freely, remembering his sermon just half an hour earlier.

“Hadn’t you better write home and ask your mother?” sneered William.

“Will, Will!” called my lord. “Our cousin Warrington is free to bet or not, as he likes. Have a care how you venture on either of them, Harry. Will is an old file, in spite of his smooth face, and as for Parson Sampson, I defy our ghostly enemy to get the better of him.”

“Him and all his works, my lord!” said Mr. Sampson, bowing.

Harry bristled. “I’ll tell you what, cousin Will,” he said. “I manage my own affairs in my own way. I make my own bets on my own judgment. And I don’t need any relation to choose them for me. But since I’m your guest, and you want to show hospitality, I’ll take your bet—there. And so Done and Done.”

“Done,” said William, glancing sideways.

“Of course it’s the regular odds in the paper you give me?” Harry asked.

“Well, no,” growled William. “The odds are five to four—that’s the fact. You may have ‘em if you like.”

“Nay, cousin,” said Harry firmly, “a bet is a bet. And I take you too, Mr. Sampson.”

“Three to one against Jason. I lay it. Very good,” said the parson.

“Is it to be ponies too, Mr. Chaplain?” asked Harry, puffing out his chest as if he held Lombard Street in his pocket.

“No, no. Thirty to ten. It is enough for a poor priest to win.”

“Here goes a great slice out of my quarter’s hundred,” thought Harry. “Well, I shan’t let these Englishmen think I’m afraid of them. I didn’t start it, but for the honour of Old Virginia, I won’t go back.”

With the betting settled, William scowled and headed toward the stables, where he liked to smoke with the grooms. The parson went off to charm the ladies, while my lord and Harry remained alone.

Since Harry’s arrival, my lord had spoken little. He was courteous, but reserved—often sitting at the head of the table without a word.

“I suppose your property is a fine one by now?” he asked.

“I reckon it’s almost as big as an English county,” answered Harry, proud of his inheritance. “And the land’s as good, too, for many things.”

“Indeed?” said my lord, surprised.

“When it belonged to my father, it did not yield much.”

“Pardon me, my lord,” said Harry sharply. “You know how it belonged to your father. It was because my grandfather chose not to claim his right.” [This matter is discussed in the Author's previous work, The Memoirs of Colonel Esmond.]

“Of course, of course,” said my lord hastily. “We of the Virginian house owe you nothing but our own.”

“And our own,” continued Harry, “and the hospitality you’re showing me.”

“You are heartily welcome to both. Were you hurt by the betting?”

“Well,” said the youth, “I am sort o’ hurt. Your welcome is different from ours. At home, we hold out a hand, give you of our best. Here, you take us in, feed us well, but don’t seem to care when we come or go. That’s what I’ve been thinking—and now I’ve said it.”

With that, he knocked a billiard ball across the table and laughed.

“A la bonne heure!” said my lord. “We are cold to the stranger within and without our gates. We don’t cry when we see our cousin. We don’t cry when he leaves—but do we pretend?”

“No,” said Harry, “you try to get the better of him in a bet.”

“Is there no such practice in Virginia? Do sporting men there not try to outwit each other? What was that story you told Aunt Emily about the British officers and Tom of Spotsylvania?”

“That’s fair,” said Harry. “It’s usual practice. A stranger must look out. I don’t mind the parson—if he wins, he may have it. But a relation! To think my own blood cousin wants money from me!”

“A Newmarket man would get the better of his father,” said my lord. “My brother has been on the turf since he rode from Cambridge. If you play cards with him—he will beat you if he can.”

“Well, I’m ready!” said Harry. “I’ll play any game I know. Or jump. Or ride. Or row. Or wrestle. Or shoot—with him—now.”

The older man smiled and held out his hand.

“Anything, but don’t fight with him,” said my lord.

“If I do, I’ll whip him! Hanged if I don’t!” cried Harry.

But a look of displeasure from my lord brought him to his senses.

“A hundred pardons, my lord!” he said, blushing. “I talked ill-mannered, angry and hurt. But to boast about prowess to my host and kinsman—that’s worse. We Americans don’t boast, believe me.”

“You are the first I’ve ever met,” said my lord, smiling. “And I take you at your word. I give you fair warning about cards and betting—that is all, my boy.”

“Leave a Virginian alone!” said Harry. “We are a match for most men.”

Lord Castlewood did not laugh. His eyebrows arched slightly, and his grey eyes turned downward.

“So you can bet fifty guineas and afford to lose them? So much the better for you, cousin. Do those great Virginian estates yield a great revenue?”

“More than sufficient for all of us—for ten times as many as we are now,” replied Harry. (*“What, he’s pumping me,”* thought the lad.)

“And your mother makes her son and heir a handsome allowance?”

“As much as ever I choose to draw, my lord!”

“Peste! I wish I had such a mother!” exclaimed my lord. “But I have only a stepmother—and she draws me.”

There was a knock at the door—the dinner bell.

“Shall we go?” said my lord, taking Harry’s arm.

In the dining room, Mr. Sampson became the centre of attention. He regaled the ladies with stories from London—whispers from Mayfair, scandals from the clubs, the latest gossip about politicians, lovers, and courtiers. He knew who had run away with whom, the last bon mot of Mr. Selwyn, the wildest bet of March and Rockingham. He spoke of the king’s quarrel with Madame Walmoden, the Duke’s new romance, the Princess of Wales’s favourites, and the hangman’s latest victim—who had behaved nobly in the cart.

The ladies laughed freely, unshocked by his plain talk. Not a blush stirred among them. They listened, enchanted, until the chapel bell rang again for afternoon service.

No sermon this time. The chaplain would return after a bottle of Burgundy.

William called for another, and the chaplain tossed off a glass before rushing out. Half an hour later, he burst back in, shouting for another bottle.

Then they joined the ladies, card tables were set, and the evening unfolded in easy play. Madame de Bernstein was a master at piquet—only the chaplain could match her. The game lasted late. The sun sank behind the elms, rooks cawed their evening song, and still they played.

The clock tolled hour after hour, unnoticed. The moon rose, stars appeared. At nine, the groom announced supper.

As they ate, the postboy’s horn echoed through the village. My lord’s letters arrived. He skimmed them, smiled, and handed the paper to William.

“Read that, Will.”

William read aloud. Then he let out a roar.

“Gracious heavens, William! What has happened?” cried one of the sisters.

“Mercy, child, why do you swear so dreadfully?” asked the mother.

“What’s the matter?” inquired Madame de Bernstein, waking from her punch-induced doze.

“Read it, Parson!” said William, thrusting the paper forward.

“Bit, by the Lord!” roared the chaplain, slamming the paper down.

“My lord read aloud: *‘The Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon was won by Jason, beating Brilliant, Pytho, and Ginger. The odds were five to four on Brilliant against the field, three to one against Jason, seven to two against Pytho, and twenty to one against Ginger.’*

“I owe you a half-year’s income of my poor living, Mr. Warrington,” groaned the parson. “I will pay when my noble patron settles with me.”

“A curse upon the luck!” growled William, reaching for another bumper.

“Nay, cousin Will,” said Harry. “It was but in jest. I can’t think of taking your money.”

“Curse me, sir,” said William, “do you suppose, if I lose, I can’t pay? That I want to be beholden to any man alive? That’s a good joke. Isn’t it, Parson?”

“I think I have heard better,” said the clergyman.

“Hang it,” said William, “let us have another bowl.”

Let us hope the ladies did not wait for it. For certain, they had already had their share.

Our young Virginian, having won a fair sum from his cousin and the chaplain at cards, felt it only right to give them a chance to reclaim their losses. Yet, had his mother or any of the more upright minds in Virginia seen him thus engaged, they might have frowned upon such a way of life. For Harry Warrington played cards far too often—more than was wise, more than was proper. Beyond the daily rounds of whist and quadrille, which began promptly after dinner at three o’clock and continued until supper, there were private games where fortunes changed hands swiftly and dramatically. All the gentlemen—including the Earl himself—joined in these contests. Since their conversation on Sunday, Lord Castlewood had grown more relaxed and open with his kinsman, betting freely and sharing in games of backgammon and piquet. Mr. William and the pious chaplain, though discreet about it, enjoyed a little hazard now and then—though this pastime remained a secret from the ladies, who had repeatedly demanded promises from Cousin Will that he would neither lead the Virginian into mischief nor involve himself in such matters. And so Will gave his word: he would never play—never. But as soon as the household retired for the night, he would slip away with a dice box and a bottle of rum to Cousin Harry’s quarters, where he, Hal, and the reverend gentleman would sit up through the hours, playing until dawn.

When Harry described his mother’s estate in America to Lord Castlewood, he meant no deception. He was not one to boast, nor to fabricate; his nature was honest and straightforward. But truth be told, life in Virginia had exposed him to all manner of rough company—horsemen, tavern idlers, gamblers, and sporting men, many of whom thrived in his native colony. With a landed aristocracy relying on enslaved laborers to cultivate tobacco and corn, entertainment was limited to hunting or games of chance around the punch bowl. Hospitality in the province knew no bounds—every man’s house was open to his neighbor—and idle gentlemen rode from one great mansion to another, finding much the same pleasures, welcomes, and coarse comforts wherever they went. The Virginian squire might ride a cobbled saddle and keep a barefoot valet, but within his ramshackle fences there was always plenty of corn for the horses, venison for the table, and liquor enough to last through the longest night. Harry had slept on straw mattresses more than once, and spent countless nights drinking claret and punch from cracked bowls until the hounds called them out again. His younger brother, by contrast, was sober and reserved—a fact Harry acknowledged with quiet regret. Such is nature’s way: some are drawn to books and tea, others to wine and wild rides across the countryside. It was clear from the start that Harry’s tastes were not those of the Puritan mind. None of his new English companions found fault with him for lacking refinement; indeed, they admired him all the more for not being a milksop. Manners, after all, were looser a century ago—tongues ran free, names were freely spoken, and deeds were done that we today would find shocking. Yes, madam, we are not like our ancestors. Should we not be grateful that time has made us so much more virtuous?

Keenly aware of those around him, and sensing rightly that his cousins sought to probe him, Harry chose to remain cautious about his own affairs. In every game of chance and every contest of sport, he proved himself no less capable than the three men he had come to know. Even in the noble game of billiards, after only a few days, he could hold his own against his cousins and their reverend pastor. His grandfather had loved the game, and had brought over from Europe one of the rare tables in the King’s province of Virginia. Though Mr. Will could best him at first, he could not gain unfair odds. After their initial wager, Harry became more guarded, and Will admitted—though reluctantly—that the American was his equal in most things, and perhaps even superior in some. Yet despite Harry’s skill—so sharp that he could beat the parson and soon match Will, who naturally outplayed both girls—why was it that in matches against the ladies, especially one among them, Mr. Warrington often came off second-best? He was profoundly courteous to every woman who wore a petticoat—an old-fashioned politeness still alive in his homeland. All the women of Castlewood adored the young man. The stern housekeeper softened in his presence; the plump cook greeted him with warm smiles; the maids, whether French or English, giggled and blushed when he passed; even the pretty daughter of the lodge keeper always had a kind word for him. Madame de Bernstein observed all this closely, though she said nothing. She watched the boy’s behavior, noting every nuance of his character.

Who can say how old Lady Maria Esmond truly was? Books of the Peerage were scarce in those days, and I cannot fix her age within a few years, let alone a decade. When Will claimed she was thirty-five, he was exaggerating—though he was known for such excesses. Maria was Will’s half-sister, born of the late Lord Castlewood’s first wife, a German lady whom he married during Queen Anne’s wars. Baron Bernstein, who wedded Maria’s aunt Beatrix—the widow of Bishop Tusher—was also a German nobleman, a Hanoverian relative of the first Lady Castlewood. If Maria was born under George I., and if George II. had reigned thirty years, how could she possibly be twenty-seven, as she told Harry? “I am old, child,” she used to say, calling him “child” when they were alone. “I am a hundred years old. I am twenty-seven. I might almost be your mother.” To which Harry would reply, “Your ladyship might be the mother of all the cupids, I’m sure. You don’t look twenty, on my word you do not!”

Lady Maria looked any age you pleased. Fair of face, with a dazzling complexion of white and red, she had a cascade of golden hair flowing over her shoulders and arms so round and lovely that they drew admiration whenever she played billiards with cousin Harry. When she stretched across the table to take a shot, Harry caught sight of a delicate ankle, a clocked stocking, and a small black satin slipper with a red heel—sights that filled him with unspoken delight. He swore there was no such foot, ankle, or slipper in the world. Yet, foolish boy! Your mother’s foot was slimmer, half an inch shorter than Lady Maria’s. But boys do not gaze upon their mothers’ ankles with such rapture.

No doubt Lady Maria was kind to Harry when they were alone. Before her sister, aunt, or stepmother, however, she mocked him—calling him a simpleton, a chit, and worse. Behind his back, and sometimes even to his face, she imitated his provincial accent, which carried the faintest trace of Virginia. Harry blushed and tried to correct his speech under the guidance of his English tutors. His aunt declared they would soon make him a fine gentleman.

Lord Castlewood, as we’ve said, grew increasingly familiar and friendly with his guest. Until the harvest was complete, there was little sport save occasional cockfights in Winchester and bull-baiting at Hexton Fair. Harry and Will rode together to many jolly fairs and races nearby. The young Virginian was introduced to several county families—the Henleys of the Grange, the Crawleys of Queen’s Crawley, the Redmaynes of Lionsden. Neighbors arrived in their heavy coaches, staying two or three days in country fashion. More would have come, had it not been for the fear the Castlewood family held of offending Madame de Bernstein. She disliked rural society; the rough talk and manners annoyed her. “We shall be merrier when my aunt leaves us,” the young people whispered. “We have cause, as you may imagine, for being very civil to her. You know what a favorite she was with our father? And with reason. She helped secure his earldom, being well connected at Court with the King and Queen. She commands here naturally—perhaps too much. We are all afraid of her. Even my elder brother fears her, and my stepmother obeys her more than she ever did my father, whom she ruled with an iron rod. But Castlewood is merrier when our aunt is not here. At least, we have more company. You will come to us in our gay days, Harry, won’t you? Of course you will: this is your home, sir. I was so pleased—oh, so pleased—when my brother said he considered it your home!”

A soft hand reached out after this tender speech. A pair of bright blue eyes, remarkably preserved, gazed warmly at him. Harry seized his cousin’s hand with eagerness. I cannot say what privileges of kinship he might have wished to claim, except that he was too shy. They call the English selfish and cold. Harry had thought so at first—but how mistaken he was! How kind and affectionate they were, especially the Earl—and dear, dear Maria! He longed to recall the letter he had written to Mrs. Mountain and his mother, in which he hinted that his welcome had been chilly. The Earl, his cousin, was everything kind—promising to introduce him to London society, present him at Court, and take him to White’s. He was to regard Castlewood as his English home. He had been rash in judging his relatives in Hampshire. All this, along with many expressions of remorse, he wrote in his second letter to Virginia. And he added—since it has been noted that the young gentleman did not yet spell with perfect accuracy—“My cousin, the Lady Maria, is a perfect Angle.”

“Ille praeter omnes angulus ridet,” muttered little Mr. Dempster, back in Virginia.

“The child can’t be falling in love with his angle, as he calls her!” exclaimed Mountain.

“Pooh, pooh! My niece Maria is forty!” said Madam Esmond. “I perfectly remember her when I was at home—a tall, awkward, carrot-haired creature, with feet like bellows.” Where, indeed, is truth? And who knows it? Is beauty truly beautiful, or is it only our eyes that make it so? Does Venus squint? Does she have a splay foot, red hair, a crooked back? Anoint my eyes, good Fairy Puck, so that I may always see the Beloved Object as a paragon! Above all, keep anointing my mistress’s dainty peepers with the strongest ointment, so that my head may always appear lovely to her, and she may continue to crown my honest ears with fresh roses!

Not only was Harry Warrington beloved by some in the drawing room and all the ladies of the servants’ hall, but his valet, Gumbo, was equally admired and respected by many in the domestic circle. Gumbo possessed a hundred talents. He was renowned as a fisherman, hunter, and blacksmith. He could style hair beautifully, learning the art under the Earl’s Swiss valet. He excelled in cooking Virginian dishes and picked up new culinary skills from the Earl’s French chef. We have heard how melodiously he sang at church; he sang sacred music as well as secular, often composing rude lyrics in the manner of his people. He played the fiddle so enchantingly that he set all the girls dancing in Castlewood Hall, and was always welcomed with a free mug of ale at the Three Castles inn, provided he brought his instrument. He was good-natured and delighted in playing for village children. Thus, Mr. Warrington’s negro servant was a universal favorite throughout the Castlewood domain.

Yet it was not hard for the servants’ hall to recognize that Mr. Gumbo was a liar—though this flaw did not diminish his charm. For example, at church, when he pretended to read from Molly’s psalm book, he sang entirely different words—words he could not possibly have read, since he could not decipher a single syllable. He claimed to understand music, so the Swiss valet handed him a score, and Master Gumbo turned the page upside down. Such instances of exaggeration occurred daily and were plain to all in the Castlewood household. They knew Gumbo lied, though they did not seem to disapprove—perhaps because they liked to believe him.

Whatever wonder or envy Gumbo may have felt upon seeing the splendor of Castlewood, he kept silent. Instead, he examined the place with cool detachment—the park, the appointments, the stables. The horses, he said, were decent, though there were fewer than at Castlewood in Virginia, where they had six times as many and fourteen or eighteen grooms to care for them. Madam Esmond’s carriages were far finer than the Earl’s—much more gold on the panels. Her gardens covered acres and grew every kind of flower and fruit under the sun. Pineapples and peaches? Those were so common they were fed to pigs in his country. They had twenty or forty gardeners—all black gentlemen, like himself. Inside the house were twenty or forty men in livery, besides countless women-servants—too many to count. “Tink dere were fifty women-servants,” he said. “All Madam Esmond’s property, worth ever so many hundred pieces of eight apiece.” How much was a piece of eight? Bigger than a guinea, he said. “Tink Madam Esmond have twenty or thirty thousand guineas a year—whole rooms full of gold and plate. Came to England in one of her ships—have ever so many ships, Gumbo can’t count how many. And estates, covered all over with tobacco and negroes, reaching out for a week’s journey.” Was Master Harry heir to all this? Of course—he was now, since Master George was killed and scalped by the Indians. Gumbo had killed many Indians and tried to save Master George, but he was Master Harry’s man. And Master Harry was as rich—oh, as rich as he liked. He wore black now because Master George was dead, but you should see his chests full of gold clothes, lace, and jewels at Bristol. Of course, Master Harry was the richest man in Virginia, and might have twenty or sixty servants—though he preferred traveling with just one, and that one, need scarcely be said, was Gumbo.

This tale was not invented at once, but slowly pieced together from Mr. Gumbo, who may have contradicted himself at first. But by the time he had repeated it twice or thrice in the servants’ hall or the butler’s private room, he had mastered his story—knowing exactly how many slaves Madam Esmond owned and how much income she earned. The truth was, four or five blacks could do the work of one white man, so American households employed far more servants than English ones. Like most Virginian landowners, Madam Esmond’s estate teemed with negroes.

Gumbo’s account of his mistress’s wealth reached the Earl through his man, and Madame de Bernstein and the ladies through their waiting-women. And, we may be certain, the story lost nothing in translation. A young gentleman in England is not less liked because he is believed to inherit vast riches. When Lady Castlewood heard of Harry’s enormous expectations, she regretted her initial coldness toward him—and her harsh pinch of her daughter’s arm when Fanny reached out to greet him too warmly. Was it too late to welcome him back into those fair arms? Lady Fanny was invited to try, and resumed her dancing lessons. The Countess offered to play the piano with all her heart. But how irritating that sentimental Maria always insisted on being present! As sure as Fanny walked in the gardens, so sure would her sister follow. As for Madame de Bernstein, she laughed and enjoyed the tales of her Virginian relatives’ immense fortune. She knew her half-sister’s banker in London and likely understood the true state of Madam Esmond’s finances. But she did not deny the rumors—nor did she suppress the amusement she took in watching how the reports affected the family’s treatment of their young kinsman.

“Hang him! Is he so rich, Molly?” asked the Earl of his elder sister. “Then farewell to our chances with your aunt. The Baroness will leave him all her money out of spite, knowing he doesn’t need it. Still, the lad is a good fellow enough. It’s not his fault he’s rich, you know.”

“He is very modest and simple in his habits for one so wealthy,” remarked Maria.

“Rich men often are,” replied the Earl. “If I were rich, I’d be the greatest miser, living in rags and eating bread. There’s no pleasure so lasting as making money. It grows on you, increases with age. But since I’m as poor as Lazarus, I dress in purple and fine linen, and feast every day.”

Maria went to the library and found *The History of Virginia* by R. B. Gent. She read about the province’s excellent climate, its abundance of fruit and grain, and the noble rivers—Potomac and Rappahannock—teeming with fish. She wondered if the climate would suit her, and whether her aunt would approve. And Harry was certain his mother would adore her—as would Mountain. When asked about the number of his mother’s servants, he said they certainly had more than in England—he didn’t know how many. But the negroes did not work as efficiently as English servants, hence the need for so many. As for other details from Gumbo, Harry laughed and said the boy was a wonderful storyteller—probably trying to speak for the honor of the family.

So Harry was modest as well as rich! His denials only strengthened his relatives’ belief in his vast inheritance. The Countess and the ladies grew ever more affectionate toward him. Mr. Will bet with him more frequently and tried to sell him bargains. Harry’s plain clothing and modest equipage only deepened the impression of his wealth. To see a young man of his rank traveling with only one servant, without horses or a carriage of his own—what humility! When he went to London, he would surely cut a better figure. Of course he would. Castlewood would introduce him to the finest society in the capital, and he would appear as he ought at St.7 James’s. No one could be more pleasant, wicked, lively, or attentive than the chaplain, Mr. Sampson. How proud he would be to show his young friend a bit of London life—to warn off rogues and keep him safe from harm! Mr. Sampson was kind; everyone was kind. Harry liked the respect shown him. As Madam Esmond’s son, he thought it perhaps his due. He accepted the image others had of him as the personage they imagined him to be. How could he know otherwise? He had never seen beyond his own province. Why should he not respect his condition when others respected it so highly? So the small circle at Castlewood House, and then the villagers, and finally the whole county, came to believe that Mr. Harry Esmond Warrington was heir to immense wealth and a man of great importance—because his negro valet had told lies in the servants’ hall.

After a fortnight, Harry’s aunt, Madame de Bernstein, began to tire of Castlewood and its inhabitants. This clever woman tired of most things and people sooner or later. She started nodding off during the chaplain’s stories, dozing at whist and over dinner, and speaking sharply to her Esmond nephews and nieces. She launched barbs at the Earl and his brother the jockey, at the widowed and unmarried ladies, who winced under her scornful remarks and endured them as best they could. The cook, once praised, now failed her; the wine was corked; the house was damp, dreary, full of drafts; doors wouldn’t shut, chimneys smoked. She began to think Tunbridge waters essential for her health and ordered the doctor from Hexton to prescribe them.

“I wish to heaven she would go!” growled the Earl, the most independent member of the family. “She may go to Tunbridge, Bath, or Jericho—for me.”

“Shall Fanny and I come with you to Tunbridge, dear Baroness?” asked Lady Castlewood.

“Not for worlds, my dear! The doctor orders absolute quiet. If you came, I’d have the knocker ringing all day, and Fanny’s lovers would never leave the house,” answered the Baroness, thoroughly weary of her sister-in-law’s company.

“I wish I could be of service to my aunt,” said the sentimental Lady Maria, demurely.

“My good child, what can you do for me? You cannot play piquet as well as my maid, and I’ve heard all your songs till I’m tired of them! One of the gentlemen might accompany me—at least make the journey and see me safely from highwaymen.”

“I’m sure I’ll be glad to ride with you,” said Mr. Will.

“Oh, not you! I don’t want you, William,” cried the young man’s aunt. “Why don’t you offer? Where are your American manners, you ungracious Harry Warrington? Don’t swear, Will—Harry is much better company than you are, and much better ton too, sir.”

“Ton, indeed! Confound his ton,” muttered envious Will to himself.

“I dare say I’ll be tired of him, as I am of others,” continued the Baroness. “I’ve hardly seen Harry at all these past days. You shall ride with me to Tunbridge, Harry!”

At this direct appeal—and to no one’s greater surprise than her own—Mr. Harry Warrington blushed, hemmed and hawed, and finally said, “I’ve promised my cousin Castlewood to go to Hexton Petty Sessions with him tomorrow. He thinks I should see how the courts operate here—and—and—the partridge-shooting will soon begin, and I’ve promised to be here for that, ma'am.” Saying this, Harry turned as red as a poppy, while Lady Maria lowered her eyes and busied herself with her needlework.

“You actually refuse to go with me to Tunbridge Wells?” exclaimed Madame Bernstein, her eyes flashing, her face flushing with anger.

“Not to ride with you, ma'am—I’d be honored to do that. But to stay there—I’ve promised…”

Young Harry Warrington’s sudden defiance took Madame de Bernstein entirely by surprise. There was no time for measured response—only a swift, stormy outburst of anger that left her standing in the doorway, eyes blazing, before she swept from the room. Her glance darted first to Lady Fanny, then to her mother, as if searching for complicity. But Lady Maria, absorbed in her embroidery at the tambour-frame, barely stirred. She did not lift her head, nor did she acknowledge the aunt’s departure or the subtle exchange of glances between mother and daughter.

“So,” the maternal gaze seemed to say, “in spite of everything, you have done it?”

“Have what?” asked Lady Fanny’s eyes, wide with feigned innocence. But the expression was too hesitant, too uncertain. If she had been guilty, she would have masked it better—her face carefully composed, her demeanor unflappable. As it was, she looked puzzled, perhaps even a little afraid. Her mother, however, stared at her with such intensity that one might have thought she wished to pluck out those very eyes.

But Lady Castlewood could not act like the monstrous figures in the stage directions of *King Lear*. When she wanted to punish her daughter, she would smile, place an arm around her waist, and later, in private, exact her retribution.

“So you don’t care to accompany the old lady to Tunbridge Wells?” she said, voice cool, face serene, with the practiced grace of someone who knows how to mask intent beneath politeness.

“And small blame to our cousin!” interjected my lord, stepping forward with a calmness that startled his family. (For just a moment, Lady Maria raised her eyes from her needlework.)

“A young man should not spend his days idly chasing pleasures,” he continued. “Let him mix useful pursuits with his amusements. He may visit the pump-rooms and fiddling halls of Tunbridge or Bath later. Mr. Warrington has responsibilities in America—a great estate to manage. Let him see how we conduct ours here in England. Will has already shown him the kennels and stables, the games we play—games, I believe, that he handles as well as any master. After harvest, we shall take him hunting; in winter, we’ll introduce him to English fowling. Though there has been some distance between us and our kinswoman in Virginia, we share blood. Before sending our cousin back to his mother, let us show him what life is like for an English gentleman at home. I would like to read with him as much as I would hunt with him—that is why I’ve urged him to stay, to be near me.”

He spoke with such open sincerity that his mother-in-law, half-brother, and sister could not help but wonder at his true intention. These three often conspired together, whispering grievances against the head of the house. When he adopted this tone, they never knew what lay beneath. He did not say, “This is true,” but rather, “This is what I wish my family to accept.” And so it became accepted: Lord Castlewood had a noble desire to foster domestic affection, to educate and guide his young relative. He had taken a genuine liking to the boy and wished him to remain nearby.

“What is Castlewood up to now?” William whispered to his mother and sister as they retreated into the corridor.

“Stop! By George, I’ve got it!” he exclaimed.

“What, William?” asked his sister.

“He wants to get him playing—and win back the Virginia estate from him. That’s it!”

“But the lad doesn’t own the estate yet,” pointed out their mother. “He can’t lose what he hasn’t got.”

“If my brother isn’t hatching some scheme, may I be—” she began, then stopped herself.

“Hush! Of course he has a plan. But what is it?”

“He can’t mean Maria,” mused William. “She’s older than Harry’s mother.”

“Pooh! With her faded hair, freckled skin, and ancient face? Impossible!” Lady Fanny declared, though her voice held a hint of sigh.

“Of course your ladyship fancied the Iroquois too!” snapped their mother.

“I trust I know my station and duty better than that, madam! If I had liked him, it wouldn’t mean I’d marry him. You taught me that much.”

“My Lady Fanny!”

“I’m certain you married our father without loving him. You’ve told me so a thousand times!”

“And if you didn’t love him before marriage, you certainly didn’t fall in love afterward,” Mr. William broke in, laughing. “Fan and I remember how our parents used to quarrel. Don’t we, Fan? And poor Esmond kept peace between them.”

“Don’t bring up those dreadful scenes, William!” cried their mother. “When your father drank too much, he became a raving madman. His behavior should serve as a warning to you, sir, who seem fond of the same disgusting habit.”

“I’m sure, madam, you weren’t much happier marrying a man you didn’t like. And your title has brought us very little,” Lady Fanny muttered.

“What use is a coronet when your jointure is no better than a tradesman’s wife? How many women in London are richer than we are? Just look at the grocer’s widow who moved into our square at Kensington—she has three gowns where I have one. And though she’s waited on by only a man and two maids, I know she eats and drinks far better than we do, with our scraps of cold meat and our grand, lazy, impudent footmen!”

“He! he! Glad I dine at the palace, not at home!” chuckled Mr. Will. (He owed his minor Court position—Deputy Powder—to his aunt’s influence with Count Puffendorff, Groom of the Royal {and Serene Electoral} Powder-Closet.)

“Why shouldn’t I be happy without any title but my own?” Lady Frances went on. “Many people are. Perhaps even happy in America.”

“Yes—surrounded by a mother-in-law who’s a perfect Turk and Tartar, Indian war-whoops echoing all around, and the constant danger of losing your scalp or being devoured by a bear every time you go to church.”

“I wouldn’t go to church,” said Lady Fanny.

“You’d go with anyone who asked you, Fan!” roared William. “And so would old Maria. And so would any woman, that’s the truth.” He laughed at his own wit.

“Pray, good folks, what is all this merriment about?” asked Madame de Bernstein, peering through the tapestried door into the gallery where the conversation had taken place.

William explained that his mother and sister had been arguing—nothing new, as his aunt well knew—because Fanny wanted to marry their cousin, the wild Virginian, and the Countess refused.

Fanny protested. Since the day her mother forbade her to speak to the young man, she had scarcely exchanged two words with him. She knew her place. She didn’t want to be scalped by Indians or eaten by bears.

Madame de Bernstein frowned. “If he’s not staying for you, then whom is he staying for?”

“At every house he’s visited, you’ve made sure to show him only women who are either frights or in the nursery. And I think the boy is too proud to fall in love with a dairymaid,” said William.

“Humph. Taste is taste, ma'am,” replied William, shrugging.

“Of Mr. William Esmond’s taste, perhaps—but not of that boy’s. The Esmonds of his grandfather’s upbringing would not court in the kitchen.”

“Well, every man to his taste,” William retorted. “A fellow might go farther and fare worse than my brother’s servants’ hall. Besides Fan, there’s only the maids—or old Maria.”

“Maria? Impossible!”

Yet as soon as the word left her lips, a thought struck Madame de Bernstein: perhaps this elderly Calypso had captured her young Telemachus after all. She recalled half a dozen cases from her own experience where young men had become infatuated with older women. She remembered Harry Warrington’s frequent absences—absences she had dismissed as mere sport. And how often, when he was gone, so was Maria Esmond.

Walks in shaded alleys, whispers behind clipped hedges, fleeting handclasps in dim corridors, secret glances on staircases—her imagination, seasoned by years of worldly observation, conjured these possibilities just as she declared them impossible.

“Impossible, ma'am! I don’t know,” William persisted. “My mother warned Fanny off him.”

“Oh, your mother warned Fanny?” the Baroness asked.

“Certainly, my dear Baroness!”

“Didn’t she? Didn’t she pinch Fanny’s arm black-and-blue? Didn’t they fight about it?”

“Nonsense, William! For shame!” both ladies cried at once.

“And now, since we’ve heard how rich he is, perhaps it’s sour grapes,” Madame de Bernstein mused. “Now that he’s been warned off the young bird, maybe he’s hunting the old one. Why impossible? You know old Lady Suffolk, ma'am?”

“William, how can you speak of Lady Suffolk to your aunt?”

A grin crossed William’s face. “Because Lady Suffolk was a favorite at Court? Well, others have succeeded her.”

“Sir!” Madame de Bernstein said sharply.

“So they have,” William insisted. “Who, pray, is my Lady Yarmouth now? And didn’t old Lady Suffolk fall in love with George Berkeley and marry him when she was quite old? Nay, ma'am, if I recall correctly—though we hear plenty of gossip at our table—Harry Estridge went mad for you when you were nearing twenty, and would have changed your name a third time if you’d let him.”

This mention of a past affair—well-known in society—did not provoke anger, as the earlier remark about her favor at King George II’s court had. Instead, it warmed her mood.
