“Au fait,” she said, tapping lightly on the table, her mind drifting to the reckless young Harry Estridge. “It’s not impossible, William, that both young and old might play the fool.”

“But I still can’t understand a young man falling for Maria,” William said. “Though he might for you, ma'am. That’s another matter, as our French tutor used to say. You remember the Count, ma'am? He—he!—and so does Maria!”

“William!”

“And I dare say the Count remembers the bastinado Castlewood gave him. A confounded French dancing-master, calling himself a count, daring to fall in love in our family! Whenever I want to make myself especially agreeable to old Maria, I just speak a few words of *parly voo* to her. She knows exactly what I mean.”

“Have you spoken ill of her to your cousin, Harry Warrington?” Madame de Bernstein asked.

“Well—I know she’s always abusing me—and I’ve said my piece about her,” William admitted.

“Oh, you idiot!” the old lady exclaimed. “Who but a fool ever speaks ill of a woman to her sweetheart? He’ll tell her everything, and they’ll both hate you.”

“The very thing, ma'am!” William burst out, laughing. “I had a suspicion, you see. Two days ago, riding together, I told Harry Warrington my thoughts about Maria. Why shouldn’t I? She’s always criticizing me, isn’t she, Fan? And your favorite turned as red as my plush waistcoat—shocked that a gentleman could slander his own flesh and blood. He trembled with rage and called me no true Esmond.”

“Why didn’t you chastise him, sir, as my lord did the dancing-master?” Lady Castlewood demanded.

“Well, mother—you see, in quarter-staff, two sticks are used,” William replied. “And my opinion is that Harry Warrington can defend himself quite well. Perhaps that’s why I didn’t offer him a beating. And now you mention it, I know he told Maria. She’s been glaring at me like battle, murder, and sudden death ever since. Which proves—”

He turned to his aunt.

“Proves what?”

“That I think we’re on the right scent. We’ve found Maria—the old fox!” And with that, the ingenuous youth clapped his hand to his mouth and gave a loud halloo.

How far had the intrigue gone? That was the question.

Mr. Will believed that at her age, Maria would move swiftly—time was short. There was little affection between William and his half-sister.

“Who will investigate thoroughly?” Madame de Bernstein mused. “Scolding won’t help. Threats only inflame. I’ve only been in danger once in my life, young people,” she said, “and I believe it was because my poor mother contradicted me. If this boy is like others of his family, the more we oppose him, the deeper he’ll become entangled. We’ll never pull him out.”

“Faith, ma'am, suppose we leave him in it?” grumbled William.

“Old Maria and I don’t love each other much,” he admitted, “but an English earl’s daughter is good enough for an American tobacco-planter, all things considered.”

His mother and sister objected loudly. They would not hear of such a match.

“Then why grudge him to Maria?” William retorted. “I think Castlewood wants her to have him.”

“Why grudge him to Maria, sir?” Madame de Bernstein asked, her voice sharp with emotion. “Do you remember who the boy is? What your family owes to his? His grandfather was your father’s closest friend, the man who gave up this estate, this title, this very castle—so you and yours might benefit. And the reward? You shut the door on the child when he knocks, and talk of marrying him to an elderly woman who might be his mother! He shan’t marry her.”

“The very thing we were thinking, my dear Baroness!” Lady Castlewood interjected. “Our branch of the family isn’t eager for the match, though my lord and Maria may be.”

“You would like him for yourself now that you know he’s rich,” Madame Beatrix snapped, turning on the women. “Mr. Warrington may be wealthy, madam, but there’s no need to remind us constantly that we are poor.”

Lady Castlewood responded with spirit. “At least there’s little difference in Fanny’s age and Mr. Harry’s. And surely you won’t claim that a lady of our name and breeding isn’t good enough for any gentleman born in Virginia or elsewhere.”

“Let Fanny take an English gentleman, Countess,” Madame de Bernstein replied. “Not an American. With her looks, accomplishments, and your support, she cannot fail to find a worthy match. But from what I know of your daughters—and what I suspect of our young cousin—I’m certain no happy union could result.”

“What does my aunt know about me?” Lady Fanny asked, flushing.

“Only your temper, my dear. I don’t believe all the idle gossip one hears in town. But temperament and upbringing speak volumes. Imagine one of you banished from St. James’s and the Mall, forced to live in a plantation surrounded by savages! You’d die of boredom—or drive your husband mad with your ill-humor. You were born to adorn courts—not wigwams. Let this boy return to his wilderness with a wife suited to him.”

The other two ladies declared in unison that, for their part, they desired no better fate. After a few more words, they departed, while Madame de Bernstein lifted the tapestry and retired to her chamber.

Now she saw the full design. She admired the ways of women, recalling a dozen small signs she had overlooked. She wondered at her own blindness. How far had the affair progressed? Was Harry’s passion deep and serious, or merely a fleeting flame? How deeply was he involved?

She feared the strength of Harry’s feelings—and the desperation of Maria’s. A woman of her age, she thought, might do anything to secure love. Scandal? Bah. She could retire to Virginia and become a princess, letting England chatter as it pleased.

Was there always something women withheld from one another? Something they agreed to conceal—not from deceit, but from modesty?

Men, as soon as they feel an inclination, seek a friend to share the joy. Women, with greater skill, bury their secrets. For weeks, had not Maria made fools of everyone—Maria, the family joke?

I refrain from probing too deeply into Lady Maria’s past. But I have my own opinions about Madame de Bernstein’s.

A hundred years ago, the world was less rigid. People were not all pure, moral, modest. Skeletons existed in closets. Schemes were hatched. Old stories were buried. Girls sold themselves for wealth. Mothers helped them.

Suppose Lady Maria tries to play her game—what then? Where is her eccentricity?

On these matters, no doubt, the Baroness pondered long and hard in the quiet of her private room.

As Lady Castlewood and her children passed through one door of the drawing-room, Lord Castlewood withdrew by another. Then, from beneath the delicate lace of her tambour frame, where she had been quietly stitching violets and jonquils, Lady Maria lifted her eyes—soft, steady, and full of quiet observation—to where Harry Warrington stood before an ancestral portrait, framed in the shadow of the great fireplace.

He was a sight to behold: flushed, trembling, his cheeks like rosebuds, his forehead glowing, even his ears tinged with crimson. A storm of emotion seemed to have gathered within him, and now it burst forth.

“Why did you refuse to go with our aunt, cousin?” she asked, her voice gentle but probing.

“Because your ladyship bid me stay,” he replied, his voice low but firm.

“I bid you stay? La, child! What one says in jest, you take as law! Are all Virginian gentlemen so dutiful that they believe every word a lady utters is a command? If so, Virginia must be a most delightful land for women!”

Harry’s breath caught. “You said—when we walked on the terrace two nights past—O heaven!” he cried, his voice breaking.

Ah, that sweet night!” murmured Maria, a softness coming into her gaze.

“When you gave me this rose from your own neck,” he blurted out, pulling a crumpled, withered bloom from his waistcoat pocket, “a rose I will never part with—no, by heavens, while this heart beats!”

“You said,” he went on, his voice rising, “‘Harry, if your aunt asks you to go, you will go—and if you go, you will forget me.’ Did you not say so?”

“All men forget,” sighed Maria, her tone distant, almost melancholy.

“In this cold, selfish country, perhaps,” Harry answered, his passion undimmed, “but not in ours. I would have lost an arm rather than deny the old lady. It tore my heart to say no—she has been so kind to me, so generous. But when she introduced me to—O heaven!” He kicked at a spaniel that had wandered too near the fire, sending it yelping away, then stepped forward toward her.

“Look here, cousin—if you bade me leap from that window, I would do it. If you asked me to commit murder, I would do it.”

“La! You need not squeeze my hand so tightly, you silly boy!” she said, though her pulse quickened beneath his grasp.

“I can’t help it—we are so different in the South. Where my heart lies, I cannot keep my tongue still. And you know where that heart is.” He paused, breathing hard. “Ever since that evening—since that moment—I’ve scarcely slept. I want to do something great, to distinguish myself, to become worthy of you. I wish there were giants in the world, as in the books I read, so I could fight them. I wish you were in danger, so I might save you. I wish you needed my blood—then I would give every drop. And when you told me not to go with Madame Bernstein…”

“I never told you such a thing,” she interrupted, her voice sharp.

“You did,” he insisted. “You said you knew I preferred my aunt to my cousin. And I said then, as I say now: ‘Incomparable Maria! I prefer you above all women and all angels in Paradise. I would go to dungeons, to death itself, if you commanded it!’ And do you think I would not stay anywhere—anywhere—so long as you wished me near?”

“Men always talk like that,” she said, hesitating, then correcting herself. “That is… I’ve heard so. What should a woman from the country know about such creatures? When you’re near us, you burn with promises and rapture; when you’re gone, you forget us entirely.”

“But I don’t want to go away,” he groaned. “I’ve grown tired of many things—books, I never cared for study much; games and sports I once loved, but no longer. Before I saw you, I dreamed only of being a soldier. I raged when my dear brother took my place on that ill-fated expedition—when we lost him. But now… now I care for nothing but one thing. And you know what that is.”

“You silly boy!” she said, half laughing, half chiding. “Don’t you know I am nearly old enough to be…”

“I know,” he cut in, “but what does that matter to me? Hasn’t your brother—or someone—told me tales against you? Didn’t they show me the Family Bible, with all your names and dates inscribed?”

“The cowards!” Maria exclaimed, her face flushing. “Who did that? Was it my mother-in-law—the grasping, odious, brazen harpy? Do you know all about her? How she married my father in his cups—the horrid hussy! And…”

“It wasn’t Lady Castlewood,” Harry interjected, bewildered.

“Then it was my aunt,” she continued, her voice rising. “A pretty moralist, indeed! A bishop’s widow, they say—but whose widow before and after? She intrigued with the Pretender, with the Hanoverian Court, and I dare say would have plotted with Rome or the Sultan of Turkey if she’d had the means. Do you know who her second husband was? A creature who…”

“Our aunt never spoke a word against you,” Harry broke in, more amazed than ever by her sudden fury.

She faltered. In his wide, earnest eyes, she saw alarm—not admiration. Her temper cooled.

“Well, well,” she said softly, “I am a fool. I only want you to think well of me, Harry.”

Her hand reached out, and without thought, he seized it, pressing it to his lips.

“Angel,” he whispered, gazing into her face with eyes that burned like stars. The warmth of her presence lit him from within. Two fish-pools under moonlight could not glow more brightly than those blue eyes, into which he looked as if seeking heaven itself. Yet, like the foolish dog who sees his own bone reflected in water and leaps in, losing the real one, he drowned himself in illusion. The surface was calm, but beneath lay depths—hidden currents, secrets, treasures dropped and forgotten.

What lies beneath some quiet faces? What golden dishes, what jewels of love, what bones and flesh have we cast into these still waters? And how many faithful dogs—how many hearts—have jumped in whole, only to be swallowed up?

When a woman is dragged down, what marvels may be found in her depths? *Cavete, canes!* Beware how you drink that water. What do they want of us, these siren sluts? A green-eyed Naiad sings, dances, winds around, whispers secrets, kisses feet, leers from the rushes—“Come, sweet youth! Hither, rosy Hylas!” Pop goes Hylas.

Surely the fable repeats itself endlessly.

Did the Siren enjoy her prey? Did she care for the man she lured? No more than a fisherman at Brighton cares for one herring among ten thousand.

Ulysses rowed past their shore, deaf and blind—he and his men. Young Telemachus wanted to jump overboard, but the tough old crew held him fast. They could not hear the song, nor see the beauty. The witches were stale, leering, old. Away with them!

I dare say they paint their cheeks by now. Their songs are as outdated as Mozart. Their hair is false. But Harry Warrington does not see that. To him, the song is fresh, the voice pure. He hears no warning.

And yet—Brother Boatswain, do you remember how lovely the opera was the first time we heard it? *Cosi fan tutti*—Mozart’s music. Now, they sing it again, with new words, new singers, new crowds. Still, it remains on the bills. Men and women with any sense, or experience, or who’ve read a novel, must know—when Harry pulled out that faded rose just now—that the story is familiar.

We all fall into the same patterns. A pair of lovers whisper in a garden alley, or glance across a room—Jenny to Jessamy—and we muse on the past. These things follow each other by a natural law, not older than the hills, but older than the people walking upon them.

When a young man pulls a decayed flower from his breast and kisses it—what more is there to say? As well tell the gardener’s name, the watering, the pruning, the soil—than explain how Harry came by it.

The rose lived its life—planted, watered, potted, pruned, bloomed, given, transferred to a boy’s pocket. It followed the fate of all roses. And why did Maria give it to him? Why did he treasure it so fiercely?

Is one story less stale than another? Are they not all alike? What good is there in retelling them?

Harry valued that rose because Maria looked at him with old eyes, met him in the garden in the old way, took his hand, whispered behind the old curtain (the ragged one, everyone could see through!), walked early in the park on a fine morning, visited Goody Jenkins with her jelly, and—of course—someone had to carry the basket.

Whole chapters might be written about such details. But *à quoi bon?*

Love-making, especially, repeats itself. I wonder, dear readers, why you still read novels.

Psha! That rose in Harry’s pocket had grown, budded, bloomed, and now rotted—like all others. You’ll want me to say he kissed it? Of course he did. What are lips for, if not to smile, to kiss, to humbug, to eat mutton-chops and cigars?

But I cannot write this part of the story. Harry never dared write it home. His letters to Maria—written, no doubt, since they were in the same house—were destroyed. Later, he remained silent. And we cannot ask her—she never told the truth about anything.

So again—*cui bono?* What good is it?

Take your story, gentle reader. Take mine. Tomorrow it will be Miss Fanny’s, walking off with her doll to the schoolroom. Next day, it will be Baby’s, screaming for his bottle.

Maria might have liked to rule Harry’s heart—but she didn’t want him to quarrel with his aunt for her sake, nor anger Madame de Bernstein. Harry was not yet Lord of Virginia—he was only the Prince. The Queen might marry, bear other princes, and primogeniture might not hold in Virginia. What did she know?

Lord Castlewood and his sister had exchanged no words about the matter. Yet they understood each other perfectly. The Earl had known Maria all her life—her ways, her tricks, her faults—through years spent in her company. He guided her schemes silently, without speech.

Three days earlier, as she walked to visit poor Goody Jenkins, ill with a sore knee, Harry happened to be strolling beneath the elms. Lord Castlewood, with his dogs and gardener, crossed the courtyard just then. He called to his sister.

“Molly, you’re going to see Goody Jenkins. A charitable soul, my dear. Give her this half-crown for me—unless Cousin Warrington has already done so. A pleasant walk to you. Let her want for nothing.”

At supper, he questioned Harry about poverty in Virginia, the care of the poor. Harry answered wisely. The Earl wished England had fewer poor than America. He advised Harry to visit all classes—farmers, artisans, city folk—to learn agriculture, trade, institutions. Harry nodded modestly. Madame Bernstein approved, nodding over her piquet game with the chaplain.

The next day, Harry sat in the Earl’s justice room. The day after, he rode with him across the estate. On their return, the Earl stopped to visit a sick tenant. Lady Maria was out that day, reading to Goody Jenkins—though Madame Bernstein likely never asked about her niece.

---

At first, I did not care for Castlewood, nor my cousins. Now, I grow accustomed. We understand each other better. With my duty to my mother, please tell her that, considering Lady Castlewood’s kindness, Madam Esmond may be reconciled to her half-sister, the Baroness de Bernstein. The Baroness was my grandmother’s daughter by her first husband, Lord Castlewood (though Grandpapa was the true lord). But that was not his fault, and he was kind to Grandpapa, who always spoke of him kindly.

Madame de Bernstein first married Reverend Mr. Tusher, a learned and good man, beloved by His Majesty—as was my aunt. He became a bishop. After his death, the King honored her, and she married a Hanoverian nobleman, holding office at Court. I believe she left him very rich. My cousin, Lord Castlewood, told me this. I have found her most kind and affectionate.

Lady Castlewood, Will, and Fanny have been described in my last letter, sent by the Falmouth packet on the 20th. The ladies remain unchanged. Will and I are close friends. We ride often. We’ve had excellent cockfights at Hampton and Winton. My cousin is sharp, but I think I’ve shown him that Virginians know their sport.

Reverend Mr. Sampson, the family chaplain, is an excellent preacher—without pretension.

My cousin the Earl grows ever more dear. By next year’s ship, I hope my mother sends him some of our best tobacco and hams. He is most charitable to the poor. So is his sister, Lady Maria. She spends hours reading good books to the sick. She is beloved in the village.

“Nonsense!” said a lady to whom Harry showed his letter. “Why flatter me, cousin?”

“You are beloved in the village—and beyond,” Harry replied, with a knowing glance. “And I’ve flattered you a little more, further on.”

“There is a sick old woman there, whom Madam Esmond would like—a most religious, good old lady. Lady Maria visits her often. It gives her comfort, she says. But though her voice is sweet—both speaking and singing—she plays the organ beautifully—I doubt Gammer Jenkins gains comfort from it. She is very deaf, due to age. But her memory is perfect. She remembers when my honored Grandmother Rachel, Lady Castlewood, lived here. She says my grandmother was the best woman in the world—gave her a cow when she married, cured Gaffer Jenkins of the colics—likely with the Pills and Drops my mother packed in my boxes when I left Virginia. I’ve never been ill since—no use for the pills. Gumbo has, eating and drinking too much in the servants’ hall.

The next angel to my grandmother,” she adds, “Gammer Jenkins says, is Lady Maria. She sends her duty to her Aunt in Virginia, remembers my Grandpapa and Grandmamma when they were in Europe, and she was a child. You know they have Grandpapa’s portrait here. I live in the rooms he occupied—rooms that are to be mine, my Lord Castlewood says.”

Having no more to say, I close with best love and duty to my honored mother, respects to Mr. Dempster, a kiss for Fanny, kind remembrances to Old Gumbo, Nathan, Old and Young Dinah, the pointer dog and Slut, and all friends, from their well-wisher,

“I have written and sent my duty to my Uncle Warrington in Norfolk. No answer yet.”

“I hope the spelling is right, cousin?” Harry asked, showing the letter to Lady Maria.

“Quite well enough for any person of fashion,” she replied, avoiding closer scrutiny.

“One word—‘angel’—I know I spelled wrong in my letter to my mother. But I’ve learned how to spell it right now.”

“And how is that, sir?”

“I think it’s by looking at you, cousin,” he said, bowing low, adding one of his finest blushes—as if offering both a bow and a bouquet.

At the next meal, the household gathered as usual, but there was no trace of the morning’s storm in Madame de Bernstein’s demeanor. Her face beamed with warmth, and her manner toward every guest—especially Harry—was gracious and affectionate. She praised the cook, declaring the fricassee divine, and insisted that no eels compared to those in Castlewood’s moats. When someone suggested the wine might be corked, she laughed it off, refusing to allow a fresh bottle for “a useless old woman” like herself. Instead, she raised her glass to Madam Esmond Warrington of Virginia, hoping Harry had secured his mother’s blessing to bring back an English bride.

Harry, though he could not recall his grandmother, found himself drawn into the Baroness’s tender recollections of her own dear mother—the beauty, kindness, and joy she’d known in her second marriage, despite the age difference between her and Colonel Esmond. “To see them together,” she mused, “was a sight to warm the heart. Their love was spoken of throughout the land. What matter if one is older than the other? Such devotion makes all differences vanish.”

My Lady Castlewood and her children remained silent, listening politely as the Baroness continued her charming reminiscences. Harry, captivated, felt his heart swell with admiration. Maria, beside him, looked on with quiet surprise. Lord Castlewood, meanwhile, could only wonder what sudden whim had transformed his aunt so completely—but he masked his curiosity with a serene expression, as though everything were perfectly natural.

The Baroness’s good humor spread through the room like sunlight. Not a single person at table escaped a kind word or a gentle jest. When Mr. Will, ever sincere, voiced his astonishment at her change of mood, she smiled and said, “Complimentary, my dear? Of course I am. I’m making amends for being dreadfully rude this morning. When I was a child, and my parents lived here, I used to behave just the same. If I’d been naughty during the day, I’d try to win them over at night. I remember sitting right here, at this very table—oh, centuries ago!—pleading with my father, my mother, and your grandfather, Harry Warrington. And there were eels for supper, just as tonight. That dish brought it all back. I was just as stubborn then, at seven, as I am now, at seventy. So I confess my sins and beg forgiveness, like a good girl.”

“I absolve your ladyship!” declared the chaplain, who sat among them.

“But you don’t know how cross I was,” she continued. “I scolded my sister, Castlewood. I scolded her children. I even boxed Harry Warrington’s ears—because he refused to go with me to Tunbridge Wells.”

“Then I shall go, madam,” said Mr. Warrington promptly. “With the greatest pleasure.”

“You see, Mr. Chaplain,” she added, “they are all so dutiful. Only I was unkind. Oh, how cruel I was to treat them so! Maria, I ask your pardon, my dear.”

“Surely, madam,” replied Maria, “you’ve done me no harm.”

“Indeed, I have—great harm,” the Baroness insisted. “Because I was weary of myself, I told you your company would be tedious. You offered to come, and I refused you rudely.”

“Nay, ma'am,” Maria said gently, “if you were unwell, and my presence troubled you…”

“But it will not trouble me now,” the Baroness interrupted. “You were kind to offer. I beg, I pray, I implore you—come with me.”

Lord Castlewood sipped his wine, his face calm and unreadable. The truth dawned upon him: this sudden affection was no mere whim—it was a plan. A maneuver.

“Anything that pleases my aunt,” said Maria, striving to appear cheerful, “will surely delight me.”

“You must stay with me, my dear,” the Baroness urged. “And I promise to be sweet and pleasant. My lord, will you spare your sister to me?”

“Lady Maria is of age,” his lordship replied with a bow. “She may judge for herself.”

“If any of us can serve you, madam,” he added, “you ought to command us.”
Which, in plain speech, meant: *Curse the old woman—she’s stealing Maria away from this Virginian boy.*

“Oh, Tunbridge will be delightful!” sighed Lady Maria.

“Mr. Sampson will arrange everything,” said my lord.

Harry traced patterns on the table with his finger. His mind swam with visions—long walks beneath ancient trees, rides through sun-dappled lanes, whispered conversations under moonlit skies, music shared in secret corners, stolen glances, tender words… The days ahead promised bliss. Soon, everyone would depart—Lady Castlewood to visit friends, Madame Bernstein to the healing waters—and he would be left alone with Maria. Alone with her, and with a rapture too vast for words.

The thought nearly overwhelmed him. He had feared this moment would never come. Now it was near. And yet—something stirred within him. A whisper: *It won’t last. Something will tear her from me.*

“Will you ride with us to Tunbridge, nephew Warrington?” asked Madame de Bernstein. “To keep us safe from highwaymen?”

Harry felt his cheeks flush. He forced his voice steady. “Yes, madam. I’ll ride with you. I’m sure you need fear no danger.”

Danger? He would welcome it. He would face a hundred thieves to protect her. He would ride beside her carriage, watch her eyes at the window, press her hand at the inn, lead her to the coach each morning. Two full days to Tunbridge—and perhaps a few more spent at the Wells. Was not a condemned man grateful for even two extra days of life?

We do not dwell long upon Harry Warrington’s state of mind. It was not madness, nor mere infatuation—it was a deep, consuming passion, such as some men carry to their graves. Some fall in love gently; others burn with it until they are consumed. And though we might laugh at such folly, let us not scorn him. For who among us has not acted foolishly when love struck? Even if the object is twice his age—have we not read of young men undone by passion for women who turned out to be their grandmothers? Let those who have never brayed mock him. But those who understand the donkey’s burden—let them pity him.

“You’ll stay with us for a day or two at the Wells,” Madame Bernstein went on. “You’ll help settle us in. Then you may return to Castlewood and the partridge-shooting, and all the fine things you and my lord will discuss.”

Harry bowed. A whole week—perhaps more—of pure happiness. Life was not without hope after all.

“And since there will be plenty of company at the Wells,” the Baroness added graciously, “I shall introduce you.”

“Company!” Harry sighed. “Ah, I shan’t need company.”

He corrected himself quickly. “I mean—I shall be quite content with just you two ladies.”

No doubt Mr. Will blinked at his cousin’s declaration.

As it was to be Harry’s final evening at Castlewood, Will proposed that he, the chaplain, and Harry meet later to settle accounts. Harry, having won several hands at cards, saw no objection. So, when the ladies retired and my lord withdrew to his chambers, the three men gathered in Harry’s small room around the punch bowl—a fixture of Will’s nightly routine.

But Will’s idea of settling debts was to draw fresh packs of cards and suggest doubling Harry’s winnings—or letting fate decide whether they were forgiven. The chaplain had little cash, and neither did Lord Castlewood’s younger brother. Harry wanted nothing from either. To take advantage of Maria’s kin, or wound the brother of the woman he adored—such thoughts were unbearable. He agreed to play, not to win, but to give them fair chance.

They began. Dice rattled. Cards flew. Harry’s mind wandered far from the game.

*Right now,* he imagined, *she sits with her golden hair spread across her shoulders, her maid brushing it. Happy maid. Now she kneels in prayer, that angelic creature, speaking to the heavens where angels like her dwell. Now she rests behind her damask curtains. Bless her, bless her.*

“Double us all round?” Will called. “I’ll take a card on each. Ten—then queen. Two natural vingt-et-uns. Since you doubled, you owe me…”

Imagine the curses from Will, the furious imprecations from the chaplain. Yet Harry remained calm. He had not played to win—he had played because he could not refuse. And fortune, ever fickle, favored him. Perhaps because his heart was elsewhere—perhaps because he was thinking of another nymph, equally capricious.

Will and the chaplain, eager to regain their losses, pushed harder. They believed the wealthy Virginian wished to let them recover. But Harry had no such intention. At home, he had played many such games—though he kept such matters quiet from his mother—and always played fairly. He expected fairness in return.

“The luck seems to be with me, cousin,” he said, in response to Will’s grumbles. “And I don’t wish to push it. But I’m not going to throw it away. I’ve already got a pile of your IOUs. If we continue, let’s put real money on the table—or its value.”

“Always the way with rich men,” Will muttered. “Never lend unless you get security. Always win because you’re rich.”

“Faith, cousin,” Harry replied, “you’ve been throwing my riches in my face lately. I have enough for my needs—and my creditors.”

“Oh, if only we could say the same!” groaned the chaplain. “How happy we’d be—and how happy the duns would be!”

“What can we bet against our conqueror?” he asked. “Here’s my new gown, Mr. Warrington. Will you set five pieces against it? I can preach in wool if I lose. Wait—I have Chrysostom, Foxe’s Martyrs, Baker’s Chronicle, and a cow and calf. What shall we wager?”

“I’ll bet one of cousin Will’s twenty-pound notes,” Harry announced, pulling out a document. “Or—my brown mare. I’ll back her red against your notes—though I prefer ready money.”

“I have my horse,” Will bellowed. “I’ll bet it against you for fifty!”

Harry accepted both bets. Within ten minutes, the horse and the bay mare had changed hands. Will swore louder than ever. The chaplain flung his wig to the floor and roared curses with the vigor of a seasoned veteran.

Yet Harry remained composed. He had played because they asked. He had known he would win. And he did—not because he sought victory, but because his soul was already conquered.

*O beloved slumbering angel,* he thought, gazing out his window toward the casement opposite—her room—where a faint light still burned. *Am I not sure of triumph when you are kind to me?*

He forgot the noise, the complaints, the losers’ rage. Under the flickering starlight, behind that quiet casement, lay his joy, his heart, his treasure.

While the venerable Bishop of Cambray, in his tale recently mentioned, lamented Calypso’s sorrow at Ulysses’ departure, I wonder if he ever noted the grief of Calypso’s maid as she bade farewell to Odysseus’s own servant. Surely, in the kitchen shadows, the two servants wept together while their masters and mistresses clung in passionate embrace in the drawing-room. They stood side by side in the fore-cabin, hearts aching, as their superiors tore themselves apart in the grand saloon. When the bell tolled for the final time, and Ulysses’s mate roared, “Now! Any one for shore!” both Calypso and her maid stepped across the same plank—palms trembling, eyes brimming with tears. Each waved a handkerchief—though of vastly different worth and weave—as they stood on the quay, watching the ship sail away. The crowd ashore and the crew on deck shouted “Hip, hip, hooray!” or whatever Greek equivalent might have echoed through the harbor. But the truth remains: if Calypso could not be consoled, neither could her maid. They shared the same grief, walked the same path of parting, and shed tears equally salt and deep—whether in marble halls or in the servants’ quarters.

Not only did Harry Warrington leave Castlewood undone by love, but Gumbo too departed from those halls, captivated by the same tender passion. His wit, charm, cheerful nature, and talents in dance, music, and cookery had won him the affection of every woman in the household. While some men might have resented him, the ladies adored him. In England at that time, there was no widespread prejudice against Black servants such as later emerged among white society. Though not equal in status, they were tolerated, even welcomed with a kind of whimsical sympathy—and especially so by women, whose kindness often knew no bounds. When Ledyard and Parke, in Blackmansland, faced persecution from men, did not the Black women show them compassion? Women have always shown tenderness toward our kind. What (mental) negroes do they not cherish? What (moral) hunchbacks do they not adore? What lepers, fools, dullards, or misshapen creatures (I speak metaphorically) do they not cradle and delight in? Gumbo was treated with more warmth than many who were no better than himself—only the male servants in the hall rejoiced at the Virginian boy’s departure. I should like to see him say goodbye. I would love to see Molly, the housemaid, slipping into the terrace gardens at dawn to gather a wistful bouquet. I’d like to watch Betty, the kitchen girl, snipping a thick lock of her chestnut curls, intending to trade it for a woolly token from young Gumbo’s head. Of course, he claimed to be *regum progenies*, a descendant of Ashante kings. In Caffraria, Connaught, and other lands where hereditary bondage once flourished, surely countless such royal bloodlines must have existed—judging by their descendants today.

On the morning of Madame de Bernstein’s departure, all the servants of Castlewood gathered at doors and passages—some hoping for one last glimpse of her ladyship’s attendants and the enchanting Gumbo, others to bid farewell to her maid, all eager to catch the Baroness and her nephew for parting gifts. It was customary in those days for departing guests to bestow generous tips upon the household staff. Both the Baroness and her nephew gave liberal rewards—to the liveried men, the gentlemen in black and ruffles, and the swarm of female servants. Castlewood had been the Baroness’s childhood home; and as for Harry, who had lived there free of charge, winning horses and money—or promises of money—from his cousin and the unfortunate chaplain—he naturally felt generous. “My mother,” he thought, “would expect me to be kind to all who served the Esmond family.” So he scattered gold pieces freely, as though he were as rich as Gumbo proclaimed him. No one came near him without receiving a token of his goodwill. From the major-domo to the shoeblack, Mr. Harry offered a peace offering to each. He gave something to the stern housekeeper in her still-room, the frail old porter in his lodge—every soul touched by his generosity. When a man falls in love with one woman in a family, how quickly he grows fond of everyone connected to her. He flatters the maids, is courteous to the butler, takes interest in the footman, runs errands for the daughters, gives advice and lends money to the younger son at college, pats dogs he would otherwise kick, smiles at old stories told by papa, drinks sweet port wine he’d otherwise curse, endures the grumpy maiden aunt, taps his fingers to little Fanny’s piano piece, and laughs when naughty Bobby spills coffee on his shirt.

Harry Warrington, in his own way and according to the customs of the age, had, for a brief time (which suggests his love had only just been declared and accepted), offered these innocent tokens of affection to the Castlewood household. Cousin Will should have reclaimed his money and welcome—or at least as much of Harry’s as the lad could spare. Yet the young man, though smitten, remained sharp, clever, and fond of fair play, and knew a good horse when he saw one. Having won all of Will’s money—plus numerous valuable autographs from Mr. Esmond—Harry was delighted to claim Will’s brown horse—the very animal that nearly threw him into the water on the night of his arrival. He had seen the horse perform many times, and even amid his romantic fervor, he took pride in owning such a sound, swift, well-bred hunter. After gazing long enough at the stars above his beloved’s window and extinguishing her candle, he retired to his room, no doubt dreaming of Maria and his new horse, imagining how sweet it would be to ride across the island with her arms wrapped around his waist. He fell asleep musing on these joys, blessing Maria in his heart, knowing he would enjoy her company for at least one more week.

Early the next morning, Chaplain Sampson sent over his small black mare, delivered by his groom, footman, and gardener—all of whom wept and kissed the horse’s white nose before handing it over to Gumbo. Both Gumbo and Harry were moved by the man’s emotion—Gumbo showing his feelings through tears, Harry by producing two guineas, which astonished and comforted the chaplain’s boy. Then Gumbo and the former groom led the mare to the stable, instructed to bring it back with Mr. William’s horse after breakfast, at the appointed hour for the Baroness’s carriages.

So respectful was he to his aunt—or so grateful for her leaving—that the master of the house even appeared at breakfast to bid farewell to his guests. The ladies and the chaplain were present; the only absent family member was Will, who left a note for his cousin, written in poor spelling: he had to go to Salisbury Races that morning but had left the horse Harry had won the previous night, which Tom, his groom, would deliver to Mr. Warrington’s servant. Will’s absence did not stop the others from sharing a peaceful cup of tea. Soon, the carriages rolled into the courtyard, servants loaded the Baroness’s extensive luggage, and the moment of departure arrived.

A large open landau carried the stout Baroness and her niece, with two male servants riding atop, pistols and blunderbusses ready in case of highwaymen. Another carriage held the ladies’ maids and a guard over the trunks—numerous and bulky, though nothing compared to the vast baggage trains of modern ladies. Mr. Warrington’s modest valises were placed in this second carriage under the maid’s care, and Gumbo planned to ride beside the window for most of the journey.

Lord Castlewood, with his stepmother and Lady Fanny, escorted their kinswoman to the carriage steps, embracing her with heartfelt farewells. Lady Maria followed in a riding dress, which Harry Wawah considered the most becoming attire imaginable. A host of servants stood nearby, begging Heaven bless her ladyship. The Baroness’s departure was known in the village, and dozens of villagers waited beneath the trees outside the gates, cheering and waving hats as the heavy carriages rolled away.

Gumbo returned with Mr. Warrington’s horses as Lord Castlewood walked arm-in-arm with his young guest through the courtyard. “I hear you’re taking some of our horses out of Castlewood?” the lord said.

Harry blushed. “A gentleman cannot refuse a fair game at cards,” he replied. “I never wanted to play, nor would have bet money had my cousin William not forced me. As for the chaplain—I hated to win from him, but he was just as eager as Will.”

“I understand, I understand. There’s no blame on you, my boy. At Rome, you do as Rome does. And I’m glad you’ve given Will a lesson. He’s mad for gambling—would stake his coat off his back—and I and the family have paid his debts far too often. May I ask how much you’ve won?”

“Eighteen pieces the first few days, plus his note for a hundred and twenty, and the brown horse—sixty. That’s nearly two hundred. But, you know, cousin, it was all fair play. I didn’t want to gamble at all. Will isn’t a match for me, my lord—that’s the truth. He really isn’t.”

“He’s a match for most people,” said Lord Castlewood. “His brown horse, you said?”

“Yes. Prince William, out of Constitution. You don’t suppose I’d set sixty against his bay, my lord?”

“Oh, I didn’t notice. I saw Will riding out this morning—perhaps I didn’t pay attention to his mount. And you won the black mare from the parson?”

“For fourteen. He’ll suit Gumbo well. Why hasn’t that fellow come back with the horses?” Harry’s thoughts were already with lovely Maria. He longed to be riding beside her.

“When you reach Tunbridge, cousin Harry, keep an eye out for sharper players than the chaplain and Will. There’s all sorts of odd characters at the Wells.”

“A Virginian learns to take care of himself, my lord,” Harry replied with a knowing nod.

“So it seems! I entrust my sister to you, Harry. Though she’s not a child in years, she’s as innocent as one. See that she comes to no harm?”

“I’ll guard her with my life, my lord!” Harry declared.

“You’re a brave fellow. By the way, unless you’re deeply attached to Castlewood, I wouldn’t rush to return to this lonely, crumbling old house. I myself plan to go elsewhere and won’t be back until partridge-shooting season. Go and look after the women—my sister and the Baroness.”

“I will indeed,” said Harry, his heart swelling with joy at the thought.

“And I’ll write when you should bring my sister home. Here come the horses. Have you said goodbye to the Countess and Lady Fanny? They’re waving from the music-room balcony.”

Harry hurried upstairs to bid the ladies farewell, making it brief—eager to rejoin his beloved. He descended to mount his newly acquired steed, which Gumbo, astride the parson’s black mare, held by the reins.

There stood Gumbo on the black mare, indeed, holding another horse—but it was not brown. It was a bay, with broken knees—an old, worn-out beast.

“What is this?” Harry exclaimed.

“Your honour’s new horse,” said the groom, touching his cap.

“This brute?” Harry protested, using one of the expressions common in England and Virginia at the time. “Bring me Prince William, Mr. William’s horse—the brown one!”

“Mr. William rode Prince William to Salisbury Races this morning. His last words were, ‘Sam, saddle my bay horse, Cato, for Mr. Warrington. He’s Mr. Warrington’s horse now. I sold him to him last night.’ And I know your honour is generous—you’ll consider the groom.”

Lord Castlewood couldn’t help laughing at Sam’s words, while Harry let loose several remarks too vulgar for polite print.

“Mr. William said he’d never part with Prince William for less than a hundred and twenty,” the groom added, looking at Harry.

Lord Castlewood laughed harder. “Will has been too much for you, Harry Warrington.”

“Too much for me, my lord? Like a man rolling loaded dice and throwing sixes—too much for me. I don’t call this betting. I call it cheating.”

“Mr. Warrington! Spare me foul language about my brother, please. I assure you, I’ll see justice done. Farewell. Ride quickly, or your coaches will reach Farnham before you.” With that, the lord waved goodbye and entered the house, while Harry and Gumbo rode out of the courtyard. The young Virginian was too eager to reunite with the carriages and his charmer to notice the unspoken devotion Gumbo cast toward a young girl in the porter’s lodge.

After the youth left, the chaplain and Lord Castlewood sat down to finish their breakfast in peace. The two ladies did not return.

“That was one of Will’s confounded tricks,” said the lord. “If our cousin breaks Will’s head, I wouldn’t be surprised.”

“He’s used to it, my lord. Still,” added the chaplain with a grin, “last night, when we played, the horse’s color wasn’t mentioned. I couldn’t escape—I had only one. And the black boy rode off on him. The young Virginian plays like a man, I must give him credit.”

“He wins because he doesn’t fear losing. I suspect he’s quite wealthy. His mother’s legal agents are my lawyers, and they report the estate is practically a principality, growing richer every year.”

“If it were a kingdom, I know whom Mr. Warrington would make queen,” said the chaplain, sycophantically.

“Who can judge taste, parson?” asked Lord Castlewood with a sneer. “All men are alike. The first woman I loved was forty—and as jealous as if she were fifteen. It runs in the family. Colonel Esmond (the one in scarlet and breastplate yonder) married my grandmother, who was almost old enough to be his mother. If this lad chooses to take an elderly princess to Virginia, we mustn’t stand in his way.”

“‘Twere a consummation devoutly to be wished!” cried the chaplain. “Shall I go to Tunbridge Wells myself, my lord, to be on hand and ready to perform my sacred duty for the young couple?”

“You shall have a pair of new nags, parson, if you do,” said the lord. And with that, we leave them enjoying a quiet pipe after breakfast.

Harry was so eager to join the carriages that he nearly forgot to remove his hat and acknowledge the cheers of the Castlewood villagers. They all liked the lad—his honest face and warm manner earned him respect wherever he went. Legends still lingered in Castlewood about his grandparents, particularly how his grandfather, Colonel Esmond, might have become Lord Castlewood but refused the title. Old Lockwood at the gate often recounted the colonel’s bravery in Queen Anne’s wars. His feats were exaggerated, and the behavior of the current family contrasted sharply with that of the old lord and lady—who may not have been popular in their day, but were seen as better folk than those now in power. Lord Castlewood was a harsh landlord, perhaps disliked more because he was known to be poor and in debt than because of his severity. As for Mr. Will, no one liked him. He’d had fights and quarrels throughout the village, suffered and dealt broken heads, had unpaid bills in neighboring towns, been brought before magistrates for seducing village girls, and been ambushed and beaten by angry husbands, fathers, and lovers. A century ago, his character might have been painted in full detail by a social observer; today, the Comic Muse merely hints at someone behind Molly Seagrim’s curtain, then passes on primly, fanning herself in horror. The village knew the young Virginian had beaten Mr. Will at riding, jumping, shooting, and finally at cards—everything was known—and they respected Harry all the more for it. Above all, they admired him for the legend of immense wealth Gumbo had created for his master. This fame had spread across the county and now preceded him on the boxes of Madame Bernstein’s carriages, where valets, descending at inns to rest the horses, told wild tales of the young Virginian’s rank and splendor. He was a prince in his own land. He had gold mines, diamond mines, furs, tobacco—what else, who knew? No wonder the honest Britons cheered him and respected him for his success, as noble-hearted people always do. I’m surprised city corporations didn’t send him formal addresses and golden boxes with the freedom of the city—he was so rich. Ah, what a proud thing it is to be a Briton, to know that nowhere else is prosperity so honored, and achievement so warmly celebrated!

Thus, leaving the villagers shouting and tossing hats in the air, Harry spurred his sorry beast and galloped forward, with Gumbo behind, until he caught up with the cloud of dust surrounding his charmer’s carriage. Breaking through the haze, he found himself at the window. Lady Maria occupied the back seat alone; by staying slightly behind the wheels, he could gaze upon her divine eyes and smile. She raised a finger to her lips. Madame Bernstein was already sleeping. Harry didn’t wish to disturb the old lady. To see his cousin was bliss enough. The landscape might have been beautiful, but what did he care? All the skies and trees of summer meant nothing compared to her face; the hedgerow birds sang no sweeter song than her soft syllables.

The Baroness’s fat horses were accustomed to short rides, gentle paces, and frequent feeding; so despite Harry’s poor mount, he managed easily to keep pace with his elderly kinswoman. At two o’clock, they stopped for two hours to dine. Mr. Warrington paid the landlord generously. What price could be too high for the pleasure of being near his beloved Maria, and having the chance to talk with her, scarcely interrupted by the soft breathing of Madame de Bernstein, who, after a satisfying meal, slipped into a pleasant half-hour nap? In low, tender voices, Maria and her young man repeated their sweet nonsense—words no one in Harry’s condition ever tires of hearing.

They were heading to a crowded spa town, where beauty and fashion would abound. Timid Maria feared that among the young beauties, Harry would find someone far more worthy of his attention than her plain face and figure. “By all the gods,” Harry vowed, “Venus herself could not lure me from your side.” Yet it was he who truly had reason to worry. When fashionable young men saw his exquisite Maria, they would surround her carriage, make her forget the rough, humble American lad who knew nothing of elegance or wit—whose only treasure was a faithful heart.

Maria smiled, looked heavenward, and declared that Harry misunderstood women. It was men, she insisted, who were famously faithless, who toyed with fragile hearts. A minor argument ensued. A clatter broke out among the dessert knives and forks. A glass tumbled and shattered. An “Oh!” escaped Maria’s lips. The disturbance came from Harry’s broad coat sleeve, stretched across the table to grasp Lady Maria’s hand, knocking over the wineglass. Was there anything more natural—or necessary—than for Harry, upon hearing his sex accused of fickleness, to seize his fair accuser’s hand and swear eternal loyalty on those lovely fingers?

What a role hands once played in courtship! How delicately they were squeezed at that stage of life! How eagerly thrust into conversation! What absurd vows and declarations passed through their touch! What purpose could there be in pulling and pressing a thumb and four fingers? I imagine Alexis laughing, reading this page beside Araminta. To talk about thumbs indeed!... Maria glanced around to see if Madame Bernstein had awakened from the crash—yet the old lady slept peacefully, so her niece deemed it safe to yield to Harry’s gentle pressure.

The horses were put back to work. Paradise ended—at least until the next opportunity. When the landlord entered with the bill, Harry stood at a distance from his cousin, staring out the window at the gathering cavalcade below. Madame Bernstein stirred awake, smiling and unaware. With profound care and reverent politeness, Mr. Warrington helped his aunt into her carriage. How demure and simple Lady Maria looked as she followed! The carriages rolled away, amid deep bows from the landlord and waiters, countryfolk gathered around the blazing inn sign, shopkeepers peering from their modest doors, boys and market-goers under the colonnade of the old town hall, and loungers along the gabled street. “It’s the famous Baroness Bernstein. That’s her, the old lady in the capuchin. It’s the rich young American just come from Virginia—worth millions and millions. Well, sure, he might have a better horse.” The procession vanished, and the little town sank back into its usual quiet. The landlord returned to his friends at the club to recount how the great ones were spending the night at The Bush in Farnham.

Let no gentle reader be alarmed for Mr. Harry Warrington’s safety, nor imagine that his fall from the broken-kneed horse has carried him beyond the bounds of life and story. Rest assured, nothing of great consequence has befallen him. Why should we so rashly dispatch our heroes in their youth, when they have barely stepped into manhood, and the tale is still unfolding? We mourn already for one of the Virginians who met an untimely end in America—surely we cannot take another in England? No, indeed. Heroes are not swept away without cause, unless there is a pressing need to remove them from the scene. If every gentleman perished at the first stumble of a horse, not only would the hero vanish, but the author himself would long since have been laid low. Yet here, the young man lies not dead, but merely sprawled upon the ground, unconscious yet breathing—soon to be brought within the sheltering walls of Madame de Bernstein’s household, where servants have rung the bell in haste.

To prove that this youngest of the Virginians still draws breath, here is a letter penned by the lady whose home received him after his fall—a letter both tender and truthful:

If Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Virginia can recall twenty-three years past, when Miss Rachel Esmond was at Kensington Boarding School, she may remember Miss Molly Benson, her classmate—now grown and mellowed with time, who has forgotten all the petty quarrels they once had (though she admits she was often in the wrong), and remembers only the generous, spirited, radiant Miss Esmond—the very Princess Pocahontas, whom so many of our schoolmates admired.

Dear madam, I cannot forget that you were once dear Rachel, as I was your dearest Molly. Though we parted on less than friendly terms when you returned to Virginia, I know how deeply we once loved each other. I still possess the gold etui your father gave me on speech-day at Kensington, when we performed the quarrel between Brutus and Cassius from Shakespeare. Only yesterday morning, I dreamed we were called before the formidable Miss Hardwood to recite our lessons, and I failed—while, as always, Miss Rachel Esmond outshone me. How vivid those memories are! How young we seem when we revisit them.

I remember our walks, our exercises, the good King and Queen strolling through Kensington Gardens, followed by their court, while we girls curtsied in perfect line. I can still name what we ate each day, point to the spot where your garden stood—always better kept than mine—and recall how neat your chest of drawers was, compared to my own disordered chaos. Do you remember the tales we spun in the dormitory, interrupted by Madame Hibou, our French governess, hooting from her bed? And the poor dancing-master, who claimed he’d been attacked by assassins—only to be revealed as having been beaten by your brother’s footmen?

My dear, your cousin Lady Maria Esmond—her father was then but Viscount Castlewood—has just visited this house. I did not mention those old sorrows to her, though I now speak of them freely to you, Mrs. Esmond.

Lady Maria stayed with us, along with another relative of yours, the Baroness de Bernstein. Both have journeyed onward to Tunbridge Wells. But one dearer guest remains under my roof—sound asleep, I trust, in the next room. His name is Mr. Henry Esmond Warrington. Now do you understand why I write to you?

Do not fear, dear madam. I know your thoughts: *My son is ill—that is why Miss Molly Benson writes.* No, my dear. Mr. Warrington was unwell yesterday, but today he is much improved. Our doctor—none other than my beloved husband, Colonel Lambert—has bled him, reset his dislocated shoulder, and assures me that within two days he will be fit to travel again.

I confess, I and my daughters are sorry he will recover so quickly. Yesterday evening, during tea, a sudden ringing at the gate startled us all—such a sound is rare in this quiet place, save when a beggar seeks charity. The servants rushed out and returned with news: a young gentleman had fallen from his horse, lying unconscious on the road, surrounded by companions. At once, my husband—ever the most compassionate of men—hurried to help. With the aid of the servants and two ladies, he brought into the house a pale, lifeless, yet strikingly beautiful young man.

Ah, my dear, how glad I am that your child found refuge beneath my roof! That my husband could ease his pain, prevent fever, and restore him to health and you!

We shall be friends again, shall we not? Last year I fell gravely ill; it was feared I might die. In those dark hours, I often thought of you—of how we parted in anger so long ago. I began a letter to you, half-written, which I never finished, telling you that if I were to depart this world, I wished to leave it in peace with every soul I had known.

Lady Maria showed deep concern for her young kinsman after the accident. I believe her heart is truly kind. The Baroness de Bernstein, though aged, was moved until Mr. Warrington regained consciousness, when she expressed a desire to continue her journey to Tunbridge, fearing illness without a physician nearby. My husband laughed and said he would not attend a lady of quality—but he would care for his young patient with all diligence. Indeed, Colonel Lambert has seen many such injuries in his military service, and I assure you, even if we summoned every doctor within twenty miles, Mr. Warrington could not receive better care.

Once settled, the Baroness and Lady Maria took their leave—Lady Maria reluctant to go. When the young gentleman is well enough, my husband will ride with him as far as Westerham, where an old army comrade of his resides. This letter will not reach Falmouth until, by God’s grace, your son is fully restored. So rest easy, dear madam. He is safe under the roof of your affectionate, humble servant,

I am delighted to hear (Mr. Warrington’s colored servant informed us) that Providence has blessed Mrs. Esmond with great wealth and a son worthy of it. Our means are sufficient, but would be small divided among our survivors. Ah, dear madam, I have heard of your loss last year. Though the Colonel and I have raised five children, we have lost two. A mother’s heart knows sorrow, and I grieved for yours. I confess, when the boy spoke of his dear brother—so gently, so tenderly—I felt a pang for him. It is impossible not to love him. I am grateful we could offer him shelter, and that in welcoming a stranger, we welcomed the son of an old friend.

There is something about certain men—written plainly upon their faces—that commands trust wherever they go. Harry Warrington bore such a countenance in youth. His eyes sparkled with honesty, his cheeks glowed with health, his expression open and true. Even those who sought to deceive him found themselves believing in him. Yet beneath that innocent air lay a mind sharper than it seemed. He was not the artless boy he appeared. Perhaps more cunning in youth than he ever became in age.

It is said that honest men grow simpler with time—learning to judge swiftly, to discard falsehoods easily, to strike truth with fewer missteps. Or is it merely the delusion of age, that our vanities fade, and we grow wiser in seeing our own faults and those of others?

Yet let us say this: young people, though fairer in face and freer in spirit, are often as clever as their elders. What little masters of deceit are our frank schoolboys! How they cheat their mothers, hoodwink their fathers, fool the housekeeper, cringe before the older boys they serve at school! What a web of lies and flattery they weave toward Dr. Birch! And their sisters—do they fare any better? Do they not learn their tricks only when they enter society?

From Mrs. Lambert’s letter, we see she, like most good women (and many not-so-good ones), was sentimental. As she watched Harry Warrington lie in her best bed—after the Colonel had bled him and set his shoulder—she held his hand and saw him drift into sleep, murmuring softly, a faint blush on his cheek. She confessed he was a lovely lad—more handsome than either of her sons. Jack, at Oxford, might have been so, had smallpox spared him. As for Charles—

“Always took after his papa,” said the Colonel, gazing at his own honest face in a little mirror with a japanned frame.

“Did I say so?” whispered Mrs. Lambert, startled.

“No,” replied the Colonel, “but you thought it.”

“How can you read my thoughts, Martin?”

“Because I am a conjurer,” he smiled, “and because you tell them aloud. You never see a young man without comparing him to your own. You never hear of one without wondering which daughter he’ll marry.”

“Don’t be foolish, sir,” she said, placing a hand over his lips.

They had quietly left the guest’s chamber and now stood in the adjoining dressing-room—a cozy, wainscoted space overlooking gardens, with India curtains, Japanese chests, fine china, and the sweet scent of lavender.

“You can’t deny it, Mrs. Lambert,” the Colonel continued. “You were just now thinking: Which of my girls will he marry? Theo or Hester? And then Lucy, at boarding school?”

“There’s no hiding anything from you, Martin,” sighed the wife.

“There’s no hiding it from your eyes, my dear. What is this strange longing all women have—to sell off their daughters? We men don’t wish to part with them. I confess, I wouldn’t care for this young fellow half as much if I thought he meant to carry one of my darlings away.”

“But surely, Martin,” she replied, looking at him with her warmest gaze, “since I’ve been so happy myself, I must wish my girls to find happiness too!”

“Then you think good husbands are common,” he teased, “that you might walk down the road and pick one up like a sack of coals?”

“Wasn’t it providential,” she asked, “that this young man should fall at our very gate—and turn out to be the son of my old schoolfriend?”

“There is more than chance in such things,” said the Colonel. “Depend upon it.”

“And this was the stranger you saw in the candle three nights running?”

“And in the fire, too,” she added. “Twice, a coal leapt near Theo. You may laugh, but these signs are not to be ignored. Did I not see you clearly returning from Minorca, and dream of you at the exact hour you were wounded in Scotland?”

“How many times have you seen me wounded when I was untouched, my dear? How many times have you foreseen my illness when I was well? You are always prophesying—and it’s lucky for you that you’re sometimes right. Come, let us leave our guest sleeping peacefully and go below to give the girls their French lesson.”

So saying, the Colonel took his wife’s arm, and together they descended the broad oak staircase of the old hall, lined with portraits of generations of Lamberts—worthy magistrates, soldiers, country gentlemen, including the Colonel himself.

He was a man of cheerful wit. The French lesson he shared with his daughters was a scene from Molière’s *Tartuffe*. He played Orgon with playful mockery, addressing his daughter Theo as “Madam” and treating her with mock solemnity. They read together with laughter and charm, and Papa especially relished Orgon’s lines:

> **ORGON:** Or sus, nous voila bien. J'ai, Mariane, en vous
> Reconnu de tout temps un esprit assez doux,
> Et de tout temps aussi vous m'avez ete chere.
>
> **MARIANE:** Je suis fort redevable a cet amour de pere.
>
> **ORGON:** Fort bien. Que dites-vous de Tartuffe notre hote?
>
> **MARIANE:** Qui? Moi?
>
> **ORGON:** Vous. Voyez bien comme vous repondrez.
>
> **MARIANE:** Helas! J'en dirai, moi, tout ce que vous voudrez!
> *(Miss Theo laughs and blushes, unable to contain herself.)*
>
> **ORGON:** C'est parler sagement. Dites-moi donc, ma fille,
> Qu'en toute sa personne un haut merite brille,
> Qu'il touche votre coeur, et qu'il vous seroit doux
> De le voir par men choix devenir votre epoux!

“Have we not read it well, Elmire?” the Colonel laughed, turning to his wife.

Elmire adored Orgon’s performance—just as she adored everything her husband did.

O reader, can you count upon the faithfulness of pure hearts? Can you call among life’s blessings the love of loyal women? Then purify your own soul, and strive to make it worthy of such devotion. Kneel, and give thanks for this gift above all others. For all the prizes of ambition—wealth, pleasure, power—are but vanity and disappointment, fiercely grasped and bitterly abandoned. But love endures beyond life. I believe it carries us beyond the grave. Do we not still give it to those who are gone? May we hope they feel it for us, and that we leave it behind in one or two tender hearts when we too pass?

And why this reflection? Because I know more of the Lamberts than you do—how could you, who have never met them before? You may not like them. Few people do when introduced with such fervent praise. You might say: *Is this all? Are these the people he admires so? The girl isn’t beautiful—the mother is kind, perhaps, but no longer youthful—and the father… well, quite ordinary.*

Granted. But do you not feel something sweet and moving in the sight of an honest man, with a loving wife at his side, and children who cherish him? When you see such a family gathered round him, their faces alight with affection, their confidence plain in every glance—can you remain unmoved? If you stay in such a house, and see them gather in prayer at dawn or dusk—do you not join humbly in their petitions, and close them with a reverent *Amen*?

That first night at Oakhurst, Harry Warrington, drugged and restless, thought he heard the Evening Hymn—and that his dear brother George was singing it at home. In that moment of illusion, he drifted back into peaceful sleep.

A gentle slumber, lulled by the soft murmur of voices and the quiet rustle of the morning breeze, carried Harry Warrington through the night. When he awoke, the sun was already climbing high in a clear summer sky, casting golden rays across the room. At his bedside stood the kind host and hostess, their faces lit with warmth and concern.

He stirred, ravenous from hunger, and the doctor, observing him closely, permitted a light meal—chicken and rice, prepared with care by one of Mrs. Lambert’s daughters. As the scent of the food filled the air, Harry’s mind wandered. He remembered faintly two young girls with bright cheeks and dark, curling hair, who had smiled at him as he lay unconscious, then vanished just as he began to stir. Then came another image—a woman older, graceful but no longer young, her hair golden under the candlelight… But no—such thoughts brought a sudden pang of shame. A wave of memory surged forward: the false pearls, the dyed locks—he recalled now, with horror, how he had once been deceived by such things. It seemed like a lifetime ago, when he was still a boy, innocent and unguarded. Now he was a man—older, wounded, bled, fevered, and drugged into deep sleep. The past felt distant, almost unreal.

“What is it, my dear child?” asked Mrs. Lambert gently, noticing his sudden distress.

“Nothing, madam,” replied Harry, clutching his shoulder. “Just a twinge. I thank you both for your kindness. You’ve taken such good care of me.”

“We are old friends, Mr. Warrington,” said Colonel Lambert. “My wife and your mother were schoolmates in Kensington, and I knew your father well. You were never a stranger to us, even before your aunt and cousin told us who you were.”

“Are they here?” Harry asked, his eyes dimming slightly.

“They must have stayed at Tunbridge Wells last night. They sent a rider from Reigate yesterday to inquire after you.”

“Oh—yes,” Harry murmured, glancing down at his bandaged arm.

“You’re recovering well,” said the Colonel. “Now, we’ll leave the rest to Mrs. Lambert and the cook.”

“Nay,” interrupted the lady, “Theo made the broth herself. And she mended your sleeve too—so it wouldn’t chafe your wound.”

“And if howling proves loyalty,” said the Colonel with a grin, “then your valet must be the most devoted creature alive.”

“He let your luggage go off with your aunt’s carriage,” added Mrs. Lambert. “You’ll have to wear my husband’s shirts—though I’m sure they’re not half so fine as yours.”

“Pish!” the Colonel laughed. “They’re good enough for any Christian. And besides, Theo and Hester stitched them themselves.”

Harry looked up at the vase of roses on the toilet table, their crimson petals glowing in the sunlight. “What beautiful roses!”

“Theo picked them this morning,” said Mrs. Lambert. “She did, didn’t she, Lambert?”

The Colonel merely nodded, though his expression suggested he might have nudged her quietly, as if to remind her of propriety.

“I thought I heard someone singing the Evening Hymn last night,” Harry said softly. “Or was it only a dream?”

“Theo again,” chuckled the Colonel. “The servants said your servant began it in the kitchen—singing like a church organ.”

“Our people sing it at home,” said Harry, his voice softening. “My grandfather loved it dearly. His wife’s father was a close friend of Bishop Ken, who wrote it. And—my brother used to love it too.” His voice trailed off.

At that moment, Mrs. Lambert’s eyes softened, as if she would have reached out to comfort him. The tenderness of the place—the quiet healing, the simple kindness—had begun to touch Harry’s heart. For weeks he had breathed the polluted air of London’s vanity, ambition, and deceit. Now, surrounded by honesty and peace, he felt something stirring within him—something purer, more true.

The Colonel sat beside him as Harry ate, and the housewife left them to their conversation. Gratitude warmed Harry’s spirit, and the fullness of his stomach loosened his tongue. Usually reserved, he found himself speaking more freely than usual. He wasn’t much of a scholar—books had never held his interest—but he could talk knowledgeably about horses, dogs, and the ways of country life. The Colonel, shrewd and experienced in men, cattle, and war, quickly sized him up.

It was only now that Harry learned Mrs. Lambert had been a childhood friend of his mother’s, and that the Colonel’s own father had fought alongside Harry’s grandfather, Colonel Esmond, during Queen Anne’s wars. Suddenly, he wasn’t just a guest—he was among kin.

“My sons are away,” said the Colonel. “Otherwise, they’d show you the country. But you’ll have to make do with my wife and daughters. Theo—our eldest—made your soup, cut the roses, and sewed your sleeve. She’s no miracle worker, though her mother thinks she is. But she’s a capable girl, cheerful and hardworking.”

“It’s very kind of Miss Lambert,” said Harry.

“She treats everyone alike,” replied the Colonel. “Does her duty. I laugh when she praises our children—though I suppose I’m just as bad myself. God has given us good children. Why hide my gratitude?”

“You don’t have a sister?” he asked.

“No, sir,” said Harry. “I am alone now.”

“Forgive me,” said the Colonel. “Your servant told us what happened last year. I served with Braddock in Scotland. I hope he recovered before he died. A wild man, but there was truth beneath the swagger. Your servant speaks freely—perhaps because he saved you?”

“Saved me?” Harry blinked.

“From dozens of Indians, on that very expedition. We didn’t know we were hosting such a wealthy gentleman. He says half Virginia belongs to you. But even if all of North America were yours, we’d give you our best.”

“Negro boys lie like the devil,” said Harry, flushing. “They think it honors us to say we’re ten times richer than we are. My mother has a good estate—better than most in England, but nothing extraordinary. All our grandeur is in Gumbo’s imagination. He never rescued me from an Indian—and would flee at the sight of one, just as my brother’s boy did when he fell.”

“A brave man can run at times,” said the Colonel. “I saw the finest troops in the world scatter before a ragged mob of Highlanders at Preston.”

“That was because they fought for their king,” said Harry.

“And what of the French Indians last year?” asked the Colonel.

“The scoundrels!” Harry clenched his fist. “I’d take the scalp of every one of them! They invaded British land. But the Highlanders fought for their king.”

“And we fought for ours,” said the Colonel, laughing. “And won.”

“If Prince James hadn’t turned back at Derby,” said Harry, “your king and mine would be King James the Third now.”

“Who made you such a Tory?” asked the Colonel.

“Not I,” replied Harry. “The Esmonds were always loyal. If we’d lived in England twenty years earlier, my brother and I would have risked our heads for the king.”

“Yours is better where it is,” said the Colonel. “I’ve seen others’ heads on poles at Temple Bar. Not a pleasant sight.”

“I’ll salute them whenever I pass,” said Harry. “If the king and court stand nearby!”

“I doubt Lord Castlewood shares your views,” said the Colonel, smiling. “Nor your aunt, the Baroness of Bernstein. She’s changed sides—sent her nephews into the Household, and looks for suitable matches for her nieces. If you hold Tory opinions, take an old soldier’s advice—keep them to yourself.”

“I trust you won’t betray me,” said Harry.

“I won’t,” said the Colonel. “But others might. Did you speak so freely at Castlewood?”

“I should have been safe among my own kin,” said Harry.

“Perhaps,” said the Colonel. “But kinsmen can play tricks. Servants have ears. Your servant talks too much.”

“Has he told about the broken-kneed horse?” Harry blushed deeply.

“To be honest,” said the Colonel, “my groom knew the story. Said it was a shame a gentleman sold such a beast—especially to a cousin.”

“I’ll not speak of it again,” said Harry.

With Gumbo’s help, Harry rose from bed. He gave the valet a stern warning—this time, not a single word about his affairs in the servants’ hall. Gumbo swore solemnly he would obey. But the reader may suspect that the words flew from his lips as soon as he stepped into the kitchen.

Mr. Lambert’s house stood on the edge of Oakhurst, a quiet town between Farnham and Reigate. It was modest but stately—a square brick building with stone-framed windows, tall chimneys, and a balustrade crowning its roof. Behind it stretched a wide garden; before it, a field where cows grazed and horses roamed. Two heraldic beasts guarded the gates, and above the central window hung a carved shield and coronet. The house had once been the jointure-house of Oakhurst Castle, whose turrets peered over the trees beyond. Though the castle loomed larger in history, the Lambert home was the most respected in the town.

After dressing with Gumbo’s aid—his fair hair neatly arranged, his injured arm supported by a handkerchief—Harry followed the Colonel down a broad oak staircase lined with ancient weapons. Into a marble hall they stepped, where pikes, halberds, pistols, and jackboots from Cromwell’s wars stood proudly displayed. There was a tattered French flag from Malplaquet, a pair of Highland swords thrown aside after Culloden, and portraits of stern Parliamentary soldiers.

“They fought against your grandfather and King Charles,” said the Colonel. “I don’t hide it. We were Whigs—more than that. John Lambert, the Major-General, was a kinsman. We liked short hair and long sermons. You don’t seem fond of either?”

Harry’s face tightened as he studied the portraits.

“Don’t worry,” said the Colonel. “We’re Churchmen now. My eldest son will enter the clergy. He’s traveling with Lord Wrotham’s son in Italy. And our women—well, they’re all for the Church. Every woman is a Tory at heart, though Pope called it a rake. Come, let’s see them.”

He opened the door to the parlour, where the ladies waited.

“Here is Miss Hester,” said the Colonel. “And this is Miss Theo—the soup-maker, the tailor, the harpsichord player, and the songstress who lulled you to sleep. Make a curtsey, girls.”

Miss Theo bowed deeply, her cheeks flaming. She was sixteen, sturdy and freckled, with rich brown curls tumbling from her cap, strong arms, and feet that needed no telescope to see. Not a beauty, perhaps, but warm and real. Harry did not fall instantly in love with her—nor could he forget the other woman who had lately captured his heart.

“Eh bien! que dites-vous, ma fille, de notre hote?” the Colonel hummed, tapping her chin.

“Nonsense, Mr. Lambert!” said Mrs. Lambert.

“Nonsense is often the wisest thing in the world,” said the Colonel.

“Do you like nonsense?” he asked Harry, seeing the youth’s confusion.

“We consume plenty of it here,” said the Colonel. “Rabelais is my favorite. My wife likes Fielding and Theophrastus. Theo prefers Tom Brown. Hetty loves Swift.”

“Our papa talks about what he loves,” said Miss Hetty.

“And what is that?” asked the Colonel.

“Sure, sir, you said it was nonsense,” she replied, tossing her head.

“Which of them do you prefer, Mr. Warrington?” asked the Colonel.

“Which of whom?”

“The Curate of Meudon, or the Dean of St. Patrick’s, or honest Tom, or Mr. Fielding?”

“And who were they?”

“They wrote books.”

“I’ve never heard of them,” Harry admitted, lowering his eyes. “I fear my schooling was neglected. My brother read everything. He could talk about them for hours.”

Mrs. Lambert glanced at Theo, who blushed.

“Never mind,” said the Colonel cheerfully. “Honesty beats book-learning any day. You can live honorably without reading these. Some might bring more pleasure than profit.”

“I know more about horses and dogs than Greek and Latin,” said Harry. “Most of us in Virginia do.”

“You’re like the Persians,” said the Colonel. “You ride well—and speak the truth.”

“Are the Prussians good riders?” asked Harry. “I hope to see their king and fight beside or against him.”

And then, silently, Miss Theo looked at her mother—and Mrs. Lambert’s face grew sad.

Why? Because young girls raised in quiet towns are not immune to dreams. Even those sheltered behind walls and aprons harbor secret hopes. Like the princess in the fairy tale, locked in a steel castle, listening for the horn that signals her champion’s arrival. The dragon is slain, the gate opens, and she rushes forth—ready, eager, dressed in her finest. That is romance. And that is why Miss Theo blushed. Because somewhere, deep in her heart, she believed the hero had come.

And so, though he did not know it yet, Harry Warrington had entered a world far different from the one he had known. Here, among honest men and gentle women, among laughter and memory, he began to heal—not just his body, but his soul.

Mrs. Lambert’s little dream had come to an end. Miss Theo and her mother, though they said little aloud, both knew in their hearts that the young man they had imagined as a hero was merely a plain, ordinary fellow. Yet no words were needed between them—love speaks louder than speech—and the mother, with gentle touches and tender glances, tried to comfort her daughter for the quiet disappointment.

“Never mind, my dear,” she whispered, pressing a soft kiss to Theo’s cheek, “our hero has turned out to be only a mortal man—and none such is good enough for my Theo. You shall have a real husband soon, if there be one left in England. Why, I was barely fifteen when your father first saw me at the Bury Assembly, and while still at school, I vowed I’d never marry any other man. If Heaven gave me such a husband—the best man in all the land—surely it will bless my child too, who deserves a king, should she fancy him!”

And perhaps Mrs. Lambert, who well knew the age and reputation of the Prince of Wales, secretly hoped he might ride past her gate one day, fall from his horse, be brought into the house, cured by her care, and cause his royal grandfather to grant Martin Lambert a regiment—while falling madly in love with Theo, of course.

Colonel Lambert and his younger daughter, Miss Hetty, stood firmly on the side of laughter and disbelief. Their mother was always dreaming up matches. Indeed, Mrs. Lambert had a deep fondness for novels, reading them with fervent emotion and often weeping over their tragedies.
