Every carriage that passed the gate stirred her hopes: surely, she thought, a noble suitor would step down and ring the bell.

Miss Hetty, meanwhile, took delight in teasing. Her tongue wagged with sharp wit, and she peppered their conversations with sly references to Prussia and Persia. She asked whether the King of Prussia was called “Shaw” or “Sophy,” and how far it was from Ispahan to Saxony—since His Majesty was currently invading the region, a matter her father studied intently in maps and newspapers. She quietly placed *The Persian Tales* upon the parlour table, where the family sat together. She declared she wouldn’t marry a Persian prince—she preferred a gentleman who kept only one wife. She began calling Harry Warrington “Theo’s prince,” “Theo’s gentleman,” and once even asked her mother if she wished her, Hetty, to take the “black prince” for herself.

She mocked her sister and mother endlessly about their romantic notions, driving them to anger before bursting into tears and rushing to embrace them, kissing each fiercely until they relented and laughed again.

Harry Warrington, meanwhile, remained utterly unaware of all this drama. A hundred jokes flew his way—about Prussians, Sophies, Shaws—but he didn’t grasp a single one. He likely thought “Sophy” was a woman’s name, and found it absurd that a man with a great black beard could bear such a title. Like a stone dropped into a still pond, he entered their lives quietly, unaware of the ripples he caused—disturbing the fish, startling the ducks, agitating the water's surface.

How could Harry know what effect his arrival had? He thought well enough of himself in many ways, but was still shy around women—just at the age when young men need encouragement and guidance. Raised in a modest household, he had grown up with limited contact with the opposite sex. So Miss Hetty’s jests floated past him like summer gnats—annoying, perhaps, but harmless.

It wasn’t that he was dull, as Hetty believed; rather, he was simple, absorbed in his own honest thoughts and concerns. And so, without knowing it, he became the subject of countless stories, secrets, and dreams—yet remained blissfully ignorant of it all.

One evening, as the sisters combed their long curls by candlelight or chatted in the large bed where, by custom, they slept together, Harry had no idea how deeply he occupied their minds.

Three days after his arrival, the family walked with him through Lord Wrotham’s beautiful park, where they were free to wander. Near a small lake, they came upon a group of swans, which the girls often fed with bread. As the birds approached, Hetty glanced sideways at her mother and sister, then at her father, standing nearby in his cheerful red waistcoat.

“Mamma’s swans are something like these, papa,” she said with a mischievous grin.

“What swans, my dear?” her mother asked.

“Something like, but not quite. They’ve shorter necks than these, and there are scores of them on our common,” Hetty continued. “I saw Betty plucking one in the kitchen this morning. We’ll have it for dinner—with apple-sauce and…”

“Don’t be a little goose!” Theo interrupted.

“And sage and onions,” Hetty persisted. “Do you love swan, Mr. Warrington?”

“I shot three last winter on our river,” Harry replied simply. “Ours aren’t as white as these—but they eat very well.”

He had no idea that at that very moment, he was being used as a metaphor—Hetty was telling a fable about him, comparing him to the swan, noble yet doomed.

In some ancient Latin text I once read, it was said that long before Virginia was discovered, people were just as slow to understand meaning. So perhaps Theo’s fluttering heart—her tender, sudden stirrings when she first saw the pale, handsome Virginian—was premature. It was not true love, not yet. Like a bird that sings at false dawn, it had awakened too early.

Return to your perch, little creature, and cover your head with your wing. It is not yet light. Rest is better than song. Soon enough, the sky will glow crimson, and you will rise into it, singing your full song to the sun.

Earlier in this chapter, I mentioned: “Three days after his arrival, Harry was walking with…” But if he could walk—indeed, he walked perfectly—he had no reason to remain at Oakhurst. His shoulder was healed, his health restored. He hadn’t even changed his clothes, relying entirely on the Colonel’s generosity for attire. Surely a young man in such condition had no excuse to linger? Duty, love, family ties, and even the washerwoman’s expectations demanded his return to Tunbridge Wells.

Why did he stay?

Could it be he didn’t want to go?

Have you noticed the mysterious S at the beginning of the previous chapter—the faint sketch of Sinbad the Sailor, crowned by that dreadful old sea-man? What if Harry Warrington is that sailor, and his fate the crushing, inevitable old man? What if, for two days now, he has felt those knees tightening around his neck? What if his aunt’s cruel purpose has succeeded, and his former love lies dead—killed not by sword or illness, but by poison from her lips, just as fair Rosamond fell to her royal rival?

Is Hero lighting the lamp and preparing supper, while Leander sits comfortably elsewhere, never thinking of swimming across the dark waters?

Since that cowardly blow struck Lady Maria Esmond’s back by her own kin, can we not feel compassion for her? Yes, she has flaws—perhaps even wears false hair and false jewels. But is she not a woman in distress? Should we mock her because of her years? Between her cruel aunt and her shattered illusions, Lady Maria must endure terrible loneliness at Tunbridge Wells.

No one protects her. Madam Beatrix holds her captive. Lady Maria is poor, hoping for money from her aunt. She carries secrets—secrets the old woman knows and uses like weapons. For myself, I cannot help but feel pity. Imagine her alone, chained like Andromeda to a rock on Mount Ephraim, offered to the dragon of a Baroness!

Succour, Perseus! Come swiftly with your winged feet and shining sword!

But Perseus does not hurry. The dragon feasts on Andromeda day after day.

Harry Warrington, who would not let a dislocated shoulder stop him from hunting, stayed contentedly at Oakhurst, finding each passing day more pleasant than the last. Perhaps he had never, since his grandfather’s death, been in such good company. At home, he lived among Virginian squires—men of fox hunts, horses, punch bowls, and broad shoulders. The ladies he knew were well-bred, pious, and proper, but narrow in spirit. His world was small—filled with pompous customs, petty rules, flattery, and gossip. Until he left, he did not realize how confined his life had been.

Here, at Oakhurst, everything was different. He was among people who had seen the world, though they lived apart from it. Both the Colonel and his wife had known good books—and better, living ones—good company that taught humility and wisdom. Society, when truly good, teaches us our insignificance and introduces us to our betters.

Young reader, if you are reading this, remember: nothing is healthier than acknowledging and learning from those above you. I would not wish my son Thomas to be the top scholar, the best oarsman, the pride of the school. Better for him to have a fair place, decent rivals, and the occasional thrashing—followed by a firm handshake. Who among us, if we could choose, would want to be a prince, surrounded only by servants and fools, while the world remains silent unless we speak?

One of the greatest gifts Harry received at Oakhurst was the realization that he was profoundly ignorant—and that there were many people far wiser than he. Arrogant with some, he became humbly attentive in the presence of those superior to him. He had admired his brother and his friend, the gallant Colonel of Mount Vernon, and considered himself equal to the gentlemen of Castlewood. But here, he met a man who had read more books than he could imagine, who had faced danger and war and emerged unscathed, whose face bore honesty and kindness—qualities Harry instinctively respected.

As for the women—kind, merry, and delightful—they were unlike anyone he had known. More charming than Parson Broadbent’s loud-laughing daughter, equally refined as the Castlewood ladies (except for Madam Beatrix, who sometimes seemed as grand as an empress). Yet after talking with Madam Beatrix, Harry would leave feeling sour, as if the world were full of deceit. But the others—no, they were not prudish. They laughed over Fielding, wept over Richardson, discussed scandals with amusement, not malice. Their neighbors greeted them with warmth, their hospitality was generous. Truly, it is good to be among good people.

Harry may not have known it then, nor fully grasped it until later, but this was a peaceful interlude—a calm, golden hour in a life that would soon be storm-tossed. Nothing dramatic happened. Only sweet sleep, gentle waking, warm welcomes, and quiet joy. The gates of Oakhurst seemed to shut out the harsh world, and within, the people were kinder, purer, more genuine.

He was not in love—not with saucy Hetty, nor with gentle Theo. But when the time came to leave, he clutched both their hands, feeling a deep affection for them. He wished to meet their brothers, sure they must be fine fellows. And Mrs. Lambert—well, she was as sentimental at his departure as if he were the final volume of *Clarissa Harlowe*.

“He is very kind and honest,” Theo said gravely, watching from the terrace as Harry rode away with her father and the servants toward Westerham.

“I don’t think he’s stupid at all now,” Hetty said. “And, mamma, I think he really is like a swan.”

“It felt just like one of the boys going off to school,” the mother murmured.

“Just like it,” Theo echoed, sadly.

“I’m glad he has Papa to ride with him to Westerham,” Hetty added, “and that he bought Farmer Briggs’s horse. I don’t like him going to those Castlewood people. I’m sure Madame Bernstein is a wicked old woman. I expected to see her ride away on her crooked stick.”

“Hush, Hetty!”

“Do you think she’d float if they tried her in the pond, like poor old Mother Hely did at Elmhurst? The other old woman seemed fond of him—I mean the one with the fair hair. She looked very sad when she left. But Madame Bernstein whisked her off with her crutch, and she had to go. I don’t care, Theo. I know she’s a wicked woman. You think everyone’s good because you never do anything wrong yourself.”

“My Theo is a good girl,” the mother said, gazing lovingly at both daughters.

“Then why do we call her a miserable sinner?”

“We are all so, my love,” said the mother gently.

“What, Papa too? You know you don’t think so,” cried Miss Hester.

And that was almost too much for Mrs. Lambert to bear.

“What did you tell John to give to Mr. Warrington’s black man?”

With a touch of shame, she admitted: “A bottle of my cordial water and a cake I had Betty make.”

“I feel quite like a mother to him,” she confessed, “and you know both our boys still carry one of our cakes to school or college.”

Mrs. Lambert, her handkerchief held aloft as a token of farewell, stood with her daughters at the edge of the road, watching the departing travellers until the curve of the lane, thick with lime trees, hid them from view. That grove had long been a silent witness to farewells—her husband marching off to war, her sons riding away to school, each vanishing behind the green screen, returning only when fate allowed. Each departure left behind a quiet ache, softened by memory and love, and nurtured by the stillness of home life. In their absence, the women of Oakhurst found time to dwell on the men who were gone: the empty room where a boy had slept, the imprint of his carpet bag still visible on the bed; the whip hanging in the hall, the fishing rod and basket left unused—silent reminders of days past.

At meals, the absence lingered: the half-eaten cherry tart, once shared with laughter and melancholy; the evening prayers said without one voice; the midnight silence when thoughts turned to the child now far from the nest. Dawn brought no comfort—only the knowledge that the world beyond the gates was hard and demanding. So the limes became more than trees; they were a veil between the domestic warmth of Oakhurst and the uncertain road ahead.

Mrs. Lambert often walked alone to the edge of the grove, her heart heavy. She once mused aloud about carving the names of her loved ones into the silver-grey bark, entwined with true-lovers’ knots—a custom of tender affection. Miss Theo, gifted with poetry, composed verses about the trees, which her mother proudly sent to a journal of the time.

“Now we’re out of sight,” Colonel Lambert called, tipping his hat as he rode past the limes with Mr. Warrington beside him. “My wife always watches from the window until we round this bend. I hope you’ll see these trees and this house again, Mr. Warrington. The boys are home now—perhaps there’ll be better sport for you.”

“I’ve never been happier,” replied Warrington, “and I feel as though I’m leaving old friends behind.”

“The man we’ll dine with tonight has a son—an old friend of our family,” said the Colonel. “My wife, ever eager for matches, would have paired him with one of my girls—had not the young fellow fallen in love with someone else.”

“Oh?” sighed Warrington. “Others have done the same. There were brave men before Agamemnon.”

“Pardon me, sir,” the younger man interjected, “but I didn’t catch the name—Aga…?”

“No,” laughed the Colonel, “his name is James Wolfe. He’s barely thirty, yet the youngest lieutenant-colonel in the army—unless we count the nobility, who take rank above us commoners.”

“Of course,” said the young companion, nodding with colonial deference to aristocratic order.

“And I’ve seen him command captains—brave men, all—some thirty years his senior, none of whom could match his merit or fortune. Yet no one envies him. We all admit he’s our superior. He’s beloved by every man in his old regiment, knows each one by name. A scholar too—he speaks many languages.”

“Ah,” breathed Harry Warrington, “I feel I’ve wasted my youth. I come to England an ignoramus. Had my brother lived, he would have carried our name with dignity. George was a scholar, a musician, a man who could hold his own among the most learned. I’m glad to be here, especially to you, if only to learn how much I don’t know.”

“If you know that,” smiled the Colonel, “you’ve already gained much.”

“At home, since my brother died, I used to think myself quite remarkable. I suppose folks flattered me. Now I see I was wrong. I wish I knew more of books and less of dogs and horses.”

“Dogs and horses are fine books too,” said the Colonel. “Some men aren’t meant to be scholars. They may still be worthy citizens. Why should all of us strive to be wise or great? His Royal Highness commands, Martin Lambert is colonel, Jack Hunt—riding behind us—is a groom. Each does his duty. Who can say which station is higher? Perhaps Jack’s currycomb, my epaulettes, or the Prince’s baton are equal in the eyes of Heaven. When I began life, I dreamed of glory. Now I dream of duty—and of those we left behind. Let us ride on. We’ll reach Westerham before night.”

At Westerham, they were welcomed by a stately matron, an elderly soldier whose service spanned forty-five years, and their son—Lieutenant-Colonel James Wolfe of Kingsley’s regiment, then stationed at Maidstone. Harry watched the young officer with interest. He was lean, pale, with red hair and sharp features—no beauty in his face. But his manners were refined, his greetings warm, and his conversation lively enough to make one forget his plain looks.

Mr. Warrington was bound for Tunbridge? Then James would accompany him, the lady said, whispering something to Colonel Lambert at supper. The Colonel raised his glass and toasted “Miss Lowther.”

“With all my heart!” cried James, draining his cup.

The hostess murmured to her friend that James and Miss Lowther were destined to marry—she came from the famed Lowther family of the North.

“If she were Charlemagne’s daughter,” said Lambert, “she’d still be good enough for James—or for any son of mine.”

“She wouldn’t be so keen on that,” James declared.

“Oh, of course,” chimed in the mother, “she’s the priceless pearl, and you’re nothing.”

“No,” said James firmly, “I agree with Colonel Lambert. If she brought all of Cumberland as a jointure, it would be my due. That’s how it goes, Mr. Warrington. We nurse our children through fevers and smallpox, send them to war, break our hearts at parting, and get them home only for a few weeks a year. Then along comes a girl with bright eyes—and our boy is gone, never thinking of us again.”

“And pray, my dear,” asked the elder Colonel Wolfe, “how did you come to marry James’s father?”

“Because he had gout and needed someone to care for him,” she replied. “Not because I liked him much.” And so the evening passed in easy talk and gentle humor.

The next day, Colonel Lambert bid farewell to his guest with heartfelt kindness, turning his horse homeward while Harry and James rode toward Tunbridge Wells.

Wolfe was eager to arrive. Warrington, perhaps less so—his thoughts lingering on Oakhurst, on the calm days spent in that peaceful home.

James praised the Lamberts warmly—father, mother, daughters, all.

“To live as Colonel Lambert lives, and to carry such a name,” said Wolfe, “seems to me the height of human ambition.”

“And glory?” asked Warrington. “Is that nothing? Would you give up fame?”

“It was my dream once,” replied Wolfe. “But now my desires are quieter. I’ve served since fourteen. I’ve known every kind of duty, visited every garrison town, served wherever there was work. I’ve done nearly all a soldier’s tasks—except command an army, which is unlikely for one of my age. Now I crave peace: books, a wife, children on my knee. I’ve imagined such a life. True love is better than glory. A quiet hearth, with the woman of your heart beside it—that is the greatest gift the gods can give.”

Harry pictured the scene. He nodded, but his expression was somber. James noticed.

“You say ‘yes’ as if a fireside and a sweetheart weren’t to your taste.”

“Well,” said Harry, “there are other things a young man might want. You’ve seen sixteen years of the world. I’ve just left my mother’s apron strings. When I’ve fought campaigns, like you, distinguished myself—then I may think of retiring.”

To this, James, his heart full of another matter, responded with a passionate defense of marriage, praising the virtues of his beloved—words that thrilled him, though perhaps not his listener, whose views on wedlock were faintly bleak.

They reached Tunbridge Wells by late afternoon, uneventfully—save for a moment when Harry, mistaking two riders for highwaymen, drew his pistol. James laughed and stopped him: “Only innkeepers’ agents—robbers only in trade.”

Gumbo, their horse, bolted briefly, causing much shouting, but was soon recovered. They entered the town, checked into their inn, and parted ways, each seeking the ladies they had come to visit.

Mr. Warrington found his aunt installed in elegant lodgings, guarded by London footmen. She greeted him warmly. Lady Maria was absent—whether he regretted this, or concealed his feelings, remained unknown. Madame de Bernstein, meanwhile, received him with several visitors: a dandy in rich brocade, two dowagers in vast hoops and rouge.

She introduced Harry as “the young Croesus from Virginia,” speaking of his estate—“as large as Kent, and infinitely richer.” She told how her half-sister, Madam Esmond, was known as Princess Pocahontas in America. She praised his mother and son endlessly—wealth, character, virtue.

The dandy shook Harry’s hand, delighted. The ladies lavished praise upon him. He blushed under their adoration.

When they departed, the Baroness turned to her nephew.

“You couldn’t have arrived at a better time,” she said. “Those three have tongues like bells. They’ll spread your name across every drawing room. I’ve already introduced you to a hundred people—and lied shamelessly about Virginia. I’ve filled it with gold mines, spices, diamonds—possibly even elephants. Your mother, I’ve claimed, rules over a kingdom with armies of negroes. It’s a magnificent dominion. I don’t know exactly how much she earns—but it’s enormous. And you, my dear, will be treated as heir to this royal lady. Don’t let it go to your head.”

“But why must I be so rich?” Harry asked.

“To open doors,” she replied. “Being thought rich is as good as being rich. People will assume you hoard your money—that’ll do you good. Mothers will smile. Daughters will curtsey. When I was young, I tried to improve my lot through marriage. Your grandmother, a saint save for a little jealousy, scolded me—called me worldly. Worldly? So is the world. We must serve it as it serves us. Give it nothing for nothing.”

“Henry Esmond Warrington,” she added, “I adore those two names. Coming here or to London, you’d have been nobody. Our protection means little. Our family has little credit—Castlewood was suspected in ’45, ruined by gambling. He’s lost everything—mortgages devour his estate. He’s tried every scheme. Once, I feared my diamonds were unsafe with him—I traveled without them. Terrible, isn’t it, to speak so of one’s own nephew? But you are my nephew too—and untouched by the world. I warn you: it is wicked.”

She spoke of Harry’s card games with Will and the chaplain—“harmless fun,” she said. “But had you played with Castlewood, you’d have lost everything. I warned him to keep his hands off you.”

“You interfered to protect me?”

“I kept his claws from you. Be thankful you escaped with flesh on your bones. Gambling has consumed our family. My brother played. Both his wives—especially the last—live only for cards. I wouldn’t leave you alone with her. The passion is too strong. They’d fleece you, then fight over the spoils. Castlewood’s position at Court is Will’s fortune—and Maria’s and Fanny’s.”

“And do they play?”

“No—Molly doesn’t. But Fanny, in London, bets her eyes out. I know the passion. I had it—like measles. Not cured. For a poor old woman, there’s nothing left but cards. You’ll see high stakes tonight. Hush—this is what I need. At Castlewood, I couldn’t win from my nieces or their mother. They refused to pay. Best to warn you now—lest you be shocked.”

A few days earlier, Harry—then fond of cards, cockfighting, betting—would have laughed at such confession. Among the Castlewoods, morality was mocked. Faith and honor were jokes. Selfishness was normal. Duties were sneered at. Sin was shrugged off. They didn’t pretend to be better than others—they lived with them, joked about them, took their share of pleasure and plunder. They lived day by day, without pretense.

Such people are rare today. Human nature has changed. Card-playing is nearly extinct—few fashionable ladies know Spadille from Manille.

“How dull you must have found those village folk,” said Madame de Bernstein, patting his cheek. “But the savages were kind, child!”

“They were very kind,” Harry replied, his face flushing. “It wasn’t dull at all. I think they’re some of the best people in the world.”

His aunt’s tone offended him. He couldn’t bear anyone slighting the new friends he’d found. He didn’t want them spoken of in such company.

The old lady, quick to anger, paused. *Those two girls—sickbed—interesting stranger—of course he’s fallen for one of them.*

Madame de Bernstein glanced mischievously at Lady Maria, who entered the room just then.

Cousin Maria made her entrance, accompanied by two gardener’s boys carrying baskets brimming with flowers—roses, sweet-williams, and other blooms—to adorn Madame de Bernstein’s drawing-room in anticipation of the evening’s guests. Three footmen in livery, their coats trimmed with elaborate worsted lace, set up twice as many card-tables as were needed. A major-domo, dressed in black with a powdered wig and ruffled sleeves that seemed to demand a sword at his side, followed behind, bearing bundles of wax candles. He placed pairs on each table and lit the silver sconces along the wainscoted walls, which now shimmered under the slanting golden rays of the afternoon sun. Beyond the windows, the green common stretched out, dotted with rocks, clusters of trees, and houses gleaming in the light. Figures in bright silks, hoops, and powdered wigs strolled across the grass, casting dappled shadows upon the earth.

On the opposite side of the Baroness’s windows lay the Pantiles, where a constant fair buzzed with activity. The clatter of voices and the hum of conversation drifted through the air, mingling with the strains of a band playing for the visitors at the Wells. Madame de Bernstein’s sitting room might not have suited a recluse or scholar, but for those who thrived on liveliness, elegance, and a view into the heart of society, it was an ideal retreat. When the lights were lit, passersby below could see that her ladyship was entertaining—and that admission to her gathering was within reach.

It struck one as curious, reflecting on the past, how dimly society lived just a century earlier. For every candle we now burn in a drawing-room, there had been scarcely one back then—let alone gaslight or electric illumination. Tallow lamps smoked and reeked in hallways; the candle-snuffer was a familiar figure even in theatres. Look at Hogarth’s prints: how dark they are! How grimy the feasts appear, as if coated in grease. In *Marriage à la Mode*, Lord Viscount Squanderfield’s grand salons—where he and his wife sit yawning before their horrified steward after a soirée—are lit by only eight candles: one per card-table, half a dozen in a brass chandelier. If Jack Briefless hosted friends for oysters and beer in his chambers at Pump Court, he might have doubled that number. Let us be grateful that Louis XIV, in all his splendour, once held court in near darkness—and bless Mr. Price and others who brought light to our lives, banishing the foul mutton-fat tapers of old.

Maria, radiant herself like a bloom among flowers, arranged the blossoms in vases and ornate jars around the room. She lingered over each vessel, her eyes darting shyly toward young cousin Harry, whose own flush would have flattered any maiden. One might have thought she meant to stay longer than her aunt intended. But the Baroness, seated firmly in her armchair with her crooked tortoiseshell cane in hand, gave orders with imperious precision. She scolded Tom for a darned stocking, John for greasing his hair too lavishly from the candle-box—maintaining strict control over her staff.

Another truth about life a hundred years ago: people shared beds—two in one, four in a single room, often in cellars—and washed in wooden troughs such as one might still find only in military barracks today.

Had Maria hoped for a private moment with Harry? Her hopes were dashed. “Where will you dine, Harry?” asked Madame de Bernstein. “My niece Maria and I shall enjoy a simple chicken in the little parlour. You should go to the best ordinary—the White Horse serves at three o’clock. We’ll hear their bell soon enough. And understand this, sir: do not stint yourself. Behave as if you were the son of Princess Pocahontas. Your trunks have already been taken to the lodging I’ve secured for you. It does no good for a young man to hover about two old women. Does it, Maria?”

“No,” replied her ladyship, lowering her eyes meekly—while the other woman’s gaze flashed triumphantly.

Andromeda, one might say, had suffered greatly beneath the Dragon’s shadow these past days. Had Perseus struck off its head, it would have been no unjustifiable act. Yet Harry did not draw sword or shield. He merely watched the lacqueys in their tawny and blue liveries creaking about the room.

“And there are fine mercers and tailors from London always present here, ready to serve the company at the Wells,” continued the Baroness. “You’d best visit them, my dear—your suit is not quite up to fashion. A touch of lace…”

“I cannot leave mourning, ma'am,” said the young man, glancing down at his black garments.

“Ho, sir!” exclaimed the Baroness, rising sharply on her cane. “Wear black for your brother until you’re as old as Methuselah, if you wish. I care not to stop you. I only insist that you dress properly, like others, and make a fitting appearance for your name.”

“Madam,” replied Mr. Warrington with solemn dignity, “I believe I have done nothing to bring shame upon it.”

Why did the old woman pause, as if struck?

Let bygones be bygones. Between them had passed many such exchanges—sharp words, quick retorts, like swords crossed and thrusts parried. Yet she respected him more for standing firm against her.

“Surely,” she said, forcing a laugh, “a finer shirt than that one won’t disgrace you, sir.”

Harry bowed, his face warming. The linen was a gift from his Oakhurst friends—a token of simplicity and sincerity. He felt oddly proud to wear it, remembering those kind souls: so pure, so honest, so full of gentle strength. In their presence, evil seemed powerless.

He promised to return after dressing in his best linen.

“Come back here, sir,” said Madame de Bernstein, “and if our guests haven’t arrived, Maria and I shall find you some ruffles!”

Under the guidance of a footman, Harry left for his new lodgings.

There he found not only spacious, elegant rooms but also a groom awaiting employment and a second valet, should he choose to hire one for Mr. Gumbo. Within minutes, messengers from a London tailor and bootmaker arrived—bearing cards and greetings from Messrs. Regnier and Tull. Gumbo laid out the finest items from Harry’s wardrobe, including the delicate linen his thrifty Virginian mother had carefully provided.

Images of home rose before him—the snow-covered fields of Castlewood, the crackling fire, the quiet ladies knitting by the hearth. For the first time, a flicker of doubt crossed his mind: perhaps his plain clothes weren’t smart enough, his homemade linen not as fine as it might be. To feel ashamed of anything connected to Castlewood? That was strange. At home, everyone took pride in what was made there. Madam Esmond, when sending her son abroad, believed no noble youth needed better provisions.

True, the clothes might have fit better or been more modern—but when Harry emerged from his chamber, fully dressed, he carried himself with grace. Gumbo summoned a chair, walked beside it, and escorted him to the White Horse ordinary, where he was to dine.

He expected to meet the gentleman he had briefly encountered earlier at his aunt’s—someone who had recommended the White Horse as the most fashionable place to dine. He mentioned the man’s name to the host, but the landlord and waiters greeted him with smiles and bows, assuring him he needed no introduction. They helped him hang up his coat and sword, offered wine—Burgundy, Pontac, or champagne—and led him to a table.

Though the most popular ordinary in Tunbridge Wells, the White Horse was not crowded that day. Monsieur Barbeau, the landlord, informed Harry that a grand entertainment at Summer Hill had drawn most of the guests away. As Harry entered, only four other men occupied the room. Two had finished their meals and were drinking wine; the other two were mid-dinner. The landlord must have whispered Harry’s name to them, for they glanced his way with interest and offered a polite bow across the table as the host bustled off to fetch his dinner.

Mr. Warrington returned their greeting. One of the younger men welcomed him to Tunbridge Wells and expressed hope he would grow fond of the place. Then they exchanged knowing looks—glances Harry could not interpret, nor understand why they directed them toward the two older men at the far end of the room.

One of these elders wore a worn velvet coat, a long queue, voluminous ruffles, and heavy embroidery. The other was short, broad-shouldered, with beetle brows and a hooked nose. His companion addressed him as “milor”—my lord—in a loud voice.

The lord, sipping wine, barely acknowledged Harry before turning to his friend.

“And so you know the nephew of the old woman—the Croesus who has just arrived?”

“You’re mistaken there, Jack,” replied the younger man. “Never could master the language.”

“Indeed,” said Jack. “But surely, my dear lord, you’ve shown energy. He’s been here less than two hours. My servants told me of him only as I came to dinner.”

“I knew him before,” said the Baron. “I’ve met him often in London with the Baroness and my lord, his cousin.”

A steaming soup arrived for Harry, carried by the smiling host.

“Behold, sir! Behold a potage of my own creation!” declared Monsieur Barbeau, placing the dish before Harry and whispering the name of the nobleman across the table.

Harry thanked him in English. The foreign gentleman turned, grinned broadly, and said, “Fous bossedez notre langue barfaidement, monsieur.”

Harry had never heard French spoken so strangely in Canada. He bowed politely in return.

“Tell me more about the Croesus, my good Baron,” continued the lord, speaking with a tone of condescension, ignoring Harry entirely—perhaps irritating the young man.

“What shall I tell you, my dear lord? Croesus is a youth like any other—tall, awkward, with black hair, as most from the Indies have. Lodgings have been taken for him at Mrs. Rose’s toy-shop.”

“I have lodgings there too,” Harry thought. “Who is Croesus? And how delicious this soup is!”

“He travels with a large retinue—four servants, two postchaises, outriders. His chief attendant is a Black man who saved his life from savages in America and refuses, under any circumstances, to be freed. He wears mourning for his elder brother, from whom he inherits his principality.”

“Could anything console you for the loss of yours, Chevalier?” asked the elder gentleman.

“Milor,” replied the Chevalier, “his property might—though you know it is not small.”

“Your brother lives on his patrimony—which you’ve told me is immense. You, by your industry, my dear Chevalier.”

“Milor!” said the Chevalier, raising his voice. “By your industry—or your esprit—how much more noble! Shall you be at the Baroness’s tonight? She ought to be a little of your parents, Chevalier?”

“Again I fail to comprehend your lordship,” said the other, rather sourly.

“Oh, come now,” the lord replied. “She is a woman of wit, noble birth, great adventures—though lacking principle. But what do we men of the world care? You intend to play cards with the young Creole, no doubt, and drain him dry. By the way, Baron—suppose this young Creole is a trap? Suppose our dear friend invented him in London, bringing him down with a reputation for wealth to prey on innocent folk here?”

“J’y ai souvent pense, milor,” said the little Baron, touching his nose knowingly. “That Baroness is capable of anything.”

“A Baron—a Baroness, que voulez-vous? I mean the late lamented husband. Do you know who he was?”

“Intimately. A more notorious villain never dealt a card. At Venice, Brussels, Spa, Vienna—he knew the prisons of every city. I knew the man, my lord.”

“I thought you would. I saw him at the Hague, where I first had the honour of meeting you. A more disreputable rogue never entered my doors. A minister must open his gates to all sorts—spies, sharpers, ruffians.”

“Parbleu, milor, how you treat them!”

“A man of my rank—of the rank I held then—must see all sorts. Entre autres, your acquaintance. What could his wife possibly want with such a name?”

“Apparently, it was better than hers.”

“Effectively! So I’ve heard of my friend Paddy swapping clothes with a scarecrow. I don’t know which name is more distinguished—the English bishop’s or the German baron’s.”

“My lord,” the other gentleman said, rising and laying a hand on a large star pinned to his coat, “you forget—I too am a Baron and a Chevalier of the Holy Roman Order.”

“—Of the Spur! Not in the least, my dear knight and baron! You will have no more wine? We shall meet at Madame de Bernstein’s tonight.”

The knight and baron left the table, fumbling in their embroidered pockets as if searching for coins. The waiter handed him his laced hat, but the nobleman waved him away with a hand adorned with rings and wide ruffles, then strode out of the room.

Only when the man called “my lord” began speaking of the bishop’s widow and the German baron’s wife did Harry realize his aunt and himself had been the subject of their conversation. Before the thought fully settled, one speaker had departed. The other turned to a nearby table and said, “What a little sharper he is! Everything I said about Bernstein applies mutato nomine to him. I knew the fellow was a spy and a rogue. He’s changed religions God knows how many times. I had him expelled from the Hague myself when I was ambassador—and I know he was caned in Vienna.”

“I wonder my Lord Chesterfield associates with such a villain!” Harry burst out.

The other diners looked up. To his surprise, the nobleman continued talking as if nothing had happened.

“There cannot be a more fieffe coquin than this Poellnitz. Why, Heaven be thanked, he has actually left me my snuff-box! You laugh? The fellow is capable of taking it.”

And my lord assumed the laughter was at his own satire.

“You are quite right, sir,” said one of the two diners, turning to Harry. “Though, saving your presence, I don’t know what business it is of yours. My lord plays with anyone who will set a pack of cards before him. Don’t worry—he’s as deaf as a post and didnI hear a word. That’s why he plays with anyone who offers cards—that’s why he consorts with this rogue.”

“Faith, I know other noblemen who aren’t particular about their company,” said Mr. Jack.

“Do you mean because I associate with you? I know my company, my good friend, and I defy most men to have the better of me.”

Meanwhile, the nobleman opposite paid no attention to Harry’s outburst. He spoke in French with Monsieur Barbeau, complimenting him on the dinner.

The host bowed repeatedly, delighted that his Excellency approved—remembering well the art he’d learned during his youth in Ireland.

“The salmi suits your lordship?” asked Barbeau.

“I have just served it to the young American seigneur opposite—the gentleman from Virginia.”

“To whom?” the lord asked, his pale face flushing slightly as he turned toward Harry.

“To the young gentleman from Virginia who has just arrived—and who speaks our beautiful language perfectly!” said Barbeau, hoping to please both parties.

“And to whom your lordship will be answerable for slanderous remarks about my family, spoken in the presence of these gentlemen!” Harry shouted, determined his opponent would hear.

“You must call into his ear,” said one of the younger guests. “Then he may perchance hear you.”

“I will ensure he understands my meaning—one way or another,” Harry declared with dignity. “I will not allow calumnies about my relatives to be spoken by him or any man!”

As Harry spoke, the nobleman opposite had not heard him—but had time to prepare his reply. He rose, wiped his mouth with a handkerchief, and placed his fingers lightly on the table.

“Sir,” he said, “you will believe, on the word of a gentleman, that I had no idea before whom I was speaking. It seems my acquaintance, Monsieur de Poellnitz, knew you no better than I. Had I known you, I assure you I would never have uttered a syllable to cause you distress. I offer my deepest regrets and apologies before my Lord March and Mr. Morris here present.”

To this, Harry could only bow and mutter thanks. The nobleman pretended to hear, bowed deeply, and said he would have the honour of visiting Mr. Warrington at his lodgings. Then he saluted the company and departed.

Within the quiet precincts of the White Horse Tavern, a well-kept bowling green stretched beside the dining room, where guests might sit at small tables beneath the shade of trees and sip punch or tea. The three gentlemen—Mr. Warrington, Lord March, and Jack Morris—had finished their dinner nearly at once, and it was Mr. Morris who proposed they adjourn to the green for a cool bottle. “Jack Morris would move to the Dust Hole,” remarked my lord, “just to find another reason for a drink.” To which Jack replied with a grin that every man had his own way of stepping into mischief—and his own weakness. For him, it was the bottle.

“My Lord Chesterfield’s weakness is deuce-ace,” observed Lord March. “He cannot stay away from cards or dice.”

“And my Lord March has not one vice,” retorted the young gentleman, “but many. He loves gambling, horse-racing, betting, drinking, eating, money, women—indeed, he loves everything. And you’ve fallen into bad company, Mr. Warrington, by coming near such a man. He’ll play you for every acre you own in Virginia.”

“With the greatest pleasure in life!” interjected Lord March.

“For all your tobacco, your spices, your slaves, your oxen, your asses—everything that belongs to you!”

“Shall we begin now?” said Lord March. “Jack, you’re never without a dice-box or a corkscrew. I’ll set Mr. Warrington against whatever he likes.”

“Regrettably,” replied Harry, “the tobacco, the slaves, the beasts—they’re not mine yet. I’ve only just come of age, and my mother, though scarcely twenty years older than I, is as likely to live long as I am.”

“I’ll wager you outlive her,” declared Lord March. “I’ll pay you now, four times what I’ll pay when she dies. Let’s settle this over this table: a fair sum against the inheritance of your estate in Virginia. What do you call your place?”

“Castlewood.”

“A principality, I hear,” said Lord March. “And I suspect its value has been inflated tenfold among these idle gossips. How did you get the name Castlewood? Are you related to my lord?”

“Oh, I know,” he added, “your mother descends from the true line of the family. That branch took the losing side in ’15. I’ve heard the tale a dozen times from my old Duchess. She knew your grandfather. A man of letters, no doubt—friend to Addison, Steele, Pope, Milton, the great men of the age. A pity he didn’t stay home and send the other branch off to the colonies.”

“I’ve just returned from Castlewood,” remarked Mr. Warrington. “I stayed with my cousin there.”

“Ah! Did you play cards with him? He’s fond of pasteboard and bones.”

“Never—only sixpences and a pool with the ladies.”

“So much the better for both of you. But did you play with Will Esmond, if he was home? I’ll lay ten to one you did.”

Harry blushed slightly and admitted that in the evenings, he and his cousin had played a few hands.

“And Tom Sampson, the chaplain?” cried Jack Morris. “Was he part of the party? I swear Tom made a third. God save you from Tom and Will Esmond together!”

“Truth be told,” said Harry, “I won from both of them.”

“And they paid you? Well, miracles never cease!”

“I didn’t say anything about miracles,” Harry remarked, smiling over his wine.

“And you don’t tell tales out of school—the volto sciolto—eh, Mr. Warrington?” asked Lord March.

“I beg your pardon,” said Harry bluntly. “French is the only language besides my own that I understand.”

“My Lord March learned Italian at the Opera,” remarked Jack Morris. “And it cost him a pretty penny.”

“We must show him the Opera,” he added. “Mustn’t we, March?”

“Must we, Morris?” replied Lord March, as if mildly offended by the familiarity.

Both men were dressed alike: small scratch wigs without powder, blue frocks with plate buttons, buckskins and riding boots, little hats adorned with narrow lace cords—no outward sign of fashion, but practical for the road.

“I don’t care much for the Opera,” said Harry, warming with the Burgundy. “But I’d like to see Newmarket. I long to watch a real English hunting field.”

“We’ll take you to Newmarket and the hunt,” said Lord March. “Can you ride well?”

“I think so,” answered Harry. “And I can shoot fairly, and jump a bit.”

“What’s your weight? I’ll bet we’re even—or I weigh more. I’ll bet Jack Morris beats you at birds or marks at twenty-five paces. I’ll bet I jump farther than you on this grass.”

“I don’t know Mr. Morris’s shooting—I’ve never seen either of you before—but I’ll take your bets, my lord, at any odds,” said Harry, now quite flushed with wine.

“Ponies on each!” shouted Lord March.

“Done and done!” echoed both men. Harry felt it was a matter of honor to accept any challenge laid before him.

“We can try the last bet now, if your feet are steady,” said Lord March, springing up and stretching his limbs. He removed his boots, then his coat and waistcoat, fastening his belt tightly around his waist and tossing his clothes to the ground.

Harry, however, held more respect for his garments. It was his best suit. He carefully removed his velvet coat and waistcoat, folded them neatly, and, seeing the tables nearby were splashed with drink, carried them inside to place them on a dry table near the open window.

At that moment, a new guest entered—the Colonel Wolfe, soberly enjoying a chicken and salad with a modest pint of wine. Harry, full of spirits, approached him. “Colonel,” he said, “I’ve got a bet with Lord March—would you stand me half?”

The Colonel smiled. “Too poor to bet, sir. But I’ll come out and see fair play.”

So he set down his glass and followed his young friend through the open window.

“Who is that tallow-faced fellow with the red hair?” asked Jack Morris, whose wine had begun to affect him.

Mr. Warrington explained: “That’s Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe, of the 20th Regiment.”

“Your humble servant, gentlemen!” said the Colonel, offering a stiff military salute.

“Never saw such a figure in my life!” exclaimed Jack Morris. “Did you, March?”

“I beg your pardon,” said the Colonel, looking surprised. “You said March?”

“I am the Earl of March, sir,” said the nobleman, bowing. “My friend, Mr. Morris, is so close to me that after dinner, we’re like brothers.”

Why isn’t all Tunbridge Wells here to hear this? thought Morris, delighted. He could not resist shouting, “Two to one on my lord!”

“Done!” called Mr. Warrington. Jack, caught up in the moment, had to cry “Done!” too.

“Take him, Colonel,” whispered Harry.

But the Colonel shook his head. “I can’t afford to lose, so I can’t hope to win.”

“I see you’ve already won one of our bets, Mr. Warrington,” said Lord March. “I’m taller by an inch or two, but you’re broader across the shoulders.”

“Pooh, my dear Will!” cried Jack. “I bet you weigh twice as much as he does!”

“Done, Jack!” laughed Lord March. “All bets are ponies. Will you take him, Mr. Warrington?”

“No, my dear fellow—one’s enough,” said Jack.

“Very good,” replied Lord March. “Now let’s settle the next wager.”

Harry, already dressed in his finest silk stockings, black satin breeches, and neat pumps, refused to remove his shoes, unlike his opponent, whose heavy riding boots and spurs were ill-suited for jumping. Before them lay a smooth stretch of grass, thirty yards long—perfect for a run and a leap. A gravel path ran around it, beyond which stood a wall with a gate bearing the Hanoverian arms: a white horse rampant between two skittles, with the landlord’s name and motto inscribed below.

Lord March placed a handkerchief on the ground as the starting point. Mr. Wolfe stood at the far end to mark where each jumper landed.

“My lord went first,” wrote Mr. Warrington later in a letter to Mrs. Mountain at Castlewood, Virginia—a letter still preserved. “He wanted me to go first, but remembering the story of Fontenoy that my dear George used to tell, I said, ‘Monseigneur le Comte, tirez le premier, s’il vous plaît.’ So he ran barefoot, and for the honor of Old Virginia, I beat him by more than two feet—two feet nine inches, to be exact. I jumped twenty-one feet three inches, measured by the tavern keeper’s tape, while his lordship managed only eighteen feet six. I’d already guessed his weight the moment I saw him. So he and Mr. Jack paid me both bets. With deepest respect to my mother—she’ll not be displeased. I bet for the honor of the Old Dominion, and my opponent was a nobleman of the highest rank, holding two earldoms and heir to a dukedom. Betting is the rage here—every young man of fashion is betting from dawn till dusk.

“I told them—perhaps that was my mistake—that there was a man back home who could beat me by a full foot. When they asked who, I said Colonel G. Washington of Mount Vernon—because he can, and he’s the only man in either our counties who can. Mr. Wolfe questioned me at length about Colonel Washington, showed he’d heard of him, and spoke of last year’s unfortunate campaign as if he knew every inch of the ground. He knew all our rivers—though he called the Potomac ‘Pottamac,’ which made us laugh. My Lord March and Ruglen were in no way upset by losing; they handed me notes from their pocketbooks, filling my own, which had grown quite empty thanks to payments to servants at my cousin’s house and the purchase of a horse at Oakhurst. I may need to draw again on my mother or her agents in London or Bristol.”

After their feats, the four men strolled from the garden into the public walk, where a crowd had gathered. Jack Morris, frank and loud, began making remarks—some of them less than polite. When Lord March made a joke (and he made many), Jack roared, “Oh, ho, ho! Oh, good Gad! Oh, my dear earl! Oh, my dear lord, you’ll be the death of me!” “It seemed,” wrote Harry sagely to Mrs. Mountain, “as if he wished everyone to know his companion was an earl!”

Indeed, the walk was filled with a wide array of characters. M. Poellnitz passed by, no more elegantly dressed than at dinner, grinning and tipping his large laced hat with tarnished feathers. Then came Lord Chesterfield, in a pearl-colored suit, blue ribbon and star, saluting the young men in turn.

“I’ll back the old boy for taking his hat off against the whole kingdom, and France too,” said Lord March. “He hasn’t changed his hat’s shape in twenty years. Look—there it goes again! Do you see that big, awkward, pock-marked man with the snuff-colored face? He barely touches his clumsy beaver in return. D—— his impudence—do you know who that is?”

“No, curse him! Who is it, March?” asked Jack, swearing.

“It’s Johnson, the Dictionary-maker. Lord Chesterfield wrote some brilliant articles to promote him when his dictionary came out. I know they were brilliant—Horry Walpole said so, and he knows these things. Confound the impudent schoolmaster!”

“Hang him—he should stand in the pillory!” cried Jack.

“That fat man walking with him is another writer—a printer named Richardson. He wrote *Clarissa*, you know.”

“Great heavens, my lord—is that the great Richardson? Is that the man who wrote *Clarissa*?” exclaimed Colonel Wolfe and Mr. Warrington together.

Harry rushed forward to look at the elderly gentleman, slowly walking with a train of admiring ladies.

“Indeed, my dear sir,” one woman said, “you are too great and good to live in such a world. But surely you were sent to teach it virtue!”

“Ah, Miss Mulso,” replied the kind, round-faced man, raising his eyes upward, “who shall teach the teacher? Even he has faults and errors. Even his age and experience do not prevent him from stumbl—Heaven bless my soul, Mr. Johnson! I beg your pardon if I trod on your corn.”

“You have done both, sir—you’ve trod on the corn and received the pardon,” said Mr. Johnson, muttering verses as he walked, eyes fixed downward, hands behind him, occasionally threatening the honest eyes of his companion with his cane.

“They don’t see well, my dear Mulso,” he said. “But even so, I would keep my lash from Mr. Johnson’s cudgel. Your servant, sir.” He bowed low and tipped his hat to Mr. Warrington, who stepped back, blushing deeply, after returning the greeting. The great author was accustomed to adoration. No gentler wind ever stirred mortal vanity. Enraptured spinsters scattered tea leaves at his feet, offered him coffee, kissed the slippers they had knitted for him. A halo of virtue surrounded his nightcap. All Europe had trembled, wept, admired over the pages of this kindly, honest man with the round belly. Harry returned glowing with pride at having received a bow from him. “Ah!” he said, “my lord, I am glad to have seen him!”

“Seen him? Why, dammy, you can see him any day in his shop, I suppose?” laughed Jack.

“My brother insisted that he and Mr. Fielding—wasn’t that his name?—were the greatest geniuses in England. He often said that when we came to Europe, his first pilgrimage would be to Mr. Richardson,” said Harry, always passionate, honest, and tender when speaking of his dear friend.

“Your brother spoke like a man,” said Colonel Wolfe, his pale face flushing. “I would rather be a man of genius than a peer of the realm.”

“Every man to his taste, Colonel,” said Lord March, amused. “Your enthusiasm—nothing personal—I assure you—it refreshes me.”

“So it does me—by gad—perfectly refreshes me,” said Jack.

“So it does Jack—you see—it actually refreshes Jack! Now, Jack, which would you rather be? A fat old printer who wrote a story about a ruined girl, or a peer of Parliament with ten thousand a year?”

“March—my Lord March, do you take me for a fool?” asked Jack, voice trembling. “Have I done anything to deserve such words from you?”

“I would rather win honor than honours. I would rather have genius than wealth. I would rather make my name than inherit it, though my father’s, thank God, is an honest one,” said the young Colonel. “But forgive me, gentlemen,” and with a quick bow, he crossed the parade toward a young lady, an older woman, and a gentleman approaching.

“It’s the beautiful Miss Lowther. I remember now,” said Lord March. “Look—he takes her arm! They say he’s engaged to her.”

“You don’t mean such a fellow is engaged to one of the Lowthers of the North?” cried Jack. “Curse me, what has become of the world—with printers, half-pay ensigns, schoolmasters, and this infernal nonsense?”

The Dictionary-maker, who had shown so little desire to bow to Lord Chesterfield earlier, now removed his beaver and bowed almost to the ground before a florid figure in a large round hat, bands, and gown. This was the Bishop of Salisbury, wearing proudly the blue riband and badge of the Garter, of which he was prelate.

Mr. Johnson stood hat in hand throughout the conversation with Dr. Gilbert, who praised Mr. Richardson extravagantly—calling him the defender of virtue, the preacher of sound morals, the pillar of religion—all of which the printer believed wholeheartedly.

Let no young lady rush to her grandfather’s bookshelf because of this praise and rashly pull down *Clarissa*. She would not care to read the volumes that once made her ancestors weep and tremble. Once celebrated from pulpits to palaces, now they gather dust. I wonder—have our women become more virtuous, or merely more sensitive? If the former, then Miss Smith of New York is certainly more modest than Miss Smith of London, who still says tables, pianos, and animals have legs. Oh, faithful Samuel Richardson! Has the news reached you in Hades that your sublime novels are now hidden away, unread, as if *Clarissa* were as forbidden as *Tom Jones*? Rise, Samuel, and reconcile yourself with your hated brother-scribe. I wonder—if a century hence, today’s novels will be locked behind wires and make maidens blush?

“Who is that strange woman in the high headdress of my grandmother’s time, speaking to Mr. Richardson?” asked Harry, as a fantastically dressed lady approached and curtseyed to the printer.

Jack Morris nervously struck Harry with the butt of his whip. Lord March laughed.

“That queer person is my gracious kinswoman, Katharine, Duchess of Dover and Queensberry, at your service, Mr. Warrington. She was once a beauty! Changed now, isn’t she? What an old Gorgon! She’s a great patron of authors. When that old frump was young, poets wrote verses about her.”

Lord March briefly left his friends to greet the duchess, while Jack explained to Harry how, upon the Duke’s death, Lord March would inherit the dukedoms.

“I suppose,” said Harry simply, “his lordship is here attending the old lady?”

Jack burst into laughter.

“Oh yes! Very much so! Exactly!” he said. “Why, my dear fellow, haven’t you heard about the little Opera-dancer?”

“I’ve only just arrived in England, Mr. Morris,” said Harry with a smile. “And in Virginia, we’ve heard little of the little Opera-dancer.”

Fortunately, the secret of the little Opera-dancer remained unspoken, for their conversation was interrupted by a lady in a cardinal cape and a hat resembling those now popular a century later. She made a deep curtsey to the two gentlemen and received their greetings.

She stopped before Harry and held out her hand, surprising him:

“Have you so soon forgotten me, Mr. Warrington?”

Off went Harry’s hat instantly. He started, blushed, stammered, and cried out, “Good heavens!” as if a celestial event had occurred. It was Lady Maria, come out for a walk. He had not been thinking of her. She had, for the moment, completely slipped from his mind—so utterly that her sudden reappearance startled him, flooding his cheeks with guilt.

No—he wasn’t even thinking of her! A week ago—perhaps a year, a hundred years—it seemed—he would not have been surprised to meet her anywhere. She had haunted his dreams, glided across garden terraces, lingered in corridors, appeared in shadows. A week ago, his heart had beaten for her. A week ago, even as he woke, her image smiled upon him. And it was only last Tuesday that his love had been wounded and died—so thoroughly that he had ceased mourning her, and indeed, forgotten her!

“You will walk with me a little?” she asked. “Or would you prefer the music? I dare say you’d prefer the music.”

“You know,” said Harry, “I don’t care much for music—except”—he hesitated, recalling the evening hymn—“except your playing.” He turned crimson as he spoke, feeling he was betraying himself terribly.

The lady herself was agitated by the flutter in her young companion. Could that tremor mean she was mistaken? That he still loved her? “Give me your arm,” she said, waving a curtsey to the others. “My aunt is asleep after dinner.” Harry could not refuse. He offered his arm and pressed the hand resting against his heart. Maria made another graceful curtsey to Harry’s companions and walked away with her prize.

In grief, rage, pain, and anguish, how a woman remembers to smile, curtsey, caress, dissemble! How resolutely she fulfills her social duties—how she offers a word, a hand, a kind phrase to the passing acquaintance who unknowingly crosses the path of tragedy, drops a light remark, and moves on. He passes, thinking, “She seemed pleased with what I said. That joke was neat. I think Lady Maria looks favorably on me—she’s a devilishly fine woman, by Gad!” O wiseacre! Such was Jack Morris’s thought as he walked away, leaning on Lord March’s arm, convinced the entire society of Tunbridge Wells was watching him. He had made clever remarks at Lady Flushington’s card game the night before, and Lady Maria had replied gracefully. And so Jack walked off, perfectly happy.

“Tell me about those children, Harry,” said Maria, as they walked slowly across the common. “The ones I saw running about at the house where you were taken in after your fall—poor dear boy, it broke my heart to see you so hurt.” She spoke gently, her voice soft with concern.

“Oh, that fall!” Harry exclaimed, gripping her arm more tightly than he meant to. “I thought I’d never recover when I saw it! But don’t squeeze like that—you know I don’t care for you?” He laughed, though his tone carried a hint of teasing.

“The people there are the kindest, most wonderful folks I’ve ever met,” he went on, warming to the subject. “Mrs. Lambert was a friend of my mother’s during her time in Europe. Colonel Lambert has seen service all over the world—Scotland, Flanders, Minorca. He’s a gentleman through and through. They treated me like their own son. No natural parents could have been kinder. How can I ever repay them? I must do something—give them a gift, I tell you!” He reached into his pocket, fingers brushing against the crisp banknotes he had just won from Morris and March.

“We could go to the toy shop,” suggested Lady Maria, smiling faintly. “Buy a couple of dolls for the children. Though I warn you—it would be ungracious to offer payment for such kindness.”

“Dolls for Hester and Theo?” Harry chuckled. “Do you think a woman isn’t a woman until she’s forty, Maria?”

Her arm under his gave the tiniest twitch—just a flicker of pain beneath the surface.

“You don’t understand,” he continued, eager now. “Hester doesn’t consider herself a child at all. And Theo—she’s older than her sister, far cleverer. They speak half a dozen languages, read endlessly—books upon books. They play the harpsichord together beautifully, sing duets, and Theo writes songs of her own.”

“Indeed?” Maria replied, surprised. “I barely noticed them. They looked so young. I had no idea they were such remarkable girls.”

“That’s just how women are!” Harry declared, laughing. “Back home, if George or I praised a woman, Mrs. Esmond or even Mountain would find fault with her!”

“I wouldn’t criticize anyone who’s been kind to you, Mr. Warrington,” Maria sighed, her voice low. “Though I know you’re not angry with me for envying them—for being the one who cared for you when you were wounded and ill, while I… I had to leave you behind.”

“You dear good Maria,” he said, squeezing her hand again.

“No, Harry,” she insisted, pulling away slightly. “Don’t be so forward. Look—there’s your black servant walking with a group of others in livery. The wretches are off to the tea-garden, no doubt to drink themselves into oblivion, just like their masters. That dreadful Mr. Morris was utterly drunk when I came to you—he frightened you terribly.”

“I’d just won big bets from both of them,” Harry said, pride swelling in his chest. “What shall I buy for you, my dear cousin?” And he began recounting his triumphs, flushed with victory and high spirits. He laughed, boasted lightly.

“For the honour of Virginia,” he declared, “I was determined to show them what real jumping was. With a little practice, I could leap two feet farther.”

Maria smiled at her young champion’s success. But then, with a note of caution, she added, “Still, you must be careful about gambling, child. You know it’s ruined our family before. My brother Castlewood, Will, poor father, even Aunt Lady Castlewood—each fell victim to it. As for Lord March, he’s the most reckless and yet most successful gambler among the nobility.”

“I don’t intend to fear him—or his friend Jack Morris,” Harry replied, fingers still tracing the edges of his winnings. “What games do you play at Aunt Bernstein’s? Cribbage, all-fours, brag, whist, piquet, quadrille? I’m ready for any of them. What time is it—surely it’s seven?”

“And you want to start now?” Maria said, voice tinged with sorrow. “You don’t care to walk with your poor cousin anymore. Not long ago, you did.”

“Hey! Youth is youth, cousin!” Harry declared, tossing back his head. “A young fellow must have his fun!” And he strutted beside her, confident, happy, hungry for pleasure.

Not long ago, he had enjoyed walking with her. Only yesterday, he had been content in the company of Hester and Theo, and kind-hearted Mrs. Lambert. But life, gaiety, the thrill of winning—these things called to him now, and he seized them without hesitation, like any other young man, blind to the hangover waiting in the morning.

As they spoke, the fiddles from the open orchestra on the Parade began tuning up, squealing in preparation for their evening concert. Maria knew her aunt was awake again—her usual routine had begun—and that she must return to her duties. Harry never asked about this burden, though he must have known it. He never pitied her. His thoughts were elsewhere.

Yet when Harry had been injured, she had suffered far more deeply than he had. He had rarely left her mind, though she buried her feelings beneath smiles and quiet composure, as women often do.

I know, dear Mrs. Grundy, you may think her an old fool. But do you suppose fools’ caps only crown bright hair? Grey locks wear them too. Be gentle with our elderly ladies, O wise Minerva of a woman! Or perhaps you’re so virtuous and enlightened that you never read novels at all. This I know: late harvests of wild oats grow just as well as early ones. From observation of myself and neighbours, I suspect *avena fatua* thrives right up to the final days of the year.

Like parents eager to escape a troublesome child and attend their evening party, Madame Bernstein and her staff had hurriedly put the sun to bed while daylight still lingered, drawn curtains over the sky, and busied themselves with cards, candles, tea, negus, and other delights.

One by one, ladies arrived at the Baroness’s door—some painted, some patched, all dressed in brocade. Gentlemen followed in gala attire. Mr. Poellnitz wore the largest star and the most elaborately embroidered coat of all. When Lord March and Ruglen appeared, he was transformed from the rough jockey Harry had met at the White Horse. His tight brown scratch hat was replaced by a curled feather wig with grey powder; his leather breeches exchanged for a rich French suit. Jack Morris wore nearly identical finery—same wig, same style of coat, tailored to resemble his lordship’s exactly.

Mr. Wolfe entered in attendance upon his beautiful mistress, Miss Lowther, and her aunt, whose passion for cards matched that of the world.

When Lady Maria Esmond arrived, her appearance belied her aunt’s description. Her figure was graceful, her dress revealing much of it. Her complexion was naturally fair, enhanced by a dark frilled ribbon around her neck, clasped with a jewel. Her cheeks bore no more colour than others’, though roses were freely bought at perfumery shops. A few artful patches, it was whispered, added sparkle to her charm. Her hoop was no larger than modern contraptions worn today. In sum, though absurd in parts, the fashion was pleasing overall.

Suppose our ladies took to bangles and nose-rings? We might laugh—but not despise them. Lovers would scarcely hesitate to lift the ring to kiss the lips beneath.

As for the Baroness de Bernstein, when she made the effort to dress grandly, she was still handsome, magnificent—but melancholy, even terrifying. Some faces carry the weight of the past; others fade into meekness. The fire dies in some eyes, as crow’s-feet deepen around them. They no longer flash with scorn, anger, or love. They gaze, but no one melts under their sapphire stare. They look—but no one is dazzled.

My fair young reader, if you are not the peerless Lindamira, Queen of the Ball—if, at night’s end, you admit you danced with only two or three partners while Lindamira drew a crowd—console yourself. At fifty, you will appear as kind and pleasant as you do now at eighteen. You won’t surrender your coach-and-six of beauty to another. You won’t walk through life alone, watching admiration flee. You won’t witness the decline of your smile, nor see fashion abandon your once-grand rooms, leaving only dust, cobwebs, and lonely placards: “To Let.”

You may never have known grandeur—but you’ll never feel abandonment. You may not have inherited millions—but you’ll avoid bankruptcy.

“Our hostess,” murmured Lord Chesterfield to a friend, unaware of his loud whisper, “reminds me of Covent Garden in my youth. Then it was the fashionable quarter. Now, noble houses are gaming dens—or you may enter with a friend and order a bottle.”

“Ah,” said Lord March, shrugging, “a bottle and a tavern have their uses. I was born after the Georges came in, though I hope to live to a hundred. I never knew the Bernstein except as an old woman. If she once had beauty, I confess I don’t know how she spent it.”

“No, hang me, how *did* she spend it?” Jack Morris laughed.

“Here’s a table!” he announced. “Shall we sit? Don’t let the Frenchman join us—he won’t pay. Mr. Warrington, will you take a card?”

Mr. Warrington and Lord Chesterfield found themselves partnered against Morris and Lord March.

“You’re late, Baron,” said the elder nobleman, stopping the other nobleman advancing toward the table. “We’ve already started. Have you forgotten Mr. Warrington of Virginia—the young gentleman you met in London?”

“The young gentleman I met at Arthur’s Chocolate House had black hair, a slight turned-up nose, and wasn’t nearly as fortunate in looks as Mr. Warrington,” the Baron replied with quick wit. “Warrington, Dorrington, Harrington? We of the continent struggle with your insular names. I assure you, this gentleman is not the one I mentioned at dinner.” With a kind glance, he sidled away to the window embrasure, where Mr. Wolfe and Miss Lowther were deep in conversation.

There, the Baron decided to engage the lieutenant-colonel in discussion of the Prussian manual exercise recently introduced into King George II’s army—a subject Mr. Wolfe knew well, and which might have interested him at any other moment. Still, the old gentleman delivered his opinions with confidence, believing himself charming.

At first, the Baroness greeted guests personally, chatting as they arrived. But as the rooms filled and games began, she grew restless and withdrew with three friends to her corner, where a reserved table awaited her. There, seated firmly, she stayed until dawn, never changing position or abandoning her game.

Now, the duty of welcoming guests fell to Lady Maria. Though she disliked cards, she dutifully attended to her aunt’s visitors, often passing by the table where Harry played with his companions.

“Come cut the cards for us,” Lord March called out as she passed. “Bring us luck, Lady Maria! We’ve had none tonight, and Mr. Warrington is winning everything.”

“I hope you’re not playing high, Harry?” she asked timidly.

“Oh, only sixpences,” Lord March replied, dealing.

“Only sixpences,” echoed Mr. Morris, though his face darkened as if losing mere coins were a disaster.

Lord Chesterfield sat opposite Harry, calmly sorting his cards. One could not tell from his expression whether fortune favoured him.

A word slipped from Morris’s lips—something less than joyful—and his partner snapped, “Hang it, Morris, play your cards and keep silent!”

Strange, considering they were only betting sixpences.

Maria lingered near Harry’s chair, hand resting on the back. She could see his cards—dozens of trumps clustered in one corner. She hadn’t taken his luck away. She smiled, pleased she had cut the pack that dealt him such advantage.

As Lord March dealt, he quietly said, “Same bet as before, Mr. Warrington—or shall we double it?”

“Anything you like, my lord,” Harry replied, calm as ever.

“Then let’s say shillings.”

“Shillings,” Harry agreed. The game continued.

The outcome of that night—and several following—can be learned from a letter never sent, but later found among Mr. Henry Warrington’s papers:

Since White’s two bottles of Burgundy and a pack of cards constitute all the joys of your life, I assume you’re currently in London, preferring smoke and faro to fresh air and haystacks. This letter will reach you by a young gentleman I’ve lately met—one you’ll be delighted to know. He plays any game, at any stake, any hour, and drinks any reasonable number of bottles during play. Mr. Warrington is none other than the Fortunate Youth of whom so many tales have appeared in the *Public Advertiser* and similar papers. He owns an estate in Virginia as large as Yorkshire, burdened only by a mother—the reigning sovereign. But since the climate is unhealthy and fevers rampant, let us hope Mrs. Esmond passes soon, leaving this virtuous youth in undisputed possession.

She is aunt to that rogue Castlewood, who never pays his debts unless he’s more honourable with you than he was with me. Mr. Warrington is of noble stock. We must include him in our circle—if only so I may win my money back.

He’s had extraordinary luck here, winning everything while his card-playing aunt loses. A few nights ago, when I first met him, he beat me in jumping (having trained among savages and fled bears in his native woods). He won bets from me and Jack Morris on my weight. That night, at old Bernstein’s, he defeated us all.

If you settle our last Epsom account, please transfer 350 pounds to Mr. Warrington—I still owe him, having emptied my purse. Chesterfield lost six hundred, though he refuses to acknowledge it, having sworn to quit gaming and live cleanly. Jack Morris, less affected than the rest—since he has no estates or retinue to maintain, and all his father’s ill-gotten wealth at hand—roars like a bull of Bashan over his losses.

We had a second night’s play, in private, with Barbeau serving us a fine dinner. Mr. Warrington keeps silence like a gentleman—none of us have spoken of our losses, but the whole place does. Yesterday, Cattarina glared at me in fury because I refused her a diamond necklace, claiming I denied her due to losing five thousand to the Virginian. My old Duchess of Q. confirms the same tale—and knows precisely how much Chesterfield and Jack have lost.

Warrington treated the company to breakfast and music. You should have seen how the women tore him apart. That fiendish Cattarina ogled him from my vis-à-vis, right under my nose, as we drove to Penshurst. I have no doubt she’s already sent him a billet-doux.

He shot Jack Morris to pieces at target practice—we’ll test him with partridges when season arrives.

He is truly fortunate. Youth unspoiled by English excesses, good health, good looks, and good luck.

In short, Mr. Warrington has won our money in the finest gentlemanly way. Since I like him—and wish to win some back—I entrust him to your saintly guardianship. Adieu! I’m heading north and returning for Doncaster.

**Yours ever, dear George,
M. et R.**

After only a few days at Tunbridge Wells, Harry Warrington found himself the most talked-about figure in the fashionable little resort. No nobleman, not even the Bishop of Salisbury himself, drew such attention. People turned to watch him pass through the streets; country folk gaped as he walked by on market day. At the assembly rooms, matrons smiled and invited him to join their circles, often contriving to leave him alone with their daughters—most of whom returned his polite glances with warm smiles. Everyone knew, down to the last acre and shilling, the size of his Virginia estate and the income it brought. At every tea-table, his winnings at cards were recounted, calculated, and admired. How curiously our neighbours know our affairs!

The fascination with Harry was so great that even his servant, Gumbo, became an object of interest. Strangers sought him out, bought him ale and cold meat, and pestered him for news of the young Virginian. Gumbo, well fed and flattered, grew plump and proud, becoming a central figure among the local valets—and never more inventive in his tales. No gathering was complete without Mr. Warrington’s presence.

Harry was both amused and astonished by this sudden fame. He bore it with good grace, though not without pride. Brought up in a household where he had always been held in high regard, he now found confirmation in the world’s admiration. Yet he did not let it go to his head. He did not boast of his victories or carry himself with arrogance. When challenged to games or races, he felt bound by a strange sense of honour to accept. To refuse would have seemed ungracious—or worse, un-Virginian. And so, when men invited him to horse-races, drinking bouts, or card matches, he responded with the same quiet dignity he’d shown back home.

He proved remarkably capable in these contests. With a steady head, a sure hand, and nerves of steel, he stood his ground against England’s finest. He shot better than Jack Morris, rode faster than Mr. Scamper, and soon held his own at tennis against Captain Batts—though he’d never played before. He faced the famed gamblers Lord Chesterfield and Lord March, who both praised his composure, gallantry, and gentlemanly conduct. Though not brilliant in books, he wrote clearly and fluently—better than many of the ton. His honest ignorance charmed Madame de Bernstein, who had once read widely and enjoyed Molière and Fielding, but whose true passion lay in life, not literature. She delighted in his simplicity and took pleasure in dressing him up: finding fine lace for his ruffles, a diamond brooch for his cravat. Soon, Harry became her favourite nephew, eclipsing all others.

Lady Maria, perhaps, was secretly pleased by his success. But her brothers—well, they must have felt a pang of envy when they heard how quickly he’d won their aunt’s favour. After two weeks at the Wells, Harry was no longer just a visitor—he was a celebrity. He knew all the best company. And if he also came to know some of the worst, could he be blamed? Was it wrong to take the world as he found it, to sip from the sparkling cup of pleasure offered so freely?

Madame de Bernstein revelled in his triumphs and encouraged him to enjoy them fully. She was no stern moralist, nor a particularly wise guide for youth. If Cattarina, the French dancer, sent him love notes, she might have advised him to reply. But Harry still carried with him the modesty of his colonial upbringing—the kind of plain honesty that went with homespun linen. In the wide-open spaces of America, libertinism was rare. The vices of London or Paris were unknown in the rough frontier towns. So when Harry heard the bold talk of his new companions, he blushed like a girl. Even Aunt Bernstein’s jokes startled him, and she would tease him, calling him “Joseph” or “simpleton.”

Yet though he remained innocent, the world assumed he was as corrupt as any other young man. How was he to know he shouldn’t walk arm-in-arm with Cattarina? He had seen Lord March driving her about in his phaeton. Surely there was no harm in offering her his arm, strolling with her in public? When she fancied a trinket at the toy shop, and his pockets were full of gold, he happily bought her the locket she desired. The next day, it was a piece of lace—again, he gave it to her. The day after, another whim—but then he stopped. With a laugh, he gently refused her request. He was generous, yes, but not reckless. He had no intention of buying diamonds for her ears. But who would believe his modesty?

Aunt Bernstein insisted he was playing Don Juan—taking Lord March’s place. She said this especially when Lady Maria was present, delighting in the pain it caused her niece. “Why, my dear,” she would say, “boys will be boys. I don’t want Harry to be the first milksop in his family!” And poor Maria, eating bread paid for by her aunt, sometimes choked on its bitterness. Oh, how cruel some women can make kindness taste!

Mr. Wolfe, meanwhile, kept coming from Westerham to court the lady he loved. Knowing the Colonel was devoted to her, Harry didn’t expect to see much of him—though he missed his conversation. It was different from the idle chatter around him. Mr. Wolfe never spoke of horses, cards, or hunting exploits. He didn’t brag about women or spread scandals. That was not a good time. The old world was far more dissolute than ours. There was a king with mistresses in open view, nobles mad for pleasure, and a looseness of speech and deed that we must record honestly, without going into details that might shock decent readers. Harry had fallen among some of the wildest people—and found an old relative living right at the heart of the merriment.

At first, Harry didn’t notice how Colonel Wolfe avoided him. When they met by chance, the Colonel’s manner was distant, cold. Harry didn’t know the stories being told. Who does? Who makes them?
