Who fathers such lies? Poor Harry had no idea of the reputation he was gaining. While riding, playing, and laughing, he was already spoken of as the most debauched, godless, and reckless young man in England.

These tales reached Colonel Lambert at Oakhurst—first one, then another, until they overwhelmed him. His kind heart filled with sorrow. His family noticed something was wrong. At first, he refused to speak. But Mrs. Lambert, anxious and persistent, wore him down. He told her what he knew of Harry Warrington. She was shocked and grieved. The sorrow passed from the bedroom to the drawing-room, then to Theo and Hester. O tender hearts! At first, Hester flushed red, clenched her fists, and swore she wouldn’t believe a word. But in the end, she did. Scandal always wins, especially over the good and innocent.

“Oh, the serpent we’ve nursed by our fire!” they lamented. “Oh, the wretched boy!” To think he walked with that painted Frenchwoman, gave her jewels, paraded his shame before all society! They wept together, then took the parson into their confidence. He preached a sermon on scandal the next Sunday, warning against judging others. But words fall short. When the next story comes, we believe it. So did the Oakhursts believe the worst of Harry Warrington.

Meanwhile, Harry was too happy to know how deeply his friends mourned him. He lived idly, pleasantly, though uselessly—unaware of the storm he stirred or the terrible name he bore.

One afternoon, after a tennis match with Captain Batts, Harry stepped out, pleased with himself and the world. He met Colonel Wolfe, returning from a visit to the woman he loved. Harry extended his hand. The Colonel took it—but his greeting was icy. Harry noticed, especially when the Colonel barely touched his hat in return, while Batts bowed deeply.

Batts walked away, looking unsettled. Harry stayed behind, speaking to his friend.

Mr. Wolfe walked beside him—upright, silent, cold.

“I haven’t seen you in days,” said Harry.

“You’ve had other companions,” replied Wolfe curtly.

“But I’d rather be with you than any of them,” Harry insisted.

“Indeed, you might find better company,” the Colonel said grimly.

“Do you mean Captain Batts?” asked Harry.

“He’s no favourite of mine,” said Wolfe. “He had a bad name in the army, and hasn’t improved since he left. You could do better than him. Pardon my frankness.”

“Friend? He’s not my friend—he teaches me tennis. He’s in league with my lord and all the fashionables here.”

“I’m not one of them,” said Wolfe.

“What’s wrong, Colonel? Have I offended you?”

“I’ll be frank,” said the Colonel. “I don’t like some of your friends.”

“But they’re the highest in England!” protested Harry.

“Exactly—too high for a hard-working soldier like me. If you keep their company, believe me, many of us humble folk can’t afford to follow you.”

“I’m here paying my respects to an honourable lady,” said Wolfe. “And yesterday, I saw you walking openly with a French ballet-dancer. You took off your hat.”

“I must frankly tell you,” he added, “I’d prefer you didn’t do that.”

“Sir,” said Harry, turning red, “do you mean I should give up your acquaintance altogether?”

“I shall ask you to, when you’re with that woman,” said Wolfe sharply—using a word too strong to repeat, though Shakespeare put it in Othello’s mouth.

“Great heavens!” cried Harry. “What shame is this? How dare anyone say such a thing about a woman?”

“You ought to know best,” said Wolfe, looking surprised. “Or the world has lied about you terribly.”

“What should I know?” asked Harry. “I see a poor French dancer, come with her mother, ordered by doctors to drink the waters. I know people of my rank don’t usually mix with hers—but why should I not offer her my arm? There are scarcely half a dozen here who speak her language. I can speak a little French. Why shouldn’t I help her? If Colonel Wolfe refuses to tip his hat when I walk with her, by George, he may leave it alone!”

“You don’t mean to say,” said Wolfe, watching him closely, “you don’t know her character?”

“Of course she’s a dancer,” said Harry. “But no better or worse than others. And if she were a duchess or your grandmother, I couldn’t respect her more.”

“You don’t mean to say you didn’t win her from Lord March at dice?”

“At what?”

“Dice. Everyone knows it. Not a soul at the Wells is unaware. I heard it myself, just now, from Mr. Richardson. The ladies said you’d become a colonial Lovelace.”

“What else have they said?” asked Harry.

Wolfe told him—stories of corruption, drunkenness, gambling, blasphemy, freethinking, and association with the worst company. Harry listened, stunned.

“I tell you these things,” said Wolfe, “so you know what people say. And because I believe, from your reaction, you’re innocent of most. I feel I’ve wronged you, and I ask your pardon.”

Harry eagerly accepted. They shook hands—this time with real warmth.

As for the charges, Harry denied most easily. As for gambling, he admitted it. A gentleman, he said, could not refuse a fair challenge—especially when he had the means. And he never played beyond what he could afford. At first, he won enough to play higher stakes. He thought play was fair—it was pleasant. Didn’t all England play, except the Methodists? Hadn’t he seen the best company at the Wells—his aunt included?

Wolfe made no comment on that. But he warned Harry plainly: the life he led might be pleasant, but it was not profitable.

“It can’t be,” said the Colonel, “that a man spends his days racing horses and playing tennis, and his nights carousing or at cards. Every man was made to work. A gentleman, if he has no duty, must create one. Do you know your country’s laws, Mr. Warrington? As a great landowner, you’ll likely become a magistrate. Have you studied the trades and industries of your land? These are worthy pursuits—better than cockfights or cricket. Do you know anything of our profession? It’s noble. There’s plenty to learn—perhaps suited to you. I mention it, not books, because I judge your genius lies elsewhere. But honour is the aim of life. Every man can serve his country one way or another. Be sure, sir, that idle bread is the most dangerous of all. Cards and pleasure may be pastimes after work—but not instead of it. And do you know, Mr. Warrington, instead of being the Fortunate Youth, as all call you, I think you are rather Warrington the Unlucky—for you are followed by daily idleness, daily flattery, daily temptation. May the Lord send you deliverance from your fortune.”

That evening, Harry did not wish to tell his aunt why he looked so grave. He meant not to drink—but the fellows at the ordinary passed the bottle round. He meant not to play—but a fourth was needed at his aunt’s table. How could he resist? He partnered her several times. He had luck—someone’s own luck, surely. And once again, he watched the dawn break, feasting on chickens and champagne as the sun rose.

At the Wells, Madame de Bernstein found ample distraction in her card games and quiet scoldings of her niece, content enough with the social rhythm of the place. Meanwhile, young Harry Warrington, still in the bloom of twenty, found himself perfectly at ease among the idle pleasures of Tunbridge. For a man of his years, few things mattered more than good company, fresh air, and a steady stream of sport and amusement. At that age, even the simplest delight feels like a triumph—every moment anticipated with eager hope, every day counted down until pleasure arrives. But as life draws on, we grow cautious, distant, and our memories turn nostalgic, recalling the joy of youth with a soft, wistful glance.

Do you not remember your first ball, Madam? How the music swelled, the lights danced, and the world seemed full of possibility? And now, sitting quietly by the fire while your daughters twirl through their dances, does not your mind drift back to those golden hours? I, for one, can recall walking three miles across the countryside just to dine with old Captain Jones—a man whose half-pay port came from the village wine merchant and cost little more than a shilling. Yet it tasted richer then, not because of the wine, but because of the warmth of the welcome, the glow of friendship, and the unburdened spirit of youth. Viximus nuper—we have lived recently, indeed.

I do not judge Harry’s idleness too harshly, as Colonel Lambert might. For there is something noble in leisure when it is free from guilt or purposelessness. Oh, blessed idleness! Divine, languid nymph! Bring me a novel as I lie wrapped in my dressing gown at three o’clock in the afternoon; mix me a sherry cobbler, and light a cigar. You may call me lazy, accuse me of sloth, name you a thousand sins—but you cannot deny that you are the most charming companion in all the world.

Lord March had departed northward, and Lord Chesterfield, disappointed by the waters’ failure to cure his deafness, returned to his solitude at Blackheath. But others remained—gentlemen who sought only recreation and relaxation—and Harry found himself well-liked among them. At the White Horse ordinary, he quickly learned to order a French dinner as deftly as any man from St. James’s, conversed fluently with Monsieur Barbeau in French, and developed a discerning eye for fine wines—able to distinguish between Clos Vougeot and Romande with remarkable accuracy.

He was the young king of the Wells, where the regulars were men of the world—easygoing, worldly, and indifferent to the rumors of gallantry and extravagance that clung to Harry’s name. Such tales had frightened Mr. Wolfe, but they meant little to these seasoned revelers. Though Harry moved freely among them, swimming in the same waters as the most carefree, he possessed a natural honesty and sharp wit that kept him clear of traps laid for the unwary.

He rarely made foolish bets with the idle fellows around him, and even the most experienced gamblers found it hard to outwit him. He played games—indoors and out—not from recklessness, but from genuine skill and love of competition. He never gambled with strangers, always settled debts promptly, and insisted on fairness above all. He would have fared poorly in a university exam, yet he carried within him prudence, loyalty, keen insight, generosity, and courage that no book could teach.

And he had moments to prove it.

When Cattarina, the opera dancer who had once caused him so much trouble, pressed her attentions beyond what Harry considered proper, he withdrew with calm dignity, leaving her to seek softer prey. Her mother soon arrived, weeping and dramatic, claiming a cruel bailiff had seized their goods, and that her husband languished in a London prison. Harry listened politely, then firmly declared that his acquaintance with Cattarina did not make him responsible for her family’s debts. He refused to act as surety for her father or settle her accounts at Tunbridge.

The woman called him a monster, then sneered, asking why he didn’t accept payment for his “services.” At first, Harry was puzzled—until she clarified. Then, with horror, he rose, declaring that in his homeland, even the fiercest savages would recoil from such a trade. He bowed her out with formal courtesy, ordered Gumbo to bar her from his lodgings forever, and let her go—no doubt vowing vengeance against the “Iroquois,” as she called him. She and her daughter fled to London as soon as their landlord allowed.

Harry faced other dangers too—those of gaming, not just of the heart. A man who plays at bowls must expect to lose some rubbers. After dinner at the ordinary, having declined another game of piquet with Captain Batts, Harry was roughly questioned. He replied honestly: he only played with gentlemen who paid, as he did. He added that he’d be happy to settle their account once it was cleared. That satisfied Captain Batts—so much so that he left without paying Harry or anyone else. The debt remained unsettled, but Harry’s integrity stood firm.

There was also the evening when a rude chairman insulted Miss Whiffler as she walked to the assembly. Harry stepped forward, challenged the man, and delivered a sound beating. Later, when Mr. Hector Buckler—famed for his sharp tongue—repeated the false tale of Harry’s affair with Cattarina in the pump-room, Harry confronted him publicly. Standing before a gathering of water-drinkers, he declared the story a lie and warned any who repeated it would answer to him.

So though Harry lived among wolves, he proved himself a worthy one. He did not merely follow the customs of the place—he upheld honor within them. And when Colonel Wolfe learned the truth, he likely hastened to correct the accusations he had once believed. There was great joy in the Lambert household when the news arrived.

“Hadst thou brought me a regiment, James,” said Mr. Lambert, “I should not have been more pleased.”

Mrs. Lambert summoned her daughters from the garden, kissed them both, and shouted the news. Hetty leapt with delight, and Theo played an extraordinary suite on the harpsichord that night. When Dr. Boyle came for his usual game of backgammon, he found the house alight with laughter and warmth. Only then did he understand—when the three ladies sang together, “We were wrong! We were wrong!”—that the sermon he had preached about mercy had come true.

“What shall we do, my dear?” asked the Colonel, leaning toward his wife. “The hay is in, the corn won’t be cut for weeks, and the horses are idle. Suppose we…”

And here, he whispered into her ear.

“My dearest Martin!” she exclaimed, taking his hand. “The very thing!”

“What’s the very thing, mother?” asked young Charley, home for his holidays.

“The very thing,” she said, “is to go to supper. Come, Doctor! Let us open a bottle of wine and drink to repentance—for all who judged wrongly.”

“Amen,” said the Doctor, “with all my heart.”

And so the family gathered, joyful and reconciled, to share a meal under the glow of forgiveness.

One bright afternoon, Mr. Harry Warrington made his usual way to the White Horse ordinary, a well-known haunt of country gentlemen and men of fashion in Tunbridge Wells. As he entered, he was greeted with familiar faces, among them the jovial and ever-cheerful Parson Sampson, whose presence always brought laughter and liveliness to the table. The parson, rosy-cheeked and full of spirits, was regaling the company with tales of London life—gossip from Kensington Palace, whispers from Pall Mall, news of Mr. Byng’s imprisonment, the latest odds at Newmarket, and who had become the toast of Covent Garden. Though not always accurate, these stories were rich in colour and charm, and more than sufficient for the tastes of the rural gentry gathered there.

The names might be mixed—Lord Squanderfield courting Mrs. Lucy instead of Mrs. Polly, Lady Jane smitten with an actor rather than Lady Mary—but such details mattered little. What mattered was the wit, the sparkle, the sense of the world beyond the countryside. And so the parson chattered on, drinking glass after glass, cheered on by his audience, who insisted he keep pouring.

A century ago, such a clergyman—a man equally at home in church, tavern, theatre, or gaming house—was not uncommon in England. He could ride with the best in the hunting field, sing a song after the play at Covent Garden, or call a hand at the card table with confidence. When Harry arrived, the parson’s face flushed deeper still—perhaps from claret, perhaps from modesty—and he whispered to the squire beside him, “Maxima debetur,” before leaping up, stumbling slightly in his haste, to greet the Virginian.

“My dear sir! My very dear sir! Conqueror of spades, clubs, and hearts!” the chaplain exclaimed, embracing Harry with warmth. “I am overjoyed to see you looking so fresh and strong!”

Harry returned the greeting with genuine pleasure. He admired the parson’s good humour and healthy glow. The squire in the drab coat, who knew Harry well, offered him a seat beside himself and called out for the parson to resume his tale about Lord Ogle and the grocer’s wife—though the place remained unnamed, as the sentence was cut short by a shout of pain: the parson had trodden on someone’s gouty toe.

Apologizing hastily, Sampson turned back to Harry and began sharing news from Castlewood: my Lord Castlewood sent his affectionate regards and had instructed him to come to Tunbridge to watch over the young gentleman’s conduct; Lady Viscountess and Lady Fanny had gone to Harrogate for the waters; Mr. Will had won at Newmarket and was now visiting the Duke; and Molly, the housemaid, was heartbroken over Gumbo, Harry’s valet.

Indeed, all the gossip of the estate had followed Sampson to the ordinary. He spoke proudly of Harry’s reputation throughout Hampshire—of his successes at Tunbridge, in every sense of the word—and expressed the hopes of many noble families that the young Virginian would not be spoiled by city life. His aunt, Madame Bernstein, would be pleased, he said, if Harry remained true to his roots.

As the guests left one by one, Harry found himself seated alone with the chaplain, their conversation growing warmer and more animated. The parson, though already well into his wine, declared cheerfully that “plenty” did not mean he couldn’t have “plenty more.” Toast after toast was raised, and Harry, now in high spirits, became generous and kind-hearted.

“Why should you pay for an inn?” he asked. “There’s a room at my lodgings—come stay with me.”

Gumbo was summoned to prepare the chamber, and Harry insisted the parson visit his stables. There, amid the scent of hay and horseflesh, Sampson recognized his own old mount—the very horse Harry had won from him in a game of cards. The beast whinnied with joy, nuzzling against the chaplain’s coat. Harry laughed and declared, “By Jupiter, Sampson, that horse is yours again—I’ll give it to you!”

The gift was accepted with emotion. The parson seized Harry’s hand, blessed him, then threw his arms around the horse’s neck and wept—not from sorrow, but from pure delight, tears mingled with Bordeaux and gratitude.

Arm in arm, they walked to Madame Bernstein’s lodging, bringing with them the fragrance of stable and saddle leather. Their cheeks were flushed, their eyes bright—evidence of a day well spent.

Madame Bernstein received her nephew’s chaplain kindly. She enjoyed Sampson’s bold jokes and lively talk, much like she relished a spicy dish or a new creation from her cook. But one pastime never grew stale: cards. “The cards don’t cheat,” she often said. “A bad hand tells you the truth plainly. And nothing flatters like a fine set of trumps.”

When in good humour, she would laughingly ask Sampson to say grace before dinner. At first, the chaplain hesitated to join the card games—he claimed her ladyship’s stakes were too high, and his pockets already empty from losing to the young Virginian. But thanks to Harry’s generosity, he soon had enough coin to take his place at the table.

Harry welcomed Sampson not only as a friend but as a mentor. He adapted quickly to English life—dressing with elegance, wearing black suits of impeccable cut, lace and linen of the finest quality. The gay Duchess of Queensberry once remarked, “With a star and ribbon, his stocking down, and his hair over his shoulder, he’d make a charming Hamlet. And I doubt he’s been the death of a dozen Ophelias—here and among the Indians.”

His possessions grew: fine shaving plates from toy-shop women, brocade bedgowns for lounging, French watches with painted backs and diamond settings, enamelled snuffboxes, swords, walking canes. A daily levee of grooms, jockeys, and tradesmen waited in his anteroom, admitted one by one by Gumbo, the groom of the chambers.

No single servant could manage such a household. Yet Harry took care to learn the arts befitting a gentleman. A French fencing master and dancing master taught him during the season, and within weeks he handled the foil with skill and grace. Lady Maria, herself a fine dancer, confessed with a sigh that no gentleman at court could walk a minuet more elegantly than Mr. Warrington.

Riding, however, he preferred his Virginian style. Though he took a few lessons from a local master, he declared that no one in England rode better than Colonel George Washington of Mount Vernon.

Sampson, meanwhile, found himself in better quarters than he had known in years. He was a man of the world, and his stories—real or imagined—delighted Harry. Young men look up to older ones, admiring their seasoned wit and worn-in anecdotes, drenched in the wine of countless dinners. To Harry, Sampson’s tales were fresh and enchanting.

In those days, such men existed—older, worldly figures who delighted in guiding young noblemen through society, teaching them manners, introducing them to gaming tables, acting as mentors at theatres and balls. They drank lemonade while the young lord sipped Burgundy, and staggered home with clear heads while their charges reeled. Mr. Sampson was one such man—perhaps the last of his kind.

And so, under Harry’s roof, he became not just a guest, but a tutor, confidant, and secretary. This is evident in the following letter, preserved in the Warrington family papers:

---

**To Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Castlewood,
At Her House at Richmond, Virginia**

Mrs. Bligh’s Lodgings, Pantiles, Tunbridge Wells
August 25th, 1756

Your letter of 20 June, delivered by Mr. Trail of Bristol, has reached me safely, and I thank you most sincerely for your kindness and wise counsel. I shall cherish the remembrances of our dear home, and I love it no less for having visited the ancestral land of our family in England.

I wrote to you by the last monthly packet, informing you of the small accident I suffered on the journey here, and of the kind friends who took me in. Since then, I have enjoyed the pleasant weather and excellent company, making many acquaintances among the nobility—friends whose company I trust you will not disapprove.

Among them are the illustrious Earl of Chesterfield, former Ambassador to Holland and Viceroy of Ireland; the Earl of March and Ruglen, heir to the Duke of Queensberry; and her Grace the Duchess, famed beauty of Queen Anne’s reign, who remembers my grandfather at Court. These and many others attend my aunt’s assemblies, which are among the most popular in this bustling resort.

On my way here, I stayed at Westerham with Lieut.-Gen. Wolfe, who served with my grandfather and General Webb in Marlborough’s wars. He has a son, Lieut.-Col. James Wolfe, engaged to Miss Lowther of the North—beautiful and well-regarded. Though only thirty, he is held in high esteem throughout the army, having served with distinction under His Royal Highness the Duke wherever British arms were deployed.

I thank you for your message regarding the quarterly allowance of £52 10s., which Mr. Trail will provide. I am not currently in need of funds, and through careful management—necessary, I admit, for maintaining horses, Gumbo, and the proper attire and equipage for a gentleman of our standing—I hope to preserve my credit without burdening you.

The clothes I brought from Virginia will serve me well for years, especially with care. While not quite as fine as those worn here, they are excellent for daily use. I may purchase a few finer shirts for grand occasions, but that is all.

I am grateful that I have not yet needed your famous family pills. Gumbo, however, has benefited greatly from them—he grows fat and cheerful on English beef, ale, and air. He sends his humble respects to you and asks Mrs. Mountain to remember him to all the servants, especially Dinah and Lily, for whom he bought posy rings at the Tunbridge Fair.

Beyond enjoying the pleasures of the place, I assure you I have not neglected my education. I have taken lessons in fencing and dancing. And when the Reverend Mr. Sampson, my Lord Castlewood’s chaplain, came here to drink the waters, he kindly agreed to take up residence at my lodgings. He breakfasts with me each morning, and we read together—Mr. Rapin’s *History*, Dr. Barrow’s sermons, Shakespeare, Mr. Pope’s translation of Homer, and (in French) a delightful collection of Arabian tales.

Several learned men have also been here—among them Mr. Richardson, author of the books you and Mountain and my dear brother so loved. When I told him his works were cherished in your library, he asked me to convey his respectful greetings to you. He is a short, stout man, with little fire visible in his eyes or manner.

My aunt and cousin, Lady Maria, send their warmest regards to you, and I enclose a note for Mountain. I remain, honoured madam,

---

*From my son. Received October 15 at Richmond. Sent: 16 jars preserved peaches, 224 lbs. best tobacco, 24 finest hams, per Royal William of Liverpool; 8 jars peaches, 12 hams for my nephew, the Rt. Honourable the Earl of Castlewood; 4 jars, 6 hams for the Baroness Bernstein; same for Mrs. Lambert of Oakhurst, Surrey; ½ cwt. tobacco. Packet of Infallible Family Pills for Gumbo. My Papa’s large silver-gilt shoe-buckles for H., and red silver-laced saddle-cloth.*

*What do you mien, you silly old Mountain, by sending an order for your poor old divadends dew at Xmas? I'd have you to know I don't want your 7l. 10, and have toar your order up into 1000 bitts. I've plenty of money. But I'm obleaged to you all same. A kiss to Fanny from—Your loving HARRY.*

*This note, which I desired M. to show to me, proves she hath a good heart, and wished to show gratitude to the family by giving up her half-yearly dividend (on £500 at 3%) to my boy. Hence I reprimanded her gently for daring to send money to Mr. E. Warrington without my knowledge. The note to Mountain is not so well spelled as the letter to me.*
*Mem.: Write to Revd. Mr. Sampson to inquire what theological books he reads with H. Recommend Law, Baxter, Drelincourt. Request H. to recite his catechism to Mr. S., which he has never fully mastered. By next ship: 3 jars peaches, ½ cwt. tobacco, hams for Mr. S.*

---

Time has long since passed the Warringtons into memory. Yet one wonders: how is it that two letters sent together—one carefully composed, the other rough and playful—could differ so much in spelling and grammar?

Perhaps Harry, eager to impress his mother, revised his letter with the help of a tutor or friend, correcting minor errors like “who I found and whom took me in.” But the note to Mrs. Mountain—written freely, without oversight—remained unpolished. Perhaps a milliner caught his eye, or a dancing bear passed by, or a jockey showed off a horse beneath his window. Such distractions are common even today.

And why should Harry write with equal care to a servant woman as to his mother? That, too, is natural. We all speak differently to different people. The letter to his mother is polite, measured, respectful—even if it omits certain truths. The note to Mrs. Mountain is honest, affectionate, and slightly mischievous.

And so, let us not judge too harshly. Every generation writes its letters with some reserve, some pretence. Parents wish their children to appear virtuous, obedient, and dignified. Children, in turn, may hide their follies, their joys, their secrets.

There must be distance between parent and child. There must be a gentle hypocrisy—a decorous fiction—that preserves dignity and affection. In the home, we are kings and queens. We expect respect, admiration, silence when we sleep, laughter at our jokes. But outside, we are free—free to dance, to tumble, to live.

So when someone says, “It was immoral of Harry to write such a prim letter while living a merry life,” let us smile and reply: “Yes, dear grandmamma, it was wrong of him. But I suppose you never had your fun when you were young.”

Of course she didn’t. And the sun never shone, the blossoms never bloomed, the blood never danced, the fiddles never sang in her springtime.

Eh, Babet! Mon lait de poule et mon bonnet de nuit!
Ho, Betty! My gruel and my slippers!

Go, ye frisky, merry souls! Dance, laugh, eat cakes and ale!

Our readers, who have followed Harry Warrington’s journey with honesty and care, know well the truth of his feelings for Cattarina—and how that tender connection was shaped by circumstance, not desire. Yet in the gossipy circles of Tunbridge Wells, where tongues wagged like windmills and reputations were as fragile as glass, such truths were buried beneath a mountain of rumor. Many of the older ladies there, particularly Madame de Bernstein, believed the young Virginian to be no better than any other reckless English nobleman—dissipated, impetuous, and given to every kind of scandalous indulgence. To her, Harry’s behavior was proof enough: he danced, he smiled, he offered tea and music at the Wells, and he spoke with charm to every woman who crossed his path. But these were not signs of vice, as she imagined—they were marks of a gentleman raised in a culture where manners mattered more than whispers.

Madame Bernstein, a woman of strong Roman pride and even stronger prejudice, had long held the belief that her nephew should live as Rome did—boldly, proudly, without restraint. So when stories began to circulate about Harry’s supposed affairs—his “Lovelace adventures,” as they were called—she swallowed them whole. She listened eagerly, nodded gravely, and repeated them with relish to anyone who would listen. And yet, though she once watched Maria closely, fearing her niece might fall under Harry’s spell, she now relaxed. Her attention drifted, distracted by her own concerns—her dinners, her rheumatism, her endless round of social duties. The fire in her eyes dimmed; her vigilance cooled. Perhaps she truly believed the danger had passed. Or perhaps, like so many elders before her, she simply stopped caring. And then there was Maria herself—so clever, so composed, so skilled in the art of quiet influence—that she may well have lulled the old Baroness into a false sense of security. At Maria’s age, girls learn quickly how to hide their hearts. And at Madame Bernstein’s age, dragons grow weary. Their claws grow blunt, their breath less fierce, their watchfulness slack. I’ve known several such women in my time—once fearsome, now gentle, their sharp edges softened by years. They no longer threaten the world; they merely sigh over it.

If the folks at Oakhurst could believe every slander whispered about Harry, why should Madame Bernstein, with her long experience of human frailty, be any wiser? Of course, every woman in her circle accepted the tales of Harry’s wild ways as gospel. When the little French dancer returned to London, it was said she’d been cast aside—abandoned by the heartless Virginian for another, whose name was guessed at, whispered, and repeated until it became fact. In Tunbridge Wells, all ranks mingled—ladies of fashion, ladies of questionable reputation, those seeking health, pleasure, or escape—all drinking from the same glasses, dancing to the same fiddles, and exchanging secrets like currency. A century ago, our ancestors gathered at Epsom, Bath, Harrogate, just as we do now at Homburg and Baden. Society never changes its nature—it only changes its dress.

So Harry’s bad name brought comfort to his aunt. It eased her mind about his feelings for Lady Maria. She was so reassured, in fact, that when the chaplain arrived to escort her home, she barely blinked. She preferred to keep Maria close, to talk of Harry’s “wild extravagances,” to whisper that boys were boys, and to confide her plans for marrying Harry off—to someone suitable, someone rich, someone respectable. All this poor Maria had to endure with patience, though her heart beat otherwise.

There lived in the last century a certain French duke and marquis, famed across Europe and America alike, who left behind a memoir so bold and candid that no decent reader should dare open it. He had played the role of Don Juan throughout his life, and in his book named countless court beauties who had fallen to his charm. What must it be like, one wonders, for descendants of those women to find their ancestresses immortalized in such a volume—flaws exposed, virtues mocked?

This nobleman once traveled to North America, where, as he had done in Europe, he expected to conquer hearts. But here, among the simple folk of the colonies, he failed entirely. Had he succeeded, he surely would have recorded it with pride. Instead, silence. Travelers often complain of American rudeness, but let me say from personal experience: the conversation of American gentlemen is modest, and the lives of their women are pure.

Harry Warrington brought that same colonial modesty with him to England. Though he heard the free talk of his new companions—men of the world, seasoned in pleasure—he remained silent, reserved. He avoided double meanings, never boasted of conquests, and blushed when others told bawdy stories. Mr. Sampson, the chaplain, had noticed this during their time at Castlewood. Once, when cousin Will shared a particularly risqué tale, Harry looked uncomfortable. Lord Castlewood had rebuked his brother sharply, telling him to save his jokes for the usher’s table at Kensington. That moment gave rise to the chaplain’s first remark upon seeing Harry: “Reverentia pueris”—respect for youth. For though Sampson lacked strength in virtue, he had grace enough not to offend an innocent boy with cynicism.

The chaplain felt genuine warmth toward Harry after the young man gave him the horse. “You see, sir,” he said, “I am of the world. I’ve led a rough life, and can’t afford to be more particular than my neighbors. Video meliora, deteriora sequor—‘I see what is better, but follow what is worse.’ That was our motto at college. I have a sister, Patty, at boarding school nearby. I keep my tongue clean when speaking to her, and expect others to do the same. So I’ll try to do the same by you.”

He praised Harry often to Madame Bernstein. She delighted in hearing it. She liked Harry—his good looks, his courage, his easy blushes, his bright eyes, his deep voice. His simplicity amused her; his shrewdness charmed her. If he had been witty or learned, she might have grown bored. But he was exactly as he was—natural, unpretentious, and full of quiet dignity. “We must find a good wife for him,” she said to Sampson. “I have a few in mind. We must set him up here. He’ll never return to his savages—or to that little Methodist mother of his.”

And here, too, Sampson had his own designs. He, too, wished to see Harry married—and not just for the sake of propriety, but because he saw a way to serve both his lord and his own interests. There had been talks at Castlewood—perhaps between Sampson and the Earl—about a marriage for Lady Maria, and a reward for the chaplain if he could help bring it about. If he could assist that anxious lady in finding a husband, Sampson was ready to act. He waited now, watching, planning, waiting to see how best to apply his influence.

Sampson proved a most agreeable companion. Within hours, he and Harry were close. The parson was cheerful, hearty, fond of good food and drink, and utterly devoid of sanctimony. He spoke plainly, laughed freely, and never forced piety on his young friend. Yet he took care not to shock him—never revealing the deeper secrets he himself knew too well. With Harry, Sampson was simply a lively, jolly companion—ready for a drinking bout, a cockfight, a game of cards, or a gallop across the common. But his talk remained decent. He aimed to amuse, not corrupt. And he succeeded.

Sampson had animal spirits and natural wit, and a lifetime of experience in the art of flattery—what some might call “toad-eating.” From the moment he entered college as a servitor, he had learned how to make his way in the world by serving others. That was satire, of course—when we say there are no toad-eaters today. But they exist still. Young men at public schools are taught early to flatter, to please, to stand beside greatness. Only now, they do it subtly—no longer bowing low or calling their patrons “sir” in public. They walk arm-in-arm, call men by their first names, borrow money, and swallow their toads in private.

But in Harry’s time, things were different. A gentleman’s toad-eater wore no mask. He openly served, called his patron “sir,” stood when addressed, and flattered by habit. Sampson took no shame in calling Harry his young patron—a Virginian nobleman recommended by the Earl of Castlewood. He was proud to walk beside him, to speak of him in public, to give orders to Harry’s tradesmen (and perhaps receive a percentage in return). He performed every duty of an aide-de-camp—though no one would have called him such. He had played the role of *ami du prince* for many young men of fashion since entering society. And Harry, despite his good intentions, had not always found trustworthy friends.

“Look at the reputation they’ve made for you here!” Sampson exclaimed, returning from the coffee-house. “Monsieur de Richelieu was nothing compared to you!”

“What do you mean?” asked Harry, puzzled. “I’ve never been to Minorca.”

Sampson explained. The widow Patcham, newly arrived, was clearly smitten. Her behavior at the rooms the night before proved it. Mrs. Hooper was another matter—her husband had already fetched her back to London. The whole place was talking.

“Who says so?” Harry demanded, furious. “I’d like to meet the man who dares say it—and confound him!”

“I wouldn’t show him to you,” Sampson laughed. “It might be the worse for him.”

“It’s a shame,” Harry continued, pacing the room. “To speak so lightly of a man’s or a woman’s character. Do you know, in our country, a fellow’s ears wouldn’t be safe? Just before I left home, three brothers shot a man for speaking ill of their sister.”

“Serve the villain right!” Sampson declared.

“They’ve already started this calumny about me—about me and that poor little French dancer.”

“I’ve heard,” Sampson said, shaking powder from his wig.

“Wicked, wasn’t it?”

“Abominable.”

“They said the same thing about my Lord March. Isn’t it shameful?”

“Indeed it is,” Sampson replied, keeping a solemn face—even though he hadnᵗt truly minded the rumors.

“I don’t know what I’d do if my mother heard these stories. It would break her heart. A military friend of mine, Mr. Wolfe, told me how terrible lies were spread about me. Good heavens! What do they think a gentleman of my name and country could possibly do? That I’m a seducer? They might as well accuse me of stealing horses or breaking houses. If I hear one man say it, I’ll have his ears!”

“I’ve read,” Sampson said, laughing, “that the Grand Seignior of Turkey sometimes receives bushels of ears. If you collected all those who’ve spoken ill of you or others, you’d fill baskets.”

“And so I would,” Harry declared. “Any man who speaks against a lady or a gentleman of honor—I’d punish him. Mark that.”

“I shall be sorry for his sake if you do,” Sampson said. “You’ll mark him in a way he won’t like. And I know you’re a man of your word.”

“You may be sure of that,” Harry said. “Now, shall we go to dinner, and then to Lady Trumpington’s tea?”

“You know, sir,” Sampson replied, “I can’t resist a card or a bottle. Let’s have the last first, and then the first shall come last.” And off they went.

That was an age when wine was drunk freely, especially since General Braddock’s army had returned to England. Harry, having heard that it was a point of honor among officers never to refuse a toast or a challenge, had grown fond of claret and bumpers. So he and Sampson drank deeply, naming a favorite lady with each glass, as was the custom.

Sampson had his reasons for wanting to know how far Harry’s feelings for Lady Maria had gone. And as the claret warmed them, their conversation grew frank, open, sincere—just as good wine often inspires. O noble vines of Aquitaine! O sunlit banks of Garonne! O dark caves of Gledstane and Morol, where the dusky flasks sleep! May we not offer thanks for the joy you bring? Can the Temperance men shout in the streets? Can the Vegetarians cry “Cabbage forever”? Must we not, as modest Enophilists, sing your praises?

For after a generous draught of good Bordeaux, there comes a moment—though not quite a pint—when the soul awakens. Wit sparkles, intellect sharpens, thoughts burst forth like birds from a cage. Kindness floods the heart, and truth stands naked before the world. We rush to aid the poor, defend the wronged. We feel ourselves capable of great deeds. But then—the next glass spoils it. The morning brings a headache. We do not enter Parliament. We do not shoot French officers who insult our country. And Jeremy Diddler knocks at eleven, asking for half a sovereign, while we lie ill in bed, unable to answer.

Yet in that golden hour, as they sat over their cups, the company gone, the bottle brought in by Monsieur Barbeau, Sampson found himself eloquent, eager to impart wisdom. And Harry, moved by emotion and wine, longed to confess everything—to tell his new friend all he felt.

“I am glad to hear how you’ve behaved with Cattarina,” Sampson said. “Truly glad. The wine is with you. You’ve shown you can resist temptation, bear down calumny. Ah, my dear sir, not all men are so fortunate. What a fine wine this is!” He sipped deeply. “A toast from you, if you please?”

“Miss Fanny Mountain, of Virginia,” Harry said, filling a bumper. His thoughts flew straight to home.

“One of your American conquests, I suppose?” Sampson teased.

“Nay,” Harry replied. “She’s ten years old. And I’ve never made any conquests in Virginia, Mr. Sampson.”

“You are like a true gentleman,” Sampson said. “You don’t kiss and tell.”

“I neither kiss nor tell. It isn’t our custom to ruin girls or consort with low women. We Virginian gentlemen honor women. We don’t wish to bring them to shame,” Harry declared, proud and handsome. “That girl I mentioned has lived in our family since childhood. I’d shoot any man who harmed her—by Heaven, I would!”

“Your sentiments do you honor!” Sampson cried, grasping his hand. “Let me shake hands with you—not as a retainer to a patron, but as a true friend. With wine like this, all men are equal. Faith, all men are rich—for a time! And Tom Sampson is as wealthy with his bottle as you are with your acres!”

“Let us have another bottle of riches,” Harry laughed. “Encore du cachet jaune, mon bon Monsieur Barbeau!” And out went Monsieur Barbeau.

“Another bottle of riches! Capital! How beautifully you speak French, Mr. Harry!”

“I do speak it well,” Harry said. “At least, Monsieur Barbeau understands me.”

“You do everything well,” Sampson said. “That’s why they say you’ve won so many hearts.”

“There you go again with the women!” Harry snapped. “I hate these stories. Confound me, Sampson, why must a gentleman’s character be blackened so?”

“Well, at any rate,” Sampson said, “there is one—unless my eyes deceive me—whose heart seems to belong to you.”

“Whom do you mean?” Harry asked, flushing.

“Nay, I name no names. It’s not for a poor chaplain to meddle with his betters’ affairs.”

“Thoughts! What thoughts, Sampson?”

“I fancied I saw a preference from a certain lovely lady at Castlewood. And a strong liking from a certain distinguished young gentleman. But I may be wrong. Pardon me.”

“Oh, Sampson!” Harry broke out. “I tell you I’m miserable. I’ve longed to confide in someone. You know, then, that something has been going on—between me and—help, Monsieur Barbeau—and—someone else?”

“I’ve watched it this past month,” Sampson said quietly.

“Confound you, sir! Are you saying you’ve been spying on me?”

“A spy? You made no effort to hide it, Mr. Warrington. Nor did she. You were always together—in the shrubberies, the walks, the village, the galleries. Plenty of eyes saw you.”

“Gracious powers! What did you see, Sampson?”

“Nay, sir,” the chaplain said, smiling. “It’s forbidden to kiss and tell. I say so again.”

Harry turned crimson. “Oh, Sampson,” he whispered. “Can I—can I confide in you?”

“Dearest sir,” Sampson said, squeezing his hand, “you know I would shed my heart’s blood for you.”

It is our pleasant duty now to reveal the secret that Mr. Lambert whispered to his wife at the close of the previous chapter—a secret that brought such joy to every member of the Oakhurst household. With the hay safely stored and the corn not yet ready for harvest, the farm horses stood idle. “Why,” asked Colonel Lambert, “should we not put them into the coach and make a journey to Tunbridge Wells? We could stop by Westerham on the way and visit dear friend Wolfe.”

Mamma embraced the idea with delight—and so did the Colonel himself. The children danced with excitement. The girls rushed off to gather their finest attire: calamancoes, paduasoys, falbalas, furbelows, capes, cardinals, sacks, negligees, solitaires, caps, ribbons, mantuas, clocked stockings, and high-heeled shoes—indeed, every article of finery they possessed. Mamma unearthed her most elegant gowns from the presses, garments reserved only for rare and solemn occasions, which would soon return to lavender-scented silence. The Colonel donned his laced hat and waistcoat, and fastened his silver-hilted hanger at his side. Charley wore a holiday suit once belonging to his father—the very coat in which the Colonel had been married—though Mrs. Lambert had to cut it down, not without a pang of sorrow.

Ball and Dumpling, the family’s best horses, had their manes and tails tied with ribbons. Chump, the old white cart-horse, took his place as unicorn leader, helping pull the carriage up the first five miles of hilly road from Oakhurst to Westerham. The vehicle itself was ancient, believed to have carried King George I from Greenwich to London upon his arrival as monarch. It had belonged to Mr. Lambert’s father and had long been regarded by the family as one of the grandest coaches in all the realm.

Brian, the family coachman—and, let it be confessed, also their ploughman—sat proudly on the box seat beside young Charley. Their valuables were packed in imperials atop the coach. The Colonel’s pistols were tucked into the carriage pockets, and a blunderbuss hung behind the box within Brian’s reach—he was an old soldier, after all. Yet no highwayman dared molest them, nor did any innkeeper demand tolls from the Colonel, whose purse was slender but whose family was large. He was not to be plundered by those who preyed on the king’s highway.

A modest lodging had been arranged by young Colonel Wolfe, at the house where he usually stayed. He rode ahead with them on horseback, and arrived just in time to welcome them. Their rooms happened to be directly across from Madame Bernstein’s residence. On Saturday evening, as the Oakhurst family settled in, they saw chair after chair arriving at the Baroness’s door, each disgorging powdered gentlemen and brocaded ladies for one of her famed card parties.

The sun had not yet set—for our ancestors began their diversions early, indulging in food, drink, or cards from three o’clock onward until dawn. From their window, the young country ladies and their mother watched the guests arrive. Colonel Wolfe identified many of them for the family. It was almost as enjoyable as attending the party themselves, Hetty and Theo agreed. Not only could they see the arrivals, but through the open casements of the Baroness’s house, they could glimpse the guests inside.

Some of these figures we’ve already met. When the Duchess of Queensberry passed by, and Mr. Wolfe explained who she was, Martin Lambert recited several lines from Mat Prior’s poem about “Kitty, beautiful and young.”

“Think that old lady was once like you, girls!” the Colonel remarked.

“Like us, papa? Well, certainly we never claimed to be beauties!” Miss Hetty declared, tossing her head.

“Yes, like you, you little baggage—like you right now, wanting to go to that drum yonder:
*Inflamed with rage at sad restraint
Which wise mamma ordained,
And sorely vexed to play the saint
Whilst wit and beauty reigned.*”

“We were never invited, papa,” said Theo. “And I’m sure if there’s no beauty worth seeing, the wit can’t be much worth hearing.”

“Oh, but Mat Prior is a rare poet!” insisted the Colonel. “Though mind you, girls, skip over any poems I’ve marked with a cross. A rare poet! And to think you’re seeing one of his heroines:
*Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way* (she always will, Mrs. Lambert!)—
*Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way,
Kitty at heart's desire
Obtained the chariot for a day,
And set the world on fire!*”

“I’m sure it must have been very inflammable,” murmured mamma.

“So it was, my dear, twenty years ago—much more so than today,” replied the Colonel.

“Nonsense, Mr. Lambert,” she said.

“Look! Look!” cried Hetty, rushing forward and pointing toward the square and the covered gallery leading to Madame Bernstein’s apartments, where a crowd of street urchins and idlers gathered.

“It’s Harry Warrington!” exclaimed Theo, waving a handkerchief—but Warrington didn’t see her.

The Virginian walked arm-in-arm with a portly clergyman in a crisp, rustling silk gown, and together they entered the Baroness’s door.

“I heard him preach a most admirable sermon here last Sunday,” said Mr. Wolfe. “A little theatrical, but striking and eloquent.”

“You seem to be here most Sundays, James,” observed Mrs. Lambert.

“And Monday, and Tuesday—right through to Saturday,” added the Colonel.

“See, Harry has already dressed himself up—his hair in buckle, and I have no doubt he’s going to the drum too.”

“I’d rather sit quietly on a Saturday evening,” said sober Mr. Wolfe. “Away from card-playing and scandal. But I confess, dear Mrs. Lambert, I am under orders. Shall I go across and send Mr. Warrington to you?”

“No,” said meek Mrs. Lambert. “Let him enjoy his evening. We’ll see him tomorrow. He won’t want to be disturbed among his fine company by us country folk.”

“I’m glad he’s with a clergyman who preaches so well,” said Theo softly. Her eyes seemed to say: *You see, good people, he is not so bad as you thought him, nor as I ever believed him to be.*

“The clergyman has a kind, handsome face,” someone noted.

“Here comes a greater clergyman!” cried Mr. Wolfe. “It’s my Lord of Salisbury, with his blue ribbon, and a chaplain following behind.”

“And whom in mercy’s name do we have here?” broke in Mrs. Lambert as a gilded sedan-chair, adorned with no fewer than five earl’s coronets and carried by bearers in richly laced clothes, approached the Baroness’s door. Three footmen in matching livery preceded it.

The Bishop, who had been about to enter, stopped and bowed deeply, stepping back with reverence as the sedan-chair drew near. He offered his hand to the woman who stepped out.

“Who on earth is this?” asked Mrs. Lambert.

“Sprechen sie Deutsch? Ja, meinherr. Nichts verstand,” joked the Colonel.

“Pooh, Martin,” said mamma.

“Well, if you can’t understand High Dutch, my love, how can I help it? Your education was neglected at school. Can you understand heraldry? I know you can.”

“I make,” cried Charley, reciting the shield, “three merions on a field or, with an earl’s coronet.”

“A countess’s coronet, my son,” corrected the Colonel. “The Countess of Yarmouth, my son.”

“And pray who is she?” asked the children.

“It has always been the custom of our sovereigns to elevate persons of distinction,” the Colonel continued gravely. “This eminent lady has been so honored by our gracious monarch, raised to the rank of Countess in this kingdom.”

“But why, papa?” the daughters asked together.

“Never mind, girls!” said mamma.

But the incorrigible Colonel persisted.

“Y, my children, is one of the last and most awkward letters of the alphabet. When I tell you stories, you’re always asking Why. Why should my Lord Bishop be bowing to that woman? Look at him rubbing his fat hands together, smiling into her face! It’s not a handsome face anymore—it’s painted red and white like Scaramouch in the pantomime. See—there comes another blue-ribbon! My Lord Bamborough, descendant of the Hotspurs, proudest man in England. He stops, bows, smiles, hat in hand. She taps him with her fan. Get away, you little blackguard boys, don’t tread on the robe of the lady whom the King delights to honor.”

“But why does the King honor her?” the girls asked again.

“There goes that odious last letter but one!” said the Colonel. “Have you ever heard of her Grace, the Duchess of Kendal? No. Of the Duchess of Portsmouth? Non plus. Of the Duchess of La Vallière? Or Fair Rosamond?”

“Hush, papa!” said the mother, placing a finger to his lips. “There’s no need to bring blushes to my dear ones’ cheeks, Martin Lambert!”

“It’s not I,” replied the son of the old republican. “It’s their sacred Majesties who are the cause of the shame. Think of bishops and the proudest nobles cringing before that painted High Dutch Jezebel. Oh, it’s a shame! A shame!”

“Confusion!” cried Colonel Wolfe, snatching up his hat and dashing from the room. He had seen the young lady he admired and her guardian walking across the Pantiles toward the Baroness’s party. They arrived just as the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden was speaking with the two lords—spiritual and temporal—and both men made the deepest bows and waited until she had entered the house on the Bishop’s arm.

Theo turned from the window with a sorrowful, awestricken expression. Hetty remained, staring with indignation in her eyes and a faint flush on each cheek.

“A penny for little Hetty’s thoughts,” said mamma, coming to the window to lead her away.

“I’m thinking what I’d do if I saw papa bowing to that woman,” Hetty said.

Tea and a hissing kettle appeared, and the family sat down to their evening meal—though Hetty begged her brother not to close the curtains, keeping command of the window from her seat. Young Charley had gone down among the crowd to inspect the armorial bearings on the sedans, no doubt, and also to spend sixpence on a cheese-cake, as ordered by mamma and desired by himself. He returned with the treat wrapped in paper.

“Look, mother,” he said, “do you see that big man in brown beating the pillars with a stick? That’s the learned Mr. Johnson. He visits our master at the Friars sometimes. He was sitting with friends just now at the tea-table before Mrs. Brown’s tart-shop. They serve tea there for twopence a cup—I heard Mr. Johnson say he’d had seventeen cups—that makes two-and-tenpence. What a sum for tea!”

“What would you have, Charley?” asked Theo.

“I think I’d have cheese-cakes,” said Charley, sighing as he bit into a large slice. “And the gentleman Mr. Johnson was with,” he continued, mouth full, “was Mr. Richardson, who wrote—”

“Clarissa!” cried all the women at once, rushing to the window to catch a glimpse of their favorite author.

By now the sun had set, stars twinkled above, and the footman lit the candles in the Baroness’s room opposite. Theo and her mother stood together, watching. There was a small illumination at Mrs. Brown’s shop, where they saw one lady retrieving Mr. Richardson’s hat and stick, another tying a shawl around his neck, and then he walked home.

“Oh dear me! He doesn’t look like Grandison!” exclaimed Theo.

“I rather think I wish we hadn’t seen him, my dear,” said mamma, known for her sentimental nature and love of novels.

They were interrupted again by Hetty, who called: “Never mind that little fat man—look yonder, mamma!”

They looked. There was Mr. Warrington being presented to the Countess of Yarmouth, still followed by the obsequious peer and prelate with blue ribbons. Then the Countess graciously seated herself at a card table, joined by the Bishop, the Earl, and a fourth partner. Soon, Mr. Warrington appeared in the window embrasure with a lady they recognized—the same one they had briefly seen at Oakhurst.

“How much finer he looks!” remarked mamma.

“What has he done to himself?” asked Theo.

“Look at his grand lace frills and rules! My dear, he’s not wearing our shirts anymore,” said the matron.

“What are you talking about, girls?” asked papa, reclining on his sofa, perhaps dozing like a dutiful house-father.

The girls told him Harry Warrington was in the window, speaking with his cousin Lady Maria Esmond.

“Come away!” shouted papa. “You have no right to spy on the young fellow. Down with the curtains, I say!”

And down they went—so the girls saw nothing more of Madame Bernstein’s gathering that night.

I beg you not to take offense if I note, merely for contrast, that while Madame Bernstein and her guests—bishop, dignitaries, noblemen—were gambling, whispering scandals, drinking champagne, and honoring the king’s favorite, the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden, our country friends knelt around their table. Brian, the coachman, came silently, his creaking boots barely audible. Mr. Lambert stood and read aloud a quiet prayer, asking Heaven to lighten their darkness and guard them from danger, and to grant the requests of those gathered.

Our young folks rose early on Sunday morning, dressed in their new finery meant to charm the people of Tunbridge, and, escorted by Charley, strolled through the town, the quaint Pantiles, and the lovely common long before breakfast or church bells rang.

It was Hester who discovered where Harry Warrington lodged, spotting Mr. Gumbo in undress, his beautiful hair in curl-papers, drawing aside red curtains and opening a window sash to breathe in the morning air. Mr. Gumbo did not see the Oakhurst children, though they saw him clearly. He leaned gracefully from the window, waved a large feather brush—used to dust the furniture—engaged in cheerful conversation with a milkmaid below, and kissed his hand to her. His fingers sparkled with rings, and his person gleamed with jewels—gifts, no doubt, from the fair ladies who adored the young African.

Before breakfast, the girls passed the window again. It remained open, but the room was empty. No sign of Harry Warrington. Neither spoke of the subject weighing on both their minds.

Hetty was annoyed with Charley, who clamored for breakfast and accused him of always thinking of food. When she asked sarcastically what he wanted, he honestly admitted he’d like another cheese-cake. Good-natured Theo laughed and said she had a sixpence—if the shop was open, Charley could have one.

It was open. Theo took out her little netted purse, made by her dearest schoolfriend, containing her pocket-piece, her grandmother’s guinea, her few shillings, and even some copper coins. She treated Charley to his beloved snack.

Fine company filled the church. There was the comical old Duchess, old Madame Bernstein with Lady Maria beside her, Mr. Wolfe next to Miss Lowther, singing from the same psalm-book, and Mr. Richardson with a group of ladies. One of them, Papa told them afterward, was Miss Fielding, sister of Harry Fielding.

“Oh, girls, what excellent company he was! And his books are worth a dozen of your milksop Pamelas and Clarissas, Mrs. Lambert. But what woman ever loved true humor? And there was Mr. Johnson sitting among the charity children. Did you see how he turned to the altar at the Belief and knocked over two or three of the frightened little urchins in leather breeches? And what a powerful sermon Harry’s parson gave—about scandal! How he stirred up some of the old harridans nearby! Why wasn’t Mr. Warrington at church? It was a shame he wasn’t.”

“I really didn’t notice whether he was there or not,” said Miss Hetty, tossing her head.

But Theo, truthful as ever, said, “Yes, I thought of him, and was sorry he wasn’t. And you thought of him too, Hetty.”

“I did no such thing, miss,” Hetty insisted.

“Then why did you whisper to me it was Harry’s clergyman who preached?”

“To think of Mr. Warrington’s clergyman is not to think of Mr. Warrington. It was a splendid sermon, and the children sang terribly out of tune. And there’s Lady Maria at the window opposite, smelling roses. That’s Mr. Wolfe’s step—I know his military tramp. Right left—right left! How do you do, Colonel Wolfe?”

“Why do you look so glum, James?” asked Colonel Lambert kindly.

“Has the charmer been scolding you, or is your conscience pricked by the sermon? Mr. Sampson, isn’t that the parson’s name? A famous preacher, I say!”

“A pretty preacher, and a pretty practitioner!” said Mr. Wolfe, shrugging.

“Why, I thought the sermon lasted less than ten minutes, and madam didn’t sleep a wink—did you, Molly?”

“Did you see when the fellow came into church?” asked the indignant Colonel Wolfe.

“He came in at the open door of the common, just in time, as the psalm ended.”

“Well, he may have been reading the service to a sick person. There are many here,” suggested Mrs. Lambert.

“Reading the service! Oh, my good Mrs. Lambert! Do you know where I found him? I went to look for your young scapegrace of a Virginian.”

“His own name is a very pretty name, I’m sure,” cried Hetty.

“It isn’t Scapegrace! It’s Henry Esmond Warrington, Esquire.”

“Miss Hester, I found the parson in his cassock and Henry Esmond Warrington, Esquire, in his bedgown, at quarter past ten in the morning, when all the Sunday bells were ringing, and they were finishing a game of piquet they’d played the night before!”

“Well, many good people play cards on Sundays. The King plays cards on Sundays.”

“Hush, my dear!”

“I know he does,” said Hetty, “with that painted person we saw yesterday—Countess what-d’you-call-her?”

“I think, my dear Miss Hester, a clergyman had better read God’s Word than the Devil’s books on that day—and so I took the liberty of telling your parson.”

Hetty looked as if she thought it was a liberty indeed.

“And I told our young friend he’d better be on his way to church than lounging in his bedgown.”

“You wouldn’t have Harry go to church in a dressing-gown and nightcap, Colonel Wolfe? That would be a sight indeed!” said Hetty fiercely.

“I’d have my little girl’s tongue not wag quite so fast,” remarked papa, patting her flushed cheek.

“Not speak when a friend is attacked, and nobody says a word in his favor? No; nobody!”

Her lips closed tightly. Her whole frame trembled. She cast a defiant glance at Mr. Wolfe and fled the room, just in time to shut the door and burst into tears on the stairs.

Mr. Wolfe looked deeply embarrassed.

“I’m sure, Aunt Lambert, I didn’t mean to hurt Hester’s feelings.”

“No, James,” she said gently—the young officer had called her Aunt Lambert since childhood—and she gave him her hand.

Mr. Lambert whistled his favorite tune, “Over the hills and far away,” tapping a rhythm on the windowpane.

“You mustn’t whistle on Sunday, papa!” cried Charley, artless as ever.

Then he added, “It’s three hours since breakfast, and I’d like to finish Theo’s cheese-cake.”

“Oh, you greedy child!” laughed Theo.

But hearing a sudden noise outside, she ran from the room, closing the door behind her.

We will not follow her. The sound was the sob rising from Hester’s overwhelmed heart. Though we cannot see, I am certain the little maid flung herself into her sister’s arms and wept upon Theo’s kind breast.

Hetty did not join the family’s afternoon walk on the common. She claimed a headache and lay in bed, watched over by her mother. Charley found a companion from Grey Friars. Mr. Wolfe naturally paired with Miss Lowther. Theo and her father took a quiet stroll in the Sabbath sunshine and found Madame Bernstein basking on a bench beneath a tree, her niece and nephew nearby.

Harry ran up to greet them, radiant with pleasure at seeing his dear friends. The elder ladies were gracious to the Colonel and his wife, who had so kindly welcomed their Harry. How noble and handsome he looked! Theo thought. She called him by his Christian name, as if he were truly her brother.

“Why didn’t we see you sooner today, Harry?” she asked.

“I never thought you were here, Theo.”

“But you might have seen us if you’d wished.”

“Where?” asked Harry.

“There, sir,” she said, pointing to the church. She held her hand up as if in gentle reproach, yet kindness shone in her honest face.

Ah, friendly young reader, wandering through life and battling temptation—may you, too, have one or two pure hearts to love and pray for you!

When Colonel Lambert learned the secret his youngest daughter had unwittingly revealed, his first impulse was anger—not at her, but at the young man who had stirred such emotion in her heart. “A plague upon all scapegraces, English or Indian!” he declared to his wife. “I wish this one had broken his nose against any doorpost but ours.”

“Perhaps,” Mrs. Lambert replied gently, “we are meant to cure him of being a scapegrace. And the fall at our door may have been no accident. You laughed at me before when I said so, Mr. Lambert; but if Heaven did not send this young gentleman to us, who did? It may be for the good of us all that he came.”

“It’s hard, Molly!” groaned the Colonel. “We raise them, love them, tend them through sickness and health. We save every penny, patch our own coats, lose sleep over their headaches, work night and day to fulfill their wishes. They call us ‘darling daddy’ and ‘dearest pappy,’ and say no father could be like ours. Then comes Tuesday morning—king of my house and family. Tuesday evening—Prince Whippersnapper arrives, and my reign is over. A lifetime of devotion forgotten for a pair of blue eyes, lean legs, and golden hair.”

“'Tis written that women should follow their husbands,” said the matron, laying a hand on his arm. “And our courtship was not long, dear Martin.”

“It’s human nature,” sighed the Colonel. “What can you expect?”

“And yet,” added Mrs. Lambert softly, “I think I did my duty to my husband—even though I left my father for him.”

“Excellent wench!” exclaimed the Colonel. “Perdition catch my soul, but I do love thee, Molly! But mind you, your father never did me any favors. And if ever I am to have sons-in-law—”

“Of course you will!” interrupted mamma. “My girls must marry, Mr. Lambert!”

“Well, when they come,” he retorted, “I’ll hate them as your father hated me—for stealing his treasure away.”

“Don’t be irreligious, Martin Lambert!” she insisted. “You’re unnatural, sir!”

“Nay, my dear,” he answered, tapping his jaw. “I have an old tooth here. 'Tis natural it should come out. But when the tooth-puller tugs it, 'tis natural I should feel pain. Do you suppose I don’t love Hetty more than any tooth in my head?”

No woman, however, resists the idea of her daughter marrying—even if fathers grumble. Mothers and grandmothers, especially, relive their youth at their children’s weddings. Their souls dress again in lace and muslin, postillions’ ribbons bloom anew, and they flutter into the carriage, off to new beginnings. Who among them has not tucked bridal favors and gowns away in lavender-scented drawers of the heart?

“It will be sad to part with her,” Mrs. Lambert murmured.

“You’ve already settled that,” laughed the Colonel. “Had I not best go order raisins and currants for the wedding cake?”

“And then I shall leave the house in their care when I go to Virginia with her,” she added. “How far is it, Martin? I imagine thousands of miles.”

“A hundred and seventy-three thousand three hundred and ninety-one and three-quarters, my dear,” he replied gravely, “by the near way—through Prester John’s country. By the other route, through Persia—”

“Oh, give me the one with least sea,” she interrupted. “Your horrid ships—I can’t bear them!”

“I hope Rachel Esmond and I shall become better friends,” she continued. “She had such spirit when we were girls at school.”

“Shall we begin the baby-linen?” asked the Colonel, now puzzled.

Mrs. Lambert likely thought there was nothing odd about it—she’d seen lovely lace caps and bibs in Mrs. Bobbinit’s shop.

That Sunday afternoon, after the discovery, little Hetty lay on her pillow—cheeks flushed, eyes closed, face full of sorrow. Her mother watched her with calm composure, even seeming pleased at her daughter’s distress. The girl was not only unhappy but furious with herself for having let her feelings show. Perhaps she hadn’t known her own heart until the sudden wave of emotion revealed it. Now, she was ashamed—as if she’d committed a crime and been caught. She raged at her weakness, vowed never to forgive herself for such humiliation.

Like a young deer wounded by a hunter’s arrow, she chafed in the forest, angry at the sting in her side, snarling at her kin, growling at her mother. Little Hetty tore at her thoughts, gnawed her pride, growled inwardly—so fierce that one might hesitate to approach her, brother or parent alike.

“What business has any young woman,” she cried, “to indulge in such nonsense? Mamma, I ought to be whipped and sent to bed. I know perfectly well Mr. Warrington doesn’t care a fig for me. He probably prefers French actresses or some milliner-girl from the toy-shop. And rightly so—they’re better than I am. Why, what a fool I am to cry like a ninny over nothing—because Mr. Wolfe said Harry played cards on a Sunday! I know he’s not clever like papa. I believe he’s stupid—I’m certain he is. But he’s not as stupid as I am. Why, of course, I can’t marry him. How can I go to America and leave you and Theo? He must like someone else—someone in Virginia, or Tunbridge, or Jericho. He’s a prince in his own land—he wouldn:think of marrying a poor half-pay officer’s daughter with twopence to her name. Remember how you used to tell me, when I was a baby, that I cried for the moon? I’m a baby now—a ridiculous, silly baby. Don’t talk to me, Mrs. Lambert, I am.”

She threatened Theo fiercely, swearing she’d never forgive her if she dared reveal the secret. As for Charley, still fixated on cheese-cakes, he’d noticed nothing. The parents and sister promised silence, each bound by the same tender secrecy.

“I begin to think we should have stayed home,” sighed Mrs. Lambert.

“Nay, my dear,” replied the Colonel. “Human nature is what it is. Hetty’s mother told me she once liked a young curate—before falling madly for a soldier of Kingsley’s. And I myself had a dozen wounds before Miss Molly Benson took my heart entirely. Our children will follow in our footsteps, I suppose. Yesterday, you scolded me for grumbling at Hetty’s early fancies. To do her justice, she hides her feelings well. I defy Mr. Warrington to guess how she feels.”

“A daughter of mine,” said the mother with dignity, “will not throw herself at a gentleman’s feet.”

“Nor the teacup either, my dear,” returned the Colonel. “Miss Het treats Mr. Warrington like a vixen. He never visits without getting boxed in some fashion. I protest she’s barely civil—but knowing what goes on in that young hypocrite’s mind, I won’t be angry at her rudeness.”

“She needn’t be rude at all, Martin,” said the mother. “Our girl is good enough for any gentleman in England or America. If their ages suit, why shouldn’t they marry?”

“If he wants her,” said the Colonel, “shouldn’t he ask her? I’m sorry we came. I’d turn the horses around and ride home tonight.”

But the mother smiled. “Depend on it, Martin, these things are wisely ordered. That Harry Warrington was brought to our gate—that he and our children met again—was not by chance. If Heaven decrees a marriage, it will be.”

“At what age,” asked the Colonel, “do women begin and stop matchmaking? If Hetty falls in love and out again, she won’t be the first. I wish we were on our way home. If I had my way, I’d leave tonight.”

“He has promised to drink tea here tonight,” said the mother softly. “Would you take away our child’s pleasure?”

The father, in his own way, was kind-hearted. “You know, my dear,” he said, “if either of them fancied our ears, we’d cut them off and serve them in fricassee.”

Mary Lambert laughed. When he was most tender, he was most grotesque. Pulling her ear, behind which her silver-streaked hair was neatly combed, he likely hurt her not at all. She may have been thinking of her own sweet courtship days—those hallowed memories of youth and love.

If youthful love is beautiful to see, how much more lovely is affection that endures through years, sorrows, fading beauty, life’s doubts and differences!

Hester had promised to hide her feelings from Mr. Warrington—and she kept her word, perhaps too well. Not only did Harry come to tea, but he invited them to an evening entertainment at the Assembly Rooms, given in their honor.

“A dance, and for us!” cried Theo. “Oh, Harry, how delightful! Can we start right now?”

“For a savage Virginian,” said the Colonel, “you’re remarkably civilized, Harry Warrings.”

“My dear,” said the Colonel, “shall we dance a minuet together?”

“We’ve done that before, Martin Lambert,” replied his wife.

Her husband hummed a tune, swept a plate from the table, and bowed with it as if it were a hat, while she curtseyed with grace.

Only Hetty remained glum.

“Why, child,” asked Theo, “have you no thanks for Mr. Warrington?”

“I never cared much for dancing,” said Hetty.

“What use is standing opposite a stupid man and dancing down a room with him?”

“Merci du compliment!” said Mr. Warrington.

“I didn’t mean you were stupid,” stammered Hetty, biting her lip—remembering her earlier words, and catching Theo’s amused glance.

But she was furious—though it was only a teasing remark.

“I hate dancing,” she declared, tossing her head. “There—I admit it.”

“Nay, you used to like it,” interposed her mother.

“That was when she was a child,” said her father. “Don’t you see she’s grown into an old woman?”

“Or perhaps Miss Hester has the gout?” suggested Theo.

“Fiddle!” snapped Hester, stamping her feet.

“What’s a dance without a fiddle?” asked her father imperturbably.

Darkness fell over Harry Warrington’s face.

“I come to please them,” he thought, “to give them joy and a dance. And she tells me she hates dancing. We don’t treat kindness so in our country. Nor speak to parents so.”

Indeed, customs have changed in the United States since then—perhaps young folks there are now quite Hettified.

But Hetty did not stop there. She mocked everyone at the Wells, especially Harry’s companions, making him feel deeply offended. Later, seeing Mrs. Lambert alone, he asked, “What have I done to offend her so?”

The kind matron felt even more warmly toward the boy after her daughter’s behavior. She longed to reveal Hester’s secret.

Theo also spoke privately to her sister.

“But Hester would not listen. In her bedroom, alone, she was as angry as she had been in the drawing-room.”

“Suppose he hates me?” she said. “I expect he will. I hate myself. I scorn myself for being such an idiot. How could he do otherwise than hate me? Didn’t I abuse him? Call him goose? All sorts of names? And I knew all along he wasn’t clever. I know I’m smarter than he is. It’s only because he’s tall, with blue eyes and a pretty nose that I like him. What a fool a girl must be to like a man just because he has blue eyes and hooked features! So I’m a fool—and I won’t hear a word to the contrary, Theo!”

But Theo thought her sister anything but foolish. She believed Hetty was worthy of any prince in Christendom.

“You’re silly sometimes, Hetty,” she said, “especially when you speak unkindly to those who mean you well—like you did to Mr. Warrington tonight. When he invited us to the Assembly Rooms, nothing could have been more gallant. Why did you say you didn’t care for music, dancing, or tea? You know you love them all.”

“I said it to punish myself,” Hetty replied. “To vex myself, to whip myself as I deserve. And besides—how can you expect an idiot like me to say anything but idiotic things? I actually enjoyed seeing him angry. I thought, *Ah!* Now I’ve hurt his feelings. Now he’ll think Hetty Lambert is an odious, sour-tempered vixen. And that will teach him—and you—and mamma—and papa—that I’m not going to set my cap at Mr. Harry. No—our papa is ten times better than he is. I’ll stay with papa. If he asked me to go to Virginia tomorrow, I wouldn’t. My sister is worth all the Virginians that ever lived.”

Then, I suppose, followed kisses between the sisters. A knock came at the door—the mother had heard their talk through the wall.

“Children,” she called, “it’s time to sleep.”

Theo’s eyes closed quickly, and she was asleep. But poor little Hetty—imagine the hours ticking by, her eyes wide open, tossing and wakeful with the agony of her wound.

“It’s a judgment upon me,” she whispered, “for speaking scornfully of him. But why should there be a judgment? I was only joking. I knew I liked him all along. But I thought Theo liked him too—and I’d give up anything for my darling Theo. If she had, no torture would have made me speak. I’d have fetched a rope-ladder to help her run away with Harry—or brought the clergyman to marry them. Then I’d have retired alone—alone—alone—to care for papa and mamma, the poor villagers, read sermons—though I hate them—and die without saying a word—not a word—and I shall die soon, I know I shall.”

But when dawn broke, the little maid slept peacefully beside her sister, a tear or two staining her rosy cheek.

Most of us play with sharp tools in youth—and cut ourselves. At first, the wound stings, we drop the knife, and cry like babies. A few unlucky ones sever their heads or stab themselves fatally—and perish. But many, alas, handle Love’s fiery arrows, sharpened on his whetstone—pricked, scarred, tattooed with wounds—and live to be lively again.

Wir auch haben das irdische Glück gekostet; wir auch haben gelebt—und so weiter. Sing your death-song, sweet Thekla! Perish, poor victim of consumption, if you choose! Had you lived longer, you’d look back on a broken heart without thinking of a grave-digger. Let us hope no sexton is needed for Miss Hetty.

Yet the moment she wakes, there it is—the pain returns, melting only briefly under the warmth of youth and tears.

Generous with his newly acquired fortune, hospitable and warm-hearted to all, our young Virginian, now fully embraced in the role of a gentleman of fashion, could not help but host an evening’s entertainment for his country friends at the Assembly Rooms. True to the customs of the day, he invited nearly every remaining guest from the Wells, ensuring no one was left out of the festivities.

Card tables were arranged in one room for those who found amusement in gaming—a pastime as common then across Europe as breathing. In another chamber, supper was laid out with generous quantities of champagne and bowls of negus, its rich, spiced warmth meant to comfort after a long day. The grand assembly hall itself was reserved for dancing, where Harry Warrington’s guests indulged in the social rituals of their ancestors—courteous, deliberate, and steeped in tradition.

Yet I cannot pretend the night was especially lively. First came the minuets, performed slowly and with solemn grace by a few couples. The most distinguished ladies took precedence: the spinsters of highest rank stepped forward first, and among them stood my Lady Maria Esmond, daughter of an earl and the most noble woman present—save for Lady Augusta Crutchley, who sat quietly aside due to her lameness. It was only natural that Mr. Warrington should open the dance with his cousin, and he did so with such elegance and poise that the entire room applauded silently. He danced more gracefully than Mr. Wolfe, who partnered Miss Lowther, and moved with a quiet confidence that drew admiration.

Having completed the first minuet, Harry courteously asked Miss Theo to join him for the next. She blushed, delighted, and glided through the steps with joy, winning smiles from her parents and sharp envy from Miss Humpleby, daughter of Sir John Humpleby of Liphook, who had hoped to follow Lady Maria herself.

After the minuets came country dances, played upon a harp, fiddle, and flageolet perched in a small balcony above the dancers. Their music, though feeble and somewhat melancholy, echoed through the room like a sigh from the past.
