One need only pick up an old manuscript and play these tunes today to understand why they seem so sorrowful. And yet, people once danced, laughed, courted, and flirted beneath their sad strains. There is a faint bitterness in almost every air—an *amari aliquid*, a trace of sorrow. Perhaps it is because they are relics now, cast into the limbo of memory, their echoes calling softly from beyond time. Or perhaps they were once bright and joyful—just as future generations may one day listen to our modern music and marvel: “Good heavens! Was this truly what amused our ancestors?”

Among the guests was none other than the Duchess of Queensberry—Colonel Lambert’s and Mr. Prior’s famed heroine. Though she turned her back on a countess present, laughed loudly, and pointed at her with her fan, the rest of the company bowed low and cringed before the countess, scarcely acknowledging the duchess’s presence or her jokes. This countess was none other than the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden, the lady whom His Majesty George the Second, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, held in high favour.

She had met Harry earlier that morning in the walks and had been kind to him, even promising a game of cards that very evening. Poor Colonel Blinkinsop, mistaking the invitation for himself, bowed deeply. “Pooh! Pooh!” exclaimed the Countess, laughing. “I don’t mean you—I mean the young Virginian!”

And so, everyone congratulated Harry on his good fortune.

That evening, the whole world seemed to gather around my Lady Yarmouth—not out of mere politeness, but in deference to her royal status. My Lord Bamborough eagerly sought to partner her at quadrille. My Lady Blanche Pendragon, a model of virtue; Sir Lancelot Quintain, a paragon of knightly honour; Mr. Dean of Ealing, a celebrated preacher; and countless noblemen, generals, matrons, and spinsters—all vied for her attention, hoping for a smile, a nod, or just a chance to stand near her card table.

Lady Maria waited upon her with humble respect. Madame de Bernstein treated her with dignified courtesy. But Harry’s bow was no lower than propriety required—and yet, Miss Hester took offense.

During their dance, she scarcely spoke to him. When he led her to the supper-room for refreshments, she remained cold and distant. As they passed the Countess’s card table, the older woman called out cheerfully: “Mr. Warrington, does your little bird enjoy dancing?”

“I thank your ladyship,” replied Miss Hester sharply, tossing her head, “but I do not like dancing, nor cards.” Then, with a curtsey stiff as a cheese, she marched away.

Harry was deeply offended. Sarcasm from youth toward age wounded him. Flippant remarks directed at himself stung. Courteous in his own simple way, he expected the same in return.

Hetty knew exactly what she was doing. She saw the flush of anger rise on his face, caught the momentary fire in his eyes—but chose to wear her innocent smile. As they approached the sideboard, she casually remarked: “What a horrid, vulgar old woman she is—don’t you think?”

“Which woman?” he asked.

“That German woman—my Lady Yarmouth—everyone is bowing to.”

“She has been kind to me,” Harry said, grimly.

“And you’ve bowed to her too! You look as if your negus isn’t pleasant,” she continued lightly.

“It’s not very good,” he admitted, swallowing.

“And the custard is terrible! I swear it’s made with bad eggs!” she declared.

“I wish, Hester,” he said, voice low, “that the evening and the company had pleased you better.”

“It’s unfortunate,” she retorted, tossing her curls, “but I suppose you couldn’t help it.”

Harry groaned inwardly—perhaps aloud. He clenched his fists and teeth. The little tormentor pressed on: “You seem upset. Shall we go to your mother?”

“Yes,” he snapped, glaring. “Let us go to your mother.” And, turning sharply, he muttered under his breath: “Curse you—why are you always in the way?”—to a waiter who happened to be standing nearby.

“La! Is that how you speak in Virginia?” asked Miss Pertness.

“We can be rough there sometimes,” Harry replied slowly, his voice quivering, “and we can’t help being disturbed.” He looked down at her, eyes blazing.

Hetty saw nothing clearly after that—only a blur until she reached her mother.

Never had she seen Harry look so noble, so striking. “You look pale, child!” her mother fretted, as all mothers do when anxious. “It’s the heat—or the cold. Thank you, Mr. Warrington.” She offered a faint curtsey, while Harry returned a deep, formal bow and walked away, lost in thought.

At first, he barely registered what was happening—so great was his anger. But soon, another quarrel erupted—this time between his aunt and the Duchess of Queensberry.

As the royal favourite passed the duchess, the latter gave her a fierce stare—her eyes, once brilliant enough to “set the world on fire,” now dimmed by age. She turned to her neighbour with a forced laugh, then launched a steady stream of giggles and sneers at the Hanoverian lady.

The Countess continued her game, unaware—or unwilling to notice—the insults aimed at her. A feud had long existed between the two noblewomen.

“How you all bow down to the idol!” the Duchess declared. “Don’t tell me—you’re just as bad as the rest, my good Madame Bernstein!”

“Oh, what a Christian country this is!” the Baroness replied. “And how your dear first husband, the Bishop, would have loved to see such a sight!”

“Forgive me, Your Grace,” said Madame de Bernstein, “if I fail to understand.”

“We are both growing old,” the Duchess said, “or perhaps we simply choose not to understand. That’s how women are, my dear young Iroquois.”

“You mentioned it was a Christian country,” the Baroness reminded her. “But I fail to grasp the point.”

“Indeed,” the Duchess replied, “there is very little point! I meant only that we are such good Christians—we forgive so easily. Don’t you remember reading, when you were young, or your husband the Bishop preaching from the pulpit, about the Jewish woman caught in sin? The Pharisees wanted to stone her. But today? We don’t stone her—we adore her! Any man in this room would crawl on his knees if she bid him. Yes, Madame Walmoden, you may raise your painted face and frown with your painted brows at me. I know I’m talking about you—and I intend to keep talking. I say any man here would kneel round the room if you commanded it!”

“I think,” said Harry firmly, “I know two or three who wouldn’t.”

“Quick, let me hug them to my heart!” the Duchess cried. “Which ones? Bring them to me, my dear Iroquois! Let us play a game of four—of honest men and women. If we can find two more partners, Mr. Warrington!”

“We are three,” said the Baroness, forcing a laugh. “Let us play a dummy.”

“Where is the third?” the Duchess asked, scanning the room.

“Madam!” the Baroness replied, rising sharply. “I leave your Grace to boast of your honesty—which I have no doubt is unblemished. But I beg you not to question mine before my family and children!”

“See how she fires up at a word!” the Duchess chuckled. “I am sure, my dear creature, you are as honest as most of the company.”

“Which may not be good enough for Her Grace the Duchess of Queensberry and Dover,” Harry interjected. “She might have stayed away, but it is the best my nephew could offer—and the best he has given you. You look astonished, Harry, my dear—and well you may. He is not used to our ways, madam.”

“Madam,” the Duchess retorted, tapping her fan, “he has found an aunt who can teach him our ways—and much more! She will teach him to welcome all guests, young or old, rich or poor. That is the Virginian way, isn’t it, Harry? She will tell him that when Catherine Hyde is angry with his old aunt, they were friends as girls—and ought not to quarrel now that they are old women. And she will not be wrong, will she, Duchess?”

With that, one dowager made a perfect curtsey to the other—and the battle, poised to begin, dissolved into silence.

“Egad,” Chaplain Sampson exclaimed the next morning, as Harry recounted the evening’s events, “it was like Byng and Galissoniere!”

“No force on earth could have stopped them from going to war,” Harry said.

“Seventy-fours at least—both of them!” laughed the chaplain.

“But the Baroness avoided battle,” Harry added, “and sailed out of danger with unmatched skill.”

“Why should she fear?” Sampson asked. “I’ve heard you say your aunt is as witty as any woman alive—no dowager’s tongue could match hers.”

“Hem!” Harry murmured. “Perhaps she had good reason to stay peaceful.”

Sampson understood perfectly. He knew the Baroness’s reputation was tarnished, her name linked to whispers too dark to repeat. Any insult thrown at Madame Walmoden could just as easily reflect upon her.

“Sir,” Harry said suddenly, “you don’t mean to suggest there’s anything against my aunt’s character?”

The chaplain looked at him with such astonishment that Harry realized there must be some hidden history.

“Good heavens!” he groaned. “Are there two in the family…?”

“Which two?” the chaplain asked.

But Harry stopped, flushing crimson. He remembered—soon we shall learn—how he’d come by knowledge of the other family secret. He bit his lip and fell silent.

“Bygones are always unpleasant,” said the chaplain gently. “Best we say nothing. No one lives long in this wicked world without some scandal clinging to them. I fear our excellent Baroness has not escaped fate’s judgment. We cannot avoid calumny, my dear young friend. You’ve already tasted it in your short time here. But we can keep our consciences clear—that is what matters.”

He raised his eyes heavenward, trying to appear as pure as the ceiling above.

“Has there been something serious about my Aunt Bernstein?” Harry pressed.

“O sancta simplicitas!” the chaplain muttered. “Stories older than you or I. Tales told about everyone—*de me, de te*—with varying degrees of truth.”

“Confound the villain!” Harry exclaimed. “If anyone dares speak ill of that dear old lady, I’ll pull his nose—sure as my name is Harry Esmond.”

“The world,” said the chaplain, “is full of lies and gossip.”

“And you’re just beginning to learn it,” the clergyman added, smiling beatifically.

“Who hasn’t been attacked?” he continued. “My lord, you, me—everybody. We must endure and forgive as best we can.”

“You may,” Harry said. “It’s your cloth. But I won’t! If anyone speaks a word against her, I’ll give them a good shove!”

And with that, he slammed his fist down on the table.

“Hello, Colonel Lambert!” he called, as the officer entered. “You find us late again, sir. Me and the reverend kept it up with the young fellows after the ladies left. I hope the ladies are well?”

“Perfectly,” the Colonel replied, grinning. “Whose nose were you pulling when I came in, Mr. Warrington?”

“Isn’t it shameful?” Harry said. “The parson told me there are villains here who attack my aunt’s character!”

“You don’t mean to say so!” the Colonel exclaimed.

“I tell Mr. Harry that everyone is slandered,” said the chaplain, adopting a clerical tone—though he winked at the Colonel, meaning: *Keep him ignorant.*

The Colonel took the hint.

“Yes,” he said, “slander’s jaws are always moving. Take that story about the dancing girl—everyone believed it about you, Harry.”

“What—everyone?” Harry asked.

“No,” the Colonel corrected. “One didn’t—Hetty didn’t. You should have heard her defend you the other day when someone brought up another tale—about a game of cards on Sunday morning, when you and a friend might have done better.”

The chaplain nodded. “Faith, I confess it. It was *mea culpa*, *mea minima culpa*—only a rehearsal of an old piquet game we’d discussed.”

“And did Miss Hester stand up for me?” Harry asked.

“She did,” the Colonel said. “But why that look?”

“She scolded me last night,” Harry admitted. “Like—like nothing I’ve ever heard. She mocked everyone—young and old—until I had to tell her that in Virginia, young folks don’t talk to elders like that. And we had a sort of quarrel. I’m glad you told me she defended me.”

He shook the Colonel’s hand, emotion glowing in his eyes.

“You won’t come to much harm if your worst enemy is Hester,” the Colonel said gravely, watching Harry’s flushed face. *Is he fond of her? How fond?* he wondered. *He knows nothing. Hetty’s been playing her tricks.* Still, he admired the boy—honest, passionate, quick to feel.

Then the chaplain asked: “And the young lady of the minuet? She danced beautifully—everyone admired her.”

“I trust Miss—Miss—”

“Miss Theodosia is fine,” the Colonel said. “Ready to dance with you right now.”

“Or wait,” he added with a twinkle, “Chaplain—do you only dance on Sundays?”

Turning back to Harry, he said: “You handled the great lady very well, Mr. Flatterer. My Lady Yarmouth has been praising you at the Pump Room. She says she has a little boy in Hanover who looks just like you—and you’re a charming young man.”

“If she were queen,” the chaplain mused, “they’d treat her no better.”

“Call her a vice-queen, parson,” the Colonel joked.

“She pocketed forty of my guineas at quadrille,” Harry laughed.

“She’ll play you again on the same terms,” the Colonel said drily. “The Countess loves games—and wins from most.”

“Why not bet her five thousand on a bishopric?” Harry suggested. “I’ve heard of a clergyman who made such a bet, lost it, paid it, and got the bishopric.”

“Ah,” the chaplain said, “who will lend me the five thousand? Will you, sir?”

“No,” the Colonel replied firmly. “I won’t give her five thousand to become Commander-in-Chief or Pope. I won’t throw stones at her—but I won’t bow either. Not like the rabble. No offence—I don’t mean you. Or you, Harry. You were right to be civil—and lose your money with good humour.”

Then, with sudden seriousness, he said: “Harry, I’ve come to bid you farewell. Our pleasures are over—my money’s gone. We must return to Oakhurst. Will you visit us again?”

“Now, sir, now!” Harry said eagerly. “I’ll ride back with you!”

“No—now is not the time,” the Colonel said quickly. “We haven’t room—we’re expecting friends.”

[“The Lord forgive me for the lie!” he muttered.]

“But—when Tom’s home—yes, when Tom’s home,” the Colonel continued. “That’ll be fun. And I want you to know, sir, my wife and I love you sincerely. So do the girls—even if they scold you. And if you ever get into trouble—such things happen, Mr. Chaplain—you may count on me. Mind that, sir!”

He turned to leave—but Harry followed him downstairs, insisting on saying goodbye to the ladies.

Instead of going straight to the Colonel’s lodgings, the two men walked toward the common. From Harry’s window, the chaplain saw them in earnest conversation. At first, the Colonel smiled roguishly. Then, as the talk progressed, he threw up his hands in surprise and agitation.

“The boy is telling him,” the chaplain thought.

When Harry returned an hour later, he found the chaplain deep in sermon-writing. His face was grave, his mood somber. He threw down his hat, sank into a chair, and muttered something like a curse.

“The young ladies are leaving—and your heart is affected?” the chaplain asked, looking up.

“Heart?” Harry scoffed. “Which one is the conqueror? I thought the youngest’s eyes followed you about at the ball.”

“Confound the little termagant!” Harry burst out. “What does she mean by treating me like a fool?”

“And no man is,” the chaplain said wisely, “with a woman.”

“Ain’t they, Chaplain?” Harry growled, letting loose more curses.

“By the way,” the chaplain asked, “have you heard anything of your lost property?”

“No!” Harry snapped, using a word too strong for print.

“I suspect,” the chaplain said, “there was more money in that book than you care to admit. I wish I could find it.”

“There were notes,” Harry said gloomily, “and papers I regret losing. What in the devil has happened to it? I had it when we dined together.”

“I saw you put it in your pocket,” the chaplain recalled. “I saw you take it out and pay for a gold thimble and workbox at the toy shop—for one of your young ladies. Have you asked there?”

“Of course,” Harry said, sinking deeper into melancholy.

“Gumbo put you to bed—at least, I think he did. I was so upset myself, I barely remember. Can you trust those black fellows?”

“I can trust him with my head,” Harry said bitterly. “With my head? I can’t trust myself with it.”

“Oh, that a man should put an enemy into his mouth to steal away his brains!”

“You may call it an enemy, Chaplain,” Harry said. “Hang it—I’ve a mind to swear off drink forever. A man says anything when he’s drunk.”

The chaplain laughed. “You, sir,” he said, “are close enough.”

In truth, for the past few days, no amount of wine could make Harry speak freely when the chaplain touched on the subject of his loss.

“And so the little country girls are gone, or going?” the chaplain asked.

“They were sweet, fresh creatures,” he said. “But I think the mother was the finest of the three. I declare, a woman at thirty-five is at her prime. What do you say, sir?”

Harry glanced sideways at him.

“Confound all women,” he muttered. “I say!”

For which sentiment, every decent person will surely rebuke him.

Colonel Lambert, no doubt, had conferred with his wife, and together they resolved to remove their daughter Hetty from the vicinity of the young man who had stirred such tender feelings in her heart. In matters of affection, absence often proves a powerful remedy—especially for men. But women, I suspect, are not so easily cured by mere distance. Some will journey far and remain apart for years, yet still carry their secret sorrows like hidden burdens. You may scold them, punish them, even wound them deeply—but still they cling to their devotion. Indeed, if I may speak from long observation, there is perhaps no surer way to secure a woman’s loyalty than through measured neglect, tempered now and then with a gentle kindness. Too much love, too freely given, breeds indifference. A woman spoiled by constant attention may grow bored with her husband, seeking solace in the company of the most ordinary man. Yet, witness Chloe—abused at breakfast, cursed before the servants at dinner—how she creeps back to her husband's side at tea, softening into affection, patting his head, playing his favorite tune. When the butler or maid enters with the bed-candles, she looks up proudly, as if to say: “See, John, how good my dear Henry is!” Gentlemen, take note: this is the art of mastery—not through indulgence, but through restraint.

I recall what Daniel O’Connell once said: “Hereditary bondsmen, know ye not that to be free, you must strike the blow?” So it is in marriage, as in politics. Rise up, then, you wronged and oppressed husbands! Women will appreciate these words, for they understand irony and humor. And I expect some young scribbler from Grub Street—whose only claim to fame is writing for three-penny papers—will cry, “He advocates beating women! He has no soul!” But I have no more soul than he has ears. Dear ladies, let me assure you: I am merely jesting. I do not endorse violence toward any woman. On the contrary, I hold your sex in higher regard than our own—for your constancy, your tenderness, your enduring fidelity.

So what purpose does it serve for Hetty’s parents to take her away? If her heart remains fixed on Harry, whether he is near or far, then distance alone will not heal her. Why not let her see him one last time before Ball and Dobbin depart? Let her say, “Good-bye, Harry—I was unkind last night, but you were kind to me.” She will show no great emotion. Ashamed of her secret, she will hide it behind a smile. Harry, preoccupied with his own thoughts, will not perceive her sorrow. He will part from her calmly, believing she is glad to return to her music, her chickens, her flower garden. He will not ride beside her carriage. He has another engagement. By the time he returns, the Lamberts are already gone from Tunbridge Wells. Their windows stand open; a card hangs in one, announcing the rooms are available again.

A fleeting pang may cross Harry’s mind when he sees the empty chambers where friendly faces once laughed and talked. But he dines at the White Horse at four o’clock, eats heartily, and demands his wine with gusto. Meanwhile, poor little Hester chokes on her tea when the family arrives at Westerham. The next morning, her cheeks are pale, dark circles shadow her eyes. It was the storm, she says—the night was hot, sleepless. She will feel better tomorrow. And tomorrow comes. They return home. There is the gate where he fell. There is the bed where he lay, the chair where he sat. How long it seems since yesterday! What a gulf between past and present! Who is that child tending chickens, watering roses? Is that girl truly Hester Lambert? She seems older than Theo, who has always been so composed, so wise beyond her years. But in just a few days, Hester has lived an eternity. So have others. No poppy nor mandragora can restore them to the peace they knew before.

Maria Esmond watched the Lamberts leave, feeling a strange relief. When Harry enters his aunt’s card room, flushed from Barbeau’s wine, she watches him closely. He laughs, answers lightly when asked which girl is his sweetheart. “I love them both like sisters,” he says cheerfully. “The Lamberts are excellent people. Why isn’t Lambert a general? He’s served with distinction. The Duke is fond of him.” Madame Bernstein suggests Harry should speak to Lady Yarmouth on his behalf. “Elle ravvole de fous, cher bedid anche!” she mimics the Countess’s German accent. The Baroness beams with pride at her nephew’s success. “You charm all the old ladies, don’t you, Maria?” she sneers at her niece, who flinches beneath the barb. “You were quite right not to notice her cheating at cards—you play like a grand seigneur,” continues Madame de Bernstein. “Did she cheat?” Harry asks, surprised. “I saw no unfair play,” he insists. “Neither did I,” replies the Baroness, “but I’m certain she did. Bah! Every woman cheats when she can. Even I, and Maria, when opportunity allows. But when playing with Walmoden, losing moderately is acceptable. Many men do it too. Cultivate her—she’s taken a fancy to your eyes. Why shouldn’t you become Governor of Virginia? Go pay your respects to the Duke and the King at Kensington. Lady Yarmouth will be your greatest ally.”

“Why don’t you introduce me, Aunt?” Harry asks. The old lady’s rouged cheek reddens further. “I am not in favor at Kensington,” she admits. “Once I might have been. But kings remember those they wish to forget. We all have something we’d rather erase. Perhaps our young gentleman here would like to wipe a few debts from his ledger. Would you not, Harry?”

Harry turns red. So does Maria. His aunt lets out a laugh—sharp, mischievous, unsettling. What secrets lie behind those crimson cheeks? What sins haunt their memories that they long to forget? I fear Madame Bernstein is right: most of us carry hidden reckonings we'd gladly escape.

Had Maria known the reason for Harry’s unease, she would have been even more distressed. For several days, he had been missing a pocket-book. He remembered having it the night he drank heavily at the White Horse, when Gumbo carried him to bed. He searched in the morning—no trace. He asked his servants, the innkeeper—nothing. He could not admit the loss. To reveal it would mean exposing letters he had written to her—letters full of confessions, satire, jealousy, declarations of love. Letters that spoke of her faults, her opinions, her private thoughts. Letters that contained family secrets, criticisms of friends, bitter complaints about other women, passionate protests of eternal devotion. The usual mix, dear madam, that every lover writes to their beloved—especially in youth. Would you want such letters read aloud? Recall what you wrote about the Miss Browns, or Mrs. Thompson’s character? Or your remarks about Edward, whom you later abandoned for Jones? Would you want Mr. Jones to see those words? Of course not. Then do not accuse Lady Maria Esmond without cause. Her letters may have been foolish—love letters often are—but that does not make them wicked. Such things are natural. Young hearts write wildly. Old ones write with regret. Still, no one wants their innermost thoughts exposed.

And so, I resolve never again to write or speak plainly about anyone. I shall say of every woman that she is virtuous and beautiful; of every man, that he is noble and clever; of every book, that it is delightful; of Snobmore, that he is gentlemanly; of Screwby’s dinners, that they are sumptuous; of Jawkins’s conversation, that it is sparkling; of Xantippe, that she is sweet-tempered; of Jezebel, that her color is natural; of Bluebeard, that he was kind to his wives—and likely they died of bronchitis. As for Messalina? Spotless, of course! Cheops? A perfect king! Oh, woe to the critic who dares question nobility!

When this tale ends, I shall discard the jaundiced tone of my earlier works. My books shall wear rose-colored covers, adorned with cherubs. All characters shall be angels. But until then, we live among mortals—flawed, human beings. Take Madame Bernstein: she sleeps after overeating and drinking too much. That is her failing. Mr. Harry Warrington plays billiards with Count Caramboli—his flaw, perhaps, is idleness. This is what Chaplain Sampson murmurs to Lady Maria, speaking softly so as not to wake the sleeping Baroness.

“A gentleman of Mr. Warrington’s means can afford leisure,” says Maria. “But surely you enjoy cards and billiards yourself, Mr. Sampson?”
“I do not claim my practice is good,” he sighs, “only my doctrine is sound. This young man should have purpose. He should appear at court, serve his country, settle down, and marry a woman of suitable rank.”

Sampson gazes steadily at her. “Indeed, my cousin wastes his time,” Maria murmurs, blushing.
“Perhaps he should visit his father’s relatives,” suggests the chaplain.
“Suffolk yokels drinking beer and hunting foxes! What benefit would come of that?”
“They are of ancient lineage,” replies Sampson. “Sir Miles Warrington has a daughter—her age, and lovely.”
“I know nothing of Sir Miles or his daughters!” Maria exclaims, flustered.

The Baroness stirs—no, she sleeps soundly. “I fear for your cousin, madam,” says Sampson. “His youth, his temptations. Folly, extravagance, intrigue—many will try to lead him astray. His lordship, my patron, sent me to watch over him. I know the ways of young men. I confess—perhaps I once walked the same path.” He adds this with solemnity, though no blush appears.

“Between ourselves,” he continues, “I fear Mr. Warrington is troubled.”
“What? Again?” shrieks Maria.
“Hush! Your ladyship’s invalid!” whispers Sampson, pointing to the sleeping Baroness.
“Do you think he has feelings for anyone—anyone in the Lambert family? For example, Miss Lambert?”
“There is nothing between them,” says Maria.
“Are you certain?”
“Women have keen eyes in such matters,” she replies coolly. “I thought she followed him.”
“Then I am mistaken again,” says the chaplain. “Mr. Warrington called her a pert, stuck-up little hussy and told her to go back to her doll.”
“Oh,” sighs Maria, relieved.
“Then there must be someone else,” says Sampson. “Has he confided anything to you?”
“To me? Where? How?” she cries.
“Six days ago, after dining at the White Horse, he lost a pocket-book containing letters.”
“Letters?” gasps Maria.
“And likely more money than he wishes to admit,” adds Sampson gravely. “He is greatly disturbed. We’ve made quiet inquiries—”
“Gracious powers! Is your ladyship ill?”

Maria gives three piercing screams and collapses from her chair.
“I will see the Prince! I have a right to see him! What is this? Where am I?” cries Madame Bernstein, waking abruptly. She shakes violently, her face flushed. She stares wildly, then staggers forward with her cane. “What—what’s happened?”
“Have you killed her, sir?”
“Only a sudden faintness,” says Sampson, alarmed. “Shall I loosen her laces? Send for a doctor?”
“What passed between you, sir?” demands the Baroness fiercely.
“I swear I did nothing. I only mentioned the lost pocket-book—then she fainted.”

Madame Bernstein splashes water on Maria’s face. A weak moan follows—she is regaining consciousness. The Baroness glares at Sampson as he departs for the doctor. Maria awakens, trembling, confused.
“What happened?” she whispers.
“You know best,” says the Baroness coldly. “What has occurred before in our family?”
“Oh, yes—the letters have been lost—ach lieber Himmel!” Maria begins speaking in her mother’s tongue.
“The seal is broken, the letters lost—it is the old story of the Esmonds,” cries the elder woman bitterly.
“Seal broken? Letters lost? What do you mean, Aunt?”
“I mean my mother was the only honest woman ever to enter this family!” she stamps her foot. “She was a parson’s daughter—no connections. Had she been born to wealth, she too would have fallen. Good heavens—must we all be...?”
“To be what, madam?”
“To be what Lady Queensberry said last night. To be what we are! You know the word!”
“What has come over our race? Your father’s mother was honest. Why did I leave her? Why couldn’t you stay so?”
“Madam!” cries Maria. “I swear before Heaven, I am—”
“Bah! Don’t ‘madam’ me! Don’t call heaven to witness—there’s no one here! And if you swore until your teeth fell out, I wouldn’t believe you!”
“Oh! You told him!” gasps Maria.
“I saw something foolish between you two,” says the Baroness. “I told him you were as old as his mother. Yes, I did. I won’t let Henry Esmond’s son waste himself on a worn-out rock like you. Not a penny of mine will go to any of you if he suffers.”
“You told him!” Maria cries, rising in defiance.
“Well then! I don’t care a penny for your petty money! I have Mr. Harry Warrington’s word—and his letters. I know he’ll die before breaking it.”
“He will die if he keeps it!” (Maria shrugs.)
“But you don’t care—your heart is stone.”
“Than my father’s sister!” cries Maria.
“Ah! Why didn I marry an honest man?” the Baroness laments. “Henry Esmond was noble. Perhaps he could have made me so. But no—we all carry the stain. You won’t sacrifice this boy, Maria?”
“Madame ma tante, do you take me for a fool?”
“Set him free! I’ll give you five thousand pounds—in my will, Maria. I swear it!”
“When you were young, you cast off Colonel Esmond for an earl, and the earl for a duke?”
“Yes.”
“Eh! Bon sang ne peut mentir! I have no money, no friends. My father was a spendthrift, my brother a beggar. I have Mr. Warrington’s word. I know he’ll keep it. And that is what I tell you!”
“Suppose my letters are published tomorrow? Apres? I know they contain things I’d rather not reveal. Things not only about me. Comment! Do you think there are no stories but mine in this family? It’s not my letters I fear—so long as I have his. Yes, his word and his letters. I trust both.”
“I’ll send to my merchant—give you the money now,” pleads the old lady.
“No,” says Maria. “I’ll have my Harry—and ten times five thousand pounds!”
“Not until your mother dies—she’s just your age!”
“We can wait, Aunt. At my age, I’m not so eager as young girls for a husband.”
“But waiting for your sister’s death—is that fair?”
“Offer me ten thousand pounds, Madam Tusher, and then we’ll see!”
“I have no such sum,” says the old lady.
“Then let me earn what I can for myself!”
“Ah, if he heard you!”
“Apres? I have his word. I know he’ll keep it. I can wait, madam,” she says, and strides from the room—just as the chaplain returns.

Now it was Madame Bernstein who needed cordials. She was profoundly shaken by the revelation that had erupted so suddenly.

Though she had clearly come off the loser in the confrontation recounted in the previous chapter, the Baroness Bernstein showed no trace of resentment when she next encountered her niece. With a calmness that belied the storm they had weathered, she addressed Lady Maria with an air of detached amusement.

“Of course, my Lady Maria,” she said, “you cannot expect me—being Harry Warrington’s near kin—to be delighted at the notion of his marrying a woman older than his mother and without a penny to her name. But if he chooses to make such a foolish match, it is none of my affair. I doubt, too, that I would have been taken seriously had I offered him five thousand pounds during our heated exchange. So it was already settled at Castlewood? Had I known how far matters had advanced, dear, I might have spared myself some unnecessary resistance. When a pitcher is broken, what use is there in railing?”

“Madam!” interjected Maria, her voice rising slightly. “Pardon me—I mean no disrespect to your ladyship’s honour or character, both of which, I am certain, are beyond reproach. Harry says so, and you say so—what more can one desire?”

“You’ve spoken with Mr. Warrington, then?” asked the Baroness.

“And he has admitted that he made you a promise at Castlewood—one confirmed in writing.”

“Indeed he has, madam,” replied Lady Maria firmly.

“Ah,” murmured the elder woman, unflinching. “And I confess I first misread the tone of your letters to him. They involve other members of the family—”

“Who have spoken ill of me and sought to turn Harry against me in every way. Yes, madam, I did write to defend myself, to justify my actions.”

“But naturally, you’re distressed at the thought that any rogue might possess damaging secrets about our family and expose them to public ridicule. That explains your agitation earlier.”

“Precisely,” said Lady Maria. “I could reveal nothing to Harry, for he is now my confidant. But that is very different from wishing the world to know the private quarrels of a noble house.”

“Upon my word, Maria, I admire you—and I’ve done you injustice these past twenty years.”

“I am heartily glad, madam, that you finally see me fairly,” replied the younger woman.

“When I saw you last night, dancing with my nephew, can you guess what crossed my mind?”

“I really have no idea what the Baroness de Bernstein might have thought,” said Lady Maria, lifting her chin.

“I recalled that you once danced that very tune with the dancing-master at Kensington, my dear.”

“Madam, that was an outrageous falsehood!”

“By which poor man received a beating for nothing!”

“It is cruel and unjust, madam, to revive such slander—and I shall request to leave this household if such talk continues,” declared Maria, with quiet dignity.

“You wish to return home? I can imagine Tunbridge will not suit you, especially if those letters surface.”

“There was not a single word against you in them, madam. On that point, I can assure you.”

“So Harry said—and gave you your due. Well, my dear, we’ve grown weary of each other. It may be best to part for a time.”

“That is exactly my own sentiment,” said Lady Maria, executing a sharp curtsey. “Mr. Sampson can escort you to Castlewood. You and your maid may take a postchaise.”

“We shall take the chaise,” echoed the younger woman. “And Mr. Sampson shall accompany me. You see, madam, I act as a dutiful niece.”

“Do you know,” the Baroness said frankly, “I suspect Sampson may have the letters?”

“The thought has occurred to me as well,” admitted Maria.

“And you intend to go home by chaise, hoping to coax them from him! Delilah! Well, they’re of no use to me. I trust you’ll succeed. When do you leave? The sooner, the better, you say? We are women of the world, Maria. We only hurl names in anger. We don’t want one another’s company—and we part on good terms. Shall we go to Lady Yarmouth’s? It’s her evening. A change of scene after such a nervous fit is just what you need, and cards drive away unpleasant thoughts better than any physician.”

Lady Maria agreed to attend Lady Yarmouth’s card party and was ready first, waiting in the drawing-room for her aunt. As Madame Bernstein descended, she noticed that Maria’s door stood open.

“She has the letters on her,” the old lady thought.

They left together, each in their own carriage, displaying toward one another the polished civility women often reserve for one another after even the most bitter disputes.

That evening, returning from the Countess’s gathering, Mrs. Brett, the Baroness’s maid, answered Lady Maria’s summons when she rang her bell before retiring.

Betty, Mrs. Brett confessed, was not fit to appear before her lady. She had spent the night carousing with Mr. Warrington’s black servant, Lord Bamborough’s valet, and several others of similar station. The liquor—Mrs. Brett was ashamed to admit—had proven too much for Betty.

Should she undress her lady?

My lady declined, saying she would manage alone, and allowed Mrs. Brett to retire.

“She has the letters in her stays,” thought Madame Bernstein.

They had exchanged a civil goodnight on the stairs.

The next morning, Betty faced a scolding from her mistress, having slept in the closet adjacent to Lady Maria’s room. She confessed, contritely, her fondness for rum-punch—a brew Mr. Gumbo was particularly skilled at preparing. She accepted the reprimand meekly and completed her duties before withdrawing.

Betty was one of the Castlewood girls who had become smitten with Gumbo, a handsome blue-eyed lass whom Mr. Case, the Baroness’s trusted man, also found appealing. Thus, between Gumbo and Case, jealousies had flared—so much so that Gumbo, though peaceable by nature, avoided the Baroness’s servants, one of whom swore he’d break Gumbo’s bones if he continued courting Betty.

Yet on the night of the punch, though Case caught Gumbo and Betty whispering in the doorway, cooled by the evening breeze, Gumbo—pale with fear—was met not with violence but charm. It was Case himself who proposed the bowl, brewed and consumed in Betty’s chamber, where Gumbo displayed his mastery of the drink. He praised Gumbo’s music. Though usually sober, Case insisted on drinking more and more until Betty became quite unsteady—precisely the state that drew her lady’s disapproval.

As for Case, who had slept outside, he was so ill from the punch that he remained in bed all day, only regaining strength enough to appear at supper-time, when his mistress gently rebuked him.

“Why, Case,” said Mr. Warrington, dining with the family, “I could have sworn it was you I saw riding hard down the London road this morning.”

“Me? Bless you, sir! I was abed, and my head felt like it would split. I ate a bit at six and drank small beer. I’m nearly myself again. But that Gumbo—bless you, I’ll never taste his punch again.”

The honest major-domo resumed his duties among the bottles and glasses.

After dinner, Madame Bernstein was cordial. She recommended strong tonics for Maria’s recurring fainting spells. These attacks were frequent. She urged her to consult her London physician and send a report via Harry.

“By Harry?” the young lady asked.

Yes. Harry was going to London for two days on business for his aunt.

“I won’t tell you, my dear, that it’s a task that will benefit him. I wish Mr. Draper to include him in my will. And since I shall be traveling soon, I think it safest to ask Mr. Warrington to carry my trinket-box to London in his postchaise. There’ve been robberies lately, and I’d rather not risk being stopped by highwaymen.”

Maria looked dismayed at the thought of Harry’s departure, but hoped he might escort her back to Castlewood, where her elder brother had returned.

“Nay,” said his aunt, “the boy has clung to us long enough. A day in London will do him no harm. He can run my errand and be back by Saturday.”

“I would offer to accompany Mr. Warrington,” said Mr. Sampson, “but I preach before her ladyship on Friday.” He wished Lady Yarmouth to judge his abilities as a preacher, and the Baroness had used her influence to secure an audience.

Harry welcomed the idea of a swift journey to London and a few days of sport. He promised his pistols were in good order and that he would deliver the diamonds safely to the banker’s vault.

Would he stay at his aunt’s London house?

No—that would be dreary, with only a housemaid and groom in charge. He preferred the Star and Garter in Pall Mall or an inn in Covent Garden.

“Oh!” said Harry, his face darkening. “I’ve often talked over this journey.”

“And with whom, sir?” asked Lady Maria.

“With one who promised to make it with me,” replied the young man, thinking, as he always did, of his lost brother with deep tenderness.

“He has more heart, my dear Maria, than some of us,” remarked Harry’s aunt, seeing the emotion in his eyes.

Uncontrollable waves of grief still swept over the young man. The memory of his brother’s death; the scene of George’s fall the previous year; the words they’d shared; the plans they’d made—all resurfaced and overwhelmed him.

“I doubt,” whispered the chaplain to Madame Bernstein after one such outburst, “whether some folks in England suffer so deeply at the loss of an elder brother.”

But sorrow, of course, could not endure forever. One could picture Mr. Warrington setting off on his journey with eager spirits, gay and relieved to be freed from his elderly attachment.

Yes. At Castlewood, on one unfortunate evening, he had offered his heart and himself to his mature cousin—and she had accepted the foolish lad’s proposal. But marriage was now impossible. He must consult his mother, the lifelong mistress of the Virginian estate. She would surely refuse consent to such a union. The decision was postponed, but the burden weighed heavily upon him, bringing remorse and unease.

No wonder his spirits lifted as he neared London, and he gazed joyfully from the windows of his postchaise at the city unfolding before him.

No highwayman halted him on Blackheath. There, gleaming beneath the trees, stood Greenwich’s domes. The Thames flowed below, crowded with ships. And there, unmistakably, rose the Tower of London.

“Look, Gumbo! There’s the Tower!”

“Yes, master,” said Gumbo, who had never heard of it.

But Harry had. He remembered reading about it in Howell’s *Medulla*, and how he and George used to play at being knights of the Tower. Now, he marveled at the prospect of seeing the armour, the jewels, the lions.

They passed through Southwark and over London Bridge—once lined with houses like a street, now reduced to a single gate, soon to vanish entirely. Then the chaise rolled through the city.

“Look, Gumbo—there’s Saint Paul’s!”

“Yes, master—Saint Paul’s,” said Gumbo, deferential but unmoved by the architecture.

So by familiar route, they reached the Temple, where Gumbo and his master stared up in awe at the rebel heads atop Temple Bar.

The chaise arrived at Mr. Draper’s chambers in Middle Temple Lane. Harry handed over the trinket-box and a letter from his aunt. The lawyer read the letter with interest and tucked it away carefully. He locked the box in his strong closet, then took his clerk into the adjoining room. Afterward, he offered to escort Mr. Warrington to an inn.

Covent Garden’s Bedford Hotel was chosen as the best lodging.

“I shall keep you for two or three days, Mr. Warrington,” said the lawyer. “The papers the Baroness requires won’t be ready yet. Meanwhile, I’m at your service to show you the town. I live outside, but I have a little cottage at Camberwell where I’d be honored to entertain you. Still, a young man likely prefers his inn and his freedom.”

Harry agreed. The postchaise, with a clerk inside, was sent ahead to the Bedford, while the two walked there together.

They sat and conversed. The Drapers had served the Esmond family for generations. The attorney regaled Harry with tales of his ancestors at Castlewood. Though no longer agent to the present Earl—whose father had fallen out with him—the firm still represented the Baroness, and Mr. Draper was pleased she favored her nephew.

As they prepared to leave, a young clerk approached his principal in the passage.

“If you please, sir, the Baroness’s papers were delivered to her man, Mr. Case, two days ago.”

“Mind your own affairs, Mr. Brown,” snapped the lawyer. “This way, Mr. Warrington. Our Temple stairs are dim. Allow me to guide you.”

Harry saw Draper cast a quick, angry glance at the clerk.

“So it was Case I saw on the London Road,” he thought. “What brought the old fox to London?”

He chose not to pry and let the matter drop.

Where should they go first? Harry wanted to visit the site where his grandfather and Lord Castlewood had fought a duel fifty-six years prior in Leicester Field. Mr. Draper knew the spot well and recounted the tale.

They could pass through Covent Garden on the way, ensuring Harry was comfortably settled.

“And order dinner,” suggested Harry.

“No,” said Draper firmly. “You must do me the honor of dining with me. In fact, I’ve already ordered a collation from the Cock.”

Harry could not refuse such a pressing invitation and walked away cheerfully, passing under the arch where the heads were, removing his hat in salute.

“They were gentlemen who died for their king,” he said. “My brother George and I always vowed we’d salute them when we saw them.”

“You’ll draw a mob if you do, sir,” warned the alarmed lawyer.

“Confound the mob, sir,” replied Harry loftily.

But the passers-by paid no heed. He walked up the bustling Strand, taking in every sight, remembering for the rest of his life the impressions of London, though keeping his emotions discreet. He did not care to reveal how deeply he was moved—or that he was a stranger.

He barely heard his companion’s chatter, though Draper spoke ceaselessly.

Nor was Draper displeased by Harry’s silence and haughty bearing. A hundred years ago, a gentleman was a gentleman, and his attorney his humble servant.

At the Bedford, the chamberlain bowed low, showing Harry to his rooms with delightful servility—for Gumbo had already announced his master’s greatness, and Draper’s clerk referred to the newcomer as “a high fellar.”

After inspecting the rooms, the two men went to Leicester Field, Gumbo strutting behind. They viewed the scene of the old wound and the tragedy of Lord Castlewood, then returned to the Temple.

Who was the shabby-looking man Harry bowed to as they left for a walk in the gardens?

That was Mr. Johnson, an author Harry had met at Tunbridge Wells.

“Take the advice of a man of the world, sir,” said Draper, eyeing the writer with disdain. “The less you associate with such folk, the better. Our office sees enough trouble with literary men.”

“Indeed,” said Harry.

He did not warm to his new friend as the latter grew more familiar.

The theatres were closed. Should they go to Sadler’s Wells, Marybone Gardens, or Ranelagh?

“Not Ranelagh,” said Draper. “There’s no nobility in town.” But seeing in the paper that Sadler’s Wells would feature a performance on eight hand-bells by Mr. Franklyn and Signora Catherina, Harry decided on Marybone Gardens—where there was music, tea, coffee, wine, and the constant stream of Draper’s conversation.

The lawyer’s obsequiousness ended at Harry’s bedroom door, where the young gentleman bid him good night with proud aloofness.

The next morning, Harry, dressed in brocade bedgown, enjoyed breakfast, read the newspaper, and savored his solitude.

He came across news from Virginia: *Williamsburg, June 7th.*

His eyes blurred. He had received letters from that packet, but his mother had not mentioned—

“A great number of the colony’s leading gentry have united under the command of the Honourable Peyton Randolph to march to the aid of their afflicted fellow-subjects and avenge the cruelties of the French and their savage allies. They wear plain blue frocks, nanquin or brown waistcoats and breeches, plain hats. Each is armed with a light firelock, a pair of pistols, and a cutting sword.”

“Ah, why ain’t we there, Gumbo?” Harry exclaimed.

“Why ain’t we dar?” shouted Gumbo.

“Why am I here, dangling at women’s trains?” Harry added.

“Think dangling at women’s trains very pleasant, Master Harry?” asked Gumbo, practical and indifferent.

Meanwhile, Harry read that the Virginia ship *The Lovely Sally* had been captured by a French privateer near port.

Then, learning that the finest mare in England and a pair of fine bay geldings were to be sold at the Bull Inn, Hatton Garden, Harry decided to go see them.

He bought the geldings on the spot, paying generously.

He said nothing of what he did that day—shy of appearing foreign—but it is believed he took a coach to Westminster Abbey, then to the Tower, Mrs. Salmon’s Waxwork, Hyde Park, and Kensington Palace. He had ordered the coach to the Royal Exchange, but catching sight of Covent Garden en route, he bade the driver return him to his inn—and tipped him a guinea.

Mr. Draper had called in his absence and promised to return. But Harry, having dined sumptuously alone, returned to Marybone Gardens, still in noble company.

The next morning, as he stepped out, the bells of St. Paul’s, Covent Garden, rang for morning prayers—reminding him that Sampson was preaching.

Harry smiled. He was beginning to form a clear, fair judgment of the value of Mr. Sampson’s sermons.

Reading the *London Advertiser* with his morning coffee, Mr. Warrington came across an announcement that stirred his interest: a grand contest of skill between two of England’s most celebrated pugilists, Sutton and Figg. The event promised to be a spectacle of manly prowess, and without hesitation he decided to attend. That very day, he set off in the phaeton he had purchased the previous afternoon, driving himself from Covent Garden toward Marybone Fields, where the famed Wooden House stood.

The young Virginian was not entirely familiar with the roads, and his journey proved somewhat circuitous. He wandered through quiet lanes behind Mr. Whitfield’s round Tabernacle on Tottenham Road, then lost his way among the open fields near Middlesex Hospital. Yet eventually, he arrived at the arena, finding it already thronged with eager spectators. A motley crowd gathered outside—louts and ruffians, beggars and cripples, all clamoring for attention or alms. Shoeblack boys tumbled over one another to polish his boots; flower girls offered nosegays; fruit-sellers called out their wares; piemen, tramps, and strolling players filled the air with noise and movement. A flag fluttered atop the building, and from the stage, a manager accompanied by a drummer and horn-blower announced repeatedly that the noble English pastime was about to begin.

Mr. Warrington paid his admission and took a seat in the gallery, where he had a clear view of the platform below. His servant, Gumbo, sat in the amphitheatre beneath, occasionally slipping out to enjoy a pint of ale or play cards with other coachmen waiting beside their masters’ carriages. The scene was alive with the bustle of servants—footmen, lacqueys, liveried men—who swarmed around every great house, chapel, and theatre. They were everywhere: in anterooms, on staircases, in halls, feasting, gambling, and demanding tips. Once a proud and dignified class, they now seemed like relics of a vanishing age—tall, melancholy figures in powdered wigs and buckled shoes, still visible on formal occasions, but doomed, like the Red Indians of America, to fade into history.

Before the main combatants appeared, lesser contests entertained the crowd. A boxing match followed, but the fighters lacked spirit, and neither suffered serious harm. The audience grew restless. Then came cudgel-play, but the injuries were minor, and the crowd began to grumble. “The masters! The masters!” they roared. At last, the champions emerged.

First came Sutton, sword in hand, who saluted the crowd with a flourish and bowed deeply to a stout gentleman seated in a private box. Shortly after, Figg entered, greeted with approval by the same man. Both fighters wore only their shirts, their heads shaved, bearing scars from countless battles. Each wore an armiger—a colored ribbon—on his sword arm. They shook hands, and as a contemporary poet once wrote, “The word it was bilboe.”

The duel began. Figg struck with such force that had it connected with Sutton’s head, it would have severed it clean as a carrot cut by a knife. But Sutton parried the blow with his own blade, and the impact was so great that Figg’s weapon shattered in his grasp. New swords were brought forth. Blood soon flowed—Sutton drew first blood from Figg’s side, sparking cheers from his supporters. But Figg appealed to the audience, particularly to the stout gentleman in the box, explaining that the wound had come from the broken sword, not from any fault in his defense. While the crowd debated this, Mr. Warrington noticed a man in riding clothes and a plain wig enter the private box. To his surprise, he recognized Lord March and Ruglen, his friend from Tunbridge Wells.

Lord March, though not overly effusive, showed marked respect to the stout gentleman, receiving banknotes with a deep bow. When he spotted Mr. Warrington, he finished his business and crossed to the young Virginian’s gallery, greeting him warmly. They watched the duel unfold—both men fought with remarkable skill and courage. After swords, they took up quarter-staves, and the battle continued long and fiercely. In the end, victory belonged to Figg, the elder champion.

As the fight raged, a thunderstorm broke overhead. Mr. Warrington gladly accepted a ride back to town in Lord March’s carriage, leaving his own phaeton for Gumbo to drive home.

The experience had delighted Harry. “This,” he declared, “is sport indeed—the finest I’ve seen since arriving in England.” As was his habit, he paused, then sighed, “I wish…”—but stopped himself. “No, I don’t,” he added.

“What do you wish?” asked Lord March.

“I was thinking of my elder brother,” said Harry. “I wished he’d been here. We used to talk of doing things together—fights, hunts, adventures. But he wouldn’t have liked this rough sort of thing. He didn’t care for fighting, though he was the bravest lad alive.”

“Was he?” asked Lord March, leaning back and studying his companion. “You should have seen him in a quarrel with a gallant officer—our mutual friend. It was absurd, but George couldn’t be held back. I’ve never seen anyone so cool—and yet so fierce. God help me, I wish he could have been here instead of you, to show us what a real Virginian gentleman is.”

“Nay, sir,” replied Harry, “I’ll do well enough. I can ride, and I think I shoot better than George. But he had the mind—oh, the head!” he said, tapping his own skull. “He read every book ever written, played fiddle and harpsichord, composed poetry and sermons. What can I do? Ride, drink Burgundy, play cards—that’s all I’m good for.”

“And yet,” said Lord March, amused, “you do those things as well as most men.”

“You’re right,” said Harry, smiling. “And I’ll back myself against any man in London.”

Lord March chuckled. “By Gad, Mr. Warrington, you ought to be put on display at Exeter ‘Change. A Virginian gentleman who genuinely misses his brother—such a breed isn’t known in this country. I believe you’d actually want him back.”

“Believe?” Harry flushed. “You mean you believe I believe I’d want him back. But you’re wrong. It’s not in human nature—not as I understand it.”

They passed through Cavendish Square, where Harry lamented the unsightly boards fencing off empty land. “There’s Montagu House turned into a museum—books, birds, rhinoceroses! And they’ve cut a road through Bedford House Gardens—New Road they call it—ruining the Duke’s pleasure, though perhaps they’ll compensate him in gold.”

“Where shall we go?” asked Lord March. “Tyburn Road and the Park? Or Swallow Street?”

“Pall Mall for dinner,” said Harry. “Or if you prefer, your place. Then we can spend the evening however you like—with the Queen of Spades, or…”

“With the Queen of Spades,” Harry agreed, blushing.

They arrived at Harry’s hotel in Covent Garden. The landlord, recognizing Lord March, bowed low, nearly touching his wig to the nobleman’s boots.

After dinner, wine flowed freely—fine vintage, even for a connoisseur like the earl. They discussed going to Vauxhall for fireworks, but Harry, who had never seen anything beyond a few squibs at Williamsburg on November 5th (which he considered sublime), yielded to Lord March’s preference for piquet.

Harry won at first, but luck soon turned. Lord March gained the upper hand, growing testy when Mr. Draper, Harry’s business agent, entered the room and was invited to sit and drink. Harry always welcomed guests warmly—sharing his bread, his meat, his water, his wine. Such generosity, he believed, was rare in London’s selfish world. Though many gave grand dinners, few possessed true kindness.

Draper, though not fond of wine, was thrilled to be in the company of nobility. He praised the game, sitting undisturbed by Lord March’s scowls.

But the game was interrupted again. A commotion erupted outside—muffled voices, then a woman’s cry. Suddenly, Mrs. Betty, Lady Maria’s maid, burst into the room, sobbing. Behind her stood Gumbo, tears streaking his face.

“Help! Help, sir!” she cried, falling to her knees.

“Help whom?” Harry asked.

“Gumbo! You scoundrel!” shouted Harry, turning sharply. “Have you done something to Mrs. Betty?”

Gumbo stepped back, placing a hand on his chest. “No, sir. Nothing happened between me and this lady.”

“It’s my mistress!” cried Betty. “She’s been taken! Here’s the letter!”

Lord March, annoyed, dismissed her. “Is it only old Molly Esmond? She’s bankrupt, no doubt. Dry your eyes, Mrs. Betty, and let us continue our game.”

But Betty refused to stop. “Oh, Mr. Harry! Your honour must come! My lady calls for you!”

“Confound you!” snapped Lord March. “Can’t you keep quiet?”

Yet Betty wept on. The game ended.

Harry rose. “My dear lord, we must cease for tonight. My relative writes in distress. I must go to her.”

“Curse her! Why couldn’t she wait till tomorrow?” growled Lord March.

Harry ordered a postchaise at once. His horses would take him to Bromley.

“Bet you won’t make it in an hour!” laughed Lord March. “Bet you won’t reach Tunbridge Wells before midnight! Bet you’ll be robbed on Blackheath!”

“Done!” said Harry.

Lord March carefully noted the wager in his pocket-book.

Lady Maria’s letter read:

> I am fallen into a trap, the work of villains. I am imprisoned. Betty will tell you all. Ah, my Henrico! Come to the rescue of your MOLLY.*

Within half an hour, Mr. Warrington was in his postchaise, crossing Westminster Bridge, galloping toward Tunbridge Wells to save his kinswoman.

In my youth, fortune brought me into close acquaintance with a gentleman of irreproachable character who hailed from an island widely regarded—by those whose judgment in matters maritime is beyond reproach—as the most exquisite jewel in the ocean’s crown. The tales he told of his kinfolk dwelling in that distant land were such that they once made my young blood run cold with horror. For there was scarcely a crime under heaven that had not been committed by one or other of them: the Ten Commandments shattered like glass; deceptions so audacious that no fiction could invent them; murders and thefts more shocking than those ever attributed to Thurtell or Turpin—all recounted with chilling accuracy and unreserved candor by my friend concerning his nearest relations, whenever anyone cared to listen.

It seemed miraculous that any member of this family still walked free, rather than rotting in a hulk. One brother, Tim, had carried his father's grey hairs to the grave with sorrowful reverence; another, Mick, had repeatedly robbed the parish church; sister Annamaroia had abandoned her Captain for the Ensign, forged her grandmother’s will, and stolen the silver spoons—a deed for which Larry the knife-boy was hanged. The house of Atreus might have seemed mild in comparison to the race of O’What-d’ye-call-'em from which my companion descended. Yet I dare not name the country from whence he came.

How then did I react when, time after time, I found these same murderers, thieves, parricides, habitual forgers of bills and letters of credit, writing to each other with affectionate phrases—"my dearest brother," "my dearest sister"—and living together in perfect harmony for months on end? With hands stained with the blood of murdered parents, Tim would mix a screeching tumbler and offer Maria a drink from it. With lips blackened by perjuries sworn in court over his grandmother’s stolen will or the murder of his brother Thady’s helpless orphans, Mick would kiss his sister Julia’s cheek, and they’d spend the night laughing, weeping, reminiscing about old times—the dear old Castle What-d’ye-call-'em, where they were born, the fighting Onetyoneth quartered there, the Major’s proposal to Cyaroloine, and the tomb of their beloved mother (who had chattered them out of the property). Heaven bless her soul! Their embraces at meeting and parting were so heartfelt, so full of emotion, that one forgot the grim stories told earlier—stories that implied they could hang each other if only they dared to speak all they knew.

What nobler gift can there be than forgiveness? What more rational act than, after hurling every insult under the sun at a man, to apologize, regret your words, withdraw the decanter you flung at his head, and return to friendship as though nothing had passed? Some people possess this admirable, angelic gift. It was beautiful, for example, to see our two ladies at Tunbridge Wells forgiving each other—smiling, jesting, almost fondling one another despite the bitter words of yesterday—yes, even forgetting past grievances, though both remembered them perfectly well. Can you and I do the same? Let us strive, my friend, to cultivate this gentle, Christian spirit.

I believe one may learn to forgive harsh language directed toward oneself—but only through practice, and only if one has grown accustomed to hearing and using it. After a quarrel marked by mutual insults, you embrace again. Heaven bless us! Bad words mean little when one is used to them; they scarcely ruffle the temper. So the aunt and niece played cards amicably, drank to each other’s health, shared a wing of chicken, pulled a bone from the merry-thought—and yet, in conversation, scratched their neighbors' eyes out, not each other’s.

We have read how Peninsular warriors, when the bugles sang truce, fraternized, exchanged tobacco pouches and wine, ready to raise their firelocks and knock each other’s heads off when the truce ended. Likewise, our seasoned soldiers—skilled in war but wise in peace—laid down their arms temporarily and enjoyed themselves gaily. Of course, while drinking with Jack Frenchman, you keep your pistol within reach, ready to blow his brains out should he make a hostile move. But meanwhile, it is *A votre santé, mon camarade!* Here’s to you, mounseer! And everything is pleasant enough.

As for Aunt Bernstein’s threatened gout? The twinges had passed. Maria was delighted! As for Maria’s fainting fits? There had been no recurrence—only a slight one last night. The Baroness was deeply sorry! Her niece must consult the best physician, take nourishing remedies, continue the steel, even after leaving Tunbridge. How thoughtful of Aunt Bernstein to offer sending bottled waters after her!

But suppose Madame Bernstein confides to her maid: “Fainting fits—nonsense! Epilepsy! Inherited from that dreadful scrofulous German mother!” What means do we have of knowing what passes between the old lady and her attendant? Suppose Lady Maria orders Mrs. Betty, her maid, to taste every medicinal glass first, declaring her aunt capable of poisoning her? Very likely such conversations occur. These are merely precautions—the firelocks loaded and cocked, lying quiet upon the grass.

With Harry’s bond safely in her pocket, the veteran Maria chose not to press for payment. She knew the world too well for that. He was bound to her, but she gave him ample time and leave on parole. It was not her intention to unnecessarily provoke or anger her young slave. She understood the difference in age, and that Harry must enjoy his pleasures and diversions.

“Take your ease and amusement, cousin,” said Lady Maria. “Frisk about, pretty little mousekin,” murmured grey Grimalkin, purring in the corner, watching with green eyes.

Of course, the ladies had discussed at length what Harry ought to see and do during his first visit to London. Both knew perfectly well what amused a young gentleman in those days, and spoke of it with the frankness typical of that easy era. Our wily Calypso consoled herself fully in the absence of her wandering youth, taking whatever diversion came her way. Mr. Jack Morris, the gentleman we’ve mentioned as enjoying the company of Lord March and Mr. Warrington, was one such diversion.

To live among titled persons was Jack Morris’s greatest joy; losing money at cards to an earl’s daughter was almost a pleasure to him. Now, Lady Maria Esmond was an earl’s daughter who was very glad to win. She obtained permission to bring Mr. Morris to the Countess of Yarmouth’s assembly, and they played cards together—everyone satisfied.

Thus, the first forty-eight hours after Mr. Warrington’s departure passed cheerfully at Tunbridge Wells, until Friday arrived—the day when the sermon was to be delivered, which we saw Mr. Sampson preparing. The company at the Wells were eager to hear it. Sampson had earned a reputation for being both amusing and eloquent; and if there were no breakfast, conjurer, dancing bears, or concert going on, the good folk of the Wells would endure a sermon.

He knew Lady Yarmouth was coming—and what power she wielded in granting livings and dispensing bishoprics. The Defender of the Faith of that day placed great trust in her opinion on such matters. So we may be certain Mr. Sampson prepared his finest discourse for her ears.

When the Great Man arrives home at the Castle and walks over to the little country church in the park, bringing with him the Duke, the Marquis, and two Cabinet Ministers—has it ever been your lot to sit among the congregation and watch Mr. Trotter the curate and his sermon? He glances anxiously at the Great Pew; falters as he announces his text, thinking: *Ah! Perhaps his lordship may give me a living!* Mrs. Trotter and the girls watch the Great Pew too, observing the effect of papa’s sermon—the familiar favorite—upon the assembled big-wigs. Papa’s initial nervousness fades; his noble voice clears, warms to the topic—he kindles—he takes out his handkerchief—he is approaching that exquisite passage which has always moved the parsonage to tears—he begins it! Ah! What is that humming sound filling the edifice, making hob-nailed Melibaeus grin at smock-frocked Tityrus? It is the Right Honourable Lord Naseby snoring in the pew by the fire! And poor Trotter’s visionary mitre vanishes with the music.

Sampson served as domestic chaplain to Madame Bernstein’s nephew. The two ladies of the Esmond family supported him. On the day of the sermon, the Baroness hosted a small breakfast in his honor. Sampson appeared rosy and handsome, wearing a fresh-flowered wig and a smart, rustling new cassock—purchased on credit from a church-loving mercer at the Wells.

Accompanied by his patronesses, their ladies’ lacqueys trailing behind them with their large gilt prayer-books, Mr. Sampson marched from breakfast to church. Everyone noted how well the Baroness looked—she laughed, was especially warm with her niece, offering a bow and stately smile to all as she moved forward with her tortoiseshell cane.

At the door, a dazzling gathering of rank and fashion entered—the fine company of the Wells trooping in, led by her ladyship of Yarmouth, conspicuous with vermilion cheeks and a robe of flame-colored taffeta. Among them were shabby figures too, though the fashionable greatly outnumbered them.

What odd-looking pair, for instance, were those in ragged coats—one with carroty hair peeking beneath a scratch-wig—who entered just as the organ ceased? No, he couldn’t have been a Protestant—he mechanically crossed himself upon entering, muttering to his companion: “Bedad, Tim, I forgawt!” From which I conclude he came from the island mentioned at the start of this chapter. Wherever they go, a rich fragrance of whisky spreads.

A man may be a heretic and still possess genius—these Catholic gentlemen came to pay homage to Mr. Sampson. Indeed, not only Catholics were present, but followers of an even older creed. Who were those two men with hooked noses and sallow complexions, who forced their way into the church despite resistance from the beadle?

Seeing the greasy appearance of these Hebrew strangers, Mr. Beadle was inclined to deny them entry. But one whispered: “We wants to be conwerted, gov'nor!” Another slipped money into his hand. Mr. Beadle raised his mace, barred the doorway lifted, and the Hebrew gentlemen entered.

The organ swelled—the doors closed. Shall we enter and listen to Mr. Sampson’s sermon, or lie on the grass outside?

Preceded by the beadle in gold lace, Sampson walked up to the pulpit—rosy and jolly as any man could wish to see. Then, as he rose from his plump cushion, why did his Reverence turn as pale as death? He glanced toward the western church door—there, on either side, stood those terrible Hebrew caryatides.

Then he turned to the vestry door, near the rector’s pew, where Sampson had sat beside his patronesses during the service. Suddenly, two perfumed Hibernian gentlemen slipped from an adjacent seat and took positions on a bench near the vestry door and rector’s pew, sitting quietly until the sermon ended, eyes cast humbly downward.

How shall we describe that sermon, if the preacher himself never knew how it concluded? Nevertheless, it was considered excellent. When it ended, the fine ladies buzzed in their pews, exchanging praise and commentary.

Madame Walmoden, seated next to our friends, declared it was *bewdiful* and made her *dremble all over*. Madame Bernstein called it excellent. Lady Maria was pleased that the family chaplain had distinguished himself. She looked up at him, trying to catch his eye as he remained seated in the pulpit; she greeted him with a flutter of her handkerchief and a wave. He barely acknowledged it—his face pale, his gaze fixed on the font, where the Hebrews still lingered.

The stream of people passed them—rushing, thronging, marching in pairs, dribbling one by one. Everyone left. The two Hebrews remained by the door.

The Baroness de Bernstein and her niece lingered in the rector’s pew, where the old lady engaged in deep conversation with the clergyman.

“Who are those horrible men at the door?” Lady Maria asked Mrs. Brett, her aunt’s maid, “and what a smell of spirits there is!”

“Farewell, doctor; you have a darling little boy—is he to be a clergyman, too?” asked Madame de Bernstein.

“Are you ready, my dear?” And the pew opened. Madame Bernstein, whose father was only a viscount, insisted her niece, Lady Maria—an earl’s daughter—go first.

As she stepped forward, the individuals she had called “horrible men” advanced. One pulled a long strip of paper from his pocket. She started and turned pale. She rushed toward the vestry, hoping to escape and bar the door behind her. But the two men followed swiftly—one actually laid a hand on her shoulder.

“At the suit of Mistress Pincott, of Kensington, mercer, I have the honour of arresting your ladyship,” he said. “My name is Costigan, madam, a poor gentleman of Ireland, bound by circumstances to follow a disagreeable profession. Will your ladyship walk, or shall my man fetch a chair?”

Lady Maria Esmond gave three shrieks and collapsed, swooning to the ground.

“Keep the door, Mick!” shouted Mr. Costigan.

“Best let in no one else, madam,” he said politely to Madame Bernstein. “Her lady-ship has fallen in a fainting fit and will recover here, at her ease.”

“Unlace her, Brett!” cried the old lady, her eyes twinkling oddly. As soon as done, Madame Bernstein seized a small bag hanging from a hair chain around Lady Maria’s neck and cut the necklace in two.

“Dash some cold water over her face—it always recovers her!” said the Baroness. “You stay with her, Brett. How much is your suit, gentlemen?”

Mr. Costigan replied: “The debt we have against your ladyship is one hundred and thirty-two pounds, in which she is indebted to Mistress Eliza Pincott.”

Meanwhile, where was the Reverend Mr. Sampson?

Like the fabled opossum who, spotting the gunner from his gum-tree, said: “It’s no use, Major—I’ll come down,” so Sampson surrendered without resistance.

“At whose suit, Simons?” he asked sadly.

Sampson knew Simons—they had met many times before.

“Buckleby Cordwainer,” said Mr. Simons.

“Forty-eight pounds and charges, I know,” sighed Mr. Sampson. “I haven’t the money. What officer is here?”

Mr. Simons’s companion, Mr. Lyons, stepped forward. “My house is most convenient,” he said, “often used by gentlemen. I shall be proud to accommodate your reverence.”

Two chairs happened to wait outside the chapel. In those chairs, Lady Maria Esmond and Mr. Sampson took their seats and were escorted to Mr. Lyons’s residence by the men we’ve just met.

Shortly after the arrests, the Baroness sent Mr. Case, her trusted servant, with a note to her niece—full of expressions of affection, but regretting that her heavy losses at cards made paying such a sum impossible. However, she had already written to Mrs. Pincott, begging for time, and would inform her niece as soon as she received a reply.

Mrs. Betty came to console her mistress. The two women searched for funds to send Betty to London—she had nearly suffered misfortune too. Both Lady Maria and her maid had lost heavily at cards, and together could muster only eighteen shillings. They agreed Betty should sell a gold chain belonging to her lady and travel with the proceeds.

Betty took the chain to the very toy-shop man who had sold it to Mr. Warrington, who had given it to his cousin. The shopkeeper, suspecting theft, threatened to summon a constable. Betty had to explain—how her mistress was imprisoned—and by nightfall, all of Tunbridge Wells knew Lady Maria Esmond was in the hands of bailiffs.

Yet, meanwhile, the money was found, and Mrs. Betty hurried to London in search of the champion whom the prisoner trusted.

“Don’t say anything about that paper being gone! Oh, the wretch, the wretch! She shall pay it me!” I assume Lady Maria meant her aunt by “wretch.”

Mr. Sampson read a sermon to her ladyship, and they spent the evening discussing revenge and playing backgammon, confidently expecting Harry Warrington to rush to their rescue upon hearing of their plight.

Though by evening’s end, every soul at the Wells knew what had happened—Lady Maria taken into custody, the house where she lay, the exact amount—nay, ten times the amount—for which she was arrested, and that she had pawned her jewelry to raise a little money to stay in jail—yet everyone maintained perfect civility. At Lady Trumpington’s card party that night, where Madame Bernstein appeared, not a word was spoken about the morning’s events as long as she remained within hearing.

Lady Yarmouth inquired after the Baroness’s nephew and learned Mr. Warrington was in London. Was Lady Maria coming tonight? No—she was indisposed, had fainted at church, and was confined to her room.

Cards were dealt, fiddles sang, wine flowed, the gentlefolk talked, laughed, yawned, chattered, footmen intercepted supper, chairmen drank and swore, stars climbed the sky—just as though no Lady Maria was imprisoned, no poor Sampson arrested.

’Tis certain, dearly beloved brethren, that the little griefs, stings, annoyances we feel acutely in ourselves do not prevent our neighbors from sleeping; and when we slip from the world, the world does not miss us. Is this humiliating to our vanity? So much the better. But on the other hand, is it not a comforting truth? And may we not be thankful for our humble condition?

If we were not selfish—*passez-moi le mot*, please—and if we cared as much for others’ sorrows as our own, how unbearable human life would be! If my neighbor’s tight boot pinched my corn; if slander against Jones set Brown into fury; if Mrs. A’s death plunged Messrs. B, C, D, E, F into despair—could we bear the burden of the world?

Let us not be angry or surprised that the company continued playing, laughing, happy, although Lady Maria had come to grief.

Countess, the deal is yours! Are you going to Stubblefield to shoot as usual, Sir John? Captain, we shall have you running off to Bath after the widow!

So the clatter goes on; the lights burn; the beaux and ladies flirt, laugh, ogle; the prisoner rages in his cell; the sick man tosses on his bed.

Perhaps Madame de Bernstein stayed until the very end, unwilling to allow the company to speak of her as soon as her back turned. Ah, what a comfort it is—once again—that we have backs, and that our ears don’t grow upon them! He who has ears to hear, let him stuff them with cotton.

Madame Bernstein might have heard folks say it was heartless of her to attend assemblies and play cards when her niece was in trouble. As if she could help Maria by staying home! At her age, it is dangerous to disturb an old lady’s tranquility.

“Don’t tell me!” said Lady Yarmouth. “The Bernstein would play cards over her niece’s coffin. Talk about her heart! Who ever said she had one? That old spy lost it to the Chevalier a thousand years ago and has lived perfectly well without one since. For how much is Maria put in prison? If it were only a small sum, we would pay it—it would vex her aunt so. Find out, Fuchs, in the morning, for how much Lady Maria Esmond is imprisoned.”

And the faithful Fuchs bowed and promised to obey.

Meanwhile, about midnight, Madame de Bernstein returned home and fell into a deep sleep, waking only late the next morning when her usual attendant arrived with her tea.

If I told you she took a dram with it, you’d be shocked. Some of our great-grandmothers used cordials in their “closets.” Have you not read of the fine lady in Walpole who said, “If I drink more, I shall be 'muckibus!'”? As surely as Mr. Gough is alive now, our ancestresses freely partook of strong waters.

After finishing her cordial, Madame Bernstein stirred and asked Mrs. Brett for news.

“He can give it you,” said the waiting-woman, sulkily.

“Who?”

Mrs. Brett named Harry, saying Mr. Warrington had arrived about midnight—and Betty, Lady Maria’s maid, was with him.

“And my Lady Maria sends your ladyship her love and duty, and hopes you slept well,” said Brett.

“Excellently, poor thing! Is Betty gone to her?”

“No; she is here,” said Mrs. Brett.

“Let me see her directly,” cried the old lady.

“I’ll tell her,” replied the obsequious Brett, and went off on her mistress’s errand, leaving the old lady peacefully resting on her pillows.

Presently, two pairs of high-heeled shoes clicked across the deal floor of the bedroom. Carpets were luxuries unknown in bedrooms of that time.

“So, Mrs. Betty, you were in London yesterday?” called Bernstein from behind her curtains.

“It is not Betty—it is I! Good morning, dear aunt! I hope you slept well?” called a voice that made old Bernstein start on her pillow.

It was Lady Maria’s voice. She drew aside the curtains and dropped a low curtsey.

Lady Maria looked radiant, rosy, and joyful.

And with the surprise of her sudden appearance through Madame Bernstein’s curtains, I think we may close this chapter.

On Saturday morning, August 25, 1756, Mr. Warrington wrote from Tunbridge Wells:

“My dear Lord March,

I am pleased to inform you that I have settled all three of our bets. I arrived at Bromley just two minutes before the hour, and my new horses performed admirably. I drove them myself, with the postilion beside me to guide the way, and my black servant inside with Mrs. Betty. I trust they found the journey agreeable.
