We were not detained on Blackheath, though two men on horseback approached us—yet, upon seeing our faces, they rode off without further trouble. We reached Tunbridge Wells at eleven forty-five, where I completed my business. This settles the score after yesterday’s game of piquet, and I shall be delighted to return your favor soon.

Yours most obliged and faithful servant,

Now, perhaps, the reader can understand how Lady Maria Esmond managed to surprise her dear aunt in bed that very morning—and slip quietly from her house of confinement. She had sent Mrs. Betty to London, expecting no return so soon. As night fell, she and the chaplain played cards after a modest supper provided by the bailiff’s wife. Suddenly, the sound of rolling wheels approached—their carriage was coming!

Lady Maria laid down her cards, her heart pounding. The wheels whirred, the coach stopped at the door. There was a brief exchange at the gate, then Mrs. Betty appeared, her face glowing with joy, though her eyes glistened with tears. And who stepped forward next? Can any reader guess?

The chaplain slammed his cards down with a joyful cry. Lady Maria, turning as pale as death, rose unsteadily, took a few steps forward, and burst into a sobbing cry, throwing herself into her cousin’s arms. How many kisses did he give her? A thousand? A hundred more? Let it pass. He had come to save her. She knew he would. He was her champion, her deliverer from captivity and disgrace. She wept freely upon his shoulder, and as she leaned against him, overwhelmed with emotion, one might say she looked more radiant than at any other moment in this tale. She did not faint this time. Instead, she walked home, leaning gently on his arm, perhaps shedding a few more tears later that night—but Madame Bernstein slept through it all, untouched by sorrow.

“You are both free to go,” Harry said, the moment they were together. “Betty, fetch my lady’s hat and cloak. Chaplain, let us smoke a pipe at my lodgings—it will refresh me after my ride.”

The chaplain, deeply moved, could scarcely contain himself. He seized Harry’s hand, kissed it, and wept openly, praying God to bless his noble, generous young patron. Harry felt a warmth spread through him. There is something noble in helping those in need, in turning grief into joy. Proud and uplifted, he marched beside the woman he had rescued, his hat tilted jauntily. It seemed as though happiness itself danced before him—smiling, singing, scattering flowers and blowing horns of celebration. “Here comes the conqueror!” the world seemed to shout. “Make way for the hero!” They led him triumphantly into the king’s house and seated him on cushions of comfort, as if he had won a battle.

Yet what had he truly done? Only kindness. With a simple gesture, he’d opened the gates of prison and silenced the tyrant who held Lady Maria captive. Let him boast a little tonight—let him swagger with the chaplain, speak of London, of Lord March, of White’s and Almack’s, with the air of a fashionable dandy. We shall not hold it against him.

Sampson, too, was utterly overcome. His emotions ran deep and fast. He was easily stirred—by pain, by joy, by laughter or sorrow. His years as a preacher had sharpened his sensibilities until he lived each feeling fully, as if acting it out. He wept real tears now, not because he needed to, but because he could. He loved sincerely while near you, mourned genuinely beside widows, and laughed uproariously with friends at the tavern. He gave money freely but never repaid debts. That night, he was in a state of rapture, overflowing with gratitude toward Harry Warrings. In all of London, there may have been no more dangerous companion than a man so emotionally charged.

He toasted Harry again and again, praising him as the noblest soul alive. And Harry, the complacent young man, accepted these words as well-earned.

“The younger branch of our family,” Harry declared, with grandeur, “has treated you poorly. But by Jove, Sampson, I’ll stand by you!”

At moments of Burgundian excess, Harry often spoke with great passion about the glory of his lineage.

“I’m glad I could help you,” he said. “Count on me whenever you need me. Did you mention having a sister at boarding school? You’ll need funds. Here—this note may cover her tuition.”

He handed over a banknote. Sampson was struck silent, then burst into tears.

“Mr. Warrington,” he whispered, pushing the note away, “I don’t deserve this kindness—by George, I don’t!” He swore it with fervor.

“Psha!” Harry replied. “I’ve plenty more. That cursed pocket-book I lost last week had no money in it.”

“No, sir,” Sampson murmured, head bowed. “There was no money.”

“Hallo!” Harry exclaimed. “How do you know?”

“I know because I’m a villain,” Sampson confessed. “I found the book that night, when you were drunk at Barbeau’s.”

“And read the letters?” Harry asked sharply, rising and flushing.

“They told me nothing I didn’t already know,” the chaplain replied. “You have spies around you—people you trust, yet suspect not. Young and naive as you are, you cannot keep secrets from such eyes.”

“Are those stories about Lady Fanny, and my cousin Will’s affairs, true?” Harry asked.

“Yes,” the chaplain sighed. “The house of Castlewood has seen better days since the elder branch left it.”

“Sir, you dare not speak ill of my Lady Maria!” Harry snapped.

“Oh, not for worlds!” Sampson replied, glancing at him with an odd expression. “I may think she’s too old for you, that it’s a pity you don’t marry someone your own age—though I admit she looks remarkably youthful, and possesses every virtue.”

“She is too old,” Harry declared, with dignity. “But she has my word—and you see how fond she is of me. Bring me the letters you found. Let me try to forgive you.”

“My benefactor,” Sampson pleaded, “let me try to forgive myself!” He hurried off to his room.

Soon he returned, pale and trembling.

“What happened?” Harry asked, imperious.

The chaplain extended a pocket-book. “With your name in it, sir.”

“My brother’s name,” Harry corrected. “George gave it to me.”

“I kept it locked in a chest this morning, before I was taken,” Sampson said. “Here is the book—but the letters are gone. My trunk and valise have been searched. I am a wretched, guilty man, unable to restore what I owe you.”

He knelt almost, hands clasped, a picture of despair. Who had entered their rooms? The landlady swore no one had come in. Harry’s chamber showed no signs of disturbance. Only Sampson’s papers were missing.

Whose interest was it to take them? Lady Maria’s? Impossible—she had been imprisoned during the theft. She was innocent.

Then why had she been arrested? Sampson knew nothing yet of the letter she had lost. Poor Maria had not shared her secret with him.

As for the stolen papers—Harry, swollen with pride over his winning bets, his rescue, and the sumptuous dinner of partridges and old Burgundy sent by Monsieur Barbeau, dismissed Sampson’s guilt. He accepted the chaplain’s tearful vows of loyalty and forgave him with a noble gesture.

When Sampson swore on his gods that he would die for Harry, the young man replied, “I believe you would, Sampson. I hope you would. Our family—Esmond—has always had faithful friends, and rewarded them. The wine’s yours, Chaplain. What toast do you call?”

“A blessing on the house of Esmond-Warrington!” the chaplain cried, tears in his eyes.

“We are the elder branch,” Harry said, voice noble but slightly blurred. “My grandfather was the Marquis of Esmond.”

“Here’s to you, Chaplain—and I forgive you—and God bless you—and if you’d been taken for three times as much, I’d have paid it. Why—what’s that I see through the shutters? By heavens, the sun’s risen again! No need for candles to go to bed, ha, ha!”

And with another blessing, he retired to sleep.

Around noon, Madame de Bernstein sent a servant to invite her nephew to join her for chocolate. Harry rose and walked to her lodgings.

She noticed a change in his appearance—his clothes sharper, his bearing more confident. He had visited tailors in London, introduced to tradesmen by Lord March.

“My dearest child,” she said, “thank you for your noble, generous care of poor Maria. That seizure in church—how it shocked me! Even worse—that I lost three hundred pounds to Lady Yarmouth Wednesday night. I am quite broke.”

“So Case went to London?” Harry asked.

“Of course. The Baroness de Bernstein cannot afford to be short of funds. Can you lend me some, child?”

“I can give you twenty-two pounds,” Harry said, blushing. “I have only forty-four left until my Virginian remittances arrive. I’ve bought horses, clothes—I’ve been extravagant, aunt.”

“And rescued your poor relations in distress—you prodigal good boy,” she said. “No, child, I don’t want your money. I’ll give you some. Here—a note for fifty pounds, vaurien! Go spend it, be merry! Your mother may repay me, though she does not love me.”

She smiled warmly, offering her hand. Harry kissed it.

“Your mother did not love me,” she continued, “but your mother’s father once did. Remember, sir—come to me when you need me.”

When she chose to charm, Beatrix Bernstein was unmatched in grace and wit.

“I can’t help loving you, child,” she said. “Yet I am so angry with you, I scarce have patience. You’ve actually engaged yourself to poor Maria—she’s as old as your mother! What will Madam Esmond say? She may live three hundred years, and you’ll have nothing to support yourselves.”

“I have ten thousand pounds from my father,” Harry said. “It will help.”

“The interest won’t even cover card games,” she retorted.

“We must give up cards,” Harry insisted. “Maria can’t control herself. She’ll pawn your coat to play. The passion runs in my brother’s blood—in mine too, I confess. I warned you. I begged you not to play with them. And now—a boy of twenty marrying a woman of forty-two—writing letters on his knees, signed with his heart’s blood (which he spells like hartshorn), swearing he’ll marry no one but his beloved cousin, Lady Maria Esmonds. Oh, it’s cruel—cruel!”

“Great heavens, madam!” Harry exclaimed, blushing fiercely. “Who showed you my letter?”

“An accident,” she replied. “She fainted when taken. Brett cut her laces. When she was carried away, we found a sachet on the floor. I opened it—without knowing what was inside. And there was your precious letter. And here—” she held up the case.

A sharp pang pierced Harry’s heart. *Why didn’t she destroy it?*

“I—I’ll give it back to Maria,” he said, reaching for the locket.

“My dear,” she said softly, “I burned the foolish letter. If you choose to betray me, I must bear the consequences. If you write another, I cannot stop you. But if you do, Harry Esmond, I’d rather never see you again. Will you keep my secret? Will you believe an old woman who loves you and knows the world better than you do? I tell you—this promise will bring misery and ruin. What is a lad like you in the hands of a cunning woman who plays with you like a toy? She has trapped you. And I’ve cut the strings. Go back. Betray me if you must.”

“I’m not angry with you, aunt—I wish I were,” Harry said, voice thick with emotion. “I—I won’t repeat what you’ve told me.”

“Maria never will, child—mark my words!” the old lady cried. “She’ll never admit she lost that paper. She’ll lie and say she still has it.”

“But I know she—she loves me,” Harry stammered. “You should have seen her last night.”

“Must I tell more lies about my own flesh and blood?” the Baroness sobbed. “Child, you don’t know her past!”

“And I must not—and I will not!” Harry cried, rising. “Written or spoken—it doesn’t matter. My word is given. Men may break promises in England, but gentlemen of Virginia don’t. If she holds me to it, she shall have me. If we’re miserable—as I fear we will be—I’ll take a firelock and join the King of Prussia—or let a bullet end me.”

“I—have nothing more to say,” she whispered. “Will you ring the bell? I—I bid you good morning, Mr. Warrington.”

She dropped a stately curtsey, rose on her tortoiseshell cane, and turned toward the door. But as she took her first step, she clutched her chest, sank onto the sofa, and shed the first tears Beatrix Esmond had wept in many years.

Harry was deeply moved. He knelt beside her, took her cold hand, and kissed it. He spoke simply, honestly, of how deeply he had felt her love—and how completely he returned it.

“Aunt,” he said, “you don’t know how vile I feel. When you told me the letter was burned—oh, I was ashamed to realize how glad I was.”

He bowed his head over her hand. Hot tears fell upon it.

She had loved this boy. For half a century—perhaps never in her life—had she felt such tender, pure emotion. Her hard heart was broken, softened, undone. She placed both hands on his shoulders and lightly kissed his forehead.

“You will not tell her what I’ve done, child?” she asked.

He swore—never! Never!

And demure Mrs. Brett, entering at her mistress’s call, found the nephew and aunt locked in a quiet, emotional embrace.

The Tunbridge season was drawing to a close, and the Esmond party, weary of the endless rounds of tea and cards, prepared to depart. Madame de Bernstein had her sights set on Bath—where life was livelier, company more plentiful, and the gaming tables ever inviting. She would make her way there after visiting a few country friends. Harry Warrington, with only mild reluctance, agreed to accompany Lady Maria and Parson Sampson to Castlewood.

As they passed through Oakhurst village once more, they came upon the same hospitable cottage where Harry had been so warmly received. Lady Maria could not resist teasing him about the young ladies of the village—how they all seemed to be setting their caps at him, how his hostess plainly wished to snare him for one of her daughters. Her remarks grew sharper, more pointed, until Harry, annoyed, declared he would ride past their door—Lady Maria’s disapproval of the family was well known, and he felt no desire to linger under their roof. That evening, at the inn several miles down the road, his mood was sour. Lady Maria’s smiles brought no warmth to his face; her tears, so readily summoned, stirred no sympathy in him. He growled back at her complaints, and when she tried to draw him into private conversation, he refused. The chaplain, as if by design, remained in the room. Had Harry ordered Sampson to stay? She sighed and retired, leaving him to bow her away with cold politeness, entrusting her care to the landlady and her maid.

Ten minutes later, a horse galloped out of the inn yard—its rider unseen, its purpose unknown.

An hour after supper, Mrs. Betty returned for her lady’s smelling salts and found Parson Sampson alone, pipe in hand. “Mr. Warrington?” she asked. “Gone to bed.” “To walk in the moonlight,” Sampson corrected. “How should I know where Mr. Harry is?”

Next morning, Harry took his place beside Lady Maria’s carriage. But his brow remained dark. The storm within had not passed. He barely spoke during the journey. *Great heavens!* thought Lady Maria. *She must have told him she stole it!*

And indeed, she had. As they walked up the steep hill near Oakhurst on the Westerham road, Lady Maria, leaning heavily on Harry’s arm and quite smitten with him, poured forth sentimental vows—affectionate declarations, poetic promises, and exaggerated raptures. The more she loved, the colder he became. The sun beat down on her face, still fresh but marked by the lines of sixty years. Poor Harry felt the weight of her arm like a burden, and the walk uphill became unbearable. To think that this—this drag—would follow him all his life! He cursed the night air, the wine, and the foolish pledge he’d made under its influence.

Her words grated on him. She quoted fragments from plays she remembered, trying desperately to charm him. “My champion,” she called him. “My Henrico, my preserver!” And again: “Molinda will be faithful forever!” She clung to him. “Ah, child!” she sighed, pressing her fingers to her heart. “Have I not your image, your hair, your writing here? Shall it not go with me to the grave? It would, sir, were I to meet unkindness from my Henrico!”

A strange revelation. Madame Bernstein had given Harry the silken case—then burned the contents. Yet here was Maria, still carrying it. At that moment, as Harry jerked his arm away, she felt the first pang of guilt—not for lying, but for being caught in the lie. Heaven help us—if every falsehood demanded penance, we’d never escape sackcloth and ashes.

At Castlewood, Harry’s temper did not improve. The lord of the house was absent; the ladies were gone. Only Mr. Will Esmond was home, returning from partridge-shooting just as the carriage arrived. His face turned pale at the sight of his cousin, who greeted him with a sullen scowl.

Still, Harry tried to appear civil. They met at supper, where conversation began politely, though without warmth. Mr. Will had been to races? Several. Successful? “Pretty well,” he said. “And you’ve brought back my horse sound?” Harry asked sharply.

“What horse?” Will replied.

“The brown horse I played against you—won from you the night before you rode off.”

“Protest, I don’t understand,” Will said.

“You remember the horse, Mr. Esmond.”

“I remember playing you for a horse,” said Will. “But mine was not brown.”

“Mr. Sampson was present,” Harry said, turning to the chaplain. “Will you serve as umpire?”

“I must admit,” Sampson said, glancing nervously toward the absent master, “that Mr. Warrington played for the brown horse.”

“And he got the other one,” Will grinned. “Sold it for thirty shillings!”

“Not a word more,” Harry said calmly. “It’s merely a matter of a bet, my dear Lady Maria. Shall I serve you more chicken?”

He was courteous, even cheerful, while she remained. When she rose, he followed her to the door, closing it with a courtly bow. Then, once she was gone, he motioned the servants to leave. After they departed, Harry locked the heavy door and pocketed the key.

The click echoed through the hall. Will, sitting over his punch, glanced up. “What the devil do you mean by that?” he snapped.

“I guess there’s going to be a quarrel,” Harry replied, blandly. “No use having servants watch two gentlemen fight.”

“Who’s fighting?” Will demanded, eyes wide, hand gripping a knife.

“Mr. Sampson,” Harry said, “you were present when I played Mr. Will fifty guineas against his brown horse?”

“Against his horse?” Will bellowed.

“I’m not such a fool as you take me for,” Harry said, voice steady. “Though I do come from Virginia.” He repeated his question.

“I must own it,” Sampson said, looking apologetic.

“I don’t own any such thing,” Will insisted, forcing a laugh.

“No, sir,” Harry said, stepping forward. “Because it costs you no effort to lie—and cheat.”

“Hands off, Mr. Chaplain!” Harry warned. “Fair play!”

Before the chaplain could react, Will hurled a wine bottle at Harry’s head. Harry ducked just in time—the bottle shattered against the wall, destroying a portrait of an ancestor and splashing port wine across Sampson’s wig and face.

“Great heavens!” the parson cried, dripping red liquid. “I beg you, gentlemen, cease!”

But gentlemen, especially when provoked, rarely heed such pleas. The bottle missed. Will grabbed a large silver-handled knife and lunged. Harry caught his wrist—just as he’d seen boxers do at Marybone—and delivered a sharp blow to Will’s nose. He staggered backward, hitting the oak paneling, then dropped the knife, which Harry kicked under the table.

Will, too, knew boxing tricks. He charged forward, head lowered like a battering ram, aiming for Harry’s stomach.

Harry had seen such tactics before—in London, and among the negroes on his mother’s plantation. He sidestepped, then struck a crushing blow to Will’s ear. The man fell, head cracking against the table, and collapsed unconscious.

“Mr. Sampson,” Harry said, breathless but composed, “you’ll bear witness—it was fair.”

He unlocked the door. Servants rushed in, startled by the crash and shouts. They found two men covered in blood—one drenched in wine, the other in his own.

“Mr. Sampson will testify I struck fairly,” Harry said. “And Mr. Esmond threw the first blow. Undo his neckcloth—see if he lives. Gumbo, fetch a fleam. Stop—he’s waking. Lift him up. Tell a maid to clean the floor.”

In moments, Will regained consciousness. His eye was swollen shut. He groaned, then began cursing freely.

“He’s coming around,” Harry said.

“Oh, praise be Mussy!” sighed Betty.

“Ask him, Gumbo,” Harry said, with dry humor, “if he’d like another.”

“Massa Harry say, wool you like any maw?” Gumbo asked, bowing low.

“No, curse you, you black devil!” Will spat, swinging at the servant. (“So he nearly cut my tongue in half!” Gumbo explained later to Betty.)

“No—that is, yes!” he added, furious. “You infernal Mohock! Why doesn’t someone kick him out?”

“Because nobody dares,” Harry said, adjusting his ruffles with calm dignity.

“And nobody won’t neither,” the men muttered. They liked Harry. Will had no allies.

“We know all’s fair,” one said. “It ain’t the first time Master William’s been served so.”

“And I hope it won’t be the last,” Betty chimed in. “To strike a poor black gentleman so!”

By now, Will had sat up, wiped his face, and slunk off to bed.

“Surely it’s manners to say goodnight,” Harry said. “Goodnight, Mr. Esmond.”

His joke was clumsy—but he laughed inwardly at his own wit.

“He’s ad his zopper, and he goes to baid!” Betty exclaimed in dialect, making everyone laugh except Will, who left trailing curses like smoke.

The next morning, Harry wrote a note to Will, asking if he wanted a ride to town. If so, he’d frighten the highwaymen on Hounslow Heath and look “very genteel” at the Chocolate House. Will responded with a furious reply, demanding Harry go to hell—*not* Hounslow.

Later, a maiden appeared at Harry’s door. Gumbo stepped forward, holding a white triangle.

Harry knew what it was. “Of course,” he groaned. A letter from Molinda—her Enrico, her beloved. She hadn’t slept. Was he sleeping well in his ancestral halls? Would he never be cruel again? Kai ta loipa. He wouldn’t quote more. Ah, golden tablets—now faded leaves. Where is the juggler who once enchanted you?

After the brawl, Harry could not remain at Castlewood. He wrote a formal letter to the lord of the house, explaining the incident—with Sampson supervising, ensuring no spelling errors. He told Lady Maria that staying after assaulting a son of the house would be ill-bred. She wept at parting. He’d go to London, see younger beauties—none, she insisted, could love him as she did. Harry showed no emotion. The moment he crossed Castlewood Bridge, he cheered up. He urged his horses to ten miles an hour, sang to them, nodded at girls by the roadside, and chucked the landlady under the chin. He was not broken-hearted. He longed for London—St. James’s, Newmarket, the fashionable world. Tunbridge’s petty society now seemed childish.

By the time he reached London, nearly all his forty pounds had vanished. More money was needed. But Harry soon eased his mind. There were two sums of five thousand pounds—his and his brother’s—over which he held control. He’d borrow a little, win it back at cards, and live as befit his station. He would explain to Madam Esmond that a gentleman of his rank could not maintain proper company or appear in society on a mere two hundred a year.

He stayed briefly at the Bedford Coffee-House, then moved to Bond Street. He took lodgings, installed Gumbo, and placed his horses at a livery stable. Tailors, mercers, and shoemakers were summoned. With regret, he discarded his mourning clothes and donned a laced hat and waistcoat. Gumbo powdered his hair—now Harry looked as fashionable as any man in the Mall. He drove in his phaeton at the Ring. Rumors of his wealth preceded him. Curiosity swirled around the “fortunate Virginian.”

Until he could join the club officially, Lord March had entered his name at White’s Chocolate-House as a distinguished American gentleman. Fashionable London was small, but a young man with money at twenty-one could thrive—even out of season. Harry meant to enjoy himself.

He ordered Mr. Draper to sell five hundred pounds’ worth of stock. What would his mother say, had she known her son was already squandering his inheritance? He dined at taverns, supped at clubs, where Jack Morris introduced him with glowing praise. Life, youth, pleasure—wine flowed freely, and Harry drank greedily. Far away, perhaps, the pious widow prayed for her son. Behind the trees at Oakhurst, a tender heart beat for him. When the Prodigal Son wandered, were not love and forgiveness still watching?

Among the unpublished letters of the late Lord Orford, one exists—omitted by editor Peter Cunningbam, perhaps doubted. I myself saw a copy in Madam Esmond’s handwriting, labeled: *“Mr. H. Walpole’s account of my son Henry at London, and of Baroness Tusher—written to General Conway.”*

“ARLINGTON STREET, Friday Night.

“I’ve come away from my devotions to our Lady of Strawberry. Have I not knelt three weeks straight? My old joints ache with rheumatism. So I took a fit to visit London—go to Vauxhall, Ranelagh. Quoi! May I not have my rattle like other elderly babies? Suppose I tire of virtue and crave cakes and ale—shall your reverence forbid me? George Selwyn, Tony Storer, and I took a boat from Westminster. Was it Tuesday? No—Tuesday I was with the Dukes of Norfolk, just returned from Tunbridge. Wednesday, then. How should I know? Wasn’t I dead drunk after a whole pint of lemonade at White’s?

“The Norfolks told me about a young savage—Iroquois, Choctaw, or Virginian—who’s been making noise in London. An offshoot of the disreputable Esmond family of Castlewood—all the men gamblers, spendthrifts; the women—well, I won’t say. My father told me both late lords were in his pay. The last one, a beau of Queen Anne’s reign, rose from viscount to earl thanks to his notorious sister, Bernstein, late Tusher, née Esmond—a great beauty, favorite of the Pretender. She sold secrets to my father, whom she later betrayed. Now she’s loyal to the Hanoverians. ‘Will Horace Walpole’s tongue never stop scandal?’ says your wife over your shoulder. I kiss your hand. I am dumb. The Bernstein is a model of virtue. She married her father’s chaplain—not out of shame, but choice. Many nobles skip marriage altogether. She wasn’t ashamed to be Mrs. Tusher, nor did she take a German Baroncino for a second husband—no one outside Hanover ever saw him. The Yarmouth bears no grudge. Esther and Vashti are friends—cheating each other at cards all summer.

“‘And what has this to do with the Iroquois?’ asks your ladyship. The Iroquois was at Tunbridge too—winning, not cheating. They say he bled Lord March of thousands. Lord March, who’s quarreled with everyone, fought everyone, ridden over everyone, and been loved by everyone’s wife—except Mr. Conway’s, and not even hers. And the Queen herself, the Countess of England, Scotland, France, and Ireland, Queen of Walmoden and Yarmouth—may Heaven preserve her.

“You know Jack Morris, that impudent creature who slips into every house in London. At Vauxhall, he nodded to a young fellow—pretty enough, leaning on Jack’s arm, delighted by the garden. Lord, how he stared at the fireworks! Gods, how he huzzayed at the singing woman—horrible, painted wench who shrieked till my ears bled! Twopence worth of glass beads and tawdry cloth are treasures in Iroquois-land, and our savage valued them accordingly.

“A buzz spread: this was the fortunate youth. He won three hundred at White’s last night—from Rockingham and my nephew. Here he was, bellowing at music, so loud it pleased the ear. I hate puppet-shows, but I love treating children to one, Miss Conway! I send your ladyship my compliments—we shall see the dolls together.

“When the singer descended, Jack introduced the Virginian. I saw him blush crimson, make a fine bow—such grace, I never thought existed in wigwams. ‘There’s a certain jenny squaw about her,’ George said—joke not as bright as a firework. Then they retreated together.

“I’d eaten and drunk too much earlier. My companions wanted chicken and rack-punch. George fell asleep. I told Tony Storer about the Virginian’s family—especially the Bernstein’s past, and Lady Maria, who was once close to the late Prince of Wales. What did I say? Not half I knew, certainly not a tenth. But then—out bursts my savage, face flushed, in war paint. He’d been drinking fire-water in the next box!

“He cocked his hat, drew his sword, demanded: ‘Which gentleman is maligning my family?’ I had to hush him—lest he wake George. ‘I assure you, sir,’ I said, ‘I didn’t know you were near. I sincerely apologize.’

“But the damage was done.”

In the time of Harry Warrington, society was deeply engaged in a debate—though our young gentleman cared little for it—about whether the ancients or the moderns were superior in literature. The learned and the world at large generally favored the ancients. But what are the moderns of that era but the ancients of our own? We now judge them as future generations will one day judge us.

As for book learning, respectable ancestors—though you had Gibbon on your side—I must say you are outmatched. Today, professors at Cambridge and Glasgow know more Greek than all the universities of Europe combined could boast in your time, even including Athens itself, if such a place existed then. In science, you were scarcely ahead of the heathens whose literary superiority you acknowledged. And what of public and private morality? Is this year, 1858, truly worse than its predecessor a century earlier? Gentlemen of Mr. Disraeli’s House of Commons: does each of you carry a price, as in Walpole’s or Newcastle’s day—or (and here is the delicate question) have nearly all of you already been bought?

Ladies, I do not claim you are a society of Vestals—but the chronicles of a hundred years past brim with scandal so shocking that you may well be grateful you did not live in such perilous times. No—on my conscience, I believe men and women are better now. Not only are there more Susannas, but the Elders are not nearly as wicked as they once were.

Have you ever heard of books like *Clarissa*, *Tom Jones*, or *Roderick Random*? Paintings by artists of their day capturing the lives and manners of men and women in full, unvarnished detail? Imagine describing the exploits of Mr. Lovelace or Lady Bellaston—or that remarkable “Lady of Quality” who lent her memoirs to the author of *Peregrine Pickle*. How the pure and outraged nineteenth century would blush, scream, flee the room, send away the young ladies, and order Mr. Mudie never again to deliver one of those odious works!

You are fifty-eight, madam, and perhaps too sensitive—too quick to cry out before any harm is done, when no offense was meant. Or perhaps the novelist’s art suffers under the restraints imposed upon it, just as many an honest statue in St. Peter’s or the Vatican is spoiled by the tin draperies ecclesiastical women have wrapped around its limbs. Yet in your prudery, there is reason. So too in the state censorship of the press. A page may contain matter dangerous to good morals. Out with your scissors, censor—cut out the prurient paragraph! We have no choice but to submit. Society, the despot, has issued its decree. We may lament that the statue looked finer without the tin covering; we may argue that the full moral tale would be better told. But away with it—no word!

I’ve never seen pianofortes in America with frilled muslin trousers draped over their legs, but I’m certain the muslin covered some notes as effectively as the mahogany, muffled the music, and hindered the player.

To what does this prelude lead? I am thinking of Harry Warrington, Esquire, in his lodgings in Bond Street, London, and the life he led—along with many other fashionable young men of his time—and how I cannot possibly take my dear young reader into such a world, any more than Lady Squeams could bring her daughter to Cremorne Gardens on an ordinary evening.

My dear Miss Diana—though I know you’re thirty-eight, despite your shy manner and your wish to appear freshly out of school—you must understand that when your grandfather was a young man about town, a member of one of the clubs at White’s, dining at Pontac’s off feasts prepared by Braund and Lebeck, riding to Newmarket with March and Rockingham, and toasting the best in England with Gilly Williams and George Selwyn (though he never understood George’s jokes, which have long since lost their flavor)—he lived a life your noble aunt, author of *Legends of the Squeams’s; or, Fair Fruits of a Family Tree*, never hinted at.

This was before your grandmother adopted the serious views that marked her later years in Bath, and before Colonel Tibbalt married Miss Lye, the heiress of a rich soap-boiler. That was when her ladyship sowed her wild oats. When she was young, she was as giddy as any other woman of fashion. At her house in Hill Street, ten card-tables were laid out every Wednesday and Sunday evening—except during the brief season when Ranelagh opened on Sundays. Every night of her life, she gambled for eight, nine, or ten hours. Everyone else in society did the same. She lost, she won, she cheated, she pawned her jewels—what else might she have pawned to feed her passion for play?

And what of that after-supper duel at the Shakespeare’s Head in Covent Garden between your grandfather and Colonel Tibbalt? They drew swords and fought in the presence of Sir John Screwby, who was drunk beneath the table. They were interrupted by Mr. John Fielding’s men, and your grandfather was carried home to Hill Street, wounded, in a chair.

Yes, those gentlemen in powdered wigs and ruffles—those who turned out the toes of their buckled shoes so delicately—were fearsome indeed. Swords were drawn constantly; bottle after bottle emptied; oaths roared through taverns; watchmen and tavern keepers were slashed and injured; chairmen beaten; citizens insulted by drunken pleasure-seekers.

You’ve been to Cremorne, I suppose—with proper vouchers, of course? Do you remember our great theatres thirty years ago? You were too refined to attend a play. Well, you have no idea what the playhouses were like, or what the green boxes were, when Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard performed before them! And I, for my children’s sake, thank that good actor in retirement who first banished such shame from the stage.

No, madam, I do not boast of my virtue. I do not claim you are naturally better than your ancestress in her wild, rouged, gambling, flaring days—or even than poor Polly Fogle, recently arrested for shoplifting, who would have been hanged a century ago. Only, I am deeply thankful that my temptations are fewer, though I still wrestle with those of my own age.

So, if Harry Warrington rides to Newmarket for the October meeting, wins or loses his money there; if he joins a party at the Shakespeare’s Head or Bedford Head; if he dines at White’s ordinary and plays macco and lansquenet afterward; if he boxes the watch or appears at the Roundhouse; if he becomes, for a time, a reckless, dissipated, harum-scarum young man—knowing human nature as I do, I shall not be surprised. And knowing my own failings, I shall not be harsh toward my neighbor’s.

Mr. Sampson was another story. In his chapel in Long Acre, he scourged Vice mercilessly; gave Sin no quarter; cursed Blasphemy with greater anathemas than others; knocked Drunkenness down and trampled it in the gutter; dragged out conjugal Infidelity and pounded her with endless rhetorical stones. Yet after service, he came to dinner at the Star and Garter, made a bowl of punch for Harry and his friends at the Bedford Head, or played whist at Mr. Warrington’s lodgings or my Lord March’s—wherever good company and supper awaited him.

Yet I often wonder—if I have taken my usual uncharitable view of Mr. Warrington during this period of his arrival in London. For I have said nothing of virtuous indignation against his conduct. If it was not wrong, then I have judged him cruelly.

O Truthful, O Beautiful, O Modesty, O Benevolence, O Pudor, O Mores, O Blushing Shame, O Namby Pamby—each with your honored capital letters! O Niminy, O Piminy! How can I dare say that a young man was ever truly a young man?

Indeed, dear young lady, I may be calumniating Mr. Warrington, as I so often do. As proof, here is a letter from the Warrington collection—Harry writing to his mother—containing not a single word suggesting he leads a wild life. And such a letter from an only son to a loving, admirable parent must surely be true:

---

I take up my pen to acknowledge your honored favor of 10 July, received via the Lively Virginia packet, forwarded by our Bristol agent. I rejoice to hear the crops look promising. 'Tis Tully who says agriculture is the noblest pursuit—how delightful when it is also profitable!

Since my last letter from Tunbridge Wells, a few incidents have occurred that I feel compelled to inform my honored mother of. Our party broke up at the end of August, with partridge-shooting beginning. Baroness Bernstein, whose kindness to me has been constant, has gone to Bath, her usual winter resort, and kindly gifted me a fifty-pound bill. I rode back with Rev. Mr. Sampson, whose instruction I find most valuable, and my cousin, Lady Maria, to Castlewood. [Could Parson Sampson have been dictating these remarks?] I paid a brief visit en route to my dear friends Colonel and Mrs. Lambert at Oakhurst House, who send their most affectionate regards to you. Their youngest daughter, I regret to say, is delicate, and her parents are anxious.

At Castlewood, my stay was short due to a quarrel with my cousin William. He is a man of violent passions and, alas, prone to drink when he lacks self-control. In a minor dispute over a horse, words grew heated, and he aimed a blow at me—or its equivalent—which my grandfather’s child, my honored mother’s son, could not endure. I responded, felled him to the ground, whereupon he was carried almost senseless to bed. I sent inquiries about his health the next morning, but hearing nothing further, left for London, where I have remained since, save for brief absences.

Knowing you wished me to see my dear grandfather’s university, I recently rode to Cambridge with friends, passing through parts of Hertfordshire and staying at the famed inn of Ware. The October meeting had just begun when I arrived. I saw students in their gowns and caps, and visited Newmarket Heath, where races were underway—Lord March’s horse Marrowbones by Cleaver winning a large stake. It was an entertaining day—the jockeys, horses, and betting vastly different from our modest races at home. The richest nobles mix freely with jockeys, betting all around. Cambridge pleased me, especially King’s College Chapel, of rich yet elegant Gothic design.

I have entered society and become a member of the club at White’s, where I meet gentlemen of the highest fashion. Lords Rockingham, Carlisle, Orford, Bolingbroke, and Coventry are among my acquaintances, introduced by Lord March, whom I have mentioned before. Lady Coventry is a fine woman, though thin. Every lady paints here, young and old—so if you, Mountain, and Fanny wish to be fashionable, I must send you some rouge pots. Everyone plays—eight to ten card tables at every house on receiving nights. I regret to say not all play fairly, nor pay fairly. I have been forced to sit down and do as Rome does. Indeed, I have witnessed ladies—whom I could name—take my counters right before my eyes!

One day, when his regiment, the 20th, was paraded in St. James’s Park, a friend, Mr. Wolfe, presented me to His Royal Highness the Captain-General. He was most gracious—a fat, jolly prince, if I may speak so without disrespect—reminding me of General Braddock, whom we knew to our sorrow last year. Upon hearing my name and learning how dear George served and fell in Braddock’s ill-fated campaign, he spoke at length with me, asking why a young man like me did not serve too, why I did not go to the King of Prussia—who was a great general—to see campaigns, and whether that would not be better than idling at routs and card parties in London? I replied that I would gladly go, but being an only son on leave from my mother, I belong to our estate in Virginia. His Royal Highness said Mr. Braddock had written home about Mrs. Esmond’s loyalty, and that he would be glad to serve me. Mr. Wolfe and I have since called upon him at his residence in Pall Mall. The latter, still quite young, fought in the Scots campaign with His Royal Highness, whom Mr. Dempster admires greatly at home. To be sure, he was too severe—though severity against rebels in arms is hard to justify.

Mr. Draper has transferred half the stock, my late father’s property, into my name. Until the painful loss in our family—whose restoration I would give my right hand for—is settled beyond doubt, the remaining stock must remain in trust for the heir. Ah, dear mother! There is no day, scarce an hour, when I do not think of him. I wish he were beside me. I feel stronger when I remember him, and would honor my family by having him represent it here instead of—

Honored madam, your dutiful and affectionate son,

P.S.—I am like your sex, who always, they say, put their chief news in a postscript. I have something to tell you about a person to whom my heart is engaged. I shall write more later—there is no hurry. Suffice it to say she is a nobleman’s daughter, and her family as good as our own.

---

My good sister,

We have been, throughout our lives, more than kin and less than kind—using the words of a poet your dear father loved dearly. When you were born in our Western Principality, my mother was not as old as Isaac’s; but even then, I was far older than you. Though she gave you all she could—her love included, though it ought to have been mine—I hope we may learn to do without affection, if we can at least have goodwill. Some small kindness you owe me—for your son’s sake, and for your father’s, whom I loved and admired more than any man I have known. He was greater than most, though he made no noise in the world. I have seen many who did, yet found few with such good heads and good hearts as Mr. Esmond.

Had we been closer, I might have advised you regarding your young gentleman’s introduction to Europe—you would have taken it or not, as people do. At least you would have said afterward, “What she counselled me was right. Had Harry done as Madam Beatrix wished, it would have been better for him.”

My good sister, it was not for you to know, nor for me to tell you—since you never wrote to me—but your boy, coming to England and Castlewood, found few friends there, except one old aunt, about whom all sorts of evil have been spoken for fifty years—and not without cause.

Now, I must tell Harry’s mother what will likely surprise her: almost everyone who knows him loves him. He is prudent in speech, generous with money, bold as a lion, with a commanding manner that suits him well. Whether he is handsome, you know best. Dear sister, I like him none the less for not being overly witty or wise. I never cared for those “set-the-Thames-afire” gentlemen who think themselves cleverer than their neighbors. Your father’s great friend, Mr. Addison, seemed to me a supercilious prig, and his follower, Sir Dick Steele, was unpleasant both in and out of his cups. And (revenons à luy), your Master Harry will certainly not burn the river with his wit.

He knows little of book learning—no more than any lord in England—and for this, I hold him none the worse. If Heaven has not given him a turn for it, there’s no use forcing him.

Considering the station he holds in his colony when he returns, and the lineage from which he comes, let me tell you: he does not have enough means to support his rank. He is likely to grow desperate, break bounds, and become extravagant—not his natural tendency, but driven by necessity. He likes to live as well as his companions, and, between ourselves, has fallen into some of the finest and most rakish circles in England. He believes it is honorable not to retreat, and often orders ortolans and champagne when he would just as soon dine on a steak and a mug of beer. From what he has told me in conversation—very naïve, as the French say—I suspect his mother has encouraged his high opinion of himself. Women like their belongings to feel important, even if they dislike paying the cost.

Will you let your lad make a fool of himself in London? Triple his allowance—at least—and Aunt Bernstein (with your permission) will add more. Otherwise, he will spend the small capital I learn he has in this country, and once a young man begins to manage, the loaf is quickly finished.

God willing, I shall leave Henry Esmond’s grandson something at my death—but my savings are small, and the pension granted me by my gracious Sovereign ends with me. As for feu M. de Bernstein, he left only debt at his passing—the officers of His Majesty’s Electoral Court of Hannover are poorly paid.

A lady currently very high in His Majesty’s favor has taken a great fancy to your lad and will soon introduce him to the Sovereign’s notice. He has met His Royal Highness the Duke. If he lives in America, why should not Mr. Esmond Warrington return as Governor of Virginia, with a title? That is my hope for him.

Meanwhile, I must be candid: I fear he has entangled himself in a foolish engagement. Even marrying an old woman for money is barely pardonable—the game ne valant guères la chandelle. Mr. Bernstein, while alive, assured me of this, and I believe him, poor gentleman. To promise oneself to an old woman without money, and marry her solely because you promised, seems to me a folly only very young men fall into—and I fear Mr. Warrington is one. How or for what reason, I do not know, but my niece Maria Esmond has extracted a promise from Harry. He knows nothing of her past—I do. For twenty years, she has sought twenty husbands. I care not how she obtained his promise. It is a sin and a shame that a woman over forty should deceive a young man and bind him to his word. She is not the woman she pretends to be. A horse jockey cannot fool him—but a woman can.

I write this news deliberately, though it must displease you. Perhaps it will bring you to England—but above all, be cautious, gentle. The slightest pressure will make his proud spirit resist. I fear the property is entailed, so threats of disinheriting him will not sway Maria. Otherwise, I know her to be so mercenary that—though she genuinely fancies this handsome youth—without money, she would not hear of him.

All I could do, and more than I ought, I have done to prevent the match. What I cannot say here, I will not write. But I am, for Henry Esmond’s sake, his grandson’s sincerest friend—and madam, your faithful sister and servant,

To Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, in Virginia.

On the back of this letter, in Madam Esmond’s handwriting:
“My sister Bernstein’s letter, received with Henry’s December 24. On receipt of which it was determined my son should instantly go home.”

Though Harry Warrington clung stubbornly to the promise he had made to his cousin, we trust no kind-hearted reader will imagine that this obligation was one he cherished—or that he did not long for a way to be free of it. Indeed, the beating he gave poor Will Esmond may well have been calculated precisely for such an end. Perhaps Harry reasoned thus: “A fight between us will surely provoke a quarrel with the family; in that quarrel, Maria might side with her brother. I shall, of course, refuse any apology or retraction. Then Will may challenge me—whereupon I shall know which of us is the stronger man. Amidst the uproar, perhaps the engagement will fall apart, and I shall regain my liberty.” So honest Harry laid his plan and set it in motion—but when the dust settled, there was no real harm done, save that William Esmond’s nose swelled and his eye turned black for a week.

Will did not send a challenge to Harry Warrington. He did not kill him, nor was he killed by him. He was knocked down—and rose again. How many sensible men would do the same if they could settle their score quietly, without witnesses to recount every blow?

Maria did not take her family’s side in the dispute. On the contrary, she declared openly for her cousin. Lord Castlewood, too, when informed of the altercation, sided with Harry. According to the chaplain’s account, Will had struck first. It was not the first—nor even the tenth—time he had been found quarreling under the influence of drink. Mr. Warrington, said the lord, had acted with proper spirit in defending himself. The fault lay with Will, not Harry. And it was Will who ought to ask forgiveness.

Harry, however, insisted he would accept no apology unless his horse was returned—or his bet paid. The chronicler has found no record in any surviving papers how this matter was ultimately resolved. But it is certain that soon afterward, the cousins met again at various social gatherings—without raising fists or drawing swords.

At first, Maria’s elder brother had been quite content with the idea of her marriage. After so many years of single life, she had accumulated more than her share of thorns, stains, and weariness. A husband from Virginia seemed a fitting conclusion to her journey. She could retire to his wigwam in the wilderness, and there find peace. Naturally, Harry would outlive her—after which he could choose whether to mourn or rejoice as he pleased.

But after a visit with Aunt Bernstein upon his arrival in London, Lord Castlewood changed his mind. He went so far as to try to dissuade Maria from the match—and even expressed pity for the young man who, through a foolish vow made at twenty-one, was doomed to a lifetime of misery.

“Misery?” Maria had asked, astonished. “Why should he suffer?”

“Pity!” echoed her brother. “I say, it’s no pity at all.”

She understood now. Her brother had spoken with Aunt Bernstein. That lady had offered money to break off the engagement. Maria saw clearly what her brother meant—but she trusted Mr. Warrington. He was a man of honour, and she believed him capable of keeping his word.

So Lord Castlewood walked away—to White’s Club, or wherever else he spent his time. It was likely that Maria had already guessed the nature of his conversation with Madame Bernstein. “And so,” he thought, “the end of my virtue is to see this fine young fellow devoured by others. There’s no point in sparing him. *Quem deus vult*—what was that old schoolmaster’s saying? If I don’t claim him, someone else will. My brother has had a taste; my dear sister wants to swallow him whole. Here I’ve been at home, pretending to protect his youth and innocence, refusing to play beyond a sixpence, acting as guardian and mentor. Why am I such a fool, fattening a goose only for others to eat? I’ve done few good deeds in my life—and this one benefits whom? Not me. Others. Talk of remorse! By all the fires and furies, the remorse I feel is for things I didn’t do—things I might have done. Why did I spare Lucretia? She hated me ever after, and her husband met his fate. Why have I let this boy go? Now March and the rest, who don’t want him, can pick him clean! And I have a bad reputation. People point at me and call me the wicked lord. Women warn their sons against me. Pardi! I’m not worse than anyone else—only far unluckier. And it’s my cursed weakness that has been my greatest enemy.”

Clearly, in recording thoughts never spoken aloud, the chronicler risks overstepping the bounds of belief. Yet must we not recall that Livy, Thucydides, and countless historians have invented speeches for their heroes—speeches we know were never uttered? If we know Lord Castlewood’s character as intimately as we do, may we not dare to transcribe what passed within his mind?

Look: a pack of wolves are hunting this lamb, and soon they’ll tear him apart. And one hungry old hunter stands aside, refusing even a single bite? Who has not admired Lord Clive’s noble words when reproached for taking too freely from India’s wealth? “Upon my life,” he said, “when I think of my opportunities, I’m surprised I took so little!”

To reveal unpleasant truths about a gentleman is always painful—especially when one hesitates to speak them until forced. Thus, though I knew from the very beginning of this history what sort of man Lord Castlewood was, and how poorly he was regarded by his contemporaries, I have held back much that was unflattering. Only gradually have I allowed the reader to see that he was not a man we should admire.

It is true that Lord March and others like him would have seen nothing wrong in betting Harry Warrington’s last shilling—and taking it. They’d use every trick, every advantage, every inside knowledge. In that, they followed the customs of their class. But when they played, they played fair. When they lost, they paid.

Madame Bernstein, however, was reluctant to tell her Virginian nephew everything she knew about his family’s failings. She was touched by Lord Castlewood’s restraint toward Harry on his arrival in Europe—and pleased that he had respected her wishes in this matter. But during their conversation about Maria’s intentions, Castlewood had spoken bluntly, as usual. He called himself a fool for having spared a young man whose ruin was inevitable. He pointed out Harry’s extravagances, his reckless friends, his nights at faro and hazard, his trips to Newmarket. “Why should I alone keep my hands off him?” he demanded.

Madame Bernstein pleaded that Harry was poor.

“Bah!” Castlewood snapped. “He’s heir to a principality that should have been mine. Our family could have been restored. (Indeed, Madame Bernstein thought Harry’s land in Virginia worth far more than it actually was.) Are there not money-lenders in town who’d lend him thousands on postobits? I know. I’ve tried them myself—during my father’s lifetime. Those cursed men swallowed two-thirds of my income.”

He spoke with such bitter honesty that Madame Bernstein began to fear for her favourite nephew. She decided to warn him at once.

That evening, she began writing a letter—but throughout her life, she disliked writing. “I never knew any good come of writing anything beyond *bon jour* or business,” she used to say. “What’s the use of writing ill when so many clever people can do it well? Even then, it’s better left unsaid.”

So instead, she sent one of her servants to Harry’s lodgings, bidding him come for tea the next day—when she intended to give him her warning.

But the next morning, she was unwell and unable to receive him. She remained in bed for several days. Then came a busy engagement. Then Harry left on a journey of his own.

In the whirl of London life, how often does one see a neighbour? A brother his sister? An old friend?

Days passed before Harry and his aunt finally met. She began gently, scolding him for his extravagance and wild ways—though in truth, she found them charming. He replied that young men must be young men, and that it was only while waiting dutifully on her that he had met the companionship he now valued most.

Then, after some preamble, she warned him about Lord Castlewood.

He burst into a bitter laugh. “The world has already told me enough about Lord Castlewood.”

“To say of a man of his rank, ‘Don’t play with him,’ is more than I care to do,” the lady continued. “But…”

“Oh, go on, aunt!” Harry said, almost with an oath on his lips.

“And have you played with your cousin already?” she asked.

“Lost and won, madam,” he answered gallantly. “I won’t say which. If we have a game in Virginia—a bottle, cards, or a quarrel—we don’t run home to tell our mothers. I mean no offence, aunt!”

Blushing, the handsome young man leaned forward and kissed her hand.

He looked splendid—rich lace, fair hair, a new velvet suit embroidered with gold. As he left, he handed his usual generous gift to her servants, who gathered around him.

It was a cold, rainy winter day. To preserve his silk stockings, he must travel in a chair.

“To White’s!” he called to the chairmen—and away they carried him to the place where he spent much of his time.

His friends might have wished he visited White’s less often. But this much can be said for Mr. Warrington: once he entered the game, he fought like a hero. He was calm in victory, undisturbed by loss. Fortune, they say, is fickle—but how many men are fickle to Fortune? How many flee from her advances, deserting her just when she might have stayed, had they not shown cowardice?

“By George, Mr. Warrington,” said Mr. Selwyn, roused by sudden enthusiasm, “you deserve to win! You treat luck as a gentleman should. While she stays with you, you behave with perfect politeness. *Si celeres quatit pennas*—you know the rest? Well, you’re not much worse off—you’ll call her coach and bow at the step. Look at Lord Castlewood over there, passing the box. Have you ever heard a man curse so fiercely over losing five or six pieces? She must be a jade indeed to favour such a niggardly rogue!”

“We don’t consider our family rogues, sir,” said Harry. “Lord Castlewood is one of them.”

“I forgot. I beg your pardon! And I offer my compliments to both him and Mr. Will Esmond.”

“The box is with me. Five’s the main! Deuce Ace! My usual luck. *Virtute mea me involvo!*” he exclaimed, sinking back into his chair.

Whether this was the occasion when Harry threw the fifteen mains mentioned in those other letters of Mr. Walpole—now lost to the editor—I cannot say. But certainly, on his first appearance at White’s, Harry enjoyed several evenings of extraordinary luck. He seemed more than ever the Fortunate Youth.

Five hundred pounds drawn from his inheritance multiplied into thousands. He bought fine clothes, horses, hosted grand dinners, gave lavish gifts, lived as if he were as wealthy as Sir James Lowther or the Duke of Bedford—yet his fortune never seemed to dwindle.

No wonder he gave freely—when giving was so easy. No wonder he was generous with Fortunatus’s purse. For such was his nature.

Other Fortunati lock up their endless purses, drink small beer, and go to bed by tallow candle. But Harry lived large.

During this golden streak, he naturally inquired about Lady Maria’s debts—and paid them all, to the last shilling. Her stepmother and half-sister, who disliked her, received magnificent presents.

“Had you not better get yourself arrested, Will?” Lord Castlewood said sardonically to his brother. “You bit him in that horse affair—the Mohock will surely pull you out of pawn.”

At that, William felt a pang of regret—not the humble kind that brought the Prodigal Son to his knees.

“Confound it,” he groaned, “to think I let this fellow slip away for forty pounds! He was worth a thousand at least.”

As for Maria, that generous soul accepted her good fortune with gratitude—and was ready to accept more. Having cleared her debts to milliners, tradesmen, and purveyors, she immediately began contracting new ones.

Mrs. Betty, her maid, went round telling the shops that her mistress was marrying a young gentleman of immense wealth—so they might extend credit freely.

Though the tradespeople had heard similar stories before, they were paid anyway—even Mrs. Pincott of Kensington, who received fresh orders without resentment.

When Maria drove from mercer to toy-shop, from toy-shop to jeweller, in a coach with her maid and Harry beside her, they thought her truly fortunate—to have captured the Fortunate Youth—even if they wondered at his choice of such an elderly beauty.

Mr. Sparks of Tavistock Street, Covent Garden, ventured to call on Harry at his Bond Street lodgings, bearing the pearl necklace and gold etwee he had purchased the day before with Lady Maria. Should he leave them at Harry’s lodging—or send them to her ladyship with his compliments?

Harry added a ring from the stock Sparks happened to carry, and bade him send the bill sumptuously. Then he took a majestic leave, and Sparks bowed low—even to Gumbo, the servant, as he departed.

His generosity did not stop there. Soon after, Harry drove up in his phaeton to Sparks’ shop and selected two trinkets—for two young ladies whose parents had been kind to him, and whom he deeply admired.

“Ah,” he thought, “how I wish I had George’s wit and talent for poetry! I’d send these gifts with sweet verses to Hetty and Theo. I’m sure, if goodwill and affection could make me a poet, I’d find rhymes easily.”

So he summoned Parson Sampson—and together they composed a note.

Mr. Harry Warrington, of Virginia, lived in grand lodgings on Bond Street in London, where he enjoyed the finest comforts and indulged freely in the pleasures of high society. Wealthy, well-born, and strikingly handsome, he was widely known as the Fortunate Youth—a title earned not just by fortune, but by charm and ease. The fashionable world embraced him with open arms, for he was young, generous, and full of life. And let us not condemn this world too harshly for favoring such men while turning a cold shoulder to those less blessed—old, plain, or unremarkable. If I choose to spend my evenings in pleasant company rather than with sour-faced misanthropes or tedious bores, why should society not do the same? Harry was liked because he was likable: he was brave, courteous, and always ready for a laugh, a song, or a game of cards. With ladies, he carried himself with modesty and warmth; with gentlemen, he shared their passions—whether hunting, riding, or drinking. To those beneath him in rank, he was lavish in kindness, never sparing effort to spare them discomfort.

In those days, when social hierarchy was still strictly observed, a gentleman’s dignity lay in his distance from inferiors—not in cruelty, but in decorum. The Secretary of State knelt before the king; the Under-Secretary stood at attention. Such customs may seem absurd now, but they were part of the order of things. And though I might find it odd to kneel before a monarch or stand all day beside a superior, I understand that boundaries exist—and I would not welcome every man who claims kinship with me simply because he writes for a newspaper or contributes to a dog magazine. There is a place for fellowship, yes—but not without distinction.

During the winter of 1756–57, Harry had every pleasure London could offer at his fingertips. He attended operas—though he found them more entertaining than many critics did, who mocked them as frivolous, foreign, and unmanly. Still, the theatres drew crowds, especially with Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard commanding one stage and Mrs. Clive another. Masquerades and ridottos glittered with nobility; private assemblies and balls filled the season with music and dance. Yet Harry preferred White’s Club, where the stakes were higher and the play fairer than at any nobleman’s card table.

One day, Lord Castlewood took Harry to court to present him to His Majesty, who had recently returned from Kensington. But the King received him coolly. “Oh,” he said, speaking in German to the Earl, “I’ve heard of you from Lady Yarmouth. Tell him he plays too much.” Then, without another word, he turned away.

Lord Castlewood looked shaken. “He disapproves of your gaming,” he whispered.
“Then if he doesn’t want us,” replied Harry simply, “we’d best not come again. I never thought that German fellow was much of a king.”

“Hush!” hissed the lord. “You don’t know what ears are listening!”

But Harry only laughed. “Look around! Just now everyone was bowing and flattering me. Now they avoid me like the plague!”

At that moment, a broad-shouldered man in a scarlet-laced waistcoat stepped forward. “Shake hands, nephew,” he said, grasping Harry’s hand firmly. “I heard what you said. I have ears like the wall. And since others turn cold, I’ll give you mine.”

It was Sir Miles Warrington, Harry’s paternal uncle—whom no one had mentioned before. “Might as well have come to see us in Norfolk,” he growled, “instead of dallying at Tunbridge Wells. Mr. Warrington—or Mr. Esmond—which do you call yourself?”

“The old lady calls herself Madam Esmond,” Harry replied, “but my mother isn’t ashamed of her father’s name, nor am I.”

“Well said, lad!” declared Sir Miles. “Come eat mutton with Lady Warrington at three o’clock in Hill Street. Don’t mind my lord here—he’ll be frightened enough as it is.”

Lord Castlewood paled. “Sir Miles,” he stammered, “you must know there are enemies everywhere in this city. I’ve avoided speaking of you because we’ve had differences. If he says anything unkind, please take it with a grain of salt.”

The Baronet grunted. “Belike he will. But you’ll come, young man. Good roast mutton waits for no one. You look like your father—smaller, younger, but often won our fights. He was henpecked, poor soul, once he married. Madam Esmond took the spirit out of him in Virginia. Virginia’s an island, ain’t it?”

Harry laughed. “No, sir, it’s not.”

“Island or not,” said Sir Miles, “you’ll come and tell us all about it. My wife’ll decide whether it’s land or sea.”

Later, at White’s, news of the royal snub had already spread. Some said the King was jealous of Harry’s closeness to Lady Yarmouth. Others claimed he was simply annoyed at the gambling. By nightfall, it was settled: another triumph for the Fortunate Youth.

At dinner in Hill Street, Sir Miles teased Harry good-naturedly. His wife, at first distant, confessed she’d given him a chilly welcome, so bad a reputation had preceded him. The daughters curtseyed primly and called him “cousin.” Only the youngest boy, Master Miles, spoke plainly.

“Are you wicked, cousin Harry?” he asked, staring into Harry’s face. “You don’t look very wicked.”

“Master Miles!” cried the tutor, blushing.

“But you said he was wicked!” insisted the child.

“We’re all sinners,” explained Sir Miles. “Haven’t you heard the clergyman say so?”

“Yes, but not *so* wicked as cousin Harry. Is it true you gamble all night and drink with bad men? And that Lady Yarmouth is wicked?”

“You’re a little pitcher,” said Sir Miles. “And my wife, nephew, is a staunch Jacobite—don’t hold that against her.”

The boy was sent off with a promise of a ride in the park, though he cried bitterly, saying he’d rather stay with his “wicked” cousin.

“You’ve got quite a name among us, nephew,” said Sir Miles. “My wife has taken to Mr. Whitfield’s sermons lately, and we’ve had a friend of the tutor’s telling sad tales about you and your brother.”

“I’ll answer for my brother,” said Harry, warming with port. “Any man who dares speak ill of George—well, he’s not fit to buckle his shoe. If I hear he’s spreading lies in Virginia, he’ll get a second caning.”

“You stand up for your friends,” said Sir Miles. “Fill your glass. You’re not as bad as painted. I’ll drink to Madam Esmond Warrington of Virginia.”

Harry drank to Lady Warrington and Master Miles. “Though,” added Sir Miles, “you’d inherit four thousand acres in Norfolk if I died.”

“God forbid,” said Harry. “Praised be that I have my own in Virginia.”

After dinner, Harry spent time with Lady Warrington and the girls. One reminded him of Fanny Mountain, and she became his favorite. When he left, the household agreed he wasn’t nearly as wicked as rumored. Lady Warrington even hoped to save him from ruin. That evening, she sent him a book—*Law’s Call*—with a note praying it might guide him. She and her daughters then went to a rout hosted by a minister’s wife.

Before going to White’s, Harry had visited Mr. Sparks in Tavistock Street and bought trinkets for his cousins—“from Aunt Warrington in Virginia,” he told them. He was generous, kind-hearted, and glowing with prosperity. Not all men are so fortunate under wealth. Some grow harder, prouder, meaner. If fate should bless me with ten thousand a year, I hope I’d have strength enough to endure it without corruption.

Meanwhile, the girls in Hill Street delighted in their gifts. They wrote a collective note, which reached their aunt in springtime—when she, Fanny, and Mountain were visiting the bleak Castlewood, now brightened by blossoming peach trees.

“Poor boy,” the mother sighed. “This was a gift he gave in his prosperity—his extravagance, perhaps. How fast his fortune has slipped away. But he always had a kind heart for poor Mountain. We must be careful now.”

They warmed themselves by one log, ate from one dish, worked by one candle. The servants, increasingly pinched, began to lie and steal. What was saved in one way was lost in another.

One afternoon, Harry sat in his Bond Street lodgings, wrapped in silk, sipping chocolate, yet weighed down by worry. A few weeks earlier, flush with luck, he’d told Parson Sampson to compile a list of his debts—promising to pay them all. Sampson had done so, listing £243—what he believed were all the debts that would truly inconvenience him.

That morning, Harry appeared pale and weak, dressed in curl-papers, barely touching his breakfast. Sampson, trembling slightly, pulled out the paper. “Here is the list, sir—every shilling I owe—thank Heaven—save those that wouldn’t trouble you.”

Harry burst into laughter—harsh, bitter, mocking. “Confound it—why didn’t you bring it on Monday?”

Sampson’s heart sank. “I—I thought—”

“It’s my luck,” Harry muttered. “The cards have been against me. Monday night, last night—both ruined. Don’t worry, chaplain—there’s money left. But I must go to the City. Sell out, sir? Yes. I borrowed a hundred from Mackreth last night. Must repay him at noon. I’ll settle your affairs tomorrow.”

Yet once Sampson left, Harry slumped forward, beating the coals with the poker, muttering curses—his spirits torn.

Then came Mr. Lambert, in military dress, having just attended the Captain-General’s levee. He was a friend, always welcome—though today Harry sensed something colder in his greeting.

“How are the ladies at Oakhurst?” he asked. “Miss Hetty—was she still poorly?”

“Better,” said Harry. “They’re staying in London with Lord Wrotham.”

“Ah,” said Lambert. “So you live at White’s, dine with the great, court at St. James’s, and attend Lady Yarmouth’s parties?”

“Other people do what other people do,” said Harry, stiffening.

“Other people are richer,” replied Lambert.

“Sir,” said Harry sharply, “I owe nothing I cannot pay.”

“I only mention it because you told me yourself,” said Lambert gently. “But I hear all sorts of stories. At the levee today, they said you’d won eighteen hundred one night—two thousand another—six or eight thousand in total.”

“Let them gossip,” snapped Harry. “Why don’t they mind their own business?”

“And you,” continued Lambert, “look as if you’re about to say something else.”

“It’s my affair,” said Harry. “And I’ll thank you not to meddle.”

Then Lambert drew a packet from his coat. “Look here, Harry. These trinkets—given with such kindness—you couldn’t afford them on two or three hundred a year. A nobleman or banker might send such gifts. But not a young man who gambles.”

“Sir,” said Harry, flushing, “I meant only kindness.”

“No,” said Lambert, voice thick. “I can’t accept them. Hester and Theodosia must not wear jewels bought with gambling winnings. It grieves me to return them. Mrs. Lambert keeps her gift—it’s small—and sends her love. So do I, Harry Warrington—with all my heart.”

His voice broke. He passed a hand over his eyes.

But rebellion flared in Harry. He rose, refusing the offered hand. “Colonel Lambert,” he said, “I’ve had enough of your advice. You volunteer it constantly, without being asked. You pry into my games, my companions. What right have you to judge my amusements? I show my gratitude with small gifts, and you return them.”

“A slight,” said Lambert sadly, “may mean nothing here—but in our country, it means war.”

“God forbid I draw sword on the father of women who’ve been like mother and sister to me,” said Harry. “But you’ve wounded me—humiliated me. This treatment I will not bear from any man.”

With that, he turned and strode to his bedroom, rustling in his brocade gown, leaving the Colonel standing alone—silent, sorrowful, and deeply shaken.

When his peace offerings were refused, the young American nobleman—once so bold and confident—was consumed by anger, not only toward Colonel Lambert but against the entire family. “He has humbled me before the girls!” he fumed in private. “And Mr. Wolfe, always preaching virtue and acting like a guardian angel, has joined hands with him to brand me as a reckless wastrel once more. They are so pious they won’t even shake my hand, and when I try to show them a little gratitude, they toss my gifts back at me!”

“Why, sir,” murmured Parson Sampson, eyeing the two morocco boxes with covetous interest, “these must be worth a fortune! Look at those golden trinkets resting on their satin cushions!”

“They cost a fair sum,” replied the young man, “but I wouldn’t begrudge ten times that amount to those who’ve shown kindness.”

“No, indeed, sir,” Sampson chimed in quickly, never missing an opportunity to flatter his patron, “not if I know your honour!”

“The repeater watch,” the young man added, “they said was a bargain—worth a hundred pounds in Paris. And little Miss Hetty once told me she dreamed of owning a repeating timepiece.”

“Oh, what a treasure!” exclaimed the chaplain, eyes gleaming. “With its pearl-encrusted back and diamond-set crown—why, it could win any woman’s heart!”

At that, Mr. Warrington’s voice rose sharply. “I’ve a mind to throw it out to that apple-woman passing by!” he declared, his temper flaring.

Later, when Harry went into the city on business—through the Strand and past the Temple—his companion did not follow far. He turned aside, confessing a deep fear of Chancery Lane and its strange inhabitants. Left alone, Harry made his way to his broker, and together they walked to the Bank, where some minor transactions took place. After signing a few papers, Harry left with a bundle of crisp banknotes tucked securely in his pocket.

The broker then escorted him to one of London’s famed dining establishments, where they dined in silence. Afterwards, he showed Harry the Virginian walk on 'Change—the very path where Harry passed with shame, imagining how his father’s estate had slipped through his fingers. “What would my mother say,” he thought, “if she knew I was carrying off such a portion of our family’s inheritance in this endless gambler’s pocket? There they all are—Virginia merchants—talking about me: ‘That’s young Esmond of Castlewood, son of Madam Esmond. He’s been losing money at cards, selling stock after stock.’”

His spirits lifted only after he crossed under the traitors’ heads at Temple Bar and stepped clear of the City. From there, he walked home, pausing briefly to glance into St. James’s Street, though no one yet stirred—everyone still bound for dinner or later engagements.

Once inside, Harry unfolded his notes. He selected three, wrapped them in paper, sealed them carefully, and wrote within: “Much good may they do you. H. E. W.” He addressed the packet to Reverend Mr. Sampson and placed it on the mantelpiece, instructing his servants to deliver it upon the parson’s arrival.

Then, with his phaeton waiting at the door, he climbed in, intending to drive through the park. But rain began to fall, or the east wind grew sharp, and he changed course, turning down St. James’s Street instead. By three o’clock, he was back at White’s Club, where few had yet arrived—dinner hour still holding sway. Yet there, lounging over the *Public Advertiser*, was his cousin, Lord Castlewood, fresh from Court duties.

Lord Castlewood yawned over the newspaper. “Shall we play a game of piquet?” he asked.

Harry saw no reason to refuse. “Just for an hour,” said Castlewood. “I dine at Arlington Street at four.”

“Just for an hour,” agreed Harry. They called for cards.

“Or shall we move upstairs?” suggested Castlewood. “Away from the noise?”

“Certainly,” Harry replied.

By five o’clock, half a dozen gentlemen had come in after dinner—some playing cards, others sipping coffee, others talking. The ordinary diners still lingered at their tables. At White’s, men often sat until midnight.

One gentleman leaned toward the window. “Whose phaeton is that?” he asked.

“The Fortunate Youth’s,” came the reply.

“Not so fortunate lately,” said the first. “Luck’s been terrible these past nights. Lost thirteen hundred last night alone. Has Mr. Warrington been here today, John?”

“He’s here now, sir,” answered John. “In the little tea-room with Lord Castlewood since three. Playing piquet.”

“What fun for Castlewood,” muttered the first man, shrugging.

The second growled. “Curse the fellow! He doesn’t belong in this club. He never pays when he loses. Gentlemen shouldn’t play with him. Sir Miles Warrington told me the other day Castlewood owes him money on a bet—three years now.”

“Castlewood doesn’t lose when he plays alone,” said the first, grinning. “A big crowd unnerves him—that’s why he avoids the table.”

“Let’s go up and stop them,” growled the second.

“Why?” countered the first. “Better just watch from the window. Look—there’s the lamplighter climbing the ladder. Good sport. And that old fellow in the chair—have you ever seen such a face?”

“Who just left the house? It’s Fortunatus! He’s forgotten his phaeton’s been waiting. I’ll wager he’s lost to Castlewood.”

“Do you take me for a fool?” the first snapped. “Look at those horses—fine beasts. How fast he’s driving them!” They watched as Harry galloped away, scattering coachmen and chairmen alike. Soon, Lord Castlewood entered a chair and departed.

Harry drove home—just a short distance—but those poor horses had pounded the wet pavement for hours. At the door, Mr. Gumbo stood chatting with a country girl, who curtsied and hurried off. Gumbo was always surrounded by admirers.

“Gumbo,” Harry called from the carriage, “has Mr. Sampson been here?”

“No, sar,” Gumbo replied. “Mr. Sampson have not been here.”

“Go upstairs and fetch a letter addressed to Mr. Sampson,” Harry ordered.

“Addressed to Mr. Sampson? Oh yes, sir,” Gumbo said, unable to read.

“A sealed letter,” Harry corrected sharply. “On the mantelpiece, in the glass!”

Gumbo obeyed slowly. As soon as Harry had it, he turned his horses around and headed back toward St. James’s Street. From their window, the two men at White’s watched the Fortunate Youth return in seconds.

As Harry left the tea-room—having played piquet with Castlewood—he noticed several men had entered the gaming room. A bank was already set up. Some players wore their gaming jackets, kept at the club for regular sessions.

Harry went to the clerk’s desk, paid his account from the previous night, and sat down at the table, calling for fresh counters. This week had been particularly unlucky—and tonight offered no relief. He called for more counters, then more again. Pale and quiet, though polite when spoken to, he could not win.

Eventually, he rose. “Hang it, stay and mend your luck!” urged Lord March, sitting beside him with a mountain of green and white counters. “Take a hundred of mine and keep going!”

“I’ve had enough for tonight, my lord,” Harry said, rising and leaving. He ate a broiled bone in the coffee-room and returned to his lodgings around midnight.

After great misfortune, sleep often comes easily. But waking is another matter. Last night you proposed to Miss Brown. You quarreled with Captain Jones and pulled his nose. You played cards with Colonel Robinson and left behind a trail of IOUs. These memories, along with a pounding headache, return in the morning light. What a chasm lies between yesterday and today! It feels like years have passed. Can you leap back? Is yesterday merely a dream?
