You lie in bed. No dawn yet. Pull the nightcap over your eyes, the blankets over your nose. Sleep away yesterday. Psha! It was only a dream! No—no. Sleep refuses to come. The watchman cries out the hour—what hour? Beneath your pillow, the repeating watch sings six times in the dark, followed by a soft chime marking the half-hour.

Poor little Hester—so bright, so innocent. He had meant for her to have that watch. What will Maria say? (Oh, that old Maria—how tiresome she’s becoming.) What will Madam Esmond think when she learns he’s lost every shilling of his ready cash—of his entire inheritance? All his winnings, plus five thousand pounds, gone in three nights. Could Castlewood have cheated? No. My lord knows piquet better than Harry does, but he wouldn’t betray blood. No—Harry was glad his kinsman had gotten the money. Not another shilling would he risk. It was only when he tallied his losses and realized they’d wiped out everything he owned that he stepped away from the table.

But oh, cursed company! Extravagance! Folly! Humiliation! Remorse! “Will my mother forgive me?” he wondered. “Oh, that I were home—never having left it!”

Dawn finally seeped through the shutters. The housemaid lit the fire and opened the windows to admit the gray morning. Gumbo followed, warming the dressing gown and setting out shaving tools. Then came the hairdresser to powder and curl his master’s hair while Harry read his letters. Finally, Parson Sampson arrived—eager, smiling, eager to serve his patron. He had intended to return the day before, but friends detained him at St. Alban’s, and they made a night of it.

“Oh, Parson!” groaned Harry. “It was the worst night you’ve ever known! Look here!”

The chaplain glanced at the broken envelope. “'Much good may it do you,'” he read aloud.

“Look outside!” Harry snapped. “It was addressed to you.”

Sampson’s face drained of colour. “Has someone opened it?” he asked, alarmed.

“Someone has,” Harry said. “I opened it, Sampson. If you’d come yesterday afternoon, you’d have found it full of banknotes. As it is, I dropped every last one at the infernal macco-table last night.”

“All?” Sampson whispered.

“Yes, all—every penny I brought from the city, every shilling I possessed. In the afternoon, I played piquet with my cousin—well, a gentleman at White’s—and he relieved me of all I had. Remembering there might still be money here—if you hadn’t taken it—I came home, fetched it, and left it at the table with every shilling I own. And—great heavens, Sampson—what’s wrong?”

“It’s my luck,” the chaplain cried, breaking into tears. “My usual luck!”

“You’re not sobbing like a child over the loss of a couple hundred pounds?” Harry roared, furious. “Leave the room, Gumbo! Confound you—why do you always stick your woolly head in that door?”

“Someone below wants to see master with a bill,” Gumbo said.

“Tell him to go to Jericho!” Harry bellowed. “I’m not at home! Let me see no one!”

A murmur, a scuffle—then silence. Harry’s anger only intensified. He turned on Sampson, who sat with his head buried in his chest.

“Perhaps you should take a bumper of brandy to steady yourself?” he said, voice laced with sarcasm. “Hang it, don’t snivel like a woman!”

“Oh, it’s not me!” Sampson insisted, lifting his head. “I’m used to it.”

“Not you? Then who?” Harry demanded.

“Myself—because someone else is hurt, and through my fault!” the chaplain said, regaining strength. “I’ve lived in London for years with a bootmaker—a decent man. A few days ago, trusting a friend who promised a loan, I borrowed sixty pounds from him—money he needed to pay his own bills. I can’t repay it. His goods will be seized. His wife and children—poor souls—will be cast out. This honest family will be ruined because of me. But as you say, Mr. Warrington, I shouldn’t snivel. I’ll remember your kindness—and bid you farewell.”

Taking his wide-brimmed hat, the chaplain walked out.

Harry burst into a curse and a bitter laugh. He was furious—furious at himself, at fate, at everyone. He didn’t know what he said. Sampson heard the laughter, then Harry’s voice from the stairs: “Sampson! Sampson! Hang you—come back! It’s a mistake! I beg your pardon!”

But the chaplain was too wounded to return. Harry heard the street door slam. It echoed in his own heart. He entered his room and collapsed into a luxurious chair. He was the Prodigal Son, among the swine—his guilt tripping him, wallowing over him. Gambling, extravagance, debauchery, reckless companions, dangerous women—they surged forward, trampling the fallen youth.

Yet the Prodigal was not entirely defeated. With a sudden surge of defiance, he shoved the demons aside, kicked away his shameful memories, and grabbed a large glass of brandy—just as he had recommended to the humiliated parson. Throwing off his fine damask robe, he rang for Gumbo.

“Not that!” he roared as Gumbo presented a green coat with gold buttons and cord. “A plain suit—the plainer the better! Bring the black clothes!”

Gumbo returned with the mourning coat Harry had worn months before.

Then Harry gathered:
1. His new gold watch;
2. The repeater—bought for Hetty—into his other fob;
3. The necklace meant for Theo;
4. Half a dozen rings—except his grandfather’s seal ring, which he kissed and placed on the pincushion;
5. Three gold snuffboxes;
6. His purse—knitted by his mother—containing three shillings, sixpence, and a silver coin from Virginia.

He put on his hat and stepped out.

At the landing, Mr. Ruff, his landlord, bowed low and handed him a long strip of paper. “Much obliged if Mr. Warrington will settle. Mrs. Ruff has a large account to settle today.” Mrs. Ruff was a milliner. Mr. Ruff was a senior waiter at White’s, serving under Mr. Mackreth.

The sight of the landlord did nothing to improve Harry’s mood.

“Perhaps your honour will settle the account?” Ruff asked.

“Of course I will,” Harry said, glowering down from the stair.

“Now, perhaps?”

“No, sir! I will not settle it now!” Harry snapped, pushing forward.

“I’m very much in need of money, sir,” Ruff pleaded. “Mrs. Ruff is—”

“Hang you! Get out of my way!” Harry roared, shoving Ruff backward, nearly sending him tumbling down the hall. He stomped down the stairs and stepped into Bond Street.

The Guards were drilling at the King’s Mews near Charing Cross. Their drums and fifes echoed as Harry passed. He looked in and saw them in formation. “I can shoulder a musket,” he thought grimly, “at least.”

Crossing St. Martin’s Lane—where he handled some business—he reached Long Acre and the bootmaker’s house where Sampson lodged. The landlady said the chaplain wasn’t home but would return by one. Since she knew Harry, she let him into the apartment. He sat down and, lacking anything better to do, picked up an unfinished sermon—on the Prodigal Son. He didn’t read it closely.

Soon, he heard the landlady’s shrill voice chasing someone up the stairs. Sampson burst in, followed by the weeping woman.

At the sight of Harry, Sampson froze. The landlady stopped mid-scream. “There’s only thirteen pounds in the house, and he’ll be here at one!” she shrieked.

“Hush, hush!” the chaplain gasped, pointing to Harry. “Don’t you see Mr. Warrington? I have urgent business with him. It will be settled—trust me!”

He coaxed the woman out, the children clinging to her coat.

“Sampson,” Harry said, rising, “I’ve come to apologize. What I said earlier was cruel, unjust—unlike a gentleman.”

“Not a word more, sir,” Sampson replied, coldly bowing, barely touching the hand Harry offered.

“I see you’re still angry,” Harry continued.

“An apology is an apology,” Sampson said. “A man of my station asks for no more from one of yours. You likely didn’t mean to wound me. And if you did—well, you’re not the only one in the family who has.” He gazed around the room, filled with sorrow. “I wish I’d never known the name Esmond or Castlewood—or that place pictured over my fireplace, where I’ve buried myself these many years. Your cousin took a fancy to me, promised to make my fortune, kept me as his dependant—until fortune passed me by. Now he refuses me my due.”

“What do you mean, your due?” Harry asked.

“Three years’ salary owed me as chaplain of Castlewood,” Sampson said. “When I couldn’t get help from you, I went to his lordship this morning. I fell on my knees and begged. He gave me civil words—though none of the money. Only five guineas, which I accepted. But five guineas among so many needs! Oh, those poor children!”

“Lord Castlewood said he had no money?” Harry exclaimed.

“He won eleven hundred pounds from me yesterday at piquet,” Harry said. “I paid him from this very pocketbook.”

“I dare say, sir,” Sampson replied, “one can’t trust a word his lordship says. But I’m thinking of execution here—ruin tomorrow!”

“That needn’t happen,” Harry said. “Here are eighty guineas, Sampson. That’s all I have. I wish I could give more—as I promised. But you didn’t come at the right time. I’m penniless until my remittances arrive from Virginia.”

Sampson stared, stunned, then turned pale. He dropped to his knees, clutching Harry’s hand.

“Great powers, sir!” he cried. “Are you an angel sent by Heaven? You scorned my tears this morning. I cannot help them now. They pour forth from a grateful heart. Even a stone would weep before such kindness! May Heaven bless you forever! May my prayers rise for you, my best benefactor! May—”

“Nay, nay!” Harry said, embarrassed. “Get up, friend—get up, Sampson!”

“I am glad to have helped you,” Harry said, feeling oddly pleased. “There—don’t kneel to me!”

“To Heaven who sent you!” the chaplain cried. “Mrs. Weston! Mrs. Weston!”

“What is it, sir?” the landlady asked instantly—she’d been listening at the door.

“We are saved!” Sampson shouted. “We are saved! Kneel, woman—kneel and thank our benefactor! Children, raise your voices and bless him!”

A chorus of sobs erupted. The chaplain led the prayer. Harry stood in the middle, awkward but delighted. They would worship him, no matter what. One child, confused, remained standing. Her mother slapped her cheek. “Drat it, Jane! Kneel down and bless the gentleman, I tell you!”

We leave them in their heartfelt gratitude. Harry walked away from Long Acre, almost forgetting the sorrows of the past days, tingling with the warmth of having done something truly good.

The young woman Gumbo had been speaking with that evening—the one he met when Harry returned from White’s—was Mrs. Molly, maid to the ladies at Oakhurst. Wherever Gumbo went, he left admirers in his wake. We mentioned it was a Wednesday evening when he and Mrs. Molly took a walk. They were exchanging tender farewells when Harry arrived, ending their twilight whispers.

We have all, no doubt, seen enough of the world to know that human nature wears many faces—some noble, some absurd, some deeply sincere, and others merely performative. Yet there is one sort of person we often see mocked in novels and plays—the religious hypocrite: the man who preaches virtue with fervor but lives without conviction, whose sermons ring hollow even as he delivers them. Such figures are common enough in fiction, but I must confess I have met very few in real life. For though men may not be wholly devoted to their faith, they are rarely so utterly insincere as to pretend belief they do not possess.

Observe, for instance, the Sunday evening procession toward church—the clatter of hobnailed boots, the rustle of ribbons worn by maids, the orderly ranks of schoolboys, the well-dressed young ladies and matrons marching with polished prayer books, the chapel bell chiming gently in the distance. There, beneath the gaslight near Ebenezer’s door, a congregation gathers—umbrellas, bonnets, pattens—all assembled like a quiet army of piety. But what goes on within? The maid thinks of her sweetheart; the grocer calculates how to buy sugar and whether the bank will accept more of his paper; the head boy reviews Latin verses for Monday; the young rascal dreams of pie after service; the clerk leading the psalm worries about his daughter’s illness, half-mumbling the words without meaning them. And when the parson bows his head, perhaps he’s thinking only of the bill due tomorrow.

These people are not saints. They are of this world—worldly, distracted, burdened with daily cares. But they are not hypocrites. Their religion is stored away, like medicine in a drawer—used when needed, trusted when ill. A woman might say to her neighbor, “My dear, you’ve been seized with spasms? These drops will cure you!” Or to a man overindulging, “You’ve taken too much wine? This pill will save you.” And so it was with spiritual matters—women especially were eager dispensers of both remedies and counsel. A hundred years ago, every country lady had her still-room, her medicine chest, her powders and potions for every ailment in the village. My Lady Warrington, for example, managed not only the health of her tenants but their souls as well. She oversaw the servants’ moral welfare with the same care she gave their digestion. Whether her remedies worked—well, Heaven knows—but she administered them with full conviction, and those around her accepted them willingly.

She believed herself among the most virtuous, self-denying, wise, and learned women alive—and by constantly repeating this belief to others, she persuaded many to agree. At Sir Miles’s dinner table, where silver gleamed and liveried footmen stood at attention, it took a sharp eye to notice the smallness of the beer served from the splendid tankard or the single joint of mutton on the grand dish. When Sir Miles raised his glass to the King, he drank as if the wine were ambrosia. He asked Harry Warrington if Virginia had such port, then declared it nothing compared to what he’d taste in Norfolk. His praise was so vivid that Harry almost believed it himself, winking into his own glass, trying to catch the richness his uncle seemed to savor.

In this household, as in many families of the time, there were two ideal daughters. One, Flora, was the beauty—fair, graceful, admired by all. The other, Dora, was the genius, the angel—so described by Lady Warrington, who proudly told Harry that Flora was engaged to Tom Claypool, the son of a baronet in Norfolk. But Dora, the “angel,” was determined to reform Harry’s character. She sang to him at the harpsichord—though, Harry thought, rather off-key for an angel—and offered advice, instruction, and conversation—so much of it, indeed, that Harry longed instead for the company of little cousin Miles, who reminded him of Fanny Mountain back home.

After dinner, Miles usually retreated to his nursery. Flora would go to her duties. Mamma wrote letters or tended to the poor. Papa dozed in his chair. And Dora remained—her duty being to guide her young cousin. The quiet dignity of the house pleased Harry. It offered a refuge from the noise and excess of his usual life. No welcome could have been warmer. The doors were always open. If Flora was absent, Dora was ready. Soon, Harry and Miles had raced horses in the park, and Harry, generous by nature, began planning to buy his cousin a better mount than the one he rode—until events intervened that shattered his fortune.

Though Sir Miles imagined Virginia to be an island, the ladies were well-informed. They eagerly questioned Harry about his homeland. He, in turn, was glad to talk. He described his estate—its rivers, forests, fields, its tobacco ships sailing from wharves along the Potomac and James Rivers. He had once practiced surveying with a friend, and now drew a map of his county, marking towns that were really little more than log cabins—though he exaggerated their size and elegance, proud to represent his land honorably. As he pointed out hills and rivers, dressed in velvet and silver lace, he looked like a prince showing his realm. And sometimes, he almost felt like one.

Not only Dora listened—he saw Flora leaning forward, her eyes bright with interest. How could Tom Claypool, with his loud voice and five thousand acres, compare to this American gentleman, speaking of March, Chesterfield, Selwyn, Bolingbroke, and the whole glittering world of London fashion? Even Dora, the angel, began to lose her composure, teasing Flora for flirting. Claypool sat silent before Harry, whose ruffles and laces made him seem more brilliant than any English heir.

Lady Warrington grew more fond of Harry each day. She worried about the spiritual state of the Indians and enslaved people in Virginia. What could she do to help Madam Esmond, whom she called “a precious woman,” in her charitable work? Her butler and housekeeper were devout, and they adored Gumbo, the young black servant, for his sweet singing and pious ways.

“Oh, Harry, Harry!” she would sigh. “You’ve been such a wild boy! Why didn’t you come to us sooner? You’ve wasted your youth among fools and wastrels. But it’s not too late. We’ll reclaim you, dear Harry! Won’t we, Sir Miles? Won’t we, Dora? Won’t we, Flora?” The three lifted their eyes to the ceiling in solemn agreement. They would rescue the prodigal. But which of them would succeed?

Dora watched Flora. Mamma, when alone with Harry, spoke more tenderly, more seriously. She wanted to be a mother to him in the absence of his own admirable parent. She gave him a hymn book, kissed his forehead, and expressed pure love, tenderness, and religious concern for her wayward yet amiable nephew.

Meanwhile, Sir Miles kept silent about his affairs—affairs that had spiraled into ruin. Fortune, who had smiled upon him for weeks, abandoned him in a matter of days. Was Lord Castlewood, his kinsman, unfair? We won’t accuse him of dishonesty. But he had won every shilling Harry possessed—and would have taken his future inheritance, too, had Harry not thrown up his hands in defeat.

Remembering the last sum he’d set aside for poor Sampson, Harry risked it at the gaming table. But that, too, was lost. Fortune fled, leaving him nearly destitute.

Yet youth and generosity shielded him from despair. He could sell his horses, carriages, reduce his staff. Where could he turn for money? His Aunt Bernstein? His kinsman who had won so much from him? Or his kind Uncle Warrington and Aunt Warrington, who professed such love and virtue?

He would ask them later. But first, Sampson’s story of his landlord’s distress moved him. To raise funds quickly, Harry sold all his trinkets to a pawnbroker in St. Martin’s Lane.

That broker was connected to Mr. Sparks of Tavistock Street—the very man from whom Harry had once taken the trinkets meant for his friends at Oakhurst. Sparks visited his brother-tradesman soon after Harry’s sale. Recognizing the diamond-handled repeater, he exploded into furious remarks—words best left unsaid, given my reputation for plain speech.

A man who knows a pawnbroker has bailiffs among his acquaintances. And bailiffs have men who, under law, treat noblemen and dandies alike. The same officers who had arrested Lady Maria at Tunbridge now turned their attention to her cousin.

They learned from chattering Gumbo that Harry was at Sir Miles’s house in Hill Street. While Gumbo flirted with Mrs. Lambert’s maid next door, Mr. Costigan and his assistant waited in the shadows.

Never had Uncle Miles been more cordial. Never had Aunt Warrington been more gracious. Flora looked unusually radiant. Dora was exceptionally kind. At parting, Lady Warrington gave Harry both hands and called down blessings from above.

Papa, in his jovial mood, said: “Hang it, nephew! When I was your age, I’d have kissed two fine girls like Do and Flo long ago—even if they were my own flesh and blood! Don’t tell me! I should, my Lady Warrington! Odds-fish! ‘Tis the boy blushes, not the girls! He, he!”

“Papa!” cried the virgins.

“Sir Miles!” said the august mother at once.

“There, there!” said papa. “A kiss won’t hurt, nor tell tales. Will it, nephew Harry?”

And so, amid these brief exchanges, the harmless gesture occurred—Harry touched the cheeks of both cousins, blushing as he did.

Descending the stairs with his uncle, Lady Warrington delivered a final speech: “What noble qualities your cousin possesses! What wisdom mixed with simplicity, what fine manners—though I care little for worldly elegance. How terrible it would be to lose such a soul! We must save him, my darlings. We must take him from those wicked companions, those dreadful Castlewoods—not that I mean to speak ill of neighbors. But I shall pray, I shall hope, that he may be rescued from his evil ways!”

She gazed upward again, resolute. The girls watched the door through which Harry had just vanished.

His uncle walked with him to the gate. “God bless you, my boy!” he said warmly, pressing Harry’s hand and repeating his blessing.

As the door closed, the hall light illuminated Harry’s face. Two men stepped forward from across the street. One pulled a strip of paper from his pocket, placed a hand on Harry’s shoulder, and declared him prisoner.

A hackney coach waited. Poor Harry was led away—sleeping that night in Chancery Lane.

To think that a Virginian prince should be slapped by a ragged bailiff’s follower—that Madam Esmond’s son should end up in a spunging-house in Cursitor Street! I do not envy our young prodigal his rest that night.

Let us strike while he is down, my dear friends. Let us imagine the sting of remorse keeping him awake on his grim pillow, the drunken laughter of hardened inmates echoing from the room beside him, the shame, the rage, the humiliation. Let us feel no pity—for surely, you, my honest young gentlemen, have never indulged in extravagance, folly, or the bitter reckoning of regret.

Harry Warrington sat in the dim, musty room of the lock-up house, his spirits a tumult of shame, anger, and unease. The reality of being arrested—of being locked away like a common debtor—struck him with sudden force. He had always moved through life as if above such indignities, a young man of fortune, charm, and consequence. Now he was confined, not by any crime, but by debt—a fate that seemed absurd to him, yet one he could not deny.

He felt genuine remorse for his reckless spending, his gambling habits, his indulgence in pleasures without thought of consequences. Yet he also resented the humiliation of it all. To be dragged from his chambers, surrounded by bailiffs and clerks, while the world looked on—this was not how a gentleman should live or fall. But Harry was certain this would be brief. Twenty friends stood ready to help him: Mr. Draper, the shrewd businessman who had always been attentive; his uncle, the Baronet, who had offered him a home and treated him like a son; his cousin Castlewood, who had won vast sums from him at cards; the noble gentlemen at White’s Club; even his Aunt Bernstein, whose affection he sometimes doubted but always cherished.

Any one of them would step forward, though perhaps with a scolding for his folly. The key, however, was discretion. Mr. Warrington cared deeply about appearances. He did not want the public to know that a man of his standing had been reduced to this. As if the world didn’t already know everything it wished to learn! As if the hole in his stocking, visible now beneath his boot, or the dinner he would eat later, could remain hidden from some curious observer. The truth was, secrets were fragile things. The world prided itself on knowing what it wanted to know—and then promptly forgot it.

People took their reputations too seriously, he mused. A man falls into prison? He thinks himself ruined. Bankrupt? He believes society will cast him out. Exposed in a bargain gone wrong? He imagines he’ll be punished. But no—society yawns. It talks, dines, laughs, dances, as if nothing had happened. If you tumble, brush off the dirt, smile, and reappear—no one notices. You are not the center of the universe, mi fili. And yet here he was, fuming as if every soul in London had felt the weight of that hand laid upon his shoulder.

“A fine sensation my arrest must have caused at the club,” he muttered. “Selwyn will no doubt be making jokes about it. March will tremble over our bet—I wonder if I’ll ever be able to pay him when I lose. They’ll be cheering at the Savage, calling me ‘the Savage’ now that I’m behind bars. How can I face anyone again?”

Yet, despite his pride and distress, Harry displayed a strange mix of cunning and simplicity. He decided not to turn immediately to family or friends. Instead, he chose Sampson—the chaplain, a man who had once found himself in similar straits and might know how to navigate the maze of legal troubles.

As dawn broke, weak and grey, Harry sent a message to Sampson in Long Acre, pleading for advice and comfort. The hours stretched slowly. The light crept into the cell-like room, the silence broken only by the occasional shuffle of feet from other inmates. When breakfast arrived, Harry ordered it eaten in silence, refusing to dine at Mrs. Bailiff’s table with the others. “I’ll be gone before dinner,” he declared to the attendant, who likely thought this a familiar boast from another young gentleman who believed escape was just around the corner.

“Very well,” the man replied, “but if you stay, there’s good beef and carrots at two o’clock.” And with that, he left Harry alone with his thoughts.

But no Sampson came. Not at ten, nor eleven, nor noon. Instead, just after midday, Gumbo burst in—his master’s servant—carrying a portmanteau and weeping uncontrollably. He flung himself at Harry’s feet, sobbing, swearing eternal loyalty, promising to sell himself into slavery again if it meant freeing his beloved master.

Harry, touched by the display, gently lifted him up. “All you need do is get me dressed and keep your mouth shut. Not a word to anyone, understand?”

“Oh no, sir, never to nobody!” Gumbo vowed, eyes wide and solemn.

And so he began dressing his master—powdering his hair, brushing his coat, arranging his cravat—until Harry looked every inch the gentleman, polished and poised as if preparing for a visit to St. James’s Palace.

Gumbo served his master with devotion, but there were limits to what even love could achieve. He could not undo what had been done. He could not stop himself from talking—especially when grief and excitement stirred his tongue. For though he swore secrecy, Gumbo had already told the tale to half of London.

He had carried the news to Colonel Lambert’s and Lord Wrotham’s servants. He’d shared it at the footman’s club, where noblemen’s retainers gathered. He’d drunk ale with Sir Miles Warrington’s butler, embellishing the story with each retelling. Then he’d visited Madame Bernstein’s household, and finally Lord Castlewood’s, spreading the news like wildfire.

So when Gumbo stood before Harry, hand on heart, tears streaming, and promised never to speak of it, the reader may judge how credible that oath truly was.

At last, late in the afternoon, a letter arrived—not from Sampson, but from him. Sealed with wet wax, the ink still fresh, it read:

> “Oh, sir, dear sir, I have done all a man can do for his patron! You did not know what you were asking of me. Else, why would I not share your prison, if I am to go to one? Indeed, I am in one myself—three doors down, at Naboth’s.
>
> As I hurried to you, knowing the danger, I was seized by two men with a writ against me. They’ve locked me up close by—so near, we could almost hear each other across the garden walls.
>
> I had much to say about your affairs, which I cannot write down. May they mend! May my cursed fortunes improve!
>
> Your afflicted Chaplain-in-Ordinary,

Thus, Sampson refused to speak further. But now, let us reveal what he dared not write.

Gumbo had not reached Long Acre, so Sampson remained unaware of the full extent of Harry’s plight until he received the message from Chancery Lane. Still grateful for the kindness Harry had shown him—having recently helped him financially—Sampson rushed to Lord Castlewood’s house, hoping to move his noble cousin to mercy.

He spoke passionately, with real emotion, of Harry’s misfortune, of his generosity, of his downfall. But Lord Castlewood cut him short.

“Did I not tell you two days ago,” he said sharply, “that I am as poor as a beggar? Has anyone left me a fortune since? The money I won from him was spent long ago. I cannot help him—and indeed, I had written this morning asking *him* for aid.”

A letter to this effect had already reached Harry’s lodgings via the penny post.

“I must find him money,” Sampson insisted. “I know he had little left after helping me. I’ll pawn my cassock, my bands—anything!”

“Go ahead,” said Castlewood, unimpressed. “Your enthusiasm is admirable. But I have no use for it.” And with that, he returned to his reading, leaving the chaplain crushed.

Meanwhile, Lady Maria, hearing of Sampson’s visit, confronted him as he left her brother’s house. Her face showed deep concern.

“What has happened to Mr. Warrington?” she asked.

“You know?” Sampson replied.

“I’ve been in agony since Gumbo brought the news last night,” she said. “We heard it at the opera—from Lady Yarmouth’s box. My lord, I, and Lady Castlewood.”

“And my lord knew?” Sampson asked.

“Benson told us when we returned from the playhouse,” she confirmed.

The chaplain exploded. “This is outrageous!” he exclaimed. He recounted his failed appeal to Castlewood—the refusal, the hypocrisy, the cruelty of winning from Harry and then turning his back when he was in need.

Lady Maria, usually reserved, erupted in a torrent of words. She spoke bitterly of her family, of their greed, their lack of honor, their betrayal of kinship. With tears and fury, she accused her brother of selfishness, of using Harry as a pawn. She called him cowardly, dishonorable, unworthy of respect.

She stormed toward Castlewood’s library door, shrieking, until the terrified chaplain fled outside.

Castlewood looked up, surprised, and launched a sharp curse at her.

But Maria was fearless now. “You sit with him at cards, take his last shilling, and refuse to give him a penny when he’s penniless!” she shouted.

“So the chaplain has been gossiping?” Castlewood snapped.

“Dismiss him! Pay him and send him away—he’ll be glad enough to leave!”

“I keep him for when one of my sisters needs marrying,” Castlewood growled.

“What kind of women are we, when our brothers are like this?” Maria demanded.

“Effectivement,” Castlewood shrugged.

“We are bad enough—but what are *you*? No courage, no honor, no decency. Since your equals won’t play with you, you take a poor lad from Virginia—your own cousin—and fleece him! It’s a disgrace!”

“We all play our own games,” Castlewood retorted. “Haven’t you played yours, Maria? Are you suddenly squeamish about the boy? Has he rejected you? Or have you found a better match?”

“I’d be a fool to expect you to act like an honest man,” Maria said coldly. “You wouldn’t help a relative in distress. You’d fleece him.”

“Fleece him? Nonsense. Look at his behavior—how could he avoid this end? If I hadn’t taken his money, someone else would. I didn’t begrudge you your schemes. Why fly into a rage because I took what he was offering freely?”

“You think this money belongs to you? It’s not yours to spend. In three months, every shilling would’ve vanished into White’s gaming tables. Better it pays your debts.”

“My good brother might have given more than kind words to the boy from whom he just took hundreds,” Maria interjected.

“Great heavens, Maria! Don’t you see this could be a chance for a clever woman?” Castlewood said, smirking. “Suppose I know of a situation—another family, another young man. A green lad comes to town, a country cousin. An elderly female relative, lonely and ambitious, extracts a marriage promise from him. He doesn’t want it. He’ll claim his mother refuses. He’ll lie. He’ll break it.”

“My lord, are you insulting me as well as your cousin?”

“Not at all. I said nothing about cheating. I simply tell a story. The aunt gets a promise—then he breaks it. That’s what happens. Like Tunbridge—your Aunt Bernstein handled it perfectly. She got the letters, hid them, and said nothing. Wise woman. You still pine for your Cherokee. Soit. A woman knows the value of a husband. What’s the loss of two or three hundred pounds?”

“Not more than three hundred?” Maria asked.

“Eh? Never mind a hundred or two. It’s a bagatelle. You’re playing for a principality. You want your kingdom in Virginia. And this little misfortune? It may be great luck for you.”

“I don’t understand.”

“C’est possible. But sit down—I’ll explain.” And so, the furious lioness collapsed into a gentle lamb at her brother’s feet.

Madame de Bernstein, upon hearing the news from Gumbo, was disturbed. She had not slept, consumed by worry. Was Harry in serious trouble? How much would it cost to free him? Had he spent all his own funds?

She liked his extravagance. He was the only person in years who had drawn her affection. She sent a messenger to Mr. Draper, her man of business, ordering him to investigate Harry’s debts and report immediately.

Draper discovered the claims: Mr. Sparks, the jeweller, for unpaid goods; the landlord in Bond Street, for board and lodging. These were manageable. He could settle them at once—with her guarantee.

“There’s no difficulty in raising a thousand pounds more or less for a gentleman of Mr. Warrington’s rank,” she said.

Draper suggested settling the matter quickly, especially the jeweller’s account—Harry had taken items on credit and pledged them to a pawnbroker. If made public, it would look dishonorable.

But the Baroness had a different idea. “I think,” she said, “my young gentleman has sown enough wild oats. When he comes out, I want him clean—no debts, no liabilities.”

“No gentleman ever tells all his debts,” Draper reminded her.

“True,” she replied. “But I want him free.”

And so, while Harry waited in silence, the web of influence, money, and family politics tightened around him—each player acting not from duty, but from self-interest, ambition, or pity. The chains of debt bound him, but the greater chains were those of expectation, blood, and social order.

Mr. Gumbo’s kindness had softened the harsh edge of Harry Warrington’s pride, and his second night in the spunging-house passed with a measure of comfort he had not known before. At least one person—his loyal servant—stood by him, offering quiet companionship and practical care. Yet though this small act of devotion eased his heart somewhat, it did little to mend his bitterness toward the world at large. To Harry, England was a land of coldness and self-interest. His pious Aunt Warrington, his noble friend March, even his cynical cousin Castlewood—all had promised aid, only to fail him when he needed them most. He would not beg from any of them again, not even if it meant twenty years in prison. What fools he had been to trust their words, to believe their friendship! There was no true loyalty here, only calculation and indifference. He would leave this place. He would go to Germany and fight under the king’s banner, or return to Virginia and vanish into the forests, hunting all day, managing his mother’s lands, becoming her steward. He might marry Polly Broadbent or Fanny Mountain—any woman who offered honest affection—and live as a simple farmer. Anything, anything but remain among these English gentlemen whose fine manners hid nothing but emptiness.

With that resolve burning within him, Harry rose early the next morning, his face calm, his spirit still aflame. Gumbo was already waiting outside his chamber, having come from Bond Street with letters. “I wanted to bring more clothes,” the faithful man said, “but Mr. Ruff, the landlord, wouldn’t let me bring anything else.”

Harry glanced at the letters without much interest. One by one he opened them—each a bill, demanding payment. Then came the fourth: a letter from the landlord, cold and firm. He would allow no more of Mr. Warrington’s belongings to leave the house. Unless the debt was paid, he would sell every item and claim the money for himself. And Gumbo, too, must find another place to sleep.

The black man sighed. “I found shelter with friends at Lord Wrotham’s house,” he said quietly. “Colonel Lambert’s people, sir.”

He looked intently at Harry. “And Miss Hetty—she fainted when she heard you were taken in. Mr. Lambert, he’s a good man. This morning he told me, ‘Gumbo, tell your master if he needs me, send word, and I’ll come.’”

At the mention of Hetty, something stirred in Harry’s heart. He didn’t believe the story about her fainting—he was used to Gumbo’s dramatic flair—but the thought that she had suffered because of him touched him deeply. Yet when Gumbo spoke of Colonel Lambert, a shadow fell across Harry’s face.

“Send to Lambert?” he muttered, grinding his teeth. “The man who insulted me, who threw my gifts back in my face? Even if I were starving, I’d rather die than ask him for a crust!”

Soon after, dressed in his finest gown, Harry called for breakfast and sent Gumbo with a brief note to Mr. Draper in the Temple, summoning him immediately. The tone of the message was stiff, almost imperious—so much so that when Draper read it, he felt affronted. “It’s as if he’s writing to one of his slaves,” he grumbled, “not to a freeborn English gentleman.” He nearly refused to go. “What right has a man in a debtor’s prison to give himself such airs? Hang him!” But he went anyway.

When Draper arrived, he found Harry seated on his bed like a prince in exile, wrapped in a brocade dressing gown, his hair neatly arranged. He motioned Gumbo to fetch a chair.

“Excuse me, madam,” Draper said, turning to Madame de Bernstein, who had been listening from the doorway, “but such haughtiness—I’m not accustomed to it!”

“Sit down, please, Mr. Draper,” she replied with a smile. “And carry on with your report.” She found his indignation amusing. She liked her nephew precisely because he remained proud even in ruin.

The plan for the meeting had been discussed between her and Draper the previous day. Draper was competent—usually effective in handling difficult clients. But today, his own irritation clouded his judgment. He could not understand the young man before him, nor the strange mixture of arrogance and vulnerability that defined him.

Perhaps, dear reader, you are one of those gentle souls who have dealt with men of lower station. Have you not noticed how easily they are offended—how a glance, a tone, a silence can wound them, though they themselves may not know why? A man who is not a gentleman often offends without meaning to. You disapprove, perhaps, and he feels it instantly. He sees scorn where there is none, and responds with fury. You speak plainly, and he thinks you mock. You are indifferent, and he hates you all the more—for you do not care enough to hurt him.

“Gumbo, a chair for Mr. Draper,” Harry commanded, folding his robe tightly around his legs. “Sit down and let us talk business. Thank you for coming so promptly. Did you hear about this unfortunate turn?”

Draper nodded. “Bad news travels fast, sir. I was eager to offer my services as soon as I heard.”

“I’ve been imprudent,” Harry admitted. “I lived beyond my means. I gambled with men wealthier than myself, and a run of bad luck left me with debts totaling five hundred pounds.”

“Five hundred pounds now in the office,” Draper confirmed.

“I thought I could settle it yesterday by appealing to a few friends,” Harry continued. “But I was mistaken. I need your help to raise the funds as quickly as possible.”

Draper frowned. “Hm.”

“You say it can be done?” Harry pressed.

“It can be done,” Draper replied slowly. “But it will take time. To access your estate in England, we must wait for your father’s death to be proven, the trustees released—none of which can happen until we hear from Lady Esmond Warrington in Virginia. That may take six months.”

“And my Bristol agent?”

“He’s authorized to pay only two hundred pounds a year.”

“So I have no choice but to turn to my aunt, Madame de Bernstein?”

“She will do anything for you,” Draper said. “She has told me so repeatedly. If she gives her word, you can walk out of here today.”

“Then go to her for me, Mr. Draper,” Harry said. “I didn’t wish to burden my family, but I cannot endure this imprisonment any longer. Tell her where I am, what has happened. Disguise nothing. And say that I trust her kindness to release me from this—this disgrace.”

His voice cracked slightly, and he rubbed his eyes.

“Sir,” Draper said, studying him closely, “I was with her yesterday. We discussed your situation—the entire matter. I won’t call it disgraceful, but it is certainly unfortunate.”

“Does she know everything?” Harry asked sharply.

“Every detail,” Draper replied. “The pawned watches, the unpaid bills.”

Harry flushed crimson.

“It’s an unfortunate affair,” Draper continued. “Pawning items you never paid for—especially when it involves credit. It could lead to legal trouble. In court, barristers don’t care about rank. When they put a man on trial—”

“Good God, sir,” Harry interrupted, rising from the bed, “do you think a gentleman of my standing couldn’t take a watch on credit without intending to cheat?”

“Of course not,” Draper said, winking. “But the law doesn’t always see it that way.”

“That’s exactly what my aunt says—‘the most imprudent thing I ever heard of.’”

“Then you agree with her,” Harry said slowly, each word measured.

“I’m only doing my duty,” Draper said. “Like a doctor telling a patient he’s ill. I must warn you of the risks.”

“And yet you can’t help me pay the debt?” Harry demanded. “You’ve come only to tell me I may be accused of fraud?”

“Of obtaining goods under false pretenses? Yes, sir. I can’t help it. But I *can* help you avoid it—if you’re willing to accept certain conditions.”

Harry stared.

“There’s money in my pocket,” Draper said. “Not mine, but your aunt’s. She’s ready to pay the debt immediately—on one condition.”

“What is it?”

“She wants you to break off your engagement to Miss Maria Esmond.”

Harry’s face brightened.

“She believes the match will ruin you,” Draper continued. “She knows you gave your word, but she also knows the promise was made under duress. It was recovered—dropped at Tunbridge, as I understand.”

“Yes,” Harry said. “She still has it.”

“She does,” Draper confirmed. “And letters compromising her family were found as well. But you were away when they were discovered. No fault of yours.”

“And you want me to break off the marriage?”

“I want you to give me your word of honour,” Draper said, stepping forward. “Say you’ll withdraw. Say yes, and I’ll pay every shilling, take you out of here, and put you in a coach—either to your aunt’s or White’s Club—with two hundred pounds in your pocket. Say yes, and shake hands with me. Don’t waste your life behind bars!”

For a moment, Harry hesitated. The thought of freedom, of escape from this humiliation, was intoxicating. His feelings for Maria had long since faded. If his aunt could free him from this bond, how grateful he would be.

“Come, sir,” Draper urged, holding out his hand. “Don’t dither. If I’d married every woman I promised, I’d be like the Grand Turk or Captain Macheath!”

But Harry stepped back. He folded his robe tighter and turned away.

“Give me an hour,” he said. “I must think.”

Draper clenched his jaw. “Very well, sir. Very well.” He grabbed his hat, stormed out, muttering curses under his breath.

“Won’t take my hand, eh?” he growled as he descended the stairs. “Will tell me in an hour! I’ll show him what an hour is!”

Back in his chambers, Draper raged, berating his clerks, sending a message to the Baroness, then going through his usual routine—seeing clients, eating dinner—before finally making his way to Cursitor Street.

“The Fortunate Youth in his room?” he asked the bailiff’s assistant.

“Mr. Warrington is in his apartment,” the man replied, “but—”

And then he winked and touched his nose.

“But what?” Draper snapped.

“My name is Costigan,” the man said proudly. “My family is noble. My native city is Dublin, Mr. Six-and-eightpence!”

A strong smell of spirits filled the air.

“Confound you!” Draper roared. “Let me pass!”

“I can hear you perfectly,” the man retorted. “Except your h’s—you drop them like stones. And don’t call me names, or your fingers and my nose will become very familiar.”

Draper pushed past, but the bailiff blocked his path. “Walk in, sir!”

As he entered, a lady hurried down the stairs, her face covered by a capuchin and handkerchief. She gasped in alarm as Draper tried to follow.

“Keep your distance!” the bailiff shouted. “This way, madam!”

He slammed the door in Draper’s face.

That evening, at six o’clock, the old Baroness paced her drawing-room, her nerves frayed. She had delayed dinner, ignored her cook’s complaints, ordered extra dishes as if expecting guests. When a coach stopped at her door, she rushed to the window.

“Mr. Draper,” the servant announced.

He bowed deeply.

“Where is the boy?” she demanded. “I told you to bring him! How dare you come without him?”

“It is not my fault, madam,” Draper said. “Mr. Warrington refuses to come.”

And he recounted the interview—every word, every gesture, every refusal.

In a fit of anger, Mr. Draper turned away from his morning meeting with Harry Warrington, convinced the young man had spoken behind him. Indeed, Harry had risen from his bed and begun to call after him—half an exclamation escaping his lips—but pride held him back. The lawyer, too, was offended, and chose not to pause. It stung Harry’s dignity to be forced into submission by mere want of money. “An hour later will do just as well,” he muttered, sinking back onto the mattress with a sullen sigh.

No, he did not care for Maria Esmond. Not truly. He was ashamed of how easily he had been drawn into that engagement—a trap laid by a woman far more cunning than he. She had played upon his youthful passion, taken unfair advantage, just as her brother had once outmaneuvered him at games. They were kin, blood of his blood—and yet they had used him. Together, they had made a fool of him, exploiting his trust for their own ends.

He thought now of how they had betrayed the sanctity of hospitality—how they had turned the guest who came in faith into a prisoner within their walls. His heart ached. His head fell against the pillow, and bitter tears traced paths through the grime on his face. “Had they come to Virginia,” he whispered, “I would have welcomed them differently.”

His thoughts were shattered by the sudden appearance of Gumbo, grinning broadly at the door. “A lady has come to see Master Harry,” he announced.

And then she entered—Maria Esmond, wrapped in her dark capuchin cloak, her face pale beneath its folds. Harry sat up abruptly, his eyes wide and hollow. Before he could speak, she rushed forward, arms outstretched, and clutched him around the neck with genuine emotion. Tears streamed down her cheeks as she pressed her face against his, kissed his cheek, and sobbed into his shoulder. “Oh, my Harry! Could I ever have dreamed I’d find you here?”

He recoiled slightly, startled by her presence, but she knelt beside the bed, seizing his feverish hand and pressing her forehead to his knee. There was real affection in her—real sorrow for the wretched place where she found him, the broken man before her. Her heart swelled with pity.

“I—I thought none of you would come,” Harry said, voice thick with grief.

She answered not with words, but with more tears, more kisses, more fervent embraces. Her hands clasped his tightly, as if afraid he might vanish. “My dear, my dear!” she wept. “I cannot bear to think of you suffering like this!”

Though hardened by life, her soul was not stone. In that moment, she seemed more mother than cousin. Her tenderness was deeper than any affection he had known. “Some of the debts,” she confessed, “were mine. My extravagance brought this upon you. You bought jewels and trinkets to please me—oh, how I hate them now! I never imagined I could feel so.” She pulled from her cloak brooches, rings, a gold watch, and a handful of guineas, pouring them all into his lap.

The sight overwhelmed him. A strange warmth surged through his chest, melting the cold despair that had gripped him. “Dearest, kindest cousin!” he choked out. Words failed him, but his eyes spoke volumes—gratitude, love, relief.

Soon enough, he smiled. He pushed aside some of the gifts—trinkets he had once given her—and told her how he’d fallen into ruin by selling goods bought on credit. He recounted how the lawyer had just insulted him over it. “I won’t take your money,” he insisted. “I’ve enough now. But these twenty guineas—your kindness—I’ll cherish them always. More than twenty thousand pounds, they are worth to me. I’ll never forget your love. I’ll tell my mother everything. May Heaven bless you for this!”

Their conversation continued warmly, filled with hope and affection, until dusk began to fall. Then Maria rose, sighed deeply, and bid farewell. As the door closed behind her, it opened again almost immediately—to admit Mr. Draper.

“Your humble servant, sir,” he said, bowing stiffly.

But his voice grated on Harry’s nerves. The lawyer’s presence felt like an intrusion. “I expected you hours ago,” Harry said curtly.

“A lawyer’s time is not always his own,” Draper replied, still reeking of port from his earlier meal at the Grecian. “Never mind. I’m at your service now. Presume it’s all settled, Mr. Warrington. Packed your trunk? Why, you’re still in your nightgown. Let me go down and arrange things while you summon your manservant to dress you. I’ve a coach waiting. We’ll be off and dine with the old lady.”

“Are you going to dine with the Baroness de Bernstein?” Harry asked.

“No such honour for me,” Draper scoffed. “I’ve already eaten. It’s *you* who’re dining with your aunt, I suppose?”

“Mr. Draper,” Harry said, standing tall in his brocade robe, “you suppose far more than you know.”

“What in God’s name do you mean?” Draper demanded.

“I mean,” Harry replied firmly, “that I’ve considered it. And having given my word to a faithful, honourable woman, I cannot break it.”

“Confound it!” Draper shrieked. “She’s lost the paper! There’s no binding contract! She’s old enough to be—”

“Enough!” Harry thundered, stamping his foot. “You seem to think you’re speaking to some petty clerk. I take it, Mr. Draper, you’re not used to dealing with men of honour.”

“Pettifogger, indeed!” Draper roared. “Men of honour? Let me tell you, Mr. Warrington, I’m every bit as honourable as you. I may not know many gamblers or jockeys. I haven’t squandered my inheritance, lived like a nobleman on two hundred a year, or bought watches on credit only to pawn them—touch me if you dare!”

With that, he lunged toward the door.

“That’s the way out,” Harry said calmly. “You can’t go through the window—it’s barred.”

“And the answer I give to my client is—NO!” Draper screamed, slamming the door behind him.

Harry stepped forward, fists clenched. “If you utter another word,” he said, “I’ll—”

The sentence died unspoken. The door shut swiftly. Draper stormed off to Madame de Bernstein, where, despite offering her the most polished version of events, he received even harsher rebuke than he had from Harry.

“What?” Harry murmured, pacing the room in his rustling robe. “Shall she trust me—and I abandon her? No. Dear, faithful, generous woman! If I must rot in prison for years, I’ll stay true to her.”

Meanwhile, at Castlewood, the desolate Baroness sat alone at the dinner table. The chair meant for her nephew stood empty. Silver gleamed, glasses sparkled, dishes were laid one after another—yet she touched nothing. The major-domo pressed her gently.

“It is eight o’clock,” he said. “You’ve eaten nothing all day. It would do you good.”

She shook her head. “I’ll have coffee. Send Case to fetch it.”

The servants cleared the table, leaving her seated before the vacant chair. Moments later, the old servant returned—without the coffee, his face ashen with terror.

“Mr. WARRINGTON!” he gasped.

The Baroness uttered a cry, rose from her chair, then collapsed back, trembling violently.

“So you’ve come, sir?” she whispered, voice trembling with joy. “Bring back the—Ah!”

Then she screamed. “Gracious God! Who is it?”

Her eyes widened in horror. Her painted face turned deathly white. She gripped the armrests as the figure approached.

It was a gentleman—tall, fair-haired, dressed in fine clothes—whose features mirrored Harry Warrington’s exactly. His voice, when he spoke, echoed Harry’s tone in uncanny fashion.

“You expected my brother, madam?” he said politely. “I am George Warrington. I’ve just arrived in London. I went to his house and met his servant at your door, carrying this letter. I thought I’d bring it to you before going to him.”

He placed the letter on the table.

“Are you…” the Baroness breathed, “are you my nephew—thought dead?”

“Was killed—and is alive,” the stranger said quietly. “I am George Warrington. And I ask you: what have you done with my brother?”

“Look, George!” she cried, bewildered. “I waited for him tonight. That chair was set for him. I’ve been waiting… till I’m faint. I don’t like being alone. Stay and sup with me!”

“Pardon me, madam,” George replied with grave courtesy. “Please God, my supper will be with Harry tonight.”

“Bring him back! Bring him back here—on any terms! It’s only five hundred pounds! Here—take it! Take it if you need it!”

“I have no need, madam,” George said softly. “I have money. And there is no better use for it than in my brother’s service.”

“And you will bring him to me? Say you will bring him to me!”

George bowed deeply—once, formally—and left the room, passing the stunned servants, calling over his shoulder, “Gumbo! Follow me!”

Had Harry received no letters from home? Had he not read the missive announcing his brother’s escape from French territory and return to Virginia?

No. No such letter had reached him. Otherwise, surely he would have told Gumbo.

“Quick, horses!” George commanded. “To Strand! To Temple Bar! This is the House of Captivity—and the Deliverer has come!”

Hurry, coachman! Drive fast through the dim lanes of London—Strand and Fleet Street—bearing George Warrington to his brother’s rescue. Any observer familiar with Hogarth’s depiction of a London hackneycoach and the city’s roads in that age might well imagine how wearisome such a journey must have been: few lights save those carried by link-boys; coaches poorly hung, jolting over uneven pavements; great holes in the road, and deep sloughs of winter mud. To young George, the ride from Piccadilly to Fleet Street felt as endless as the long trek from Marlborough to London he had made earlier that very day.

He had written to Harry, announcing his arrival at Bristol. Before that, he had sent word of his own return—news of his survival after months of captivity, of his miraculous escape from death beneath Braddock’s command. At the time, war raged between England and France, and French privateers prowled the seas, seizing British merchant vessels even within sight of port. The letter carrying news of George’s return must have been aboard one of the many American ships captured by the French. It never reached Harry. Instead, it lay unopened in his lodgings, delivered on the third morning after Harry’s imprisonment—just as Mr. Ruff, furious at the loss of his lodger’s belongings, refused to surrender a single item.

George’s first stop upon arriving in London was Harry’s apartment in Clarges Street. He asked for his brother. The maid who answered the door screamed at the sight of him—so strikingly like her master—and fled to her mistress. The woman, unwilling to admit the truth—that poor Harry was imprisoned by her husband’s suit—said only that Mr. Warrington had left, and she did not know where he had gone.

But George knew Clarges Street was near Bond Street. He had studied London maps often. Aunt Bernstein would know where Harry was. Perhaps she was with her now. George remembered Harry’s letters to Virginia, full of gratitude for Aunt Bernstein’s kindness. Even Madam Esmond had been moved by it—especially by the letter from the Baroness that had prompted George to rush across Europe without delay. She had hoped, sincerely, that Madam Beatrix had found cause to repent her past ways. At her age, it was long overdue. Heaven knows, she had much to regret!

Rachel Esmond never spoke of her eldest daughter. Madam Esmond Warrington never mentioned her sister. And though the order for remission had been issued, though the words were written on the floor of the Temple—there remains a sin some will never forgive. Especially among women. Female virtue, once wounded, can be implacable.

Perhaps the Virginians’ agent at Bristol had painted a grim picture of Harry’s downfall. But when George reached his aunt’s door, Gumbo—the faithful negro servant—stood there, trembling. As the boy recovered from his shock at seeing the master he believed dead, he managed to stammer out a few words about Harry’s whereabouts and his pitiful state. That was enough to harden George’s manner when he approached his aunt.

To him, it seemed natural that family should come to a brother’s aid in distress. Oh, George, how little you know of London and its ways! How many poor men do you pass in your walks? If every philanthropist tried to free them all, even the wealth of America would not suffice. Yet as George rattled through the darkened streets toward the bailiff’s house, he began to feel a pang of remorse. The old lady’s agitation, her quiet sorrow—it touched him. “She does care,” he thought, “for my poor Harry’s plight. I judged too quickly.” Again and again in life, George would find himself rebuked for this same fault—haste in judgment. How many of us are not guilty of it? And alas, once the harm is done, no repentance can mend it.

“Quick, coachman!” he called. “We move as slowly as you do.”

Gumbo knew the way well. Once more, the bell rang. The outer door opened, then shut tightly behind them. They stood in a narrow passage, lit by a flaring tallow torch held by a small Jewish janitor. A second door creaked open, and they entered the house.

The porter stared, startled, as the torchlight revealed a second Mr. Warrington. “Come to see the gentleman?” he asked. “Yes. But wait—this is Mr. Warrington’s brother from America.” Gumbo was sent to prepare the master. “Step into this room,” said the porter. “There’s a gentleman already here about Mr. W.’s business. Another upstairs with him. No end of people have been calling.”

The room into which George was ushered was small, known as Mr. Amos’s office. By the flicker of a guttering candle, a stout man in a cloak and laced hat sat talking with the bailiff. The young porter carried his candle ahead, so the space was well lit.

“We’re not angry anymore, Harry!” said the stout gentleman, rising cheerfully and stepping forward with an outstretched hand. “Thank God, my boy! Mr. Amos says there’ll be no trouble—James and I will stand bail, and we’ll settle everything by breakfast tomorrow. Why… Angels and ministers of grace! Who are you?”

He stepped back, surprised, as the newcomer grasped his hand. But the stranger held tighter. “God bless you, sir!” he said. “I know who you are. You must be Colonel Lambert—whose kindness to my brother Harry he wrote of. And I am the brother you’ve heard of—left for dead in Braddock’s battle, living again after eighteen months among the French. I live to thank God—and you—for your kindness to my Harry.”

“James! James! News!” cried Mr. Lambert, turning to a gentleman in red who entered the room. “Here are the dead risen! Harry Scapegrace’s brother has returned—and with his scalp still on his head!” (George had removed his hat and stood in the light.)

“This is my brother-bail, Mr. Warrington,” said Mr. Lambert. “This is Lieutenant-Colonel James Wolfe, at your service. There’s been a little difference between Harry and me, Mr. George. Is he pacified, James?”

“He is full of gratitude,” replied Mr. Wolfe, bowing to George. “Harry wrote home about me, sir,” said the young man, “and I hope my brother’s friends will be kind enough to welcome me as their own.”

“I wish he had none but us, Mr. Warrington,” said Mr. Wolfe. “Poor Harry’s fine folks have been too fine for him—and ended by bringing him here.”

“Nay, gentlemen,” interjected Harry’s landlord, “I’ve done my best to keep the young gentleman comfortable. Knowing your honour—when you came before to bail Captain Watkins, and knowing your security is good—if you wish, the young gentleman may go free tonight. I’ll settle with the lawyer in the morning.”

“The debt is five hundred and odd pounds?” asked Mr. Warrington.

“With a hundred thanks,” said the landlord, “I can pay it now into the officers’ hands—take the usual acknowledgment and caution. But I shall never forget, gentlemen, that you helped my brother in his need. For that, I say thank you—and God bless you—in my mother’s name and mine.”

Meanwhile, Gumbo had hurried upstairs to Harry’s chamber. The young man would likely have scolded him for returning so late—but he was already softened by the conversation he’d just had with the friend who had left him. He sat smoking a pipe of Virginia tobacco, lost in thought. Even Maria’s kindness and devotion, shown just moments before, had not fully comforted him. He had begun to dread the consequences of that very love—how it bound him, how it shaped his future.

Then the door opened, and Mr. Wolfe entered—his homely face bright with warmth, his hand outstretched. “Lambert’s below,” he said. “And he’s come to help you.”

In spite of himself, Lambert would be kind. In spite of Harry’s ill temper and unjust anger, the good man meant to help him—even against Wolfe’s own advice. “For you were wrong, Mr. Warrington,” said the Colonel plainly. “You wouldn’t listen. You used harsh words to your senior—and one of the finest men alive. See what your pride has brought you. Will you bear with a friend who speaks honestly?”

“You have acted as always,” said Harry, “as the best Christian, the best friend, the most generous man. Nay, if you want proof of his goodness—here it is: He has turned me around. I was angry with you, but he brought me down here to be your bail. Let us both cry *Peccavimus*, Harry—and shake hands with our friend. He waits below. He would not come up until he knew how you’d receive him.”

“I think he’s a good man,” groaned Harry. “I was wild and angry when we last met, Colonel Wolfe. Perhaps he was right to send back those trinkets—though it hurt me. Go down to him, will you? Tell him I’m sorry—ask his pardon—and—God bless him for his generosity.”

And he turned his face away, rubbing his eyes.

“Tell him yourself, Harry,” said the Colonel, taking his hand. “No deputy will say it half so well. Come with me now.”

“You go first—I’ll follow,” said Harry. “On my word, I will. See? I’m in my morning gown! Just let me put on a coat. Give him my message first—prepare him for me!”

Wolfe smiled as he left—knowing well the young man’s hesitation. As he opened the door, Gumbo burst in—so excited he nearly forgot to bow. His eyes rolled, his mouth grinned, his hands trembled. “What, Gum? What’s happened?” asked Harry.

“No new sweetheart, mas’r,” said Gumbo, grinning wildly. “I’ve seen a ghost!”

“A ghost? Whose? Where?”

“Whar? Saw him at Madame Bernstein’s house. Came with him in the coach! He’s downstairs now—with Colonel Lambert!”

As Gumbo spoke, putting on Harry’s coat, his head wagged, his lips twitched, his whole body quivered with joy.

“What ghost?” demanded Harry, agitated.

“Is anyone—is—my mother come?”

“No, sir! No, Master Harry!” Gumbo’s head spun nearly off. Harry looked at him oddly, then flung open the door and raced down the stairs.

He reached the bottom just as a voice from within the little office—its door wide open—said, “And for doing so, I say thank you, and God bless you, in my mother’s name and mine.”

“Whose voice is that?” shouted Harry, his own voice trembling.

“It’s the ghost’s, mas’r!” yelled Gumbo from behind.

Harry ran forward—into the room.

There, if you please, we pause for a moment—before we enter.

When we were first introduced to Sir Miles Warrington at the King’s drawing-room in St. James’s Palace, I must confess that, upon seeing his jolly round face, broad waistcoat, and hearty country manner, I immediately thought I had found an admirable acquaintance—perhaps even the noblest specimen of humanity: the celebrated English country gentleman. To be such a man is, indeed, to stand close to the divine, perched atop the summit of earthly happiness. To possess a generous estate, free from encumbrances, with rents paid promptly by farmers who bless their stars for having such a landlord; to have only one tenant perhaps holding back, not out of malice but to afford the good old gentleman the opportunity to display his boundless charity; to hunt three days a week, adore the sport above all else, and enjoy perfect health and appetite as a result; to have not just appetite, but a sumptuous dinner; to sit in church amid a chorus of blessings from villagers, the foremost man in the parish, its benefactor, aware of his own worth—though he does mutter “Have mercy upon us, miserable sinners” only because the book demands it, and to set an example—yet how can a man so healthy, wealthy, and beloved truly believe himself a wretched sinner? Allons donc! Give any man robust health, temper, five thousand pounds a year, the admiration of his community, and the love of his family, and you’ll find it impossible to make him feel deeply dissatisfied with his spiritual state. If you were a Royal Highness, arriving at church in perfect comfort, the parson waiting to begin until your grace entered, would you consider yourself a miserable sinner? Perhaps only when afflicted with gout, isolated, death looming, your doctor having forbidden claret and prescribed arrowroot and sherry—then, yes, humility might come. But under the sun, in high spirits, the word *miserable* is mere form. You don’t truly believe you’re pitiable. If misery must be endured, what then of Colin Ploughman, suffering from ague, supporting seven children, paying two pounds a year rent, and earning eight shillings weekly? No—such a man is far more deserving of pity than the rich, jovial country gentleman, who, if he is a sinner, has few to tell him so.

He may grow selfish, but at least he is content with himself. For miles around, none rival him in goodness or greatness. His excellent wife serves him—and the entire parish. His children revere him. The vicar respects him. He commands authority at quarter-sessions. Poachers tremble before him. At market, hats fly off in his presence. Around his grand coach, where his spotless daughters and noble lady sit, tradesmen bow bareheaded, farmwives curtsey endlessly. From their seats, the ladies look down with benevolent smiles, nodding kindly to the poor. They buy a yard of ribbon with graciousness, purchase an ounce of salts or a packet of flower-seeds with condescension, deign to bargain over a goose. Their journey resembles a royal progress. A happy people presses about them, blessing them. Tradesmen bow, farmers’ wives bob, town boys wave ragged hats and cheer the red-faced coachman driving the fat bays, shouting, “Sir Miles for ever! Throw us a halfpenny, my lady!”

But suppose the market-woman hides her plump goose when the coach approaches, fearing the lady might insist on buying it cheaply? Suppose no coppers ever emerge from the coach window? Suppose Sir Miles offers his tenants thin beer and his poor a watery broth? This may well be the way of our ideal English gentleman. There have been many such gentlemen and ladies—those who patronized the poor without relieving them, who shouted “Amen!” at church as loudly as the clerk, who observed every ritual of piety and every custom of English gentility, who bought virtue as though it were a bargain, believing they honored it through purchase.

Poor Harry, in distress, turned to his relatives for help. His aunt sent him a tract and her blessing. His uncle was out of town and could not reply. How common is this kind of behavior in respectable society? One might imagine Lord and Lady Macbeth plotting murder, meeting afterward with awkwardness. But what of Lord and Lady Skinflint, consulting in their bedroom about aiding their unfortunate nephew, deciding against it, then descending to family prayers, greeting their children and servants, speaking virtuously before them, and retiring to talk privately—what thoughts pass between them? What do they think of the kinsman left to suffer, groaning unaided? How can they maintain their pious airs? How dare they look each other in the eye? Do they believe they’ve done wrong? Is Skinflint tormented by guilt over the plea ignored, the hunger sent away empty? Not at all. He is angry at Prodigal for being foolish. He feels no shame for being stingy. “A young man with such prospects throwing them away?” he thinks. “A fortune wasted on gamblers and wastrels? Horrible, horrible! Take warning, child, from this young man’s folly—see the ruin of extravagance.”

According to the great and ever-established Church of the Pharisees, this is a perfect moment for moral instruction and the assertion of virtue. “And to think he deceived us so!” exclaims Lady Warrington. “Very sad, very sad, my dear,” says Sir Miles, wagging his head. “To think of so much extravagance in one so young!” cries Lady Warrington again. “Cards, bets, tavern feasts of wicked profusion, fine horses, the company of the wealthy and profligate of his sex, and, I fear, of the most iniquitous women.” “Hush, my Lady Warrington!” interrupts her husband, glancing toward the spotless Dora and Flora, who lower their blushing heads at mention of the last. “No wonder my poor children hide their faces!” continues mamma. “My dears, I wish even the existence of such creatures could be kept from you!” “They can’t go to an opera or the park without seeing them,” says Sir Miles. “To think we should have introduced such a young serpent into our family! And left him with that guileless darling!” She points to Master Miles. “Who’s a serpent, mamma?” asks the boy. “First you said cousin Harry was bad, then good, now bad again. Which is he, Sir Miles?” “He has faults, like all of us, Miley, my dear. Your cousin has been wild—you must take warning by him.” “Was not my elder brother, who died—my naughty brother—was not he wild too? He never gave me money, nor toys, nor rode with me, nor—why do you cry, mamma? Sure I remember how Hugh and you were always fighting—” “Silence, sir!” cry papa and the girls together. “Don’t you know you’re never to mention that name?” “I know I love Harry, and I didn’t love Hugh,” says the bold little rebel. “And if cousin Harry is in prison, I’ll give him my half-guinea that my godpapa gave me, and anything I have—yes, anything, except—except my little horse—and my silver waistcoat—and—Snowball and Sweetlips at home—and—yes, my custard after dinner.” This was in response to a hint from sister Dora. “But I’d give him some of it,” adds Miles after a pause. “Shut thy mouth with it, child, and then go about thy business,” says papa, amused. Sir Miles Warrington possessed a considerable fund of easy humor.

“Who would have thought he’d ever be so wild?” murmurs mamma. “Nay, youth is the season for wild oats, my dear.” “That we should have been so misled in him!” sigh the girls. “That he should kiss us both!” cries papa. “Sir Miles Warrington, I have no patience with that sort of vulgarity!” declares the majestic matron. “Which of you was the favourite yesterday, girls?” continues the father. “Favourite, indeed! I told him over and over again of my engagement to dear Tom—I did, Dora—why do you sneer?” says the handsome sister. “Nay, to do her justice, so did Dora too,” says papa. “Because Flora seemed to wish to forget her engagement with dear Tom sometimes,” remarks the sister. “I never, never, never wished to break with Tom! It’s wicked of you to say so, Dora! It is you who are always envious because I happen—because gentlemen imagine I’m not ill-looking, and prefer me to some folks, in spite of all their learning and wit!” cries Flora, tossing her head and looking at the mirror. “Why are you always looking there, sister?” asks artless Miles junior. “Sure, you must know your face well enough!” “Some people look at it just as often, child, who haven’t near such good reason,” says papa gallantly. “If you mean me, Sir Miles, I thank you,” cries Dora. “My face is as Heaven made it, and my father and mother gave it me. ’Tis not my fault if I resemble my papa’s family. If my head is homely, at least I have brains in it. I envious of Flora, indeed, because she has found favor in the sight of poor Tom Claypool! I should as soon be proud of captivating a ploughboy!” “Pray, miss, was your Mr. Harry, of Virginia, much wiser than Tom Claypool? You would have had him for the asking!” exclaims Flora. “And so would you, miss, and have dropped Tom Claypool into the sea!” cries Dora. “I wouldn’t.” “You would.” “I wouldn’t”—and da capo goes the conversation—the shuttlecock of wrath briskly passed between the sisters.

“Oh, my children! Is this the way you dwell together in unity?” exclaims their excellent mother, laying down her embroidery. “What an example you set to this Innocent!” “Like to see ‘em fight, my lady!” cries the Innocent, rubbing his hands. “At her, Flora! Worry her, Dora! To it again, you little rogues!” says facetious papa. “’Tis good sport, ain’t it, Miley?” “Oh, Sir Miles! Oh, my children! These disputes are unseemly. They tear a fond mother’s heart,” says mamma, with majestic gesture, though bearing the wound with remarkable calm. “What cause for thankfulness ought we to have that watchful parents have prevented any idle engagements between you and your misguided cousin. If we have been mistaken in him, is it not a mercy we discovered our error in time? If either of you had any preference for him, your excellent good sense will teach you to overcome, to eradicate, the vain feeling. That we cherished and were kind to him can never be a source of regret. ’Tis a proof of our good-nature. What we have to regret, I fear, is that your cousin should have proved unworthy of our kindness, and, coming away from the society of gamblers, play-actors, and the like, should have brought contamination—pollution, I had almost said—into this pure family!”

“Oh, bother mamma’s sermons!” says Flora, as my lady begins another harangue—of which we only record the beginning—but during which papa, whistling, quietly slips from the room on tiptoe, while the artless Miles winds up his top and pegs it beneath his sisters’ robes. The top hums, stumbles, tumbles, and expires in its usual drunken manner long before Lady Warrington finishes her sermon. “Were you listening to me, my child?” she asks, placing her hand on her darling’s head. “Yes, mother,” says he, whipcord in mouth, winding up his toy. “You was a-saying that Harry was very poor now, and that we oughtn’t to help him. That’s what you was saying; wasn’t it, madam?” “My poor child, thou wilt understand me better when thou art older!” says mamma, turning toward the ceiling, her habitual refuge. “Get out, you little wretch!” cries one sister. The artless one has pegged his top at Dora’s toes and laughs at her discomfort.

But what is this? Who comes here? Why does Sir Miles return to the drawing-room, and why does Tom Claypool, striding behind him, wear such a disturbed countenance?

“Here’s a pretty business, my Lady Warrington!” cries Sir Miles. “Here’s a wonderful wonder of wonders, girls!” “For goodness’ sake, gentlemen, what is your intelligence?” asks the virtuous matron. “The whole town’s talking about it, my lady!” says Tom Claypool, puffing for breath. “Tom has seen him,” continues Sir Miles. “Seen both of them, my Lady Warrington. They were at Ranelagh last night, with a regular mob after them. So alike, that but for different ribbons you’d hardly tell one from the other. One in blue, the other in brown; but I’m certain he’s worn both suits here.” “What suits?” “What one, what other?” call the girls. “Why, your fortunate youth, to be sure.” “Our precious Virginian, and heir to the principality!” says Sir Miles. “Is my nephew, then, released from his incarceration?” asks her ladyship. “And is he again plunged in the vortex of dissip----” “Confound him!” roars the Baronet, with an expression I fear was stronger still. “What should you think, my Lady Warrington, if this precious nephew of mine should turn out to be an impostor; by George! no better than an adventurer?” “An inward monitor whispered me as much!” cries the lady; “but I dashed from me the unworthy suspicion. Speak, Sir Miles, we burn with impatience to listen to your intelligence.” “I’ll—speak, my love, when you’ve done,” says Sir Miles. “Well, what do you think of my gentleman, who comes into my house, dines at my table, is treated as one of this family, kisses my—” “What?” asks Tom Claypool, flushing as red as his waistcoat. “—Hem! Kisses my wife’s hand, and is treated in the fondest manner, by George! What do you think of this fellow, who talks of his property and his principality, by Jupiter!—turning out to be a beggarly SECOND SON! A beggar, my Lady Warrington, by——” “Sir Miles Warrington, no violence of language before these dear ones! I sink to the earth, confounded by this unutterable hypocrisy. And did I entrust thee to a pretender, my blessed boy? Did I leave thee with an impostor, my innocent one?” the matron cries, fondling her son. “Who’s an impostor, my lady?” asks the child. “That confounded young scamp of a Harry Warrington!” bawls papa; whereupon the little Miles, after a puzzled look and some hidden emotion, bursts into tears. His admirable mother tries to clutch him to her heart, but he rejects the embrace, crying louder and kicking wildly in her lap, as the butler announces: “Mr. George Warrington, Mr. Henry Warrington!”

Miles is dropped from his mother’s lap. Sir Miles’s face matches Mr. Claypool’s waistcoat. The three ladies rise and make three frigid curtseys as our two young men enter. Little Miles runs to them, holds out a hand. “Oh, Harry! No! which is Harry? You’re my Harry,” and he chooses rightly this time. “Oh, you dear Harry! I’m so glad you are come! And they’ve been abusing you so!” “I am come to pay my duty to my uncle,” says the dark-haired Mr. Warrington; “and to thank him for his hospitalities to my brother Henry.” “What, nephew George? My brother’s face and eyes! Boys both, I am delighted to see you!” cries their uncle, grasping each hand affectionately, his honest face glowing with pleasure. “This indeed hath been a most mysterious and a most providential resuscitation,” says Lady Warrington. “Only I wonder that my nephew Henry concealed the circumstance until now,” she adds, casting a sidelong glance at both young gentlemen. “He knew it no more than your ladyship,” says Mr. Warrington. The young ladies exchange glances, lowering their eyes. “Indeed, sir! A most singular circumstance,” says mamma, with another curtsey. “We had heard of it, sir; and Mr. Claypool, our county neighbour, had just brought us the intelligence, and it even now formed the subject of my conversation with my daughters.” “Yes,” cries a little voice, “and do you know, Harry, father and mother said you was a—a imp----” “Silence, my child! Screwby, convey Master Warrington to his own apartment! These, Mr. Warrington—or, I suppose I should say nephew George—are your cousins.” Two curtseys—two cheeses—two hands extended.
