Mr. Esmond Warrington makes a profound low bow, embracing (and it is the only embrace he offers) all three ladies. He lays his hat to his heart. “It is my duty, madam, to pay my respects to my uncle and cousins, and to thank your ladyship for such hospitality as you have been enabled to show to my brother.” “It was not much, nephew, but it was our best. Ods bobs!” cries the hearty Sir Miles, “it was our best!” “And I appreciate it, sir,” says Mr. Warrington, looking gravely around the family. “Give us thy hand. Not a word more,” says Sir Miles. “What? Do you think I’m a cannibal, and won’t extend the hand of hospitality to my dear brother’s son? What say you, lads? Will you eat our mutton at three? This is my neighbour, Tom Claypool, son to Sir Thomas Claypool, Baronet, and my very good friend. Hey, Tom! Thou wilt be of the party, Tom? Thou knowest our brew, hey, my boy?” “Yes, I know it, Sir Miles,” replies Tom, with no particular rapture. “And thou shalt taste it, my boy! Thou shalt taste it! What is there for dinner, my Lady Warrington? Our food is plain, but plenty, lads—plain, but plenty!” “We cannot partake of it to-day, sir. We dine with a friend who occupies my Lord Wrotham’s house, your neighbour. Colonel Lambert—Major-General Lambert he has just been made.” “With two daughters, I think—countrified-looking girls—are they not?” asks Flora. “I think I have remarked two little rather dowdy things,” says Dora. “They are as good girls as any in England!” breaks out Harry, to whom no one had spoken a word. His reign was over. He was nobody. What wonder, then, that he should not be visible? “Oh, indeed, cousin!” says Dora, glancing at the young man, who sits with burning cheeks, chafing at the humiliation, yet unsure how or whether to respond. “Oh, indeed, cousin! You are very charitable—or very lucky, I’m sure! You see angels where we only see ordinary little persons. I’m sure I could not imagine who those odd-looking people were in Lord Wrotham’s coach, with his handsome liveries. But if they were three angels, I have nothing to say.” “My brother is an enthusiast,” interposes George. “He is often mistaken about women.” “Oh, really!” says Dora, looking slightly uneasy. “I fear my nephew Henry has indeed met with some unfavourable specimens of our sex,” remarks the matron, groaning. “We are so easily taken in, madam—we are both very young yet—we shall grow older and learn better.” “Most sincerely, nephew George, I trust you may. You have my best wishes, my prayers, for your brother’s welfare and your own. No efforts of ours have been wanting. At a painful moment, to which I will not further allude—” “And when my uncle Sir Miles was out of town,” says George, looking toward the Baronet, who smiles with affectionate approval. “—I sent your brother a work which I thought might comfort him, and I know might improve him. Nay, do not thank me; I claim no credit; I did but my duty—a humble woman’s duty—for what are this world’s goods, nephew, compared to the welfare of a soul? If I did good, I am thankful; if I was useful, I rejoice. If, through my means, you have been brought, Harry, to consider—” “Oh! The sermon, is it?” breaks in straightforward Harry. “I hadn’t time to read a single syllable of it, aunt—thank you. You see I don’t care much about that kind of thing—but thank you all the same.” “The intention is everything,” says Mr. Warrington, “and we are both grateful. Our dear friend, General Lambert, intended to give bail for Harry; but, happily, I had funds of Harry’s with me to meet any demands upon us. But the kindness is the same, and I am grateful to the friend who hastened to my brother’s rescue when he had most need of aid, and when his own relations happened—so unfortunately—to be out of town.” “Anything I could do, my dear boy, I’m sure—my brother’s son—my own nephew—ods bobs! you know—that is, anything—anything, you know!” cries Sir Miles, clasping George’s hand with a generous smack. “You can’t stay and dine with us? Put off the Colonel—the General—do, now! Or name a day. My Lady Warrington, make my nephew name a day when he will sit under his grandfather’s picture and drink some of his wine!”

“His intellectual faculties seem more developed than those of his unlucky younger brother,” remarked my lady, when the young gentlemen had taken their leave. “The younger must be reckless and extravagant about money indeed, for did you remark, Sir Miles, the loss of his reversion in Virginia—the amount of which has, no doubt, been grossly exaggerated, but, nevertheless, must be something considerable—did you, I say, remark that the ruin of Harry’s prospects scarcely seemed to affect him?” “I shouldn’t be at all surprised that the elder turns out to be as poor as the young one,” says Dora, tossing her head. “He! he! Did you see that cousin George had one of cousin Harry’s suits of clothes on—the brown and gold—that one he wore when he went with you to the oratorio, Flora?” “Did he take Flora to an oratorio?” asks Mr. Claypool, fiercely. “I was ill and couldn’t go, and my cousin went with her,” says Dora. “Far be it from me to object to any innocent amusement, much less to the music of Mr. Handel, dear Mr. Claypool,” says mamma. “Music refines the soul, elevates the understanding, is heard in our churches, and ’tis well known was practised by King David. Your operas I shun as deleterious; your ballets I would forbid to my children as most immoral; but music, my dears! May we enjoy it, like everything else in reason—may we—” “There’s the music of the dinner-bell,” says papa, rubbing his hands. “Come, girls. Screwby, go and fetch Master Miley. Tom, take down my lady.” “Nay, dear Thomas, I walk but slowly. Go you with dearest Flora downstairs,” says Virtue. But Dora took care to make the evening pleasant by talking of Handel and oratorios constantly during dinner.

Across the way, dear reader, if you’ll kindly step with us, we find ourselves at Lord Wrotham’s residence—lent by his lordship to the General and his small household party, those same individuals we met earlier at Oakhurst and Tunbridge Wells. James Wolfe has promised to join them for dinner, but as it happens, he is currently occupied with Miss Lowther, whose glance holds more value in his eyes than any delicacy prepared by Lord Wrotham’s finest cook or the sumptuous dessert that awaits us. You, gentle reader, will make the sixth guest. Feel free to take Mr. Wolfe’s seat—he won’t be coming. As for me, I shall remain at the sideboard, observing and reporting.

Observe first the joy on the women’s faces! When Harry Warrington was seized by bailiffs, I had meant to tell you how Mrs. Lambert, upon hearing of his misfortune, rushed to her husband, pleading, beseeching, demanding that Martin lend a hand. “Forget his rebelliousness from the other day—forget his anger when his gifts were returned; anyone would be angry, especially a spirited boy like Harry! Forget our poverty, forget that every spare penny goes to the boys at college—there must be a way to help him. Didn’t you rescue Charles Watkins two years ago? He paid you back every farthing. And you made an entire family happy—blessed be God! Mrs. Watkins still prays for you and blesses you daily. I believe everything has prospered for us since then. And I’m certain your kindness helped make you a major-general—no doubt about it,” she insisted, full of fervor.

Martin Lambert, ever ready to do a kind deed, needed little convincing. He resolved to seek out James Wolfe and post bail for Harry. Taking his hat and bidding farewell, he squeezed Theo’s hand—she seemed to sense his purpose (or perhaps their mother had already spilled the secret)—and kissed little Hetty’s flushed cheek before stepping out of the room, though not before being followed by his wife.

Alone with him, Mrs. Lambert could no longer contain herself. She threw her arms around his neck, kissed him a hundred times over, called down blessings from heaven, wept freely upon his shoulder—so overcome with emotion that she was discovered in this tender state by old Mrs. Quiggett, the housekeeper, who was bustling through the halls. The sight, I imagine, startled her greatly.

“We’ve had a disagreement and are making up! Don’t go spreading gossip, Mrs. Quiggett!” the gentleman said, walking off.

“Well, I never!” exclaimed Mrs. Quviggett, bursting into a shrill, cackling laugh, like an ancient cockatoo—indeed, she bore a striking resemblance to such a bird: white-haired, hooked-nosed, long-lived, and perpetually animated. “Well, I never!” she repeated, shaking her sides until her keys and ribs clattered together.

“Oh, Quiggett!” sobbed Mrs. Lambert, “what a man he is!”

“You’ve been quarreling, have you, mum, and now making up? That’s good.”

“Quarrel with him? He never told a bigger lie. My General is an angel, Quiggett. I’d worship him. I’d fall at his boots and kiss them, I truly would! There’s never been a man so good as my General. What have I done to deserve such a husband? How dare I possess such a noble soul?”

“My dear,” replied the old housekeeper, “I think there’s a pair of you.” Then, with a twinkle in her eye, she added, “Now, what would you like for supper?”

When Lambert returned late that evening, bearing news that Harry was free and his brother had come to his rescue, the household erupted into jubilation. If Mrs. Lambert had thought her husband an angel before, what could she call him now? If she had wanted to embrace his boots in the morning, what deeper expression of devotion might she offer in the evening? Little Hetty quietly crept to her father, silently drinking a sip from his glass. Theo and her mother glowed with happiness, radiant as twin moons.

After supper, at a silent signal, all four knelt together—offering solemn yet joyful homage, a prayer of repentance and renewal, filled with the purest delight angels might know. Just then, a loud knock echoed at the door. Who could it be? Lord Wrotham was miles away in the country. It was past midnight—their talk had carried on long into the night. But Mrs. Lambert knew instantly who stood outside.

“This is George,” said a young man, ushering in another. “We came from Aunt Bernstein’s. We couldn’t sleep without thanking you too. You dear, dear, good—” His words trailed off. Aunt Lambert was already embracing Harry. Theo snatched up Hetty, pale as death, and held her close, breathing life back into her. George Warrington stood with his hat in hand. When Harry’s reunion was complete, George stepped forward and kissed Mrs. Lambert’s hand. The General passed a hand across his eyes. I assure you, they were all wrapped in tenderness and joy. Generous hearts often feel most deeply when wrong is forgiven, peace restored, and love returns after being lost.

“We came from Aunt Bernstein’s,” Harry explained. “We saw lights here, and couldn’t go to bed without saying goodnight to all of you. Could we, George?”

“A famous nightcap, indeed,” said the General with a smile. “When shall you dine with us? Tomorrow?”

“No,” said George, “we must visit Madame Bernstein tomorrow.”

Then the next day? Yes, they would come then—and that very day is the one we write of. This is the dinner where, in place of Lieutenant-Colonel James Wolfe—absent on private business—you, dear reader, have just been invited to sit.

To sit down—and why, pray? Not merely for a feast of empty promises, no—but to hear **MR. GEORGE ESMOND WARRINGTON’S ACCOUNT**, which he is about to deliver. Here they all sit—not in Lord Wrotham’s grand dining hall, but in the cozy study or parlour ahead. The cloth has been removed, the General has given the King’s health, the servants have left, and the guests sit in quiet expectation. After a moment of hesitation and a blush, Mr. George begins:

“I remember well, at our General’s table, how the sharp-witted Philadelphia agent—whose cleverness we admired at home—voiced the very concerns that later proved justified by the disaster. ‘Of course,’ he said, ‘once your Excellency’s troops reach Fort Duquesne, such a weak outpost cannot withstand your general, your army, your artillery.’ But he asked, ‘Have you considered the difficulty of reaching it? Your march will be through nearly untouched woods, over roads you must build yourself. Your line stretches four miles long. Such a slender column, moving through dense forest, will be vulnerable to constant attacks—front, rear, flank—from enemies you cannot see, men trained in ambush.’

‘Psha!’ the General scoffed. ‘The savages may frighten your raw American militia’—as if acknowledging Washington’s presence at the table—‘but the Indians will never trouble His Majesty’s regulars.’

‘I sincerely hope not,’ Mr. Franklin sighed. Naturally, the General’s companions sneered at the postmaster—a civilian, they thought, meddling beyond his understanding.

We underestimated the Indians. Our commander dismissed them. Our officers insulted the native chiefs accompanying us, behaving outrageously toward their women. Only seven or eight remained with our force. Had two hundred stood before us on that fateful 9th of July, the outcome might have been different. They could have repelled the French Indians, prevented the panic and surprise that followed. Now we know the French had even begun preparing to surrender, never imagining resistance possible. Even the French Indians protested against attacking such overwhelming numbers.

I was with the General when the firing began. One aide-de-camp after another was sent forward. At first, our advance guard responded bravely, cheering with spirit. But soon our fire slackened, while single shots rang out from behind every tree and bush. Men fell one after another. We marched in order—skirmishers ahead, colors and two small guns in the center, baggage guarded at the rear—over open ground for a mile or two, flanked by thick tangled woods.

After a short time, enemy fire opened from both sides. Men dropped rapidly—officers more than soldiers. At first, we cheered and returned fire. Our guns fired into the woods, seeming to silence the hidden Frenchmen. But then the rifle shots began again. Our men halted, huddled together despite shouts and orders to advance. They fired wildly into the brush—useless, of course. Those in front fled back, wounded and terrified. They reported five thousand Frenchmen and a legion of shrieking Indian devils ahead, scalping our fallen. We heard their cries from the surrounding woods as our comrades fell.

No amount of urging could make them move forward. Aide-de-camp after aide-de-camp was sent—none returned. Finally, it was my turn. I was sent with a message to Captain Fraser of Halkett’s regiment—one I would never deliver.

I had barely advanced thirty yards when a rifle ball struck my leg. I fell immediately. I saw Indians and Frenchmen rush forward, the former screaming war cries, the latter as fierce as their allies. I was stunned to see how few whitecoats there were—no more than a score passed me. In truth, fewer than fifty fought in the battle that shattered two of Britain’s bravest regiments.

One man—half Indian, half French, wearing moccasins and a white coat with a cockade—saw me lying there and turned back, musket raised, intent on killing me and looting my body. I had my fusil, given to me by Harry before the campaign—it had fallen near me. I grabbed it and shot him dead at six yards. I was saved—for the moment—but bleeding heavily, fainting. I nearly passed out trying to reload. The gun slipped from my grasp, and my hand went limp.

I was barely conscious, the screams and gunfire echoing dimly, when I saw an Indian approaching. He was rifling the Frenchman I’d killed, tearing open his coat, searching his pockets. Then he scalped him, knife bloody in his mouth, and came toward me.

I saw him through a haze, as in a dream. I could not move. He placed his knee on my chest, seized my hair with one bloodied hand, lifted my head, and in doing so revealed a French officer advancing behind him.

‘Good God!’ I cried. ‘A moi, Florac! C’est Georges! Aide-moi!’

He froze, ran to me, laid a hand on the Indian’s shoulder, and ordered him to stop. But the savage didn’t understand French—or refused to. He gripped my hair tighter, waved his knife, signaling Florac to leave me to him.

‘Ah, canaille, tu veux du sang? Prends!’ Florac cursed, and with a grunt, plunged his sword into the Indian’s chest. He fell over me, dead.

Florac looked around. ‘Eh! La belle affaire! Where are you wounded? In the leg?’ He bound my leg tightly with his sash. ‘Others will kill you if they find you here. Ah, tiens! Put on this coat and hat with the white cockade. Call out in French if anyone passes. They’ll think you’re one of us. You’re Brunet of the Quebec Volunteers. God guard thee, Brunet! I must go forward. It’s a general rout, and all your redcoats are fleeing, my poor boy.’

What a rout it was! What a day of shame for England!

Florac’s rough bandage stopped the bleeding. He helped me lean against a tree, loaded my fusil, and placed it within reach. He gave me the gourd of the French soldier I’d killed—the drink inside refreshed me greatly. He marked the tree and the terrain so he could return, then hurried forward. ‘You see how much I care for you, George,’ he said. ‘I stay behind in a moment like this.’

I don’t recall telling you, Harry, that Florac owed me something. I won money from him at cards in Quebec—only because he begged me to play—and there was trouble paying. I forgave his debt and lit my pipe with his note of hand. You see, sir, you’re not the only gambler in the family.

At dusk, after the pursuit ended, Florac returned with two Indians, each carrying fresh scalps. He told them I was a wounded Frenchman, his brother, captured early in the day. They laid me on a blanket and carried me groaning, with Florac beside me. Had he abandoned me, they would have left me for dead, looted me, and added my scalp to theirs. He promised brandy at the fort if they brought me safely. I remember little of the journey—my wound was agony—I fainted several times. Eventually, we reached the fort. I was taken to the officer’s log cabin and laid on Florac’s own bed.

Thank heavens I was unconscious. I had arrived as a wounded French soldier. Later, I learned that during my delirium, the few British prisoners taken that day were dragged under the walls of Duquesne by their Indian captors and burned, tortured, butchered—before the eyes of the garrison.

As George speaks, a shiver of horror runs through the listeners. Theo takes Hetty’s hand, alarmed. Harry slams his fist on the table. “The bloody, murderous, red-skinned villains! There’ll be no peace until every last one is hunted down!”

“They offered a hundred and thirty dollars per Indian scalp in Pennsylvania when I left home,” George says calmly. “Fifty for women.”

“Fifty for women, my love?” the Colonel exclaims, lifting his wife’s hair. “Did you hear that, Mrs. Lambert?”

“The murderous villains!” Harry shouts again. “Hunt them down, sir! Hunt them down!”

“I don’t know how long I lay fevered,” George continues. “When I regained consciousness, Florac was gone. He’d been sent on a mission against an English fort in Pennsylvania, claimed by the French. In Duquesne, only thirty Europeans remained. The place could have been retaken a dozen times—if anyone had dared return after defeat.

My old enemy, ague-fever, returned as I lay by the river. It’s a miracle I survived. But for a kind half-breed woman in the fort, who pitied me and cared for me, I would never have recovered. My poor Harry would have become, as he imagined yesterday, our grandfather’s heir, our mother’s only son.

I remembered how Florac had placed my money, watch, and trinkets under my pillow when he laid me in his bed. When I woke, they were gone. A gruff old sergeant—the only officer left—told me, cursing, that I was lucky to be alive. My white cockade and coat had saved me from the fate others deserved.

When I recovered, the fort was nearly empty. The Indians had left, rich with plunder. Most French regulars had gone north on expeditions. Florac had left me in charge of an invalided sergeant. Monsieur de Contrecoeur had joined one of these missions, leaving an old lieutenant named Museau in command.

Museau had long served in the colonies, far from France. His record there was likely poor, and knowing promotion in France favored nobility, he saw no future. He had taken my guineas, I suppose, along with my watch—I once saw it pinned to his chest.

Monsieur Museau and I became fairly friendly. I told him I could be exchanged or sent home, and my mother would pay handsomely for my ransom. This idea stirred his greed. When a trapper arrived in winter, while I still lay ill, Museau agreed I could write home—but only in French, only if he approved it, and only if I claimed I was in Indian hands and wouldn’t be ransomed unless ten thousand livres were paid.

I protested—I was a prisoner of His Most Christian Majesty, entitled to treatment as a gentleman and officer. But Museau swore the letter would go, or he’d throw me out or hand me to his savage allies. He forbade the trapper to speak with me except in his presence. Life and liberty are precious. I resisted briefly, but weakened by fever, I wrote the letter he demanded. The trapper took it, promising to deliver it to my mother in Virginia in three weeks.

Three weeks passed. Six. Twelve. No messenger returned. Winter came and went. The plantations near the fort—where French soldiers had cleared fields and planted gardens, peach and apple trees—bloomed in spring. Heaven knows how I endured.

When I grew stronger, I drew portraits of the soldiers, the half-breed woman and her child (Museau’s child), and Museau himself—though I admit I flattered him terribly. An old guitar remained in the fort. I played French airs, sang, and tried to win favor with my captors. The months dragged on. The messenger never returned.

Finally, word came: the trapper had been shot by British Indians in Maryland. My hope of ransom vanished. Museau grew furious—especially when his sergeant accused the Indian woman of favoring me, which, I believe, she did. I was always gentle with her, grateful to her. My small talents amazed her. I was sick and unhappy—always claims to a woman’s heart.

A captive weakened by illness, a cruel jailer, and a young woman moved by his plight—surely you expect some tragic tale to unfold? You, Miss Hetty, are about to guess she saved me?

“Why, of course she did!” cries mamma.

“What else is she good for?” says Hetty.

“You, Miss Theo, have already painted her as a dark beauty—isn’t that right? A swift huntress—”

“Diana with a baby,” says the Colonel.

“—Who roams the plains with her nymphs, brings down game with unerring aim, queen of the forest—and I see by your expressions you think I’m madly in love with her?”

“Well, I suppose she’s interesting, Mr. George?” Theo says, blushing.

“What think you of a dark beauty, the color of new mahogany, with long straight black hair, usually oiled with a pomade unpleasant to approach, small eyes, high cheekbones, a flat nose sometimes pierced with a ring, rows of glass beads around her tawny throat, her cheeks and forehead tastefully tattooed, fond of finery, and passionately devoted to—oh! Must I confess?”

“For coquetry. I know what you’re going to say!” Miss Hetty interrupts.

“For whisky, my dear Miss Hester—in which appetite my gaoler also indulged. Often, when I was in favor with Monsieur Museau, I sat by and watched him and the woman drink together until they could barely hold the mug. These evenings included singing, dancing, quarreling, knocking things over. And when I was in favor, I was allowed to join them—for Museau, jealous of his dignity, refused his men access to his private revels.

While the trapper’s fate remained uncertain, and Museau and I expected ransom payment, I was treated reasonably. I was allowed to walk the fort, even venture into nearby fields and gardens—always keeping my parole, returning before gun-fire. I practiced a bit of deception, which I hope you’ll forgive. Once my leg healed—the bullet exited in winter, after pain and inflammation—I chose to walk as if still crippled. I hobbled with sticks, moaning Ah! and Oh! every minute, hoping one day I might finally run.

For months, life at the fort dragged on in a monotonous rhythm of hardship and routine. The commandant and I endured our share of quarrels and reconciliations, passed the time with greasy card games, and filled the silence with dismal duets—his wheezing flute and my cracked guitar. La Biche, the poor Fawn, bore her beatings and the liquor poured down her throat as her master saw fit. She nursed her papoose, tended to Museau when his gout flared up, and cared for me during my fevers. Such was our existence until the early autumn of the previous year, when a hunter arrived with news that stirred the entire garrison.

The Marquis de Montcalm had dispatched a strong force to reinforce French-held forts and seize new positions within British territory. Troops had departed from Quebec and Montreal, sailing up the St. Lawrence and across the lakes in bateaux, laden with artillery and supplies. Museau would be replaced by an officer of higher rank—one who might exchange me or hand me over to the Indians in retaliation for the cruelties committed by our frontier men against French soldiers. The men of the fort were thrilled by the prospect: they dreamed of marching into Pennsylvania and New York, capturing Albany and Philadelphia, driving the “Rosbifs” into the sea, and claiming all America from the Mississippi to Newfoundland.

Yet despite this promise of triumph, Museau remained troubled.
“Eh, commandant!” I said, “It’s all very fine, but what of your farm in Normandy? Your pot of cider? Your trippes à la mode de Caen? Where are they now?”

“Yes, yes,” he replied, “it’s all well enough, my garçon. But where will you be when poor old Museau is removed? Other officers aren’t so companionable as I. Very few men possess my humanity. When the garrison swells, will your next commander grant you the same indulgences I have? You’ll be shut in a sty like a pig awaiting slaughter. As surely as one of our men falls into the hands of your frontier brutes and suffers, so surely will you pay with your skin. You’ll be delivered to our red allies—the brethren of La Biche there. Did you see what they did to your countrymen after Braddock’s defeat? Roasting was the least of it, ma foi—was it not, La Biche?”

He went on with vivid, jocular descriptions of torture—eyes burned out, teeth and nails torn away, limbs hacked open. I turned pale, dear Miss Theo. But I’ll spare you the gruesome details, though honest Museau recounted them with grim amusement.

La Biche showed no such emotion. She had seen such horrors before. A Seneca woman, she came from villages near the great cataract between Ontario and Erie. Her people fought for the English, then against them; they had clashed with other tribes, and in war between us and them, it was hard to say which side was more savage.

“They may chop me into cutlets and broil me,” I said coolly, “but still, commandant—you’ll never have your farm in Normandy.”

“Go fetch the whisky-bottle, La Biche,” Museau commanded.

“And it’s not too late,” I added. “I’ll give a generous reward to anyone who brings me home. And I swear, as a man of honour, ten thousand livres to whoever returns a token—say, my watch and seal bearing my grandfather’s arms—I’ve seen it somewhere in this fort.”

“Ah, scelerat!” roared the commandant, laughing hoarsely. “You’ve eyes, you do! Everything is fair game in war.”

“I dream of a house in my village,” I continued, “a field with half a dozen cows, a fine orchard heavy with fruit.”

“And Javotte at the door with her spinning wheel, and a rascal child or two with cheeks as red as the apples! O my country! O my mother!” he sobbed. “Quick, La Biche—get the whisky!”

That night, Museau was deep in thought. La Biche sat apart, silent and melancholy, nursing her child. Whenever I glanced her way, I saw her watching me. The infant began to cry, and Museau, cursing, sent her off to her own hut. Once she was gone, we spoke freely. I laid my arguments before him—arguments he could not resist.

“How can you be sure,” he asked, “that this hunter will help you?”

“That’s my secret,” I replied. But since we’re not bound by honour now, I’ll tell you. Hunters often linger a day or two at the settlements for rest, drink, and company. Our visitor loved all three. He played cards, traded furs for liquor, sang, danced, gambled. He enjoyed himself at the fort. And I—being idle—often sang and scraped my guitar. The men joined in chorus or danced to my tunes until the drums called them to retreat.

Our guest attended one or two of these gatherings. I decided to test whether he understood English. After we’d sung our French songs, I said, “My lads, I’ll give you an English song.” To the tune of *‘Over the hills and far away’*—a favourite air my grandfather used to hum in Marlborough’s camp—I made up some clumsy words:

> *This long, long year, a prisoner drear,*
> *Ah, me! I'm tired of lingering here:*
> *I'll give a hundred guineas gay,*
> *To be over the hills and far away.*

“What is it?” he asked. “I don’t understand.”

“A girl to her lover,” I said—but I saw the twinkle in his eye. He understood.

The next day, when no one else was near, he passed me and hummed softly, perfectly in English: *“Over the hills and far away.”*

“If you’re ready,” he said, “I am. I know who your people are, and how to reach them. Talk to the Fawn—she’ll tell you what to do. What! You won’t play with me?” He pulled out cards and spoke in French as two soldiers approached. “Milor est trop grand seigneur? Bonjour, my lord!”

He bowed mockingly and walked away, shrugging, to find another game.

Now I knew the Biche was to be my agent—and Museau had agreed. The poor Fawn carried out her role faithfully. I needed no further words with Museau. The understanding was complete.

She had long been allowed free access to me—had nursed me through wounds and sickness, helped with my chamber, cooked for me. She was permitted to leave the fort, go to the river, gather corn and vegetables for the garrison.

After gambling away most of his fur money, the trapper gathered his flints, powder, and blankets and left. Three days later, La Biche gave me the signal: the time had come.

When first wounded, I’d been placed in the officers’ room by kind Florac. Later, with only the old lieutenant remaining, I stayed in my quarters—sometimes free, sometimes locked up, sometimes sharing meals with my drunken keeper.

The officers’ house was log-built, like the others in the fort, which mounted only four small guns—one behind my cabin. From there, looking westward, you could see a small island at the confluence of the Ohio and Monongahela rivers, where Duquesne stood. On the opposite shore, a cluster of trees marked the rendezvous.

“You see those trees?” La Biche whispered the day before, in broken French. “He waits for you behind them.”

By day, my door stood open. That afternoon, she returned from the fields with a pickaxe and a basket of greens. She sat on a bench outside my door, the pick leaning against it, the basket beside her. We talked for a while—though I confess I was so dull-minded I wouldn’t have thought to use the pick if she hadn’t pushed it through the door into my room.

“Hide it,” she said. “Need it soon.”

That same day, she pointed out the trees.

The next morning, she came in pretending to be angry. “My lord! My lord! Why didn’t you come to the commandant’s dinner? He’s very ill! Entendez-vous?” She peered into the room and tossed a coil of rope at me.

“I’m coming, La Biche,” I said, hobbling after her on my crutch. As I entered the commandant’s quarters, she murmured, “Pour ce soir.” Then I knew—tonight was the night.

Museau knew nothing. Not a word. He growled at me, complained the soup was cold. He stared at me steadily, chatted about this and that—not just in front of his servant, but later, as we smoked pipes and played piquet. La Biche sat huddled in a corner as usual.

His whisky bottle was empty. “Must have another glass,” he said, with a knowing glance. “We both need one tonight.” Rising, he shuffled to his inner room, where he kept his fire-water locked away—well beyond La Biche’s reach.

As he turned his back, she rose. No sooner was he gone than she knelt at my feet, kissed my hand, pressed it to her heart, and burst into tears upon my knees. I confess I was deeply moved—by her silent devotion, greater than I’d ever imagined. When Museau returned, I was still shaken, though La Biche had retreated to her corner, wrapped in her blanket.

He noticed nothing unusual. We sat down to play. My thoughts were elsewhere; I barely saw the cards.

“I gain everything from you tonight, milor,” he said grimly. “We play on parole.”

“And you may count on mine,” I replied.

“Eh! That’s all you’ve got!” he laughed.

“Monsieur,” I said, “my word is worth ten thousand livres.” We continued.

At last, he said he had a headache and would retire. I understood—I was to follow. “Good night, mon petit milor,” he said. “Wait—without your crutch, you’ll fall.” His eyes twinkled, his face twisted into a sarcastic grin. In my excitement, I’d forgotten my lameness and was walking briskly.

“What a vile night!” he muttered, glancing out. Indeed, a storm raged—wind howling, rain pouring. “Bring a lantern, La Tulipe, and lock my lord safely in his quarters!” He watched me from the doorway. For a moment, I glimpsed La Biche behind him.

The rain was so heavy the sentries stayed in their boxes, leaving me undisturbed. The log house stood on upright posts sunk deep into the ground, with horizontal logs laid across. I began digging beneath the lowest log, working in darkness shortly after tattoo. It took hours before I felt rain falling on my hand under the log. Then, for two more hours, I worked cautiously, until I crawled through to the parapet and silently threw my rope over the gun—heart pounding, fearing the sentry might spot me and shoot.

The wall was only twelve feet high. My fall into the ditch was easy. I waited, staring under the gun, trying to see the river and the island. Above, the sentry paced, humming a tune. Slowly, the darkness cleared. The moon rose, illuminating the river and the dark rocks and trees of the island.

I hurried toward the mark, racing for the clump of trees. Oh, what relief when I heard a low voice humming: *“Over the hills and far away!”*

When Mr. George reached this point, Miss Theo, seated at the harpsichord, turned and played the tune. The little gathering burst into the cheerful chorus.

“Our path,” George continued, “lay through a broad forest on the right bank of the Monongahela, familiar to my guide. By daylight, we came to open land, and my trapper—Silverheels, he called himself—asked if I’d ever seen the place before. It was the fatal field where Braddock fell—the very spot from which I’d been rescued the summer before. Now, the leaves were turning to the brilliant colours of autumn.”

“Ah, brother!” cried Harry, seizing his hand. “I was gambling and wasting myself at Bath and London while you fled for your life through the wilderness! Oh, what a wretched spendthrift I’ve been!”

“But I think you are not unworthy to be called your mother’s son,” Mrs. Lambert said softly, her eyes glistening. Indeed, in Harry’s remorse, his love, his joy, his generosity—we saw hope for the repentant, kind young sinner.

“We crossed the river,” George resumed, “and followed the base of the western Allegheny slopes through a magnificent forest of oaks, maples, and towering poplars, some a hundred feet high without a single branch. Our danger came not only from the French patrols, but from the Indians—always uncertain allies, now especially hostile due to our past mistreatment and the French victory two years prior.”

I was still weak. Our journey through the wilderness lasted over two weeks. As we advanced, the woods grew redder. Frost nipped sharply at night. We lit fires at our feet and slept wrapped in blankets. At this season, mountain hunters gathered maple sap to make sugar. We met several families camping near their trees by mountain streams. They welcomed us at their fires and shared venison. So we crossed the Laurel Hills and the Alleghenies.

On the final day, my faithful guide and I descended Will’s Creek—a wild, magnificent pass between cliffs nearly a thousand feet high—bare, white, and jagged like fortress towers. Eagles circled the peaks, guarding their nests in the crags.

From there, we descended to Cumberland, where we had marched the year before. Now, it held a substantial garrison of our own men. Oh, you may imagine what joy it was to see English colours once again flying over the banks of our native Potomac!

The previous evening, George Warrington had recounted his tale to Madame de Bernstein—though not in full, for the old lady dozed off repeatedly during his account. Only when he paused would she stir, murmuring, “Most interesting,” and urging him to go on. The young man fumbled through his words, stammering and blushing, clearly ill at ease. He spoke far less confidently than he had before his small, attentive audience in Hill Street—where Hetty’s wide-eyed wonder, Theo’s sympathetic gaze, his mother’s gentle smile, and his father’s amused expression had all served as encouragement enough. His father once joked that his wife’s tears were as powerful as Mr. Addison’s trunk-maker’s: if she were cast in a tragedy, she’d make it a success simply by weeping in the front row. That was why they’d chosen Lord Wrotham’s house as the stage for George’s first performance—to give him an audience that would truly appreciate him, not one like Madame Bernstein, whose indifference and weariness had dimmed his delivery.

“Very good and most interesting, I am sure, my dear sir,” said Madame Bernstein, raising three delicate fingers adorned with lace mittens to conceal a twitch of her lips. “And your mother must have been delighted to see you.”

George shrugged slightly and bowed low, catching his aunt’s sharp glance. “Have been delighted to see you,” she continued dryly, “and killed the fatted calf, and all that sort of thing. Though why I say *calf*, I don’t know, nephew George—for you were never the prodigal son. I may say *calf* to thee, my poor Harry! Thou hast been among the swine, surely. And evil companions have stripped you of your money and your coat.”

“He came to England, madam,” George replied, his voice rising slightly, “and his friends were yours.”

“Could not have come to worse advisers, nephew Warrington,” she snapped, lifting her chin. “I should have told my sister so earlier, had she condescended to write to me through him, as she has done through you.”

That night, as she prepared for a rout, she muttered to her maid: “This young gentleman’s mother is half sorry he’s alive again—I could see it in his face. She’s half sorry, and I am perfectly furious! Why didn’t he stay dead under that tree? And why did that young Florac carry him to the fort? I knew those Floracs in Paris, in the time of Monsieur le Régent. They were of the Ivry line—no great house before Henri IV. His ancestor was the king’s favourite. His ancestor—he! he!—his ancestress! Brett! *Entendez-vous*? Give me my card-purse. I don’t care for this young Monsieur George’s airs. Yet he bears a striking resemblance to his grandfather—the same look, sometimes the same tone. You’ve heard of Colonel Esmond when I was young? This boy has his eyes. I suppose I liked the Colonel because he loved me.”

Engaged in a card party—an amusement she never missed, whether weekday or Sabbath, so long as she could hold her trumps or sit upright—Madame Bernstein soon dismissed her two nephews after George finished speaking. To the elder, she offered a formal curtsey and a few fingers; but to Harry, she gave both hands and a warm pat on the cheek.

“My poor child,” she said, “now thou art disinherited, thou wilt see how differently the world treats thee. There is only one person in all London—a wicked, heartless old woman—who will treat thee as before.” She handed him a pocketbook. “Do not lose it at Ranelagh tonight. That suit does not become your brother nearly as well as it did you. You shall present your brother to everyone and walk up and down the room for at least two hours. Were I you, I would then go to the Chocolate-House and play as if nothing had changed. While you are there, your brother may return to me and eat a bit of chicken. My Lady Flint gives dreadful suppers, and I wish to discuss your mother’s letter with him. *Au revoir*, gentlemen!”

She departed for her toilette, her chairmen and torchbearers already waiting at the door.

The brothers went to Ranelagh, where only a few of Harry’s acquaintances happened to be present. They walked the rounds, met Mr. Tom Claypool and some countrymen, listened to music, and drank tea in a box. Harry acted as host, introducing George to the marvels of the place. George, in turn, was more excited than Harry had ever been on his own first visit—thrilled by the music, especially the full orchestra and a satisfying rendition of Handel. It was notable, too, that Harry showed respect for George’s passion for music at a time when playing the violin was considered effeminate and unmanly in England. Patriotic prints mocked such “frivolous accomplishments” as those of Squallini or Monsieurs. But today, no Briton boasts of ignorance. Conceit is rare. Dullness is unknown. Arrogance is extinct. Art, once an outsider, now holds near-equal status. If Mrs. Thrale were to marry a music master today, her friends would not flinch. If she had fortune and a good cook, people might even dine with her—despite the match—and treat Mr. Piozzi with civility.

After Ranelagh, following Madame Bernstein’s advice, George returned to her house while Harry went to the club, where gentlemen gathered nightly to dine and gamble. No one mentioned Harry’s recent absence. Mr. Ruff, his former landlord, greeted him with solemn courtesy, as though nothing had passed between them. Harry had already removed his belongings from Bond Street, and the brothers now lived elsewhere.

When supper ended and the men prepared to ascend to the gaming tables, Harry declared he would not play again. “I’ve burned my fingers already,” he said. “I can afford no more extravagance.”

“Why,” said Mr. Morris lightly, “you must have won more than you lost, Mr. Warrington, all things considered.”

“And of course I don’t know my own affairs as well as you do, Mr. Morris,” Harry replied sternly, remembering Morris’s coldness upon hearing of his arrest. “But I have another reason. A few months—or days ago—I was heir to a vast estate. I could afford to lose a little. Now, thank God, I am heir to nothing.”

He looked around, flushing slightly, at the group of gamblers lounging about the tables or near the fire.

“What do you mean, Mr. Warrington?” asked Lord March. “Have you lost Virginia too? Who has won it? I always fancied playing you myself for that stake.”

“And grow an improved breed of slaves in the colony,” added another.

“The rightful owner has won it,” Harry said. “You’ve heard me speak of my twin elder brother?”

“The one who died in Braddock’s affair two years ago? Yes. Good heavens, I hope he hasn’t come back to life!”

“He arrived in London two days ago. He was imprisoned in a French fort for eighteen months, escaped recently, and left our house in Virginia shortly after.”

“You haven’t had time to order mourning, I suppose?” asked Mr. Selwyn cheerfully. Simple Harry barely understood the joke until his brother explained it.

“Hang me, if I don’t believe the fellow is actually glad his brother’s come back!” exclaimed Lord March, as the conversation continued after Harry had left.

“These savages still practice simple virtues—affection, for instance,” yawned Selwyn. “They’re barely civilized in America yet.”

“They love their kin,” piped Mr. Walpole, “and scalp their enemies. It’s not Christian, but natural. Shouldn’t you like to witness a scalping-match, George? See a man skinned alive?”

“A man’s elder brother is his natural enemy,” said Mr. Selwyn calmly, arranging his counters.

“Torture is like broiled bones and pepper,” Horry continued. “You wouldn’t enjoy hanging afterward, George!”

“I’m hanged if there’s any man in England who’d want his elder brother alive,” declared Lord March.

“No more than his father, my lord!” cried Jack Morris.

“First time I’ve known you had one, Jack. Give me counters for five hundred.”

“I say,” Jack went on, “it’s all very fine about dead brothers coming back to life. But who’s to say it wasn’t a scheme between these two? Here comes a young fellow calling himself the Fortunate Youth, claiming to be a Virginian prince and heaven knows what, and getting into our society—”

A laugh broke out at Jack’s phrase “our society.”

“Who’s to know it wasn’t a cross?” Jack pressed. “The younger one comes first. He marries an heiress. Then, when he’s secured her, up rises the elder brother! When did this elder brother appear? Just when the younger’s plan was blown and all was lost! Who’ll tell me the older brother hasn’t been living in Seven Dials, eating tripe and cow-heel, until the younger was disposed of? Dammy, as gentlemen, I think we ought to take notice. This Mr. Warrington has taken a most outrageous liberty with the whole club.”

“Who put him up? Was it March?”

“Yes. But my lord thought he was putting up someone else. Didn’t you, March?”

“Hold your confounded tongue and mind your game!” the nobleman snapped.

Yet Jack Morris’s view found many allies. Many believed it indecorous for Harry to have ever accepted his brother’s death. The young man’s sudden appearance and behavior seemed suspicious. In short, there was growing unease about foreigners, adventurers, and such. One must be cautious.

Though Harry was free from prison, possessed Madame Bernstein’s generous gift, and had his brother restored—without once lamenting his return, as his friends at White’s imagined he would—though Maria had shown remarkable grace through his ordeal—yet when alone, Harry felt no joy. He smoked his pipe of Virginia tobacco with a troubled heart.

It was not the loss of his inheritance that distressed him. He knew his brother would share fairly, as he would have shared with him. But after all his struggles, doubts, and hopes, to find himself poor and bound irrevocably to his elderly cousin—yes, elderly indeed. When she visited that dreadful den in Cursitor Street and her tears washed away her rouge, she looked as old as his mother—her face wrinkled, yellowed. Thinking of her brought the same queasy feeling he’d felt when she fell ill in the coach en route to Tunbridge.

What would his mother say when he brought her home? What battles would ensue? He might flee to one of the plantations—far from home—and manage a few slaves, farm modestly, hunt often. But at Castlewood, or in any home he could build for her—what a life for poor Maria, who had grown up attending court, cards, balls, assemblies every night?

If only he could be overseer of the estates! He would be an honest factor, make up for his wasted years and reckless spending. Five thousand pounds—his entire fortune, accumulated over his minority—gone in six months! He was a beggar, except for George’s kindness. All he had left was an old wife—though a lovely one, dressed in velvet and silver lace, the poor lad in his best clothes. What a figure he had cut in Europe! What a fine end he had come to!

With all his grand friends at White’s and Newmarket, with all his extravagance—had he been happy a single day since arriving in Europe? Three days. Four. Yesterday evening, when he was with dear Mrs. Lambert and her kind daughters, and that brave Colonel. And the Colonel was right to rebuke him for his wasteful ways. He had been a brute to fly into a rage. God bless them all for their generosity!

These thoughts filled Harry’s pipe, and he smoked them quietly, waiting for his brother’s return from Madame Bernstein’s.

The Colonel Esmond, maternal grandfather of our Virginians and a man whose name has echoed through these pages, had spent many quiet years in the New World after leaving England behind. In the solitude of his American estate, he devoted part of his long leisure to writing down the story of his earlier life. These memoirs, though never published, were rich with personal recollections—and among them, Madame de Bernstein, known in her youth as Beatrice Esmond, held a prominent place. George Warrington had read these writings over and over again, so that by the time he met his aunt in person, he already knew her—knew her not as she was now, but as she once had been: young, radiant, and fiercely independent, a woman who had once stirred hearts and commanded attention.

Now, however, her beauty had faded; her eyes, once bright and bold, were dimmed by time; her spirit, once so lively, seemed dulled by the weight of years. And yet, as George watched her return from her evening gathering, rouged and adorned with diamonds, he could not help but think of what she must have been in her prime. Was it sorrow or satisfaction, he wondered, for such a woman to look back upon those days? When the heart grows cold, does it ache to remember how it once burned? When strength wanes, do we still find joy in recalling the fire of youth, the ease of laughter, the eagerness with which life was lived?

So it is with all things—roses bloom and fall, summer gives way to winter, and even the grandest palaces become ruins. “And that,” George thought, “was a beauty once.” He saw her now—this woman who had once been the center of admiration—surrounded by relics of her former glory. Crowds of lovers had once courted her; men had fallen silent before her presence. But now, only shadows remained.

He remembered a fireworks display at Williamsburg on the King’s birthday—the dazzling bursts of light, the sudden silence after the last spark died out, the hollow framework of the wheel left standing like a skeleton. That was what Aunt Beatrice’s past felt like to him now: brilliant, fleeting, and gone.

Harry had read the manuscripts too, but unlike George, he had no taste for reflection. Books did not interest him; introspection was not his nature. If he had pondered the words of his grandfather, he would not have drawn the same conclusions as his brother—nor would he have found any moral lesson in the tale of a woman’s lost splendor.

George said nothing about how intimately he knew his aunt’s history. There was no need. The truth stood plainly before him.

After dinner, the Baroness pointed to her escritoire with her cane and instructed her maid to fetch the letter beneath the inkwell. George recognized the handwriting immediately—it was the letter he had carried from Virginia.

“From this,” she said, fixing her nephew with a sharp glance, “it seems your return has brought some disagreement between you and my sister.”

“I did not know Madam Esmond mentioned it,” George replied.

She adjusted her spectacles—once famed for their fiery gaze—and scanned the letter before handing it to him.

It began:

> RICHMOND, VIRGINIA, December 26th, 1756
> HONOURED MADAM! AND SISTER!—I have received, and thankfully acknowledge, your ladyship’s letter of October 23rd, sent via the Rose packet. I reply at a season meant for peace and goodwill, though Heaven has seen fit to burden us still with sorrow and trial. My answer will be delivered by my eldest son, Mr. Esmond Warrington, who returned to us miraculously from the Valley of the Shadow of Death—as our previous correspondence has informed my poor Henry. He wishes, and I consent, to visit Europe, though he has been with us only briefly.

> I grieve deeply that my dear Harry should have presented himself in England under false pretenses—as if he were the rightful heir—when my son George, though dead to us, is still alive. Ah, madam! For eighteen months of captivity, what anguish have his mother’s and brother’s hearts endured! Harry’s heart is the tenderest of any man living. In the joy of seeing Mr. Esmond Warrington restored, he will forget the worldly loss he suffers. He will return to (comparative) poverty without regret. The most generous, the most obedient of sons, he willingly yields the inheritance that was his by birth—except for fate’s cruel twist—and the providential return of George.

> Your kindness toward my dear Harry will be doubly welcome now that he must live on a younger brother’s modest share. Many years ago, an excellent opportunity arose to secure his future here in Virginia—he might now own a noble estate, slaves, and stand well among the gentry, had his mother’s wishes been followed and his father’s small fortune invested wisely. But legal formalities, and—I regret to say—my elder son’s scruples, prevented it. This chance was lost. Yet Harry’s savings have been carefully preserved—may he long enjoy them! May Heaven bless you, dear sister, for whatever aid you may offer!

> From your letter, I understand the sum allotted to him has not covered his expenses among fine company. And rightly so—being the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, one who nearly succeeded to his lordship’s title, he deserves equal footing with any nobleman in Britain. I have a sum set aside, always intended for his establishment. I entrust it to my eldest son, who, to his credit, holds deep affection for his brother, to use as best suits Harry’s needs.

At this point, George interrupted: “It took him out of prison yesterday, madam. I think that was the best use we could make of it.”

“Nay, sir!” she retorted sharply. “Why not buy him a commission? Or help him acquire land and slaves, if he fancies home? Besides, I had a mind to pay that debt myself.”

“I hope you’ll let him handle it,” George said calmly. “I ask leave to act as my brother’s banker. I’ve borrowed much from my mother—let me repay it to Harry.”

“Do you indeed?” she said, raising an eyebrow. “Give me a glass of wine. You’re a spendthrift, nephew! Read on—you’ll see your mother agrees. Here, drink to your health. Good Burgundy. Your grandfather never cared for Burgundy—he drank claret, when he drank at all.”

George continued:

> This remittance should cover any expenses Harry may have incurred due to the misunderstanding of his status. I wish I could trust my elder son’s prudence as fully as I do my Harry’s! But I fear Mr. Esmond W. has learned little humility during his captivity—though I have always taught it to my children. Should you show him these lines, when the Great Ocean divides us, he shall know that a mother’s prayers and blessings follow both her sons. No act I have ever done, no desire I have ever expressed—however little he may have obeyed—has not been for their welfare.

There was a scratch on the paper, made with a penknife, and a large stain, as if water had fallen upon it.

“Your mother writes well,” the Baroness remarked. “Did you two quarrel?”

“Yes, ma'am,” George answered quietly. “Many times. The last was over money—ransom promised to the old lieutenant who helped me escape. I told you he had a mistress, a poor Indian woman who aided me. Six weeks after my return, she arrived in Richmond, having traveled the same path I did. She brought me the token Museau had promised—a sign he’d assisted my flight. A new commander and reinforcements had reached Duquesne. Charges—of corruption, though unclear—were laid against Museau. He was arrested, tried to flee, but failed. Shot on the ramparts, he sent the woman to me with my grandfather’s watch and a note written in blood: *Send ce que je scavais* to a notary in Havre de Grace, France, to be forwarded to his family in Caen. Silverheels, the hunter, helped her reach safety. Without him, she might have been scalped.

“But at home, they received her coldly. They gave her no real welcome. I won’t say what suspicions they harbored—about her and me. She fell into drinking whenever possible. I ordered food and shelter for her, but she became a joke among the servants, a subject of gossip in town. Fortunately, the Governor was reasonable. I persuaded him to grant her passage back to her people. Her grief at parting only confirmed their doubts. A preacher condemned me from the pulpit—I believe. I had to cane another man. And I argued fiercely with Madam Esmond—our quarrel remains unresolved—because I insisted on paying the ransom to Museau’s heirs, as I had promised.

“You see,” George concluded, “scandal thrives at the edge of the wilderness, just as it does in the Old World.”

“Ah,” said Madame Bernstein softly, “I have suffered from it myself, my dear. Fill your glass. A touch of cherry brandy—’twill do you good.”

The letter continued:

> As for my poor Harry’s marriage—though I know, from bitter experience, the dangers youth faces, and would keep my boy from them at any cost, even if I wished him to marry a woman of rank, as befits his birth—Lady Maria Esmond is entirely out of the question. Her age is nearly mine. And I know my brother Castlewood left his daughters with the smallest portions. My Harry is so obedient that a word from me will be enough to end this imprudent match. Some once believed I myself considered a second marriage—with someone far above our station. No! I knew what was due to my children. Mr. Esmond W., as successor to this estate, is amply provided for. Now, my task is to save for his less fortunate brother. And since I do not wish to live alone, let him return soon to his loving mother.

> Your account of Harry fills my heart with gratitude. He is everything a mother could desire. A year in Europe will refine him beyond what Virginia can offer. Mr. Stack, our minister in Richmond, has a letter from Mr. Ward—my children’s tutor—who knows Lady Warrington and her admirable family. He reports that Harry has been with his cousins lately. I am thankful he has such good influence. May he heed their counsel and walk the path of true wisdom. Adieu, dear madam and sister! Accept the heartfelt thanks of a mother’s love. Though we have been apart, may these ties grow stronger. I am grateful you spoke kindly of my dear father—he truly was one of the finest men. He, too, thanks you for your kindness to one of his children. His daughter,
> With sincere thanks, your ladyship’s most dutiful and grateful sister and servant,

> P.S.—I have spoken with Lady Maria, but there is no need to tell her or Harry that either you or I hope to increase his fortune. The match is wholly unsuitable.

When George finished reading, he laid the letter down.

“As for myself, madam,” he said, “your letter reveals nothing new. I always knew Harry was the favorite son—deservedly so. He possesses qualities I lack. He has better looks—”

“Nay,” the Baroness interjected, glancing at him slyly, “that is not your fault. Were it not for his fair hair and your dark skin, one might pass for the other.”

George bowed slightly, a faint blush rising on his pale cheek.

“His disposition is bright, mine dark,” he went on. “Harry is cheerful; I am not. He wins affection easily; I have few friends.”

“My sister and you have your little disputes,” the Baroness observed. “We had such in our family. And if Madam Esmond takes after our mother—”

“My mother always called hers an angel upon earth,” George broke in.

“Eh!” she snapped. “That’s what people say when they’re dead! Rachel Castlewood was an angel, if you like—but angels are often inconvenient to live with. Perhaps they’re too pure for our sinful world. The air down here doesn’t agree with them. My poor mother was so perfect she couldn’t forgive me for being otherwise. Ah, mon Dieu! How she oppressed me with her heavenly airs!”

George lowered his eyes, remembering his own lonely youth. He did not wish to reveal more of his family secrets to this worldly woman, who seemed to read his thoughts despite his silence.

“I quite understand you, sir,” she said, “even when you speak not a word. A sermon every morning, one at night, and three on Sundays—that’s what people call goodness. Every pleasure forbidden. Balls are abominations. Theater is sin. Cards are damnation! What a life! Mon Dieu, what a life!”

“We played cards every night when we pleased,” George smiled. “And my grandfather loved Shakespeare so much, my mother never objected to his favorite author.”

“I recall,” she tapped her fan, “he could quote whole passages. Though I prefer Mr. Congreve. And then there was that dreadful Milton—whom he and Addison pretended to admire!”

“If you don’t care for Shakespeare,” George said gently, “you won’t quarrel with my mother for being indifferent to him. Indeed, I believe you misjudge her. Wherever there are the poor, she helps them. Wherever there are the sick—”

“She poisons them with her foul purges and pills!” the Baroness exclaimed.

“Of course,” George said, “just as your mother did.”

“She does her best!” he insisted. “She acts in good faith, doing what she believes is right.”

“I don’t blame you,” she said, “for keeping your counsel. But there is one thing we all agree on—this foolish marriage must be stopped. Do you know how old the woman is? I can tell you, though she tore the first page from the family Bible at Castlewood.”

“My mother knows her cousin’s age,” George replied. “She finds the difference shocking. A city-bred woman of that age, used to London society, would find our plantation a dismal place. And the house—such as it is—is not Harry’s. He is welcome, Heaven knows—perhaps more welcome than I, who inherit it by right. But I doubt his wife would—would like our colony.”

The Baroness laughed sharply.

“He, he! Nephew Warrington! Speak freely. I’ll tell no tales to your mother—though I know she has a temper and loves her own way. Harry has kept quiet, but it needed no wizard to see who ruled the household. I love my niece, Lady Molly, so dearly I’d wish her three years in Virginia under your mother’s rule. You look alarmed! Harry has said enough to show me who governs.”

“Madam,” George said, smiling, “I may say this: I don’t envy any woman coming into our house against my mother’s will. And my brother knows this well.”

“What? You two have discussed it? Of course you have. And the fool thinks himself bound by honor—of course he does, the gaby!”

“He says Lady Maria behaved nobly,” George explained. “When he was imprisoned, she brought him her jewels and every guinea she owned. That touched him deeply—he feels more obligated than ever. But I confess, he seems bound by duty rather than love—such is his present feeling.”

“My good creature,” the Baroness said, “don’t you see? Maria brings trinkets and a few guineas to Mr. Esmond, the heir of a great Virginia estate—not to the second son, who is penniless and has squandered every shilling. I swear, on my honor, that knowing Harry’s stubbornness and the misery awaiting him, I tried to bribe Maria to break off the engagement. I failed—because I couldn’t bribe high enough. When he was in prison, I sent my lawyer to him, offering to pay his debts—if he would leave her. But Maria had already acted. Harry refused to go back on his word.”

Then, with a wicked twinkle, she recounted the affair in full—the cynical terms, the sharp truths, the kind of language that passed among the elite in her day, though we no longer utter such things in polite company. And perhaps that is for the better. We may not be more virtuous, but we are more decent. We may not be purer, but we are cleaner.

She talked so long, so cleverly, that she was delighted with herself and her audience. As Mrs. Brett helped her retire, she declared she had changed her opinion of George—now he was handsome, witty, far superior to poor Harry (whose intellect, she admitted, was sadly limited), and possessed a certain melancholy dignity that reminded her of the Colonel.

Had she ever told Brett about the Colonel? Many times, no doubt. And tonight, she told her again.

Meanwhile, George, walking home late, was not so pleased. What a strange picture of life he had seen! How bitterly she mocked everyone—yet revealed, in her scorn, the selfishness of her own family, the petty ambitions, the grasping desires, the endless pursuit of trivial rewards. The scenes of faded pleasures, hollow triumphs, and wasted lives—how they painted the world around her!

“Are these the heirs of noble blood?” he asked himself, passing houses where guests were leaving, chairmen yawning over dying torches. “Are these the proud bearers of ancient names and ancestral honors? Our family tree bears coats-of-arms and titles older than the Conquest. Did knights of old turn away from a friend in need? Did noble lords deceive defenseless women? Did chivalry cheat at dice or lie about horses? Can it be that this worldly woman has deceived my poor Harry? That her tears are false, and she will abandon him when she learns he is poor? Shall we pack our trunks and sail home?”

He reached his door, still turning over these thoughts. Gumbo came forward, yawning, candle in hand. Inside, Harry sat asleep before the cold hearth, his pipe ashed out beside him.

He woke suddenly, eyes clouded by sleep—then lit with joy at the sight of George.

“There he is, flesh and blood, thank God!” he exclaimed, throwing an arm around his brother. “I was dreaming of you—Ward giving us our lesson! Remember the ruler, Georgy? Bless my soul—it’s three o’clock! Where have you been, Mr. George? Supped? I ate at White’s, but I’m hungry again. I didn’t play—no, no! Not for younger brothers! And Lord March paid me fifty pounds he lost to me. I bet against his horse and backed the Duke of Hamilton’s! They raced this morning—Lord March was under weight. He lost. Paid up. And was as sour as a bear. Let’s have one pipe, Georgy—just one.”

And after the smoke, the brothers went to bed. May they rest well—for there is no greater comfort than to see brothers who love one another.

Of course, the two young men had spoken at length of home—of the people they knew, the happenings in their absence, and all that had shaped their lives since last they met. How were Harry’s dogs? Was little Dempster still as lively as ever? What of old Nathan, who had served their family for generations? And was Mountain well? Had Fanny grown into a fine young woman? George listened with amusement as Harry recounted how Parson Broadbent’s daughter had become engaged to Tom Barker of Savannah, and how they were planning to settle in Georgia.

Harry confessed he had once been deeply smitten by the parson’s daughter—so much so that he’d spent more than his share of pocket money at cards and consumed gallons of strong spirits just to keep near her. But, as he ruefully admitted, Madam Esmond would never have allowed such a match. “She’d have said I was throwing myself away on Polly Broadbent,” he laughed. “And she was right—though I did love her enough to make fools of myself.”

George then shared news of Colonel Washington’s wife—a pleasant, attractive woman of good fortune whom he had brought to Richmond. He described, with wry humor, the formalities of the visit between his mother and the new Mrs. Washington, and how his mother had greeted her with an almost comical politeness. “Never mind, George,” Mrs. Mountain had said, chuckling. “The Colonel has taken another wife, but I’m certain two young gentlemen I know nearly ended up with a six-foot-two stepfather!”

Indeed, Mountain was always imagining matches where none existed. Two people could hardly sit down to tea or play a hand of cards without her declaring it was clearly a sign of destiny. It was she—the busybody—who had first whispered about the Indian woman, Biche. When Parson Stack mentioned it to Madam Esmond, she dismissed the idea with scorn: “I’d as soon believe Mr. Esmond stole the silver spoons or married a kitchen maid.” Yet though she refused to believe the accusation, her coldness toward Biche was unmistakable. The poor woman, hurt and humiliated, withdrew into the servants’ quarters, where she drowned her sorrow in drink.

George painted a bleak picture of his time at home. “The birthright is mine, Harry,” he said, “but you are the favorite—and God help me, I think my mother resents that. Why must I be the elder? If you had come first, you’d have had the best cellar, the finest horse, the most respect in the county. Instead, I am the one no one trusts, the one who frightens them with my silence. I should have been second son—gone to law, or come to England for my degrees, become a parson, and said grace at your table. But fate has placed me here, and now I’m cursed with being the one who must fix what’s broken.”

“Why, Georgy,” Harry replied, grinning, “you’re quoting poetry now! You sound like some scholar from a book.”

“I suppose someone spoke those lines before me,” George said, smiling faintly. “It’s from one of your books. You read every word ever written, don’t you?”

“That’s true,” Harry admitted, voice thick with emotion. “And I remember how you used to talk about them—how much they meant to you. That’s why I liked seeing the authors at Tunbridge. I took off my hat to them—not because I cared for their writing, but because I remembered how much they mattered to you.”

He paused, eyes glistening. “To see you again—it feels like a dream. Do you remember that bloody Indian with his knife at your throat? I’d give anything to repay Monsieur de Florac for saving you—but I’ve nothing left but my gold knee-buckles. They’re worth less than two guineas.”

“You have half of what I possess,” George said gently. “We’ll divide it when I’ve paid the Frenchman.”

At this, Harry erupted not only in praise but in fervent oaths—outbursts born of deep affection and relief. He swore there had never been a better brother than George. For days after his arrival, Harry followed him with his eyes. He’d drop his knife and fork mid-meal, or lay aside his newspaper, just to watch George and smile to himself. Walking through Hyde Park or along the Mall, he’d turn to the crowd as if to say, “Look—this is my brother! This is the man who was dead and now lives again! Is there any other brother in Christendom like him?”

He insisted George fulfill his promise to pay Museau’s heirs the twelve thousand livres he’d pledged for his ransom. But this had caused great distress at home. With Museau dead, Madam Esmond argued passionately—nearly angrily—that the bargain was void. The man had been a rogue, she declared. She refused to reward sin. Mr. Esmond had his own inheritance; let him spend it if he wished. But she would not consent to giving money to peasants in Normandy—enemies of England—who would likely send every penny to priests and the pope. It was extravagance, wickedness. If George wanted to squander his father’s fortune (and she noted he hadn’t shown such eagerness before, especially when Harry’s inheritance was at stake), why not give it to his own blood—to poor Harry, suddenly stripped of his future? Why send it across the sea?

This argument had raged between mother and son throughout George’s final days in Virginia. It remained unresolved. On the morning of his departure, Madam Esmond came to his bedside after a sleepless night and asked whether he still intended to throw away his father’s property. He answered, heavy with grief and duty, that his word was given—he must honor it. She replied that she would continue praying Heaven might soften his proud heart and help her bear her burdens. The last image George carried of her was of her standing beside his bed—pale, silent, eyes dry—before slowly turning and leaving.

“Where did you learn to win everyone over, Harry?” George asked later. “How is it that you and everyone else begin as friends? Teach me some of your secrets—though I may not want to learn them. I find it oddly pleasing when people hate me.”

At first, in Richmond, he had been admired. Mr. Esmond Warrington, the sole survivor from Braddock’s defeat, had been welcomed with kindness—by the town, by the clergy, even by Madam Esmond herself. The parson preached a sermon praising his escape; neighbors visited him; the family coach was sent out. There were whispers of admiration—perhaps even flirtation. But Mother swiftly quashed any warmth. Her haughtiness frightened people away. His popularity faded before the final blow: the appearance of Biche.

He wasn’t jolly enough for the officers, who preferred drinking, dice, and coarse talk. Too sharp-tongued for the ladies, whose endless gossip bored him as much as the men’s boasting. “I can’t tell you, Harry,” he said, “how lonely I felt among all that noise and scandal. I missed my prison—even Duquesne—where I had peace and freedom of thought.”

He was shy, he admitted. He could speak freely to few. Most of the time, he sat in silence. At home, it had been Harry who carried the conversation at meals, occasionally earning a smile from their mother. When George and she were together, they had little in common—no subject to discuss until they clashed over theology or law.

So the gentlemen deemed him aloof and dull. The ladies found him cold, sarcastic—never sure if he meant what he said. Before long, they decided he was unpleasant. Then came Biche.

“Oh, what a character they made of me!” George cried, furious. “What a life they gave me after Museau’s messenger arrived! Boys hooted at her if she walked the street. Ladies offered half-curtseys and crossed to the other side. That hypocritical clergyman went from tea party to tea party preaching about seduction and the sins of popish lands. And when Biche returned home weeks later—well, they declared it was a plot between us. Some said she waited on the other side of the river until I signaled her to cross. Officers mocked me at the coffeehouse, cracking jokes about the woman I’d chosen.”

“The world,” he spat, “is a cruel place.”

He considered fleeing to Castlewood—his mother found the estate dreary, and her only comfort was Mr. Stack’s sermons—when news reached him of Harry’s troubles. “That gave me a reason to leave,” he said. “And I think we were all glad to have an excuse.”

“I’d like to see any of those scoundrels who spoke against you,” Harry roared, pacing the room. “I’d break their bones! I did something similar for Bob Clubber.”

“For that sneaking, backbiting, toad-eating wretch who follows my lord around Greenway Court?” George asked. “If you whipped him, I hope you gave him a proper beating!”

“We were bound over to keep the peace,” George replied. “I offered to go to Maryland and settle things there—but of course, the good folk said, ‘Well, he’s already broken the seventh commandment—why not the sixth?’ So, with that and that—I left home, Harry, with a reputation worse than any young man ever earned—though I’m as innocent of the crime as you are.”

Ah, what a chance this offers for moralizing! If only the reader and I could gather—could write down, could publish with illustrations—all the lies told about each of us since we became men—what a harrowing, thrilling tale it would make! Not only do people know everything about us, but far more. Recently, the postman delivered a paper containing a critique that stated: “This author claims he was born in such-and-such a year. It is a lie. He was born in another.” The critic knew better—of course he did. Another, from the land that gave birth to Mulligan, warned a friend: “Don’t mention New South Wales to him. He has a brother there, and the family never speaks his name.”

But such subjects are too vast for a single paragraph. One day, I shall prepare a memoir—or better yet, let a society of literary men compile a series of biographies—lives of gentlemen, as told by friends they never knew.

Having laid bare his trials, George now turned to hear Harry’s story. Harry spoke frankly of his feelings toward the family of Castlewood—not for losing at cards, for he was honest in games, but for refusing aid to the chaplain in need and dismissing him with false excuses. As for Mr. Will, Harry had settled matters after the horse-dealing affair, marking his disapproval plainly upon the man’s face.

Regarding the Countess and Lady Fanny, Harry spoke cautiously but not kindly. He had heard stories—about the Countess as a card-playing old woman, Lady Fanny as a reckless flirt. Who told him? A person who knew them well—Maria herself, during those days of open trust mentioned in the previous volume. Maria had confided many tales about her stepmother and half-sister, none of which reflected well on either.

But when it came to Lady Maria, Harry was firm. “It may be imprudent,” he said. “I won’t deny it. I may be a fool—I think I am. I know there will be a terrible fight at home. Madam and she will clash. But we can live apart. Our estate is large enough. I can go elsewhere—anywhere but Richmond or Castlewood. When you inherit, you’ll give me a portion—at worst, Madam will rent it cheaply. Or I’ll become a farmer or factor. I cannot, I will not, leave Maria. She has done so much for me—she brought every jewel she owned, dear brave soul, and threw them into my lap with her last guinea. God bless her!”

Here he wiped his eyes with his sleeve, stamped his foot, and declared, “No, brother—I won’t part from her. Not even if I were made Governor of Virginia tomorrow. And you—my dearest old George—would never advise me to do so.”

“I am here to advise you,” George said quietly. “I am here to try to end this engagement—if I can. I cannot imagine a more unfortunate match. But I cannot counsel you to break your word, my boy.”

“I knew you couldn’t,” Harry replied, darkly. “What’s said is said, George. I’ve made my bed. Now I must lie in it.”

Such was their understanding when they first discussed Harry’s love affair. But after George’s conversation with his aunt, and the deeper insights gained from Mr. Warrington—whose skeptical nature led him to question everything—doubt began to creep in. Was Maria truly in love with Harry, or was it his wealth? His looks? Were the stories Aunt Bernstein had told true? Certainly, he could not urge Harry to break his promise. But perhaps—just perhaps—he could devise a way to test her sincerity. And it was this thought, this quiet calculation, that shaped the actions he would take next—actions that seemed unkind, but were born of concern.

My Lord Castlewood possessed a grand house in Kensington Square, spacious enough to accommodate his noble household and conveniently situated near the palace when His Majesty resided there. Her ladyship entertained guests with evening gatherings and card parties, though Kensington was still considered remote from London a century past—so much so that George Selwyn once confessed he dared not venture there after dark, fearing either highwaymen masked in crape or ladies in rouge at the quadrille table, though which danger was more likely no one could say.

On the morning following Harry Warrington’s unexpected reappearance at White’s Club, the entire family gathered for breakfast—Mr. Will included, who was to take up duties in the royal service later that afternoon.

The ladies arrived first, sipping chocolate; Mr. Will joined them in full court attire; finally, my lord appeared, languid and unshaven, still clad in bedgown and nightcap, his wig yet unfastened. He took up his *Daily Advertiser* as Will burst into the room with news he had brought from the Star and Garter the previous night, where he’d dined with men who’d heard it whispered at White’s and seen it confirmed at Ranelagh.

“Heard what? Seen what?” asked the head of the house, scanning the paper.

“Ask Maria!” said Lady Fanny.
