My lord turned to his elder sister, whose face wore an expression of profound sorrow, her pallor stark as linen.

“Only one of Will’s usual polished inventions,” Maria declared.

“No!” swore Will, throwing out several oaths. “It wasn’t invented. Tom Claypool of Norfolk saw both brothers at Ranelagh. Jack Morris came straight from White’s, where he heard it from Harry Warrington himself—his own lips! Curse him—I’m glad of it!” he roared, slapping the table. “What do you think of your Fortunate Youth, your Virginian, whom you praised so highly, turning out to be a second son?”

“The elder brother not dead?” asked my lord.

“No more dead than you are. Never was. I suspect it was some kind of mix-up between the two.”

“Mr. Warrington is incapable of such deceit!” cried Maria.

“I never encouraged the fellow,” said my lady. “I assure you, nor did Fanny—nor we, indeed!”

“Nor we, indeed!” echoed Lady Fanny.

“The man is nothing but a beggar,” continued Will, “and probably hasn’t paid for the clothes on his back. I’m glad of it—hang him, I loathe him!”

“You don’t look upon him kindly, especially since he blacked your eye, Will,” grinned my lord. “So the poor lad has found his brother—and lost his estate.” Here he turned to Maria, whose grief seemed almost comical to the humorist beside her. After a moment’s gaze, he burst into a sharp laugh that flushed her cheeks and soon brought tears to her eyes.

“It’s a shame! It’s a shame!” she sobbed, hiding her face in her handkerchief.

Her stepmother and sister exchanged glances. “We never quite understand your lordship’s humour,” the former remarked gravely.

“I don’t see why you should,” replied my lord coolly. “Maria, my dear, please forgive me if I’ve said—or done—anything to wound you.”

“Done anything? You stripped the boy of everything in his prosperity, and now mock him in ruin!” Maria rose, glaring around the table. “You’re known throughout the world as the man who feeds on his own flesh and blood. Now that you have taken all he had, you make sport of his downfall!”

And with that, she swept from the room, casting defiant looks at each member of the assembly.

“Tell us what happened, Will,” said my lady, “and let my sister’s distress not interrupt us.” And Will recounted, with great detail and immense satisfaction at Harry’s misfortune, the tale now spreading through London: George Warrington’s sudden appearance.

Lord Castlewood felt genuine pity for Harry. He was a good, brave young man, and despite their differences, he had liked him—as people often like one another in this world, not for virtue, but for convenience. True, he had played cards with Harry and profited from market dealings—but why not? If others would pluck the fruit, he might as well eat it. Indeed, if that were all his conscience reproached him for, he needn’t fret much. “Where does Mr. Warrington live?” he asked.

Will shrugged, expressing readiness to enter eternal damnation if he knew or cared.

“He shall be invited here,” said my lord, “and treated with every respect.”

“Including piquet, I suppose?” growled Will.

“Or will you send him to the stables and sell him one of your bargain horses, Will?” asked Lord Castlewood. “You’d have won from Harry fast enough—if you could. But you cheat so clumsily that you got hit with a cudgel. I insist that our cousin Warrington receive every courtesy.”

“And that you won’t be disturbed when you sit down to play, of course, my lord?” Lady Castlewood interjected.

“Madam, I desire fair play—for Mr. Warrington, for myself, and for every member of this amiable family,” retorted my lord sharply.

“Heaven help the poor gentleman if your lordship means to be kind to him,” murmured the stepmother with a curtsey.

No one knew how far the argument might go—until, at that very moment, a phaeton drew up before the house, carrying the two young Virginians.

It was the carriage Harry had bought in his days of wealth. He still drove it; George sat beside him, their negro servants behind. Harry had offered to surrender the reins and the vehicle entirely. “What use have I, a poor devil like me, for horses and carriages, Georgy?” he had humbly said. “Beyond the coat on my back and the purse Aunt gave me, I have nothing. Take the driving seat, brother—it’ll ease my mind.”

George laughed, saying he didn’t know the way, but Harry did. As for the carriage, he claimed only half—just as he had already divided his wardrobe. “But a bargain is a bargain,” he added. “If I share thy coats, thou must divide my breeches’ pocket, Harry—that’s fair dealing.”

Again and again, Harry insisted there had never been such a brother on earth. How the horses clattered over the road! How proud and joyful he was to drive such a brother! They arrived in high spirits, and Gumbo’s thunderous knock upon Lord Castlewood’s door was worthy of the most imposing footman in St. James’s.

Only Lady Castlewood and her daughter, Lady Fanny, were in the drawing-room when the young men were announced. Will avoided facing Harry; my lord was not dressed; Maria remained absent—perhaps until her tears had dried.

When we arrive at friends’ homes today, with our coaches-and-six, John announcing our names, and we enter the drawing-room in our finest hats and smiles, does it ever happen that we interrupt a family quarrel? That we glide in smiling, stepping over the smoldering embers of a domestic fire still hot beneath the ashes? That just between the hall and the parlor, the Joneses have arranged themselves into a carefully composed tableau—the girl arranging flowers, one reclining over a devotional book, mother on the sofa with the butcher’s ledger hidden under a cushion, knitting in hand, a little foot extended prettily—while honest Mr. Jones, instead of muttering, “Curse that Brown, always calling here!” extends a welcoming hand and exclaims, “What, Brown, my boy! Delighted to see you! Hope you’ve come to lunch!” I ask: does it ever happen that we become unwitting victims of domestic artifice, spectators of comedies staged solely for our amusement? Oh, let us be grateful—not only for faces, but for masks! Not only for honest welcome, but for hypocrisy, which hides the unwelcome from our sight! While I speak thus lightly, what right have you, good sir, to know what truly passes within my mind? Perhaps I’m suffering from gout, or my eldest son has just sent me a thousand pounds in college bills, or I’m writhing from the sting of the *Stoke Pogis Sentinel*, or perhaps dinner is dreadfully skimpy, the leftovers of a party I didn’t invite you to—and yet I conceal my pain, wear a cheerful smile, and say, “What! Come to take pot-luck with us, Brown, my boy! Betsy! Put a knife and fork for Mr. Brown. Eat! Welcome! Fall to! It’s my best!” I call this deception beautiful self-denial—hypocrisy, true virtue. Oh, if every man spoke his mind, how unbearable society would be!

As the young gentlemen entered, Lady Castlewood approached them with ease and warmth. “We’ve heard, Harry,” she said, fixing a particular kindness on him, “of this extraordinary turn of events. My lord said at breakfast he would call on you today, Mr. Warrington. And cousin Harry, we mean not to love you any less because you’re poor.”

“We can now show it’s not your acres we love, but you,” added Lady Fanny, following her mother’s lead.

“And I, to whom the acres have fallen?” said Mr. George, bowing with a smile.

“Oh, cousin, we shall love you for being like Harry!” replied Lady Fanny archly.

Ah! Who has traveled the world without admiring the astonishing grace with which fine ladies drop you and then pick you up again? The ladies now addressed themselves almost exclusively to the younger brother. They were civil to George, but with Harry they were tender, familiar, gentle, affectionate—reproachful even. Why hadn’t Harry come to visit them in days?

“Better to have shared tea and piquet with us than with others,” said Lady Castlewood. “If we’d won enough to buy a paper of pins from you, we’d have been content. But young gentlemen never know what’s good for them,” she added.

“Now you have no money to play with, you can come and play with us, cousin!” exclaimed Lady Fanny, lifting a finger. “So your misfortune becomes our fortune!”

George was baffled. This reception was unlike anything he’d expected. All these attentions lavished on the younger brother, who had no guinea left! Perhaps these people weren’t so bad after all? The Blackest of all Blacks is said not to be quite as dark as some describe him.

This warm conversation lasted twenty minutes, when my lord appeared, wig in place, sword at side. He greeted both young men politely—equally. “Had you come to us earlier—though I rejoice to see you now—how regrettable it would have been! A certain evening of piquet might never have occurred. A younger son would have shown more prudence.”

“Yes, indeed,” said Harry.

“Or a kinsman more compassion. But I fear the passion for play runs in our blood. I inherited it from my father, and it made me the poorest peer in England. Those fair ladies before you are not exempt. Poor Brother Will is a martyr to it. What I win one day, I lose the next. The rage for play in England is shocking. All of my poor cousin’s banknotes left me within twenty-four hours of receipt.”

“I’ve played, like other gentlemen,” said Mr. Warrington, “but never to harm myself, nor ever truly cared for the game.”

“When we heard my lord played with Harry,” the ladies chimed in, “we scolded him terribly.”

“But had it not been me, cousin Warrington,” said my lord, “some other would have taken your money. A poor consolation, but such as Harry must accept—glad that friends won his money, who care for him, rather than strangers who cared nothing and fleeced him.”

“Eh! A tooth out is a tooth out, even if your brother pulls it, my lord,” said Mr. George, laughing. “Harry must bear the consequences of his faults, pay his debts like any man.”

“I have never said otherwise,” replied Harry. “It’s not English to be sulky when beaten.”

“Your hand, cousin!” exclaimed my lord delightedly. “You speak like a man!” The ladies smiled at each other.

“My sister in Virginia knows how to raise her sons as gentlemen!” declared Lady Castlewood, enthused.

“I protest you must not grow so amiable now you’re poor, cousin Harry!” said Fanny. “Why, mamma, we didn’t know half your good qualities when you were only the Fortunate Youth and Prince of Virginia! You’re exactly like him, cousin George—but I vow you can’t be as amiable as your brother!”

“I am the Prince of Virginia,” said George gravely, “but I fear I am not the Fortunate Youth.”

Harry began, “By Jove, he is the best—” when the sound of a harpsichord drifted from above.

The lad blushed. The ladies smiled.

“That’s Maria,” said Lady Castlewood. “Let some of us go to her.”

They rose and moved toward the door, Harry following, deeply embarrassed. George stepped forward, but Lord Castlewood detained him. “Nay, if all the ladies follow your brother,” he said, “let me at least enjoy your company. I long to hear the story of your captivity and rescue, cousin George!”

“Oh, we must hear that too!” called one of the ladies, lingering.

“I am greedy,” said my lord, looking sternly at her, “and would prefer to have it all to myself.” He followed the women to the door and closed it with a low bow.

“Your brother has doubtless told you of all that has transpired here, cousin George?” asked his kinsman.

“Yes,” replied George, “including the quarrel with Mr. Will and the engagement to Lady Maria.”

“I may be forgiven for saying he has met with ill fortune here, my lord.”

“Which no one deplores more than I. My brother lives among jockeys and trainers, the wildest of town rakes. There is little sympathy between us. We live together only because we are so poor. This house belonged to our grandmother before she went to America and married Colonel Esmond. Much of the furniture was hers.” George looked about the panelled room with interest.

“Our house has not prospered in twenty years, though we gained a title two decades ago thanks to court influence. But the plague of gambling has ruined us all. I am its miserable victim—too proud to sell myself and my title to a commoner, as many noblemen have done. Pride is my fault, cousin. I remember how I was born!” And he placed a hand on his shirt-frill, turned out his toe, and looked George squarely in the eye.

Young George Warrington naturally believed everyone who spoke to him. Once deceived, however, he became utterly skeptical. He inwardly laughed at my lord’s speech, though kept his face grave and allowed no scorn to show.

“We all have our flaws, my lord. Gambling has been forgiven countless times among gentlemen of our rank. Having forgiven my brother, I cannot presume to judge you. Instead of losing, I wish you had both won!”

“So do I, with all my heart,” sighed my lord. “I take heart from your words, cousin—your wisdom and understanding of the world seem greater than most young men of your age possess. Your brother Harry has the finest heart, though I wonder if his head is strong.”

“Not very strong, indeed. But he wins friends wherever he goes. Despite his recklessness, most people love him.”

“I do—we all do, as if he were our own brother!” exclaimed my lord.

“He often described his welcome here in his letters. My mother keeps them all. Harry’s style is not learned, but his heart is so good that reading him is better than wit.”

“I believe his brother possesses both heart and wit,” said my lord, stubbornly gracious.

“I am as Heaven made me, cousin. Perhaps I’ve endured more experience and sorrow than most young men.”

“This misfortune—no, this good fortune—your sudden reappearance—has not left Harry entirely without resources?” Lord Castlewood asked gently.

“Only what my mother can leave him, or I may spare him at her death. What is the usual portion for a younger brother here, my lord?”

“Ah, a younger brother here…” said my lord, shrugging. “Everyone knows what a younger brother is.”

George pressed on: “We are friends, but we are flesh and blood. I do not pretend to give him more than is customary. Why give him money? To squander it at cards or racing? We have cards and jockeys in Virginia too. My poor Harry has already distinguished himself in his own country before coming to yours. He inherits the family failing for dissipation.”

“Poor fellow, poor fellow—I pity him!”

“Our estate is large, but our income small. We earn little more than what we get from England for our tobacco—and even that is scarce, for it comes back in goods: cloth, leather, groceries, ironmongery, even wine and beer for ourselves and our people. Harry may return and share all this: a horse in the stable, venison on the table, a little ready cash, a coat or two yearly. This continues while my mother lives—unless, as is likely, he quarrels with Madam Esmond. Then, while I live, he’ll have access to the house and all it holds. If I die leaving children, he’ll be less and less welcome. His future, my lord, is bleak unless some miracle occurs. Henceforth, he is doomed to dependence—and I know no worse fate than relying on a woman like our mother. The means he used to command respect at home, he has wasted here. He has thrown his inheritance to the dogs. Poverty and servitude are now his only lot.”

Mr. Warrington delivered this speech with spirit and fluency. His cousin listened respectfully.

“You speak well, Mr. Warrington. Have you considered public life?”

“Of course,” replied George. “Like every man of my station—every man who cares for something beyond dice or stables. I hope to find my place, and my unfortunate brother must accept his. I say this advisedly, having heard of certain engagements he has made—engagements that would bring misery to all if he attempted to fulfill them now.”

“Your logic is compelling,” said my lord. “Shall we go see the ladies? There’s a portrait upstairs said to be by your grandfather. Before you go, cousin, please fix a date when our family may honor you with a visit. Castlewood is always your home when we are there. It’s somewhat like your Virginian Castlewood, from your description. We have beef, mutton, ale, wood—in plenty. But money is sadly lacking among us.”

They ascended to the drawing-room, where only one lady remained—Lady Maria, emerging from a window embrasure where she had been speaking with Harry.

George bowed deeply; Maria curtsied low. “You resemble your brother wonderfully,” she said, offering her hand. “And from what he tells me, cousin George, I believe you are as good as he.”

At the sight of her swollen eyes and tear-streaked face, George felt a pang of remorse. “Poor thing,” he thought. “Harry has been praising my generosity to her, while I’ve been playing the selfish elder brother downstairs. How old she looks! How could he ever have loved such a woman?” How? Because he didn’t see with your eyes, Mr. George. He saw rightly now—with his own. I never know whether to pity or congratulate a man on coming to his senses.

After the introduction, a brief conversation ensued—Lady Maria managing it with effort. But after a few sentences, she broke down, sobbing, motioned Harry away, and fled the room.

Harry rushed forward but stopped—checked by her gesture. My lord explained his sister was prone to nervous fits and had already been unwell that morning.

After this, the young men deemed it unnecessary to linger. Lord Castlewood escorted them downstairs, admired their horses in the phaeton, and waved a friendly farewell.

“And so,” said George to his charioteer, “we’ve been cooing and cuddling by the window, and part good friends, Harry? Is it not so?”

“Oh, she is a good woman!” Harry cried, lashing the horses. “You’ll see when you know her.”

“When you take her to Virginia? A pleasant welcome our mother will give her. She’ll never forgive me for not breaking off the match, nor you for making it.”

“I can’t help it, George! Don’t you keep popping your ugly head so close to my ears, Gumbo! After what’s passed between us, I’m bound by honor to stand by her. If she sees no objection, I must find none. I told her everything. I told her Madam would be stiff at first—but that she loves me and will relent. And about the property—I told her I knew my dearest George so well, I could count on sharing with him.”

“The deuce you did! Let me tell you, my dear, that I’ve been telling my Lord Castlewood a different story. That as elder brother, I intend to claim all my rights—there, don’t flog that near horse so—and that you can expect only poverty and dependence.”

“What! You won’t help me?” Harry gasped, turning pale.

Madame de Bernstein was no less delighted than her Virginian nephews by the outcome of Harry’s final meeting with Lady Maria. George sent her a letter that very evening, detailing what had transpired; and shortly after, her nephew Lord Castlewood—whose visits to his aunt were few and far between—arrived to pay his respects and speak openly about the affair. No man understood the value of candour better than my Lord Castlewood, and now that the matter between Maria and Harry was settled, there was no need for pretense or reserve. The game was played, the cards laid bare: he saw no reason not to recount every move, every trick, every subtle maneuver.

“She is my own sister,” said the lord affectionately. “She won’t have many more chances—such chances as this—to marry and secure her future. I may not have approved of the match in every way, and I may have pitied your ladyship’s young Virginian favourite; but such an opportunity could not be wasted. I was bound to stand by my own flesh and blood.”

“Your honesty does you credit, my lord,” replied Madame de Bernstein, “and your devotion to your sister is truly admirable.”

“Nay,” said the nobleman, bowing slightly, “we lost the game, and I speak without rancour. It is not for you, who have triumphed, to bear ill will.”

The Baroness protested she had never been in better spirits. “Now, confess, Eugene—was it your idea for Maria to visit Harry at the spunging-house? That touching gesture of returning all his gifts—was that your doing?”

“It was pity for the young man,” replied Lord Castlewood demurely, “and a sense of duty to Maria’s affianced lover in his hour of misfortune. Surely those were motives enough.”

“But you advised her, my good nephew?” pressed the Baroness.

With a shrug, Castlewood admitted he had. “Yet we would have won, despite your ladyship—had not the elder brother made his appearance. And I’ve been trying to console poor Maria by showing her how fortunate it was, after all, that we lost.”

“Suppose she had married Harry, and then George arrived?” mused the Baroness.

“Effectivement,” exclaimed Eugene, taking snuff. “As the grave was to give up its dead, let us thank it for disgorging in time! I must say, Mr. George Warrington seems a man of sound judgment, no more selfish than any other eldest son or worldly gentleman. My poor Molly fancied he might be—how shall I put it?—a greenhorn, like his younger brother. She hoped he’d be inclined to share everything equally with Twin junior. So infatuated was she with the lad that I believe she would have taken him anyway. ‘Harry Warrington, with half a loaf, might do very well,’ I told her, ‘but Harry Warrington with no bread at all, my dear?’”

“And no bread?” asked the Baroness.

“Well,” said Castlewood, “no bread except at his brother’s side-table. The elder brother said as much.”

“What a heartless creature!” cried Madame de Bernstein.

“Oh, bah!” retorted the lord, playing his cards openly. “Mr. George only did what anyone else would have done. We have no right to resent him. Indeed, Molly herself came around once her initial grief passed, and I brought her to reason. The silly old thing—to be so smitten with a young man at her age!”

“It was real passion, I almost believe,” said the Baroness. “You should have heard her say farewell to him. C’etait touchant, ma parole d’honneur! I wept. Before George appeared, I couldn’t help myself. There he stood, muddy stockings, hair falling into his eyes, bursting into our dinner party, making his offer to Molly in frank, noble terms—and she answered him. Begad, it reminded me of Mrs. Woffington in that new Scotch play Lord Bute’s man wrote—Douglas, was it? She clung to the boy, bid him adieu in heart-rending tones, stepped from the room in stately despair—no more chocolate, thank you. If she’d made a faux pas, no one could have withdrawn with greater dignity. A masterful retreat after defeat. We were driven from our position, but we left with all the honours of war.”

“Molly won’t die of disappointment,” observed the Baroness, sipping her tea.

Lord Castlewood gave a snarl of a grin, revealing his yellow teeth. “He, he! She’s had the malady before—twice or thrice—and recovered perfectly. It doesn’t kill, as you know, at Molly’s age.”

How could she know? She didn’t marry Doctor Tusher until late in life, and became Madame de Bernstein even later. Old Dido, as poets say, knew sorrow well—and thus learned compassion for others in distress. In the little world, people quarrel, fight, abuse each other, and remain estranged for years. But in the great world, wisdom prevails. Differences arise, meetings cease—but then reconciliation comes, unspoken, unexamined. A wandering prodigal—or a stray puppy-dog—is welcomed back under amnesty, though he may have roamed with unsavoury company.

For six months, since the Castlewoods and Madame de Bernstein had vied for control over poor Harry Warrington, these two branches of the Esmond family had kept apart. Now, with the matter resolved, they were free to reunite as if no rift had ever existed. Madame de Bernstein drove her grand coach to Lady Castlewood’s gathering, and the Esmond ladies smiled brightly at Madame de Bernstein’s festivities, loving each other just as fervently as before.

“So, sir,” said the Baroness, delighted and tapping George with her walking stick, “I hear you’ve behaved like a heartless monster toward your poor brother Harry!”

“I acted on your ladyship’s suggestion,” replied George, turning red. “I wanted to see whether your kin sought him for himself—or for his supposed fortune.”

“Maria could not marry a man utterly penniless,” countered the Baroness, “especially when his elder brother declared he’d give him nothing!”

“I did it for the best, madam,” George insisted, still blushing.

“And so you did, O thou hypocrite!” laughed the old lady.

“Hypocrite, madam? Why?” demanded Mr. Warrington, straightening himself with dignity.

“I know all, my infant!” said the Baroness in French. “Thou art very like thy grandfather. Come—let me embrace thee! Harry has told me everything, including how thou hast shared thy small inheritance with him.”

“It was natural,” said George, his voice softening. “We’ve had one heart and one purse since birth. I merely pretended harshness to test those people yonder.”

“And thou wilt divide Virginia with him too?” asked Madame de Bernstein.

“I don’t say so,” replied George. “It wouldn’t be fair. The land belongs to the eldest born, and Harry would not claim otherwise. Perhaps I shall die, or my mother live longer than both of us. But half of what is mine is his. And remember—he was extravagant only because he believed he was heir.”

“Ah!” exclaimed Madame de Bernstein, turning to her attendant as she prepared for bed. “It is a knight of old, a Bayard, the grandfather reborn!”

That evening, when the young men left her, she bestowed a tender kiss upon Harry’s hand—and a rouged cheek to George, who blushed nearly as deeply as the rose often painted on her face, touched by such favour from his ancient kinswoman.

Though Harry Warrington was among the least envious of men, and held his brother in the highest regard as chief, guide, and superior, it was natural that a deep sense of humiliation and sorrow weighed upon him after being stripped of his title as the Fortunate Youth and heir to vast Virginian lands. His friends at Kensington promised they would love him all the more for his fall. Harry bowed low and thanked them graciously—but he could not ignore the reality. When he accompanied George to the grand reception hosted by Lord Castlewood for his newly discovered kinsman, he saw plainly that George was the centre of attention: receiving all the conversation, compliments, and attentions, while Harry was scarcely noticed—except by poor Maria, whose eyes followed him with wistful longing, reproachful glances, as though blaming him for accepting her freedom too readily.

“Ah!” her eyes seemed to say. “It’s very generous of you, Harry, to accept the liberty I granted you—but I never meant for you to be so pleased at being released.”

She gave him up, yet did not quite forgive him for taking her at her word. She refused him, yet could not fully let go. Oh, my dear young readers, how sweet the beginning of love is—and how undignified the end can be! What a romantic vista lies ahead for young Damon and Phillis (or their middle-aged counterparts) when, their innocent affection revealed, they entwine their arms and gaze upon the lovely pays du tendre stretching beneath them! Together, they’ll wander through life, facing rocks and roaring rivers—yet Damon’s steadfast love will carry Sweetheart across them all. Dragons and dangers may lie in wait—but his brave sword will cut them down. At dusk, they’ll rest close together, like two children in the wood, moss for a bed, stars for a canopy, arms for pillows. This is the wise plan youth sets forth when embarking on the journey of love—and yet—O me!—they’ve barely walked a mile when they meet a towering wall and must turn back.

They’re squabbling with the post-boy at Barnet (the first stage on the Gretna Road), and lo—Strephon has no money, or Papa arrives with a horsewhip, takes Miss back, and locks her in the schoolroom, weeping. Heartbreaking, yes—but years later, when Strephon has become a prosperous barrister or a broken-down raff, and Delia a banker’s wife with eight children, and they meet again—what a ridiculous reunion!

Still, I hope no young man falls in love unless he believes his passion eternal. Doubt creeps in only after second or third loves. But some women remain romantic to the end—from eighteen to eighty-five, always expecting their hearts to break.

In short, when you’ve loved and no longer do, when the King of France, with twenty thousand men, colours flying, music blaring, marches up the hill—only to march down again—you find yourselves in an absurd position. This, no doubt, was Harry Warrington’s feeling when he returned to Kensington and met Maria’s melancholy, accusing eyes.

Yes—it is foolish, indeed. But how melancholy to return to a house once lived in, and see blackened windows and emptiness where once fires burned warm. Melancholy? Yes—but how bitter, how absurd, to pass sentimentally by No. 13 and see someone else grinning from the window, clearly on excellent terms with the landlady.

I always feel wounded—even at a familiar inn—if I see others’ trunks and boots outside rooms once mine. Did those boots rest on the sofa I once reclined upon? I kick you from before me, you muddy, vulgar highlows!

Thus, knowing his time of occupation was over, and Maria’s rooms—though perhaps not yet occupied by another—were certainly available for rent, Harry felt uneasy in her presence, and she likely in his. He found either nothing to say, or what she said was dull and commonplace. And now, the red lip of a white-necked pipe of Virginia tobacco was far more agreeable to him than Maria’s softest words or most sorrowful expression.

When George went to Kensington, Harry cared little to follow, citing other engagements. At his uncle’s house in Hill Street, the poor lad fared no better. He was barely acknowledged by the virtuous household. The ladies did not hesitate to deny themselves when he visited. He could scarcely believe such insincerity after their earlier embraces, welcomes, and repeated declarations of affection. Yet, sitting with the Lamberts for an hour after calling on his aunt, he saw her chairmen arrive with an empty carriage. His aunt stepped out, entered the vehicle, and did not even blush when he bowed from the opposite window.

To be denied by one’s own relations—to have a door that once opened wide slammed shut in his face! Poor simple Harry could not have believed such a thing possible.

Perhaps he thought the knocker had a kind heart, and was not made of brass. But the change in his Aunt Lambert’s face—just as cold and stern as the knocker itself—was no less shocking.

“My father’s own brother’s wife! What have I done to offend her? Oh, Aunt Lambert, Aunt Lambert—have you ever seen such cold-heartedness?” Harry burst out, as usual, with impulsive emotion.

“Do we make any difference to you, my dear Harry?” asked Aunt Lambert, casting a sideward glance at her youngest daughter.

“The world may look coldly upon you,” she continued, “but we do not belong to it. You may come to us in safety.”

“In this house, you are different from others,” replied Harry. “I don’t know how, but I always feel quiet and happy when I come here.”

“Quis me uno vivit felicior? aut magis hac est Optandum vita dicere quis potuit?” called out General Lambert.

“Do you know where I got these lines, Mr. Gownsman?” he asked his son from college, who had come to spend Easter with his parents.

“You took them from Catullus, sir,” replied the scholar.

“I took them from no such place,” said the General. “I took them from my beloved Democritus Junior—from old Burton, who has supplied many indifferent scholars with learning.” And Montaigne, too, were favourite authors of the good General.

It had long been the fashion among the young Virginians to embrace Jacobite sentiments with a fervour that, while not uncommon for their age, was more than mere youthful fancy. They admired the exiled Stuart line, and in particular the banished prince who had once acknowledged Madam Esmond’s father as Marquis of Esmond. Though she might have taken umbrage at such royal favouritism, Madam Esmond bore no ill will toward a family so quick to recognize her own noble lineage. As for the whispered scandal involving her sister, Madame de Bernstein, and the Old Chevalier—well, she dismissed it with a wave of her hand, declaring with unshakable truth that the first two Hanoverian monarchs were scarcely better in private virtue than any of the Stuarts. Yet, she acknowledged one undeniable fact: the king who sat on the throne, though not by birthright, was the king in practice. He had been solemnly crowned and anointed in church; he had vanquished his rival in battle. Thus, in her mind, duty called upon her sons to appear before him—not merely out of loyalty, but because they owed themselves that respect.

And if His Majesty should see fit to bestow a post, or a ribbon of blue or red upon either of them, Madam Esmond would not be surprised. She believed the King knew the Virginian Esmonds as well as any other noble house in the land. So it was that her sons were commanded to present themselves at court—and had they known, she would have been furious to learn that George wore Harry’s laced coat on the day of his visit to Kensington.

A century past, the King’s drawing-room stood open nearly every day to nobility and gentry alike. Loyalty, especially since the war had begun, found ample satisfaction in seeing the sovereign in person—perhaps a dozen times a month. The threat of enemy warships made sea voyages perilous, and thus the King, though longing for his native Hanover, remained reluctantly within England. A Hanoverian lady, beloved for her grace and devotion, endeavoured to ease his sorrow. From the lips of the Countess of Walmoden—honoured with a British title by imperial grace—the monarch could hear the voice of home.

It was to this sovereign that Mr. Warrington, through his uncle—a diligent courtier—requested introduction. Since Mr. Lambert too was bound for court to thank the King for his recent promotion, the two set off together, hiring a hackney-coach for the journey, as my Lord Wrotham’s carriage was now occupied by its rightful owner, who had returned to town.

They arrived at Kensington Palace Gate, where the sentries recognized and saluted General Lambert, and then walked modestly on foot to the summer residence of the Crown. Passing beneath the portico, they entered the gallery leading to the grand black marble staircase—richly adorned by Mr. Kent—and moved through several chambers hung with tapestry and lined with portraits and busts until they reached the King’s great drawing-room. There, amid masterpieces of art, hung Titian’s famed “Venus,” Rubens’ “St. Francis adoring the infant Saviour,” and other treasures of the brush. Here, among the courtiers, the gentlemen waited, as the King concluded his private council with those whom the newspapers of the time called his M-j-ty’s M-n-st-rs.

George Warrington, never having stepped inside a palace before, found himself entranced. He gazed upon paintings he had only read about—Vandyck’s portrait of Charles I with his Queen and children, Tintoretto’s “Esther before Ahasuerus,” its figures draped in opulent Venetian finery. He lingered so long in admiration that he barely heard General Lambert whispering names into his ear.

“There,” said the General, “are two of His Majesty’s Lords of the Admiralty—Mr. Gilbert Elliot and Admiral Boscawen. That last is your Boscawen, whose fleet fired the first shot in your waters two years ago.”

“That stout gentleman, all gold-braided, is Mr. Fox—the former Minister, now content with being Paymaster, though he still carries the auri fames on his person. Why, his waistcoat is a perfect Potosi!” laughed George.

“Aliena appetens—how goes the text? He loves to get money and spend it,” added Lambert.

“Yonder is my Lord Chief Justice Willes, speaking with my Lord Salisbury, Doctor Headley. If he serves God as he serves the King, Heaven will grant him high advancement. He lived in your grandfather’s time, loved by Dick Steele, hated by the Dean. With them stands my Lord of London, the learned Doctor Sherlock. The lords of lawn sleeves have lost half their honours now. I remember when I was a boy, my mother made me kneel before the Bishop of Rochester—the one who crossed the water and became minister to someone unnamed—Perkin’s Bishop.”

“The fair man beside him is Admiral Smith. President of poor Byng’s court-martial—he tried in vain to save him. Tom of Ten Thousand, they call him in the fleet. The French ambassador broke him when he was a lieutenant, for making a French ship lower its topsails. The King made him captain the next day.”

“And that tall, proud fellow?” asked George.

“My Lord George Sackville. Now that I am Major-General myself, he’ll treat me less like a footman. I wish Blakeney were here—soldier’s darling, brave and kind, unlike yonder poker of a nobleman.”

At this moment, the nobleman approached.

“I am your lordship’s very humble servant,” said Lambert, turning fully to his companion. “This is a young gentleman from America, recently returned from Braddock’s unfortunate expedition.”

“Oh, indeed!” replied the nobleman. “I have the honour of speaking to Mr.——?”

“To Major-General Lambert, at your lordship’s service. And this, sir, is Mr. Warrington. I must present you to His Majesty if Sir Miles tarries much longer.”

As he spoke, Lambert addressed only the young man, ignoring his colleague entirely. The nobleman retreated, startled, as if offended by such boldness. In those days, nobility was nobility, and expected reverence.

Soon, Sir Miles Warrington appeared in his bright red waistcoat, greeted warmly by both Lambert and his nephew. Their affection was evident. Sir Miles embraced the General, calling him “dear friend,” and lamented his departure from the house.

“We miss you terribly, General,” he declared. “My daughters fell in love with your ladies—upon my word, they did! My Lady Warrington and I debated endlessly how to make acquaintance with your charming family. We feel as if we’ve known you for years. And we love you—for your kindness to our dear nephews, though we confess we were jealous when they visited you so often.”

He passed a hand over his eyes, choking with emotion. “Carry my deepest respects to Mrs. Lambert,” he continued. “Thank her for her care of these boys—my own flesh and blood, my brother’s sons!”

While they conversed—George suppressing laughter with admirable restraint—the door to the King’s apartments opened. Pages preceded His Majesty, followed by his corpulent son, the Duke of Cumberland, resplendent in blazing scarlet. Behind them came various officers and ministers, among them George recognized instantly: Mr. Secretary Pitt—tall, stern-faced, with an eagle eye and a presence that commanded silence.

Even from a hundred years’ distance, I feel a shiver of awe as I see him pass. Not from fear of George II, nor dazzlement at the Duke’s imposing figure—but from the sheer weight of Pitt’s presence. The Great Commoner, the terrible Cornet of Horse! He strides across history like a colossus, wrapped in flannel, gouty shoes clumping, thunderbolt hands clenched. Perhaps dark words had passed between him and the King—long speeches, eloquent yet tedious, repulsive to the sharp old monarch who detested fine phrases and pompous brose.

Pitt moved solemnly through the crowd. The company drew back respectfully. The King walked slowly around the room, his son trailing behind, speaking briefly to select individuals.

The monarch was small, keen-eyed, fresh-complexioned, dressed plainly in snuff-coloured clothes and brown stockings, adorned only by the blue ribbon of the Garter. He spoke in a German accent, yet with ease and wit, addressing those he chose, bowing to others.

He knew General Lambert well—from Dettingen, from Scotland—and congratulated him heartily on his promotion.

“It is not always,” the King observed, “that we can do as we please. But I was glad, for once, to give myself that pleasure in your case, General. Your army holds no better officer.”

Lambert blushed deeply, humbled and proud.

Then the King turned to Sir Miles and the young man beside him.

“Who is this?” he asked, pointing to George Warrington, who stood in respectful silence, clad in Harry’s finest embroidered suit.

Sir Miles bowed low. “Your Majesty, this is my nephew, Mr. George Warrington of Virginia, who begs leave to pay his humble duty.”

“This, then, is the other brother?” the King remarked kindly. “Had he come late, the other would have spent all the money.”

He turned to the Bishop of Salisbury. “Why do you come out in this bitter weather? You’d do better staying at home.”

And so he passed on.

Sir Miles was visibly moved. He clasped George’s hands. “God bless you, my boy,” he exclaimed. “I told you you’d see the greatest monarch and finest gentleman in the world. Is he not so, my Lord Bishop?”

“That, that he is!” the bishop cried, raising his ruffled hands to heaven. “The best of princes and men!”

“Ah,” said Lambert, “that is Master Louis, my Lady Yarmouth’s favourite nephew.”

Just then, the Duke of Cumberland approached.

“Congratulate you on your promotion, Lambert,” he said cheerfully.

Sir Miles’s eyes nearly popped out of his head with joy.

“I owe it, sir, to your Royal Highness’s good offices,” the General replied.

“Not at all,” the Duke said. “You deserved it long ago. Always been a good officer. Perhaps there’ll be employment soon. This is the gentleman James Wolfe introduced to me?”

“His brother, sir.”

“Oh! The real Fortunate Youth! You were with poor Ned Braddock in America—a prisoner, lucky to escape. Come and see me in Pall Mall. Bring him to my levee, Lambert.”

And with that, the Duke turned away.

“It’s raining!” Sir Miles cried. “You came on foot, General? You and George must come home in my coach. You shall come with me—I say so! By George, you must!”

So he drove them back to Hill Street, presenting Lambert to Lady Warrington and the girls—Flora and Dora—and insisting they partake of a collation.

“What? Only cold mutton?” Sir Miles joked. “Well, an old soldier can eat cold mutton. And a good glass of my Lady Warrington’s own cordial—prepared with her own hands—will keep the cold wind out. Delicious cordial! Capital mutton! Our own, my dear General—six years old if a day. We keep a plain table, but the Warringtons have always loved mutton since the Conqueror. Our meal may look scanty—but we are plain people. I keep my servants on board-wages. Can’t afford seven-year-old mutton, you know.”

In front of George, Sir Miles recounted the court visit in glowing terms—so flattering that George felt almost embarrassed, unsure how to respond, how to contradict such praise before the family.

Lambert sat quietly, eyes wide. He had been to Kensington too—but had seen none of the wonders described.

“We are proud of you, dear George,” Sir Miles declared. “We love you—my dear nephew—we all love you, we’re all proud of you—not because you’re wealthy, nor blessed with lands and ancient name—but because you’ve used your talents wisely. Because you’ve fought and bled for your country, your king. You are truly worthy of the King’s favour.”

To Lambert, he added, “You’ve kindly dropped in on a country family. We hope to see you again, when our hospitality is a little less homely. Yes, by George, you must name a day when you and Mrs. Lambert, and your dear girls, dine with us. No refusal now—I won’t take it!”

Lady Warrington rose. “Will you accompany us to my drawing-room?”

Lambert declined, but the ladies refused to let George go.

“No, positively,” said Flora. “You shall not go. We must meet our cousin. We must hear about that dreadful battle, and your escape from the Indians.”

Tom Claypool entered, catching some of the tale. Flora listened, handkerchief pressed to her eyes.

“Why do you take your handkerchief, Flora?” asked little Miles. “You’re not crying a bit.”

When Lambert returned home, he could not resist telling his wife about the new family he had met.

A certain word—“humbug”—had lately entered fashion. And the General used it freely to describe the Warringtons.

He recounted the father’s eager hospitality, the mother’s exaggerated flattery, the daughters’ admiring glances, the tough mutton, and the abominable cordial.

Mrs. Lambert could not help comparing Lady Warrington’s treatment of poor Harry with her current enthusiasm for George.

“Is Miss Warrington really handsome?” she asked.

“Yes,” said the General, “very handsome—and the most astonishing flirt I’ve ever seen.”

“The hypocrite!” she exclaimed. “I have no patience with such people!”

To which the General replied, simply:

“Bo!”

“Why ‘Bo’, Martin?” she asked.

“I say ‘Bo!’ to a goose, my dear,” he answered.

And his wife swore she didn’t know what he meant—or what he was thinking.

And the General said:

“Of course not.”

The true fabric of life, I suspect, occupies but a small part of the novelist’s craft. When he writes of war—where courage is tested, where danger and devotion shine forth—the writer may venture close to reality, for such moments stir the soul and demand grand gestures. But beyond that arena, daily existence—whether it be selling spices, poring over legal tomes, or measuring coats in a tailor's shop—rarely finds its way into fiction. What can a storyteller say of the quiet, grinding routine of Ficulnus the merchant, Causidicus the lawyer, or Sartorius the tailor? Would readers endure a tale spun from hobnails and eighteenpence a day? Not likely.

In the age we describe, poets painted shepherds not in rough wool, but in pink breeches and chintz waistcoats, dancing before their flocks with flageolets tied in blue satin ribbons. And so, I reply to critics who would have us depict life as it truly is: the novelist cannot hope to capture the ordinary—save perhaps in war. Law, stockbroking, theology, drapery, apothecary work—all these must remain beneath the surface, unexplored. Our task is to show men not at their trade, but in passion, laughter, love, sorrow, and folly; to reveal their inner lives while leaving their professions unspoken, almost unheard.

Thus, when we speak of past or present times, we wander through theatre lobbies, coffee-houses, pleasure gardens, and ballrooms—places of leisure, not labour. Meanwhile, the real world plods on in offices, workshops, and fields. Corydon must cart manure and thresh barley before he can woo Phillis; Ancillula must wash clothes and serve meals before she dares whisper sweet nothings to Boopis the policeman. The city’s pavements wear down under his heels long before he can steal a kiss or a cold pie. We glimpse our characters only in these brief respites from duty—away from their burdens—and so, though they live full lives, we see them only when they are free.

Harry Warrington found himself increasingly shunned by the fashionable set. The macaronis of White’s and Arthur’s turned their backs on him with cold indifference, and soon he avoided their company altogether. The gaming tables of the Ring and the Mall no longer knew his face. Madame de Bernstein urged her nephew to stand firm against the world’s neglect. “You must have courage,” she declared. “If you’re slighted now, bear it with a smile. One day, you’ll repay them tenfold.” She spoke with authority, recalling her own trials. “I’ve eaten humble pie more than once,” she said. “We all must. Now that you’re no longer the Fortunate Youth, become the Clever Youth. Go everywhere. Be civil to everyone—especially women. Show your spirit, but do it with grace. With economy and your brother’s generosity, you can still appear well-born. You’re handsome—there’s no reason you can’t win a rich heiress. Go to the merchants in the City. They won’t know you’re out of fashion at Court.”

Yet this same woman, once so fond of Harry, now treated him with icy formality. Where once she had smiled and kissed him, she now scolded and mocked him before guests. Her servants, once eager to serve him, barely acknowledged his presence. When he called on Lady Yarmouth, she was always ill or otherwise engaged. Her staff did not offer him refreshment, nor ask if he’d stay. The days when he was welcomed as a companion of the great were gone.

Heartbroken, Harry confided in Mrs. Lambert. “She used to love me,” he said, voice thick with grief. “Now she turns on me. It hurts—I don’t understand why people I care for should turn away.”

The ladies listened quietly. Miss Hetty, ever bold, said, “Well, you’re not very lively, Harry.”

“Why should he be?” asked Theo gently. “He’s hurt. He has a good heart. Isn’t that enough?”

“But I’d never let anyone see me hurt,” Hetty insisted, clenching her fists. “And I’d smile even if that horrid old painted woman boxed my ears. She’s dreadful, mamma! You think so too, don’t you, Theo? You said so last night—you mimicked her coming in on her crutch!”

“I may dislike her,” Theo replied, blushing, “but I won’t call Harry’s aunt names in front of him.”

“You’re always right!” Hetty snapped. “That’s what makes me angry. I’m sorry, Harry. I shouldn’t have spoken like that.”

“It’s not the others,” Harry said softly. “But this one—it feels cruel. I cared for her. It’s hard when someone you love turns away.”

“Suppose George did?” Hetty asked.

“That’s impossible,” Harry replied sharply, rising. “You don’t know George like I do. You wouldn’t dream of suggesting he could do anything unkind.”

Hetty went pale. She looked up at him, then said nothing.

Before leaving, Harry added, “I’m sorry if I was harsh, Hetty. I didn’t mean to be unkind. But I’ll always defend George.”

She gave him her hand and curtseyed stiffly.

Later, alone with Theo, Hetty whispered, “I thought seeing him every day would be wonderful. But now I keep offending him. I can’t help it. He’s not clever, Theo—but oh, isn’t he good? Brave? Didn’t he look noble when he was angry?”

“You silly thing,” Theo teased. “You always try to make him look heroic.”

Among these young people, it was Theo and Hetty, Harry and George—a quartet bound by friendship. General Lambert, no doubt, nicknamed his wife “Bo” as a gentle tease, mocking her sentimental nature and her tendency toward matchmaking—traits common among women whose hearts matter. It hinted that Madam Lambert was foolish to imagine the two Virginian brothers might fall for her daughters. Little Hetty might dream, but dreams fade. “And you know, Molly,” the General would say, “you fancied someone else before you fancied me.” Mrs. Lambert couldn’t deny it. Yet Harry clearly wasn’t smitten with Hetty. And now, with George older and more commanding, Harry felt overshadowed—even his coat no longer felt entirely his own.

“Oh yes,” Mrs. Lambert sighed. “Now he’s poor, they’ll throw him out. Just like everyone else.”

“And I always do that, don’t I, Molly?” the General asked. “Turn my back on friends in trouble?”

“No, dear,” she said, dabbing her eyes. “I’m the goose. I admit it.”

“Let the boy come here,” the General said warmly. “Our house is one of the few where he’s welcome. He’s unhappy, and being here brings him peace. Let him stay—God willing.”

So whenever Harry needed a meal or a place to rest, Mr. Lambert’s table had room for him. George came too, though less warmly at first. He was quieter, more reserved than his brother. But the Lamberts’ kindness touched him. He saw how deeply Harry suffered, and began to feel for him. Often, with a dry wit, George would mock himself: “Dear Harry, I’m George the Unlucky, while you’ve ceased to be Harry the Fortunate. If Florac hadn’t killed that Indian, I’d still have my scalp—and you’d be safe from all this.”

“I never know whether you’re joking or serious,” Harry said.

“Precisely my own case,” George replied.

“But one thing I know: there’s never been a better brother. Or kinder people than the Lamberts.”

“Never truer words,” George said, taking his hand.

“And if I’m miserable,” Harry continued, “it’s not your fault—or theirs—or maybe even mine. It’s fate. It’s having nothing to do. I must work—but how, George?”

“We’ll wait to hear from mother,” George said.

“I don’t think I want to go back to Virginia,” Harry murmured.

“In love with one of the girls here?”

“Love them like sisters—with all my heart. But after what happened, thanks to you, I don’t want to return. Not because of that. It’s just… hunting, duck-shooting, planting tobacco, playing whist, going to church—over and over. That’s all there is. What else is there? What can I do? That’s what makes me miserable. It wouldn’t matter for you—you’re clever. You’d succeed anywhere. But for me? No chance. Until I do something, I’ll never be happy.”

“Have I not always said so?” George asked. “Are you finally agreeing with me?”

“What opinion?”

“You know everything I think, I think,” Harry said.

“That Florac should have left the Indian alive, my dear.”

At that, Harry laughed and shook his head. They sat together, smoking pipes in peaceful companionship.

They lived apart, each following their own path, yet bound by affection. Harry never disturbed George’s studies, sitting silently while his brother read. Soon they moved from the Court end of town, much to Madame de Bernstein’s disapproval. But George took a liking to Sir Hans Sloane’s new reading-room and museum in Montagu House, and rented cheerful lodgings in Southampton Row, Bloomsbury, overlooking the green fields near Hampstead. Lord Wrotham’s family moved to Mayfair, and Mr. Lambert, busy in London, relocated to furnished apartments in Soho—near the young men’s home.

Harry often stayed with the Lamberts, finding comfort in their warmth. George visited too, and as time passed, he grew more drawn to their circle. Their company suited him better than Aunt Bernstein’s gamblers, Sir Miles Warrington’s port-and-mutton dinners, or the noisy coffee-houses. Both families were newcomers to London, and they shared its pleasures: Vauxhall, Ranelagh, Marybone Gardens, the Tower, and above all—the theatre.

General Lambert loved innocent joy for his children, and George, generous by nature, liked to treat his friends—especially those kind to his brother.

Above all, Mr. Warrington adored the theatre. He had never known such entertainment in Virginia, only once or twice in Canada. Now, in London, with Drury Lane and Covent Garden at their peak, he believed he could never tire of it. Anything he enjoyed, he wished to share. Naturally, he invited his friends to join him. “Shall we go to Drury Lane or Covent Garden, ladies?” he asked.

Drury Lane offered Garrick and Shakespeare. But the ladies wanted to see the new play at Covent Garden—the work of a rising genius.

At that moment, a brilliant star had risen in British drama. Mr. John Home, a Scottish clergyman, had written a tragedy so refined, so classical, that many called it the finest since ancient times. Why had Garrick refused it? Some said Shakespeare, though great, contained barbarisms unfit for polite ears. Home, however, wrote with elegance—even in sorrow. His death scenes were not merely tragic, but graceful and moving. He never stooped to farce or puns, unlike earlier playwrights. Moreover, the play had been praised by the highest circles—by royalty and scholars alike. Even Mr. Gray of Cambridge claimed it matched the best of dramatic art. In Edinburgh, where it premiered, the audience roared in dialect: “Where’s Wully Shakspeare noo?”

“I’d like to see the man who could beat Willy Shakspeare,” the General chuckled.

“Mere national pride,” said Harry.

“Beat Shakspeare, indeed!” Mrs. Lambert scoffed.

“Pooh! You’ve cried over Richardson more than Shakespeare,” the General retorted. “Most women say they love Shakespeare, but they don’t.”

“Oh, papa!” the three girls exclaimed, throwing up their hands.

“Well, then, why do you all prefer *Douglas*?” he asked. “And you boys—Tories both—will you attend a play by a Whig Scotsman, imprisoned at Falkirk?”

“Relicta non bene parmula,” said Mr. Jack, the scholar.

“Nay,” said the General. “It was relicta bene parmula. The Highlanders threw down their targes and fought fiercely. Had they done so at Derby—”

“I know which side would be rebels,” George interrupted. “And who’d be called the Young Pretender.”

“Hush,” said the General. “Remember my cloth. My cockade is black, not white. But if politics don’t sway you, George, there’s another reason to like Home.”

“I may be a Tory,” George replied, bowing, “but I can respect a good Whig. Why should I like him?”

“Because he’s a Presbyterian minister who dared write a play. His fellow clergymen excommunicated him. They stripped him of his livelihood. He’d have starved—if not for the Young Pretender on our side, who gave him a pension.”

“If persecuted by parsons, he deserves support,” George smiled. “From now on, I shall attend his sermons.”

“Mrs. Woffington is divine in it,” Harry said. “Barry draws tears from everyone. Garrick is furious he refused it. Girls, bring six handkerchiefs! Mamma must stay home—I can’t trust her.”

But Mrs. Lambert insisted on going. “If I must cry, I’ll do it in a corner.”

So they all went to Covent Garden—the most of them prepared for a masterpiece. Could they not quote Congreve? Had they not wept over Otway and Rowe? Alas, how quickly glory fades. Who remembers where those old dramatists lie buried? Poor, forgotten Muse of the past! You sing, and we refuse to dance; you mourn, and we refuse to weep. And what of our own heroes? How soon will they too be dead and buried? How many will survive?

Off they went to Covent Garden to see the immortal John Home. The ladies and General arrived in a glass coach, meeting the young men at the door. Through torch-boys and footmen they made their way. Little Hetty clung to Harry’s arm; Miss Theo was handed into the box by George. Gumbo held their seats until they arrived, then bowed and retreated to the footman’s gallery.

They had fine seats in a front box, with a pillar behind which Mrs. Lambert could weep in privacy. Opposite them sat the Prince of Wales, with his mother, the Princess Dowager, greeted with loyal but lukewarm cheers. Behind the Prince stood Lord Bute, the poet’s patron, whose court had already wept over the play.

And so, under the glow of candlelight and expectation, the curtain rose on a tragedy that would echo through the ages.

When the play ended, our friends took a coach to Mr. Warrington’s lodgings, where the Virginian brothers had arranged an elegant supper. Mr. Warrington was eager to entertain them in the most generous manner, and General Lambert and his wife accepted with pleasure, delighted at the opportunity to repay their young hosts’ kindness. The gathering included the General and his wife, their son John from college, their two daughters—Miss Theo and Miss Hetty—and Mr. Spencer of the Temple, a recent acquaintance George had met at a coffeehouse. Together, they enjoyed the landlady’s fine fare with good spirits.

The seating arrangement remains uncertain, but it is clear that Miss Theo sat beside the chickens and Mr. George Warrington, while Miss Hetty shared her attention between a ham and Mr. Harry. Mrs. Lambert must have been seated to George’s right, leaving only the positions of the General, his son, and Mr. Spencer to be settled. Mr. Spencer had attended another performance earlier in the week, where he had introduced George to the greenroom.

Conversation soon turned back to the evening’s drama. Some guests professed great admiration for the play. “As for what our gentlemen say,” Mrs. Lambert declared to Mr. Spencer, “you must not believe a word of it. It was a delightful piece, and my husband and Mr. George behaved as ill as possible.”

“We laughed in the wrong places and cried when we shouldn’t have,” the General admitted with a smile. “That’s the truth.”

“You caused all the people in the boxes around us to turn and cry ‘Hush!’” Mrs. Lambert continued. “You made the pit shout, ‘Silence in the boxes, yonder!’ Such behavior I never saw, and I blushed for you, Mr. Lambert!”

“Mamma thought it was a tragedy,” the General said, “and we thought it was pure fun. George and I behaved perfectly well, didn’t we, Theo?”

“Not when I was looking your way, papa!” Theo replied.

At this, the General chuckled. “Was there ever such a saucy baggage seen?”

“I didn’t speak till I was bid,” Theo answered modestly. “I confess I was deeply moved by the play, especially by Mrs. Woffington’s performance. I was sorry the poor mother found her child and then lost him. And I’m sorry, too, papa, if I oughtn’t to have felt that way,” she added, smiling.

“Women aren’t as clever as men, you know, Theo,” Hetty remarked from the other end of the table, glancing slyly at Harry.

“The next time we go to the theatre, brother Jack,” she said, “please pinch us when we should cry, or nudge us when it’s time to laugh.”

“I wish we could have seen the fight,” General Lambert mused. “The battle between little Norval and the giant Norwegian—that would have been splendid! You should write to Mr. Rich, the manager, Jack, and suggest it.”

“I haven’t seen that,” Harry said gravely. “But I saw Slack and Broughton at Marybone Gardens.” He paused, wondering if he’d said something witty, for everyone burst into laughter.

“It wouldn’t take a giant to knock over that little fellow in red boots,” Harry added. “I, for one, could throw him over my shoulder.”

“Mr. Garrick is small,” Mr. Spencer observed. “But there are moments when he seems like a giant.”

“How grand he was in *Macbeth*, Mr. Warrington!” the Templar exclaimed. “How terrifying that dagger scene was! You should have seen our host, ladies! I introduced Mr. Warrington to Mr. Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard in the greenroom, and Lady Macbeth did him the honor of taking a pinch from his box.”

“Did the wife of the Thane of Cawdor sneeze?” the General asked, lowering his voice dramatically.

“She thanked Mr. Warrington in tones so hollow and tragic that he jumped back—and must have spilled some of his rappee, because Macbeth sneezed three times.”

“Macbeth, Macbeth, Macbeth!” the General thundered.

“And the great philosopher standing beside Mr. Johnson said, ‘You must mind, Davy, lest thy sneeze should awaken Duncan!’ who, by the way, was chatting with the three witches as they sat against the wall.”

“Oh, I’d give anything to go behind the scenes!” Theo sighed.

“To see the ropes pulled, smell the tallow candles, look at the pasteboard gold and tinsel jewels, and the painted old women, Theo? No—don’t look too close,” George warned, demurely sipping a glass of hock.

“You were angry with your father and me,” he added.

“Nay, George!” Theo protested.

“Nay? I say yes!” George countered. “You were angry because we laughed when you wanted to cry. If I may speak for both of us, sir,” he said, bowing to General Lambert, “I think we weren’t inclined to weep like the ladies, because we stood behind the author’s scenes. Looking closely at the young hero, we saw how much of him was mere rant and glitter. As for the pale, tragic mother—her pallor was white chalk, and her sorrow, her handkerchief. Now, Theo, admit you thought me unfeeling?”

“If you can find it out without my confessing,” she replied, “what’s the use of my owning it?”

“Suppose I were to die,” George went on, “and you saw Harry grieving—you’d see real sorrow, a true tragedy. But if you saw the undertaker in mourning clothes and a black cloak, you wouldn’t feel a thing.”

“Indeed, I would!” Mrs. Lambert insisted. “And so would any daughter of mine.”

“Perhaps we might find our own mourners, Mr. Warrington,” Theo said softly.

“Would you?” George asked, and both his cheeks and Theo’s flushed crimson—likely because they noticed Hetty’s bright eyes watching them.

“The older writers understood little of the pathetic,” Mr. Spencer remarked.

“What do you think of Sophocles and *Antigone*?” John Lambert called out.

“Faith, our wits don’t trouble themselves much about him—unless an Oxford man reminds us!” Spencer replied. “I meant only to go back as far as Mr. Shakespeare, whom we all agree doesn’t handle the elegant or the pathetic as well as modern playwrights. Has he ever approached Belvidera, Monimia, or Jane Shore? Can you find in his comic women the grace of Congreve?” He offered snuff to both sides.

“Do you suppose Mr. Spencer himself has tried his hand?” someone asked.

“Many gentlemen of leisure have,” Spencer replied. “Mr. Garrick, I confess, once read a piece of mine and returned it.”

“And I’ve four acts of a play tucked away in one of my boxes,” George confessed.

“I’ll bet it’s better than any of theirs,” Harry whispered to his neighbor.

“Is it a tragedy or a comedy?” Mrs. Lambert asked.

“Oh, a tragedy,” George replied. “With at least two or three dreadful murders!”

“Let us perform it,” the General declared. “And let the audience watch their eyes!”

“Then fetch the tragedy at once, Gumbo!” Mrs. Lambert called to the servant.

Gumbo bowed low. “Tragedy, madam? Yes.”

“In the great cowskin trunk, Gumbo,” George said solemnly.

Gumbo bowed again. “Yes, sir,” he replied, even more gravely.

“But my tragedy is buried under linen, packages, books, and boots, Hetty,” George added.

“Never mind,” Hetty said cheerfully. “Let’s have it and toss the linen out the window!”

“And the trunk is at our agent in Bristol,” George explained. “So Gumbo must get post-horses. We can keep the performance going until he returns the day after tomorrow.”

The ladies groaned in mock despair. “Oh!” they chorused.

The General, perhaps more seriously, said, “Let us be thankful for the escape. Let us think of going home. Our young gentlemen have treated us nobly. Let us all raise a final toast to Madam Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, Virginia. Suppose, boys, you return home to find a tall, handsome stepfather waiting? Women as old as she have married before.”

“To Madam Esmond Warrington, my old schoolfellow!” Mrs. Lambert toasted. “I shall write and tell her how lovely her sons have treated us. And Mr. George, I won’t say how poorly you behaved at the play!”

With that, the company took their leave. The General’s coach and servant, bearing a flambeau, waited to carry his family home.

After such a gracious evening, what could be more natural than for Mr. Warrington to call upon his guests the next day to inquire how they had fared? Their coach might have taken the open road behind Montague House toward Oxford Road—where footpads lurked in the fields. The ladies might have caught cold or slept poorly after the emotional strain of the play. In short, there was no need for apology. So he closed his books early at the Sloane Museum and walked away, perhaps remembering little of what he had read.

Yet what was the meaning of his hesitation as he approached the door of the General’s lodgings in Dean Street? Why did he pause, knock with trembling hands, and study the footman who answered? Does any young man truly read? Does any old man remember? Does any weary, broken heart recall the days when it beat full and strong?

It has been many years since some of us were young; we forget—but not all. No, madam, we remember with advantages, as Shakespeare’s Harry promised his soldiers: if they survived Agincourt and St. Crispin’s Day, they would remember it well.

Old chargers turned out to grass may still kick up their heels and gallop once more when the trumpet sounds over the hedge. I no longer care for clowns or pantaloons; I find fairies ugly and their verses unbearable. Yet I enjoy seeing children at a pantomime. I no longer dance or eat supper, but I delight in watching Eugenio and Flirtilla whirl in a waltz, or Lucinda and Ardentio pull a cracker.

Burn your little fingers, children! Blaze out warm sparks from each other’s eyes! Then draw close and read the motto—yes, that old, sentimental motto, stale yet ever new—let her lips read it, and his interpret it. Divide the sweetmeat, young lovers, and crunch it together. I have no teeth. Bitter almonds and sugar disagree with me. But shall not bonbons melt on the tongue?

We follow John upstairs to the General’s rooms, entering with Mr. George Esmond Warrington, who bows with exaggerated politeness. Only one lady sits near the window—a place not often touched by sunshine in Dean Street. She is not especially beautiful, but spring is in the air, and she blooms like a young plant. A bouquet of fresh roses glows in her cheek. Her eyes, perhaps, are violets.

A hundred years ago, we would have told Mr. Sylvanus Urban that her neck was a lily, her form a nymph’s. We would have composed an acrostic and celebrated Lambertella in verse—between a neat engraving of Prague and the King of Prussia’s camp, and a map of Maryland.

Here is Miss Theo, blushing like a rose. What could her mother have meant an hour earlier, insisting she was pale and tired, best kept indoors? They had gone to thank Lord Wrotham’s ladies for their hospitality. The General was at the Horse Guards, likely expecting a new command—though his wife trembled at the thought of another posting abroad.

“My brother and yours have gone to visit our younger brother at his school at the Chartreux. My brothers are both destined for the clergy, I believe,” Theo said, busy hemming a boy’s shirt.

A century ago, young ladies stitched shirts without shame. I don’t claim they were better or worse for it. I have no desire, dear girl, that you make puddings—or that I black boots.

Harry has been visiting them often, almost daily.

“He likes us better than the fine folk,” Theo added, smiling. “They don’t care for him now—now that he’s no longer one of them.”

“Why don’t you embrace fashion?” she asked. “Why not frequent chocolate-houses and racecourses, Mr. Warrington?”

“Has my brother gained so much from his gay life that I should imitate him?”

“You might at least visit Sir Miles Warrington. His arms are wide open. Her ladyship came today in her chair, praising you! She says you’re on the path to preferment. The Duke spoke highly of you at court. When you become great, will you forget us?”

“Yes,” George said, “when I am great, I will.”

“Well, Mr. George, then—”

“—Mr. George!”

“When papa and mamma are here, I suppose we need no Mister,” Theo said, glancing out the window, slightly flustered.

“And what have you been doing, sir? Reading or writing more of your tragedy? Will it make us cry—as we like—or just frighten us—as you do?”

“There’s plenty of killing,” George replied, “but not much crying. I haven’t met many women. I’ve not been intimate with them. I daresay what I’ve written comes from books or poems I’ve read and imitated like other young men. Women don’t talk to me, generally. I’m told I have a sarcastic way that displeases them.”

“Perhaps you never cared to please them?” Theo ventured, blushing.

“I displeased you last night. You know I did.”

“Yes,” she said, “but it wasn’t really displeasure. Later, I realized I was wrong.”

“Did you think of me when I was away, Theo?”

“Yes, George—that is, Mr.—well, George. I thought you and papa were right about the play. As you said, it wasn’t real sorrow, only affectation. I wonder whether it’s fortune or misfortune to see so clearly. Hetty and I agreed we’d be careful in the future about enjoying tragedies. So be careful when yours comes. What’s its name?”

“He’s not christened yet. Will you be godmother? The lead character is—”

But at that moment, Mrs. Lambert and Miss Hetty returned from their walk.

“I never expected to see Mr. Warrington today,” the mother said quickly. “Well, I thought he might come. That is, it’s very kind of him. The play and supper were charming—except that Theo had a slight headache this morning.”

“I dare say it’s better now, mamma,” Hetty said.

“Indeed, my dear,” Theo replied, tossing her head, “it never mattered. I told mamma so.”

They began talking about Harry. He was downcast. He needed something to do. He was always at the Military Coffee-House, studying the King of Prussia’s campaigns. It was unfair to keep him in London after his fall from grace.

He said nothing, but one could see how he regretted his idle past and resented his current dependence. Passing the guard at St. James’s with John Lambert, he had whispered, “Why can’t I be a soldier too? I’m as tall as that fellow, and I can shoot as well as any man. But I earn less than sixpence a day. I’ve squandered my own bread and now eat half my brother’s. He’s the best brother, but it’s shameful I live off him. Don’t tell my brother, Jack Lambert.”

“And my boy promised he wouldn’t,” Mrs. Lambert said.

The girls were out of the room when she spoke.

George said he had written to his mother, offering half his inheritance—perhaps the whole, if needed—for Harry to buy a commission or pursue any venture that might bring him purpose.

“He has a good brother,” the lady sighed. “Let us hope for better days.”

“The Danes always come pour qui scait attendre,” George murmured.

“You heard that? Ah, George! My Theo is an—ah, never mind what she is, George Warrington,” the mother said, eyes brimming.

“Bah! I’m going to make a fool of myself, just as I did at the tragedy.”

But Mr. George had been planning a private scheme for his brother’s benefit. After his presentation to the Prince at Kensington, several people—including General Lambert—had mentioned that the Duke had inquired about him and wondered why he hadn’t come to his levee. Such royal interest could not be ignored.

A day was set, and George and the General visited the Prince at his house in Pall Mall. When it was George’s turn to bow, the Prince was especially gracious. He spoke at length about Braddock and the war, pleased by the young man’s modest and intelligent replies.

George attributed the expedition’s failure not only to panic and surprise, but more to delays caused by colonial greed and selfishness toward the King’s troops.

“If we had moved a month sooner,” George said, “the fort would have been ours, and the army never defeated.”

The Prince fully agreed.

“I’m told you saved yourself mainly through your knowledge of French,” the Duke remarked kindly.

George modestly explained his youth in the French colonies, where he had learned the language.

The Prince, known for his charm when pleased, asked who had taught him—and joked that French ladies were the best teachers.

George bowed low and said it was not for him to contradict his Royal Highness.

The Duke, laughing, called him “a sly dog.”

Still silent, George waited.

Then the Prince said, “I take the field immediately against the French, who threaten His Majesty’s Electoral dominions. If you wish to join me, your language skills may prove useful. I hope we’ll be more fortunate than poor Braddock!”

Every eye turned to the young man receiving such an offer from a prince.

And now George delivered his finest speech.

“Sir,” he said, “your Royal Highness’s proposal does me infinite honor, but—”

“But what, sir?” the Prince asked sharply.

“But I have enrolled at the Temple to study law and prepare for my duties at home. If my wound in service gives me any claim to your favor, I humbly ask that my brother—equally fluent in French, stronger, braver, and more gifted in military affairs—be allowed to serve in my place.”

“Enough, enough, sir!” the Prince snapped, visibly irritated. “I offer you a favor, and you hand it to your brother? Wait till I offer you another!”

And with that, he turned abruptly away—just as he would later turn on the French.

“Oh, George! Oh, George! Here’s a pretty kettle of fish!” General Lambert groaned as they walked home together.

The news of Mr. George Warrington’s refusal to join the Duke of Cumberland’s army stirred a storm of indignation among loyal Britons. To decline an invitation from the beloved son of King George II, Captain-General of the British forces, was seen as nothing short of sacrilege. What a chance for advancement had been cast aside! What a rare favour spurned! Esmond, ever prone to fiery rhetoric, could scarcely contain his wrath. “That cursed young Mohock,” he raged, “is cutting his own throat!” He took grim satisfaction in imagining the consequences of such ingratitude.

Cousin Castlewood offered a more charitable interpretation: “A savage gentleman may scalp himself if he chooses.” Or perhaps, he added with quiet sympathy, “our cousin heard enough war-whoops at Braddock’s defeat and has lost his taste for battle.”

Mr. Will, meanwhile, rejoiced that the younger brother had gone to ruin—and hoped the elder would follow. “The next time I see him,” he declared, “I’ll make sure he knows exactly what I think.”

“Then you’d best be careful,” Lady Maria interjected sharply, “that Harry isn’t within earshot!”

Will muttered darkly—likely something about twins and their shared disgrace.

“My Lord Hervey,” said the Duke, stepping into the fray with a smile, “we can’t all be warriors in one family.”

“And your lordship never claimed to be one?” Maria retorted.

“Never, my dear. Quite the contrary. Will is our champion. One warrior is quite enough for any household. And so, I suppose, with the two Mohocks—George is the scholar, Harry the soldier. When you chose to quarrel, Will, how unfortunate it was you didn’t have George on your side instead of the other!”

“Your lordship’s hand is famous—at piquet,” Mrs. Hervey observed dryly.

“It is a fine hand,” the Duke replied, examining his fingers with a faint smirk. “My Lord Hervey’s glove and mine were of a size. Yes, my hand is better suited to cards than to swords. Yours, my Lady Castlewood, is remarkably dexterous too. How I bless the day you gave it to my lamented father!”

Such banter delighted the Duke—he possessed both wit and coolness, and often outmanoeuvred his family in verbal duels.

Madame de Bernstein, upon hearing of George’s refusal, flew into a rage. She scolded her servants, nearly lashed out at George himself—but age and caution held her back. She feared her nephew, and though she disapproved, she could not bring herself to confront him directly.

“You will never rise at court, nephew,” she sighed when George came to call shortly after his rejection.

“It was never my wish, madam,” George replied with calm dignity.

“But you might have helped Harry. You could have served your brother by accepting the Duke’s offer. Princes do not take kindly to refusal. It’s no wonder his Royal Highness was offended.”

George turned slightly red. “General Lambert said much the same. I now see I was wrong. But please remember—I’ve never known court life. I don’t expect to shine there.”

“I fear you won’t, my good nephew,” the Baroness replied, taking snuff.

“And what then?” George asked.

“I’ve never sought that kind of glory. I’m content without it. When His Royal Highness spoke to me—kindly, I must say—my thought was this: I am no soldier, but my brother Harry is. He has every quality the profession demands; I lack them all. If the Duke were wounded and fell from his horse, as poor Braddock did, would he not be better off with a mount that could carry him through fire and storm than one that couldn’t bear his weight?”

“Au fait,” the old lady murmured. “His Royal Highness’s charger must be strong indeed, my dear.”

“Expende Hannibalem,” George muttered, shrugging.

“Your Hannibal weighs no trifle,” the Baroness noted.

“I don’t quite follow you,” she said.

“When Wolfe and Lambert remonstrated with me, just as you have, madam,” George replied with a laugh, “I gave this very argument. I told them I offered the Prince the best soldier in the family. They admitted my mistake had some excuse. Perhaps they’ll still speak well of me to His Royal Highness. My experience of war has taught me my true inclinations lie elsewhere.
