The other night, we saw the Scottish play everyone’s talking about. When the hero, young Norval, said he longed to follow a warlike lord to battle, I thought, ‘How like Harry!’—except that he doesn’t brag. Harry dreams of red coats. He follows the King of Prussia everywhere. He fears neither man nor god. As for me, I prefer books and peace. I read battles in Homer or Lucan—not fight them.”

“Then why become a soldier at all?” Madame de Bernstein asked. “And why not send Harry with Braddock instead of going yourself?”

“My mother loved her youngest son best,” George answered, voice low and dark. “And when the enemy invaded our land, it was my duty—as head of the family—to go. Had I been a Scot twelve years ago, I should have been a——”

“Hush, sir!” the Baroness snapped, though her face betrayed amusement. “Or I shall be more angry than ever!”

George’s explanation may have satisfied the Baroness—a woman whose principles were, we suspect, not rigid. But to Sir Miles Warrington and his wife, the news struck like a blow.

“I thought,” Lady Warrington said, “from my sister Esmond’s letters, that her widowhood had preserved her sense and judgment, and that she had raised her sons with proper decorum. Yet what are we to make of an education that produced such failure in both boys?”

“The elder speaks Latin fluently,” Mr. Claypool remarked, “and French and German too. I heard him converse with the Hanover Envoy at the Baroness’s gathering. He jabbered French easily. When he lacked High Dutch, he and the envoy switched to Latin—talked away till the whole room stared.”

“It’s not language, Thomas Claypool,” Lady Warrington insisted, “but principle. What must George’s principles be, if he could refuse an offer from his Prince? The more he speaks, the more he should have accepted it! Look at our son, look at Miles!”

“Hold up thy head, Miley, my boy!” Sir Miles declared.

“I trust, Sir Miles,” the matron continued, “that as a Member of Parliament and an English gentleman, you’ll attend His Royal Highness’s levee tomorrow and declare—if such an offer had been made for our child—we would have accepted it, even though he’s only ten.”

“Faith, Miley,” said Sir Miles, “thou’d make a fine little drummer or fifer!”

“Shouldst like to be a little soldier, Miley?”

“Anything, sir, anything!” the boy cried. “A Warrington ought to be ready at any moment to be cut in pieces for his sovereign!”

He roared loudly—then was promptly removed by Screwby.

Next day, obedient to his wife’s command, Sir Miles attended the levee. There he paid solemn homage to the Prince, who graciously accepted his declaration, saying: “Nobody ever supposed Sir Miles Warrington would refuse any office offered to him.”

A compliment echoed throughout London, repeated by Lady Warrington as proof of the royal family’s full trust in the Warringtons’ loyalty.

Thus, when George returned home, he was met not with anger, but with a sorrowful pity—the kind reserved for those who have failed spectacularly: the bankrupt, the disgraced, the one who walks into a room where they’ve just been condemned. Who does not recognize that face? Whose kin hasn’t mourned them, not dead, but living?

Not you? Then, sir, if you’ve never stumbled, never sown wild oats, never spoken imprudently, never sinned and repented, never been foolish and regretted it—then you’re a wise man, and this tale is not for you.

Yet it was unjust of Sir Miles to turn on George. For Sir Miles himself had once agreed with George’s decision: to pursue a civilian life, not a military one. This was precisely the plan Madam Esmond had outlined in her letters from Virginia. George had announced his intention to enter the Temple, to train for the civil and judicial duties he would one day assume. And no one had praised this choice more heartily than Sir Miles himself, who introduced George to a respected lawyer under whose tutelage we imagine the young man studying diligently.

Madam Esmond approved fully. She wrote to Sir Miles and his wife, expressing gratitude and affirming that the British Constitution was the envy of the world—a subject every English gentleman should study with admiration.

Her only objection? That George would dine in the Temple mess hall—cutting mutton, drinking small beer from tin pannikins beside rough students in clerical gowns. Harry, too, shared this disdain. “Anything is good enough for me,” he said. “I’m the younger son. I can endure hardship.” But George, in a gown, eating off pewter platters beside nobodies? Harry could not stomach it. He wished fervently that an application had been made to the Master of the Temple, declaring that Mr. George Warrington was of noble birth and great American wealth, and therefore deserved a seat among the elite.

But when Harry shared this idea with their friend Mr. Spencer at the coffee-house, Spencer burst into laughter. And history, as recorded in the Warrington papers, shows no such petition was ever sent.

Beyond law, George pursued literature and history—his true passions. He attended Westminster courts, listening to Henley, Pratt, Murray—men famed for eloquence and patriotism. He followed debates in both Houses of Parliament. Gradually, he gained notice among members of the Bar and Commons, who spoke of him as a young man of intelligence and refinement. Their regard softened Sir Miles’s heart, and Dora and Flora began to smile upon him again.

This reconciliation came at a turning point: after the Duke of Cumberland’s defeat at Hastenbeck, he signed a capitulation the King refused to ratify. Humiliated, the Duke resigned his commissions, laid down his baton—though truth be told, he had wielded it poorly—and withdrew from public life forever.

Though he never blamed his father, the loss of power and prestige diminished his standing. With it, Sir Miles’s anger toward George faded.

One day, walking in St. James’s Park with Mr. Lambert, the brothers encountered the Duke—dressed plainly, without star or staff. They bowed deeply. The Prince stopped, smiled, and asked Mr. Lambert how he liked Lord Ligonier, the new Commander-in-Chief, and his duties at Horse Guards.

Then, recognizing the young men, he turned to George: “You did well, sir, not to come with me when I asked you in the spring.”

“I was sorry then, sir,” George replied, bowing low, “but I am more sorry now.”

“Thank you, sir,” the Prince said, touching his hat, and walked on.

When Harry wrote this account to his mother, she treasured it. She recounted it hundreds of times until all her friends knew it by heart—and likely grew weary of it.

As the three men walked toward the Strand, Mr. Lambert pointed to the lion atop the Earl of Northumberland’s house at Charing Cross.

“Harry Warrington!” he said. “Your brother is like yonder lion.”

“Because he is as brave as one,” Harry replied.

“Because I respect virgins!” George laughed.

“Because you’re a stupid lion,” Harry shot back. “Because you face west, saluting the setting sun. Why, child, what good comes from being civil to a man in disgrace? Your uncle will be angrier than ever—and so am I, sir.”

But Mr. Lambert only chuckled, unbothered. He was always laughing—never truly angry.

If Harry Warrington had any passion for war and military life, he was fortunate to live in a time when Europe trembled with conflict and every London drawing-room buzzed with talk of battlefields and kings. Though our own beloved Prince of the House of Hanover had suffered defeat, the Protestant Hero—the King of Prussia—was spreading his name across the continent with dazzling victories. I am grateful, on my own account, that Harry did not take part in those great campaigns; for then I would have been compelled to describe battles already immortalized by another pen. I am truly glad that Harry Warrington was not at Rossbach on that famous Gunpowder Day, November 5th, 1757, nor at Leuthen, where the Prussian king delivered such a crushing blow just a month later. These mighty events shall be told in other volumes—volumes that all the world eagerly awaits. Would this history dare to rival such grand narratives? Could my light-hearted yellow park phaeton challenge the thundering chariot of war? Could my gentle Pegasus meet the charge of a steed with flaming nostrils and bit of fire? Dear reader—kind, patient, dear reader—let us both be thankful that Harry Warrington did not follow the King of Prussia, as he once intended. For then I would have had to recount wars that Thomas Carlyle himself will paint with greater power. And I do not wish you to compare me with such a master.

Yet Harry did not join the King of Prussia—not because he lacked desire, but because fate held him back. Instead, he lingered in idle sorrow, a man without purpose or direction. He wandered through military coffee-houses, reading nothing but newspapers. Books were not his calling. He found novels absurd, and could not understand how ladies wept over Richardson’s tales. He laughed heartily—though often too late, after the joke had passed. Why must every gentleman be a scholar? And do we despise friends simply because they never composed a single verse? Ruined, idle, dependent upon his brother for support, Harry read only to fall asleep. His strong hands had no work to do. How lucky it is that he avoided deeper ruin! Even Achilles, sent by his mother to the court of King Lycomedes to keep him safe from war, found himself stirred by longing and pride among women. And what became of Pyrrhus? A bold young hero should not be bound by women's care, nor kept idle with distaffs and tea-cups. When he is not fighting, such a man is likely to fall into worse mischief still.

The two elder Lambert ladies—gentle, compassionate souls—had deep pity for Harry, a kindness only certain women can give. Who comforts a man in grief? Who soothes him in anger? Who doubles his joy, shares his triumph, and stands beside him when disgrace strikes? Who binds the wounds made by Fortune’s cruel arrows? Only woman, if you please. You who have known hardship—have you not found such tender healers beside you? Thank the gods for their presence. What gentleman has not his rock, his chain, his liver torn by daily pain? But the sea-nymphs come—soft, kind, understanding—they kiss our wounded feet, wet our dry lips with their tears, and comfort us Titans in our downfall. They do not abandon us when we fall.

Theo and her mother felt profound sympathy for Harry. But Hetty’s heart was harder, sharper. She resented his idleness, his lack of glory. The world was at war—why could he not carry a musket? It was harvest season, and thousands reaped with flashing sickles—could he not cut down his own sheaf of honor?

“Why, how fierce she is with him!” said Papa, after one of Hetty’s usual sharp exchanges with Harry, who came daily like a target set up in Mrs. Lambert’s drawing-room.

“Her behavior is abominable!” cried Mamma. “She deserves to be scolded and sent to bed.”

“Perhaps,” Theo ventured gently, “it’s because she likes him more than any of us do. Perhaps she is angry for his sake. If I loved someone deeply, I would want to admire him always—to believe everything he did was right—and to think my gentleman better than all others.”

“That’s true, my dear,” replied Mrs. Lambert. “Your father is so much better than anyone else—he has spoiled us all. Have you ever seen anyone like him?”

“Very few,” Theo admitted, blushing.

“Few indeed. Who is so good-tempered?”

“I think no one, mamma,” Theo said softly.

“Or so brave?”

“Well, Mr. Wolfe, or Harry, or Mr. George, are certainly brave.”

“Or so learned and witty?”

“Oh, Mr. George seems very learned, and witty in his way,” Theo said. “His manners are exquisite—Madame de Bernstein says so, and she has seen the world. He has a noble bearing, unlike others. In books, he chooses the finest, most noble things, even though he mocks them. He is satirical, yes—but only toward the petty and weak. No gentleman has a softer heart. Just yesterday, after he spoke so sharply, I looked out the window and saw him stop to buy apples for a whole crowd of children. And the day before, when he brought me Molière, he gave money to a beggar—so gracefully! And he reads French beautifully. I agree with him about *Tartuffe*, though it is clever and lively—it’s too mean a villain to be the center of a great play. Iago, Mr. George said, is nearly as wicked—but he isn’t the main character; Othello is, with his noble weakness. But Molière’s portraits of gentlemen and ladies—Mr. George thinks them splendid—but oh, I can’t repeat the verses after him.”

“But you know them by heart?” asked Mrs. Lambert.

“Oh yes, mamma—I know them by... Nonsense!”

I imagine here a blush, a flutter, and Miss Theo hurrying away, cheeks glowing like roses. Why had she stopped? Because her mother was watching her oddly. And why did Mamma watch her so? And why had she followed Mr. George with her eyes when he left, and waited for him when he returned? Ah, and why do cheeks flush, and why do flowers bloom? Time still flies. Old spring, old summer, old autumn, old winter—when trees stand bare or white with snow.

A few minutes after George arrived, Theo would descend with a fluttering heart, perhaps, holding a fresh nosegay—just gathered, as it were, in his honor. I suppose she watched the street constantly, eager to see his generosity to the sweep or his purchase from the apple-woman. But if it was Harry who knocked, she stayed in her room, working or reading, sending her sister to greet him—or her brothers, if the elder was home from college, or Doctor Crusius had given the younger leave.

Our friends were welcome at Mr. Lambert’s house, free to come and stay as they pleased. One day, Harry sat on a couch, sunk in a mood of unusual weariness and despair, when who should appear but Miss Hetty? It was curious—though the girls would never admit it—that when Harry came, Hetty appeared; when George arrived, Theo somehow materialized. Thus, according to custom, it was Miss Lambert, junior, who now entered to entertain the younger Virginian.

After polite greetings, she said:

“And pray, sir, what makes your honor look so glum this morning?”

“Ah, Hetty,” he sighed, “I have nothing else to do but look glum. I remember when we were boys—I was a lazy one, you may be sure—I’d always ask my tutor for a holiday, spend it swinging on a gate or making ducks and drakes on the pond. Those idle days were always the most melancholy. What have I to do now, from morning till night?”

“Breakfast, walk—dinner, walk—tea, supper, I suppose,” said Hetty, tossing her head. “And a pipe of your Virginia.”

“I tell you,” Harry went on, “when I returned with Charley to the Chartreux the other night, I almost said to the master, ‘Teach me, sir. Here’s a boy who knows more Latin and Greek at thirteen than I do at twenty-three. I’ve nothing to do all day—I might as well return to my books and try to mend my youth.’ Why do you laugh, Hetty?”

“I laugh at the thought of you at the head of a class, called up by the master!” she exclaimed.

“I wouldn’t be at the head,” Harry said humbly. “George might lead any class. But I’m not a scholar, you see. As a boy, I neglected myself. We wouldn’t let our tutors cane us much at home—but if we had, it might have helped.”

Hetty tapped her foot, looking at the young man—strong, idle, sorrowful.

“Upon my word, it might help you now!” she thought. “What does Tom say about being caned at school? Does his story make you long for it?”

“My brother’s account,” Harry answered simply, “makes me realize I wasted my time when I should have worked. I have no gift for books. So what am I good for? Only to spend my patrimony when I come abroad, or loiter at coffeehouses or racecourses, or chase hounds when I’m home. I’m good for nothing. That’s what I am.”

“What, such a big, brave, strong fellow—good for nothing?” Hetty retorted. “I wouldn’t confess that to any woman, even if I were twice as useless!”

“What am I to do?” Harry asked. “I’ve begged to join the army, but Madam Esmond hasn’t answered. That’s the only thing I’m fit for. I have no money to buy a commission. I’ve spent all mine—and so much of my brother’s. I won’t ask for more. If my mother would send me, I’d go in a heartbeat.”

“Eh!” said Hetty. “A man of spirit doesn’t need a woman to buckle his sword or clean his musket! Remember what Papa told us yesterday about Sir John Armytage?”

“Sir John Armytage? I knew him at White’s and the clubs—a fine, noble young man, heir to a great estate in the North.”

“And engaged to a famous beauty—Miss Howe, Lord Howe’s sister—but surely that’s no obstacle?”

“To what?” asked Harry.

“To glory!” Hetty declared. “I don’t think any woman of spirit would say ‘Stay!’ even if she adored her lover. When her country calls, she lets him go. Sir John volunteered for the coming expedition. Yesterday at court, His Majesty asked when he’d be ready. ‘Tomorrow, please your Majesty,’ he replied. And the king said, ‘That’s a soldier’s answer.’ Papa himself longs to go, though he has us all at home. Oh dear, oh dear! Why wasn’t I born a man? Both my brothers are going into the Church—but I know I’d make a fine little soldier!” And as she spoke, she paced the room, radiating courage, bold as Joan of Arc.

Harry watched her with quiet admiration. “I think,” he said, “I wouldn’t like to see a musket on that small shoulder, or a wound on that pretty face, Hetty.”

“Wounds? Who fears wounds?” she snapped. “Muskets? If I could carry one, I’d use it. You men think we’re only good for puddings and samplers. Why wasn’t I a man? George read Tasso to us yesterday—look, here’s the book, with the mark where we left off.”

“With the mark?” Harry asked.

“Yes. It’s about a woman disappointed because her brother won’t go to war. She says—

‘Alas! why did not Heaven these members frail
With lively force and vigour strengthen, so
That I this silken gown...’”

“Silken gown?” Harry asked, puzzled.

“Well, sir, I know it’s only Calimanco—but so it is in the book—

‘... this silken gown and slender veil
Might for a breastplate and a helm forgo;
Then should not heat, nor cold, nor rain, nor hail,
Nor storms that fall, nor blust'ring winds that blow,
Withhold me; but I would, both day and night,
In pitched field or private combat, fight—’”

“Fight? Yes, that I would!” Hetty declared. “Why must both my brothers become parsons? One of my father’s children ought to be a soldier!”

Harry smiled—softly, kindly—as he looked at her. He couldn’t imagine hurting such a delicate warrior.

“Why,” he said, holding up a finger, “this finger is nearly as thick as your arm. How would you stand against a big, strong man? I’d like to see any rogue try to harm you. You little, tender creature! Do you think any villain would dare touch you?” Excited, he began pacing, imagining a Frenchman daring to offend Miss Hester Lambert.

It was this silent strength he seemed to possess that drew Hetty to him—the courage she believed he had—that made her admire him. Yet Hetty herself was no warrior. She was no more bold than Erminia, whose words she had just recited—whose name Harry had never heard. He may have been present when George read poetry to the ladies, but his thoughts were elsewhere, lost in Clotildas and giants and enchanted forests. No, Miss Hetty—no, I believe—had no trace of the Amazon in her nature. Otherwise, she would have liked a soft, literary man, or one who played the flute. And who has not noticed how great, strong men are drawn to fragile, gentle women? How tender women are drawn to powerful, honest men? How mighty warriors often end up henpecked? If Harry Warrington falls in love with a woman like Miss Lambert—and marries her—without magic, we can all guess the outcome.

So while Hetty fired her sharp remarks at Harry, he scarcely felt them, letting her shoot on without even flicking the tiny arrows from his skin. Did she mean to stir him into action? He was too generous to grasp such subtle hints. Did she mean to shame him by saying she, a weak woman, would wear armor and fight? He either melted at the thought of her in danger—or burst into laughter.

“What good is a strong hand if you only use it to hold silk for my mother?” Hetty demanded. “And what’s the point of being strong in a drawing-room? Nobody wants you to throw someone out the window, Harry! A strong man, indeed! There’s probably a stronger at Bartholomew Fair. James Wolfe isn’t strong. He looks weak and ill. Last time he was here, he coughed all day, pale as if he’d seen a ghost.”

“I never understood why a man should fear a ghost,” Harry said.

“Have you seen one, sir?” asked Hetty, sharp as ever.

“No,” he replied. “I thought I once—at home, when we were boys. But it was only Nathan in his nightshirt. I wasn’t frightened. I think ghosts don’t exist. Nurses lie about them.” He paused. “George was a little afraid—but then, he’s…”

“Then George is what?” Hetty pressed.

“George is different from me,” Harry said. “Our mother is as bold as any woman—but she screams at mice. Can’t help it. It’s her nature. So perhaps George can’t bear ghosts. I don’t mind them.”

“George always says you’d have made a better soldier than he.”

“So I think I would—if I’d been allowed to try. But he can do a thousand things better than anyone. Why didn’t he let me volunteer on Braddock’s expedition? I might have died—and then I’d be as useful as I am now. At least I wouldnーt have ruined myself, brought shame on the Warrington name. Why can’t I go on this new expedition, and volunteer like Sir John Armytage? Oh, Hetty! I’m a miserable fellow—that’s what I am,” he groaned, pacing quickly.

“What a compliment to us! Thank you, Harry!” she said, then softened at his look. “Are you—thinking of going home?”

“And have all Virginia laughing at me? Not a gentleman there would accept me—except one, and my mother doesn’t like him. I’d be ashamed to return. You don’t know my mother, Hetty. I’m not afraid of most things—but somehow, I am of her. What shall I say when she asks, ‘Harry, where’s your inheritance?’ ‘Spent, mother,’ I’ll have to say. ‘What have you done with it?’ ‘Wasted it, mother—and ended up in prison.’ ‘Who got you out?’ ‘Brother George, ma'am. He took me out. Now I’m back—useless, with no profession, no future—only to tend negroes, be scolded at home, or sleep through sermons, or gamble, drink, and cockfight at taverns.’ How can I face the gentlemen of Virginia? I’m ashamed to go home like this. I must do something! What shall I do, Hetty? What shall I do?”

“What did Mr. Wolfe do at Louisbourg?” Hetty asked. “Ill as he was, in love as we knew, he didn’t wait to be nursed by his mother or dally with his sweetheart. He went into the King’s service and returned covered in glory. If there’s another campaign in America, Papa says he’s sure of a command.”

“I wish he’d take me,” Harry moaned. “And that a bullet would finish me.”

“You speak as if it were my fault you’re not in the army,” Hetty said, shrugging. “When you know I’d give—give, what have I to give?—yes! My life—to go into service!”

“Life indeed!” Hetty said, dismissively.

“You don’t seem to value it much,” Harry remarked sadly. “No more it is—anyone’s life. I’m a poor, useless fellow. I’m not even free to throw it away, as I’d like—because I’m under orders here and at home.”

“Orders?” Hetty scoffed. “Why under orders? Are you not tall enough, old enough to act for yourself? Must you have George as your master here, and your mother as your schoolmistress at home? If I were a man, I’d do something great before I was twenty-two. I’d make the world talk of me. I wouldn’t waste time at apron-strings. I wouldn’t curse my luck—I’d make it. I swear I would!”

For the first time, Harry flinched at her words.

“No slave on our plantation is more enslaved than I am,” he said, turning red. “But then, Miss Lambert—we don’t blame the poor man for not being free. That’s not generous. That’s not honor. Perhaps it’s different for women. Or maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I shouldn’t be hurt by a girl telling me my faults. Maybe my faults aren’t faults—only bad luck. You’ve talked so long about this man volunteering, that man winning glory, praising their courage as if I had none. I suppose I’m as well equipped as any gentleman. I don’t brag—but I’m not afraid of Mr. Wolfe, nor Sir John Armytage, nor anyone I’ve ever met. How can I buy a commission when I’ve spent my last shilling? Or ask my brother for more, when he’s already shared half with me? A gentleman of my rank can’t enlist as a common soldier—else, by Jupiter, I would! And if a bullet ends me, I suppose Miss Hetty Lambert wouldn’t mind. It’s unkind, Hetty—I didn’t think you’d say that.”

“What have I said?” she asked. “Only that Sir John Armytage volunteered, and Mr. Wolfe gained honor. And now you scold me! How can I help it if Mr. Wolfe is brave and famous? Is that reason to be angry?”

“I didn’t say angry,” Harry said gravely. “I said I was hurt.”

“Oh!” Hetty exclaimed. “I thought such a tiny creature as I couldn’t hurt anyone! It’s flattering to hear that a girl whose arm is no bigger than your little finger can wound a man as strong as you!”

“I never expected you’d try, Hetty,” he said. “You see, I’m not used to this kind of reception in this house.”

“What is it, my poor boy?” asked Mrs. Lambert, appearing at the door, seeing Harry’s distressed face.

“Oh, we’ve heard it all before, mamma!” Hetty said quickly. “Harry’s complaining again about having nothing to do. He’s unhappy—and keeps saying so over and over.”

George Warrington did not let his legal studies eclipse the pleasures of life or endanger his health. In letters, Madam Esmond had reminded him that though he wore a student’s gown and dined among nameless scholars at hall-commons, he carried with him a name of ancient lineage—one that entitled him to rank among the foremost in his own country. She urged him to study as a gentleman, not as a mere drudge of the law. He followed her counsel faithfully. Thus, while others toiled in the ranks of legal apprenticeship, George stood apart—more like a volunteer in the service of justice than a conscript. Though less rigid in those days than she would later become, the law even then demanded devotion; it was a jealous mistress who asked for near-exclusive attention. Murray, they say, might have been an Ovid, but chose instead the ermine of Lord Chief Justice. Perhaps George Warrington could have risen to a peerage, seated on the woolsack, had he pursued the law with greater diligence, had he mastered courtly ways and won favor among attorneys. But such was not his nature. He honored Themis with respect, yes—but his heart belonged to letters. The black-letter verse of Chaucer stirred him far more than the Gothic pages of Hale and Coke.

In those times, letters were truly revered. Authors were authorities. Gentlemen cited Virgil or Lucan in Parliament or the courts. What said Statius? What thought Juvenal? Let alone Tully or Tacitus—what did they declare on this matter? Their influence has faded now. The good old pagan gods are no longer worshipped—no more than their poetry or ethics. The age of economists and accountants has taken over, and Tooke’s Pantheon stands deserted, absurd. Now and again, perhaps, a Stanley sacrifices a kid, a Gladstone waves a laurel wreath, a Lytton burns incense—honoring the Olympians. But what do they care at Lambeth, Birmingham, or Tower Hamlets for ancient rites or divinities? Who, indeed, are the Muses? And what use is there in all that Greek and Latin nonsense? What is Helicon? Who cares? Who was Thalia, and how long is her *i*? Is Melpomene pronounced in three or four syllables? And from whose design did I borrow that figure of Tragedy which graces the initial G of this chapter?

It has already been told how, in his youth, and during the long idle hours at home and in his imprisonment within the French fort on the banks of Monongahela, George Warrington passed his time courting Melpomene—the Muse of Tragedy. The result of their union was a play, one omitted from Bell’s Theatre, though surely no worse than many printed there. Most young men, when first drawn to literature, turn first to tragedy—just as they often fall in love with women older than themselves. Let the honest reader admit, if ever he felt a spark of literary ambition, that his dreams were once grand—so lofty that only epic or tragic works seemed worthy of his hand. As years passed, he may have lowered his expectations, thinking that translating a Horace ode or rendering a Waller song into decent alcaics was about the height of his talent. But in youth, nothing less than the highest prize would suffice.

Thus, upon arriving in London, George frequented the theatres at both Drury Lane and Covent Garden. He visited theatrical coffee-houses, listened to critics, and could often be seen between acts at the Bedford, or supping at the Cecil with actors and wits after performances. There, he gradually made friends with players and writers known to the public. The tough old Macklin, the lively Foote, the vivacious Hippisley, and the sprightly Mr. Garrick himself sometimes appeared at these gathering places. George, with his wit and modest charm—and perhaps also because of his well-known wealth—grew popular among them. Actors willingly shared a bowl of punch with him, and critics dined at his expense with great ease. To be close to an author or actor has always been a dream for many young men. To hobnob with Bobadil or Henry V, to accept a pinch from Aristarchus’s own box, to help Juliet into her coach or guide Monimia to her chair—these were privileges any poet-hearted youth would cherish. No wonder George loved the theatre. Moreover, he took secret delight in knowing that his mother disapproved of plays and playhouses, making them feel like forbidden fruit.

He gave several elegant dinners for the players, and it was whispered that one or two distinguished geniuses had even borrowed money from him.

As he refined his masterpiece, he sought advice from trusted friends, who offered praise and guidance. Mr. Spencer, his new acquaintance from the Temple, hosted a breakfast in his chambers at Fig Tree Court, where George read part of his play. The gentlemen present declared it possessed unusual merit. Even the learned Mr. Johnson, invited as guest, acknowledged the piece showed talent. “True,” he added, “it violates the unities—but others have done so before. You may break them as well as another.” He noted that George’s tragedy bore echoes of both Coriolanus and Othello. “And two very fine plays, sir!” George replied. “Well,” said Mr. Spencer, “there can be no doubt. Your catastrophe is terrible, just, and since it draws on truth, it is all the more awful.”

The plot of George Warrington’s tragedy was rich with battle and bloodshed. One of his grandfather’s favorite books had been the life of George Frundsberg of Mindelheim, a colonel in the Imperial army during the Battle of Pavia and the wars of Constable Bourbon. Among Frundsberg’s comrades was a certain Carpzow—or Carpezan—as George named his hero. The first act, as preserved in Sir George’s manuscript, unfolds before a convent on the Rhine, besieged by Lutherans under Carpezan’s command. These Lutherans were godless: they’d torn the beards of Roman friars, stripped veils from religious women. Inside the walls, a score of nuns tremble, awaiting surrender unless reinforcements arrive by midday. For now, there is armistice. The sentries watch hungrily as soldiers and camp followers gamble outside the gate.

Twelve o’clock strikes—ding, ding, dong!—on the convent bell. No relief has come. Open the gates, warder! Admit the famed Protestant hero—the terror of Turks on the Danube, of Papists in Lombardy—Colonel Carpezan! Here he comes, clad in full armor, his war hammer slung over his shoulder—once used to shatter infidel fortifications. His banners fly, his trumpets blare.

“Hold your tongues, my men,” says Carpezan. “The wine is yours, and the convent’s larder and cellar are fair game. The church plate shall be melted. Any soldier who wishes to join Gaspar Carpezan will be paid well. No harm to the ladies! I have promised them safe passage. Anyone who touches them hangs—mind that, Provost Marshal!”

The Provost Marshal—a massive man in a red doublet—nods.

“We’ll see more of that Provost Marshal,” Mr. Spencer remarks to the guests.

“A most agreeable companion, I’m sure,” says Mr. Johnson, wagging his head over his tea. “This scene—soldiers, camp followers, their wild games—is fresh and exciting, Mr. Warrington. My compliments. The Colonel has entered the convent, I believe? Let us hear what he intends.”

The Abbess and a few elder nuns appear before the conqueror. Though defeated, they heard him in their sacred halls. They know of his past violence in religious houses. That hammer—he carries it always—has shattered countless holy images. They’ve heard of his melting of convent silver—the sacrilegious plunderer! No wonder the Abbess-Princess of St. Mary’s, noble-born, outspoken, and deeply prejudiced, resents the lowborn heretic now ruling her house. She speaks plainly to Carpezan, scolding him with boldness. This scene—where the woman gains the upper hand—was particularly admired by the audience at the Temple. Though terrifying in war, Carpezan stumbles at first under the Abbess’s sharp words. Conqueror though he is, he seems momentarily conquered by his prisoner.

But such a hardened soldier could not be bested forever by any woman. “Madam,” he says calmly, “how many sisters remain here? I will ensure transport for all.”

The Abbess, troubled and angry, replies, “Besides myself, twenty-three—twenty-three noble sisters of Saint Mary’s House.” She hesitates—had she nearly said twenty-four?

“Ah,” asks Captain Ulric, one of Carpezan’s liveliest officers, “why the hesitation?”

Carpezan pulls a letter from his coat. “I demand,” he says sternly, “the body of Lady Sybilla of Hoya. Her brother was my favorite captain, slain beside me in Milan. With his death, she inherits his lands. It is rumored her greedy uncle brought her here and imprisoned her against her will. The lady shall decide—remain cloistered, or return to freedom as Baroness of ———.”

The Abbess is shaken. “There is no Lady Sybil here,” she retorts. “Every soul in this house is under your protection and sworn to go free. Sister Agnes was a professed nun. Her lands and wealth belong to the Order.”

“Give me the body of Lady Sybilla of Hoya!” roars Carpezan. “Or I give the signal to my Reiters—and this convent goes to war!”

“Faith,” murmurs Captain Ulric, “if I led the charge, I wouldn’t choose your Lady Abbess—but rather some plump, smiling, red-lipped maid like—like—” He glances beneath the veils of two attendant nuns.

“Silence!” cries the Abbess, furious. “The lady you seek has passed beyond sin, temptation, vanity. Three days ago, our Sister Agnes—died.”

At this, Carpezan is thrown into turmoil. The Abbess calls upon the chaplain to confirm. Pale and trembling, he admits that Sister Agnes was buried three days prior.

Enough! In Carpezan’s mail coat lies a letter from Sister Agnes herself—confessing she would be entombed alive in a dungeon, kept on bread and water, or left to starve. He seizes the Abbess by the arm, while Ulric grabs the chaplain by the throat. The Colonel blows his horn. His Lanzknechts rush in—crash, bang! They batter the walls. Flames rise, screams echo, slaughter ensues. And then—Carpezan enters, carrying a fainting woman on his shoulder. It is Sybilla herself. A young nun (that same red-lipped girl) had pointed out the way to Sister Agnes’s dungeon—and revealed her fate to the Lutheran leader.

“The convent is crushed,” says George Warrington. “We end Act I with its burning, the soldiers’ shouts, the nuns’ shrieks. They’d best change their robes soon—they’ll be court ladies in Act II, as you’ll see.” The gentlemen discuss casting. Mrs. Pritchard might not relish playing the Abbess—she appears only in Act I. Miss Pritchard could play Sybilla, Miss Gates the nun. Mr. Garrick, though not tall enough, might still dominate as Carpezan—especially when roused, when no one sees him as anything less than a giant. Mr. Johnson agrees Woodward would make a fine Ulric, given his flair for Mercutio roles. Gradually, the audience imagines the play staged, the parts assigned.

In Act II, Carpezan has married Sybilla. Wealthy, ennobled by the Emperor, he lives in splendor at his castle on the Danube.

Yet despite riches and title, Lord Carpezan is not happy. Perhaps his wild life—leading mercenaries for both sides—has left him haunted by guilt. Or perhaps his rough soldier ways clashed too sharply with his highborn bride. She tormented him—mocking his humble origins, his vulgar companions whom he loved around him. At times, he wished he’d never rescued this lovely, quarrelsome vixen from the dungeon where he pulled her out. After the chaos of Act I, this act is quieter—centered on the bickering between Baron and Baroness Carpezan—until horns sound: the young King of Bohemia and Hungary approaches, hunting nearby.

Act III takes place in Prague, where the King invites Carpezan and his wife, offering nobility to her—Baron to Count, Colonel to General-in-Chief. Sybilla becomes the most dazzling lady at court. And as for Carpzoff—

“Oh, wait—I know your tale now,” interrupts Mr. Johnson. “It’s in ‘Meteranus,’ in the Theatrum Universum. I read it at Oxford—Carpezanus, or Carpzoff—”

“That’s Act IV,” says George. In Act IV, the King’s attentions toward Sybilla grow increasingly evident. Carpezan fights jealousy, refusing to believe until proof overwhelms him—until Sybilla’s guilt is undeniable. Then, convinced, he summons the executioner who follows his regiment and orders her killed in her own palace. The curtain falls just after the deed—inside a chamber lit by moonlight through a great oriel window, beneath which the King arrives with his lute, singing the tune meant to signal their tryst.

This song—written in the old style and repeated earlier in Act III at a royal festival—Mr. Johnson praises as a clever imitation of Waller’s manner. Its cheerful repetition amid murder and horror deepens the tragedy.

“But what happens next?” he asks. “In the Theatrum, Carpezan is later welcomed back by Count Mansfield—perhaps he kills others on the reformed side?”

Here, George departs from history. In Act V, King Louis of Hungary and Bohemia—deeply shaken by the bloody end of his affair—learns that Sultan Solyman invades his Hungarian lands. Two nobles enter, reporting that at the King’s council, Carpezan stormed in, broke his sword, flung it at the King’s feet—along with a glove, daring him to wear it, swearing he’d claim it one day. Then, enraged, he fled Prague. None have heard from him since—except rumors that he joined the Turkish invaders, donned a turban, and now serves in the Sultan’s camp, whose white tents gleam across the river. The King prepares to march against him.

Now the King enters his tent with generals, issuing battle orders. He dismisses them, keeping only an aged knight—his master of the horse—to whom he confesses regret for past sins, admiration for his wronged queen, and resolve to face battle like a man.

“What is this field called?”

“Mohacz, my liege,” answers the old warrior. “Before sunset, Mohacz will witness a battle bravely won.”

Trumpets sound—alarms ring. These are the cymbals and barbaric music of the Janissaries. We are in the Turkish camp. Yonder, surrounded by turbaned chiefs, walks the Sultan’s friend—the conqueror of Rhodes, the dreaded Grand Vizier.

Who is that warrior in Eastern dress, yet with a glove tucked in his cap? It is Carpezan. Even Solyman knows his courage and ferocity. He understands the Hungarian army’s weaknesses—how their cavalry, powerful as it is, should be lured into a marsh where death awaits. He begs for command in the front, near where King Louis will fight. “Well,” says the grim Vizier, “our invincible Emperor surveys the battle from yonder tower. At day’s end, he will reward your valor.”

Signal-guns fire. Trumpets blow. Turkish captains retreat, swearing death to the infidel, eternal loyalty to the Sultan.

Battle begins. Christian knights clash with Turkish warriors. Alarms continue. Troops advance and retreat. Carpezan, glove in cap, hammers all before him, roaring for King Louis. About to strike down a warrior, he recognizes young Ulric—his former captain. He lowers his hammer. “Fly, Ulric. Think of Carpezan.” Moved by seeing his old friend, he remembers their shared victories for Protestantism. Ulric urges him to return—but that is impossible. They fight. Ulric falls beneath the hammer. The renegade weeps at his wounded comrade—then sees King Louis, plumes torn, sword hacked, shield battered by a thousand blows.

Ha! Who is this? The guilty king tries to flee—but Carpezan is upon him. All softness vanishes. He rages like a fury. “A fair fight!” he roars. “Traitor against traitor! Stand, King Louis! False king, false knight, false friend—by this glove in my helmet, I challenge you!” He tears it from his cap and hurls it at the monarch.

They duel. The king falls under Carpezan’s mighty mace. He dies, muttering words of repentance. Carpezan leans on his weapon, delivering a heartbroken soliloquy over the corpse. Turkish warriors gather. The day belongs to them. The dark Vizier stands, surrounded by Janissaries—bows and swords weary from drinking death. He watches the renegade over the king.

“Christian renegade,” he says, “Allah has granted us victory. The Sublime Emperor’s arms triumph everywhere. The Christian king fell by your hand.”

“Peace to his soul,” gasps Ulric, dying on the field. “He died like a good knight.”

“In this battle,” continues the Vizier, “no man fought more bravely than you. You are made Bassa of Transylvania. Archers—fire!”

An arrow pierces Carpezan’s chest.

“Bassa of Transylvania,” the Vizier declares, “you were a traitor to your king—now slain by your hand. Yet you contributed more than any soldier to our victory. Thus, my sublime Emperor rewards you. Sound trumpets—we march for Vienna tonight!”

The curtain falls as Carpezan crawls toward his dying comrade, kisses his hands, and whispers:

“Forgive me, Ulric.”

When George finishes reading, he turns modestly to Mr. Johnson and asks, “What say you, sir? Is there any chance for me?”

But the critic cannot reply—for Mr. Johnson has been asleep for some time. He admits frankly he missed the final scenes.

The small audience hums and stirs as the reading ends. George may have been nervous at first, but all agree he read the last two acts superbly. Compliments are exchanged on both content and delivery. Perhaps everyone is in good spirits simply because the play is over. Mr. Spencer’s servant brings refreshments. The Templars sip negus and voice their opinions.

Mr. Fountain suggests the Vizier should not say “Fire!” when ordering archers—since bows don’t “fire.” A note is made.

Mr. Figtree, sentimental, regrets Ulric couldn’t survive and marry the comic heroine.

“Nay,” says Mr. Johnson, “there was a total annihilation at Mohacz. Ulric must die with the rest. He could only live by fleeing—and we wouldn’t want a hero run away. Sentence him to death, but let him die with honor.”

Messrs. Essex and Tanfield exchange glances at the odd, impertinent guest Spencer has invited—someone who contradicts everyone. They suggest a boat ride up the river for some fresh air after the drama.

Gumbo could not bear the thought of his master’s departure. When he heard that Mr. Harry had enlisted, the boy fell into such a frenzy of sorrow—howling, weeping, and wringing his hands—that one might have sworn his heart would break. No wonder he sought solace among the maids at Mr. Lambert’s lodgings. Wherever Gumbo went, he gravitated toward women, as if their gentle hearts were the only refuge for his own troubled soul. They, in turn, showed him kindness, not because of his station or skin, but because they saw in him something tender and true beneath the dark exterior. Indeed, history has shown that many Africans—like the famed Chevalier de St. Georges—have found favor with the fair sex, and Gumbo, though humble, was no exception. The servants wept with him; the maids treated him not just as Harry’s man, but as a brother.

Hetty, however, could not help laughing when she saw Gumbo sobbing over the fact that Master Harry had gone off as a volunteer—and without taking him along. “He’d die for Master Harry,” Gumbo declared, “and be cut into twenty thousand pieces before he’d let harm come to him!” Yet even in grief, he managed to eat—plenty of cold meat and beer in the kitchen, where nature demanded her due.

Greedy, idle, and prone to exaggeration, yes—he was all those things. But Hetty still gave him half a crown, and treated him with unusual tenderness. Her usual sharp tongue, once so quick with jests, now lay quiet. She moved through the house like a shadow—meek, subdued, almost reverent. She spoke softly to her mother, thanked John and Betty for serving dinner, endured Polly’s tugs on her hair during combing, and bore Charley’s clumsy footfalls without complaint. In her father’s presence, she was silent—so silent it seemed as if she had been transformed into a different girl altogether.

If Papa had asked her to roast the mutton or walk to church arm-in-arm with Gumbo, she would have curtsied low and said, “Yes, if you please, dear papa.”

But what did it matter? What kind of meal were poor volunteers eating, with cannonballs flying overhead? And church—how could she pray when the very words “Thou shalt do no murder” echoed in her ears, making her knees tremble as she knelt? She lowered her head whenever the parson read from the communion rail, afraid he might be looking directly at her. She thought constantly of travelers—by land or sea—and sickened each time she ran to fetch the newspaper, hoping for news of the expedition. She watched her father closely when he returned from the Ordnance Office, searching his face for signs of good or ill fortune. Was he well? Had he become a general? Was he wounded—or worse? Perhaps both legs had been taken by a single shot, like that old pensioner seen in Chelsea Garden the other day?

She would gladly wear wooden legs all her life—if only his could bring him home safe. At least, she vowed, she would never rise from her knees until he did.

“Have you heard of people whose hair turned grey in a single night, Theo?” she asked one day. “I wouldn’t be surprised if mine did—wouldn’t be surprised at all.” And she stared into the mirror, half-expecting to see silver strands already creeping through the brown.

“Theo,” her elder sister replied gently, “you weren’t this nervous when Papa was away in Minorca.”

“Oh, Theo,” Hetty sighed, “one can easily see George is not with the army—he’s safe at home.” At this, Theo blushed and looked down, her thoughts drifting elsewhere.

Indeed, if Mr. George had been in the army, matters would have been quite different.

But enough of such sorrow. We shall not prolong the anguish. Let us say plainly: Harry Warrington, for the moment, was as safe as any officer stationed in Regent’s Park Barracks.

His first campaign was neither glorious nor decisive—but it was real. The British Lion, after all, does not always meet a worthy foe. Sometimes, he sets out to battle a tiger and finds only a goose. He may roar and paw, but the goose is quickly dispatched. Lions must eat, just as men must live. But suppose, instead of one tiger, six emerge from the forest? Then the lion turns tail and retreats—wise to do so. To charge six tigers would make him no hero, but a fool.

Such was the case with Harry Warrington.

On June 1st, he sailed with about thirteen thousand others from the Isle of Wight. By dawn on the 5th, the fleet stood in the Bay of Cancale, Brittany. From their ships, the volunteers enjoyed a view of the French coast while the Commander-in-Chief and Commodore reconnoitered in a cutter. Cattle grazed nearby; dragoons trotted off into the distance. A small fort with two guns dared fire upon the officers in the boat. By two o’clock, the entire British fleet was anchored, and signals were sent for grenadiers from eleven regiments to board flat-bottomed boats and gather around the Essex, the Commodore’s ship.

Meanwhile, Admiral Howe hoisted his pennant aboard the frigate Success and sailed close to shore, followed by other frigates, to protect the landing. Under Lord George Sackville and General Dury, the volunteers, grenadiers, and three battalions of guards rowed ashore.

But no heroic deeds were possible. The French, who should have fought, fled. The frigates silenced the fort’s guns, and the army stormed it, capturing the entire garrison—just one old gentleman, who fired both cannons gallantly before surrendering. “If every Frenchman had acted like me,” he told his captors, “you would not have landed at Cancale at all.”

The advance force occupied the village of Cancale and rested under arms all night. There, Harry was teased by comrades for his eagerness to go on the war-path and bring back scalps. But no scalps came his way. The only death of the day was a French nobleman riding with his servant, whom Lord Downe surprised marching ahead with Kingsley’s company. My Lord offered quarter, which the man refused. Both he, his servant, and their horses were shot.

The next day, the full force landed and marched to St. Malo. Villages emptied before them; roads were narrow, forcing single-file march. Hedges rose high—had there been enemies, they could have been ambushed. At dusk, the army reached St. Malo, greeted by artillery fire from the town—though darkness limited damage. Under cover of the shots, the British set fire to ships, warehouses, pitch and tar stores, creating a blaze that burned through the night.

No resistance came. Though it was believed a strong French force remained in the town, they chose not to emerge. So the Duke of Marlborough and Lord Sackville decided not to attack. Instead, they withdrew to Cancale—and then boarded their ships again.

Had this been fiction, one might have sent Harry off on grander adventures. But history is not so obliging.

Exactly four weeks after leaving England, Harry arrived back at Portsmouth. He wrote to his brother George, who rushed to Dean Street with the letter in hand.

“Glorious news, ladies!” George announced, finding the Lamberts at breakfast. “Our champion has returned! He faced dangers—dragons, even! He says so himself!”

“Dragons?” Mrs. Lambert asked, startled.

“Not killed any,” George added, laughing. “But he saw them.”

“What does he mean?” Hetty cried.

“Immense creatures with long tails and steel scales,” Papa explained, “who breathe fire and devour virgins. Haven’t you read *The Seven Champions*?”

“St. George’s flag scared them off,” George said.

“I’ve read of them,” little Charles from Chartreux chimed in solemnly. “They eat women. One tried to eat Andromeda. Jason killed another guarding the golden apples.”

Harry’s letter continued:

> “Dearest Brother—
> I am glad to tell you I am returned—without commission, without wounds, without glory—but alive and hearty. Our ship was as crowded as poor Mr. Holwell’s Black Hole at Calicut. We had rough seas, and some of the gentlemen volunteers grumbled. Their stomachs are dainty. After Braund’s cookery and White’s kick-shaws, plain rum and biscuit didn’t sit well. But I, having sailed before, took my rations and flip with contentment. I meant to show our English macaronis that a Virginia gentleman is as good as the best.
>
> I wish I had more to brag about. But all I can say is—we went to France and came back. Why, I don’t think even your tragic pen could make anything of such a campaign. We landed on the 6th at Cancale Bay. We saw a few dragons on a hill—who rode away without fighting. We slept under canvas. We marched to St. Malo and burned many privateers. Then we returned to ship—never crossed swords with an enemy, except a few poor devils plundered by the troops. Better luck next time! This wasn’t glorious—but I liked it. I smelled powder, rosin, and pitch. I saw the enemy. Slept under canvas. Was dreadfully crowded and sick at sea. I liked it.
>
> Best compliments to Aunt Lambert. Tell Miss Hetty I wasn’t very frightened seeing the French horse.
>
> Your most affectionate brother,

Hetty’s fears were not eased by this news. But soon after, Mr. Lambert visited the troops at Portsmouth, and George accompanied him. They found Harry greatly changed—spirited, healthy, eager to learn military drills. He was no longer the listless youth who lingered in coffeehouses and drawing rooms. Now he was alert, cheerful, and full of energy—a new man entirely.

George walked arm-in-arm with him through the streets of Portsmouth, recalling his own brief military service two years prior. He marveled at the size of the army compared to the disastrous one he had once joined. Though the campaign was unglorious, morale was high. The nation celebrated—claiming victory over the proud Gaul, even if no great battle had been fought. What valour, after all, could compare to British valour?

And then came the next expedition—one that promised more glory.

This time, a distinguished volunteer led the charge: His Royal Highness Prince Edward. He boarded the Essex in a twelve-oared barge, the English standard flying proudly. The Admiral followed, then the captains in order of rank. The fleet sailed forth, Harry waving his hat from the deck as friends cheered from the shore.

He would surely earn his commission soon. George believed it was only a matter of time. Money was available to buy it—but better yet, if Harry could win it through courage and conduct. The regiment’s colonel praised him highly; officers and men alike liked him. He was clearly a young man of promise.

Ten days later, news arrived that thrilled the nation.

On August 7th and 8th, His Majesty’s troops had landed in the Bay des Marais, west of Cherbourg, facing a large enemy force. But the French fled. Cherbourg surrendered. The English flag flew over three outer forts. Twenty-seven ships were burned, dozens of brass cannons captured. Iron guns were destroyed, the harbor basin demolished, and both piers at the entrance shattered.

London erupted in celebration. Captured colors from Louisbourg were brought to St. Paul’s, escorted by life-guards and horse-grenadiers. At the West Gate, the Dean and Chapter received them—then the Tower and Park guns thundered in salute.

Next day, the Cherbourg cannons rolled through the streets—adorned with lilies, crowns, and mottoes. People shouted and cheered. The Teneraire, the Malfaisant, the Vainqueur—what a triumph!

And Hetty? She believed Harry had dragged every cannon from the batteries himself, vanquishing the gunners single-handed. His name soared. Madame de Bernstein inquired after him. Lady Maria begged George to visit and give her news.

George, once the center of attention, felt suddenly overshadowed. Wit, learning, tragedy—what were these compared to victories and brass cannons?

Still, hope burned bright. Fifteen thousand Britons—why not march on Paris itself? Some ladies believed it possible.

They embraced, congratulated one another, and dreamed of triumphs.

But then—clouds gathered.

The commanders, emboldened by success, returned to St. Malo, determined to destroy it this time. They landed in the Bay of St. Lunar, marched toward the town, and intended to finish what they had begun.

But the harbor proved unsafe. The fleet moved to St. Cas, maintaining supply lines.

Then came word: St. Malo was now defended by a full French army sent by the Governor of Brittany. The surprise attack was impossible.

So the British retreated to their ships, waiting in the Bay of St. Cas.

As they marched down to embark, they discovered a French army advancing from Brest.

Two-thirds of the troops and all the artillery were already aboard when the enemy descended.

Four companies of Guards and the grenadier units formed up on the beach, holding the rear. The rest were carried off in boats.

But as the French advanced, these defenders left their strong position—a raised dyke along the shore—and marched forward to attack, outnumbered ten to one.

After a brief struggle, they broke and fled to the boats—“Sauve qui peut!”

Seven hundred of the eleven hundred were killed, drowned, or captured. The General fell. And—where was Harry?

A man of peace myself, I confess I care less for the battlefield than for those left behind.

Jack the Guardsman and La Tulipe of the Royal Bretagne—facing each other, striking for blood. It is their nature. Like lions and bears, they must fight. But what of the girl at Tower Hill who clung to Jack before he left? Or the lass in Quimper who gave her lover tobacco and a brule-gueule before he stepped onto the noir trajet?

What have you done, poor hearts, that you must grieve so?

My concern is not with armies, but with the people they leave behind.

And so—what state must Miss Hetty Lambert be in, hearing of the disaster? What agony grips George Warrington? What sorrow fills Martin Lambert’s eyes as he sees his daughter’s face, pale and trembling?

Howe, the brave Commodore, rowed under fire, rescuing scores in his boats. Many drowned. Hundreds were prisoners or slain on the beach.

And among them—where was our Virginian?

Great Powers! Will the vanity of men—especially Frenchmen—ever cease? Can it be believed that, after the skirmish at St. Cas—a mere matter of cutting off a rearguard, as we all know—they had the gall to fire cannons at the Invalides in Paris and shout their triumph over our misfortune? Is there any nobility in huzzahing because five or six hundred brave soldiers were surrounded by ten thousand on a beach, and met the fate said to befall the last in line? I once thought of painting a vivid picture of London’s rejoicing over our victory at St. Malo—the polished guns paraded by our gallant sailors, the horse-grenadiers prancing proudly, the crowd waving hats, roaring cheers, stealing pockets, while friends watched from a balcony in Fleet Street, blessing this scene of British glory. But now that the French have so vulgarly copied our celebration and raised their own St. Cas against our St. Malo, I refuse to dwell on such stale pride. I say *Nolo*, not *Malo*—content enough, for my part, if Harry has returned from one campaign to another with his life intact. And have I ever hinted he was hurt? Have I not, out of kindness to my fair young reader, declared him as well as ever he’d been in his life? The sea wind had bronzed his cheeks, but the bullet that whistled past his curls left them unscathed. The ocean soaked his boots and clothes, yet spared his body. True, he had exposed the lapels of his coat to the enemy—but only briefly, withdrawing from sight as quickly as possible. And what are lapels, pray, but reverses? Coats have them, just as men do—and our duty is to wear them with courage and good humor.

“I can tell you,” said Harry, “we all had to run. When our line broke, the luckiest were those who reached the boats first. The French cavalry and infantry chased us down to the shore, mingling among us, slashing at our men, bayoneting them where they fell. Poor Armytage was shot ahead of me and dropped; I lifted him and staggered through the surf toward a boat. It was lucky the sailors in our boat weren’t frightened—though bullets flew around their ears, shattered their oars, and riddled their flag. But the officer in charge stayed calm as if sipping punch at Portsmouth—which we did, I assure you, the moment we landed. Poor Sir John wasn’t so fortunate. He never made it to the ship. The service has lost a fine soldier, and Miss Howe a true gentleman for her husband. These things happen, you see—and his brother inherits both the baronetcy and the commission.”

“It’s the poor lady I think of,” said Miss Hetty (to whom Harry was recounting his tale), “and the King. Why did His Majesty send Sir John Armytage into battle? A gentleman cannot refuse a command from such a source. And now he’s dead! Oh, how grieved must the King be!”

“I doubt not His Majesty will be deeply moved,” replied Papa, nodding sagely.

“Now you’re laughing!” Hetty exclaimed. “Do you mean to say that when a gentleman dies in service—almost at the King’s feet—the King of England won't feel for him?”

“If I thought that,” retorted Papa, “I’d be for the Pretender!”

“The sauce-box would make a fine head for Temple Bar,” remarked the General, who understood Hetty’s meaning beneath her words, sensing the storm of remorse, shock, and gratitude swirling in her heart now that the danger was past.

“No,” he continued, “my dear. If kings wept for every fallen soldier, what a burden they’d bear! I hold His Majesty in higher regard than to believe him so weak. And if Miss Hester Lambert got her Pretender, I suspect she wouldn’t be much happier. That family has never been famed for excessive emotion.”

“But if the King sent Sir John—Harry, I mean—to war, where he died, oughtn’t His Majesty to repent?” asked the young lady.

“If Harry had fallen, no doubt the court would have gone into mourning,” observed the General. “As it is, gentlemen and ladies wore colored clothes yesterday.”

“Why shouldn’t we light bonfires for a defeat, and don sackcloth and ashes after a victory?” asked George.

“I protest I don’t want to thank Heaven for helping us burn the ships at Cherbourg,” he added.

“Yes, you do, George,” said Harry. “Not that I have the right to speak, and you’re far cleverer than I. But when your country wins, you’re glad—I know I am. When I flee before Frenchmen, I’m ashamed—I can’t help it, though I’ve done it.”

“It doesn’t seem right,” he added gravely, “that Englishmen should have to do it.”

George smiled, but chose not to ask what the Frenchman himself might think.

“It’s a bad business,” Harry went on, still solemn. “But it’s lucky it wasn’t worse. The story goes that the French governor, the Duke of Aiguillon, was rather a wet hen. Our entire retreat could have been cut off—though, truth be told, we were in such a hurry to move ourselves. The local militia fought bravely, I’m glad to say, and many gentlemen volunteers stood firm at the front. They say the Chevalier de Tour d’Auvergne joined the fight despite the Duke’s orders. Officers who came back with lists of prisoners and wounded told General Bligh and Lord Howe about it. He’s a lord now—since news of his brother’s death reached home, George. He’s a brave man, whether noble or common.”

“And his sister—she was to marry poor Sir John Armytage—think what she must be going through!” sighed Miss Hetty, growing more sentimental by the day.

“And his mother!” cried Mrs. Lambert. “Have you seen her address in the papers to the electors of Nottingham? ‘Lord Howe being absent on public service, and Lieutenant-Colonel Howe with his regiment at Louisbourg, it rests upon me to beg your votes and support so that Lieutenant-Colonel Howe may fill his late brother’s place in Parliament.’ Isn’t she a gallant woman?”

“A Laconic woman,” quipped George.

“How can sons fail to be brave when raised by such a mother?” mused the General.

Our two young men exchanged glances.

“If one of us were to fall defending our country,” said George, “we’d have a mother in Sparta who’d write and think just so.”

“If Sparta is anywhere near Virginia,” remarked Mr. Harry, “then we do.”

“And to think we both faced the enemy—and both were beaten by him, brother!” he added pensively.

Hetty looked at him, seeing not the man of today, but the figure she remembered: staggering through the waves, his comrade bleeding on his shoulder, enemies close behind, bullets flying. And it was she who had driven him into that danger! Her words had provoked him. Yet now, returned, he gave her no rebuke. Except when questioned, he spoke little of his ordeal. With Hetty, he was grave and courteous; with the rest of the family, open-hearted and tender. But her taunts had wounded him deeply.

“Little hand,” his eyes seemed to say, “you should not have raised yourself against me. It is wrong to scorn anyone—much less one who has given so much for you and yours. I may not be quick-witted, but in spirit, in heart, I stand equal to the best—and the best of my heart has always belonged to your family.”

His silence, his quiet strength, and his dignified endurance won back in Hetty’s esteem the place he had lost during months of idle disgrace. She now honored him not for rank or wealth, but for courage. No longer sharp-tongued or mocking, she became humble, changed, better. And as she changed, so did the world around Harry.

He was no longer sulky or idle. He no longer doubted himself or defied others. His colonel reported his conduct as model and recommended him for one of the commissions freed by casualties. Though the expedition ended poorly, it brought him fortune. His fellow volunteers, returning to St. James’s Street, praised him highly. Their deeds became the talk of the town. Had Harry been a general slain in victory, Sir John Armytage could scarcely have drawn more sympathy than these volunteers received.

Newspapers brimmed with letters in their honor. Men of wit and feeling competed to write epitaphs for the fallen. The fate of Sir John’s fiancée was mourned. She was, as we’ve said, the sister of the courageous Commodore who had just returned from the ill-fated campaign and inherited his elder brother’s title—an officer as noble as himself, who had recently fallen in America.

My Lord Howe himself spoke warmly of Mr. Warrington, and thus Harry shared in the public adoration showered upon the volunteers. Doubtless thousands served as well or better—but the English love their gentlemen, and admire them when they distinguish themselves. These volunteers were hailed as paladins, heroes, by unanimous acclaim.

And so, as young noblemen do, they accepted their fame with grace. White’s and Almack’s lit up in their honor. St. James’s welcomed its new knights. Harry regained full favor among them. Hands reached out eagerly to greet him again. Even his relatives congratulated him. A letter arrived from Castlewood—where Aunt Bernstein had taken refuge—praising his valor and enclosing a small banknote as a token of her affectionate approval. It bore the frank of Lord Castlewood, who sent his regards to both cousins and invited them to visit his country seat.

And then, through the post, came a private letter—not perfectly spelled, but in a handwriting that made Harry smile. His cousin Maria Esmond wrote that she always loved to hear his praises (now echoing everywhere), sympathized with his fortunes, and begged him to keep a small place in his heart for her. Parson Sampson, she added, had preached a moving sermon on the terrors of war and the heroism of men who volunteered for danger in defense of their country.

Soon after, the chaplain himself wrote a passionate letter, saluting Mr. Harry as his friend, benefactor, and glorious hero. Even Sir Miles Warrington sent a basket of game from Norfolk—one bird, shot while perched, tied with a string and note reading “With love to my cousin”—the first victim of young Miles’s fowling piece.

Then, radiant with joy, Mr. Lambert visited the young men at their lodgings in Southampton Row and announced that Henry Warrington was to be officially appointed Ensign in the Second Battalion of Kingsley’s, the 20th Regiment—now reorganized as the 67th. Its colonel had not accompanied the regiment to Brittany; he was at Cape Breton, engaged in capturing the guns from Louisbourg—those very guns whose arrival in England had sparked such national jubilation.

Some of my dear readers may be familiar with the famous garden in Regent’s Park, where birds, beasts, and fish alike are housed and displayed for our delight and edification. There, amid the quiet bustle of nature and human curiosity, I found myself one day—still musing on the fortunes of our Virginia friends—gazing into the glassy depths of the aquarium. A creature glided past, swift and elegant, its form cutting through the water in graceful arcs: now showing its dark, shimmering back, now turning to reveal a pale, silken breast. It was, as it turned out, none other than the humble flounder—the very same fish we’ve all devoured at Greenwich, unaware that beneath its plain exterior lay such beauty and agility.

So it is with men, and so with flounders. When placed in their proper element, both thrive—strong, noble, and full of life. Remove them from it, and they falter, their grace lost, their purpose gone. The flounder, cast upon dry land, flops helplessly, gasping its last breaths. Yet lift him gently, return him to the Thames, and he will swim once more, free and proud. But let us not dwell too long on this analogy—for surely the proverb “a fish out of water” has been told before by wiser naturalists than I.

Harry Warrington had long been out of his element. For years he had drifted, uncertain and unmoored. But when he stepped into the army, something within him stirred. Like the flounder returned to the river, he revived. Health, strength, spirit—all rushed back into him. With a single tap of an epaulet upon his shoulder, he became a new man. He embraced his calling with eagerness, mastering every detail of military life with astonishing speed. Had I the gift of my friend Lorrequer, I would follow him into camp—through marches, messes, parades, and the camaraderie of the field. I would share his laughter over wine, sleep under canvas beside him, and learn the art of war from the ground up. But since I cannot do so, I must leave the reader to imagine the scene: Harry Warrington in his bright red coat and golden trimmings, proud to wear the King’s colours, eager to serve, and content at last to find his place in the world.

George, too, rejoiced in his brother’s success. He wrote to their mother in Virginia, pouring out his admiration for Harry’s progress and his own joy at seeing him flourish. He spoke of how Harry had earned his first rank through merit alone, and how he, George, hoped to ask their mother’s permission to help fund a higher commission for him. It gave him great pleasure, he confessed, to assist his brother—especially since Harry’s sudden return to fortune had deprived him of an inheritance he had thought rightfully his. In his innocence, Harry had lived beyond his means, believing himself heir to greater wealth. Now, George felt it only fair—and almost like a thank-offering for his own rescue—that he should contribute generously to his brother’s advancement.

And then, having spoken of Harry, George turned to matters closer to his own heart. He addressed his beloved mother on a subject that weighed heavily upon him. She knew well the kindness of Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, the family who had become their closest friends in England. While their own kin had often proved distant or indifferent, the Lamberts had offered warmth, generosity, and unwavering support. General Lambert was respected throughout the army; his wife, a former schoolfellow of Madam Esmond, had nurtured both her children with deep affection. And now, George confessed, he had come to love the elder Miss Lambert—Theo—with a passion that, he believed, would determine the course of his entire life.

He had not yet made a formal proposal, nor spoken plainly to her parents—but he had not hidden his feelings. Indeed, they seemed to be met with gentle encouragement. Theo, he said, was everything a woman should be—modest, kind, intelligent, and devoted to duty. Her devotion to her mother had been admirable, and he trusted she would carry the same care into her marriage. He described her as a model of perfection, and declared that his future happiness depended entirely on whether he could win her hand.

Why not publish this letter? some sentimental soul might ask. Why withhold the tender words of a young man’s heart?

Because love is sacred. To expose the private confessions of youth—to read aloud the trembling vows, the whispered hopes, the secret sighs—is to trespass on a holy ground. Shall we pry behind closed doors, count the glances exchanged at twilight, record the tremor in a voice, or trace the pulse beneath a maiden’s breast? No. Let us respect silence where tenderness dwells. Love is not meant for public display. It belongs to two souls, and to no third party. As the ancients warned: *Qui Deae sacrum vulgarit arcanae*—he who reveals the sacred secrets of the goddess, desecrates them. Beware the man who dines with you today, for tomorrow he may print your most intimate talk. Sail with him, and he may cast you overboard.

While Harry sought glory in battle—charging into smoke and fire, carrying wounded comrades from the fray—George pursued a quieter, gentler war. His battlefield was the moonlit walk beneath Theo’s window, his weapons verses penned in secret, flowers plucked from Covent Garden, and notes passed between hands that trembled with longing. He walked to St. James’s Church, singing hymns without hearing the sermon, his mind fixed on her. He charmed her younger siblings, bantered with her sister Hetty, and won the affections of her mother, whom Martin Lambert claimed was already half in love with him.

Gumbo and Sady were ever busy shuttling between Southampton Row and Dean Street. In summer, outings were planned—Ranelagh, Hampstead, Vauxhall, Marylebone Gardens—each invitation a chance to be near her. George asked Theo to copy out a famous tragedy for the stage, knowing full well her handwriting was among the most beautiful in London. As the pages passed between them, so did little notes—questions, thanks, compliments—each one a spark in the growing flame.

Here lies a packet marked in George’s neat script: “T’s letters, 1758–9.” Should we open it? Should we expose those virgin lines, written only for one ear? Years later, perhaps, the husband read them again—his heart stirred by memory, his eyes moist with tenderness. But to show them now would be sacrilege. Let us trust that the letters were pure, modest, and full of reverence. That is enough.

In truth, we have said little—but in these last months, George Warrington had come to know certainty. He had found the woman of his dreams. Not necessarily the most beautiful—there were others, Flora, Coelia, Ardelia—yet her face held a sweetness that no other could match. She might not be the cleverest, but her voice was music to his ears. And in her presence, he felt himself rise—witty, eloquent, generous, noble. He was better when she was near. And she, no doubt, saw him as the hero of her dreams—endowed with every virtue, every charm, every quality she could desire.

When George’s letter reached Virginia, it stirred excitement around Madam Esmond’s hearth. So he was in love—and wished to marry! A natural thing, and one that would keep him safe from reckless pursuits. If he chose a well-bred Christian girl, Madam saw no harm.

“Of course they’ll set their caps at him,” Mountain remarked. “They think his wealth matches his estate. He doesn’t say if she has money. I fear otherwise.”

“And people here would try to catch Mr. Esmond Warrington for their daughters,” Madam replied grimly, eyeing her servant. “Who are no richer than Miss Lambert.”

“I suppose you mean me?” Mountain asked. “My Fanny is poor, as you say. Kind of you to remind me.”

“I said people would set their caps at him. If the cap fits, *tant pis!* as my father used to say.”

“You think I’m scheming to keep George for my daughter? I thank you, sir! A good opinion you have of us after all these years!”

“My dear Mountain,” Madam said with dignity, “I know you better than to believe you’d ever imagine your daughter a fit match for a gentleman of Mr. Esmond’s rank.”

Mrs. Mountain cried out. “Then you *did* think of marrying her to my son! I shall write to Mr. Esmond Warrington and tell him how sorry I am you’re disappointed!”

And so, we may suppose, Mrs. Mountain was indeed disappointed—perhaps harboring ambitions for her daughter. Else why such anger at the idea of George’s marriage?

Madam Esmond replied warmly. She praised George’s fraternal care for Harry, and agreed that it was right to help him recover what he had lost. As for funding Harry’s promotion, she would gladly bear half the cost, grateful that his courage had earned him his first step. This act of generosity, she added, was far more pleasing than certain other extravagances—like the ransom paid to the French captain’s family—a sum she had refused to cover. She had a firm will, like her son. What she called his pride, he called persistence. Whether she herself was proud, only time could judge. But people then, as now, liked to have their way.

George, meanwhile, had spent much of his patrimony—on his own ransom, his brother’s debts, and half the price of Harry’s advancement. Yet he did so willingly. His mother always reminded him of his grandfather’s name, urging him to uphold the dignity of the Esmonds. She sent him commissions—goods to buy, clothes to order, horses to purchase—even though her remittances were small. Still, she spoke constantly of their exalted lineage, of the need to move in the highest society, to frequent court, to live with distinction. George believed, without question, that her funds would arrive when needed. And so he lived accordingly.

The records of the time show bills for fine dinners, tailor-made court suits, liveries for servants and chairmen, receipts from horse dealers—evidence that George, too, was living with considerable expense. But unlike his brother, he was not reckless. No scandals of gambling or racehorses stained his name. His table was generous, his carriages elegant, his purse never empty. His inheritance was vast, and known to all. These facts, I mention, because they likely shaped both George’s conduct and the views of those around him.

The young heir of Virginia was abroad, travelling for pleasure and education. His mother, the queen, wrote to him daily, urging him to live with the grandeur befitting his station. She ordered him to make purchases—twelve new sets of wagon harness, an organ capable of playing fourteen specific psalm tunes. George obeyed dutifully. Though payment had not yet arrived, he assumed it would eventually. He never discussed these matters with his friends, nor questioned his mother’s affairs. They, in turn, took it for granted that he was secure—and while not mercenary, the Lamberts were pleased to see their daughter attached to a man of such character, talent, and prospects.

Mr. Esmond Warrington was honest in word and deed. He carried himself with a quiet dignity, neither haughty nor supercilious. Toward strangers, especially the great, he was reserved. But toward women, he was courteous; toward friends, warm, kind, and lively. It was no wonder, then, that one young woman came to believe him the finest man in the world—even above her father.

A true love makes a man better, in the eyes of the beloved, than all others. George himself marveled at how witty, wise, and eloquent he became when speaking to Theo. Yet we must not linger on such whispers. Those soft words were never meant for the page. If you are inclined to sentiment, put down the book and remember—remember the feeling that once clung to your arm, the tears that fell upon your heart. Perhaps it is gone—buried, forgotten. But in a moment, it rises again, smiling, whispering, alive. And yet—so far away. The hearth is cold, the ship has sailed. The roses are gone.
