But enough of sentiment. As for George and Theo—no one doubted the outcome. The Lamberts were fully satisfied. Though no formal proposal had been made, everyone knew what the answer would be. Only Mama might grow impatient.

“Psha! my dear,” the General said, “there’s time enough. Theo is barely seventeen; George is under forty. Besides, he must write to Virginia and wait for mamma’s reply.”

“But suppose she refuses?”

“That would be a sad day for us all,” the General replied. “Better to say—suppose she consents? I can’t imagine anyone refusing Theo anything she sets her heart on. And I’m sure her heart is set on this match.”

So they waited—eagerly, anxiously—until the letter from Madam Esmond arrived. And they trembled, fearing the packet-ship might fall prey to French privateers before it reached English shores.

James Wolfe, Harry’s new colonel, returned from America just weeks after the Virginian had joined his regiment. Previously lieutenant-colonel of Kingsley’s, Wolfe had been rewarded for his gallantry at Cape Breton with command of a second battalion. Harry visited him with genuine respect and warmth, eager to pay his duty to a man now drawing the world’s attention—many believing he was destined for greatness in arms. The recent campaigns in France had revealed the shortcomings of once-revered officers. The Duke of Marlborough proved no worthy heir to his legendary ancestor, and doubts already surrounded Lord George Sackville’s abilities—doubts confirmed by his misjudgment at Minden. The nation yearned for military glory, and the ministry sought a leader who might satisfy that hunger. With both Wolfe and Lambert stationed in London, their friendship rekindled, and none was more pleased than Lambert at his younger friend’s rise.

When not on duty, Harry could not get enough of Wolfe’s tales of the previous year’s campaigns. He spoke openly, without reserve, revealing a mind as candid as it was courageous—a quality later seen in Nelson. He discussed battles frankly, unburdened by pride or pretense. While some at court might sneer at his simplicity, among friends he found eager listeners. The young general possessed a boyish romanticism: he loved music and poetry deeply. On his final day, he confessed he would rather have written Gray’s *Elegy* than won a battle. It is certain such a man would have drawn George Warrington into intimate conversation. Both were lovers, both accepted, both longing for happiness—no doubt their talks were full of sentiment, though we lack precise records to recount them.

In one of his later letters, Warrington wrote:

“I had the honour of knowing General Wolfe during his last stay in London. We shared a conversation so absorbing it never failed to delight us both. I admired his simplicity, his honesty, and the noble courage that marked every word and gesture. He was deeply in love, and craved laurels to carry to his beloved. 'If it be a sin to covet honour,' he often said, quoting Harry the Fifth—his passion for plays and verse was boundless—'I am the most offending soul alive.' On his last day, he enjoyed a triumph that satisfied even the most ravenous appetite for glory. He hungered for it—not merely as a soldier fulfilling duty, but as a knight chasing dragons. My own country has lately produced a very different kind of leader, of a quite opposite nature. I scarcely know which to admire more—the Briton’s chivalrous fire, or the Roman-like steadfastness of our great Virginian.”

While Lambert remained in London on official business, his family stayed contentedly with him. Warrington, too, seemed content with the quiet life of Southampton Row and the beauty of Bedford Gardens, choosing not to leave London for long. He did make a pilgrimage to Castlewood, spending a few days there in the chamber once occupied by Colonel Esmond as a boy. He was welcomed warmly by those of the family present—but no doubt he preferred the city, where he found greater joy in the company of a young woman whose presence surpassed all others, even if Lady Maria and her circle were courteous and gracious. Lady Maria especially delighted in the tragedy George and Parson Sampson read aloud to the ladies. The chaplain praised it enthusiastically, and indeed, it was through his support—rather than Mr. Johnson’s—that the play ever reached the stage. Though Johnson urged Garrick to produce it at Drury Lane, Garrick had already committed to a tragedy by Home, author of *Douglas*. Thus, *Carpezan* went to Covent Garden, where Mr. Rich accepted it.

On the night of its premiere, Warrington hosted an elegant dinner at the Bedford Head in Covent Garden, after which he and his guests proceeded en masse to the theatre. A few lingered behind with the young author, awaiting news from inside. Barry played Carpezan with force; Shuter took the role of the old nobleman; Reddish excelled as Ulric; and the King of Bohemia was portrayed by a young Dublin actor, Mr. Geoghegan—known on stage as Hagan—who captivated audiences with his grace and presence. Mrs. Woffington appeared somewhat aged in the first act, but her death scene in the fourth stirred terror and awe. Miss Wayn sang the ballad sung by the king’s page at the moment of execution, and all agreed Barry was profoundly moving in his portrayal of Carpezan, especially during the final scene. Hagan’s elegance drew universal admiration. Mr. Rich staged the production with care, though some questioned the inclusion of a favourite elephant—used in pantomimes—during the Janissary march. One of Warrington’s black servants marched beside it in Turkish costume, while another sat in the footman’s gallery, weeping and cheering at key moments.

The execution of Sybilla marked the turning point. Once her head fell, George’s friends breathed easier, and messengers arrived at the coffee-house one after another, reporting the play’s overwhelming success. Amid thunderous applause, Barry announced the piece would return—and revealed it was the work of a young gentleman from Virginia, his first venture into drama.

We wish we could have watched Theo’s anxious flutter during the uncertain moments, and seen the flush and sparkle in her eyes when victory was assured. Harry, pale as death during the tense fourth act, turned whiter than Barry himself, covered in chalk. Yet when the curtain fell, he roared louder than any giant could have clapped. Wolfe and Lambert cheered wildly. Mrs. Lambert wept—though Hetty teased, “Why do you cry, mamma? You don’t want any of them alive again; you know it serves them all right.” Still, the girl was thrilled, as was little Charley from the Chartreux, granted leave for the evening, and Miss Lucy, brought from boarding school expressly for the occasion. My Lord Castlewood and Lady Maria attended; the former left his box to congratulate Barry and the cast, while Parson Sampson led the applause from the pit, having instructed Gumbo to watch him from the gallery and follow his lead.

That night, celebrations followed—many of them. Mr. Gumbo hosted a gathering for gentlemen of the shoulder-knot who had supported his master’s masterpiece. Henry Warrington gave a supper at the Star and Garter in Pall Mall for ten officers from his new regiment, who had come specifically to champion *Carpezan*. Finally, Warrington entertained the three principal actors, his family from the side box, Mr. Johnson, his clever friend Mr. Reynolds the painter, Lord Castlewood and his sister, and others. Lady Maria sat beside the young actor playing the King. Somehow, Warrington ended up next to Theo, and no doubt they passed a pleasant evening together. The room buzzed with joy and camaraderie. When toasts were called, Lady Maria cheerfully offered “The King of Hungary.” The actor, full of spirit and charm, declared he had already died once that night and hoped to die a hundred times more on the same field—but dead or alive, he vowed he would remain her humble servant. Ah, if only he had a real crown instead of pasteboard and tinsel—he would lay it at her feet with joy! Neither Lord Castlewood nor Mr. Esmond approved of the actor’s bold gallantry—no doubt partly due to the wine and punch he’d consumed freely. Theo and her sister, new to society, were startled by his fervor, but Lady Maria, more worldly, took it in stride.

Late into the night, coaches were summoned. Gentlemen escorted the ladies home, then returned to the supper room. The end came with Carpezan carried away in a chair, the King of Hungary nursing a terrible headache, and the poet astonished the next morning when half a dozen guests appeared at his door—guests he had invited overnight but barely remembered.

As he helped Mrs. Lambert and her daughters into their coach the night before, all the ladies were flustered, excited, overjoyed. Naturally, the young man was with them the next day, talking endlessly about the play, the audience, the actors, and the beauty of the performance. Mrs. Lambert had heard warnings about actresses being dangerous companions for young men. She hoped George would avoid the greenroom too often.

George smiled and said he had a safeguard against such temptations—one he feared not at all. As he spoke, he looked into Theo’s eyes, as if they held the amulet that would protect him from all harm.

“Why should he fear?” asked the maiden simply. She knew nothing of danger or deceit.

“No, my darling, I don’t think he need,” said the mother, kissing her.

“You don’t suppose Mr. George would fall for that painted old creature who played the lead?” asked Hetty, tossing her head. “She must be old enough to be his mother.”

“Do you suppose,” replied the mother sharply, “that at our age no one can care for us? That we have no hearts left? I believe—indeed, I hope and trust—your father thinks otherwise. He is perfectly satisfied, miss. He does not sneer at age, however little girls may choose to. And they had better be back in school, and remember what the fifth commandment says—yes, Hetty!”

“I didn’t mean to break it by saying an actress was as old as George’s mother,” pleaded Hetty.

“George’s mother is as old as I am—when we were at school. And Fanny Parker—Mrs. Mountain now—was seven months older, and we were in the French class together. I see no reason why our age should become a subject of ridicule for our children. I will thank you to spare it, please. Do you consider your mother too old, George?”

“I’m glad my mother is of your age, Aunt Lambert,” said George, in the most sentimental tone.

Strange how passion distorts reason! At some point before marriage, men often grow fond of their mothers-in-law. At this time, our dear General swore—with some justification—that he was jealous. Mrs. Lambert doted on George more than anyone else in the family. She dressed Theo beautifully to meet him, constantly caressed her, and consulted her whenever he spoke. “Don’t you think he looks well?” “Doesn’t he look pale today, Theo?” “Has he been reading too late?” If he caught a cold, she would have made gruel and soaked his feet in hot water. She sent him health recipes of her own invention. When he was away, she never stopped speaking of him to her daughter. Theo likely enjoyed the topic. When he arrived, she was always needed elsewhere—always leaving Theo to care for him until her return. But could you not hear her voice outside the door, chatting with servants or children? When she reappeared, George was usually seated at a distance from Theo—except once, when she dropped her scissors and he naturally bent down to pick them up. Why was she blushing? Were not cheeks meant to blush, and roses to bloom in spring? Mamma never noticed the blushes, but began a casual conversation as she sat down, brimming with happiness at her worktable.

Then came a letter from Virginia, penned in Madam Esmond’s familiar hand. George trembled and blushed before breaking the seal. It was in reply to his letter about Harry’s commission and his own feelings for Miss Lambert. She fully approved of his choice regarding Harry. As for his marriage, she was not opposed to early unions. She would accept a portrait of Miss Lambert, allowing for the exaggerations common in lovers’ likenesses, and hoped—sincerely—for his sake—that the young lady matched his description. From his letter, she gathered he had little money, which saddened her, though their family owned vast lands, even if cash was scarce. Still, by God’s blessing, there was plenty for generations to come, and her sons’ wives would share all she possessed. After hearing more from Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, she would write further. She admitted she had higher hopes for her son—given his name and prospects, he might have aimed for the highest lady in the land—but since Heaven had guided his heart toward her old friend’s daughter, she accepted it. She would welcome George’s wife as her own child.

Madam Esmond concluded with affectionate greetings to Mrs. Lambert and her blessing to the future daughter-in-law.

The letter was not warm, and the writer clearly only half-hearted in her approval—but it contained formal consent. How eagerly George rushed to Soho with the long-awaited news! His friends must have read it in his face—else why should Mrs. Lambert take her daughter’s hand and kiss her so passionately when he announced the news? Then, voice trembling, face pale, he turned to Mr. Lambert: “Madam Esmond’s letter, sir, is in reply to mine, in which I told her I had formed an attachment in England, and asked her permission. She gives it, I am grateful to say. I humbly ask my dear friends to be equally kind to me.”

“God bless thee, my dear boy!” said the good General, placing a hand on George’s head. “I am glad to call thee my son, George. There, there—don’t kneel, young folks! George may, of course, and thank God for giving him the best little wife in all England. Yes, my dear, except when you were ill, you never caused me a heartache. Happy is the man who wins thee!”

No doubt the young couple knelt before their parents, as was the custom. Mrs. Lambert kissed them both and wept copiously into her handkerchief. Hetty was absent during this emotional scene. When she heard of it, she laughed bitterly, saying, “Is this all the news you’ve got for me? I’ve known it for months. Do you think I have no eyes or ears?” But privately, she softened. She threw herself into her sister’s arms, vowing no one would ever love Theo as she did. With Theo, she became gentle and humble. She couldn’t resist teasing George, but he was too joyful to mind, too generous to resent her jealousy.

When the families read Madam Esmond’s letter, they found it vague—only promising a reception at her house, with no mention of settlement. The General frowned, having overlooked the letter until after the engagement. Now, it gave him little comfort.

“Bah!” said George. “I’ll earn three hundred pounds from this play. I can write one a year. If worst comes to worst, we can live on that.”

“And your inheritance,” added Theo’s father.

George hesitated, explaining how much he’d spent—on his mother’s bills, Harry’s commission and debts, and his own ransom. His own patrimony was nearly gone.

Mr. Lambert’s expression grew graver—but seeing his daughter’s alarmed eyes, he pulled her into his arms and vowed that, come what may, his darling would not be denied her happiness.

About returning to Virginia, George confessed he disliked the idea of being entirely dependent on his mother. He described life at home, and how little freedom it allowed. No—why not stay in England? Write more plays, study law, seek a position? Why not? Already, he sketched a new tragedy, bringing drafts to Theo and her sister. Hetty yawned, but Theo declared it even more beautiful than the last—which she thought perfect.

The engagement was announced to both families. Sir Miles Warrington received a formal letter from his nephew. For a time, he saw no objection—though, given George’s name and prospects, he might have expected higher. In truth, Sir Miles believed Madam Esmond had made a generous settlement, assuming George’s circumstances were comfortable. But when he learned George was entirely dependent on his mother, and his own small fortune exhausted—just as Harry’s had been—Sir Miles’s anger erupted. He could not express his horror at the imprudence of both young men. He felt compelled to speak his mind and wrote to Madam Esmond, condemning the match. Could respectable people like the Lamberts truly lure a penniless youth into marrying their equally poor daughter? He laid out his views plainly, gave George half a finger whenever he visited, and refused to invite him to drink the famous family small-beer. Toward Harry, he was slightly softer—Harry had served well, earned praise, and seemed to reform. But George? A reckless prodigal racing to ruin. His name was spoken only with groans.

Are there still such youths today, I wonder, whose families turn on them, curse them, stone them, and pass stones to neighbours to join in? All patrimony spent! Gracious heavens! Sir Miles paled at the sight of his nephew. Lady Warrington prayed for him as a dangerous sinner. Meanwhile, George walked the town, unaware of the storm he had stirred. He took little Miley to the play and brought him back. He sent tickets to his aunt and cousins—they couldn’t refuse, or it would seem too obvious. So they accepted, and when country members came to town, they asked for more, whispering that George’s intimacy with the theatre meant disgraceful relations with actresses. When an august personage praised the play to Sir Miles at Saville House, the old man modified his opinion and spoke of it more respectfully henceforth.

Yet George lived on, indifferent to the judgment of uncles, aunts, and cousins alike.

Few things stir the soul more deeply than parting—yet we shall not dwell upon the ache in Harry Warrington’s heart as he bids farewell to his brother and friends. Such farewells are not rare; they are the common lot of men caught in the currents of duty and war. Was Mr. Wolfe not also leaving behind a mother to kiss, and a sweetheart to embrace one last time? His father, brave and gone before him, had fallen during the great campaign at Louisbourg. And what of Admiral Holmes, whose fleet—the Somerset, the Terrible, the Northumberland, the Royal William, the Trident, the Diana, the Seahorse—sailed westward under his flag on the Dublin? He too must have stood ashore, heart heavy, saying goodbye to his wife and daughters. Admiral Saunders, who followed soon after, was no less touched by sorrow. These were men of steel and courage, yet their hearts beat like any other man’s when it came to love and loss.

So it was with William and his crew, sailing through the churning sea, while Black-eyed Susan watched from the shore until the ship vanished into the golden haze of sunset. It slipped into the West, swallowed by twilight. The night fell over the ocean like a shroud. They were gone—but their thoughts remained, clinging to those left behind.

In silence, each man carried a burden of tender emotion. How many prayers rose that night—on deck beneath the stars, in homes where mothers knelt beside empty beds, children huddled close, and lovers whispered hopes into the dark. On land and sea, grief and hope mingled in the same breath.

The next morning dawned. Life resumed its rhythm. George stayed in Portsmouth with Harry for a few days, waiting for wind and tide. He shook hands with Mr. Wolfe, looked long at his pale, resolute face, and saw the ships vanish beyond the horizon amid the clangor of bells and the thunder of cannon. Then, alone again, George returned home—to a life that, though full of purpose, felt strangely selfish now. He passed by Harry’s old room, seeing half-burnt papers still smoldering in the grate—a quiet echo of absence.

Soon he was back in Dean Street, walking softly toward the firelight where Theo waited, wrapped in the warmth of his return. She was radiant—so happy she almost felt ashamed. How could she be joyful when poor Hetty sat in silent sorrow? “Don’t,” Theo murmured, her voice barely audible, perhaps in a moment of dimness between the flickering flames. “I ought to be wretched. If I’m not, it’s very wicked.” One could feel her gentle guilt, her soft-hearted remorse.

But then servants entered with supper and light. The family gathered. Conversation flowed freely. The destination of the fleet was known: Canada. With such strength and under an officer like Wolfe, the French would be met with force and resolve. Though Wolfe looked ill, his spirit was strong. The nation placed its trust in him. After dinner, as custom dictated, Mr. Lambert led the household in prayer—George among them—asking blessings on all travelers. Theo and her sister knelt together, their voices joining in quiet supplication.

And so, as the ship sailed farther into the West, love followed it across the miles. Night passed. The sun rose. A few days later, life settled back into routine. George Warrington, celebrated playwright, turned once more to his work.

His tragedy *Carpezan* had run for nearly thirty nights, drawing crowds and praise. Yet soon others took the stage. Some wondered how audiences could tire of such a masterpiece—how actors could don new costumes, recite new lines. But George, ever skeptical, accepted the shift with calm. He collected his earnings—hundred pounds from Dodsley, two hundred more from the theatre manager—and found satisfaction in the acclaim. Critics praised him, friends admired his talent. He began drafting another play, hoping to surpass his first triumph.

Months passed in this peaceful pursuit. Happy months—perhaps the happiest of youth. Love was spoken and answered. Eyes sparkled with joy every day. Lips never tired of whispering secrets. Each “Good night” held the promise of tomorrow. Hearts overflowed, generous to all. Days ended in glad prayers, mornings broke with hopeful dreams. Doubt seemed cowardly, misfortune impossible, poverty merely a test of devotion.

Theo’s elders, recalling their own youthful joys, watched quietly, content to witness the unfolding of this sweet drama.

In one of his letters to his wife, written during a brief absence, George confessed he had walked past the windows of the old house in Dean Street, wondering who now sat in the room where he and Theo had once shared so much. And through his letters to Harry, we learn how time unfolded for those left behind.

“From the old window opposite Bedford Gardens, 20th August 1759.”

Why do you return to rocks and cold shores, when you might have won laurels in Germany? Kingsley’s regiment returns covered in glory, like Jack-a-Green on May Day. Our six regiments did wonders. Our cavalry could have done more—had my Lord George Sackville allowed them. When Prince Ferdinand shouted “Charge!”, his lordship either didn’t hear or couldn’t translate the German word for “Forward.” So we defeated the French, but did not crush them as we might have, had Lord Granby or even Mr. Warrington commanded. Now he’s back in town, demanding a Court-Martial. He stood tall in victory, and in defeat, he remains stubbornly proud—almost admirable in his arrogance. He looks as if he envies poor Byng, and the failure to shoot him is a slight against him.

The Duke has been warned—he must prepare for departure from this world of glory and ruin. A stroke has struck him. Death has peeped through his door, whispering, “I will call again.” Tyrant though he was, he has shown nobility in downfall. No king ever had a truer servant than our sovereign has in his son. Why do I always sympathize with the losing side? Why do I wish to rebel against the victors?

I’ve heard your famous Mr. P---- in Parliament twice or thrice. I loathe his grandiloquence. I wish some small David would bring down this swollen Goliath. His speech is always posed, theatrical. I prefer Barry’s style, though the other is more commanding.

*Pocahontas* progresses well. Barry enjoys playing Captain Smith. Though he insists on red coat and blue facings, I’d rather dress him like one of Queen Elizabeth’s gentlemen at Hampton Court—ruff, square beard, square shoes. “And Pocahontas—would you like her tattooed?” Uncle Lambert asked. Hagan, cast as the warrior who loves her and saves the captain out of honor, should be a hit. A curious fellow, Hagan—full of stage talk and melodrama, yet honest and brave. He’s furious about being cast as Sir O’Brallaghan in Macklin’s farce *Love A-la-mode*. He says he wonches to disgrace his tongue with imitations of that rascal brogue. As if anyone needed imitation when he has such a natural twang!

Shall I tell you something? Shall I hide it? Hurt your feelings? Stir jealousy? Know this: though *Carpezan* is long dead, cousin Maria still comes to the playhouse. Tom Spencer sees her every night—in the gallery. She comes especially when Hagan performs. Quick, Burroughs! Get Mr. Warrington’s boots and portmanteau! Order a chaise and four to Portsmouth immediately! That letter I burned at breakfast—I can confess now, since the cat has run so far—was from cousin M., warning me not to speak of her. But I can’t help whispering: Maria is consoling herself as fast as she can. Should I spoil the fun? Tell her brother? Is it any concern of mine? What have the Esmonds done for us but win our money at cards? Yet I admire our noble cousin. He might have been good—if only he’d been given the chance. He’s been led astray, and it may be too late to save him.

O blessed farmers! Our Virginia was dull, but thank God we were raised there. We were little slaves, but not slaves to vice, gambling, or bad company. It wasn’t until Harry left home that he fell among thieves—great thieves, who ambushed him on English roads. I don’t blame you for being robbed. You were the unlucky one. But now you go westward to make your name, to slay French dragons, to rise as a commander. Our mother will speak proudly of her son—the Captain, the Colonel, the General—and have his portrait painted with stars and epaulets. While I remain a mere poetaster—or, if fortune smiles, a placeman with a little box at Richmond or Kew, and a dozen little picaninnies bobbing curtseys at the garden gate when their uncle the General rides up on his great charger, his aide-de-camp’s pockets filled with gingerbread.

It is your destiny to wield Mars’s sword. Mine is peace: a quiet home, a small library, and someone sweet—dulce ridentem, dulce loquentem—sitting by the fire as I write. I am so content with this dream, so utterly happy, that I fear speaking of it—even to you, dearest Hal—lest it slip away.

What is ambition to me, with this certainty? What do I care for war, when peace smiles so near?

Mynheer Van den Bosch, our mother’s friend, has returned from Holland, having found kinfolk there. Miss—intended by maternal design to be your bride—has spent six months at Kensington School and is now emerging with a hundred accomplishments, polished into a perfect lady. Her father brought her to Dean Street to curtsy—and what a graceful curtsy it was! Though barely seventeen, she moves with the ease of a dowager of sixty. She conversed with Aunt Lambert as an equal, treated the girls like children—enraging Hetty and amusing Theo. She discussed politics with the General, gossip with the ladies, fashion and opera with perfect ease. Only a few slips betrayed her origins. You might have thought Miss Lydia was born in Mayfair.

She says she’ll live at the Court end of town and has no patience for her father, who lodges in Monument Yard. For lovers of brown beauty, she is a lovely mignonne. But my taste, dear brother, as you know…

Here the letter continues with pages of poetic effusion, raptures, and verses—too personal, too tender, for the editor to reproduce. Let us leave them unsaid.

Gentlemen and ladies of a certain age may recall their own such moments—when words spilled forth like spring rain, when love was sung in every line, when youth bloomed and birds sang without pause. The branches may now be bare, the leaves fallen. But let us remember the vernal time.

And you, young readers—whose April or May has not yet begun—need not linger here. When your season comes, nature will awaken your hearts. Your flowers will bloom, and your songs will rise.

George Warrington had written in his letter—quoted earlier—that despite Lord Castlewood’s past dealings with Harry, the nobleman and George remained on cordial terms, bound by a kinship that transcended petty grievances. If George needed letters of introduction, access to court circles, or even a seat in the House of Lords to witness a debate, his cousin was always ready to assist. He was a man of charm and wit, generous in spirit when it came to advancing the interests of those close to him—provided such actions did not undermine his own.

Now, Lord Castlewood went so far as to promise George he would use his influence to secure him a position in government or society, an offer eagerly embraced by the Virginian. For George, England was no longer just a temporary refuge—it had become home. He found the life of London infinitely more stimulating than anything Virginia could offer. Though he might have accepted a planter’s existence if it meant true independence, in reality, he was merely the first among many subjects under his mother’s rule, and one who felt especially burdened by her expectations. The thought of returning with his young bride to a life of rigid routine, constant subordination, and inevitable disputes filled him with dread. Better, he believed, to remain in England—poor but free, surrounded by congenial company and the faint possibility of future distinction—than endure the suffocating monotony and social constraints of colonial life.

Thus, Lord Castlewood’s pledge carried great weight for George. True, the earl had done little for his own brother, and his own standing as a peer was far from enviable. But hope often distorts perception, and George chose to believe in his cousin’s sincerity. Unlike the Warringtons, who were reserved and distant, Lord Castlewood proved remarkably gracious upon learning of George’s engagement to Miss Lambert. He visited her parents, complimented both George and Theo, and behaved with such charm and warmth that the family, already inclined toward kindness, forgot the rumors that followed him like shadows. To them, he seemed transformed—witty, lively, almost innocent in their presence. As if shedding his worldliness with his coat, he entered their drawing-room a different man—one who left behind the storms of high society to rest in a haven of peace.

It was no pretense, either. In truth, Lord Castlewood may have been better while among these good people, at least for a time. And perhaps, in that moment, he was not a hypocrite at all.

His admiration for Miss Theo was open and unreserved, though modestly expressed.

“It doesn’t trouble my sleep,” he said, “nor will I break my heart if Miss Lambert chooses another. But I wish, madam, that when I was young I’d met someone as pure and kind as your daughter. She might have kept me out of much harm. Yet such girls never fell into my path—or if they had, they might have made me better than I am.”

“Surely, my lord,” Mrs. Lambert replied gently, “it is not too late?”

He started, startled by the suggestion.

“Not too late?” he echoed.

She blushed. “Not too late to win your daughter’s hand, my lord—but not too late to repent. Scripture says it is never too late to turn from sin. If others are welcomed at the eleventh hour, why should you despair?”

“I know my own heart better than you do,” he answered, voice tinged with melancholy. “I speak French and German fluently—because I learned them in childhood. A man who picks them up later can never truly master them. So it is with virtue: I cannot learn it now. I can only watch others practice it and admire them. When I stand on the other side of Lazarus’ gate,” he continued, “will Miss Theo give me a drop of water? Don’t frown—I know I shall be there. Some men are born doomed. I think some of our family are among them. Others waver, uncertain which way the scale will fall. But some are predestined angels—born to soar, naturally drawn to Heaven, no matter what they do.”

“Oh, my lord,” she said, “why should you not be one of the predestined? While there is a day, an hour—there is still hope!”

“I see what lies behind your words, dear lady,” he said softly. “I read your prayers in your eyes. But how can they help? You don’t know all. You don’t understand what our lives are—how early they begin, how selfish nature, necessity, and upbringing shape us. Fate holds the reins of our chariot; we cannot escape our destiny. I know this. I see goodness in others. I go my own way—but it is not mine. It is Fate’s. And yet, Fate has mercy: it allows us, from time to time, to meet souls like yours.” He took her hand, looked deeply into her eyes, and bowed with quiet dignity.

Every word was true. The greatest mistake is to assume that flawed men lack feeling or sensitivity. They feel deeply—but their emotions do not last. Sometimes, tears themselves become a form of indulgence, much as old libertines once found sorrow in their victims’ grief to heighten their pleasure. But Mrs. Lambert knew nothing of these inner struggles. To her, he was a sinner in need of grace—and so she prayed for him with tender persistence. He was, she believed, much better than he appeared. He was interesting, compelling. There was still hope—for him, for all.

Which of them judged him more rightly? Time would tell. But if the gentleman spoke the truth, then the lady’s prayers, though powerless to change him, could do no harm. Kind-hearted women—like doctors tending a dying patient—care for the reprobate not because they expect recovery, but because compassion compels them. Once healed, the patient is forgotten; the physician moves on.

Yet while the illness endured, Mrs. Lambert could not resist seeing more of her sick man. A genuine intimacy grew between Lord Castlewood and the Lamberts. One might suspect worldly motives mingled with spiritual ones—even in such a devout woman. After all, who can say where worldliness won’t slip into Eden, even if guarded by flaming swords?

Her son was preparing for ordination. Lord Castlewood feared his current chaplain, Mr. Sampson, whose careless habits and unorthodox views might lead him to resign. Should that happen, the small parish would become vacant—and the earl hinted it might be offered to a young clergyman of sound principles and gentle manners, content with modest income and a small but faithful congregation.

Thus began a connection between the two families. The ladies of Castlewood, ever mindful of propriety, paid visits to Mrs. Lambert’s drawing-room. They were polite, courteous, respectful. My Lady Castlewood invited the Lamberts to her card parties. There was gambling, certainly—everyone gambled, from the king to bishops, peers to peeresses. But no one was forced to play. And surely, no one should object when such lofty figures indulged freely.

Mrs. Lambert herself attended several of these gatherings, grateful for the welcome and pleased by the attention her daughters received.

Earlier, mention had been made of an American family of Dutch descent, brought to England by Madam Esmond’s recommendation to her sons abroad. Her letter had been clear enough for Mrs. Lambert to grasp its intent. George, however, was already engaged. And poor Hetty’s suitor, Harry, was away on military duty—a circumstance for which Hetty’s mother may not have regretted. With a laugh, she told George he ought to heed his mother’s advice: break off with Theo and pursue Miss Lydia, who was ten times—no, a hundred times—richer than her daughter, and undoubtedly more beautiful.

“Yes, indeed,” George replied, “she is handsomer, richer, perhaps even cleverer.”

(These praises, Mrs. Lambert half resented.)

“But suppose she is all these things,” he continued, “so is Mr. Johnson cleverer than I. So is Mr. Hagan the actor taller and finer-looking. So is Sir James Lowther wealthier. Yet, pray, ma'am, do you think I’d be jealous of any of them—or believe Theo would leave me for their sake? Why should I deny that Miss Lydia is lovely, rich, clever, vivacious, well-bred—if you insist—and even angelic, if you wish? Theo is not afraid. Are you, child?”

“No, George,” Theo replied, her gaze honest and steady—so sincere it could shame suspicion itself.

And if, after such words, Mrs. Lambert leaves the room—on some errand, real or imagined—to fetch scissors, thimbles, slippers, or even the cross atop St. Paul’s—then returns minutes later to find George near Theo, her face flushed, his hand just released from hers—would she really know what passed between them?

Would you, madam? Do you remember what happened when Mr. Grundy came courting? And you, who weren’t present, dare cry *fie* and *for shame*? Then fie and for shame upon you, Mrs. Grundy!

With Harry gone and Theo and George irrevocably betrothed, Madam Esmond’s matchmaking plans were thwarted. But why should Mrs. Lambert not have her own? If a rich, handsome, beautiful girl crossed Jack Lambert’s path, why shouldn’t he claim her? So thought the ever-marriage-minded mother—though General Lambert, as usual, called her a goose.

At any rate, beauty and wealth were no objection. Madam Esmond had urged hospitality to this family. It wasn’t her fault Harry had departed for Canada. Would the General want him to return, abandon his career, come to England, marry the American, and break Hetty’s heart? Let us spare further debate—and refrain from suggesting Mr. Lambert was right to call his wife such a foolish bird.

In those days, distinctions between court and city were vast. Mr. Van den Bosch, upon arriving in London, associated only with city folk. He lived near his agent in the commercial district. When his daughter returned from school for holidays, they took walks to Islington or Highgate, or strolled through the Artillery Ground in Bunhill Fields. They attended Baptist services in Finsbury Fields, and once or twice, secretly, watched Mr. Garrick or the mischievous Mr. Foote at the Little Theatre. A Lord Mayor’s feast was a grand event for a man of his rank; dancing with a young mercer at Hampstead Assembly gave the daughter immense joy.

When George first visited his mother’s friends, he found Mr. Draper of the Temple, attentive and eager. The married lawyer warned George: “Look out—this young lady has a fortune.”

Mr. Drabshaw, a Quaker gentleman and nephew of Madam Esmond’s Bristol agent, also frequented the household, growing anxious when George arrived.

To honor his mother’s neighbors, George hosted a gathering at his own apartments. Naturally, his Soho friends joined them. Not one failed to praise Miss Lydia’s beauty. She had the foot of a fairy, the arms and neck of a huntress, flashing eyes that sparkled with life. She carried a soft, plaintive accent from America—one I, speaking now, have heard mocked a hundred times in Cockney imitation, yet which, when spoken by a charming woman, is enchanting. Who dares say otherwise? Miss Whittington, whose h’s are lost? Miss Nicol Jarvie, with her northern burr? Miss Molony, with her Dublin lilt? All accents are sweet when spoken by beauty. Who sets the standard—rose, thistle, shamrock, or star and stripe? Miss Lydia’s accent, I believe, was never offensive. Had it been, George, a man of taste, would have noticed—and her schoolmistress at Kensington would have failed her.

After six months at the Kensington Academy, Miss Lydia returned to her grandfather, eager to enter society. At first, her world was narrow—but she was determined to expand it. Wherever she led, her grandfather followed. He had been thwarted in youth; he’d punished his son too harshly, with unfortunate results. For Lyddy, he vowed, life would be as pleasant as possible.

“Do you think I’m wrong, Mr. George?” he asked.

There was talk in Virginia—though he didn’t know its source—that the Castlewood boys might have been happier if Madam Esmond had allowed them more freedom. George could not contradict that rumor, nor persuade the kindly old man to change his plans.

As for the Lamberts, how could they refuse such a generous, loving father, a friend of Madam Esmond?

When Lydia returned from school, her grandfather moved from Monument Yard to a fine house in Bloomsbury. Their city friends followed—merchants from Virginia Walk, respectable tradesmen with whom he dealt, and their families, all gracious toward Miss Lyddy.

But gradually, the old circle faded. No more outings to Belsize or Highgate, no Saturday trips to Deputy Higgs’ villa, no country dances at Mr. Lutestring’s in Hackney. Even Sunday worship changed—oh, the horror! Mr. Van den Bosch left Bethesda Chapel in Bunhill Row and actually took a pew in Queen Square Church!

Queen Square Church—and Mr. George Warrington lived nearby in Southampton Row! It was obvious whom Miss Lyddy favored.

Mr. Draper, once full of praise for the grandfather and granddaughter, now warned George with new caution. Mr. Van den Bosch, he claimed, was no noble Dutchman—he was from Albany, nobody’s son. He’d made his fortune through land speculation, privateering (nearly piracy), and the Guinea trade. His son had married an assigned servant—marriage being questionable—and was disinherited, falling into vice, dying quietly in his bed.

“Mr. Draper has told you bad things about me,” the old man said calmly to George. “We are all sinners. Some truths may be said of all, and many falsehoods. Did he tell you my son was unhappy with me? I told you that myself. Did he spread wicked tales about my family? He liked it so much he wanted to marry Lyddy to his brother. Bless her! I’ve had many offers. And you—you’re the man I would have chosen. I like you none the less for preferring someone else—though I must say, I fail to see what you find in your Miss compared to my Lyddy.”

“There is no accounting for tastes, sir,” George replied, with his most elegant air.

“No, sir,” the old man agreed. “It’s a wonder of nature, happening every day. When I ran my store in Albany, a gentleman of your class might have married my dear daughter—had she lived—along with a good fortune. But since my father and I quarreled, Lyddy would have been penniless. Instead of my beautiful Bella, he chose a plain creature, no prettier than your Miss, without a dollar. The fool of it, saving your presence, Mr. George.”

“Please don’t save my presence,” George laughed. “I suppose the gentleman had promised the other lady, seen her first—hence, indifferent to your charming daughter.”

“Ah, yes,” the old man mused. “When a young man gives his word to commit folly, he sticks to it. But Lord, Lord, what am I talking about? Twenty years ago! I was well-off then, but Heaven has blessed my store—now I’m three times richer. Ask my agents how much they’ll pay for Joseph Van den Bosch’s bill at six months on New York—or sight, perhaps, for forty thousand pounds. I warrant they’ll discount it.”

“Happy he who holds the bill, sir,” George said, bowing with amusement.

“Lord, Lord,” the elder exclaimed, “how mercenary you young men are! Always thinking of money! Happy he who has the girl, I should say—the money isn’t the point when it comes with such a lovely young thing as that—though I humbly say it, who shouldn’t, and who is her fond, silly old grandfather.”

“We were talking about you, Lyddy darling—come, give me a kiss, my blessing!” he said, embracing her. “We were discussing you and Mr. George said he wouldn’t take you with all the money your poor old grandfather can give you.”

“Nay, sir,” George protested.

“Well, you’re right to say nay,” the old man chuckled. “I didn’t mean all. When Heaven takes me to a better place, Lyddy will be a rich little Lyddy. But she doesn’t want me to go yet, does she?”

“Oh, you darling dear grandpapa!” she cried.

“This young gentleman won’t have you,” he declared. (Lyddy sent him a playful, arch “Thank you, sir” from her brown eyes.) “But at least he’s honest—more than we can say of some folks in this wicked London. Oh, Lord, how mercenary they are! Did you know, in Monument Yard, they all swarmed around my poor little Blessing for her money? Tom Lutestring, Mr. Draper—your precious lawyer—Mr. Tubbs of Bethesda Chapel—all buzzing like flies around honey.”

“To avoid the flies, of course!” Miss Lydia said, tossing her head proudly.

“Where my brother-tradesmen live,” the old man continued. “Else why should I consort with your grandees and fine folk? I don’t care for fashion, Mr. George; I don’t care for plays or poetry, begging your pardon. I’ve never been to a play in my life—except to please this little minx.”

“Oh, sir,” she exclaimed, “it was lovely! And I cried so, didn’t I, grandpapa?”

“At what, my dear?”

“At—Mr. Warrington’s play, grandpapa.”

“Did you, my dear? I dare say. It was mail day—my letters had come, my ship *Lovely Lyddy* had arrived in Falmouth, Captain Joyce reported escaping a French privateer—my head was full of gratitude for that escape, which saved me much money, Mr. George—ships insured at scandalous rates these days, so I often prefer to risk rather than insure—that I barely listened to the play. I only went to please this little Lyddy.”

“And you pleased me, dearest Gappy!” she cried.

“Bless you! Then it’s all I want. What more does a man need here below than to please his children? Especially me, who knew unhappiness when young, and repented of treating this darling’s father too harshly.”

“Oh, grandpapa!” she whispered, clinging to him.

“Yes, I was too hard with him, dear. That’s why I spoil my little Lydkin so!”

More kisses followed. The girl flung her arms around the old man’s neck, pressed her lips to his wrinkled cheek, showered his wig with powder, and glanced at George as if to say: *See, sir? Would you not like me to do the same for you?*

We confess—we confess much. George certainly told Theo of his visit with Lyddy and Gappy, and the old man’s revelation of his granddaughter’s wealth. But did he tell all? For Theo remained amused, warm, and entirely unbothered when next the two young ladies met.

We must now, before continuing with Miss Lydia’s story, clarify that passage in Mr. Warrington’s letter to his brother concerning Lady Maria Esmond—a sentence that may still puzzle some gentle readers. How, indeed, could anyone of decent sensibility imagine such a turn of events? How might an innocent young person suppose that a woman of noble lineage, ancient descent, and mature years—whom we ourselves saw deeply in love only a few months past—could so abandon herself as (oh, my fingers tremble at the thought!) not only to fall for a man of humble birth and many years her junior, but actually to marry him, openly, or rather, secretly, beneath the very eyes of society? For it was not exactly public; no grand ceremony marked the union. No, Parson Sampson quietly tied the knot in his chapel in Mayfair, away from prying gazes.

But pause before you condemn her entirely. Because Lady Maria once entertained a foolish fondness for her cousin, does that mean she should never again feel love? Are men alone permitted to change their hearts, while women are condemned for seeking comfort in new affections? What greater rudeness, what more unfeeling judgment, than Hamlet’s tirade against his mother’s remarriage? The truth is likely simpler: that tender, clinging creature needed something to hold onto—and when Hamlet Senior was gone, she wrapped herself around Claudius. Indeed, we have known women so eager to attach themselves that they’ve managed to entwine round two gentlemen at once. Why, then, should there not be marriage tables after funeral feasts? If you gave thanks yesterday for your meal, does that mean you cannot hunger today? Your appetite remains keen, your relish strong—surely tomorrow evening at eight, you’ll need dinner again. I, for one, when Flirtilla or Jiltissa took a fancy to me (let us imagine them both of dazzling beauty and high rank), always reminded myself that time would come when their hearts would turn elsewhere. We are served à la Russe, devouring one dish at a time, like those poor souls in Polyphemus’s cave. *Hodie mihi, cras tibi*—there are anthropophagi who consume dozens of us: the old, the young, the delicate, the tough, the plump, the lean, the plain, the fair. There is no escape. One by one, we vanish down their vast maws.

Look at Lady Ogresham! Last year we all watched how she seized upon poor Tom Kydd—devoured him, picked his bones clean, and cast him aside. Now it is Ned Suckling who lies within her grasp. He quivers beneath her great eyes, helpless, entranced. See the small, trembling creature panting under her gaze! She draws nearer, he moves closer. Soon there will be a faint cry for mercy—and *hobblegobble*—he will disappear! Ah, how sad it is. I knew, for instance, that Maria Esmond had lost her heart many times before Harry Warrington found it; yet I liked to believe he would keep it—though mischance and troubled times might have kept her love safe, cherished in quiet celibacy. If I were to fall madly in love tomorrow, I would still pretend I’d secured the full ownership of my beloved’s heart—not merely leased a battered furnished apartment, where the wine glasses are clouded by countless lips, and the sofas stained by the boots of previous tenants. Dear, dear nymph! To be loved and beautiful! Suppose I once felt a fleeting passion for Glycera (and truly, her complexion was as pure as polished Parian marble); suppose you once admired Telephus, with his low collars and absurd neck—those infatuations are long gone, aren’t they? We love each other now, don’t we? Yes, forever. Let Glycera go to Bath, and let Telephus take his *cervicem roseam* to Jack Ketch, *n’est-ce pas*?

No, we never think of changing, my dear. However the winds blow, however time flies, however spoons stir our potage—now piping hot—it shall never grow cold. We may have allowed ourselves passing fancies in the past; and truly, your attachment to Telephus (do not frown so, my darling, and deepen those lovely lines on your brow)—I say, it was the talk of the town. And Glycera? She behaved abominably toward me. Well, well—now that we understand each other, our hearts are united forever, and we can look at Sir Cresswell Cresswell and snap our fingers at his wig. But this Maria of the last century was a woman of disordered mind. You, my love, who know the world, understand that in her life much must have transpired unfit for light, unsuitable for telling. You know (not that I mean you’ve experienced such things, but you’ve heard—heard your mother speak) that an old flirt, having played the fool with one passion, will soon play it again with another. Flirting, like drinking—once the brandy is gone, Glycera, who has taken to drinking, will turn to gin. So if Maria Esmond has found a successor to Harry Warrington, and set up a new sultan in the empire of her heart, what, after all, could we expect from her? That realm was like the Low Countries—long accustomed to conquest, perpetually open to invasion.

And her present captor was none other than Mr. Geoghegan—or Hagan—the young actor who had performed in George’s tragedy. His voice thrilled, his eyes sparkled, his bearing was noble; clad in gilt leather armor and a large buckled wig, delivering the poet’s fiery lines, he stirred the lady’s heart as Ariadne’s was stirred by Bacchus when her affair with Theseus ended. The young Irishman was touched and uplifted by the noblewoman’s affection. He might have preferred a Lady Maria Hagan younger in years, but one more tender-hearted he could scarcely find. She clung to him closely. When their marriage became known and her furious relatives disowned her, she withdrew with him to his modest lodgings in Westminster.

General Lambert brought the news home from Whitehall one day, sharing it with laughter and jests. In those simpler times, humor was broad, and even fine ladies laughed at Fielding’s bawdy pages and wept over Clarissa’s letters—letters that would make your modern ladyship recoil in horror. The General made all manner of witticisms about the marriage—about George’s role in bringing it about, about Barry’s jealousy when he learned of it. He swore it was cruel that cousin Hagan hadn’t chosen George as groomsman; that the first child should be named Carpezan or Sybilla after the play. They wouldn’t quite afford a coach, but perhaps they could borrow a chariot and pasteboard dragons from Mr. Rich’s theatre. The baby might be christened in Macbeth’s caldron, and Harry and Harlequin ought certainly to be godfathers.

“Why shouldn’t she marry him if she likes him?” asked little Hetty. “Why should he not love her because she is a little old? Mamma is a little old, and you love her none the worse. When you married my mamma, sir, I’ve heard you say you were very poor; and yet you were very happy, and nobody laughed at you!”

Thus spoke the impudent child, unaware of Lady Maria’s past indiscretions.

“So her family has deserted her?” George recounted the fury they had shown—how Lady Castlewood had gone into mourning, how Mr. Will had sworn he’d have the rascal’s ears, how furious Madame de Bernstein was, above all. “It is an insult to the family,” said haughty little Miss Hett, “and I can imagine how noble ladies must be outraged by their relative marrying someone of Mr. Hagan’s condition. But to abandon her is a different matter.”

“Indeed, my dear,” replied mamma, “you speak of things you do not understand. After Lady Maria’s conduct, no respectable person can visit her.”

“What conduct, mamma?”

“Never mind,” said mamma. “Little girls should not inquire too closely into such matters. Suffice it to say, I am shocked she ever came here, and I repeat: no honest person should associate with her!”

“Then, Aunt Lambert, I must be whipped and sent to bed,” said George, with mock solemnity. “I confess (though I did not sooner, since it was not my affair) that I have visited my cousin the player, and his lady. I found them in very shabby lodgings in Westminster, where the wretch keeps not only his wife, but his old mother and a younger brother whom he sends to school. I met Mr. Hagan, and left with a liking, even a respect for him—though I admit he has made a most imprudent marriage. But how imprudent some people are about marriage, aren’t they, Theo?”

“Improvident, if they marry spendthrifts like you,” said the General. “Master George found his relations, and I’ll wager he left his purse behind.”

“No, not the purse, sir,” said George, smiling gently. “Theo made that. But I must admit it came empty. Mr. Rich is furious. He says he hardly dares put Hagan on stage, fearing a riot—like the one Garrick faced over foreign dancers. This will be a gentleman’s riot. The macaronis are furious, swearing they’ll pelt Hagan and cudgel him afterward. My cousin Will at Arthur’s has vowed he’ll have the actor’s ears. Meanwhile, since the poor man doesn’t perform, they’ve cut his salary. Without it, these unfortunate lovers have no means to buy bread and cheese.”

“And you brought them food, sir? It was like you, George!” said Theo, adoring him.

“It was your purse that carried it, dear Theo,” replied George.

“Mamma, I hope you’ll go see them tomorrow!” pleaded Theo.

“If she doesn’t, I’ll get a divorce, my dear!” joked papa. “Come and kiss me, you little wench—that is, *avec la bonne permission de monsieur mon beau-fils*.”

“Monsieur mon beau fiddlestick, papa!” said Miss Lambert, and I suspect she obeyed without hesitation. And thus, for the first time, George Esmond Warrington, Esquire, was called a fiddlestick.

Any man—even today—knows the price of an imprudent marriage: the scorn, the wrath, the pity of his family. If your respectable kin cry out when you marry the curate’s daughter—one in ten of whose children are charming—or engage yourself to a young barrister whose only income comes from court reports and who must pay his Oxford bills from your slender fortune—if your friends protest such matches, imagine the outcry when Lady Maria Hagan’s family learned of this union.

First, there is old Mrs. Hagan. Her son had supported her diligently and comfortably since leaving Trinity College after his father’s death, appearing as Romeo at Crow Street Theatre. His salary had lately sustained his brother at school, helped his sister working as a companion, and provided fire, clothing, tea, dinner, and warmth for the widow of a clergyman. And now, a fine lady with extravagant habits arrives, claiming the humble home, dividing the scant loaf and mutton! Had Hagan not been proud, and the old mother afraid of him, I doubt Lady Maria’s life in those Westminster lodgings would have been peaceful. It was selfish, perhaps, to take a seat at that small table, to claim the cream of the milk, the wings of the chickens, the best half of everything when there was barely enough. No wonder the poor old mother-in-law grumbled. But what was her complaint compared to the uproar in Kensington among Lady Maria’s noble kin? Think of the gossip across the city! The whispers at the Princess’s court, where Lady Fanny held a position; the jokes of Mr. Will’s fellow officers at the usher’s table; the witticisms in newspapers and magazines; the outrage of moralists; the laughter of clubs and the sneers of the irreverent!

At the news, Madame Bernstein fell into fits and fled to the solitude of her beloved rocks at Tunbridge Wells, where she saw no more than forty people a night at cards. My lord refused to see his sister; and the Countess, in mourning as we’ve said, paid a visit to a gracious Princess, who offered her condolences upon the disgrace and calamity that had struck her house. For three whole days, the town buzzed with scandal—then came other news: a victory in Germany, uncertain reports from America, a general returning to face trial, a new soprano from Italy—and the public forgot Lady Maria in her garret, eating the hard-earned meal of the actor’s family.

This is an extract from Mr. George Warrington’s letter to his brother, describing personal matters and his visit to the newlyweds:

“My dearest little Theo,” he writes, “was eager to accompany her mother on this charitable errand; but I thought Aunt Lambert’s visit best suited the circumstances, without the presence of her little spinster aide-de-camp. Cousin Hagan was out when we arrived; we found her ladyship in loose dress, hair loosely pinned, playing cribbage with a neighbor from the second floor, while good Mrs. Hagan sat opposite the fire with a glass of punch and *The Whole Duty of Man*.

“Maria—your Maria once—cried a little when she saw us; and Aunt Lambert, of course, offered her sympathy. While she comforted Lady Maria, I paid the best compliments I could to the elderly lady. When conversation between Aunt L. and the bride flagged, I turned to the latter, and together we did our best to make the dreary visit pleasant. We spoke of you, of Wolfe, of war—you must be facing the French by now, and God send my dearest brother safe and victorious from battle! We follow your steps anxiously—we imagine you at Cape Breton. We have plans of Quebec and charts of the St. Lawrence. Shall I ever forget your joy when you saw me return safely from that little skirmish with the little Frenchman? So will my Harry return from his battle. I feel certain of it, elated by the prospect of your success and safety. And I’ve shared this cheerfulness with everyone here. We speak of the campaign as over, Captain Warrington’s promotion assured. Pray Heaven, all our hopes may be fulfilled soon.

“How strange it is that you, the bold one (you know you are), have escaped quarrels thus far, while I, a peaceful youth wishing no harm to anyone, am thrust into battles! What do you think of my having another affair on my hands—this time with whom, pray? With none other than your old enemy, our kinsman, Mr. Will.

“I cannot guess what provoked him. Spencer (who acted as my second—don’t be alarmed, it’s all over, and no one is hurt) thinks someone incited Will, but who? His behavior has been outrageous. We’ve met often lately at good Mr. Van den Bosch’s house, where his pretty granddaughter was entrusted to both of us by our dear mother. Oh, dear mother! Did you know the little thing would become a *causa belli*, sparking duels and endangering lives? Yet so it has. To show his spirit, or doubt mine, whenever Will and I meet at Mynheer’s—he’s always there—he treats me with open rudeness, requiring extraordinary patience to endure. He contradicted me once, twice, thrice in front of the family, plainly out of spite. Is he courting Miss Lydia and her father’s ships, slaves, and forty thousand pounds? I suspect so. The old gentleman talks endlessly of money, adores his granddaughter, and since she’s beautiful, many here adore her too. Was Will vile enough to think I’d trade Theo for a million guineas, slaves, and Venus herself? Could such baseness enter his mind? I don’t know if he accused me of stealing Van den Bosch’s silver or robbing on the highway. But for one reason or another, he’s jealous of me. Though I’ve answered his insults with dry sarcasm (always civil in company), I may have angered him. Miss Lydia, unknowingly, fueled the fire—especially yesterday, when we spoke of you.

“‘Ah!’ says the careless little thing, ‘it’s lucky for you, Mr. Esmond, that Captain Harry isn’t here.’

“‘Why, miss?’ asks he, using one of his usual conversational ornaments. He must have offended a fairy in youth, cursed to drop oaths like the girl who spat toads and serpents. (I know someone whose gentle lips only yield pearls and diamonds.) ‘Why?’ says Will, roaring with curses.

“‘O fie!’ says she, covering her prettiest little ears with her prettiest fingers. ‘O fie, sir! Such naughty words. It’s lucky the Captain isn accountability, or he might quarrel with you. Mr. George is so peaceful, he won’t. Have you heard from the Captain, Mr. George?’

“‘From Cape Breton,’ I reply. ‘He is well, thank you—that is—’ I couldn’t finish, so furious was I.

“‘From the Captain, as you call him, Miss Lyddy,’ says Will. ‘He’ll distinguish himself as he did at Saint Cas! Ho, ho!’

“‘So I apprehend he did, sir,’ says Will’s brother.

“‘Did he?’ asks our dear cousin. ‘Always thought he ran away; took to his heels; got ducked, and ran off as if a bailiff chased him.’

“‘La!’ says Miss, ‘did the Captain ever have a bailiff after him?’

“‘Didn’t he? Ho, ho!’ laughs Mr. Will.

“I suppose I looked fierce, for Spencer, dining with us, trod on my foot. ‘Don’t laugh so loud, cousin,’ I said gently. ‘You might wake good old Mr. Van den Bosch.’ The old gentleman slept in his armchair, as he often does after dinner.

“‘Oh, indeed, cousin,’ says Will, turning to wink at a friend, Captain Deuceace—whose own and whose wife’s reputation you may have heard of in the clubs, and whom Will has introduced into this simple household as a man of the highest fashion. ‘Don’t be afraid, miss,’ says Mr. Will, ‘nor my cousin needn’t be.’

“‘Oh, what a comfort!’ cries Miss Lyddy. ‘Keep quiet, gentlemen, don’t quarrel, and come up when I send for tea.’ And with a sweet curtsey, she vanishes.

“‘Hang it, Jack, pass the bottle, and don’t wake the old gentleman!’ continues Mr. Will. ‘Won’t you help yourself, cousin?’ he adds, particularly facetious in the word *cousin*.

“‘I’m going to help myself,’ I said, ‘but I won’t drink it. And I’ll tell you what I’ll do with it, if you’re quiet, cousin.’ (Desperate kicks from Spencer.)

“‘And what the devil do I care what you do with it?’ asks Will, looking pale.

“‘I’m going to fling it into your face, cousin,’ I said—and did so.

“‘By Jove, and no mistake!’ cries Mr. Deuceace. As he and William shouted curses, old Van den Bosch woke, removed his handkerchief, and asked what was wrong.

“I said it was just a glass of wine spilled. The old man replied, ‘Well, well, there’s more where that came from! Let the butler bring what you want, young gentlemen!’ and sank back to sleep.

“‘From the back of Montagu House Gardens, there’s a fine view of Hampstead at six in the morning; and the statue of the King on St. George’s Church is elegant, cousin!’ I resumed.

“‘D---- the statue!’ begins Will.

“‘Don’t, cousin!’ I said. ‘Or you’ll wake the old gentleman. Shouldn’t we go upstairs to Miss Lyddy’s tea-table?’

“We arranged a meeting for the next morning—our bodies might have lain under a coroner’s verdict by now—but just as we were to duel, three of Sir John Fielding’s men intervened, carried us to Bow Street, and bound us over to keep the peace.”

The brief dispute between George Warrington and his cousin William had, for the time being, severed their connection with Bloomsbury Square. Mr. Will, ever more zealous in his attentions, now carried himself with such unmeasured arrogance that George found it increasingly difficult to restrain his temper. The once cordial visits ceased entirely, though not without a lingering sense of unease—particularly as both men had been bound over to keep the peace, rendering any further confrontation legally perilous.

Lydia Van den Bosch, ever the impulsive and artless child, seemed utterly transformed by the events. Six weeks earlier, she had been consumed by jealousy at George’s evident regard for another; now, however, her manner toward Theo Lambert was marked by an almost maternal warmth. “Miss Theo,” she would declare, “is so quiet, so gentle—such a perfect match for George! I’m truly grateful that the quarrel never came to bloodshed.” She spoke with a softness that belied her usual vivacity. “Had the constables not arrived just in time, dear Mr. George, you might have lost your life. And how foolish Mr. Esmond looked, raging about his ruined duel!”

She added, with a demure smile, “You won’t stay to meet him at dinner today? You don’t like his company? But he can do you no harm—and you’ll do him none.”

Such innocent remarks, spoken aloud in the presence of others, were not calculated to endear George to the family. Yet they carried a subtle weight, especially when uttered by a young woman whose charm had long captivated him.

News of George’s encounter with Mr. Esmond reached Dean Street only after some delay. He had chosen to withhold it from the household, not wishing to disturb their tranquility. But once the truth emerged, the reaction was swift and intense.

“You were actually going to take a man’s life!” exclaimed Theo, appalled. “And you came here, said nothing? Oh, George, it was shocking!”

“I could not let him call us both cowards,” George replied, defending himself. “Could I sit silent while he insulted my brother and me?”

The General sat quietly, his face grave. “You know, papa,” he said, “you’ve often said dueling is un-Christian, and that gentlemen ought to have the courage to refuse.”

“Refuse?” muttered Mr. Lambert, still brooding. “It requires immense strength of mind.”

“And I think,” Jack Lambert added, darkly, “that if any man called me a coward, I’d forget my orders.”

“See?” George retorted. “Brother Jack stands with me.”

“I must not oppose you, Mr. Warrington,” Jack replied stiffly.

“Mr. Warrington!” George blushed. “Would you, a clergyman, have me break the Commandments and commit murder?”

“I am a soldier’s son,” Jack replied dryly. “Besides, Mr. Warrington has committed no murder. We shall soon hear from Canada—the great question of racial supremacy will be decided there!”

He turned away as he spoke, and George watched him with astonishment.

Hetty, pale at this unexpected turn, was discreetly led from the room by her sister. George rose and followed them to the door.

“Great powers, gentlemen!” he declared, returning. “I believe, on my honour, you’re accusing me of shirking this affair with Mr. Esmond!”

The clergyman and his father exchanged glances.

“A man’s nearest and dearest are always the first to insult him,” George snapped.

“You mean to say, ‘Not guilty’?” the General cried, suddenly moved. “God bless thee, my boy! I told thee so, Jack.” He rubbed his eyes, blushed deeply, and gripped George’s hand with fervor.

“Not guilty of what, in heaven’s name?” Mr. Warrington demanded.

“Nay,” the General said, “Mr. Jack brought the story. Let him tell it. I believe ’tis a —— lie, with all my heart.”

And with that, he stormed out of the room.

Jack Lambert looked profoundly embarrassed.

“And what is this—this d——d lie, sir, that someone has been spreading about me?” George asked, grinning.

“To question a man’s courage is always an offence,” Jack replied. “And I rejoice that yours has been misrepresented.”

“Who told the falsehood, sir?” George bellowed. “I insist on knowing the name!”

“You forget,” Jack reminded him, “you are bound over to keep the peace.”

“Curse the peace!” George roared. “We can fight in Holland! Tell me the man’s name!”

“Fair and softly, Mr. Warrington,” Jack said, raising his voice. “My hearing is excellent. It was not a man who told me the story—I confessed it to my father.”

“What?” George exclaimed, realization dawning. “Was it that clever, mischievous little vixen in Bloomsbury Square?”

“Vixen?” Jack protested. “That word applies to no young lady, George Warrington—least of all Miss Lydia. Artful? She is the most innocent creature in Heaven! Wicked? That angel! With heartfelt joy that the quarrel ended, with deep gratitude that consanguineous blood was spared, she praised you for declining the duel—and expressed profound sympathy for your choice of the painful but only method of avoiding it.”

“What method?” George demanded, stamping his foot.

“Why, laying an information, of course!” Jack replied.

George exploded into a torrent of furious language—too violent to repeat—directed squarely at Miss Lydia.

“Do not speak thus!” the parson interjected, now visibly angry. “Do not defile, in my hearing, the most charming, the most innocent of women! If she erred in judging you, and doubted your willingness to commit what, after all, is a crime—homicide, the most dreadful of sins—you have no right to slander her character! You, who are innocent yourself, should honor her purity as well as her beauty! Oh, George, are you to be my brother?”

“I hope to have that honour,” George answered, smiling faintly. He began to grasp Jack’s intent.

“And what, then—though it is too much bliss for sinful man to hope—what if she should one day be your sister? Who could resist her charms? I confess I am enslaved. Those Latin Sapphics in the September issue of *The Gentleman's Magazine*, beginning *Lydicae quondam cecinit venustae*—with an English version by my friend Hickson of Corpus—are mine. I have told my mother what has passed between us. My mother agrees: the most lovely of her sex has deigned to look upon me with favour. I have written a letter—she another. She intends to visit Miss Lydia’s grandfather today, and bring me the answer that will make me either the happiest or most wretched man alive!”

He paused, then added, “In the course of family talk, I mentioned her sentiments to my father. Perhaps I spoke lightly of your courage—which I do not doubt, by Heaven, I do not doubt. But perhaps she, too, has erred. Perhaps the fiend jealousy has gnawed at my heart—and horror!—perhaps I thought my sister’s lover received too much favour from her. I would have it all to myself. Ah, dear George, who knows his own faults? I am beside myself with passion. Confound it, sir! What right have you to laugh?”

At that moment, the General burst in, catching the tail-end of the laughter.

“What, have you two boys made it up?” he asked, grinning.

“I was giving my opinion to Mr. Warrington on laughter—on his laughter in particular,” Jack retorted, fuming.

“George is bound over to keep the peace, Jack! You cannot fight him for two years. In that time, I trust you’ll reconcile. Dinner is ready, boys! Let us drink to absent friends, and put an end to the war—no fighting outside the profession!”

George excused himself with a business engagement and left early. Jack followed shortly after. When George returned to his lodgings and went to Mr. Van den Bosch’s house in Bloomsbury Square, he found Jack already speaking with a servant.

“His master and mistress left town yesterday,” the servant reported.

“Poor Jack! And you had the decisive letter in your pocket?” George asked.

“Well, yes,” Jack admitted. “And my mother has ordered a chair—she’s coming to wait on Miss Lyddy,” he whispered, distraught.

George, too, had a note in his pocket—one he hadn’t shared with Jack. His errand at home had been to write a sharp letter to Miss Lydia, addressed to the gentleman who had spread the tale of his having given information about the duel.

With the family gone, George decided not to leave his note. “If cousin Will was the slanderer,” he thought, “I’ll go and make him recant.”

“Will the family return soon?” he asked the servant.

“They’re visiting the quality,” the man replied.

George read the address on a slip of paper: “The box from Madam Hocquet’s to be sent by the Farnham Flying Coach; addressed to Miss Van den Bosch, at the Right Honourable the Earl of Castlewood’s, Castlewood, Hants.”

“Where?” Jack gasped.

“Their lordship and ladyships have been here often,” the servant said proudly. “The families are quite intimate.”

This was strange. Lyddy had mentioned only one visit from Lady Castlewood.

“And they’ll be staying some time,” the man added. “Miss took a power of boxes and gowns with her!”

The two young men walked away, each crumpling their letters in their pockets.

“What did you say?” George asked Jack.

“Distraction! I am beside myself, George! I—don’t know what I’m saying,” Jack groaned. “She’s gone to Hampshire—and Mr. Esmond is gone with her!”

“Othello could not have spoken better!” George laughed. “And she has a pretty scoundrel in her company!”

“Ha! Here is your mother’s chair!” they heard.

Aunt Lambert appeared, swinging down Great Russell Street, preceded by her footman.

“It’s no use going farther, Aunt Lambert!” George called. “Our little bird has flown.”

“What little bird?” she asked.

“The bird Jack wished to pair with—the Lyddy bird, aunt. Why, Jack, I protest you’re swearing again! This morning it was the Sixth Commandment you wanted to break—and now—”

“Confound it! Leave me alone, Mr. Warrington, do you hear?” Jack growled, striding far beyond the reach of his mother’s bearers.

“What is the matter, George?” Aunt Lambert asked.

George, annoyed by Jack’s behavior all day, replied, “Brother Jack has no fine temper, Aunt Lambert. He tells you I’m a coward and reproaches me for being angry. He finds his mistress gone to the country and begins to swear and stamp. O fie! Oh, Aunt Lambert, beware of jealousy! Did the General ever make you jealous?”

“You’ll make me very angry if you speak to me this way,” she said, distressed.

“I am respectfully dumb. I make my bow. I withdraw,” George said, bowing low, and turned toward Holborn.

His soul burned with anger. He felt the need to quarrel with someone. Had he met cousin Will that night, the sureties might have faced ruin. He sought Will at every haunt—Arthur’s, his own house—but learned only that Mr. Esmond had likely joined the family in Hampshire.

He wrote a letter:
“My dear, kind cousin William,
You know I am bound over and would not quarrel with anyone, least of all a dear, truthful, affectionate kinsman whom my brother insulted by caning. But if anyone says I prevented the meeting by giving information, please tell them I believe it is not I but someone else who is the coward. I also write to Mr. Van den Bosch, informing him and Miss Lyddy that some rascal has been spreading lies about me, and begging them to beware such persons.”

After dispatching these letters, George dressed and attended the play, supping cheerfully at the Bedford.

A few days later, a letter arrived on his breakfast table, franked “Castlewood” and signed by the nobleman himself.

“Dear Cousin,” Lord Castlewood wrote, “our family has suffered much lately. It is time our quarrels ended. Two days ago, my brother William brought me a furious letter signed G. Warrington, and informed me, to my grief, of a quarrel between you—your conduct, to say the least, violent. It is ill to waste good wine on poor uses—such as you applied to good Mr. Van den Bosch. Before an old man, youth should show more respect. I admit William’s words and behaviour are often irritating. He has tried my temper within the past twenty-four hours.

“Ah! Why cannot we all live in harmony? You know, cousin, I have always held you in sincere regard. I admire the admirable young lady to whom you are engaged, and offer my warmest compliments to her. I wish to live in peace with all my family where possible—especially since I hope to welcome a Countess of Castlewood.

“At my age, it is not unusual to choose a young wife. My Lydia (you may divine I am happy to call her the elegant Miss Van den Bosch) will naturally survive me. After soothing my declining years, I shall not begrudge her choosing a worthy successor. Though of noble Dutch descent, she admits her rank is not equal to mine—a fact she is pleased to share. I, in turn, shall welcome descendants to my house, and through my Lady Castlewood, restore its former splendour, diminished by improvident predecessors.

“My Lydia, seated beside me, sends her warmest regards to you and the Lambert family.

“The marriage will take place soon. May I hope to see you at church? My brother will not attend—he took the news poorly, spoke harsh words he will regret, and is visiting neighbours. The Dowager Lady Castlewood keeps the Kensington house; we have our own establishment, where you will always be welcomed.

Yours affectionately,

From the *London Magazine*, November 1759:
“Saturday, October 13th, married at his seat, Castlewood, Hants, the Right Honourable Eugene, Earl of Castlewood, to the beautiful Miss Van den Bosch, of Virginia. 70,000 pounds.”

CHAPTER LXXII. (From the Warrington MS.) In which My Lady is on the Top of the Ladder

Looking across the fire, towards her accustomed chair—my dear companion for the better part of my life—I often find myself asking (as middle-aged gentlemen may, with the indulgence to repeat their jokes and questions) whether any two young people were ever more reckless and ill-advised than we were when we married, in the year of the old King’s death? My son, who has taken some astonishing leaps during fox-hunts, tells me he looks back upon those daring crossings of rivers and chasms with a kind of horror, marveling at his own boldness; yet there is no more spirited rider in either county than Miles. He loves his sport so thoroughly that nothing else matters. He has broken his collarbone, endured a hundred falls—great cause of anxiety to his mother—but so too have I, once thrown over my old mare’s head as she slipped on a stone while we both drifted along a park road at four miles an hour, lost in thought—perhaps composing a line or rehearsing a speech for Quarter Sessions.

Miles’s reckless joy in hunting has been the delight of his life, just as my marriage has been the blessing of mine. I never reflect upon it without gratitude. Yet I do not hold up our union as a model. I would not advise young folk to marry on a mere twopence a year—though such advice might draw stern glances at vestry meetings. Still, my wife is known far and wide as a matchmaker of fierce determination. When Hodge and Susan appear before me in my justice room, whispering about allowances, we encourage them to spend their half-crown at home, add a little from our own purse, and summon the vicar.
