When I pose a question to my dear oracle, I already know the answer. That is, no doubt, why I so frequently consult her. A certain look upon my face, and my Diana instantly mirrors it. Suppose I say, “My dear, did you not think the moon looked like cream cheese tonight?” She replies, “Well, papa, it certainly did—there’s no one like you for whimsical comparisons.” Or if I remark, “My love, Mr. Pitt’s speech was impressive, though I fear he does not reach the heights of his father,” she responds, “No one could match Lord Chatham.” Then one of the girls will exclaim, “But I’ve heard Papa call Lord Chatham a charlatan!” To which mamma says, “How much she resembles her Aunt Hetty!”

As for Miles, Latin or Greek—Tros Tyriusve—is all one to him. He reads only the sporting columns in the Norwich paper. So long as the scent is good, he cares not a whit for the state of the nation. I suspect he has never read my poems, let alone my tragedies—though I mentioned Pocahontas to him recently, and he thought she was a river in Virginia! And how can he grasp my Latin verses when I know he cannot translate Corderius? This notebook lies openly on the small table beside my fireside, with my spectacles resting on its cover—anyone who takes the trouble to lift them may read. But Miles has never done so.

I have tucked into the loose pages caricatures of him—jokes at his expense—and yet he neither sees nor minds them. Once, instead of my neat China-ink sketch of Miles asleep after dinner—a drawing so lifelike that even Bunbury claimed it was his own—I found a crude portrait of myself tumbling over Sultana’s head, labeled *The Squire on Horseback, or Fish out of Water*. The fellow roared with laughter, and the girls tittered when I came upon the page. My wife confessed she had never felt such fright as when I opened the book. But I can bear a joke at my own expense—I have heard many, though (strange to say, given my years among the wits of the age) I have never encountered a truly clever one in my life.

Never mind, Miles—though thou art no wit, I love thee none the less. There has never been a quarrel between wits in a family. Though thou hast no great beauty, thy mother thinks thee as handsome as Apollo—or His Royal Highness, the Prince of Wales, born in the same year as thee. Indeed, she insists Coates’s portrait of the Prince bears a striking resemblance to her eldest son, and keeps the print in her dressing-room to this day.

[Note, in a female hand: “My son is not a spendthrift nor a breaker of hearts, as some gentlemen are. But that he resembled H.R.H. as infants is most certain—the Duchess of Aneaster herself remarked it in St. James’s Park, where Gumbo and my poor Molly used to take him for an airing. Th. W.”]

In that very year, with such different destinies, my Lord Esmond, son of Lord Castlewood, also entered the world. At that time, my Lord C. and I had already grown cool toward one another, and heaven knows, my honest Miles’s godmother brought no golden pap-boats to his christening! Matters have improved since—laus Deo, indeed! For I suspect neither Miles nor his father would ever have managed well by their own devices.

Castlewood House now presents quite a different appearance from the venerable structure I knew in my youth—once scarred by time, war, and weather, its façade etched with the marks of centuries. I cherish the memory of it as it stood when young Mr. George Warrington descended upon it at the owner’s invitation, to attend the marriage of his lordship to Miss Lydia Van den Bosch—“an American lady of noble Dutch descent,” as the county paper proclaimed her.

Then the towers stood as they had under the Colonel’s gaze—Warrington’s grandfather, whom Madam Esmond fondly called the Marquis. The woods, though thinned somewhat, remained largely unchanged; perhaps the very same rooks cawed above them that the Colonel had seen sixty years prior. His portrait hung in the hall—might have been his, had he chosen wealth and title over love and loyalty. As I walked those ancient corridors, dew-damp terraces, and shadowed avenues, I felt for a moment as if I were one of Walpole’s cavaliers—ruff, rapier, buff-coat, gorget—and feared at every turn that an Old Pretender or Jesuit spy might emerge from behind a tree or carved cupboard.

Strange, melancholy, and delightful fancies filled my mind. I imagined intrigues, serenades, sieges—Oliver’s Roundheads battering the walls, or Hal’s Beefeaters charging across the plain. I was then courting a certain young lady—madam, your eyes needed no spectacles then, and the brow above them bore no wrinkle or silver hair—and I wrote reams of romantic descriptions under my Lord Castlewood’s frank, letters she never tired of reading. Now, when I am away in London or elsewhere, I send her only three lines—so as not to weary your aged eyes, my dear.

Mr. Warrington deemed himself justified in ordering a fine new suit for the wedding, and with Mons. Gumbo in attendance, arrived at Castlewood several days before the ceremony. I must mention that it had been necessary to send my faithful Sady back to Virginia aboard a ship. A severe inflammation of the throat and lungs—fatal in many cases during Wolfe’s expedition—had nearly killed my boy. Doctors advised that his native air was the best cure. We parted in tears, and Gumbo shed as many when his master departed for Quebec. But Gumbo had ties here and no taste for military life, so he stayed in my service.

We found Castlewood teeming with guests—friends, relatives, and visitors. Lady Fanny was present, albeit reluctantly, as a sulky bridesmaid. Some local maidens attended the young Countess. The Baroness Beatrix, widow of a bishop, brought a holy brother-in-law from London to officiate the marriage between Eugene, Earl of Castlewood, and Lydia Van den Bosch, spinster. For weeks before and after the nuptials, the old Hampshire house wore a festive air unfamiliar to it for years.

Country families flocked to pay their respects to the newlyweds. The bride’s fortune became the talk of the land—no doubt growing in the telling. Scandalous tales circulating in town, spread by her disappointed suitors, took time to reach Hampshire. When they did, the locals chose civility over curiosity. Had she rejected one man and mocked another? It mattered little—they cared only for her money, and she was no more mercenary than they.

To the Hampshire folk, it was a blessing to see Castlewood House reopened—beer in the cellars, horses in the stables, spits turning before kitchen fires. The new Countess assumed her place with dignity. All acknowledged her rare talents and sharp intellect. Was it not stated in the marriage announcement that she brought her noble husband seventy thousand pounds? On a *beaucoup d’esprit* with seventy thousand pounds. The people said that was but a fraction of her wealth. When the grandfather passed, they believed many plums would fall from that old tree.

That quiet, keen-eyed old man soon set about restoring Castlewood’s finances, long neglected through poverty and carelessness. His life’s work became improving the estate—raising rents where possible, cutting expenses. He watched every yard of worsted lace on the footmen’s coats, every pound of beef served at dinner. A vigilant eye noted each flagon of beer drawn from the buttery, ensuring no waste in the larder. Servants were fewer, but paid regularly. Liveries were cleaner, and tailors no longer pursued payment. Gardeners and grooms grumbled, though wages were no longer overdue. But horses grew fat on less corn, and fruit and vegetables abounded—such was the precision of my lady’s grandfather, watching from his solitary chamber in the turret.

These changes, though summarized here in a few lines, took months and years at Castlewood. Through thrift, order, and wise spending—though my lord sometimes lamented he had no funds—the estate flourished. No one denied it was a prosperous, economical household—not even the dowager lady and her two children, who now rarely crossed Castlewood’s threshold. My lady regarded them as enemies—what gentleman, after all, would welcome a stepmother-in-law?

The reigning Countess gave the dowager battle and routed her swiftly. Though educated in the colonies and unversed in polite society, Countess Lydia possessed a mastery of language and a strength of will that all who opposed her had to acknowledge. The dowager and Lady Fanny proved no match for the young American. They fled to their jointure house in Kensington—and no wonder their absence was not mourned by my lord, who seldom regretted anyone whose back was turned.

Could cousin Warrington, whose hand his lordship clasped so warmly on arrival and departure—whose companion he was so gay and open with—expect that his lordship would grieve at his passing, or any misfortune befalling him? Cousin Warrington knew better. Always skeptical, Mr. W. took grim pleasure in observing his neighbors’ quirks, and could admire this one, despite his lack of courage or heart.

Courage? Heart? What do these mean to us in the world? A man may possess private virtues as he may hold half a million in government stock. What society demands is liveliness, charm, a decent appearance, and the ability to keep up one’s end.

Colonel Esmond Warrington’s grandfather—whose history and dwelling-place fascinated Mr. W.—might once have owned Castlewood and its titles. The gentleman often studied the Colonel’s portrait, still hanging in the saloon, a copy of which Mr. Warrington cherished from Virginia.

“He must have been a little touched here,” my lord said, tapping his own tall, placid forehead.

There are actions—simple, common to some—that others cannot comprehend, dismissing them as lies or madness. “I do you the justice to think, cousin,” Mr. Warrington said, “that you would never surrender any advantage for a friend.” “Eh! I am selfish,” replied my lord, with a French shrug and a pinch from his snuffbox. “But am I more selfish than the rest?”

Once, while walking in the fields, my lord wore a bright scarlet coat. A cow charged toward him, and the usually languid nobleman sprang over a stile with the agility of a schoolboy. He did not hide his fear, nor his natural timidity.

“I dare say you respect me no more than I respect myself, George,” he would say, candidly, and launch into a sardonic discourse on human frailty—why Heaven had not made us all brave, tall, handsome, and rich?

As for Mr. Warrington, who likely enjoyed being the center of attention, he could not help admiring this kinsman—so witty, graceful, polished, high-born—yet utterly his inferior. Like the creature in Sterne’s famous tale, “Do not beat me,” his lordship seemed to say, “but if you wish, you may.” No man, save a bully and coward himself, treats such a spiritless soul harshly.

We all know, dear children, from our favourite fairy tales, how in every wedding or christening there is always someone left out—some poor soul who feels slighted and swears revenge. So it’s no wonder that good cousin Will should rage and curse when he heard the news of his brother’s engagement to the colonial heiress. At first, Will stormed out of the house, swearing he would never return. But no one truly believed him—not even he himself. The prodigal son, though unrepentant, came back after a day or two, drawn by the scent of the wedding feast. He couldn’t bring himself to give up his place at Castlewood’s table. He returned, ate, drank, and toasted the young bride with a glass of wine, while muttering curses under his breath. When her father gave her away in the chapel, and my lord vowed to love, honour, and cherish her, Will responded with muffled imprecations. He was not alone in his grumbling; Mr. Warrington knew well that many had spoken ill of the new Countess and her grandfather.

The old gentleman’s City friends, his legal adviser, the Dissenting clergyman who had led their services upon arrival in England, and poor Jack Lambert—the orthodox young minister whose eloquence the old man had hoped might have won the girl over in private—all resented her perceived betrayal. Each had a tale of being deceived, encouraged, then jilted by the clever American. The lawyer, who had compiled such an exact list of her properties, estates, slaves, ships, and expectations, now declared it must be false—there was no such place as New York or Virginia, or at least Mr. Van den Bosch owned nothing there. There was no Guinea trade, and the negroes were mere fabrications conjured by the cunning planter. The Dissenting pastor lamented his lost lamb—though such a wily, mischievous creature could hardly be called a lamb at all. Poor Jack Lambert confessed to his mother that he still kept a lock of her black hair, which he wept over and addressed in language quite unfit for a clergyman. As for Mr. William Esmond, he unleashed his usual torrent of shrieks and oaths—even in the presence of his sister-in-law—swearing before Acheron that no devil more artful than Miss Lydia existed. He called her an infernal Cerberus and invoked every wrath of heaven and earth upon his brother, whom he accused of deceiving him with sweet words and stealing his prize.

“Why,” said Mr. Warrington, when Will ranted on about these matters, “if she’s truly the kind of woman you describe, then you’re better off without her. If she intends to poison her husband, as you say, how fortunate for you that you’re not the one! You ought to thank the gods, Will, instead of cursing them, for sparing you such a fury. And what greater revenge could you have on Castlewood than letting him have her all to himself?”

“All very well,” Will replied, perhaps not unfairly, “but my brother remains a scoundrel for cheating me out of the fortune I expected—and which I risked my life to win.”

George Warrington wondered how Will had ever come to risk his precious life—perhaps, he thought, a rope’s end would have been a fitting end for it. But Will, with full candour, told him how the little Cerbera had actually brought them together, only for Sir John Fielding’s men to interrupt their meeting. She constantly mocked George for sneering at Will, and Will for ignoring the taunts. She claimed George was a coward, and Will a poltroon. Then, during Braddock’s expedition, George had fled in terror and nearly died of fright. “Deuce take me,” said Will, “I was never more surprised, cousin, than when you stood your ground so coolly in Tottenham Court Fields. My second and I wagered you wouldn’t show up!”

Mr. Warrington laughed and thanked him for the compliment.

“Though,” he added, “it was lucky for me the constables arrived, or you’d have run your sword through me in another minute. Didn’t you see how clumsy I looked standing before you? And you turned pale and trembled with anger!”

“Yes, curse me,” said Will, now turning red, “that’s how I show rage. And I was furious with you, cousin! But now it’s my brother I hate—and that little devil of a Countess—a countess! A pretty countess, indeed!” And with another thunderous volley of oaths, he saluted the reigning member of the family.

“Well, cousin,” said George, looking him sharply in the eye, “you let me off easily. I dare say I owe my life to you—or at least a whole waistcoat. I admire your restraint and courage. What a pity such bravery should be wasted as a mere court usher! You’re a loss to His Majesty’s army. You truly are!”

“I never know whether you’re joking or serious, Mr. Warrington,” growled Will.

“I should think few gentlemen would dare joke with you, cousin, if they cared for their lives or ears!” retorted Mr. Warrington, who delighted in teasing his noble kinsman and watching him choke back his curses, grind his teeth in helpless fury, and smother his cowardly rage.

“And you should moderate your language, cousin, regarding the dear Countess and my lord your brother,” Mr. Warrington continued. “They speak of you most kindly. Her ladyship has told me everything.”

“What everything?” asked Will, aghast.

“As much as women ever do tell, cousin. She admitted she thought you had been a little enamoured of her. What woman can help liking a man who admires her?”

“She hates you, and says you were wild about her, Mr. Warrington!” exclaimed Mr. Esmond.

“Spretae injuria formae, cousin!”

“For me—what’s for me?” asked the other.

“I never cared for her, and thus perhaps she does not love me. Don’t you remember the case of the wife of the Captain of the Guard?”

“Which guard?” asked Will.

“My Lord Potiphar,” said Mr. Warrington.

“Lord Who? My Lord Falmouth is Captain of the Yeomen of the Guard, and my Lord Berkeley of the Pensioners. My Lord Hobart held it before. Suppose you haven’t been long enough in England to know who’s who, cousin!” remarked Mr. William.

But Mr. Warrington explained he meant the Captain of the King of Egypt’s Guard, whose wife persecuted Joseph for refusing her advances. Will responded that Egypt, he believed, was a confounded long way off, and if Lord What-d’ye-call’s wife lied about him, it was typical of her sex—women, he supposed, were the same everywhere.

In truth, when Mr. Warrington visited Castlewood for his marriage, he had heard from the Countess herself her version of the quarrel between Will and her. This account differed in some ways, though he did not claim it was more truthful than Will’s straightforward tale. The lady regretted how she had been misled by her brother-in-law. She feared his time at court had corrupted the noble principles all Esmonds were born with. She doubted Will’s word, believing his loose living and financial troubles had made him mercenary, dulled his honour, perhaps even weakened the chivalrous courage “which we Esmonds, cousin,” she declared, tossing her head, “must always possess—at least you, me, my lord, and my cousin Harry do, I know!”

“Oh, cousin George!” she went on, “and must I confess I began to doubt yours—without which a man of ancient and noble lineage like ours isn’t worthy to be called a man! I shall try, George, as a Christian lady and head of one of the first families in this kingdom and the world, to forgive my brother William for speaking ill of a family member—even if a younger branch by the female side—and making me doubt you. He did. Perhaps he told me many bad things you had said about me.”

“I, my dear lady!” cried Mr. Warrington.

“Which he said you said of me, cousin, and I hope you didn’t, and pray you didn’t. I can afford to despise them. And he paid me court—that’s true—and others have done so too. I’m used to it. He might have prospered better than he did (for I didn, at the time, know my dear lord nor value his great qualities as I do now, out of the fulness of my grateful heart!). But oh! I found William lacked courage, and no man without it can ever earn Lydia, Countess of Castlewood’s esteem—no, not that much!” And she snapped her fingers. “Noblesse oblige. A man of our blood who lacks courage—well, I don’t care a pinch of snuff for him—there, now, I don’t! Look at our ancestors, George, around these walls! Haven’t the Esmonds always fought for country and king? Is there one of us who, when the moment comes, isn’t ready to prove he’s an Esmond and a nobleman? If my eldest son showed the white feather, ‘My Lord Esmond!’ I would say to him (for that’s the second title in our family), ‘I disown your lordship!’” And with that, the intrepid little woman surveyed the portraits of her forebears—painted by Lely and Kneller—adorned the walls of her drawing-room.

Over that room, and indeed over the entire house, estate, and village, the new Countess soon established absolute rule. It was astonishing how quickly she learned command. Though she didn’t follow English customs of precedence, she invented her own rules, announced them, and enforced them. Having grown up a Dissenter and unfamiliar with the Established Church rites, Mr. Warrington noted she made a few mistakes—such as not knowing when to face east during service, a practice not observed in most Reformed churches. But between his first and second visits to Castlewood, she mastered her duties perfectly. She entered chapel on her cousin’s arm, her two footmen bearing her great Prayer-book behind her, as demurely as the pious old devotee in Hogarth’s famous painting *Morning*, as if she had always had a chaplain at her side.

She patronized not only the new chaplain but the church itself, as if she had never heard a Ranter preach in a barn. She made the oldest families in the land—grave baronets and their wives, worthy squires of twenty generations—know their place, and grant her the pas. She acquired an ancient heraldry book and sought instruction from a remarkable old maid from Winton, renowned for etiquette and genealogy, who had known Queen Anne’s court. Soon, she prattled fluently about gules and sables, bends and saltires—sometimes inaccurately, but with relentless energy. She made small progresses to nearby towns in her gilt coach-and-six, or to the village in her chair, asserting a quasi-regal right to homage from tenants and villagers alike.

She lectured the parson on theology, the bailiff on farming, instructed the astonished housekeeper in preserving and pickling, and would have taught the London footmen how to leap behind the carriage—had her little frame not been too small to mount it. She gave the village gossips advice on nursing and child-rearing before she had any children of her own. And when it came to medicine, Madam Esmond of Virginia was no more stubborn about her remedies than Miss Lydia, the earl’s new bride. One wondered, recalling the tale of the Fisherman and the Genie in the *Arabian Nights*, how such a vast spirit could be contained in such a tiny body.

When Mr. Warrington returned to London after his first visit, she sent gifts to his young friends in Dean Street—Theo, older, and Hetty, barely younger than herself. She sent a trinket to one and a book to the other—G. Warrington insisting Theo’s was a doll, and Hetty’s a nursery book with single-syllable words. As for Mr. Will, her younger brother-in-law, she treated him with maternal gravity and tenderness, often speaking to him with a protective air that amused Warrington, though it only intensified Will’s oaths and blasphemies.

As for old age, my Lady Lydia had little patience for it. Once the settlements were secured, she treated the elderly Van den Bosch and his large periwig with no more ceremony than Dinah, her black attendant, whose ears she would pinch and woolly head pull without hesitation when offended—so at least Dinah told Gumbo, who told his master. The entire household quivered before the Countess: the housekeeper, once feared even by my lord and the dowager; the pampered London footmen, who once quarreled over cards and complained loudly as they drank endless beer, now moved swiftly at her call. Even old Lockwood, gate-porter for half a century or more, tried to gather his failing wits when she entered his lodge to inspect his window, wood-closet, and order his dogs outside. Lockwood bowed his bald head before his new mistress, glanced pleadingly at his niece, and trembled before her authority.

Gumbo, dressing his master for dinner, spoke of Elisha—whom the chaplain had read about that morning—“and his bald head and de boys who call um names, and de bars eat em up, and serve um right,” said Gumbo. But the Countess, discussing the old porter with her cousin, dismissed him with a wave. “Pooh, pooh! Stupid old man! Past his work, he and his dirty dogs! They’re as old and ugly as those old fish in the pond!” She pointed to two ancient carp in the garden pond—rumoured to have lived for centuries, their backs covered in grey mould. “Lockwood must go. The workhouse is where he belongs. I’ll have a smart, tall fellow in the lodge, one who’ll do credit to our livery.”

“He was my grandfather’s man, served him in Queen Anne’s wars,” interposed Mr. Warrington.

“Oh, Lord! Queen Anne’s dead, I suppose, and we’re not going into mourning for her,” snapped the Countess.

This matter was debated at dinner, when she announced her intention to dismiss the old man.

“I am told,” said Mr. Van den Bosch gravely, “that English law provides admirably for poor servants and the aged. I wish we had such an asylum at home, and were spared the cost of keeping our old hands.”

“If a man can’t work, he ought to go!” declared her ladyship.

“Yes, indeed, that’s a fact!” agreed grandpapa.

“What! An old servant?” asked my lord.

“Mr. Van den Bosch may have been independent when young,” remarked Mr. Warrington.

“Greased my own boots, opened my own shutters, sanded and watered my own——”

“Sugar, sir?” asked my lord.

“No—floor, son-in-law!” chuckled the old man. “Though there are tricks in grocery stores, saving your ladyship’s presence.”

“La, pa! What should I know about stores and groceries?” said her ladyship.

“He! Remember stealing the sugar, and what came of it, my dear ladyship?” said grandpapa.

“At any rate, a handsome, well-grown man in our livery will look better than that shrivelled old porter!” insisted the Countess.

“No livery is so becoming as old age, madam, and no lace as handsome as silver hairs,” said Mr. Warrington. “What will the county say if you banish old Lockwood?”

“Oh! If you plead for him, sir, I suppose he must stay. Hadn’t I better send him a couch from my drawing-room and some of the best wine from the cellar?”

“Indeed, your ladyship couldn’t do better,” Mr. Warrington replied, very seriously.

And my lord yawned, “Cousin George is perfectly right, my dear. To turn away such an old servant as Lockwood would look ill.”

“You see, those mouldy old carps are a curiosity, and attract visitors,” Mr. Warrington continued gravely. “Your ladyship must allow this old man to remain. It won’t be long. Then you may hire the tall porter. It’s hard on us, Mr. Van den Bosch, that we must keep our old negroes when they’re past work. I shall sell that rascal Gumbo in eight or ten years.”

“Don’t tink you will, master!” grinned Gumbo.

“Hold your tongue, sir! He doesn’t understand English ways,” said Mr. Warrington. “He thinks an old servant has a claim on kindness.”

The next day, to Warrington’s surprise, the Countess actually sent a basket of fine wine and a cushion for Lockwood’s armchair.

“I thought of what you said last night, when I went to bed. I guess you know the world better than I do, cousin. It’s best to keep the old man, as you say.”

And so the affair ended, Mr. Warrington wondering inwardly at this strange little character from the West—her naivety, simplicity, and heartlessness that would have shamed the most hardened dowager in St. James’s.

“You tell me to respect old people. Why? I don’t see anything to respect in the old ones I know,” she said to Warrington. “They aren’t funny, and they certainly aren’t handsome. Look at grandfather; look at Aunt Bernstein. They say she was a beauty once! That portrait painted from her! I don’t believe it. No one shall tell me I’ll ever be as bad as that! When they reach that state, people shouldn’t live. No, they shouldn’t.”

At Christmas, Aunt Bernstein came to visit her nephew and niece, accompanied by Mr. Warrington. They travelled slowly in the Baroness’s own landau, the old lady in excellent health and spirits, the weather crisp but not too cold. As they neared Castlewood, Aunt Beatrice regaled her companion with stories of the house and bygone days. Though often sluggish and irritable, she could suddenly blaze with liveliness, her wit sharp, her memory rich with anecdotes of a vanished age and society. How cruel it is, I thought, that beauty should not enjoy its own span, but be forced to surrender it after forty years at most. As she spoke of her former lovers and admirers—of whom I knew far more than she suspected—I studied her face, trying to reconstruct her beauty in youth. What a sermon I read there! The courts overgrown with grass, towers crumbled, doors ajar, gilded halls tarnished, tapestries cobwebbed and torn. That ruined palace had once thrived with music and splendour, its windows blazing with light. What balls and feasts had taken place here, what laughter and passion! I could imagine secret meetings, hidden intrigues, though the curtains were drawn tight. I often felt like saying to her, “Madam, I know the story wasn’t as you tell it—but so and so.” (I had read at home the history of her life, written by my dear old grandfather.) My mind wandered through her, as I had walked through our father’s house at Castlewood, meditating on vanished glories, imagining ancient times.

When Aunt Bernstein arrived at Castlewood, her relatives respected her not for her wealth, but for her commanding presence, sharp wit, and imperious nature. She expected the same deference from the new Countess, whom she welcomed with special warmth. After all, she had orchestrated the match. “Since you, you silly creature, refused the heiress,” she said, “I was determined she wouldn’t leave the family.” She chuckled over her schemes to bring the marriage about. She had given the girl a coronet and her nephew a hundred thousand pounds. Naturally, she deserved a warm welcome. She admired the Countess’s boldness in overcoming the Dowager and Lady Fanny. Always fond of attractive people, Madame Bernstein praised her niece Lydia’s bright eyes and lovely figure. The marriage was ideal. The old man was an obstacle, yes, and rather homely in speech and appearance. But he would soon be gone. “He’ll want to go to America, or perhaps farther,” she shrugged. “As for the child, she has fire and vivacity, a Cherokee manner that has charm,” said the pleased Baroness. “Your brother had it—so do you, Master George! Nous la formerons, cette petite. Eugene lacks character, but he’s a finished gentleman. Between us, we’ll make the little savage perfectly presentable.”

Thus we talked on the second afternoon as we journeyed toward Castlewood. We stayed the first night at the King’s Arms in Bagshot, where the Baroness was always received with deep respect, then drove post to Hexton, where she had arranged for my lord’s horses to wait. But they were not there, and after two hours we continued with our Bagshot horses to Castlewood.

Our kin at Castlewood kept us in their company until the dawn of the new year. After a fortnight’s absence—what seemed an eternity to the young man, so utterly captivated by love—he returned to the side of his beloved. Madame de Bernstein, for her part, was not displeased to leave the home of her father. As we distanced ourselves from that place, she began to speak more freely.

What transpired during the tense encounter between her and her niece—when the two women stood locked in a battle of wills—she never revealed. But from that moment forward, the old lady spoke no more of shaping *cette petite* into a proper noblewoman. Indeed, when she mentioned the young Countess at all, it was with a nervous laugh, devoid of malice. Her nephew Eugene, she declared, would be henpecked for the rest of his days—something she saw clearly enough. A little order in the household, she insisted, would do him more good than any grand schemes. The little American gentleman, though vulgar in manner, appeared shrewd enough to serve as steward—a role he might well fill with advantage.

As for the Countess’s mother—well, she had heard rumors that the woman had been a convict transported from England, likely having spent years in prison beating hemp. But such gossip need not be shouted from rooftops. And truly, when it came to certain kinds of people, what did birth matter? The girl herself would now act with honesty for her own sake. She was clever, and would learn English soon enough. And the name she carried—one of great standing—was sufficient to open doors in any society. Was Mr. Van den Bosch a grocer? A smuggler? A slave-dealer? What did it matter? The Countess of Castlewood could afford to be anyone’s daughter. Once my nephew presented her, said the old lady, it would be our duty to stand by her.

Bound by ties of blood, Madame de Bernstein was expected to extend the same affection to her niece as she did to her nephew. Mr. Warrington hoped she would be generous toward Lady Maria, and spoke of his visit to Mr. Hagan and his wife, begging her aunt’s favor for them. But the old lady remained firm in her refusal. She begged that Lady Maria’s name never again be spoken, and then proceeded for two hours recounting anecdotes about her niece—tales so intimate and pointed that, since this book lies open before the innocent eyes of youth, I shall refrain from recording them. Yet let me say this: if the young woman erred, she was not alone in sin within her family. And if she repented, others would do well to follow her example.

Hagan, it is known, led an exemplary life after leaving the stage. He was renowned for both elegance and eloquence in the pulpit. His wife, though she embraced extreme views, was deeply respected in her religious circle. When I last saw her, she spoke of possessing a peculiar spiritual illumination—an idea I suspected at the time stemmed from overindulgence in drink. But I remember when she and her husband were kind to me and mine, during a time when sympathy was rare and many a self-righteous soul turned away.

I have told how easily one rose and fell in my fickle aunt’s favor, how each of us brothers, in turn, was embraced and then cast aside. My moment of glory came after the success of my play. I was introduced to the wit of the town, held my place among them with modest success, praised as “pretty well bred” by the macaronis and men of fashion. Had my purse lasted longer, or had I chosen that path, I might have carved out a respectable career among them. But I loved, at that time, a pair of kind eyes more than the brightest orbs of the Gunnings or Chudleighs, or all the painted beauties of Ranelagh.

Because I loved your mother, children, can you believe it was said that my tastes were low? That my genteel family deplored my way of life? It was so. Both my godly Lady Warrington and worldly Madame Bernstein laid their heads together and lamented my choices.

“Why,” said Religion, ever watchful of Heaven and the main chance, “with his name, he might marry anyone!”

“I meddle with no man’s affairs,” said Uncle Warrington, “and I admire genius. But it is a pity you consort with poets and authors, and that sort of people. When you might have had a lovely creature with a hundred thousand pounds, you let her slip and courted a country girl without a penny.”

“But if I had promised her, uncle?” I asked.

“Promise, promise!” he replied, turning sharply on his heel. “These things are matters of arrangement and prudence. You committed yourself to little Miss Lambert before you’d seen the lovely American lady your mother wished you to marry—as any good mother would. Your duty to her, nephew, your duty to the Fifth Commandment, would have justified breaking with Miss L. and fulfilling your mother’s intentions regarding Miss—what was the Countess’s Dutch name? Never mind. A name is nothing. But a plumb, Master George, is something to look at! I have my dear little Miley at dancing school with Miss Barwell, Nabob Barwell’s daughter. I don’t disguise my hope that the children may form an attachment that endures through life. I tell the Nabob so. We went from the House of Commons one dancing day and saw them. It was beautiful to see the young ones walking a minuet together—it brought tears to my eyes. For I have a feeling heart, George, and I love my boy!”

“But if I prefer Miss Lambert, with twopence to her fortune, to the Countess with her hundred thousand pounds?”

“Then, sir,” said the old gentleman, “you have a singular taste—that’s all.” And with that, he left me.

I understood perfectly his vexation at my inability to see the world as he did. Nor did Aunt Bernstein approve of my engagement or the family with whom I spent so much time. Their simplicity wearied her, perhaps even annoyed her, just as certain persons (not so black as they’re painted) dislike holy water. She chafed at my constant presence beside my sweetheart. Having risen high in her favor, I began to fall again. Harry once more became the favorite—and his brother, Heaven knows, was not jealous. He was now our family hero.

He wrote brief letters from the seat of war where he served. At first, Madame Bernstein paid little attention to them—their tone plain, their content unexciting. But we had already learned in London of the battle fought on the glorious first of August at Minden, where Wolfe’s old regiment was among the six British units that helped secure victory on that famed day. At the very same hour, the young General lay sick in his bed near Quebec, stricken by fever and perhaps rage and disappointment at the setback his troops had just endured.

Arriving in the St. Lawrence in June, the fleet carrying Wolfe and his army landed them on the last day of the month on the Island of Orleans, opposite the towering cliffs of Quebec. After the great action in which his General fell, the dear brother who had accompanied him wrote home one of his simple letters, describing his modest role in that glorious day. He added nothing new to the many accounts already written of the battle of September 13th, except one detail: from the testimony of a fellow aide-de-camp who stood beside him, the General never spoke a word after receiving his mortal wound. Thus, the famous phrase attributed to the dying hero must be considered no more authentic than a speech by Livy or Thucydides.

From his position on the island, which lies in the river’s main channel north of the city, the General watched constantly for an opportunity to attack. Above and below the city, he landed forces—here and there—ever seeking an opening. It was surely a grave error on the part of the Marquis of Montcalm to accept battle on equal terms, for the British General had no artillery. When we scaled the heights and reached the Plains of Abraham, we were closer to the city, certainly—but still as far off as ever from entering it.

The game played between these two brave commanders, lasting from July until Mr. Wolfe won the final stake in September, must have been one of the most compelling matches ever fought. On the very night after landing, as my brother recounted, the contest began. At midnight, the French sent a squadron of fire-ships downriver toward the British vessels discharging stores at Orleans. Our sailors thought it sport to tow them clear of the fleet and ground them ashore, where they burned out.

As soon as the French commander learned our ships had entered the river, he marched to Beauport, ahead of the city, and took up a strong position. Once our supplies and hospitals were established, our General crossed from the island to the left bank, drawing nearer to his enemy. He had the fleet behind him in the river, but the entire countryside lay hostile before him. Indians in the forest seized our advance parties and tortured them horribly. The French were as cruel as their Indian allies.

The Montmorenci River flowed between Wolfe and his foe. He could neither attack them nor the city beyond. Determined to find another point of assault, he circled around Quebec and skirted the left shore. Everywhere, defenses were strong—both in front and behind. After enduring the batteries’ fire up and down the river, he returned to his post at Montmorenci.

On the right flank of the French position, across the fordable Montmorenci River, stood an enemy redoubt. He wanted that. Perhaps its defense would force the French commander to abandon his lines and bring on a battle. Wolfe decided to risk it. He would move his army from the Island of Orleans and attack from the St. Lawrence. He timed the assault so that at low tide, his lieutenants Murray and Townsend could cross the Montmorenci.

On the last day of July, he launched this desperate gamble. First, he and General Monckton—setting out from Point Levi—crossed the St. Lawrence from their respective stations, met with a storm of shot and artillery as they rowed to shore. No sooner were the troops landed than they rushed toward the redoubt without order, were cut down in great numbers, and forced to retreat.

At the prearranged signal, the troops on the other side of the Montmorenci advanced across the river in perfect order. The enemy evacuated the redoubt and fell back to their lines—but from there they met the attackers with such fierce fire that any impression was impossible. The General had no choice but to withdraw.

The Battle of Montmorenci—fought over and over again by my brother Harry and me over our wine—formed the grim burden of the first dispatch from Mr. Wolfe to reach England, plunging us all into gloom. What could one expect from such a rash commander? What disasters might not follow? Was ever a plan so reckless as bringing three large bodies of men across broad rivers, under murderous batteries, merely to provoke an entrenched enemy into battle?

It was the talk of the town. No wonder sober men shook their heads and prophesied further disaster. The General, weakened by fever, would live barely six weeks longer—and die immortal.

How does greatness come to pass? Is it merit—or madness? Frolic or fortune? Fate? Does the just cause always prevail? How did the French take Canada from the savages, and we from the French? And after which conquest should we sing Te Deum?

We always invoke Heaven in our quarrels, summoning the gods to intervene, no matter the knot. Does Broughton, after pummeling Slack, raise his bruised eye to Jove and thank him for the victory? And if ten thousand boxers do so, why not one? If Broughton is grateful, what must Slack feel?

“By the list of disabled officers—many of rank—you may see, sir, that the army is greatly weakened. The nature of this river deprives the most formidable part of our armament of its power. Yet we face nearly the entire force of Canada. In this situation, I am at a loss. Great Britain demands vigorous action; yet courage should be used only where there is hope. The admiral and I have examined the town for a general assault—he would join in any measure for public service—but I cannot propose such a dangerous undertaking, promising so little success... I found myself so ill, and remain so weak, that I begged the generals to consult for the public good. They agree we should send a corps of four or five thousand—nearly our whole strength—to draw the enemy from their position and force a battle. I have agreed, and preparations are underway.”

So wrote the General—whose noble letters clearly were not penned by our dear scribe—from his headquarters at Montmorenci Falls on September 2nd. Then, on October 14th, the Rodney cutter arrived with the sad news in England: the attack had failed, the chief was ill, the army dwindling, the city too strong for assault. “The only chance,” he wrote, “is to fight the Marquis of Montcalm on less disadvantageous terms, and, if possible, draw him from his position.”

Would the French commander—whose military genius was known across Europe—fall into such a trap? No wonder faces grew pale in the City, doubt and gloom spreading wherever the news reached.

Three days later came the famous letters announcing the astonishing turn of fortune that ended Mr. Wolfe’s remarkable life. If no man is truly happy until death, what shall we say of this one? His end was so glorious that I protest not even his mother nor his mistress should mourn it—or wish him alive again.

I know we speak of a hero. Yet I confess I scarcely know whether to admire the triumph of genius, invention, and daring—or the boldness of a gambler winning against impossible odds. Suppose his ascent had been discovered half an hour earlier? Suppose his men had been beaten back? Suppose the Marquis of Montcalm had refused to leave his entrenchments? Suppose these points—none of which depend on Mr. Wolfe—and what becomes of the glory of the young hero, the minister who discovered him, or the nation drunk with self-congratulation?

What fate shapes our ends—or those of nations? In the many risky games Lord Chatham played, he won this greatest one. And as the greedy British hand seized Canada, it dropped the United States from its grasp. Of course, wisdom after the fact is easy. Now, we marvel at Wolfe’s rashness, and blame others for their mistakes. What generals are we on paper! What sharp retorts come to mind after the deed is done! And once the game is over, how well we see how it should have been played!

Writing thirty years later, it is easy to criticize. But when we first heard of Wolfe’s deeds on the Plains of Abraham—of the army marching in darkness, carried silently up the midnight river—of the rocks scaled by the intrepid leader and his men—of the enemy’s miraculous unawareness, their acceptance of our challenge, their defeat on the open field by sheer valor—we were all intoxicated in England by the news.

The whole nation rose up, feeling stronger for Wolfe’s victory. Not only those who fought, but those at home who had condemned the plan, felt themselves heroes. Our spirit soared as theirs faltered. Friends embraced. Coffee-houses and public places teemed with people eager to talk of the news. Courtiers rushed to the King and the great Minister whose wisdom had guided the campaign. When he appeared, the people followed him with shouts and blessings.

No one mourned the dead warrior—only admired his peaceful passing. Should James Wolfe’s friends grieve and wear mourning because a chariot from heaven had come to carry him away? Let them watch in awe, and see him departing radiant, rising above us, superior.

To have known someone near him was to be honored. Every soldier who fought with him became a hero. In our small circle, it was a distinction to be Harry’s brother. Even Uncle Warrington wrote letters praising Heaven and congratulating himself and me on Harry’s share in the glorious achievement. Aunt Beatrix opened her house and welcomed guests in celebration of the victory. I, too, became a hero—by virtue of my resemblance to my brother.

And Parson Sampson preached a sermon so fiery that his listeners—some warned in advance—could barely be stopped from huzzaing him. They were mobbed as they left the chapel.

“Don’t talk to me about grief,” General Lambert said to his wife, who, dear soul, wanted to allow herself a small indulgence on the day Wolfe’s remains were buried at Greenwich. “If our boys could die like James, you wouldn’t stop them from being shot. You’d scale the Abraham heights to see it done! Wouldst thou mind dying in the arms of victory, Charley?” he asked the little hero from the Chartreux.

“That I wouldn’t,” said the boy. “And the doctor gave us a holiday, too.”

Harry’s promotion was assured after his role in the battle. Our aunt announced her intention to purchase a company for him.

Had your father, young folks, possessed even the commonest measure of prudence, this chapter would never have been written—nor would you yourselves have ever come into being to plague him in a hundred ways: to shout and laugh in the corridors when he seeks quiet at his books; to wake him after dinner, as any healthy country gentleman should be allowed to doze; to misplace his spectacles, steal his newspaper when he wants to read it, and burden him with tailors’ bills, mantua-makers’ bills, tutors’ fines—all of which you now inflict upon him with such cheerful regularity. You break his peace at night when you fall ill, though he would sleep undisturbed if only your silly mother could keep still for half an hour. And when Joan cannot sleep, what use is there in Darby putting on his nightcap? Every little ailment one of you has suffered has terrified her so that I confess I’ve never known true tranquility. Were I not the most patient creature alive, I’d have wished to be rid of you all.

Now, when you’ve grown past childhood, long petticoats, chicken-pox, smallpox, whooping-cough, scarlet fever, and those other delightful afflictions of youth, what must that stubborn woman propose but to turn the south rooms into a nursery for possible grandchildren, and set up Captain Miles with a wife—marry him early, just as we did! She says he’s too fond of Brookes’s and Goosetree’s when he’s in London. With perverse wisdom, she hints that while an entrée to Carlton House may be pleasant, it’s perilous for a young man. She wants Miles to live away from temptation, sow his wild oats, and marry—just as we did. Marry! My dear, we had no business to marry at all! By every rule of reason and duty, I ought to have broken off my engagement with Miss Theo—she would have married someone else—and chosen a wealthy wife instead. Your Uncle John was a parson and couldn’t fight; poor Charley was still at school; and your grandfather was too old to challenge me with sword or pistol. I say again: never was a more foolish match than ours. Our relatives were perfectly right to be angry with us. What are relations for, after all, but to find fault and quarrel?

When Hester marries, Master George, remember to argue with her if she does not take a husband of your choosing. When George secures his living—after becoming senior wrangler and fellow of his college—Miss Hester, you must lift your nose disdainfully at any young lady he fancies. As for you, my little Theo, I cannot bear to part with you. You must stay with your old father; he likes you to play Haydn for him, and peel his walnuts after dinner.

[On the blank leaf opposite this paragraph is written, in a large, girlish hand: “I never intend to go.--THEODOSIA.” “Nor I.--HESTER.” They both married, as I see by the note in the family Bible—Miss Theodosia Warrington to Joseph Clinton, son of the Rev. Joseph Blake, later Master of Rodwell Regis Grammar School; and Miss Hester Mary, in 1804, to Captain F. Handyman, R.N.—ED.]

While they enjoyed the blessing (so they thought!) of meeting daily, billing and cooing like lovers in a dream, your parents lived in a fool’s paradise, heedless of the world around them and its gossip and interference. Rinaldo was as brave a warrior as ever slew a Turk—but you know he loved lingering in Armida’s garden. Pray, my Lady Armida, what did you mean by casting your spells over me in youth, so that neither glory nor fashion, nor gaming tables, nor the society of witty men whom I met, could keep me long from your apron-strings, or out of reach of your gentle, simple talk? Pray, my dear, what did we say to each other during those endless hours together? I never slept after dinner then. Which of us was wittier? Was it I—or you? And how came our conversations to be so delightfully sweet? I remember that year I didn’t even care to go see Lord Ferrers tried and hanged, though all London was running after him. The King of Prussia’s capital had fallen; had the Austrians and Russians encamped around the Tower, there could scarcely have been greater stir in London. Yet Miss Theo and her young gentleman felt no real emotion—no pity, no indignation. What mattered to us the fate of Leipzig or Berlin? The truth is, that dear old house in Dean Street was an enchanted garden of joy. I’ve been idle since, but never so happy.

Shall we order the postchaise, my dear, leave the children to run the household, and drive up to London to see if the old lodgings are still available? And you can sit in your old window seat, waving a little handkerchief as I walk down the street. Say our actions were imprudent. Would we not do it all over again? My good friends, if Venus herself had walked into the room and challenged the apple, I was so infatuated I would have given it to your mother. And had she had the choice, she would have preferred her humble servant in a threadbare coat to my Lord Clive with all his diamonds.

Once, indeed, and for a brief time that year, I had thoughts of taking to the highway to be caught and hanged like Lord Ferrers; or joining the King of Prussia and asking some of his enemies to end my life; or enlisting for India, where I might perform some desperate feat that would end in death. Ah me! That was truly a dreadful time. Your mother dares not speak of it now, save in a whisper of fear; nor think of it—it caused her such cruel pain. She remained unhappy for years afterward on the anniversary of that day, until one of you was born on it. Suppose we had been parted—what would have become of us? What would my life have been without her? When I think of that possibility, the whole world becomes a blank.

I do not say we would be parted now. God has granted us thirty years of union. We’ve reached autumn. Our successors are ready. And whichever of us departs first knows the other will follow soon. But we *were* parted in our youth—and I shudder to think what might have happened, had not a dearest friend brought us back together.

Unknown to myself, and perhaps meaning only my good, my relatives in England wrote to Madam Esmond in Virginia, describing what they called the folly of my engagement. Every one of them sang the same tune. I saw the letters later—burned them all years after when my mother showed them to me in Virginia. Aunt Bernstein was quick to advise. A young man with no striking looks, no family, no fortune—was ever such an imprudent connection? And should it not be broken off for dear George’s sake? She had several suitable matches in mind for me. With my name and prospects, it was a shame I should throw myself away on this girl. Her sister ought to intervene—etc., etc.

My Lady Warrington also wrote—her letter adorned with scripture texts. She wrapped her worldly concerns in religious garb. She pointed out how I was living among actors and such people—whom she wouldn’t say were entirely without religion (Heaven forbid!), but who were deplorably worldly. She refrained from saying an artful woman had ensnared me for her daughter, having failed to capture my younger brother. She said nothing harmful about the young woman I had chosen, but insisted Miss L. had no fortune, and her parents might naturally wish to avoid a scandal. She had taken counsel, sought guidance, and felt bound to act. Sir Miles, a man of excellent judgment in worldly matters (though he knew and sought a higher), fully agreed with her and urged her to write, to beg her sister to interfere before the marriage took place.

And who else but the new Countess of Castlewood must insert her finger into the pie? She wrote a majestic letter to Madam Esmond, declaring that Providence had placed her at the head of the Esmond family, and thus it was her duty to warn her kinswoman to break off this marriage. I believe the three women conferred beforehand, sending packet after packet of warnings across the Atlantic.

One raw April morning, as Corydon went to pay his usual visit to Phillis, he found not his beloved with her usual smile, but Mrs. Lambert, eyes red with tears, and the General as pale as death. “Read this, George Warrington!” he said, as his wife buried her face in her hands, placing a letter before me—whose handwriting I instantly recognized. I can still hear the sobs of dear Aunt Lambert. To this day, the sound of fire irons stirring a fire above gives me a chill. I heard such noises that day in the girls’ room, where the sisters sat together. Poor, gentle child! Poor Theo!

“What can I do now, George, my poor boy?” asked the General, pacing the room with desperation etched on his face.

I did not finish reading Madam Esmond’s letter—faintness seized me. But I fear I could recite parts of it now by heart. Its tone was polite, its words measured, though they implied that Mr. and Mrs. Lambert had tricked me into the marriage; that they knew such a union was beneath me; that (as Madam E. understood) they had desired a similar match for her younger son—a plan abandoned, perhaps wisely, when it became clear Mr. Henry Warrington was not the heir to the Virginian estate. If Mr. Lambert was a man of honor, as he was reputed, Madam Esmond doubted he would persist after her representations. She would not command her son, whose temperament she knew well—but for the sake of Miss Lambert’s reputation and peace, she urged the engagement be dissolved by her family, not by Rachel Esmond Warrington of Virginia refusing to marry.

“God help us, George,” the General said, “and give us strength to bear this grief and these charges your mother has laid upon us. They are harsh, but they matter less now. What matters most is sparing my poor girl as much sorrow as we can. I know you love her deeply—you’ll help me and her mother make this blow as light as possible on that tender heart. Since she was born, she’s never hurt a soul—and it’s cruel that she should suffer.”

As he spoke, he passed a hand over his dry eyes.

“It was my fault, Martin! It was my fault!” wept the poor mother.

“Your mother gave us her word,” said the father. “And do you think I will withdraw mine?”

“I will not!” I cried, swearing a thousand frantic oaths—vows they already knew—that I was bound to Theo before Heaven, and nothing could tear me from her.

“She will demand the separation herself,” said the General. “She is a good girl, God help me! And dutiful. She won’t want her parents accused of scheming, or treated with scorn. Your mother may not have known what she was doing—but it’s done. You may see the child, and she will tell you as much. Is Theo dressed, Molly? I brought the letter home from my office last night after you left. The women had a terrible night. She knew at once by my face that news had come from America. She read the letter calmly. Said she’d like to see you and say farewell. Of course, George, you’ll give me your word of honor not to try and see her again. As soon as my duties allow, we’ll leave this place—but mother and I think we’re best together. Perhaps you should go. But give me your word, at least, that you’ll not seek her out. We must spare her pain, sir! We must spare her pain!”

The good man sank into a deep anguish, and I, though not yet overwhelmed by my own grief, felt his pain, and pitied him.

Could it be that the lips I had kissed yesterday were to speak to me only once more? We were all here—together, loving each other, sitting in the room where we met every day. My drawing lay on the table beside her little workbox. She was upstairs. She would come down soon. Who opens the door?

I see her sweet face. It looked like little Mary’s when we feared she would die of fever. Even a smile played upon her lips. She comes forward and kisses me.

“Good-bye, dear George,” she says.

Great Heaven! An old man sits in this room—my wife’s workbox across from me, and she but five minutes away. My eyes grow dim and full—I cannot see the book before me. I am twenty-three again. I relive every stage of that agony. Once, I suffered it sitting in my own postchaise, with my wife actually beside me. Who dared defile her pure love with suspicion? Who had the right to stab such a soft heart? Don’t you see my ladies sharpening their knives, and the poor child baring hers?

My wife enters. She has been serving tea or tobacco to some of her pensioners.

“What makes you look so angry, papa?” she asks.

“My love,” I say, “it is the thirteenth of April.”

A pang crosses her face, followed by a tender smile. She has endured the martyrdom—and in the midst of pain, a halo of forgiveness appears.

I cannot forgive—not until the days of dotage come, and I cease remembering anything.

“Hal will be home for Easter,” she says. “He’ll bring two or three friends from Cambridge.” And immediately she begins planning how to entertain the boys. When is she ever occupied, but with plans to make others happy?

A gentleman in spectacles, seated before an old ledger, writing down pitiful memories of his own life, is a curious and absurd sight. My corns ache, I know—but I suspect my neighbor’s shoes pinch him too. I will not howl over my own grief, nor dwell long on this one. Many another man, I dare say, has had the light of his life suddenly extinguished, joy snuffed out, and left to darkness and vague torment. I tried to read Howell’s Letters at that time—and when I reached the part about Prince Charles in Spain, the whole tragedy rose again before me. I went to Brighthelmstone, stayed at the inn, had a room facing east, watched the sun rise many mornings after nights of wakefulness, and smoked my pipe of Virginia in his face. When I’m there by chance and see the sun rising now, I shake my fist at him, thinking: O orient Phoebus, what terrible grief and savage wrath have you not seen me endure!

Though my wife is mine for so long, I remain angry—just the same. Who dared, I ask, make us suffer so?

I was forbidden to see her. I kept my promise and stayed away—from that dreadful meeting and parting. But at night, I would go and watch her window, see the lamp burning there. I’d go to the Chartreux (where I knew another boy), call for her brother, and feed him with cakes and half-crowns. I’d invite her elder brother to dine, almost kiss him when he left. I used to breakfast at a coffeehouse in Whitehall just to see Lambert go to his office; we’d salute each other sadly, pass without speaking.

Why did not the women come out? They never did. They were working on her, persuading her to forget me. Oh, the weary, weary days! Oh, the maddening time!

At last, a doctor’s carriage began appearing daily before the General’s house. Was she ill? I confess I was almost glad she was. My own suffering was so unbearable I greedily wanted her to share it. And would she not? What grief of mine has her gentle, compassionate heart not felt? What pain would she not endure to spare me even a pang?

I sought out the doctor. I had an interview with him. I told my story, laid bare my heart with a passion so sincere it moved him to sympathy. My confession helped him understand his young patient’s illness—one his medicines could not cure. I had promised not to see her or go near her—I kept my word. I had promised to leave London—I left. Twice, thrice I returned, poured out my sorrows to him. He accepted my fee now and then, always received me kindly, let me speak.

Ah, how I clung to him! I suspect he had known sorrow himself—he knew how to comfort the broken-hearted.

He did not tell me how dangerously ill she was, though he did not hide how gravely sick she had become. I told him everything—that I would marry her, defy every risk, that without her, I was utterly ruined, cared not what became of me. My mother had once consented, but now withdrew her approval—when the bond between us had, as I believed, grown stronger than filial duty.

“I think, sir,” said the doctor, “if your mother heard you and saw Miss Lambert, she might relent.”

Who was my mother to hold me in bondage? To claim the right to make me miserable? To take this angel from my arms?

“He cannot,” he said, “be a message-carrier between pining young ladies and lovers shut out from their hearts’ gates. But this much I will say: I have seen you, and I am prescribing for you too.”

Yes, he must have suffered once. I saw him, you may be sure, on the very day he kept his promise to me. He said she seemed comforted by hearing news of me.

“She bears her suffering with angelic sweetness. I prescribe Jesuit’s bark, which she takes—but I am not sure the news of you has not done more good than the medicine.”

Later, the women admitted they had never told the General about the doctor’s new patient.

I know not what wild expressions of gratitude I poured out to the good doctor for the comfort he brought me. His treatment healed two souls. ‘Twas but a drop of water—but to a man raging in torment, a drop is enough.

I loved the ground he trod, blessed the hand that held mine, the pulse he felt. I had a ring with a pretty cameo of Hercules. Too small for his finger—and he wore no ornaments. I fastened it to his watch-chain, hoping she might see it and recognize it as mine.

How I clung to Spencer at this time—my friend from the Temple, who also had an unfortunate love affair—we walked from my apartments to the Temple, and he back to Bedford Gardens. Our talk was always of our women. I doubt I told everyone my grief. My kind landlady and Betty the housemaid pitied me. My son Miles, who for once has been reading my manuscript, says, “By Jove, sir, I didn’t know you and my mother were so deeply smitten. The year I joined, I was struck hard myself—an infernal little jilt who left me for Sir Craven Oaks of our regiment. I thought I’d go mad.” And he gives a melancholy whistle and walks away.

The General had to leave London soon for a military inspection, as the doctor casually mentioned. But since I had sworn not to present myself at his house, I kept my vow—though I made use of the physician’s permission to visit him and learn of his dear patient. His reports were far from encouraging.

“She does not rally,” he said. “We must send her back to Kent, or to the sea.”

I did not know then that the poor child had begged so piteously not to be moved that her parents, sensing perhaps why she wished to stay in London, and fearing it might be dangerous not to indulge her, had yielded and agreed to remain in town.

At last, one morning I came, as usual, and took my place in the doctor’s front parlour, where patients were called in turn to the consulting room. I sat there, idly browsing the books on the table, paying no attention to anyone. Soon the room emptied—save for me and one lady, veiled.

I usually stayed till the end, for Osborn, the doctor’s man, knew my purpose: I wasn’t there for my own health.

When only I and the lady remained, she reached out two small hands and whispered, “Don’t you know me, George?”

And the next moment I had my arms around her, kissed her as passionately as I ever had—and gave way to a flood of emotion so refreshing, for my parched soul had raged and tormented for six weeks. This was a glimpse of heaven.

Who was it, children? You think it was your mother the doctor brought to me? No. It was Hetty.

The initial surprise and greeting had passed, and at once the young girl began her charge. “So you’ve finally come to ask after Theo—and now you feel sorry that your neglect has made her so ill? For six weeks she’s been unwell, and not a word from you! Very kind of you, Mr. George, I’m sure!”

“Kind!” Mr. Warrington gasped. “Do you call it kind to be with her every day for a year, and then leave without a word?”

“My dear,” I replied, “you know my promise to your father.”

“Promise!” Miss Hetty retorted, tossing her head. “A fine promise indeed—to make my darling ill, and then one bright morning say, 'Good-bye, Theo,' and walk away forever. I suppose gentlemen make such promises because they intend to keep them. But if I were a man, I’d never toy with a child’s heart and abandon her afterward. What has she ever done but love you too much? By what right do you take her from us all, only to desert her because some old woman in America disapproves of her? She was happy before you came. She loved her sister—there never was such a sister—until she saw you. And now, because your mother thinks you might do better, you must leave her?”

“Great powers, child!” I exclaimed, furious at her injustice. “Was it I who drew back? Is it not I who am forbidden this house? Did not your father demand, on my honor, that I should never see her again?”

“Honor!” she spat. “And you’re the ones who pretend to be our superiors—the ones we’re meant to admire and respect! I declare, George Warrington, you ought to go back to your Virginia schoolroom, have your black nurse tuck you into bed, and ask permission from your mother before stepping out. Oh, George! I never dreamed my sister would give her heart to a man without the courage to stand by her—only to flee at the first obstacle. When Doctor Heberden said he was attending you, I decided to come and see you—and you *do* look ill, which pleases me. I suppose it’s your mother you’re afraid of. But I won’t tell Theo you’re unwell. She hasn’t stopped caring for you. She can’t simply walk out of a room, break her solemn vows, and return to life as if nothing happened. That’s left to men—our so-called superiors in courage and wisdom. To abandon an angel—yes, an angel ten thousand times too good for you—an angel who adored me until she saw you, and who was the very blessing of our lives—is this what you call honor? Don’t speak to me of honor! I despise you all! You claim to be our betters? We are to worship and wait upon you? I don’t care for your wit, your tragedies, or your poetry—they’re often absurd. I won’t stay up copying your manuscripts, nor watch hour after hour at a window, wasting my time, just to glimpse your worship walking down the street with your hat cocked. If you’re leaving, go ahead—but give me back my sister! Give me back my darling, the one who loved us all until she saw you. And you’re leaving her because your mother thinks she can find someone richer? Oh, you brave gentleman! Go marry whom your mother chooses, and let my dear die here, abandoned!”

“Great heavens, Hetty!” I cried, stunned by her logic. “Is it I who wish to leave your sister? Did I not offer to keep my promise? Was it not your father who refused me, forcing me to swear I would never see her again? What do I have but my word, my honor?”

“Honour indeed!” she shot back. “You keep your word to him, but break it to her! A fine honor! If I were a man, I’d soon show you what I thought of your honor! Only—I forgot—you’re bound to keep the peace and can’t… Oh, George, George! Don’t you see how distraught I am? I’m beside myself, barely knowing what I say. You mustn’t leave my darling. They don’t know it at home. They don’t believe it—but I know her best. She will die if you leave her. Say you won’t! Have mercy on me, Mr. Warrington—give me back my dearest!”

Thus, the passionate, broken-hearted girl swung from fury to pleading, scorn to tears. Was my little doctor correct in diagnosing her sister’s condition so gravely? Was there truly no other remedy than the one Hetty demanded? Had not others endured the same agony of separation, suffered the same fever and despair, lain hopeless of survival, only to recover and limp through life? Perhaps—had love not been selfish, had ours not been so intense and unique that we believed no other lovers could suffer like us—we might have found in Hetty’s fervent defense a proof that a devoted heart could endure, silently bear, and ultimately heal.

What had happened in Hetty’s own case? Her sister and I, in our easy triumphs and intimate confidences, had often spoken of it. Egotists though we were, perhaps we had drawn secret comfort from her lesser fortune. It was like sitting by a fire while winter raged outside, or walking beside a great river and watching a ship tossed by the waves. We clung closer to each other, wrapped in our own joy, viewing others’ sorrows with quiet pity.

Be that as it may. Grant that we might have been parted, and lived through it—my skeptical old age might concede that. Yet at the time, I was eager to share Hetty’s fears, willingly believing that the life most precious to me would perish if torn from mine. Was I wrong? Not now would I say so. I may doubt myself—or not—I know not—but of her, never. And Hetty found in me a willing partner in her anxieties.

I tried to share some of these thoughts with the doctor, but he silenced me. “Hush,” he said, his face comically alarmed. “I must hear none of this. If two people happen to meet and talk in my patient’s room, I cannot help it. But matchmaking and love-making? I am your humble servant! What will the General do when he returns to town? He’ll have me behind Montagu House as sure as I’m a living doctor—and alive I wish to remain, my good sir!” And with that, he leapt into his carriage and left me standing, lost in thought.

“And you and Miss Hetty must have no meetings here again,” he had warned earlier.

“Oh no!” I assured him. “Of course not! We are gentlemen of honor—and our word is our bond. Besides, seeing Hetty was a gift beyond measure. Would we not be eternally grateful?”

Refreshed by the sip of water I’d taken, I felt capable of enduring anything. I walked with Hetty to Soho, never once thinking of arranging another meeting. But the little emissary was more thoughtful. “Are you going to the Museum now to read?” she asked.

“Oh yes, sometimes,” I replied. “But I’m too wretched for reading now. I can’t see the words on the page. I don’t care about my books. Even Pocahontas bores me.”

I might have gone on, but she interrupted: “Nonsense!” she snapped, stamping her foot. “George, you’re more foolish than Harry!”

“What do you mean, my dear?” I asked.

“When do you go? You leave at three o’clock. You cross over toward Tottenham Court, walk through the village, and return by Green Lane—the one leading back to the new hospital. You know you do! Walking there for a week won’t hurt you. Good morning, sir! Please don’t follow me any farther.” And with that, she curtseyed and walked away, her veil drawn.

Green Lane, north of the new hospital, is now lined with houses. In my time—when King George II still reigned—it was a shabby rural escape from London, so perilous that city folk returning from their villas at Hampstead or Highgate would travel in groups, escorted by servants with lanterns, to guard against footpads lurking at the edges of the town. The churches of Hampstead and Highgate, crowning their hills, framed the view as one turned from London. For three days, Mr. George Warrington had the pleasure of seeing this landscape and walking back along the lane toward the hospital.

Along the way stood small inns and taverns. I recall one place, where cakes and beer were sold under the sign of the Protestant Hero. On the third or fourth day, a decent woman smiled at me, curtseying in her clean apron. “It appears the lady doesn’t come, sir,” she said. “Your honor had best step in and try a can of my cool beer.”

Then, on May 25th—O day to be marked with white stone—as I walked back through Tottenham Road, a little beyond Mr. Whitefield’s Tabernacle, I saw a landau ahead. On the box-seat, beside the driver, sat my young friend Charley, waving his hat. “George! George!”

I ran forward, my knees trembling so violently I feared I’d fall at the wheel. Inside the carriage, I saw Hetty—and beside her, my dearest Theo, propped with a pillow. How thin her hand had grown since last it lay in mine! Her cheeks were flushed and sunken, her eyes unnaturally bright, and the faint tremor in her voice when she spoke sent a shock through me—whether grief or joy, I couldn’t tell; they were so entwined.

“I’m taking her for an airing to Hampstead,” Hetty said calmly. “The doctor says the air will do her good.”

“I’ve been ill,” Theo whispered, “but I’m better now, George.”

As she spoke, a sudden burst of music erupted from the chapel nearby. I took her hand. Her eyes met mine. It felt as if we had never been apart. I shall never forget that hymn. I’ve heard it all my life—my wife played it on her harpsichord, our children sang it. Now, do you understand, young people, why I love it so? Because it was the music of our reunion. Because it sang hope into my life at its darkest hour. Yes, the darkest: for even the dreary confinement at Duquesne had its tender moments—the poor Biche, my drunken jailer, the forest birds’ reveille, the military music of my prison. I remember them fondly.

Master Charley looked down from the box-seat, watching his sister and me in silent rapture, Hetty listening to the music. “I think I’d like to go and hear it,” she said. “And perhaps Mr. Whitefield is preaching today! Come in with me, Charley—and George can drive dear Theo to Hampstead and back.”

Charley seemed less enthusiastic about Mr. Whitefield’s sermon and suggested I take Hetty instead. But she wouldn’t be denied. “I’ll never help you in another religious exercise as long as you live, sir,” she declared, “if you don’t come.”

And so the youth climbed down, and they entered the chapel together.

Can any moralist, mindful of my earlier promises, excuse me for leaping into the carriage and seating myself once more beside my beloved Theo? Suppose I broke my word—will he blame me much? Reverend sir, you are welcome. I broke my promise. And if you would not do the same, good friend, you are welcome to your virtue. Not that I suspect my own children will ever be so bold as to claim hearts of their own and give them freely. No, my young people, you will let papa choose for you—eat when he tells you, drink when he commands, and arrange your children’s marriages later.

Now, I know you’re eager to hear what happened when papa jumped into the landau beside poor little mamma, propped up by her pillows.

“I’m coming to your part of the story, my dear,” I said, turning to my wife as she sewed.

“To what, pray?” she asked.

“You should skip that part and go straight to the grand battles and your heroic defense of—”

“Of Fort Fiddlededee in 1778, when I pulled off Mr. Washington’s epaulet, gouged General Gates’s eye, cut off Charles Lee’s head, and pasted it back on!”

“Let us hear all about the fighting,” the boys insisted.

Even the Captain condescends to listen—though only because it’s from a militia officer.

“Fair and softly, young people!” I said. “Everything in its turn. I’m not yet at war. I’m just a young gentleman stepping into a landau beside a young lady I promised to avoid. I’m holding her hand—which, after a little hesitation, she leaves in mine. Do you remember how hot it was, how it trembled, how it beat a hundred and twenty times a minute? And as we trot toward Hampstead, I address Miss Lambert thus—”

“Ah, ah, ah!” the girls chorus, joined by Mademoiselle Eleonore, who adds, “Nous ecoutons maintenant. La parole est à vous, Monsieur le Chevalier!”

Here they all sit in a circle: mamma at her side of the fire, papa at his; Mademoiselle Eleonore (at whom the Captain glances rather sweetly—eyes off, Captain!), the two girls listening like nymphs to Apollo, and John and Tummas (with dull ears) bringing in tea trays and urns.

“Very good,” says the Squire, pulling out the manuscript and waving it. “We’re about to reveal your mother’s secrets—and mine.”

“I’m sure you may, papa,” cries the house matron. “There’s nothing to be ashamed of.” A blush rises across her kind face.

“But before I begin, young folks, allow me a few questions.”

“Allons, toujours des questions!” Mademoiselle sighs, shrugging her pretty shoulders. (Florac recommended her to us, and I suspect the little Chevalier has a soft spot for this lovely Mademoiselle de Blois.)

To the questions, then.

You, Captain Miles Warrington, have the honour of winning the favour of a lady—or perhaps many ladies—let us say, the Duchess of Devonshire, Mrs. Crew, Mrs. Fitzherbert, the Queen of Prussia, the Goddess Venus herself, or Mademoiselle Hillisberg of the Opera. Never mind whom, in truth. But if you do win a lady’s good graces, do you always rush to the mess and boast of it?

“Not such a fool, Squire!” replies the Captain, adjusting his side curl in the mirror. “Have you, Miss Theo, told your mother every word you whispered to Mr. Joe Blake, junior, in the shrubbery this morning?”

“Joe Blake, indeed!” cries Theo junior, scandalized.

“And you, mademoiselle?” he continues, turning to her with a twinkle. “That scented letter which arrived under Sir Thomas’s frank—have you revealed all its contents? Look at her blush! As red as the curtain, I swear! No, mademoiselle—we all keep our secrets,” says the Squire, bowing with exaggerated grace. “No, Theo, there was nothing in the shrubbery—only nuts, my dear child!
