No, Miles, my son, we don’t tell all—even to the most indulgent of fathers—and if I ever reveal what passed between us in a landau on the Hampstead Road on the 25th of May, 1760, may the Chevalier Ruspini pull out every tooth in my head!”

“Pray tell, papa!” cries mamma. “Or, since Jobson, who drove us, is now in your service, perhaps you’ll summon him from the stables! I insist upon knowing!”

“What is this mystery?” asks mademoiselle, in her delicate French accent, turning to my wife.

“Eh, ma fille!” whispers the lady. “Thou wouldst ask me what I said? I said ‘Yes!’—and that is all.”

So it is my wife who has betrayed me, not I; and that was the sum of our conversation as the carriage—far too swiftly, as I thought—galloped toward Hampstead and returned.

Theo had not consented to defy her parents—not at all. But she would marry no other man, not even if she lived to be as old as Methuselah, not even the Prince of Wales himself. Her heart had been given away—with her father’s approval, nay, his command—it was no longer hers to reclaim. A kind father must relent one day; and if George kept his promise—now, in twenty years, or in another world—she knew she would never break hers.

Hetty’s face lit up with joy when, after my brief meeting with Theo, she saw her sister’s serene expression. All the doctor’s medicines had done her no such good, the devoted sister declared. The girls returned home after their act of quiet disobedience. I gave up the seat I had occupied during my brief happiness beside my dear invalid. Hetty skipped back into her place, and Charley climbed onto his box. He later confessed that he had heard a very dull sermon. The little fellow was too devout to appreciate dissenting preachers.

Hetty was not alone in noticing her sister’s changed countenance and renewed spirits. On their return, their mother embraced both girls—especially the invalid—with greater warmth than usual. “There’s nothing like a country ride,” Aunt Lambert remarked, “to restore dear Theo’s health. She went to Hampstead, did she? Then she must go again tomorrow. Heaven bless us, Lord Wrotham’s horses are at our disposal three or four times a week—why, the sweet child might enjoy them daily!”

As for the idea that Mr. Warrington might have met the girls on their drive, Aunt Lambert never once entertained it—at least, never mentioned it. Let those interested guess whether she could possibly have imagined her daughter and her lover would ever meet again.

Do women help each other in matters of love? Do they scheme, whisper, devise little plans, tell small lies, arrange secret meetings, hang up rope ladders, coax, wheedle, mislead guardians or servants, and turn their backs while Strephon and Chloe embrace in twilight, or flee in a postchaise to Gretna Green?

My dear young friends, yes—there are some who do. And some gentle souls, who once loved deeply and truly, continue to show kindness and tenderness toward younger lovers playing the same tender game. Miss Prim does not. If she hears of two young people in love, she either mocks them as fools or imagines the worst about them. Because she bears a burden herself, she seeks to wound others. I suspect she’d throw a stone at a pair of turtles cooing in a wood rather than watch them. But I speak of your grandmother, Aunt Lambert—a woman whose heart was a great syllabub of human kindness. And as for the matter at hand, how can I possibly know whether she suspected anything?

All she said to Theo upon her return was: “My child, the country air has done you immense good. I hope you’ll take another ride tomorrow—and another, and another.”

“Don’t you think, papa,” Aunt Lambert asked the General when he came in for supper, “that the ride has done the child wonderful good? Shouldn’t she be encouraged to go out in the fresh air?”

“Yes, indeed,” said Lambert. “If a coach-and-six will benefit my little Theo, she shall have it. Or I’ll drag the landau up Hampstead Hill myself, if no horses are available.” He would have spent his guineas, his breath, his very blood, to give his child pleasure. He was enchanted by his daughter’s improved appearance—she ate a bit of chicken with appetite, drank a little negus he made for her. It seemed better than any medicine the kind doctor had prescribed, which, God knows, had done little good.

Mamma was radiant. Hetty was bright and cheerful. It felt like an evening at Oakhurst. Not in months—certainly not since that terrible, cruel day no one spoke of—had they enjoyed such a night.

Yet though the other women might coax and flatter, Theo herself was too honest to sustain the illusion for long. When the General returned to the topic of her recovery—“What has done it? The country air? The Jesuit’s bark? The new medicine?”—she placed a trembling hand on his, eyes wide and clear.

“Can’t you guess, dear?” she asked softly. “It’s because I’ve seen him again, papa.”

The two women turned pale. Theo’s own heart began to race, her cheeks grew white as she stared into her father’s stricken face.

“It wasn’t wrong to see him,” she continued quickly. “It would have been wrong not to tell you.”

“Great God!” groaned the father, pulling his hand back, his face twisted with anguish. Hetty rushed to her sister, clutching her tightly. “Theo knew nothing of it, sir! It was all my doing—I planned it!”

Theo collapsed onto her sister’s shoulder, kissing her neck over and over.

“Women, women!” cried the father, breaking into a fierce cry. “Are you mocking my honour?”

Aunt Lambert sobbed wildly. “Martin! Martin! Don’t say a word to her!”

But Hetty staggered backward, fainting against the wall, for Theo had fainted into her arms.

I was taking breakfast the next morning when my door opened, and my faithful servant announced, “General Lambert.”

At once I saw the storm in his face—he knew everything.

“Your accomplices did not confess,” he said as soon as we were alone. “They sided with you against their father—a proof of how desirable clandestine meetings are. I learned it from Theo herself—she admitted she had seen you.”

“Accomplices, sir?” I replied, perhaps eager to divert attention. “You know how deeply and dutifully your children regard you. If they oppose you now, it is because justice is on their side. A man like you cannot expect *sic volo sic jubeo* to be the only law in his household.”

“Psha, George!” he exclaimed. “Though we are parted, God forbid I should wish our friendship ended. I had your promise not to seek her.”

“I did not go to her, sir,” I said, feeling my face grow warm. For though it was true, it was also untrue.

“You mean she came to you?” he asked, agitated. “Is it behind Hester’s petticoat you hide? What a fine defence for a gentleman!”

“Well, I won’t shelter behind the poor child,” I replied. “To deny it was an attempt to evade the truth—one I am unaccustomed to making. I did not break the letter of my agreement—but I broke its spirit. From this moment, I annul it entirely.”

“You break your word to me!” he shouted.

“I recall a hasty promise made in a moment of extreme emotion and distress. No man should be bound forever by words spoken under such circumstances. And more—no man of honour or humanity, Mr. Lambert, would try to bind another so.”

“Dishonour to me, sir!” he thundered.

“If the word is to be tossed between us,” I retorted hotly, “then let it be. There can be no question of love, age, or difference when that word is used. Were you my own father—and I love you more than a father, Uncle Lambert—I would not endure it! What have I done? I have seen the woman I consider my wife before God and man. If she calls me, I will come. If she comes to me, here is my home and half of what I possess. You have no right—having given me the gift—to reclaim it. Because my mother unjustly taunts you, are you to punish this tender, innocent girl? You claim to love her, yet you cannot bear a wounded pride for her sake. Better she perish in misery than an old woman in Virginia accuse you of scheming to marry one of your daughters. Say that to satisfy what you call honour—and I call selfishness—we part, we break our hearts, we rally, we try to forget—can any man be to me what she is? Can any woman be to me what she is? You may marry her to the Prince of Wales tomorrow—it would be cowardice and treason. How can we undo the promises we made before Heaven? You may separate us—but she will die as surely as Jephthah’s daughter. Have you sworn to Heaven to murder her? Kill her if you believe your promise binds you. But this I swear: I am glad you came, so I might formally cancel a hasty pledge, and declare that whenever she calls, I will come to her!”

No doubt I spoke with the heat and passion of youth, convinced death awaited us both if we were torn apart. Who does not believe his first love eternal?

Now, having watched the world, seen passions rise and fade—alas, I must say it—I smile at my own youthful fervours. Yet if it is a superstition, I prefer to hold it. I would rather believe neither of us could live with another, that Heaven itself ordained these two souls to be joined.

“We must come to what I had hoped to avoid,” the General said, in reply. “An unfriendly separation. When I meet you, Mr. Warrington, I must know you no more. I shall order—my family and children will obey—never to acknowledge you. Since you refuse to show me the respect due to my age, the courtesy of gentlemen, I must treat you as an enemy. An enemy to my home’s peace, my children’s honour! And so I shall deal with you when you molest me.”

He waved his hand, put on his hat, and left abruptly.

I stood stunned. War, I thought, had begun. The fleeting joy of yesterday was gone, replaced by deeper sorrow—the agony of parting now mingled with the bitterness of quarrel. I was not only alone but friendless.

In a year of close companionship, I had come to revere and love Lambert as I had never loved any man except Harry. To see his face turned from me in anger was like losing the sun. Darkness surrounded me.

Yet I knew I had acted rightly in retracting my promise. My loyalty to Theo—hers to me—was above all duty or obedience. Ceremony or none, I was hers, first and foremost. Promises made before Heaven could not be undone by any parent. Even all the priests in Christendom could only confirm what we had already sealed in silence.

I met Jack Lambert by chance that day, walking toward the library of the new Museum. Overcome by grief, I pulled him aside, led him through the gardens, and poured out my story.

I didn’t care much for Jack—truthfully, he was somewhat pompous, fond of Latin quotes, and wearisome—but in my sorrow, I clung to him. Having suffered himself in his affair with the American girl, he understood pain. He listened sympathetically.

I told him of my meeting with Theo, my confrontation with her father, my resolve never to part from her.

When I saw he leaned toward my side—quoting Greek and Latin authors—I thought him wise, clung to him fiercely, and showered him with affection he rarely received from me.

We walked to his father’s lodgings in Dean Street. I watched him enter, gazed at the house with longing, hoping to glimpse Theo within. At the coffee-house where I waited, I ordered a bottle of wine—Jack’s Coffee-House, as it was called—and then another.

I called him Brother when he left. I clung to him like a condemned man to a jailer or parson.

I drank a whole bottle, then another. I feared Jack would never return.

He finally appeared, looking startled. He poured himself several bumpers from my second bottle and began his tale—most interesting to me.

My poor Theo, he said, was confined to her room, deeply agitated. He returned just in time for dinner. Afterward, his father spoke freely, relieved to have his eldest son present and Theodosia absent.

The General recounted our conversation. He silenced Hester, who sat dumb as a mouse. He chided Aunt Lambert for her handkerchief drama and cursed the women—“pimps,” he called them—for aiding each other.

Then he turned to Jack: “What is your view?”

To everyone’s surprise, Jack defended me.

Citing ancient authorities (which I didn’t catch), he argued the matter was beyond parental control. Once consent was given, the elders had stepped outside the realm. Though he didn’t agree with the sacramental views of marriage held by many divines, he believed it even more sacred—binding before Heaven, regardless of ceremony.

“It is not merely,” Jack said, turning to his father, “those whom I, John Lambert, Priest, have joined, let no man put asunder. It is those whom God has joined—let no man separate.”

(Here he removed his hat, as he told me.)

“My views are clear,” he continued. “And surely these young people were joined—or permitted to plight themselves—by your consent. My views are clear. I shall lay them out in a series of discourses, no doubt satisfying you.”

On hearing this, the General said, “I am satisfied already, my dear boy.”

And Hetty whispered, “Jack, mother and I will make you a dozen shirts, as sure as eggs is eggs.”

“While we talked,” the General resumed, “Theodosia appeared—pale, agitated. She kissed me, sat beside me, and took a sippet of toast, dipping it in my negus.”

“You should have been here to hear Jack’s sermon!” said Hester.

“Has he?” asked Theodosia, too weak to care.

“He has preached for three quarters of an hour by Shrewsbury clock,” said the General—though Jack insisted it was far shorter.

“And his discourse has been you, my dear,” said papa, playing with her hand.

“Me, papa?”

“You and—Mr. Warrington—and—George, my love.”

At this, Theodosia leaned closer, laid her head on his shoulder, and wept.

“This is different, sir,” said Jack, “from a passage I remember in Pausanias.”

“In Pausanias? Indeed!” said the General. “Who was he?”

I smiled at my father’s ignorance before his children.

“When Ulysses took Penelope from her father,” I explained, “the king pursued them, begging his daughter to return. Ulysses offered her a choice—return or go with him. She covered her face with her veil. For lack of a veil, my sister has taken refuge in your waistcoat, sir.”

We all laughed—though my mother vowed she would have returned home with her father if such a choice had been offered.

“But I am not a girl of spirit, dear mother!” said Theodosia, still resting in her father’s lap.

I don’t recall such affection being common in my youth, Jack added.

After more talk, he remembered me and left his parents pleading with Theodosia to return to bed. The events had weakened her greatly.

“I’ve experienced,” he said, “how full of anxiety and fear this passion is. It racks the soul. I have no doubt it harms health when carried too far—especially among women who lack philosophy.”

He bowed and said, “My service to you, brother.”

From grief to hope—how swift the change! Joy flooded my soul. Landlord, more port! I would have drunk a cask if Jack had asked. His sympathy was vast, generous all day. I refused to tally the bottles. Let the waiters’ calculations stand.

Jack was my dearest, best brother. I swore my friendship would last forever. If I could serve him—were it a bishopric—by George, he should have it.

I awoke the next morning with a splitting headache, yet joyfully, rapturously. I did not yet grasp the full extent of my happiness—or the transformation of my noble enemy from the previous day.

It must have been painful for an older man to yield to arguments so undutiful. But the true Christian gentleman, wounded by my harshness and moved by his daughter’s suffering, withdrew thoughtfully. Later, he went to church—his private sanctuary—and knelt in prayer.

There, submitting his case to the divine guidance he often sought, it seemed to him that his daughter was right—fidelity to me was just—and he was wrong to demand blind submission.

Thus Jack’s cause was won before he began. The brave, gentle heart—unable to bear pain, unwilling to assert authority—was only too eager to return to love and affection.

Years later, while going through old papers at home, I came upon a letter sealed and labeled in my mother’s familiar hand: “From London, April, 1760. My son’s dreadful letter.” When it became mine, I burned it—no family record should preserve the tale of that domestic sorrow and rupture for future Warringtons to read, or disobedient sons to cite as precedent. For the same reason, I destroyed the reply she sent me during that time of anger, defiance, and unrest.

Consumed by the agony of separation from my beloved, and justifiably blaming Mrs. Esmond for the deepest pain I had ever known, I wrote to Virginia a letter that might have been more measured—but in which I strove to maintain decorum and restraint. I did not know what motives had driven her, but I held her accountable for the ruin of my life, which she had chosen to shatter with her own hand. She had torn apart my union with a virtuous, innocent young woman whose hopes, health, and joy were now forever crushed by her interference. The deed was done, as I feared, and I would say no more about the doer—she stood before God alone. Yet I could not hide from my mother the depth of the injury she had inflicted: so great and fatal that neither her life nor mine could undo it. My allegiance to her was broken; I could never again be the dutiful, respectful son I once was.

Madam Esmond answered with a letter of remarkable dignity—her writing always elegant, refined, and precise. She uttered no reproach, no harsh word. Coldly, she informed me that she had laid our dispute before the tribunal of God, seeking His guidance. As a mother, she said, she was ready, in humble submission, to face divine judgment. Might I, as a son, be equally prepared to answer for myself when the Great Judge called? Would I be able to prove that I had honored my father and mother, as the law demanded? O popoi! My grandfather quoted a line of Homer in his memoir—how in every trial, we summon the gods to witness our suffering. When pride, greed, ambition, or desire to rule over others takes hold, how often do we cry out to Heaven, demanding justice on our side? In our great American conflict, both sides appealed to the skies, sang Te Deum at victory, and declared with confidence that right must prevail. Was America right because she won? Then was Poland wrong because she lost? How have I strayed into this digression about Poland, America, and all manner of things—while all the while thinking of a small woman now gone, who turned to Heaven and cited its own scriptures, as if to challenge the Almighty itself, because her son wished to marry whom she disapproved?

We appeal, we curse, we kneel, we beg for blessings, we demand judgment—yet the world moves forward. We struggle, rage, weep, reconcile, race, win, lose, pass away, and new strugglers take our place. Our days end; night falls; morning dawns, but shines no more upon us.

I showed my letter—declaring my rebellion and refusal to obey—to Mr. Lambert, in duplicate. I wanted him to understand my position, and my resolve: whatever threats or quarrels the future might bring, I would never regard my separation from Theo as anything but forced. Whenever I could see her again, I would. My promise to her was eternal—*in secula seculorum*, or at least as long as I lived. I implied that she, too, was bound to me, and her poor father knew it well. He might separate us—as he might give her poison, and she, gentle and obedient, would take it and die—but the death or division would be his doing. Let him bear the guilt. He was tender-hearted, almost weak in his affection for his children, especially her. He could not bring himself to inflict such torment. We had tried to part—we could not. He had attempted to keep us apart—it was beyond his power. The bars were raised, yet the young couple—the maid within, the knight without—still loved each other. The wall was built, but Pyramus and Thisbe whispered across it. Even amid his grief and confusion, Uncle Lambert had a sense of humor. He could not help seeing how absurd his role had become. Light began to pierce through the plaster and lime of that wall—the lovers’ hands reached through, then their heads—indeed, the wall's best course was to step aside.

I do not recall the events day by day, nor does it matter much for posterity. When my descendants face their own love troubles, they will find their own way out. I believe I did not return to Dean Street. Instead, driving in open air was considered good for Miss Lambert’s health. I acquired a fine horse and rode beside her carriage. The old woman at Tottenham Court grew quite familiar with us, nodding and winking as we passed. I suspect she had seen many such pairs before and welcomed them into her cottage with quiet kindness.

Doctor Heberden and the country air worked wonders on Miss Lambert. Hetty remained her constant companion, and sometimes, on holidays, Master Charley rode my horse while I took the carriage. How much love-making did Hetty hear—and with what admirable patience she listened! I don’t say she stopped attending Methodist sermons, but when we had a closed carriage, she kindly looked out the window. And then there were the letters—countless ones—running back and forth! Gumbo’s legs were always in motion between my lodgings and Dean Street; and Mrs. Molly, the girl’s maid, was constantly shuttling messages from Bloomsbury. By autumn, when the leaves turned pale, Miss Theo’s cheeks were rosy again, and Doctor Heberden pronounced her fully restored. What else occurred during this blessed time? Mr. Warrington completed his great tragedy *Pocahontas*, which this time was accepted by Mr. Garrick (Dr. Johnson having spoken favorably of it), and my cousin Hagan was cast as Captain Smith. Hagan’s engagement was made only when needed. I had helped him and his family financially—perhaps beyond my means, especially given my feud with Madam Esmond. Her reply to my angry letter of April reached me in autumn, written from Virginia—war for war, control for control. But these threats frightened me little. My mother’s thunder could not reach me. My conscience—or my casuistry—offered alternative interpretations of her scriptural texts, so her words carried no weight against my purpose. I told no one—neither maternal nor paternal kin—about my new love. Why argue with them? It was better to live in the moment, savoring sweet joys, and let the critics grumble or the elders advise at their leisure.

Besides Madam Esmond, in my fury, I wrote scathing notes to Uncle Warrington, Aunt Madame de Bernstein, and my Lord or Lady of Castlewood (I forget which), thanking them for spoiling the greatest happiness of my life, and promising them equal gratitude from their devoted relative. Business brought the jovial Baronet and his family to London earlier than usual. Madame de Bernstein was never sorry to return to Clarges Street and her cards. I saw them. They found me well. They assumed the match was off—I chose not to correct them. The Baroness, heartened by my cheerfulness, made many sly jokes about my philosophy and worldly wisdom. She remained determined to find me a rich match—and I fear I paid many compliments to a wealthy young daughter of a soap-boiler from Mile End, whom she wished to place in my arms.

“You court her with infinite wit and esprit, my dear,” she said, pleased. “But she understands half of what you say, and the other half frightens her. This tone of persiflage is fine among us, but spare it, my dear nephew, among these common folk.”

Miss Badge married a gentleman of royal blood, though reduced fortune, from a neighboring island. I trust Mrs. Mackshane has forgiven my jests. There was another at my aunt’s house who understood my banter no better—this was an elderly lady who had lived through James II’s reign and remained as worldly as ever under King George. I loved her company. But since my children may read this, I cannot tell a hundred tales of the great figures she knew—George I and his ladies, St. John and Marlborough, the reigning king and the late Prince of Wales, and their quarrel—but my modest muse sings only for boys and virgins. Son Miles cares not for court gossip, or if he does, he has fresh news from Carlton House, just as scandalous. No, my dear wife, you need not shake your powdered locks at me! Papa will not disgrace the nursery with ancient scandals, nor bring shame to our chaste bread-and-butter.

Yet one story I cannot omit. My aunt told it with great relish—for, to do her justice, she despised pretentious virtue and delighted in mocking the self-righteous. In her later years, she wore no mask. And in that, she was better than some whitewashed saints. To the tale. My Lady Warrington, one of the tallest and most pious women of her time—always speaking of goodness and “Heaven in her eye” like the heroine in Addison’s tedious play (which still survives on stage, unlike others)—had the world in her other eye, and a sharp desire to rise in it. When my marriage with you seemed broken off, what did she do but try the very arts she’d used on poor Harry—with similar failure—and fail again with me? It was not Beauty—Miss Flora was already claimed by my master—(and what a master! I bow in awe at such noble connections!)—it was Dora, the Muse, who was set to languish for me, pity me, read my “godless” tragedy, applaud me, console me. Meanwhile, what of Beauty? Can it be believed that my stern aunt gave a grand entertainment for my Lady Yarmouth, presented her boy to her, and placed little Miles under her protection? That much is certain. But could it be that she sent her daughter to stay at my lady’s house, which our gracious lord visited daily, with the aims old Aunt Bernstein attributed to her? “Had it not been for that apoplectic fit,” Bernstein said, “your aunt meant to make a Countess of her own blood in the Warrington family!” [Compare Walpole’s letters in Mr. Cunningham’s edition. See the supper at N. House, showing what noblemen would do for a king’s mistress, and the amusing account of waiting for the Prince of Wales before Holland House.—EDITOR.] My neighbor and kinswoman, my Lady Claypole, is dead and buried. Grow white, ye daisies, upon Flora’s tomb! I can see my little Miles, in a bright uniform of the Norfolk Militia, led by his parent to the lady the King delighted to honor, and the kind old Jezebel placing her hand upon his curly head. I am accused of being a lukewarm royalist; but surely I can compare those times with ours, and acknowledge the difference between the late sovereign and the present—one born a Briton, who has set an example of decency and virtue for every family in the empire. [The Warrington MS. is dated 1793.—ED.]

Thus my life flowed in the sweetest occupation. Happy myself, I could afford to forgive those who, after all, had done me no real harm—only added spice to my joy by briefly blocking my path. No firm plans were made, but Theo and I knew a day would come when we would never say farewell again. Whether it came in a year or ten, we were ready to wait. Day after day, we discussed our dreams, with Hetty as confidante. On our drives, we spied cottages we thought suitable for young people of modest means, devised economies, and dreamed of simple joys. We were Strephon and Chloe, indeed. A cottage and a brown loaf would satisfy us! Gumbo and Molly would serve us—as they have done ever since. At twenty, who fears poverty? Our trials would only strengthen our bond. The “sweet sorrow” of each parting made the next meeting sweeter. And when we parted, we rushed home to write those precious letters—written by young men and women in such circumstances. Though my wife keeps them all in a tin sugar-box in her bedroom, and I confess I once glanced at them, even finding some charming—I hereby charge my heirs and executors to burn them unread at our deaths. Especially I instruct my son the Captain (who, I know, finds reading manuscripts unpleasant) to carry out this duty. Those secrets whispered to the penny-post, or exchanged between Molly and Gumbo, were meant for us alone. No descendant shall overhear them.

We received brief letters telling us how our dear Harry continued in the army, serving as aide-de-camp to General Amherst after the death of his own illustrious commander. By mid-October, news arrived of the Capitulation of Montreal and the fall of Canada. Hal added a postscript: he would request leave and visit the old lady at home, who wrote as sourly as a bare-headed captain, as Warrington noted. I guessed why—though her claws could not reach me. I had written thoroughly to my brother about my affairs in England.

Then, on October 25th, came the news: His Majesty had died suddenly at Kensington, and George III now reigned. We grieved little. What do hearts tuned to love care for the Atridae? A modest, handsome, brave new prince—we gladly accepted the common belief that he possessed every virtue, and joined the loyal crowd in hailing his accession. It mattered little to us, as we thought, two young sweethearts whispering love stories in our corner.

But who knows how great events affect individuals? Did not our little Charley, at the Chartreux, wish impiously for a new king—because on the new monarch’s accession, Doctor Crusius granted his boys a holiday? He, I, Hetty, and Theo (now strong enough to walk many miles) heard the heralds proclaim the new king before Savile House in Leicester Fields. A pickpocket stole a gentleman’s watch and chain nearby, was caught, and taken to Bridewell—all due to the king’s accession. Had the king not died, the gentleman wouldn’t have been in the crowd; the chain wouldn’t have been stolen; the thief wouldn’t have been caught and whipped. In this way, many of us, more or less indirectly, were touched by the great change, and even we humble souls felt its ripple.

For instance, my Lord Wrotham, a close friend of the Savile House family, admired Martin Lambert deeply—calling him one of the finest gentlemen in the world. And my Lord Bute, newly powerful with the king, eager to reward merit, was strongly inclined toward Mr. Lambert thanks to Wrotham’s influence.

Parson Sampson, my old friend (and Harry’s), who had been in and out of jail countless times lately, harbored enduring hatred for the Esmonds of Castlewood but lasting affection for me and my brother, was staying in Hal’s room at my lodgings (hunted from his own by bailiffs). I liked having him near—a more entertaining Jack-friar never walked in cassock. He also shared my rhapsodies about Miss Theo, never tired (so he swore) of hearing me speak of her, admired *Pocahontas* and *Carpezan* with honest passion, and could recite passages with such force that Barry or cousin Hagan couldn’t surpass him. Sampson served as go-between for Lady Maria and her relatives who hadn’t disowned her. Always in debt, he was happiest drinking ale or sharing tears with friends in similar straits. His knowledge of pawnbrokers’ shops was vast—he claimed he could get more money on an item than any man in his profession. He never paid his debts, but readily forgave others’. Poor as he was, he always found ways to help his sister. A more generous, kind, amiable rogue never grinned behind bars. Some say I enjoy parasites around me. I admit I greatly liked Sampson and valued him more than many better men.

When he heard Lord Bute entered the cabinet, Sampson vowed he must appoint me to a post worthy of my birth and merit. He insisted I attend his levee. I refused? The Esmonds were proud as Lucifer; and my lineage was as noble as any in Europe. Demmy! Where was Bute when the Esmonds ruled counties, fought wars, and went on Crusades? Where were they? Beggarly Scots, barely clothed—by George! tearing raw fish in their islands. But now the times had changed. The Scots were in luck. Mum’s the word! “I don’t envy him,” Sampson said, “but he shall provide for you and my dearest, noblest, heroic captain! He SHALL, by George!” he’d roar. When the king ordered *Richard III* at Drury Lane, my chaplain cursed, swore, but insisted we go to Covent Garden to see *Carpezan* too.

One morning, he burst into my room, where I lay late, waving the newspaper and shouting “Huzza!” with all his might.

“What is it, Sampson?” I asked.

“Not your brother’s promotion—though he’ll get it soon enough. But someone else’s! Huzzay! His Majesty has appointed Major-General Martin Lambert Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Jamaica!”

I leapt up. News indeed! Mr. Lambert would go to his government. Who would go with him? I had supped with young gentlemen at the Cocoa-Tree. Gumbo had a note from my dear mistress the night before, delivering the same news, but delayed delivery. Theo begged me to meet her at the old place at noon the next day—without fail. [In the Warrington MS., nothing is said of what the “old place” was. Perhaps a reader of Notes and Queries can enlighten us, and who Mrs. Goodison was.—ED.]

There was no little alarm when we reached our meeting place. Papa had accepted the appointment and would depart soon. A frigate would be provided, and his family would accompany him. Merciful powers! Were we to be parted? Theo’s pallor returned. Aunt Lambert feared she would faint. One of Mrs. Goodison’s girls ran with a bottle of salts from the workroom. “Going away? Going in a frigate, Aunt Lambert? Taking her from me? Great God! Aunt Lambert, I shall die!” She improved when mamma came up with the salts. You see, the women met me—knowing Theo’s delicate state, how could they not feel for her? But the General was too busy with levees, ministers, and settling affairs to learn of our walks. Even when orders were issued for the ladies’ outfits, Mrs. Goodison—once a seamstress to Miss Molly Benson, who remembered Miss Esmond of Virginia perfectly—“even when the order was placed for three ladies,” she said demurely, “I thought I could do no harm in completing it.”

Need I say how agitated Mr. Warrington was returning to his lodgings that evening? No more walks, no rides to dear Hampstead or Islington, no more letters carried by Gumbo and Molly! Gumbo wept so profusely that I was moved by his loyalty and gave him a crown-piece to share supper with the girl—turns out she was his sweetheart. What, you too, unhappy Gumbo, torn from the maid you love? I was ready to shed tears with him.

We, who had played our parts in the morning’s secret drama, felt a deep and bitter guilt when we saw how deeply it had wounded the man we loved and revered most. The blow we had dealt—though not meant in malice—had struck him with a force that left us trembling with remorse. His beloved daughter had deceived him; his entire family had turned against him in silent conspiracy. Oh, dear friend and father! We know now—though then we could not see—that you forgave us, even as you stood among the pure spirits of heaven, where love and mercy are the only laws. For you, forgiveness was natural, as easy as breathing. To wound you was to strike at innocence itself, to lash a child or harm one who nurtured others. And so, after the deed was done, we all knelt in shame before the man we had wronged.

I will not linger on the scenes of reconciliation, of prayer together, of quiet farewell as he departed for his government, the ship sailing away beneath a sky still heavy with sorrow. We stood upon the shore, hand in hand, silent, abashed, guilty beyond words. My wife did not come to me until he was gone. Between the wedding ceremony and his departure, she stayed at home, by her father’s side, sharing her sister’s bed. He remained kind as ever, but the women—my aunt Lambert especially—were cold, restless, unkind. Little Hetty, feverish and distant, whispered over and over, “I wish we were gone. I wish we were gone.”

Though forgiven, I kept myself apart during those last days. I saw my wife only briefly, in passing, never truly hers until the ship had vanished from sight. Then we went to Winchester and Hampton for what might be called our honeymoon. It was not joyous, but rather a quiet retreat, haunted by absence. For a time, we felt utterly alone, as though we had buried our father—or driven him into exile through our disobedience.

I sent Sampson to announce our marriage in the papers. (My wife later told me she blushed every time she saw him.) I brought Mrs. Warrington back to my old lodgings in Bloomsbury, where space was generous and life modest. There, our married life began.

I wrote to my mother in Virginia, telling her nothing of the turmoil, only that Mr. Lambert was departing for his post abroad, and that I felt bound by honor to fulfill my promise to his daughter. I added that I intended to complete my legal studies, qualify for the Bar, and eventually serve in Virginia or another colony. My good Mrs. Mountain replied, at Madam Esmond’s request, saying that for peace’s sake, correspondence should pass through her.

When I returned to London, I found my relatives in a fury—amusing, indeed, to watch. At my uncle’s house in Hill Street, the butler’s face when he said, “Not at home,” was a mask of icy disdain—worthy of Garrick in *Macbeth*. My little wife walked beside me, laughing at the fellow’s stiff welcome, when suddenly we met Lady Warrington in her carriage, stopped in the street.

I doffed my hat and bowed low. “I affectionately ask after my dear cousins,” I said.

“Do you dare look me in the face?” she gasped.

“Nay, don’t deprive me of that precious privilege!” I replied. “Move on, Peter,” she screamed to her coachman.

“You would not impale your own husband’s flesh and blood,” I said gently.

She slammed up the window of her chair in rage. I kissed my hand and bowed again—my finest bow yet.

Later, walking in Hyde Park, I met my cousin Miles riding with a groom behind him. As soon as he saw us, he galloped forward, the groom shouting, “Stop, Master Miles, stop!”

“I’m not to speak to my cousin,” said Miles, “but sending love to Harry isn’t speaking, is it? Is that my new cousin? I’m Miles, son of Sir Miles Warrington, and you’re very pretty!”

“Now, duee now, Master Miles,” said the groom, touching his hat. The boy trotted off, laughing, glancing back at us.

“You see how they treat me,” I said to Theo.

“As if you married me for their sake!” she answered, her eyes bright with love.

Ah, how happy we were! How brisk and warm the winter seemed! How cozy the kettle by the fire—where the abashed Sampson sometimes came to make punch—and how delightful the nights at the theatre, where friends gave us tickets, and we waited each day for our new play, *Pocahontas*, to outshine all past tragedies.

The fickle old aunt in Clarges Street, who had scorned me on my first arrival with my wife, soon softened. Once she met Theo—whom she’d once called a plain country girl—she fell instantly in love with her. She invited us daily to tea and supper when no other guests came. “As for company,” she would say, “I don’t ask you. You’re no longer *du monde*. Your marriage has put that entirely out of the question.” So she welcomed us as entertainment, letting us enter by the back stairs.

My wife took it all in good humor. And truthfully, I must say that her servants treated us with more respect than any duke and duchess might expect. Madame de Bernstein found my tale of Lady Warrington and the chair endlessly amusing. I acted it out for her, and regaled her with stories of the pious Baronet’s lady and daughters, which delighted the lively, mischievous old woman.

The Dowager Countess of Castlewood, now settled in Kensington, offered us the polite welcome reserved for poorer relatives. We visited her once or twice at her gatherings, but quickly gave them up—losing too much at cards, spending too much on coaches. We were soon forgotten, like others swept from fashion by death, debt, or circumstance. But Theo didn’t mind at all. She had appeared once at one of these parties, wearing ornaments left by her mother—gems the old lady cherished—but I thought her bare white neck far more beautiful than any sparkle. And there were dowagers whose wrinkled faces blazed with rubies and diamonds—jewels they’d gladly trade for Theo’s simple grace.

No one spoke to her—except Beau Lothair, a friend of Mr. Will’s, who later prowled around Bloomsbury and even sent my wife a note. I met him in Covent Garden shortly after and threatened to break his face if I ever saw him near my lodgings. After that, Madam Theo was left in peace.

Only one relative came to visit: our dear Maria, with her husband, Mr. Hagan. They often shared our humble dinners. We also had friend Spencer from the Temple, who admired our quiet happiness and asked for sympathy in his own romantic disappointments. Twice or thrice, the famous Doctor Johnson dropped by for a cup of Theo’s tea.

A cup? A pailful! “And a pail the best thing to feed him, sar!” exclaimed Mr. Gumbo indignantly—for the Doctor’s appearance was not pleasant, nor his linen clean. He snorted, flushed, sputtered, flung food about, and bellowed contradictions. He annoyed Theo, whom he professed to admire, by declaring every time he saw her, “Madam, you do not love me. I see it in your manner. Though I admire you, and come here for your sake. Here is my friend Mr. Reynolds—he shall paint you. No ceruse in his box is as brilliant as your complexion.”

So Mr. Reynolds, a gentleman of perfect manners, would have painted my wife. But I knew his price and chose not to pay it. I wish I had now—for the children’s sake, to see what she looked like thirty-five years ago. To me, madam, she remains the same. And you, my lady, are always young!

What troubled Mrs. Warrington most about Dr. Johnson wasn’t his sputtering or dirty nails, but his harsh judgment of my new tragedy. Hagan once suggested he read some scenes after tea.

“Nay, sir,” said the Doctor, “conversation is better. I can read for myself or hear you at the theatre. I’d rather hear Mrs. Warrington’s artless talk than your declamation of Mr. Warrington’s decasyllables. Tell us about your household affairs, madam. Is your father well? Did you make the pudding and butter sauce? The butter sauce was delicious!” (He had preserved a large portion in the bosom of a very dingy shirt.)

“You made it as though you loved me,” he declared. “You helped me as though you loved me—though you don’t.”

“Faith, sir,” said Hagan, spiritedly, “you’re taking some of the present away with you in your waistcoat.”

“Sir, you are rude!” roared the Doctor. “You are ignorant of the first principles of politeness—courtesy before ladies. Having received an university education, I am surprised you haven’t learned such basics. I respect Mrs. Warrington. I would never insult her guests before her!”

“Then why,” said Hagan fiercely, “did you speak of my theatre?”

“Sir, you are saucy!” thundered the Doctor.

“De te fabula,” said the actor.

“I think it’s your waistcoat that’s saucy. Madam, shall I make some lemonade? My papa has sent us fresh limes. May we send some to the Temple?”

“Madam,” said the Doctor, “if they stay in your house, they’ll lose their quality and turn sweet.”

“Mr. Hagan,” he bellowed, “you are a young sauce-box! Ho! ho! It is I who have been wrong.”

“Oh, my lord, my Polidore!” cried Lady Maria, alone in my wife’s drawing-room. “‘Oh, I could hear thee talk for ever thus, Eternally admiring,--fix and gaze On those dear eyes, for every glance they send Darts through my soul, and fills my heart with rapture!’”

“You know not, my Theo,” she sighed, “what a pearl and paragon of a man my Castalio is—my Chamont, my—oh, dear me, child, what a pity it is that in your husband’s tragedy he must take the horrid name of Captain Smith!”

This tragedy was not just my literary hope—it was the foundation of my financial future. My brother’s debts paid, my mother’s drafts honored, my own expenses covered—nearly all my inheritance had been spent. This was the moment I chose to marry. I could raise money on my estate, though costly. My mother would not leave her eldest son without support, despite our quarrels. I had health, strength, wit, friends, reputation—and above all, this famous tragedy, promised by the manager to perform. I counted on its success to sustain me.

But what becomes of youth’s arithmetic? How do we reckon a hundred pounds as a fortune, a thousand as a fortune? How could I dare gamble so boldly with Fortune?

I managed to convince my dear General, who left home believing his son-in-law had at least two hundred pounds ready. He and Molly had begun life with less, and the ravens had fed them. As for the women, poverty was a romantic idea. Aunt Lambert declared it wicked to doubt God’s provision. “Was the righteous ever forsaken? Did the just ever beg bread? I know better! No, no, my dears—I won’t fear for you. Look at me and my General!”

Theo believed me—because she wished to believe.

So we began life on a capital of Five Acts and about three hundred pounds in cash.

Soon, the day of the tragedy’s premiere drew near. My friends canvassed the town to gather supporters. I am ill at begging favors from the great—but when Lord Wrotham came to London, I went with Theo to call on him. He received us kindly, out of regard for her father—though he good-naturedly wagged a finger at me (and my wife hung her head) for having stolen a march on the General. Still, he promised to help his old friend’s daughter. He hoped for success, praised the play, and secured places for himself and friends.

But that was all I had. “Mon cher,” said the Baroness, “at my age, I should bore myself to death at a tragedy—but I’ll do my best. I’ll send my people to the boxes. Case in his best black looks like a nobleman; and Brett in one of my gowns has a *faux air de moi* that is quite distinguished. Put down my name for two front boxes. Good-bye, my dear. Bonne chance!”

The Dowager Countess sent compliments (on the back of the nine of clubs), held a card party that night, and regretted she and Fanny couldn’t attend.

As for my uncle and Lady Warrington—they were out of the question. After the sedan-chair incident, asking them to Drury Lane might as well have been asking Queen Elizabeth to go to the theater.

These were all my allies—the aristocratic connections poor Sampson had bragged about. On their strength, the manager had given Mr. Hagan his engagement.

“Where was Lord Bute?” the manager snapped, taking snuff—how different from the cheerful, eager man of six months past. “Had I not promised his lordship would come?”

“Yes,” said Mr. Garrick, “and her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales, and his Majesty too.”

Poor Sampson confessed he had, in his delusion, promised the presence of these august figures.

The next day, at rehearsal, matters grew worse. The manager was furious.

“Great heavens, sir!” he shouted. “Into what a trap have you led me? Read this letter!”

It read:

I have seen his lordship and conveyed Mr. Warrington’s request that he honor *Pocahontas* with his presence. His lordship is a patron of the drama and a generous friend to the arts. But he desires me to say he cannot consider attending himself, much less invite his Gracious Master to witness a performance in which a principal role is played by an actor who has secretly married a daughter of one of His Majesty’s nobility.
—Your well-wisher,
Mr. D. Garrick, Theatre Royal, Drury Lane.

My poor Theo had a nice dinner waiting for me after rehearsal. I blamed fatigue for my pallor. I dared not tell her the dreadful news.

The English public, not being as familiar with the tale of Pocahontas as we Virginians—whose hearts still hold fond remembrance of that gentle and noble spirit—Mr. Warrington, at the urging of his friends, composed a short ballad about the Indian princess. It was printed in the magazines just days before the premiere of his tragedy. Sampson and I found this maneuver both clever and cunning.

“It’s like ground-bait, sir,” declared the enthusiastic parson, “and you’ll see the fish rise in swarms on the great day!” He and Spencer swore the poem had been widely discussed and praised in several coffeehouses, even credited to Mr. Mason, Mr. Cowper of the Temple, and—most absurdly—to the famed Mr. Gray. I suspect poor Sam himself spread these rumors; had Shakespeare been named as the author of the play, he would have declared *Pocahontas* one of the Bard’s finest works.

I first met Captain John Smith as a boy, reading his adventures in my grandfather’s library. There, perched on his knee, I’d pore over the pages of my favorite volume, tracing the bold exploits of our Virginian hero. I loved every tale: his travels, his imprisonments, his escapes—not only across America but through Europe. Now, standing before the shelves in England, I pull down that same book, and instantly, memories flood back—the scent of old paper, the warmth of the hearth, the sound of my grandfather’s voice painting scenes for me: Smith battling Turks on the Danube, led into death by savage Indians. Ah, what a fierce fight it was when he faced three Turkish champions! And how I thrilled at the story of his duel with Bonny Molgro—the last and most fearsome of them all! What a name! What a figure: a monstrous turban, a scimitar flashing, whiskers bristling! After slaying two foes and severing their heads, Smith met Bonny Molgro in combat. The book describes it thus: “They fell to with their battle-axes, whose piercing bills made sometimes the one, sometimes the other, scarce able to keep their saddles. Especially the Christian received such a wound that he lost his axe, whereat the supposed conquering Turk gave a great shout from the ramparts. Yet, by the readiness of his horse and his great judgment, he not only avoided the Turk’s blows but, drawing his falchion, pierced him under the cutlets, through back and body, so that though he alighted from his horse, he stood not long ere he lost his head, as the rest had done. For this deed, Duke Segismundus granted him three Turk’s heads on a shield for arms and three hundred ducats yearly as a pension.”

In my play, I dared to transplant these heroic deeds to the banks of the Potomac and James River, defying time and place—privileges, after all, granted to poets. My “ground-bait” verses went like this:

> Wearied arm and broken sword
> Wage in vain the desperate fight—
> Round him press the countless horde,
> He is but a single knight.
> Hark! a cry of triumph shrill
> Through the wilderness resounds,
> As, with twenty bleeding wounds,
> Sinks the warrior, fighting still.
>
> Now they heap the fatal pyre,
> And the torch of death they light—
> Ah! 'tis hard to die of fire!
> Who will shield the captive knight?
> Round the stake with fiendish cry
> Wheel and dance the savage crowd,
> Cold the victim's mien and proud,
> And his breast is bared to die.
>
> Who will shield the fearless heart?
> Who avert the murderous blade?
> From the throng, with sudden start,
> See, there springs an Indian maid!
> Quick she stands before the knight,
> "Loose the chain, unbind the ring,
> I am daughter of the king,
> And I claim the Indian right!"
>
> Dauntlessly aside she flings
> Lifted axe and thirsty knife;
> Fondly to his heart she clings,
> And her bosom guards his life!
> In the woods of Powhattan,
> Still 'tis told, by Indian fires,
> How a daughter of their sires
> Saved the captive Englishman.

I need not detail the plot further—my children may find it any day upon the shelves. Nor shall I rush to read it aloud again, especially since Captain Miles and the parson both dozed off last Christmas when I recited a few acts at mamma’s request. But anyone familiar with drama or fiction can easily imagine the scene from this sketch: an Indian king, a devoted princess, her attendant secretly in love with the English captain’s servant, a traitor within the fort, a brave warrior pining for Pocahontas, a treacherous medicine-man and priest (played superbly by Palmer), capable of every crime, determined to see the English prisoner tortured and slain—all set against the wilds, war-dances, and cries (which Gumbo mimicked perfectly from memory), culminating in the arrival of the English fleet, echoing recent victories in Canada, and affirming Britain’s eternal destiny to rule in America. Some of us believed these elements might well ensure success.

Yet I must speak of the ill omens preceding the night: the petty obstacles erected by a jealous, timid management; the open hostility from certain powerful quarters. Is it any wonder, then, that *Pocahontas* failed?

I laugh at the critics who scorned the performance. Fools, indeed, who hailed *Carpezan* as a masterpiece while sneering at a far more polished work! I maintain that Hagan played his part with such brilliance that even a leading actor-manager might have envied him. Had it not been for the conspiracy outside the theatre, the play would have triumphed. The order had been given: the play must fail. So said Sampson. “The house swarmed with Macs, by George,” he swore, “and they should have the galleries washed with brimstone.” He insisted Mr. Garrick himself could not have saved it—and he raged throughout the second act, when Smith (poor Hagan) stood bound to the stake, and Pocahontas rushed forward to save him. The audience trembled with emotion—yet laughter broke out.

Anyone curious may consult the published version—either the octavo or the later quarto edition of my *Collected Works*. Let them judge whether the scene lacks merit, whether the verse is not elegant, the language noble and rich.

One reason for failure was my strict adherence to history. I studied a portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh at the Museum—a man in frill and beard—and, with Theo lending some of her mother’s finest lace, we dressed Hagan precisely as depicted. No man looked more regal. Miss Pritchard, as Pocahontas, I dressed in authentic Indian attire, drawn from my own experiences in Virginia. Can it be believed that the audience tittered when she first appeared? They grew accustomed, yet just as she threw herself into Smith’s arms—many weeping—a man in the pit shouted, “Bedad! Here’s the Belle Savage kissing the Saracen’s Head!” A roar of laughter erupted, continuing in fits through the entire performance.

As the wag in Sheridan’s *Critic* says of morning guns—“they were not content with one, but fired two or three”—so too did this tavern joke take root. The ignorant audience didn’t know that *Belle Sauvage* was the very name derived from Pocahontas herself! My friend in the pit repeated it endlessly, naming each character after a tavern: the governor (with long beard) became “the Goat and Boots”; Barker, the lieutenant (broad-faced), “the Bull and Mouth.” And so on!

The curtain fell amid shrieks of whistles and hisses—especially aimed at poor Hagan whenever he spoke. Sampson saw Master Will in the green boxes, with some fair companions, and had no doubt he was a chief instigator. “I would have thrown him into the pit,” Sampson vowed—and he was the sort of man who would have done it—“but I saw a couple of Mr. Nadab’s men lurking in the lobby and had to back off.”

So our eggs were shattered before market. Our hopes lay in ruins.

Before the curtain rose, I peered from the stage and saw the house nearly full. Mr. Johnson sat in the front boxes, wearing a laced waistcoat, with Mr. Reynolds beside him—neither could see nor hear, so they came together, *à deux*, to form an opinion of my poor tragedy. Lady Maria I recognized by her hood, seated in the lower gallery, once more watching her beloved actor in a leading role. As for Theo, she confessed she’d rather not attend unless I commanded it—and I let her stay away. To see her suffer would have been agony. I myself, being naturally composed, took a light dinner at the Bedford and arrived at the theatre shortly before the play began, resolved to stay until fate decided the outcome.

But truth be told—I couldn’t help sensing disaster. There was a gloom about everything. Miss Pritchard had a headache. The barber had powdered Hagan’s wig like a madman. Every face in the greenroom wore uncertainty. The manager—a flippant, impertinent fellow—dared say to me, “For Heaven’s sake, Mr. Warrington, go get a glass of punch at the Bedford. Don’t frighten us with your dismal look!”

“Sir,” I replied, “for five shillings I have a right to comment on your face—but you’ve no authority to critique mine.”

“Sir,” he snapped, “I wish I had never seen your face at all!”

“Yours, sir,” I said, “has often amused me. When painted for *Abel Drugger*, it’s exceedingly comic.” Indeed, I always thought Mr. G. unmatched in low comedy.

I bowed and walked off to the coffee-house. For five years, I said nothing to him—until he apologized at a nobleman’s gathering. I claimed I’d forgotten the incident entirely, adding, “On the first night of a play, author and manager are both flurried.” Then I added, “After all, there’s no shame in not being made for the theatre. Mr. Garrick—you were.” A compliment he seemed to appreciate.

Fidus Achates came rushing to me at the end of the first act: “All’s going well—though there was tittering when Miss Pritchard appeared, dressed exactly as an Indian princess.”

“I cannot help it, Sampson,” I said, filling him a bumper of punch, “if Indians dress so.”

“Well,” he retorted, “would you have had Caractacus painted blue like an ancient Briton, or Bonduca in nothing but a cow-skin?”

Perhaps fidelity to history *was* the cause of ridicule—and if so, I’m not ashamed of the defeat.

After the second act, my aide-de-camp returned with grim news. Strange, how I grow calm in disaster, though nervous before action. [The writer seems to contradict himself here, having earlier claimed equanimity. Perhaps he misjudged himself, as many do.—ED.]

“Are things going badly?” I asked. I paid my bill, put on my hat, and marched to the theatre as calmly as if dining at the Temple—Sampson at my side, pressing my elbow, kicking link-boys aside, shouting, “By George, Mr. Warrington, you’re a man of spirit—a Trojan, sir!”

There were men of spirit in Troy—but alas, fate was stronger.

No one could say I didn’t bear my misfortune with dignity. I could no more control the audience’s clamor than a captain can stop a storm’s fury as his ship sinks. But I resolved to remain *impavidum ferient*, and I believe I endured without flinching.

“Not Regulus,” Sampson told my wife, “could step into his barrel more coolly.”

It’s unjust to accuse those of parasitic nature of deserting in adversity. Whether I prospered or suffered, the wild parson remained true—sharing our crust as eagerly as our feasts.

I took my place on the stage, watching my actors and the audience that condemned me. I suppose the performers kept their distance out of pity. I must admit, I felt no more moved than any spectator. No one would have guessed I was the unfortunate hero of the night.

But when I returned home, Theo’s face was pale and strained. I saw at once the news had reached her before I did.

Spencer, Sampson, cousin Hagan, and Lady Maria were to come after the play to congratulate the author—God wot! (Poor Miss Pritchard had sent word she was too ill to dine.)

My gardener at Bedford House had sent Theo the finest flowers to decorate the table. There they stood—painted standards—while the battle was lost.

I had borne the defeat bravely enough. But seeing my wife’s sweet face across the table, and those innocent tokens of welcome meant for a victor—I confess, my courage cracked. A pang struck me as keen as any I’ve ever known.

Our meal was somber. We tried to talk, but it brought little cheer. Fortunately, old Mrs. Hagan was gravely ill—her condition a blessing in disguise. We spoke of His Majesty’s approaching marriage. (How clearly I remember the trivial details of the day—even the tune a carpenter whistled beside me just before the curtain fell!) We discussed the death of good Mr. Richardson, author of *Pamela* and *Clarissa*, whose books we all adored. As we talked of *Clarissa*, Theo wiped her eyes and whispered, “You know, my love, mamma and I could never help crying over that dear book. Oh, my dearest, dearest mother—how I wish she were here now!”

This brought fresh tears—natural, for a young woman mourning her absent mother.

We mixed a dark bowl with Jamaica limes and toasted the Governor’s health. Then, smiling, I filled a bumper and raised it to “our better fortune!”

That was too much. The two women threw themselves into each other’s arms, sobbing and soaking each other’s handkerchiefs.

“Oh, Maria! Is not—Is not my George good and kind?” Theo sobbed.

“Look at my Hagan—how great, how godlike he was!” gasped Maria.

“It was a beastly cabal that ruined him—and I could plunge this knife into Mr. Garrick’s black heart—the odious little wretch!” she cried, clutching a dagger at her side.

Then, dropping it, she rushed to me, threw her arms around me, and embraced me before the small company.

I’m not sure if someone else did the same. We were all in a state of wild emotion. In the midst of sorrow, Love appears—the consoler—softening pain with tenderness, making one almost forget the loss.

A few days later, on our birthday, a letter arrived in my study. It bore these lines:

> Returning from the cruel fight,
> How pale and faint appears my knight!
> He sees me anxious at his side:
> “Why seek, my love, your wounds to hide?
> Or deem your English girl afraid
> To emulate the Indian maid?”
>
> Be mine my husband’s grief to cheer,
> In peril to be ever near;
> Whate’er of ill or woe betide,
> To bear it clinging at his side;
> The poisoned stroke of fate to ward,
> His bosom with my own to guard;
> Ah! could it spare a pang to his,
> It could not know a purer bliss!
> ’Twould gladden as it felt the smart,
> And thank the hand that flung the dart!

I won’t pretend the verses are masterpieces—but I love them as if they were. And when I entered her drawing-room, saw her blushing, hearing her soft voice as I hummed the lines—her face seemed more beautiful than anything I could imagine, even from Heaven.

I have already spoken of my feelings—now an old man—regarding that impetuous leap into marriage which I persuaded my dear wife to take with me when we were scarcely more than boys and girls. As a husband and father, with the weight of daily bills, the baker’s ledger, and a brood of spirited children who might at any moment decide to run off to Scotland, citing our own example as justification—I know I ought to approach this early chapter of George Warrington’s married life with caution. I should confess my sins, sit demurely in my armchair, and wear the white sheet of repentance, offering myself up as a warning to reckless youth.

Yet truth be told, that very marriage—about which my kin had prophesied so darkly—proved far kinder than they ever imagined. It had its trials, yes, but I recall them without bitterness. There were passionate sorrows, softened by time, which God has mercifully seen fit to console. There were days of true want, endured not in silence but with quiet dignity, to the astonishment of well-meaning relatives watching from afar. And then there were joys—so deep, so sacred—that I hesitate even to speak of them here, save with reverence and before One Ear alone, to whom all hearts turn in prayer and gratitude.

To marry without means is indeed unwise, perhaps even unjust to society. But how many thousands do it every year, trusting only in Heaven, health, and honest labour? Must young people wait until their cottage is fully furnished, their cellar stocked, their plate gleaming, and their strongbox brimming before they dare begin a home? If such rules governed all, the world would cease to grow. The gentlefolk tremble at the edge of poverty, clad in silk and fine shoes, waiting years for a bridge or a gilded barge to carry them across. The poor, barefoot, plunge straight into the stream, trusting their strength and fate to bear them through.

Who would wish his daughter into hardship? Who would urge his son to face the perils of a poor marriage—debt, sickness, loneliness, privation? I look at my own wife and feel shame for having placed such a burden upon one so tender-hearted. I remember her endurance, and I am grateful—for her love, her constancy, the grace with which she carried every trial. On the subject of marriage, I cannot claim impartiality: mine was rash, yet blessed beyond measure. So I will not counsel youth. I have known poverty, but never found it unbearable. Had I not known it, I could not have learned the kindness of friends, the sweetness of gratitude, nor the quiet pleasures that sometimes accompany a meagre meal and a small fire—the comfort that can warm even the longest day of toil. This much is certain: too often, the decent poor are pitied needlessly. Wealthy folk, stepping briefly into our narrow world, see shadows where we see light. They stumble over obstacles invisible to us. They marvel at our calm acceptance of thin beer and cold mutton—while we, though poor, ate with contentment and gave thanks.

My father-in-law, the good General, had married Molly when he was no more than a junior officer, his purse barely fuller than my own. Their lives had known both rise and fall. I suspect—though my wife denies it—they wedded young, without seeking parental leave. [The Editor searched Burn’s Registers of Fleet Marriages and found no record of Martin Lambert and Mary Benson.] Yet they were so pleased with their own union that they did not begrudge their children’s choices, nor fear the hardships we might face.

When I presented my financial state to Mr. Lambert, I may have exaggerated. Believing me to possess two thousand pounds, he left for Jamaica with ease, confident in his daughter’s future. After paying for the family’s journey, he returned little richer than I. My Theo’s dowry consisted of a few trinkets, some lace from Aunt Lambert, and twenty new guineas tucked into a purse stitched by her mother and sisters.

In valuing my own estate, I counted as a debt a sum my mother refused to acknowledge—even on her deathbed. She insisted the money I spent on her was for the upkeep of land destined for me. Any surplus, she claimed, belonged to my brother, who had nothing. He believed himself sole heir to the Virginian estate—until a mere half-hour’s difference in birth changed everything. He now served the king with distinction. To buy his promotion, she said, was surely his duty—and hers, too. When I finished my legal studies and my theatrical escapades, Madam Esmond informed me I was welcome to return to Virginia, to the place my birth entitled me to. She repeated this through Mountain, long before word of my marriage reached her.

Needless to say, her reaction upon learning of my marriage was fierce. When Harry, my brother, visited Virginia after the pacification of Canada, he described the reception he received. Castlewood, abandoned since our departure for Europe, reopened its doors. My mother hosted splendid feasts in honour of her son—the friend of Wolfe, the soldier of Quebec—honoured by all the colony.

But disputes arose. Harry remained steadfast in his friendship with Colonel Washington of Mount Vernon, whose virtues he praised endlessly. I admit the man had merit. In the later struggles that brought ruin to England, I can admire, as others do, Washington’s unwavering resolve and triumph.

If these arguments between Harry and our mother were frequent—as his letters suggested—I wondered why he stayed so long. A thought occurred to me, one I hesitated to share with Mrs. Warrington. We had discussed Hetty’s secret affection for him, marveling that he never noticed. Perhaps, I mused, he had found another woman in Virginia—one more suited to his taste.

Then came a letter—not a full confession, but a hint. A figure was described, unnamed—a creature of beauty and perfection, like any young lady under similar circumstances. My wife asked to see it. I handed it over, feeling sorrowful. To my surprise, she read it calmly, showing no sign of pain.

“I’ve thought about this before,” I said. “I feel for you, my love, regarding poor Hetty.”

“Ah, poor Hetty,” Theo murmured, eyes fixed on the carpet.

“It would never have worked,” I added.

“No,” she sighed. “They wouldn’t have been happy.”

“How strange he never discovered her secret!” I continued.

She looked at me sharply, a curious expression on her face. “What does that look mean?” I asked.

“Nothing, dear—nothing! Only I’m not surprised,” she said, blushing.

“What?” I asked, my mind stirred. “Do you mean to tell me… that you once cared for someone else?”

“Oh, George,” she whispered, “when I was at school, there was a boy—Dr. Backhouse’s school—sat in the loft next to ours. He had lovely eyes. I was so shocked when I saw him behind the counter at Mr. Grigg’s, buying a cloak for baby. I wanted to tell you, but didn’t know how!”

I went to find this boy with the lovely eyes. My wife described his clothes—blue camlet coat, red hair tied with a dirty ribbon. I saw him: a slight, bandy-legged fellow. I refrained from reproaching my wife—and I’ll never tell her I saw him, unless she reads this page. If wives saw us as we truly are, would they still love us? Are we not just as mistaken about them as they are about us? I gaze into one honest face, and believe I’ve never been deceived.

To prevent younger readers from imitating my folly, I won’t detail how little capital Mrs. Theo and I began with. Our tragedy brought us nothing—though recent reviewers have praised it, and Mr. Kemble himself commended it. Lord Wrotham offered to publish it by subscription, sending me a banknote for a hundred copies. But I disliked that method and locked away the manuscript, with my wife’s verses at the front. I don’t know why it offended court—perhaps because an actor who’d eloped with an earl’s daughter played a lead role. Or maybe because the Indian characters criticized British ambition and rule. Whatever the reason, royal favour slipped from my grasp.

What then? Months after the play failed, I counted what remained of my fortune (a brief calculation). I decided to leave my pleasant Bloomsbury lodgings. I gave notice to our landlady, telling her my wife needed country air. We moved only as far as Lambeth, Gumbo and Molly following. Though we were as poor as beggars, we still had a maid and a lackey in livery—like any household of standing. Naturally, relatives condemned our extravagance. Aren’t they always the ones to point out our faults?

One day, returning from London, I saw a grand gilt carriage near our lodgings—bearing the arms and livery of the Castlewoods. A crowd gathered, awed by the footmen in the sun, drinking ale. Inside, I found Lady Castlewood seated opposite my wife. Theo, with her lively way of recounting scenes, told me all.

“I’ve been here ages,” she said, “gossiping with cousin Theo while you were at the coffee-house, making merry. Guess she finds it lonely here, stitching caps and hemming frocks. Never mind, dear—you’ll soon have company to amuse you when cousin George is gone. What a nice lodging! Ours is twenty times bigger, covered in gold—but I like this better. Bless you, being rich isn’t better than being poor. When we lived at Albany, I did all the work—scoured rooms, boiled the kettle, helped wash. Just as happy as I am now. We had one old negro to keep store. Why don’t you sell Gumbo, cousin George? He’s idle, dawdling, making love to the maid. Fogh! These English people aren’t particular!”

She chattered cheerfully until it was time to go. Then she pulled out a fine repeating watch. “Time to call on Her Majesty at Buckingham House,” she declared. “And mind you come to us, George.” She waved from the coach. “Theo and I have settled all.”

“There,” I said, as the footmen climbed aboard, “is one who fears neither our poverty nor forgets her own.”

“Ashamed?” Theo resumed her needlework. “To do her justice, she’d make herself at home in any kitchen or palace. She taught me and Molly twenty lessons in housekeeping. She says she roasted, baked, swept, milked the cow.” (Madam Theo pronounced “cow” in our American fashion, mimicking the Countess delightfully.)

“And she has no pride,” I added. “It was kind of her to invite us to dine. When will Uncle Warrington ever offer us a crust—or a glass of his famous beer?”

“Yes, it was kind,” Theo replied, smiling. “But you don’t know the conditions!” She laughed, imitating the Countess. “She took out her book and told me her schedule. Monday: Duke and Duchess, several members of my lord’s household. Tuesday: earls, bishops, ambassador. ‘Of course you won’t come those days?’ she said. ‘You’re so poor—fine company isn’t good for you. Father doesn’t dine on company days—he eats cold meat.’ So I told her Mr. Warrington only cares for the best company, and suggested she invite us when the Archbishop dines. She agreed. And she’s economical—‘I thought of bringing my baby’s caps, but they might be needed again.’ So we lose that wardrobe addition.” Theo smiled. “‘When people are poor,’ she said, ‘they’re poor, and must get on.’ What shall we do for poor Maria? Goodness knows—we can’t ask her to visit as we can you, though you’re so poor. An earl’s daughter marrying a play-actor! La, my dear, it’s dreadful. His Majesty and the Princess have both spoken of it! Every noble family pities us. But I have a plan—to help them.’ She sent Simons, her groom, to tell Hagan to return to Dublin College, finish his terms, take orders, and become chaplain at home.”

This plan was fulfilled months later, when I could assist Hagan myself. Castlewood kept his word—Hagan became chaplain and received a colonial appointment. But not a penny did he spare for his sister or kinsman. I never asked him for aid—thank God. And though he expressed genuine joy when my poverty ended, I knew he meant it.

As for Uncle Warrington and his virtuous family—let me be fair. Throughout my trial, their sorrow for my condition was constant. I heard reports from acquaintances who visited them. Not once did they say a kind word about me or my wife. They called my tragedy a crime, me a reprobate, wandering Grub Street in rags. They offered no hand. My wife could cry in pain, but they had no twopence. They attended church six times a week, subscribed to charities. Their kind was known eighteen centuries ago and will endure. They thank Heaven they are not like others—and leave the suffering to fend for themselves.

I shudder to recall the doubts that haunted me—the plans I tried and failed. I turned to my friend Mr. Johnson. I remember his warmth, and blush at the sharp words I once spoke about his manners. I told him my story—my marriage, my prospects. He refused to see them as grim. “You have chances,” he said. “A position in England—slim, but possible. Your inheritance—natural, or soon to come. You have cash for now—though, to be frank, after your tragedy, I doubt nature gave you the gifts for literary fame.” And finally, “return to Virginia—plenty and a home await you.”

“Why, sir!” he exclaimed. “That sum would have been a fortune for me at the start. My friend Goldsmith would set up a coach-and-six on it. With youth, hope, and two hundred pounds—no young man need despair. You have a year. Who knows what may happen? Your relatives might help. You might inherit. You might win a fortune!”

I did not—though he did. Lord Bute granted Mr. Johnson a pension, setting Grub Street ablaze. Still, he did not abandon my literary efforts. He promised to secure work from booksellers—and kept his word. “But,” he warned, “you must not appear among them *in forma pauperis*. Have you no friend’s coach? Wear your best hat and waistcoat. We must seem to be doing *them* a favour.”

It worked—at first. Respect followed. But when the booksellers realized I expected payment, they stiffened. One, formerly a footman, told his boy: “Oh, it’s Pocahontas? Let him wait.” I stormed in. “Wait, sir?” I roared. “I’m not accustomed to waiting—but I’ve heard you are.” I marched out into Pall Mall, furious.

Yet Mr. D. was right. I came not to beg, but to bargain. It was my place to wait. Later, in better times, I apologized. The author of *The Muse in Livery* forgave me instantly.

So ends this chapter—of poverty, pride, and the quiet strength of love.

It was not long after the birth of the Prince of Wales that our own little son made his entrance into the world—though, unlike the royal infant, his arrival passed without fireworks or fanfare. No golden rails or noble nurses stood guard at his cradle; only Gumbo, steadfast and loyal, and Molly, kind-hearted and gentle, watched over him with all the devotion they could muster. Our child came into a humble life, yet born under skies no less bright for their simplicity.

Why did we not name him George, like the prince, or like his father? Because in those days, when affection from my own blood was scarce, one small soul had touched me deeply—a cousin, a boy of my family’s line, named Miles. He had been a wild, spirited lad, but full of warmth and mischief, and though he’d passed on, his memory lived in my heart. Theo and I agreed: our son should carry that name—not as a jest, but as an echo of love, of kinship, of a bond that mattered more than rank or title.

We wrote to inform my parents of the joyous news, and boldly announced the birth in the *Daily Advertiser*, noting the place—Church Street, Lambeth—as plainly as if it were a palace courtyard. Aunt Bernstein replied with a note both sharp and tender: “How could you expose your dwelling so publicly?” she wrote. “But I kiss the little mamma, and send a remembrance for the child.” That remembrance arrived in the form of a rich silk coverlid, edged with lace fit for a prince. It was beautiful, though scarcely practical—the cost of the lace alone might have fed us for weeks. Still, Theo and Molly rejoiced in its finery, and our son’s cradle gleamed with a dignity that matched any nobleman’s.

Dr. Heberden, kind and wise, visited often, ensuring my wife’s recovery. He recommended a local surgeon who proved attentive and skilled. The care needed was minimal—Theo was strong, and our landlady, along with Molly, tended her with quiet competence.

Then came Lady Castlewood again, her chariot flashing through the narrow lane as if it belonged to some grand procession. She brought a pot of jelly—no doubt once served at her own table—and spoke of court ceremonies, of the splendour surrounding the new heir to the throne. Mr. Johnson happened to be visiting that day, and he bowed low before her, awkwardly but respectfully. She called me “cousin” with gracious ease, and helped transfer the jelly from her silver dish to our crockery with a smile. Dr. Heberden tasted it and declared it exquisite.

“The great,” he said, “are fortunate in every way. They gather the finest cooks, the most witty companions. If this jelly has indeed graced his lordship’s table, then it has done so in company worthy of its sweetness. It has trembled beneath the gaze of famed beauties, kissed by ruby lips, shared among lords and ladies whose conversation must have sparkled like wine.”

And so he ate a generous portion—though I must confess, Theo found it unpalatable, and Molly, sniffing it sharply, declared it mouldy.

Yet our boy had one distinction few could claim: an earl’s daughter as his godmother. Lady Maria, our dear cousin, took the role with heartfelt devotion. Having known no children of her own, she poured her tenderness into ours, watching over mother and child with a love that stirred even the hardest heart.

Captain Miles—our own gallant son—now wears the fine uniform of the Prince’s Hussars, resplendent in gold braid and polished buttons.
