But let us hope he never forgets that his first garments were once meant for a poor player’s child. Sampson, the same man who married us in Southwark’s chapel, baptized him there too. Never had I heard the words of the Prayer-book spoken with such grace—until, at the final blessing, his voice broke, and all present wiped away tears. “Mr. Garrick himself,” Hagan remarked, “could not have read them more nobly. And never did a child enter the world with such sincere prayers.”

Now, how did he come by the name Miles?

A few days before the christening, while we still debated whether to name him George, the sound of hooves clattered up our street. At the gate stood young Miles—our cousin—dismounted, breathless, his little boots dusted with road-grime. I fear he had ridden off without permission, driven by restless spirit and loyalty.

“You know,” he said, “Cousin Harry gave me my horse. And I can’t help liking you—you’re just like Harry, and people always talk about you at home, and it’s not fair. So I’ve brought my whistle and coral—my godmamma Lady Suckling gave them to me—for your baby. And if you’re poor, Cousin George, here’s my gold moidore. It’s worth a lot, and I can’t spend it anyway. It’s no use to me.”

We lifted him to Theo’s room—proud in his tramping boots, cheeks flushed with effort. She kissed him, thanked him, and held the coin close. From that day, the moidore stayed in her purse, a token of innocence and generosity.

My mother, writing through her usual envoy, expressed her dismay upon learning my son bore the name Miles—one unknown in the Esmond line. I did not explain then. But years later, when I told Madam Esmond the truth, I saw a tear trace her wrinkled cheek. And afterward, I learned she had questioned Gumbo many times about the boy who gave his name to our Miles—our Miles Gloriosus, who would one day ride through Pall Mall, Valenciennes, Almack’s, and Brighton, remembered not for wealth or title, but for the kindness that began with a single gold coin.

In the early days of our return to England, when Harry and I were such wayward pupils under our tutor’s stern eye, who would have guessed that Mr. Esmond Warrington of Virginia would one day become a bear-leader himself? My mother—when we met again—could never speak plainly of those years. She only alluded to them as “that terrible time, my love, which I can’t bear to think of,” or “those dreadful years when there was difference between us.” Though the man who had once been my pupil—a generous and grateful soul—sent me several barrels of the very beer that built his fortune, Madam Esmond referred to him only as “your friend in England,” “your wealthy Lambeth friend,” never by name. And she never touched a drop of it. We brew our own at Warrington Manor, but every year, good Mr. Foker sends two butts of his finest entire to Ipswich. His son is now a fine young gentleman, married to an earl’s daughter; the father remains a kind and worthy man. It was through the luck of meeting him that I received some of the most welcome guineas I ever knew.

It wasn’t so much the money, but the dignity and purpose granted by the office of Governor that I took upon myself, which made those years so precious. Mr. Foker’s brewery—since moved—once stood near Pedlar’s Acre in Lambeth. The surgeon who attended my wife during her confinement also cared for the brewer’s family. He was a Bavarian, originally named Voelker. I suppose Mr. Lance, the surgeon, introduced us. This kindly doctor often smoked Virginia tobacco in my garden, and grew fond of me and mine. He brought his patron to my house. When Mr. Foker discovered I could speak a little German and sing “Prinz Eugen the noble Ritter”—a song my grandfather brought back from the Marlborough wars—he formed a deep affection for me. His wife placed her chair and chariot at Mrs. Warrington’s disposal; his little daughter adored our baby (and truth be told, the Captain, though now as unprepossessing as any man with a queue, was beautiful as an infant). [The very image of the Squire at thirty, everyone says so. M.W. (Note in the MS.)] And since Master Foker was bullied at Westminster School for his father’s trade, the parents asked if I might take charge of him, offering a fair sum for his education.

Mr. Foker was a sharp businessman, and because he and his family genuinely cared for us, I shared my financial affairs freely with him. He praised my honesty and said my accounts only deepened his respect. He laughed at our tales of aid from noble kin—my aunt’s coverlid, Lady Castlewood’s mouldy jelly, Lady Warrington’s cold treatment. But he wept when I spoke of little Miles’s moidore. As for Sampson and Hagan, “I wow,” he declared, “dey shall have so much beer als ever dey can drink.” He sent his wife to call on Lady Maria, treating her with utmost deference whenever she visited. It was at Mr. Foker’s home that Lady Maria stayed when Hagan went to Dublin to finish his studies, and the brewer’s purse helped supply our friend’s needs.

When Mr. Foker fully understood my circumstances, he spoke of me with great admiration, calling my conduct a mark of rare virtue. I’ve already told how my mother saved for Harry, and how both brothers owed me. Yet when Harry spent, he did so believing the money was his own. My mother never grasped that she was wronging me—the funds were gone, and that was that. By the end of ’62, Harry sent a substantial remittance for his promotion, reminding me he still owed me, and urging me to draw on his agents if needed. He didn’t know how dire my need was, nor how my small capital had vanished.

To take his money would delay his advancement, so I refused, though I confess I was tempted. And knowing General Lambert’s modest means, I wouldn’t burden him. These acts of restraint, my dear brewer thought, were feats of noble character. So what does he do but write privately to my brother in America, praising me and my wife as the finest humans alive, and summon Madame de Bernstein—who never mentioned her visit to me, though I noticed her sudden kindness toward us, surprising in one I saw as selfish and worldly. Later, I asked her how she’d gained access to the Baroness. She laughed: “De Baroness!” she said. “I knew de Baron when he was a valet at Munich, and I was a brewer-apprentice.” I think our family should not pry too deeply into our uncle the Baron.

Thus, a period that ought to have been bleak became instead one of warmth and unexpected blessings. The bear I led was a gentle cub, dancing readily to my pipe. Better to lead him than loiter outside booksellers’ doors, waiting on the whims of managers! During our exile, we passed many pleasant evenings with these kind friends. We weren’t without intellectual joys either: Mrs. Foker and Mrs. Warrington sang beautifully together, and when I felt inclined, I read my play *Pocahontas* aloud—better than Hagan ever did, Mr. Foker insisted.

After the incident with Miles Warrington junior, I saw nothing more of him, and heard little from my paternal relations. Sir Miles was ever busy at court—though I suspect he would have thrived even at Nero’s. Once, when Mr. Foker told me he’d heard on ‘Change that they were making my uncle a “Beer,” I blinked in confusion. “A Beer?” I asked. “Can’t you understand de vort, ven I say it?” the irritable old man replied. “Vell, veil, a Lort!” Indeed, Sir Miles was the humble servant of whichever minister held power. I wonder he didn’t adopt a Scotch accent during the first favourite’s brief reign. I saw him and his wife returning from court when Mrs. Claypool was presented to the Queen on her marriage. I carried my son on my shoulder. My uncle and aunt stared stiffly from their gilt coach window. The footmen looked blank over their nosegays. Had I worn the Fairy’s cap and been invisible, my father’s brother could not have ignored me more completely.

We rarely accepted Lady Castlewood’s odd invitation to tea and supper when no other guests came. Old Van den Bosch, clever as he was at amassing wealth, was dull in conversation—except to his daughter, who discussed household matters, City dealings, stock trading, and farming with the same sharpness as her father. Lord Castlewood was seldom home, and his absence was neither mourned nor missed by his wife. The Countess confided all this to my wife simply: “Guess,” she said, “my lord and father don't pull well together nohow. Guess my lord is always wanting money, and father keeps the key of the box—and quite right, too. If he could handle all our money, my lord would soon make away with it, and then what's to become of our noble family? We pay everything, my dear—except play-debts, and them we won't have nohow. We pay cooks, horses, wine-merchants, tailors, and everybody—lucky for them too—reckon my lord wouldn't pay 'em! And we always see he has a guinea in his pocket, so he goes out like a real nobleman. What that man owes us—what he owed before we came—gracious goodness only knows! Me and father do our best to keep him respectable—but it's no easy job, my dear. Law! he'd melt the plate, only father keeps the key of the strong-room; and when we go to Castlewood, my father travels with me, and papa is armed too, as well as the people.”

“Gracious heavens!” my wife exclaimed. “You don’t mean to say you suspect your husband of—?”

“To what? Oh no, nothing, of course! And I’d trust our brother Will with untold money, wouldn’t I? As much as I’d trust the cat with the cream-pan! I tell you, my dear, it’s not all pleasure being a woman of rank and fashion: and if I bought a countess’s coronet, I paid a good price for it—that I did!”

And so had Lord Castlewood paid dearly to free his estate from debts, furnish his houses and stables, and clear his accounts. He was enslaved by his wife and her father. No wonder the old man’s company was unpleasant to the poor victim, who fled to clubs when he could afford it—or to any society but his own. Leading a bear, as I did, was hardly glorious; waiting in a bookseller’s anteroom until his honour finished dinner and granted audience was sometimes hard for a man of my pride. But would I have traded my poverty for Castlewood’s humiliation? Or preferred his wretched dependence to my own? At least I earned my wage, however small. And no one can say I flattered my patrons or bowed to them—I was sulky, overbearing, and frankly intolerable.

Yet there was one person with whom Fate had paired me, who bore our poverty with such grace and sweetness that even stingy Fortune softened. Like a fairy tale’s gentle creature, her constant cheerfulness melted the heart of hardship. No matter how poor she was, everyone who knew her saw a true lady. Tradespeople and neighbours treated her with respect equal to the richest among them. “I think, my dear,” said kind-hearted Mrs. Foker, when they rode in her carriage, “you look like the mistress of the vehicle, and I only your maid.” Our landladies adored her; shopkeepers rushed to fulfill her smallest requests as eagerly as if a duchess had ordered them. I often thought of the lady in *Comus*, moving through chaos with serene purity.

Often, the generous parents of my young bear lent us their carriage to visit friends. Once, we drove to the Protestant Hero and enjoyed syllabub in the garden; the hostess insisted on calling my wife “her ladyship” all afternoon. We visited Mr. Johnson and took tea with him—Mr. Goldsmith was there, too. The Doctor waited on my wife to her coach. But our most frequent visits were to Aunt Bernstein. I must admit, I was not jealous when my aunt began to show a remarkable fondness for Theo.

This affection grew so strong she wanted her nearly every day, or even to live with her entirely. She saw Theo’s husband and child as mere nuisances, and hated us amusingly for keeping her favorite away. Not that my wife lacked merit—she was worthy of anyone’s affection—but her frequent absences and the difficulty of reaching her stirred my aunt’s attachment into something almost passionate. She wrote notes like love letters, her servants hovered around our kitchen. If my wife didn’t come, she sent tearful pleas, scolding me fiercely when I visited her. Once, when the child fell ill—Fate has spared our Captain to be a great trial and test of patience—Madame Bernstein came three days in a row to Lambeth, insisting there was nothing wrong with the baby, nothing at all, and that we merely pretended illness to torment her.

The reigning Countess of Castlewood was just as easygoing with her old aunt as with anyone else. “What air you all about, scraping and bowing to that old woman, I can’t tell, noways!” she’d snap. “She a fine lady? Nonsense! She ain’t no more fine than any other lady: and I guess I’m as good as any of ‘em with their high heels and grand airs! She a beauty once? Take away her wig, rouge, and teeth—and what becomes of your beauty, I’d like to know? Guess you’d put it all in a bandbox, and there’d be nothing left but a shrivelled old woman!” And indeed, the little homilist spoke painfully true. Beauty fades for all. Here was old age without reverence, grey hairs hidden or painted, the world still clinging to her crutch. For eighty years she had lived, eaten of the forbidden and permitted tree. She had known beauty, pleasure, flattery—but what secret rages, disappointments, humiliations? What thorns beneath roses? What stinging bees in the fruit? “You are not a beauty, my dear,” she’d say to my wife, “and may thank your stars you’re not.” (If she contradicted herself, perhaps we all do.)

“Don’t tell me your husband likes your face, and you want no one else’s admiration!” she’d continue. “We all do. Every woman would rather be beautiful than anything else—rich, good, or gifted with fairies! Look at that picture—though I know it’s bad, and Kneller couldn’t paint my eyes, hair, or complexion. What a shape I had then—and look at me now, this wrinkled neck! Why must our beauty last so short a time? I remember Mademoiselle de l’Enclos at my age, fresh as ever. We can’t hide our years—they’re written in Mr. Collins’s books. I was born in King James’s last year. I’m not old yet—I’m seventy-six. But what a wreck, my dear! Isn’t it cruel our time is so brief?”

Then my wife would gently point out that all our time here below is short.

“Ha!” the Baroness would cry. “Did not Adam live near a thousand years, and Eve remain beautiful? I used to puzzle Mr. Tusher with that—poor creature! What have we done since that our lives are so shortened?”

“Has your life been so happy you’d wish to prolong it?” the listener would ask. “Have you, who love wit, never read Dean Swift’s description of the deathless people in *Gulliver*? My papa and husband say it’s one of the finest sermons ever written. Better not to live at all than to live without love. And I’m sure,” my wife would say, dabbing her eyes, “if anything happened to my dearest George, I’d wish to go to Heaven that moment.”

“Who loves me in Heaven? I am quite alone, child—that is why I’d rather stay here,” the Baroness whispered, frightened and pitiful. “You are kind to me, God bless your sweet face! Though I scold and have a frightful temper, my servants will do anything to comfort me, rise at any hour, and never say a cross word. I still like my cards. Life would be a blank without them. Almost everything is gone except that. I can’t eat now since I lost those last two teeth. Everything slips away in old age. But I still have my cards—thank Heaven, I still have my cards!” Then she’d begin to doze, waking sharply if my wife stirred, imagining Theo was leaving. “Don’t go away—I can’t bear to be alone. I don’t want you to talk. Just let me see your face, my dear! It’s much pleasanter than that horrid old Brett’s, who’s scowled in my bedroom for years.”

“Well, Baroness! Still at your cribbage?” (Imagine a noble Countess interrupting a card game between Theo and Aunt Bernstein.) “Me and my Lord Esmond have come to see you! Go shake hands with grandaunt, Esmond! Tell her ladyship your lordship’s a good boy!”

“My lordship’s a good boy,” the child replied. (Madam Theo used to act these scenes for me with great liveliness.)

“And if he is, I guess he don’t take after his father,” shrieked Lady Castlewood, pretending Aunt Bernstein was deaf and shouting at her.

“Your ladyship chose my nephew for better or worse,” Aunt Bernstein replied, flustered in the presence of the young Countess.

“But he is a precious deal worse than I ever thought! I’m speaking of your Pa, Ezzy. If it wasn’t for your mother, my son, Lord knows what would become of you! We’re going to see his little Royal Highness. Sorry to see you not looking quite so well today. We can’t always stay young and law! How we do change as we grow old! Go up and kiss that lady. She has a little boy, too. Why, bless us! Have you got the child downstairs?” Indeed, Master Miles was below—sometimes accompanying his mother on visits to Aunt Bernstein. Our aunt liked her so much she reluctantly endured the child. “So you’ve got the child here? Oh, you slyboots!” the Countess snapped. “Guess you come after the old lady’s money! Law bless you! Don’t look so frightened. She can’t hear a word I say. Come, Ezzy. Good-bye, aunt!” And the Countess swept out.

Did Aunt Bernstein hear her? Where was the wit that once made her famous? Was that fire extinguished along with the sparkle in her eyes? With others, she remained sharp and quick-witted. When the Dowager of Castlewood and Lady Fanny visited (these ladies treated my wife with perfect indifference and charming manners), the Baroness was stately, poised, even commanding. She would mischievously caress Mrs. Warrington before them, later boasting of her good breeding, saying my nephew had made a foolish match, but I certainly had chosen a charming wife. “In a word, I praise you so to them, my dear,” she’d say, “that I think they’d like to tear your eyes out.” But before the little American, she trembled and fumbled. She was so afraid she dared not refuse her door, and when the Countess turned her back, she didn’t even rebuke her. Despite their dislike, they never tore out Theo’s eyes.

Once, they drove to our cottage at Lambeth, where my wife sat at the open window, holding our child. A towering footman marched through our garden and delivered their visiting cards. Their hatred hurt us no more than their visit pleased us. The next time we borrowed the Brewer’s carriage, Mrs. Warrington drove to Kensington, and Gumbo handed back our cards to the giant who had delivered theirs.

The Baroness had a coach, but rarely offered it to us. She’d let Theo, her maid, and baby start from Clarges Street in the rain, with a weak excuse that she feared asking her coachman to take the horses out. But twice, on her return, my wife was frightened by rough men on the other side of Westminster Bridge. I finally told my aunt I’d forbid Mrs. Warrington from visiting unless she could be brought home safely. Reluctantly, grumbling Jehu drove through the darkness. He complained about my shillings—he didn’t know how few I had. Our poverty wore a decent face. My relatives never offered help, nor did I complain before them. I don’t know how Sampson came by a windfall of guineas, but once he brought me six. They were more welcome than any money I’d ever received. He’d been checking on Mr. Miles’s crib while the child slept; when the parson left, I found the coins in the baby’s tiny hand. Yes, Love is best of all. I hold many such gifts close in my heart—precious springs rising in deserts, kind lights brightening our darkest hours.

This devoted chaplain willingly gave his company to Madame de Bernstein, whether for cards or theology. Having known her for years, Sampson saw her decline and warned us of her growing frailty. Speaking of her failing health and likely end, he spoke tenderly of preparing for another world, of the emptiness of this life, and the hope of happiness for repentant sinners.

“I have been a sinner,” the chaplain said, bowing his head. “God knows, and I pray Him to forgive me. I fear, sir, your aunt, the Lady Baroness, is not in a state fit for the change coming. I am but a poor weak wretch, and no prisoner in Newgate could confess more humbly. Recently, I’ve tried to speak with her on this matter, but she received me harshly. ‘Parson,’ she said, ‘if you come for cards, it’s mighty well, but I’ll thank you to spare me your sermons.’ What can I do, sir? I’ve called several times, and Mr. Case told me his lady was unable to see me.” In truth, Madame Bernstein told my wife—whom she never refused—that the chaplain’s tone was unbearable, and as for his theology, “Haven’t I been a Bishop’s wife?” she said, “Do I need this creature to teach me?”

The worst of times had passed for me, and poverty was no longer a shadow over my life. The death of my young cousin, though a sorrowful event, brought with it a change in fortune—my prospects improved dramatically. I became the next heir to a substantial estate. With no more children expected from my uncle and his wife, the path seemed clear. Sampson had once warned me that Lady Warrington might go to great lengths to thwart me, but in truth, she proved no such villain. Stricken by grief at her son’s loss, she turned inward, guided by her clergyman, who urged her to accept the will of Heaven. “While your son lived,” he told her, “your heart was drawn away from the higher world. You desired rank and title, even an earthly coronet. But now, what use is such glory to one who has but a few years left on earth? How can it compare to the crown of heaven, for which you are already assured?”

The tragedy stirred deep emotion across the community. In the chapels of the fervent sect to which she now fully aligned herself, sermons were delivered in memory of the child. I do not wish to judge the course she took—anyone who seeks solace in faith after suffering deserves respect. Even so, she sought reconciliation with me. A year after her loss, while visiting London, she requested a meeting. I went to her, and she delivered a sermon-like lecture, as was her custom. She marveled at the divine decree that allowed—and then punished—her son’s disobedience (he had gone out with his gun without her knowledge). Though this act brought me benefit, she saw it as a punishment from above.

She expressed hope that, should I ever inherit the family estate—though the Warringtons were generally long-lived, save for my father, whose life had been shortened by reckless youth—I would reform my ways. She prayed I would abandon my unsuitable companions, leave behind the theatre and its immoral crowd, and turn instead to the peace found only in religious duty. She filled her words with scripture, which I have no desire to repeat. When I left, she gave me a packet of sermons for Mrs. Warrington and a little book of hymns by Miss Dora, later known for her piety and marriage to the preacher Mr. Juffles. She forgave me, yet could not bear to see our boy.

After we lost our second child, my aunt and her daughter came swiftly to comfort us. They even invited us to their home. But my uncle now visited us nearly every day. He spent hours watching our infant, bringing endless toys and sweets. He begged the child call him “Godpapa.” When I felt the depth of my own grief—still sharp after twenty-five years—I understood his pain. My wife, however, sensed his sorrow before she knew what it meant to lose a child. Her mother’s heart had already felt the ache of paternal grief; mine, less tender, learned compassion only through experience. It was our baby’s coffin that finally reconciled me to my uncle.

He sent his coach to follow the modest funeral procession, and afterward took little Miles with him. The child chattered endlessly, forgetting his sadness in the delight of new black clothes and a carriage ride. His innocent talk pierced my wife’s heart. Could we ever wish that wound healed? I know her face well enough to recognize when, even now, she remembers that child—not as a distant memory, but as a living presence in heaven.

We returned soon to our cheerful lodgings in Bloomsbury. My young son, whom I could no longer lead about like a pet bear, was sent to Chartreux School. There, his friend Charley ensured he was treated fairly and not beaten beyond measure. Thanks to his excellent private tutor, he earned and kept a good position. He liked the school so much that he declared, if ever he had a son, he would send him there too.

I could no longer lead my bear, because I had other duties. Reconciled to us—perhaps more so for the sake of Mr. Miles—my uncle, who was such a loyal supporter of government that I often wondered how the Minister ever entrusted him with anything (since his vote was certain), used his influence on my behalf. I was appointed one of His Majesty’s Commissioners for licensing hackney-coaches—a post I held with pride until a dispute with the Minister (to be detailed elsewhere) cost me the office. I also completed my studies at the Temple and appeared in Westminster Hall in gown and wig. This year, my dear friend Mr. Foker, having business in Paris, invited me to accompany him. I was warmly welcomed by my American benefactor, Monsieur de Florac, who introduced me to his noble family and many of Paris’s most refined society. Yet I remained faithful to Foker, whose circle lay among the bourgeoisie—especially Monsieur Santerre, a brewer of some repute, though one who later made a name for himself not in beer, but in blood.

Foker needed me as interpreter, and I was glad to serve him, repaying the kindness he had shown me. Meanwhile, our wives stayed at Foker’s villa in Wimbledon, where they enjoyed the letters I sent them—dispatched through Mr. Hume, then at the Embassy—letters that would later be published in a neat volume.

While I quietly fulfilled my duties in London, unrest began to stir in the colonies—unrest that would culminate in separation from the mother country. When Mr. Grenville proposed the stamp duties, I told my wife the bill would cause discontent. We always wanted to extract as much as possible from England and pay back as little as we could. But I never imagined the fury it would ignite. It was like a family quarrel: a single incident sparks anger, but the real roots lie in old resentments. Years of petty tyranny, English arrogance toward foreigners and colonists alike, the belief that our rivers were inferior to theirs, and the natural resentment against imperial overreach all fueled the conflict. And the blunders of British policy pushed it to a breaking point—one I do not regret.

Had I been in Virginia, I might have joined the colonial side—not from principle, but perhaps from opposition to the domineering lady of Castlewood, who could have driven me into rebellion just as England drove the colonies. Was the Stamp Act the true cause of revolution? A tax no greater than what was paid in England itself. Ten years earlier, when France threatened our borders and we pleaded for help, would the colonies have rebelled then? Most people see the tax collector as a natural enemy. Against Britain in America stood thousands of brave and proud men—but even more who saw profit in the conflict or had personal reasons to join. I cannot say whether my feelings were selfish or patriotic, nor which side was right. Both, perhaps. I am sure England had no choice but to fight. And once defeated, I believe the loser felt no lasting bitterness.

Why did brother Hal write such fiery patriotic letters from Virginia, though he seemed reluctant to leave? My kind and devoted brother was always influenced by others—by me when we were together (he believed in my wit and wisdom so completely that if I said the weather was fine, he’d ponder it as if it were a maxim of the Seven Sages), by someone else when I was away. Who inspired these passionate declarations? “He is rebelling against Madam Esmond,” I said. “Some colonial woman, perhaps,” suggested my wife. But Hal never told us who “that lady” was. Indeed, he asked me not to mention the matter in my letters. “Madam wishes to read them all,” he wrote, “and I want to say nothing about you know what until the proper time.”

His affection shone through every letter. When he heard—through the same source I mentioned—that I had kept only a hundred pounds from his aunt’s legacy, despite my own dire straits, he was ready to mortgage his newly acquired estate. He quarreled with his mother on my behalf, speaking with more boldness than I ever would. Only when she accused him of ingratitude—after years of sacrifice for him—did he learn that our mother had cut off my allowance to favor him. By then, the deals were done, and I was fortunate to be free of want.

Every scrap of paper we ever wrote, our thrifty parent at Castlewood preserved—taped, labeled, stored away. We boys were less careful. I especially, perhaps too dismissive of my younger brother’s writings. But my wife, more generous, kept many of Harry’s letters, along with those of the angelic girl we would soon call sister.

“To think whom he has chosen, and whom he might have had! Oh, 'tis cruel!” my wife exclaimed when we received the letter in which Harry first revealed the name of his beloved.

“She was a pretty little girl when I left home—she may be a beauty now,” I remarked, reading the longest private letter Harry had ever written.

“But can she compare to my Hetty?” Mrs. Warrington asked.

“We agreed Hetty and Harry were not meant to be happy together,” I replied.

Theo kissed her husband. “My dear, I wish they had tried,” she sighed. “I feared—feared Hetty might lead him. She has the better head. But from reading this, it seems the new lady has taken command of poor Harry.” She handed me the letter:

“My dearest George has been prepared by earlier letters to understand how a certain lady has won my heart, which I have given up in exchange for something infinitely more precious—her own. She sits beside me as I write. If there is no bad spelling—such as you used to mock—I owe it to my lovely dictionary, which makes no mistakes, not even in the longest word. For I believe she is perfection.

“Since Madam Esmond reads all your letters, I dared not hint at a delicate matter—but now it is no secret, known throughout the country. Mr. George is not the only one in our family to make a secret marriage and be scolded by his mother. As a dutiful younger brother, I followed his example. Now I may tell you how it came to pass.

“I had not been home long before I saw my fate was sealed. I will not describe how beautiful Miss Fanny Mountain had become since I left for Europe. She says, ‘You’ll never believe it,’ and I’m glad—because she is the only thing in life I’d deny my dearest brother.

“That neither Madam Esmond nor my other mother (as Mountain is now) saw our attachment is a wonder—only explained by the fact that love makes others blind. My love for Fanny grew stronger seeing how she was treated by Madam Esmond, who was harsh and haughty. She bore it with sweetness so angelic (though she’ll order me not to write such nonsense). She was treated worse than a servant—our negroes speak more freely before Madam than Fanny ever could.

“And yet, Fanny says she does not regret it—for without it, I might never have become what I am to her. Oh, dear brother! When I recall your goodness—how you paid my debts, rescued me from prison, lived in poverty needlessly because of me, refused to reclaim what was rightfully yours, choosing my welfare over your own comfort—I am overwhelmed. Should I not thank Heaven for such a wife and such a brother?

“When I wrote asking you to send my aunt’s legacy, for a very urgent purpose, I had no idea you were yourself in poverty. That you, the head of our family, should serve as governor to a brewer’s son—that you should write for booksellers (except when your genius prompted you)—never entered my mind, until Mr. Foker’s letter arrived. It would never have been seen—Madam kept it hidden—had it not been for the disagreement between us.

“Poor Tom Diggle’s estate and slaves were for sale, due to his losses at play and his father’s debts. Madam Esmond saw this as a chance to provide for me. With six thousand pounds for land and stock, I could take possession of a fine property—near Richmond, between Kent and Hanover Court House. The house is not elegant compared to Castlewood, but the land is excellent, and the people remarkably healthy.

“This was a rare opportunity, Madam said—one that might never come again. By selling my commissions and using her savings, I could cover half the price, borrowing the rest. Money was scarce here, so it would be hard and costly. At this moment, with our new relative Mr. Van den Bosch bidding against us (his agent furious we might buy ahead of him), my aunt’s legacy arrived just in time. Now I am master of a good house and slaves in my native land. I shall likely be called to the House of Burgesses, and hope to welcome my dear brother and family beneath my roof. To sit by my own fire, ride my own horses, hunt with my own hounds—is better than soldiering now that war is over and no French to fight. Indeed, Madam Esmond insisted I leave the army and stay home when she gave me her 1750 pounds. She had lost one son who chose to write plays and live in England—let the other remain with her.

“But after buying the estate and sending papers to sell my commission, my mother wished me to marry someone of her choosing—certainly not my choice. Do you remember Miss Betsy Pitts of Williamsburgh? She is far worse than before, her face scarred by smallpox. Though Madam says she has every virtue, I find them unappealing. Her eyes don’t look straight; one leg is shorter than the other. And brother, did you never notice Fanny’s ankles when we were boys? Neater than any I’ve seen at the Opera.

“When it was decided I would leave the army, a certain dear girl—can you guess her name?—burst into tears of joy one day when we were alone. I could not help but feel deeply moved.

“‘Ah!’ she said, ‘Do you think the thought of your revered benefactress’s son going to battle doesn’t fill me with terror? Ah, Mr. Henry! Do you suppose I have no heart? When Mr. George was with Braddock, did we not pray for him? And when you were with Mr. Wolfe—oh!’

“Here she hid her face in her handkerchief, struggling not to let her mother see she was crying. But my dear Fanny insists she might have secretly hoped for such a thing (she admits it now), though she never imagined it for a moment. Nor did my mother, who thought Sam Lintot, the apothecary’s lad, was Fanny’s suitor—an absurd fellow I nearly kicked into the James River.

“But when the commission was sold and the estate bought, Fanny fell into deep melancholy. I found her weeping one day in her mother’s room, where they were trimming hats for my slaves.

“‘What! Crying, miss?’ I said. ‘Has my mother been scolding you?’

“‘No,’ she replied. ‘Madam Esmond was kind today.’

“And her tears fell upon a cockade she was sewing onto a hat for Sady, the head groom.

“‘Then why, miss, are your eyes so red?’ I asked.

“‘Because I have the toothache,’ she said, ‘or because—because I am a fool.’ Then she broke down. ‘Oh, Mr. Harry! Oh, Mr. Warrington! You’re leaving us, and it’s best. You’ll take your place in your country, as you should. You’ll leave us poor women in solitude and dependence. You’ll visit from time to time. And when you’re happy and honored, among your gay companions, you’ll remember your—’

“She could say no more, hiding her face as I, I confess, took her hand.

“‘Dearest, sweetest Miss Mountain!’ I said. ‘Oh, could I think the parting from me brings tears to those lovely eyes! Indeed, I fear I’d almost be happy! Let them look upon your—’

“‘Oh, sir!’ she cried. ‘Oh, Mr. Warrington! Consider who I am, and who you are! Remember the difference between us! Release my hand, sir! What would Madam Esmond say if—if—’

“‘If what?’ I asked, but our mother entered.

“‘What would Madam Esmond say?’ she cried. ‘She’d say you’re an ungrateful, artful, false, little—’

“‘Madam!’ I said.

“‘Yes, an ungrateful, artful, false, little wretch!’ she cried. ‘For shame, miss! What would Mr. Lintot say if he saw you making eyes at the Captain? And you, Harry, bring none of your garrison manners here! This is a Christian family, and my house is not for captains and their misses!’

“‘Misses, mother!’ I shouted. ‘Gracious powers, do you ever dare call Miss Mountain by such a name? Miss Mountain, the purest of her sex!’

“‘The purest of her sex! Can I trust my ears?’ she asked, turning pale.

“‘I mean,’ I said, ‘if anyone questioned her honor, I’d throw him out the window.’

“‘You mean you—your mother’s son—are actually paying honorable attention to this young person?’

“‘He would never dare offer anything else!’ Fanny cried. ‘Nor any woman but you, madam, to think so!’

“‘Oh, I didn’t know, miss!’ mother said, curtsying. ‘I didn’t know the honor you were doing our family! You propose to marry into us, do you? Do I understand Captain Warrington aright—that he intends to offer me Miss Mountain as a daughter-in-law?’

“‘It remains to be seen, madam, that I have no protector, or you would not insult me so!’ my poor victim said.

“‘I should think the apothecary protection sufficient!’ mother replied.

“‘I don’t, mother!’ I cried, furious. ‘And if Lintot offers her any liberty, I’ll brain him with his pestle!’

“‘Oh! If Lintot has withdrawn, sir, I suppose I must be silent. But I did not know. He came, as I thought, to court Miss—’ she paused. ‘We all thought the match equal, and I encouraged it.’

“‘He came because I had the toothache!’ Fanny said—and indeed she did. He pulled it out for her, and the rumors and suspicions of women know no end.

“‘What more natural than that he marry my housekeeper’s daughter? It was a suitable match!’ Madam continued, taking snuff. ‘But I confess,’ she added, ‘I didn’t know you intended to jilt the apothecary for my son!’

“‘Peace, for Heaven’s sake, peace, Mr. Warrington!’ my angel cried.

“‘Pray, sir, before you decide, had you not better look around my family?’ Madam said. ‘Dinah is a tall girl, not very dark; Cleopatra is promised to Ajax the blacksmith, but we could break it. If with an apothecary, why not a blacksmith? Martha’s husband has run away, and—’

“Here, dear brother, I confess I broke out swearing. I can’t help it—when a man is angry, oaths relieve him.

“‘Curses, blasphemy, ingratitude, disobedience!’ mother said, leaning on her tortoiseshell stick, waving it like a queen in a play. ‘These are my rewards!’ she cried. ‘O Heaven, what have I done to deserve this punishment? Does God visit the sins of my fathers upon me? Where do my children inherit their pride? When I was young, did I have any? Did I refuse my father’s choice? Did I ever disobey? No, sir. My fault, I admit, was loving you too much—perhaps neglecting your elder brother. I turned from Esau, clung to Jacob. And now I have my reward! I fixed my thoughts on this world, its honors. To see my son advanced was my ambition. I toiled, spared, to give him wealth. I took unfairly from my eldest son’s share, so my younger might prosper. And now—now I see him seducing the daughter of my housekeeper under my own roof, and answering my just anger with oaths and blasphemies!’

When my mother learned that I had accepted a position in England, I sensed her displeasure. It was not beyond her to cut off my allowance—perhaps even to starve me into submission, forcing me back to Virginia and under her control. Yet we never spoke plainly of the financial rift between us. She withdrew her support; I said nothing. I lived on what I could manage without her aid. I never heard her express regret or acknowledge injustice—except through Harry’s quiet words to me later. Years passed, and when we met again, she treated my wife with such unexpected kindness and affection that I thought it might be her way of admitting she had been wrong. But she never apologized, nor did I ask for one.

Harry, now secure in his own life, had always been a concern to her. With him settled, all her savings and careful plans were directed toward me, her heir. Once, a few guineas would have meant more than hundreds I might one day inherit. But by the time Madam Esmond and I crossed paths again, necessity was long behind me. I no longer needed to pinch pennies or begrudge the doctor’s fee. I had enough—and more could only add to it. I suspect she suffered privately, knowing her grandchildren had gone hungry while she turned away from them, proud and unyielding. Proud? Was she prouder than I? A simple word of understanding might have healed us years sooner—but neither of us spoke. When I do wrong and later see it clearly, I often seek forgiveness—not for others’ sake, but for my own peace. To apologize is to reclaim something lost within myself. And so, perhaps out of pride in that inner self, I’ve rarely stooped to acts of humility.

I showed no sign of surrender to my mother in Virginia. We lived apart for years, exchanging only brief messages—births, deaths, little things—passed between my wife and her. After our troubles in America over the Stamp Act, new trials came to me in London. Though I stood with the Tory side in the dispute—believing the Crown had full right to tax the colonies—I wrote an outspoken letter to a member of the House of Burgesses in Virginia. It questioned the long-standing arrogance of Britain toward its colonies, and expressed views so unpalatable to those in power that I lost my post as hackney-coach licenser. My uncle was horrified. He could never abide anyone disgraced. He adored my wife and our son, but toward me he held a pitying disdain that amused me deeply. He loathed poverty and admired success above all. Any deviation from convention frightened him; truth-telling made him pale. Yet despite everything I did to shock him, he continued to visit Theo and the child—and even me, offering a solemn nod when we met. He saw me not as a man, but as a broken creature beyond redemption.

Still, I pressed on. The repayment of Harry’s debt gave me breathing room. I could live, at least for a season. How strange youth seems now! How bold we were, so poor and yet so unshaken.

Then came the death of His Majesty’s royal uncle, the Duke of Cumberland. Strangely, his passing marked a turning point in my fortune. Sir Miles Warrington, ever eager for courtly affairs, missed no ceremony. He attended christenings, balls, funerals—any event where nobility gathered. When the duke died, he insisted on attending the funeral, standing bareheaded in the rain. He caught a chill, developed throat inflammation, and soon after, a lawyer arrived at my lodgings in Bloomsbury—bearing a formal salutation: “Sir George Warring-ton.”

The storm had passed. The rocks were avoided. The ship had found harbor. We laid Sir Miles to rest beside his young son in the family churchyard, where generations of our name lie buried. Little Miles and I were chief mourners. The tenants bowed low and curtsied, eager to win favor from the new master. The dowager and her daughter retreated to Bath. I took possession of the house—a home I would rule for thirty years.

“Do not hurry, my son,” I once said. “Have patience. One day, I too shall sleep beneath those yew trees, and the people will cheer for Sir Miles.”

The records of a peaceful country life are simple. The steward’s ledgers show rents paid and forgiven, crops grown in rotation. Visitors who came, how long they stayed. The pensioners my wife cared for, their illnesses, their deaths. The year I served as sheriff, the hunts near our gates—all these are written in our household journals, waiting for any heir who chooses to read.

We couldn’t afford the grand mansion in Hill Street my predecessor had occupied. Instead, we chose a smaller house, though we spent more on it. We made less display—no liveries, no lavish carriages, no silver plate like my uncle’s. But our beer was stronger, and my wife’s charities more generous than the dowager’s ever were. No doubt she believed there was no harm in spoiling the Philistines. She charged exorbitant prices for the goods left behind—potted plants in the greenhouse, a dreadful old spinet in the drawing-room, framed needlework by Dora and Flora, which she valued as if they were Titian masterpieces. Still, I paid without complaint. We were kinder to the poor than she had been. Yet for a time, we earned the worst reputation in the county. Whispers followed me—stories of cruelty, of mismanagement.

I had hoped to succeed my uncle in Parliament. But I discovered, somehow, that I was seen as dangerously radical. I refused to bribe. I refused to force my tenants to vote for me in the election of ’68. A man from Whitehall arrived with a pocketful of banknotes—proof I had no chance against my opponent.

Ah, well! Now that we were secure, now that tenants bowed before us and we rode in the great family coach with four fat horses—did we not sometimes miss poverty? Did I not long for the dear little cottage at Lambeth, where Want always lingered at the door? Did I not wish to return to bear-leading, or to translate books for publishers—work I once thought drudgery?

When we visited London, we made sentimental pilgrimages to our old haunts. My wife embraced every landlady she remembered. We invited friends from those days to share our new life. The Reverend Mr. Hagan and his wife came more than once. His sermon at B------ caused quite a scandal. Sampson, another unfortunate Levite, was welcomed as long as he wished to stay. Mr. Johnson mentioned coming—but delayed, then disappeared. Perhaps our house was dull. I know I grew silent for days. My moodiness must have tried even the sweetest woman in the world.

I cared little for field sports. Killing one partridge seemed no different from another. I marveled how men could spend days chasing such slaughter. Their fox-hunting tales began at four o’clock, lasting until supper. I sat silent. I listened. Day after day, I fell asleep. No wonder I was unpopular.

What confession am I making? Here, the storm is past. The ship has reached port. And yet, am I truly content? Was Susan—the woman I longed for across the sea—really the beauty I expected? Let her look in William’s logbook. I won’t write secrets there. No, Susan, I never kept secrets from you. I never loved another. I’ve seen greater beauty, but none who suited me as you did. I’ve met Mrs. Carter, Miss Mulso, Mrs. Thrale, Madam Kaufmann, the angelic Gunnings, the Duchess of Devonshire—and many others far less divine. But none dazzled me.

Yes, young folks, I may have made your mother’s life weary. I may have been a Bluebeard—though I had no other heads in the closet. But once the crown was placed upon my head, I soon grew tired of wearing it. The captain wears it differently. He rides five days a week, finds sport thrilling. He’d hear the same sermon fifty times and not yawn. But I—sweet Joan, beloved Baucis—your faithful husband and true lover—am ashamed of being testy. Arrived at happiness, Philemon asks pardon for falling asleep so often after dinner.

There came a time when I reached the peak of joy—and found myself bored. I yawned in Eden. “Is this all?” I asked. “No lions to bite? No rain to fall? No thorns in the rosebush? Only Eve, forever sweet, and figs for breakfast, dinner, supper—week after week?”

Shall I confess? Listen.

* * * * * *

Here three pages are torn from Sir George Warrington’s manuscript. The editor regrets the loss.

I understand the rites and practices of the Roman Church. But raised in a different faith—and skeptical by nature—I cannot help questioning whether Catholics truly confess all. Do Protestants? Has education made them so different? Among us, we don’t assume Catholic priests or laymen are more open than ourselves. Which brings me back: does any man confess all?

Does the woman beside me know everything about my life? She has shared it for thirty years. Whenever I’ve spoken of sorrow, she’s soothed it with gentle grace. When I’ve been silent, she’s remained still—or worn smiles, pretending ease, so I might believe she felt no care. Oh, the dear hypocrite! Have I not watched her hide the boys’ mischief from me? Have I not known she secretly spent from the household to cover their small debts? She’d talk to me with an artless face, as if unaware our revered captain had dealings with gentlemen in Duke’s Place, or our learned collegian had urgent reasons to wear oak at term’s end against university tradesmen.

From the very beginning, you wise woman, you’ve concealed things from me—this one stealing jam, that one failing at school, that rebellious boy throwing an inkstand at mamma in rage, while I was told only the gown and carpet were ruined by accident.

We all hide. We all carry secrets. We are all alone. We sin in silence—and, let us hope, repent.

She would give her foot to spare mine a twinge of gout. But when I suffer, the pain is in my slipper.

At the end of novels or plays, heroes marry or die—and the poet huzzas, or shovels them into the grave. But when Mr. Random and Mr. Thomas Jones wed, is it truly over? Are there no quarrels at home? No Lady Bellastons abroad? No constables to outrun? No temptations to conquer—or be conquered by?

The Sirens sang after Ulysses long after his marriage. The suitors whispered in Penelope’s ear. They endured doubt and fear—and so do we all.

Money troubles ended with my inheritance. But does Atra Cura sit behind baronets as well as equites? My London friends congratulated me on my happiness. Who wouldn’t want a good house, a good estate? But can Gumbo shut the hall door on blue devils? Can claret drown them forever? Does a man sleep better with twenty-four hours to doze? Do his thoughts brighten after a sermon from the dull vicar, ten minutes of flattery from the village apothecary, or the conversation of Sir John and Sir Thomas with their ladies, who travel muddy miles to eat a haunch and play a rubber?

It’s pleasant to have tradesmen bow at your carriage door, a place at quarter-sessions, your wife taken down second or third to dinner. But pleasures fade. They bring inconveniences.

For seven years after we came to Warrington Manor, our two best neighbors were Lord Tutbury and Sir John Mudbrook. We are older than the Mudbrooks—so Lady Tutbury fell to my lot when we dined together. She was deaf and slept after dinner. If I had Lady Mudbrook, she chattered incessantly, so foolishly that even my wife—consummate hypocrite as she is—could barely keep her composure, knowing I seethed.

In London, I consulted Dr. Heberden. I listed my complaints. “Psha, my dear Sir George!” he said. “Headaches, languor, bad sleep, bad temper—” (“Not bad temper,” my wife interjected. “Sir George has the sweetest temper in the world—only sometimes melancholy.”) “Bad sleep, bad temper,” the doctor repeated. “My dear lady, his inheritance has been his ruin. A little poverty and much work would do him more good than all this.”

No, Harry should have been squire—then my son Miles. Harry’s letters were full of joy. His estate thrived. His slaves multiplied. His crops were bountiful. He was a member of the House of Burgesses. He adored his wife. If only he could have a child, his happiness would be complete.

Had Hal been master here, he would have been loved throughout the land. He’d have been steward at races, the liveliest hunter, welcome at every mansion where my glum face was scarcely greeted.

As for my wife—everyone liked her. Everyone pitied her. Somehow, the rumor spread: I treated her cruelly, jealous as Bluebeard. Ah, me. It is true—I have had dark hours. Days of silence. Conversations with fools make me irritable. When I feel contempt, I often fail to conceal it.

I hope I grow more charitable with age. Because I do not love bawling after a fox like the captain, I am not his superior—but I humbly admit he is mine in that regard. He feels joys I cannot understand. Because I am blind, the world is not dark.

Now I try to listen when Squire Codgers speaks of the hunt. I strive to laugh at Captain Rattleton’s stories. I step up to the harpsichord with old Miss Humby and pretend to enjoy her ancient songs. I play whist, laboriously. Am I not doing my duty? And may I not be garrulous and egotistical, having read Montaigne all morning?

I was not surprised, knowing Harry’s inclinations, to find his name among the Virginia burgesses who declared that the sole right to tax the colony rests legally and constitutionally with the House of Burgesses—and called upon other colonies to pray for royal intervention in defense of American rights.

And it was then, after three years in our English home, that correspondence began between us and Madam Esmond. It was my wife who, with some feminine pretext, rekindled the connection. Our son Miles contracted smallpox—miraculously recovering without losing his beauty. Upon his recovery, his grandmother wrote the most charming letter to the child’s grandmother, filled with modest phrases and humble goodwill. She recounted anecdotes of the boy’s precocious genius (what became of that brilliant mind, I wonder?) and sent a lock of his hair—surely smuggled past Williamsburg customs.

In return, a gracious letter came from Lady Castlewood. She lamented the dangerous spirit spreading in the colony. She feared her son was associating with rebels. She could not blame him, given his advisers. How could a wife from a menial background sympathize with noble persons devoted to the Crown? If monarchy faced hard times—and the Americans refused taxes, demanding everything free—she recalled how the Esmonds, especially her father the Marquis, had always stood loyal.

She didn’t know what opinions were fashionable in England—though she might judge from my admiration for Lord Chatham. She prayed at least one of her sons was not on the side of rebellion.

Years later, reviewing old papers in Virginia, we found “Letters from my daughter Lady Warrington,” tied with ribbon. Theo insisted I not open them. The truth, I think, is they praised her husband so lavishly, she feared my vanity might suffer.

When Madam began writing, she shared brief news of Harry and his wife. “The two women,” she wrote, “still govern everything at Fannystown—how he calls his house. They must save money; I hear their hospitality is shabby. The Mount Vernon gentleman remains his close friend, and he votes as advised. Why he is so stingy, I cannot understand. Of five negroes sent with his equipages to Lord Bottetourt’s, only two wore shoes. I saved, because I had sons to provide for. He has no children—spared grief, though Heaven surely means our good through the trials it sends via our children.”

She added: “His mother-in-law has been ill. Since his marriage, poor Henry has become the puppet of these two clever women. They rule him entirely. Nothing, my dear daughter, is more contrary to sense and Scripture than this. Are we not told, ‘Wives, obey your husbands’? Had Mr. Warrington lived, I would have enforced that sacred law. Nothing becomes a woman more than humility and obedience.”

An appeal from our mother such as this would have softened even the hardest hearts—certainly ours, though we had grown somewhat stubborn with time. We spoke of making a swift journey to Virginia and hiring all the cabin space aboard the *Young Rachel*. But fate intervened: our child fell ill, and the voyage was deemed too perilous. A mother could not bear to part from her sick child, so the ship sailed without us that year.

The next season brought another obstacle—my worship’s first bout of gout, which occupied me deeply. It was a trial, but in truth, it cleared my mind and stirred new energy within me. Yet again, plans were postponed—this time by sorrowful news from Jamaica.

Some two years after we settled at the Manor, our dear General returned from his governorship. He came back slightly wealthier than when he left, yet burdened by a loss no riches could mend. He had chosen to leave the West Indies behind, unable to endure life without her. My Theo’s beloved mother—the most tender and devoted friend I ever knew, save one—had died abroad of fever. Her last regret was that she would not live to see her children and us prosper.

“She sees us now, even if we do not see her,” her husband said. “And she thanks you, George, for being kind to her children.”

We feared he would not long survive her. His love for her had shaped every moment of his life. To be parted from her was like living in exile. It pained us to watch him sit among us, quiet and withdrawn. My wife, in her manner, voice, and gestures, often reminded him of the woman he had lost. We did what we could to comfort him, but little Hetty became his greatest solace under Heaven.

She had refused several advantageous matches in the island, the General told us. When she returned to England, Lord Wrotham’s heir had laid himself at her feet. But she chose to remain with her father. “As long as he wants me,” she said, “I care for no husband.”

“Then let the General stay six months with us at the Manor,” we suggested. “You can have him at Oakhurst for the other half.”

But Hetty insisted her father could never return to Oakhurst now that her mother was gone—and she would marry no man for his title or fortune. Not she! The General, when we discussed it, said gravely that perhaps she had suffered some early disappointment, something she never spoke of. We respected her silence, and so did he.

By then, my brother Lambert had secured a college living near Winchester and, naturally, a wife to grace his parsonage. We welcomed her kindly, though we found ourselves only moderately fond of her. Mrs. Jack—a woman given to loud opinions and sharp tongues—was convinced Hetty’s refusal to marry stemmed not from grief, but from pride.

“My dear Sir George,” she declared, “I’ve told Theo many times I wouldn’t keep a pretty sister in my house just to make tea while I’m upstairs, or fetch things from the kitchen, or always look neat and dressed up when I’m baking pies or tending the children. I trust Jack completely—he’d never look at another woman, indeed! And I trust Jemima too—but they don’t come together in my house when I’m above stairs. That I promise!”

“And am I to understand,” the General asked coldly, “that you’ve done my Lady Warrington the favour of warning her against her sister—my daughter Miss Hester?”

“Yes, pa, of course I have. A duty is a duty. A woman is a woman. A man is a man, as I know very well. Don’t tell me otherwise! Every man is a man, no matter how sanctimonious he pretends to be!”

“You yourself have a married sister whom you were visiting when my son Jack first met you,” the General observed.

“Yes, of course I do. Everyone knows that. And I’ve been like a mother to her children, I have!”

“And are you suggesting your presence proved a temptation to her husband?”

“Law, General! How can you say such a thing? I never said anything like that!”

“Yet you imply it—about yourself, and about my daughters.”

“Never, never, never! As a Christian woman, I swear it! And it’s cruel of you to accuse me! I do say a sister is best out of the house—that I do! And since Theo’s time is coming, I warn her, that’s all.”

“Have you discovered,” the General pressed, “whether my poor Hetty has taken any of the silver spoons? This morning, when I came to breakfast, my daughter was alone, and there must have been a score of pieces on the table.”

“Law, sir! Who ever said a word about spoons? Did I accuse the poor dear? If I did, may I drop dead right here on this rug! And I won’t stand being spoken to like this! Jack and I both noticed it. I’ve done my duty, I have!” With that, Mrs. Jack stormed out, tears streaming down her face.

“And has this woman had the audacity to tell you this, my child?” the General asked, when Theo—delicate in health—joined us at tea.

“She tells me every day since she arrived. She comes into my dressing-room, my nursery—‘Ah, I wouldn’t have a sister prowling about my nursery!’ she says. How delightful it is to have such charming relatives, I say.”

“Your poor mother was spared this woman,” the General groaned.

“Our mother would have made her better, papa,” Theo replied, kissing him.

“Yes, dear.” And I saw them both fall into prayer.

It must be admitted: loving one’s kin is not always easy. Living with neighbours can be tedious. From Jack Lambert’s behaviour the next day, I knew his wife had shared her version of the exchange. He was sullen, not dignified. Angry, yet still hungry. He preached a sermon that was entirely dull. Little Miles, once more in mourning clothes, sat beside his grandfather, his small hand clasped in the old man’s.

Would he stay and manage the household during our trip to Virginia? The housekeeper would be under Hetty’s command. The butler’s keys would pass to him. Gumbo, who had married Mrs. Molly and raised a family of tawny children in my park, was to accompany us—not with great enthusiasm, I suspect.

Under the care of our General and his daughter, we left our home. We journeyed to London, then to Bristol, where our obedient agent professed prayers for our safety and declared that no children as beautiful as ours had ever graced a ship before. Our voyage passed without incident.

How strange it felt stepping ashore at Richmond! A coach waited, along with a host of negroes. Nearby, a gentleman on horseback, also attended by men in our livery, dismounted and rushed forward to embrace us. It was our dearest Hal. He rode with us to our mother’s door. There she stood on the steps, waiting. Theo knelt to receive her blessing.

Harry rode with us only as far as the house. He declined to enter with us. “She sees me,” he confessed, “and we’re fairly decent friends. But Fanny and she—well, they’re better apart. No love lost between them, I assure you. Come visit me at the Tavern when you’re free, George. Tomorrow I’ll present her sister to Theo. I only heard the ship was sighted yesterday—I stayed to see you. I sent a negro boy home to my wife; she’ll come to pay her respects to my Lady Warrington.” Then Harry leapt from the carriage and left us to meet our mother alone.

Since I had last seen her, I had encountered fine society—Theo and I had paid our respects to the King and Queen at St. James’s—but none compared to the dignity of the woman who greeted us now. I lifted my wife from her knees, embraced her, and led her inside. The house was plain, wood-built, with a gallery around it—typical of Virginian homes. Yet if it had been a palace with an empress within, our welcome could not have been more gracious.

Old Nathan remained major-domo. A dozen black faces grinned their greetings. Some I remembered as children were now strong young adults; others, once bald-headed, now wore silvery hair. Newborns peered from doorways, barefoot and wide-eyed. “I’m little Sip, Master George!” “I’m Dinah, Sir George!” “I’m Master Miles’s boy!” cried a lad in a new livery and boots polished with natural black.

Before the day ended, every servant had found a reason to pass before us, bowing and grinning. I cannot say how many meals were served. In the evening, my Lady Warrington received all the gentry of the town with perfect grace. I shook hands with a few old acquaintances—old enemies, I nearly said—but I had come into a fortune and was no longer the reckless prodigal.

A drove of fatted calves was slaughtered in my honour. Poor Hal attended the feast, but he looked glum and defeated. His mother spoke to him, but it was as a queen addressing a rebellious prince—her son, not yet forgiven.

Theo and I slipped away from the gathering and went to our rooms. Just as we began to talk freely, our mother appeared with a candle, her face pale. “Do you need anything? Is everything to your liking?” She had peeked in on the children, who slept like cherubs. She cooed over them, delighted by Miles’s commanding air and little Theo’s smiles and dimples. “Supper is ready, Sir George. If you prefer our cooking to the tavern’s, Henry, I beg you to stay.”

How different her tone was toward each of us! Hal lowered his head and followed silently to the dining room. A clergyman offered a blessing, speaking with skill and eloquence of our safe return, of God’s mercy through stormy seas, and of the divine forgiveness awaiting us when life’s tempests ceased.

This was a new clergyman—unlike those I remembered from earlier days. I praised him, but Madam Esmond shook her head. “I fear his principles are dangerous,” she whispered. “Others have adopted them. Have you seen the paper signed by the burgesses and merchants at Williamsburg last year—the Lees, Randolphs, Bassets, Washingtons… and oh, my dear, I hate to say it, our name—that is, your brother’s (by what influence I dare not speak), and that unfortunate Mr. Belman, who begged a blessing last night?”

If there had been disputes in our colonial society when I left, what were they compared to the feuds I found upon my return? We had sent the Stamp Act to America and repealed it. Then came new duties on glass, paper, and so on—also repealed, except for tea. From Boston to Charleston, tea was seized. Even my loyal mother gave up her favourite drink. My wife would have had to follow suit, but we had brought a private supply aboard, already taxed fourfold in England.

Not that I hesitated to pay duties. The home government needed revenue; without it, its authority was meaningless. They say the colonies were oppressed—I say the home government was tested and overwhelmed. [It is history now. We tried, and failed. The matter is settled as firmly as the Norman conquest of Britain.]

From conviction, I took the British side. In my brief military experience, the army’s cry was that Braddock’s expedition failed due to negligence, selfishness, and greed among those whose defence it was meant to protect. The colonists wanted everything done for them, yet did nothing. They made unfair deals with defenders, broke contracts, provided scant supplies, delayed action until it was too late. The disaster that followed need never have happened but for their indifference.

What joy erupted when the great British minister triumphed in conquering Canada! Monsieur de Vaudreuil was right: that victory marked the beginning of American rebellion. Lord Chatham, who helped achieve it, did more than anyone in England to complete it. The colonies revolted—and he cheered their defiance. How many wavering souls must he have encouraged? Like a general saying to a mutinous army, “God save the king! You have a right to rebel!” No wonder they erected his statue in one town, hung his portrait in another, and hanged governors in effigy elsewhere.

In Williamsburg, some proposed bringing over a portrait of Lord Chatham—dressed as a Roman orator, pointing to Whitehall and the window from which Charles I was executed. A clever allegory, and a flattering tribute to a British statesman! Though I hear the head was painted from a bust, so it was taken without his knowledge.

My country is England, not America or Virginia. I stood—and still do—on the English side. My heart belonged to home, where I was now a squire and citizen. Had I planted tobacco on the banks of the James or Potomac, my views might have changed. When I visited my brother at his new plantation, I found him and his wife as staunch Americans as we were Britons. We argued, as many did in those troubled times—but without bitterness. Even my new sister tried her best to inflame us, especially in private lectures she doubtless gave her husband. Yet we trusted each other so fully that even Harry’s loyalty to his wife could not make him quarrel with me.

He loved me from childhood, when my word was law. He still claimed every Virginian gentleman was loyal to the Crown. War had not yet begun. Gentlemen of differing views treated one another with courtesy. At public dinners, the King’s health was toasted loudly. Each colony’s assembly, though preparing for Congress and resisting taxation, expressed deep affection for the King as “our Father,” pleading with him to dismiss evil advisers and listen to reason.

Until the end, Virginia’s gentry remained grave, orderly, aristocratic—firm in their dignity. Later generations spoke of equality and fraternity. Among Europe’s nobility, I’ve never known a man who held his station with greater dignity than Mr. Washington—not even the King he fought against. To the French court, who rejoiced in their war against us for Canada, he was an *anax andron*—a true leader. They acknowledged no greater figure in Versailles.

Though they opposed the Governor, the House of Burgesses maintained respectful relations with him. When Lord Bottetourt arrived in splendour, all the gentry visited him, including Madam Esmond. At his death, Lord Dunmore succeeded him, bringing a fine family, and was treated with private respect—though publicly, the Assembly and Governor were at odds.

Their conflicts belong to history. For me, they mattered only because, the year after my arrival, the burgesses convened on March 1st. We decided to visit the capital and pay our respects to the Governor. Since Harry’s marriage, Madam Esmond had not performed this duty—though she had always done so before. Now, with her eldest son returned, she insisted we must attend. Perhaps we were glad to escape Richmond and enjoy the pleasures of the provincial capital.

Madam engaged, at great expense, the finest house in Richmond for herself and her family. Now I was rich—yet her generosity surprised me. I often had to intervene (her servants, too, puzzled by her new ways) and beg her not to spend so lavishly. But she gently replied that in former days she had needed to save—now she did not. Harry had enough, surely, with a wife taken from the housekeeper’s room. If she wished to be extravagant, why should she hesitate? She no longer had her dearest daughter and grandchildren with her every day—she adored them all and spoiled them beyond measure. Besides, in earlier years, I could never accuse her of extravagance. That, I believe, was her only reference to our financial differences.

So she dressed her people in their finest, shipped her best wines, plate, and furniture from Castlewood by sea—at great cost. She wore the dress she had worn at her wedding in George II’s reign. We believed our coach made the grandest impression—save the Governor’s. We hired Signor Formicalo, the Governor’s own major-domo, to oversee the feasts given in my honour. More fleshpots simmered in our kitchens in one month than had been seen in the family since the boys left.

Theo’s influence over our mother was so strong that she actually persuaded her to receive our sister Fanny—Hal’s wife—who would rather have stayed on the plantation than face Madam Esmond. But trusting Theo’s promise of forgiveness, Fanny came to town, curtsied, and was accepted.

Rather than be forgiven so, I confess I would have preferred damnation or lifelong persecution.

“You know these, my dear?” Madam Esmond asked, pointing to her silver sconces. “Fanny cleaned them often when she lived with me at Castlewood. And this dress—Fanny knows it, I daresay? Her poor mother cared for it. I always trusted her.”

A flash of anger lit Fanny’s eyes—eyes our mother, who had forgiven her, did not notice.

“Oh, she was a treasure to me!” Madam continued. “I could never have nursed my boys through illness without your mother’s care. Colonel Lee, permit me to introduce you to my daughter, my Lady Warrington. She is a neighbour of your relatives, the Bunburys, in England. Here comes his Excellency. Welcome, my lord!”

Our princess executed one of those elegant curtseys she prized. I fancied I saw a few guests suppress smiles.

“By George, madam,” said Mr. Lee, “since Count Borulawski, I’ve not seen a bow so graceful.”

“And pray, sir, who was Count Borulawski?” Madam asked.

“He was a nobleman in high favour with the Polish king,” Lee replied. “May I ask you, madam, to present me to your distinguished son?”

“This is Sir George Warrington,” Madam said, pointing to me.

“Pardon me, madam. I meant Captain Warrington, who stood by Mr. Wolfe when he died. I would have gladly shared his fate—so long as I stood near him.”

The ardent Lee stepped forward, took Harry’s hand with respect, and offered compliments. I forgave him his earlier impertinence. My dear Hal walked through his mother’s rooms in his old uniform, the same he had worn in the famous regiment he had left behind.

We had met often—moments the stern mother could not break—where the instinctive bond between us, unshakable and deep, could speak freely. Though utterly different in tastes, pursuits, and opinions—his life full of sport and fieldwork, mine spent in books and quiet reflection—we shared a sympathy deeper than any woman’s love. My poor Hal confessed as much to me, simply and honestly, when we left wives and women behind and spent a week together at Castlewood.

What strange twist of fate has it been that I should always find myself standing apart, outnumbered, and out of step? Were a law proposed to surrender this realm to the Pretender in Rome or even to the Grand Turk—were we to bow our heads to a foreign faith—I am certain I would be the one voting against it. Yet in my own home, in Virginia, I found myself no less isolated. The Patriots called me a Tory, though I confessed myself one; the Tories, in turn, branded me a dangerous Republican. The world seemed turned upside down.

No sooner had I settled into Virginia than I longed for the banks of the Waveney, for the quiet life I had left behind. But events were too turbulent to allow such a retreat. My mother, alone and vulnerable, could not be abandoned to face war and ruin. Nor would she leave her homeland at such a time. And so, as any man of spirit must, I stayed. At His Excellency’s table, over glasses of rich claret, many like-minded souls vowed allegiance to the Crown. “We are all Cavaliers,” they declared, “and we will stand by the standard!” Governor Dunmore spoke with fire and pride, and his words stirred us all.

Of all those I came to know in Virginia, none stood more firmly in her convictions than Madam Esmond. When news reached Williamsburg of the Boston Port Bill, a wave of outrage swept through the colony. The House of Burgesses passed a formal protest, declaring a day of fasting and prayer, beseeching Heaven to avert civil war. Yet the ball for the Governor’s lady had already been announced and accepted. The gentlemen decided to proceed with the event, then don sackcloth and ashes afterward.

“*A ball!*” exclaimed Madam Esmond. “I shall not attend a celebration hosted by rebels who will soon publicly insult His Majesty! I would rather die!” She wrote to the stewards, explaining that given the perilous state of the nation, she could not, in good conscience, participate.

Imagine her surprise when, on her next outing in her chair, she was greeted by a hundred people—white and black alike—shouting, “Huzzah, Madam! Heaven bless your ladyship!” They believed her refusal to go to the ball was an act of patriotism. To make sure there was no misunderstanding, she leaned out of the carriage and shouted, “God save the King!” The crowd echoed her cry. In those days, “God save the King” rang from every tongue.

On the night of the ball, my poor Harry, now a Burgess and one of the hosts, donned his red coat—once worn by Wolfe—and went off with Madam Fanny. My Lady Warrington and I, being strangers and Englishmen, were permitted to attend, though Madam Esmond refused to join. I had the honor of dancing a country dance with the lady of Mount Vernon, whom I found charming and lively. But when my wife recounted the evening to my mother, the old lady received her praise with a grim silence. “Could not Sir George have danced with my Lady Dunmore or her daughters?” she muttered. “Why must he choose Mrs. Washington? She once surveyed roads for a guinea a day!”

Indeed, the pride of these provincial upstarts knew no bounds. And what was worse, Lord Dunmore’s favor toward Sir George had clearly inflated his head. I cannot speak for Mr. Washington’s pride—but I do know that my mother never warmed to him or anything belonging to him. She disapproved of his attending the ball, and even more so three days later, when he joined the service held on the appointed day of fast and humiliation.

That day, she invited Mr. Belman and several colonial officials to dinner. The clergyman excused himself. Madam Esmond tossed her head. “Let him do as he pleases,” she said. She made a show of a grand dinner, lighting her house while the rest of Williamsburg remained dark and somber. She begged Mr. Hardy, one of His Excellency’s aides, to sing “God save the King.” The people outside listened, thinking it part of some religious observance. Then she called for “Britons, strike home!” The young gentleman, fresh from Europe, began to sing—when suddenly a great yell rose from the street, and a stone crashed into the punch bowl before me, scattering its contents across the room.

My mother rushed to the window, undaunted. I can still see her—small, stiff, arms outstretched in her frilled sleeves—singing in full voice: “Britons, strike home! strike home!” The crowd roared back: “Silence! For shame! Go back!” But she would not yield. “Throw more stones if you dare!” she challenged.

Gentlemen from the Raley Tavern stepped forward, calming the mob. “You mustn’t insult a lady,” someone said—a voice I thought I recognized. “Huzza, Colonel! Hurrah, Captain! God bless your honour!” the crowd cried, and the disturbance ended.

My mother insisted the evening was over and urged Mr. Hardy to sing another song. But he gave a weak smile and said, “I really don’t care to sing to such accompaniments.” The music ceased. Yet that night, scoundrels returned, terrified my wife nearly out of her wits, and shattered every window in our front façade. “Britons, strike home!”—it was perhaps too much. She should have stuck to “God save the King.”

Meanwhile, militia drilled, bullets were cast, ammunition stockpiled, and schemes devised to thwart royal orders. But everywhere, “God save the King” was still the cry. When I objected to the patriots’ plans, warning them they were courting separation and bringing down the wrath of the greatest power on earth, their answer was always the same: “We mean no separation. We are loyal Britons. We glory in our name.” So they claimed.

The powder barrels were stacked in cellars, the fuse laid—but Mr. Fawkes, in his duty, only petitioned the King and Parliament, meaning no harm. True, when I spoke of British strength, I assumed it would be used wisely. I never imagined we’d try to crush three million fellow Britons with a few battalions, half a dozen generals from Bond Street, and thousands of German mercenaries. Why must we send Hessians and Indian warriors to fight our own people? Was our great quarrel to be fought with foreign auxiliaries and savage allies?

Ah, now that we’ve lost, it is easy to point to maps and say how things should have been. Long Island could have destroyed Washington’s army. He should never have escaped Valley Forge alive. The South was ours after Camden—if only the Commander-in-Chief at New York hadn’t interfered, paralyzing the only capable British general, sending him into the trap at Yorktown, where he could only surrender.

Oh, for one more week, one more day, one more hour of darkness or light! Now, reviewing our American campaigns—from their ill-fated start to their dishonorable end—we can see how a single march, a single advance, might have brought the enemy to our mercy.
