But it was ordained by Heaven, and for the good of both empires, that the Western Republic should break away. And the gallant soldiers who fought for her—above all, her indomitable leader—earned glory not just by facing seasoned troops well-supplied and battle-hardened, but by enduring starvation, cold, betrayal, and disunity within their own ranks. Only the unquenchable flame of patriotism kept them going.

What constancy! What magnanimity! What perseverance against fortune! On the battlefield, Washington was no greater than hundreds who fought beside or against him—many mocked him as “Fabius.” But as commander of a nation in arms, leading divided factions, calm amid conspiracy, serene before open foes and hidden enemies, inspiring order into ragged, hungry troops, stung by ingratitude yet never showing anger, forgiving constantly, invincible in defeat, generous in victory—never more sublime than when he laid down his sword and retired to peace—here was a man worthy of admiration and reverence. A life without stain, a fame without flaw. *Quando invenies parem?*

In the larger work I have begun on this great war, I hope I have done justice to his character. [And I trust that in expressing my opinions about him, I have shown fairness and generosity—even toward those who view me with hostility. For my brother Hal, visiting Mount Vernon, showed General Washington some early pages of my history. Though the General read little and cared nothing for literature, he remarked: “If you’ll have my opinion, my dear General, I think Sir George’s projected work, from the specimen I’ve seen, is certain to offend both parties.”—G.E.W.] This came not from bias, but from respect for his virtues.

With the young Mr. Washington of my youth, I never shared much sympathy. My brother, more open-hearted than I, was his close friend in early days—when they were equals—and later, when the General, as I confess, became the superior of all mankind.

I have spoken of the contradictions in our natures—the traits that placed us on opposing sides in the coming conflict, which raged for five years until the mother country acknowledged defeat. Harry should have been the Tory, and I the Whig. Theoretically, my views were far more liberal than his. After his marriage, he became what our Indian nabobs call a Bahadoor—ceremonious, proud, demanding respect.

When Lord Dunmore suggested freeing the slaves to rally them to the King’s cause, Hal wanted to hang the Governor and his Black Guards. “If you’re fighting for freedom,” I said, “then surely the negroes may fight too.” Harry roared, shaking his fist: “Infernal villains! If I meet one, they’ll die by this hand!” My mother agreed—this idea of slave rebellion was the most abominable, parricidal notion ever born in her land. She was more consistent than Harry. She demanded obedience from both black and white. Harry, however, admitted freedom only for the latter.

To prove her point, both Madam Esmond and Harry pointed to Gumbo, a servant in our household. Having earned his freedom from me as a reward for loyalty during hard times, Gumbo returned to Virginia—only to be unwelcome among my mother’s servants. He was free; they were not. He strutted like a king among them, boasting of his friends in England (“at home,” as he called it), his adventures abroad. He drew the others around him, like a monkey who’d seen the world.

Sady, Hal’s boy, who had come to America of his own will, was not free. Jealousy flared between him and Gumbo, leading to frequent boxing matches—learned at Marybone Gardens and Hockley-in-the-Hole. Sady was not alone in his resentment. Nearly all the servants hated Gumbo for his airs. Even Molly, his wife, was jealous—though she was faithful to him. The blacks despised her for marrying one of their kind. She received no respect, could not command, and constantly complained to my mother about theft, laziness, lies among the other servants. Finally, she accused Gumbo of jealousy toward Dinah—or Diana—whom I hope was as innocent as the moonlight visitor of Endymion.

Madam Esmond, in matters of morality, was a Draconess. Accused, one was guilty. She charged Gumbo, who responded angrily. Forgetting he was a free man, she ordered him whipped. Molly flew at her, her fury over her husband’s supposed infidelity replaced by rage at the indignity. Rebellion broke out in Castlewood.

I sided with Gumbo. Hal and Fanny supported my mother. This disagreement, though brief, brought a rare closeness between Madam and her younger children. But it was clear the symbol of insurrection had to leave. We decided Gumbo and Molly would return to Europe.

My wife and I wished to go with them—God knows, our son was sickly, weakened by fever in the swampy land. But my wife was expecting our second child, Henry, and I had promised to remain. We agreed to send them. When I offered Theo to accompany them, she refused—her place was with her husband. Her father and Hetty would care for the children. I barely saw a tear in her eyes as she prepared them for departure.

Do you remember, madam, the silence in the sewing rooms as tiny shirts were folded for the journey? The secret visits to the children’s beds while they slept? The heartbreak of parting, as our barge carried servants and children to the ship, and you stood on shore?

Had the Prince of Wales sailed on that voyage, he could not have been better provided. Where, sirrah, is the Tompion watch your grandmother gave you? And how did you survive the boxes of cakes the good lady packed into your cabin?

The ship that carried my poor Theo’s children returned with the Reverend Mr. Hagan and my Lady Maria, who humbly resigned her title and was known simply as Mrs. Hagan in the colony—soon to be no colony at all.

When I was in favor with Lord Dunmore, he granted a living in Westmoreland County to our kinsman, who arrived in time to christen our son Henry and preach sermons on the dire state of affairs—sermons Madam Esmond pronounced “prodigious fine.”

I believe Lady Maria won her heart by insisting on leaving the room after her. “My father was an earl,” she said, “but you know your ladyship is a marquis’s daughter. I could never claim precedence over you.” So fond did Madam become of her niece that she allowed Hagan to read plays—even mine—and admitted, grudgingly, that my tragedy *Pocahontas* had merit, especially when delivered with passion by our parson.

Hal and Fanny rarely visited Castlewood or Richmond while the chaplain and his wife were with us. Fanny was curt and rude to Maria, giggling strangely in her presence, reminding her repeatedly of her age—much to my mother’s confusion. “Is there any quarrel between my niece and my daughter-in-law?” she would ask.

I kept silent, moved by the quiet endurance of the elder woman. Fanny loved to torment her in front of her husband—poor fellow, blissfully ignorant of his wife’s past. The other bore it with stoicism, wincing only slightly.

I often reproached Madam Harry: “Are you a Red Indian, that you torture your victims so?”
“Have I not suffered enough?” she replied, her eyes hard.
“Nay,” I said, “you were raised in our wigwam. I remember only kindness.”
“Kindness!” she cried. “No slave was ever treated as I was. The deepest wounds are those never aimed. Those who hate us are not the ones we’ve wronged.”

I thought of little Fanny in our childhood—silent, smiling, eager to run errands for us. And I grieved for my poor brother, who had taken this sly creature into his heart.

In the days when Britain ruled over its American colonies, one of the many uses we found for the New World was to send our unwelcome citizens there—those whose misdeeds or misfortunes made them unfit for life in the old country. Convicts, indentured servants, and younger sons who had outlived their welcome were shipped across the Atlantic, along with those whose debts and vices had driven them from England’s courts and homes. We sent them not as exiles, but as settlers, hoping they would start anew among the wilds and forests of Virginia, Maryland, and beyond. In this way, we exported not only men, but also the flaws of our society—like sending a specimen of English folly to be studied in foreign soil.

I myself may have played a small part in such an enterprise. I once helped secure a living in America for Hagan, husband of my cousin—the worthy man whom I knew to be honest and devout. Though he could find no place in England, I arranged for him to take up a pulpit in Virginia. He proved himself a loyal minister to his flock and to the Crown, fulfilling his duties with integrity. When Madam Theo heard of my hesitation on the matter, she reminded me that my actions were guided by principle, not prejudice. And perhaps she was right. Yet I confess—I would never have given him our parish at home. Nor would I have chosen him and his wife to serve our own community. I believed in Maria’s sincerity, yes—but I confess I was secretly relieved when she left for the wilderness. Such is the pride that stains even the noblest hearts.

Maria was not alone in being sent away. Another of our family, the Honourable William Esmond, Esquire, had long since exhausted every avenue of respectability in England. After borrowing, stealing, and cheating until nothing remained to take, he was dispatched to New York. His noble brother, Lord Castlewood, was glad enough to see the back of him. But soon after the troubles began, news reached us of what he was doing in his new home.

Lies and mischief followed William wherever he went. My Lord Dunmore informed me that William had publicly declared our estate of Castlewood belonged not to us, but to him—only so long as his brother pleased to allow it. He claimed that our father, out of affection for Madam Esmond, his half-sister, had granted her the estate for life—and now, he said, he was negotiating with Lord Castlewood to buy the reversion! It was a bold falsehood. The deed was safely stored at Castlewood and officially registered in Williamsburg. Still, the intent behind the lie was dangerous. Hal and I resolved, should we ever meet William, to force him into confirming his own absurd tale.

Madam Esmond’s reaction, when she heard it, was fierce. “What!” she exclaimed. “My father, the Marquis of Esmond, was a liar? And I am a cheat?” She raged that William would steal her son’s inheritance upon her death. She threatened to write not only to Lord Castlewood in London, but to His Majesty himself at St. James’s. Only my assurance—that William’s lies were common knowledge, and that no one expected him to tell the truth—prevented her from taking such drastic steps.

Soon we learned that William had become one of the most vocal Loyalists in New York. He rose to the rank of Captain, then Major, in a volunteer corps, sending letters of loyalty to every colony and declaring his readiness to die for the mother country. Meanwhile, in Virginia, the situation grew more tense. We could scarcely stay in a house without fear of unrest. Madam Esmond shut the shutters of our hired mansion in Williamsburg and fled to Richmond, where the Assembly had already dissolved. Captain Hal and his wife returned early to their plantation. I, increasingly uneasy about the course of events, divided my time between my own household and that of the Governor, who welcomed my counsel despite our differing political views.

Though tensions ran high, personal animosity had not yet taken root. Even after the Assembly disbanded—its members gathering in a tavern to discuss forming a continental congress—we still maintained friendly relations with the Governor. Gentlemen of opposing views dined together, hunted side by side, and shared the pleasures of the season. Once the session ended, the gentry returned to their counties and held meetings. With Assemblies dissolved across the colonies, it was agreed that a general congress must be convened. Philadelphia, the largest city on the continent, was chosen as the meeting place. There, the debates began—angry, passionate, and unmistakably the prelude to war.

We still professed loyalty to the King. Petitions were drafted, prayers offered. But when I visited my brother Harry at Fanny’s Mount—his new plantation near ours, separated by the Rappahannock River and close to Mattaponey—events took a turn I could not ignore.

One morning, Harry rode out on business. That afternoon, I decided to ride as well. One of the grooms told me he’d seen Master heading toward Willis’s Ordinary. Thinking nothing of it, I followed. Emerging from the woods onto a clear stretch of land near Willis’s, I came upon a surprising sight: Captain Hal on horseback, surrounded by thirty or forty men, armed with pikes, scythes, muskets, and fowling pieces. He stood with several young officers, drilling them in formation.

As I approached, a strange look crossed Hal’s face. “Present arms!” he commanded, and the ragged troop attempted the salute. “Captain Cade,” Hal said, “this is my brother, Sir George Warrington.”

“Colonel,” replied the captain, “as a relation of yours, the gentleman is welcome.” He extended his hand.

“And—” Hal added, flushing slightly—“a true friend to Virginia.”

“Yes, God willing!” I said.

At that, the entire group erupted in cheers, huzzaying for the Colonel and his brother.

After the drill, the men urged a drink at Willis’s, but Hal declined. We rode home together in silence for a while.

“So,” I said finally, “the cat’s out of the bag.”

He gave me a hard stare. “There are wilder cats in the basket,” he replied. “It must come to this, George. And you mustn’t tell Madam.”

“Good God,” I cried, “do you mean to say you’re preparing to fight the greatest nation and finest army in the world—with men like those?”

“We’ll likely get thrashed,” Hal admitted, “but then, George”—he smiled gently—“we’re young. A good whipping might do us good. Won’t it, Dolly?” He flicked his whip playfully at an old dog trotting beside him.

I did not try to argue further. I had done so before, in vain. I tried to appeal to reason—to the British cause, to duty, to the strength of the Crown. But Hal always replied the same way: “All mighty well, brother. You speak as an Englishman, and have cast your lot with your country—as I have with mine.”

And truly, there was no answer to that. The argument led only to conflict. Who had the right in the wars of the last century? The King or Parliament? The victor claimed it. And history showed that the victor, though often harsh, was usually more humane than the defeated might have been. Suppose, I thought, that the Tories had won in America—what horrors would have followed? What gallows, what executions? It was a chilling thought. I stood with the Crown, yet I found myself wishing the Whigs would prevail.

Hal, meanwhile, fought with honor. He never spoke ill of the enemy. “The officers of the British army,” he said, “are gentlemen—at least, I’ve not heard they’ve changed much since my time. There may be scoundrels among their ranks, as there are among ours. Our job is to beat His Majesty’s forces—not slander them. Any fool can do that.”

Because of a nickname given by Mr. Lee—“Chevalier Baird”—he became known throughout the Continental army. He was indeed a knight: fearless, upright, without reproach.

When I asked how such a motley crew could possibly stand against the British army, Hal answered with quiet confidence. “They can beat them,” he said. “That’s what they can do.”

“Great heavens!” I exclaimed. “You mean you’d lead that rabble against five hundred trained soldiers?”

“With my company of the 67th,” he replied, “I’d go anywhere. I admit, I know more about soldiering than they do. But suppose I’m placed on that open ground where you found us—armed as you please, with half a dozen friends hiding in the woods with rifles. Which side wins? You know best, Mr. Braddock’s aide-de-camp.”

There was no arguing with such resolve.

“You know my thoughts, Hal,” I said. “And since I’ve stumbled upon your secret, I must inform the Governor.”

“Tell him, of course,” Hal said calmly. “You’ve seen our county militia training. You’ll see the same in every colony from Georgia to the Saint Lawrence. As an old soldier, they elected me colonel. What else could I do? Come, brother—let’s ride on. Dinner will be ready, and Mrs. Fan doesn’t like me to keep it waiting.”

So we rode to his house—a wide-open dwelling, typical of Virginian gentlemen, where every friend, neighbor, and stranger was welcomed with warmth.

“So, Mrs. Fan,” I said as we entered, “I’ve discovered what game your husband has been playing.”

“I trust the Colonel will have plenty of sport ere long,” she replied, tossing her head.

My wife thought Harry had been hunting. I did not correct her. But what I had seen—and what Hal had confessed—left me deeply troubled.

When my visit to my brother had ended, and my wife and child had returned to our family home in Richmond, I made it my duty to travel to Williamsburg, where our Governor resided at his country estate, to discuss the mounting signs of war that were spreading across the colonies. Rumors of armed conflict reached us from every corner—Massachusetts stood on the brink of open hostilities with British troops; Maryland and Pennsylvania still seemed inclined toward loyalty; the Carolinas and Georgia remained firmly aligned with the Crown; and Virginia, proud of its heritage and ancient allegiance, was expected to stand firm. Though we had few regular troops, our gentry prided themselves on their descent from the Cavaliers, and around the Governor gathered a throng of zealous Loyalists eager to draw sword against what they called the rebellious rabble.

At these gatherings, I could not avoid hearing harsh words about my brother Harry. All agreed—perhaps justly—that his wife had influenced him toward extreme anti-British views. He was said to be blindly devoted to the gentleman of Mount Vernon, whose opinions Harry followed closely, and who daily deepened himself in the perilous path of resistance. “This is your friend,” the Governor’s circle would say, “the man you once trusted, who shared your table and your confidence!” Much of this was true, though what some called treason was really nothing more than a desperate desire to preserve loyalty to the Crown, to exhaust every avenue of reconciliation before embracing revolt.

Let traitors arm! Let villains raise the parricidal blade! We, at least, would remain faithful. England’s strength would prevail, and the wayward provinces would be punished and brought back into submission. After our banquets, we toasted His Majesty with fervor, swearing to die defending his rights. We dreamed of a prince from the royal house returning to rule over these ancient dominions.

In light of my own and my mother’s unwavering loyalty, perhaps my brother’s misguided course could yet be corrected. Was it too late to offer him a military command? Might I intercede on his behalf? I knew he respected me, and I believed I had influence over him.

Back in Williamsburg, our councils swayed between hope and despair, triumph and dread. We spoke of reinforcements from England, cursed the rebels, and trembled at the uncertain future. I promised to speak with Harry, and wrote to him—though with little expectation of success—repeating arguments I had used many times before. My mother also tried her hand, appealing to scripture and authority, warning of divine punishment for disobedience to earthly powers. She cited the example of Harry’s elder brother and hinted, rather cruelly, at his subjection to his wife—the worst possible argument in such a matter.

She did not show me her letter, but she did let me read his reply. To my surprise, it was composed with great clarity and elegance—so much so that I thought even his wife might have been incapable of writing it. It turned out Harry had enlisted the aid of Mr. Belman, the New Richmond clergyman, a staunch Whig who had preached and published sermons denouncing Hagan, one of our own faction, and who had clearly won the debate.

My entreaties, like my mother’s, were met with silence. When pressed further by the Governor’s allies, I rashly wrote that I would visit Harry at Fanny’s Mount at the end of the week. But upon arrival, I found only my sister, who welcomed me warmly but told me Harry had gone far into the countryside—toward the Blue Mountains—to inspect horses, and would be away for an unknown length of time.

Then I knew all hope was lost.

“Dear sister,” I said, “from the signs of the times, it seems inevitable that the fuse lit years ago will soon ignite. Harry is riding away—God knows where.”

“The Lord prosper the righteous cause, Sir George,” she replied.

“Amen,” I answered. “But you and he speak as Americans; I as an Englishman. Tell him this: if anything natural happens to our mother, I shall resign all my lands in Virginia to him. I have enough for myself and mine in England.”

“You don’t mean that, George?” she exclaimed, eyes brightening.

“Well, yes,” she said after a pause. “It’s only fair. Why should you, eldest by a mere hour, have everything—lands in England, plantations here, title, children—while poor Harry has nothing? Still, it’s generous of you. Handsome, proper—never expected it. And you don’t take after your mother in this, Sir George, nohow. Give my love to sister Theo!”

She offered me her cheek to kiss as I prepared to leave.

With such a woman guiding him, how could I ever hope to turn Harry?

Frustrated by my failure, I returned to the Governor. Together, we decided it was time to prepare seriously for war. The Court was agitated, furious in its denunciations of the Whigs, shouting “Old England forever!” with reckless zeal. They longed for the day when they could ride down the rebels in battle.

I left the Governor with thanks from his Excellency and a commission to raise a force in defense of the Crown. Thus began the Westmoreland Defenders—a regiment I was honored to command. News of my appointment spread quickly through the county, and officers stepped forward readily. But recruits were slow to come—and quicker to vanish.

Hagan, ever loyal, volunteered as chaplain. Madam Esmond presented our colors and traveled the region recruiting volunteers. But the most passionate recruiter was my old tutor, little Mr. Dempster, who had fought for the Jacobites in Scotland. He journeyed into the Carolinas, seeking descendants of exiled Highlanders who still wore the white cockade of Prince Charles and remained loyal to the Crown.

Meanwhile, Harry’s journey took him beyond the Blue Mountains, through Annapolis and Baltimore, and finally to Philadelphia, where a second Continental Congress was assembling. By then, history had already begun to unfold. Lexington had seen the first shots fired. The war for independence had begun.

We continued to profess loyalty to His Majesty, yet declared our resolve to die or be free. Twenty thousand loyalists gathered around Boston, armed and ready, having seized cannon from government stores. Arnold launched his bold campaign with the capture of two forts. Three generals from Bond Street advanced with reinforcements to aid General Gage.

Soon, armies clashed. At Breed’s Hill, the British made a costly blunder—fortifying instead of advancing—while Congress debated who should lead the colonial forces. The choice fell, famously, on a Virginian.

Among the regiments marching to join the new commander-in-chief was one led by Henry Esmond Warrington, formerly a captain in His Majesty’s service. Beside him rode his young wife, whose courage would later become legend. I was relieved she had left Virginia. Had she stayed, my mother might have challenged her to battle—though I am grateful that such a scene never occurred.

Farmers and country folk rushed northward to join the army. The selection of a Virginian for supreme command flattered our pride. The news of Lexington sparked fury across the colonies. Men raged against the “bloody British invader”—though the soldiers were merely doing their duty, facing armed men resisting their lawful actions. Yet anger blinds reason. The colonists had chosen sides, and with fiery spirit, they resolved to test their strength against the mighty mother country.

Breed’s Hill became a symbol—like a mountain crowned with Liberty, Victory, Glory. Farmers and ploughmen had held their ground. Civilians had outmaneuvered seasoned officers. If Britons could conquer the world, their children could now match them—even surpass them.

I do not know which side deserves greater credit—bravery or pride. We mock the French for their boastfulness, but who matches the unshakable self-confidence of the British—or their American offspring?

Most of those around us supported the people’s cause. As for me, my regiment began poorly manned and dwindled further after news of northern battles—and worse, after the conduct of our Governor.

He had vowed to raise the King’s standard and rally loyal gentlemen. I recall many names—gentlemen now serving in the U.S. government—who once pledged to die beneath the flag, or challenge the rebels to single combat. But history records that our Governor, a peer of Scotland and the Crown’s representative, was the first to flee.

He abandoned his post, slipping away at night to board a warship off York. He sent a message to the Assembly, begging them to continue their sessions, claiming he had fled only from popular fury.

What became of the sheep when the shepherd ran?

The Assembly pleaded with him to return, promising safety. But he refused. His ship became his seat of government. He demanded the House of Commons come to him.

This was raising the standard indeed.

Our Governor was gone. The Assembly ruled in his stead. A mob followed him to sea. Negroes deserted plantations to join his fleet. He landed in darkness, burning and destroying. He not only invited runaway slaves—he sent envoys to the Indians, urging them to join his banner.

When the people resisted, as at Norfolk and Hampton, he retreated to his ships again.

Even my mother, once so certain of victory, grew fearful. She saw the rebellion as both dangerous and cowardly—especially the arming of slaves. The loyal gentry suffered ruin, robbed of their property. Dozens fled to his fleet, some killed, others hanged for plundering under his command.

Yet despite the destruction, and the incompetence of the Crown’s chief officer, my mother never wavered. She became more fiercely loyal than ever. Her oddities were known throughout the province—her tales of the Marquis, her family’s grandeur—but so too were her kindnesses. Many rebels, as she called them, secretly respected the proud little Tory lady.

As for me, though my regiment shrank to nothing after the Governor’s disgrace, I escaped serious danger. After he burned the stores at Hampton and issued his proclamation calling slaves to arms, I went aboard his ship to remonstrate. I begged him to return to Williamsburg, where thousands would defend him. I spoke plainly, showing clear contempt for his actions.

He flew into a rage. “You’re a rebel like the rest!” he shouted, ordering me arrested.

As a militia officer—I often wore a red coat to show my allegiance—I demanded a court-martial. I asked two officers present to bear witness to our exchange. They may have sympathized with me. In the end, I was released unguarded.

Word spread among the Whigs. I had spoken boldly to the Governor—no Whig could have been more liberal in speech.

When riots broke out in Richmond, many Loyalists fled to the ships. But my mother’s house and property remained untouched. Our family was still hopeful of reconciliation.

“Aha!” a distinguished Whig once told me. “If all Tories were like you, we and the people at home might soon be united again.”

That was before the Fourth of July, before the Declaration of Independence made peace impossible. Later, when passions hardened, other motives were attributed to me. I was said to be a “liberal Tory” only because I was cunning, wishing to protect my estate no matter the outcome.

And this, I must admit, is the view held in high circles at home—where personal interest is supposed to explain all.

But there were only a few who knew the truth: I had resolved to cede my life-interest in our American lands to my brother—though I had not told my mother.

Why bother to correct the record? What worth has life if one must endure endless slander?

And I still do not fully understand how my mother, that notorious Loyalist, remained unmolested for years at Castlewood, even as Continental troops were occasionally quartered upon her.

I cannot say for certain. But I suspect it had something to do with Madam Fanny.

After a campaign before Boston, she returned to Fanny’s Mount, leaving her husband behind. My modest Hal, who would accept no rank higher than colonel, believed he served better leading a regiment than commanding a division.

Madam Fanny came back changed. Her bitterness toward my mother vanished. She showed affection for her and her estate. She was close to the new Governor and influential members of the Assembly. My mother, they said, was harmless—and for Harry’s sake, her errors deserved leniency.

So it was that for years, she remained safe—except for heavy requisitions, which she paid willingly. Only when the redcoats approached our house did real harm come.

In which we both fight and run away

What good was a Colonel without a regiment? The Governor and Council, who had once paraded their gratitude when they gave me my commission, were long gone—fleeing aboard ships, leaving behind only scattered acts of arson and piracy along the coast. My Lord Dunmore’s black allies drove off his own people; and worse still, we heard he had sent envoys to the southern tribes, urging them to descend upon us in force and teach our colonists “good behaviour” with tomahawks. “And these are to be our allies?” I said to my mother, exchanging a look heavy with dread, remembering with chilling clarity the savage whose face loomed over mine on Braddock’s Field, his knife at my throat—until Florac struck him down.

We fortified Castlewood as best we could, but truth be told, we feared less the rebels than the Indians and the enslaved men now armed by the Crown. I never saw my mother lose her courage—except once, when she recalled how our father had been killed in an Indian raid more than forty years before. One night, seeing shadows moving near the house, nothing could calm her; she fell to her knees, crying, “The Lord have mercy upon us! The Indians—the Indians!”

Lord Dunmore’s black troops vanished with his fleet, seeking plunder or pay elsewhere. But the painted warriors from the south never came. Still, I looked at my mother’s silver hair, my wife’s dark curls, and our child’s golden ringlets—and felt a cold fear that they might become victims of this brutal war. And it was we who had raised such forces, enlisted such allies! Though I dare not claim to interpret divine will—nor point out Heaven’s hand in every turn—I would say that using Indians and German mercenaries brought its own retribution. On the field, when the mercenaries faced the Provincials, they broke. Their defeat lifted the spirits of the Continental army. And the murder of one woman—Miss McCrea—by a handful of drunken Indians did more harm to the Royal cause than any lost battle or destroyed regiment.

Once the panic of the Indians passed, Madam Esmond regained her composure—but she grew deeply anxious about the danger I ran, and the risk I placed upon others by staying in Virginia.

“What can they do to me?” she said, “a poor old woman? If I have one son, a colonel without a regiment, I have another leading two hundred Continentals under Washington. If the Royalists come, they’ll spare me for your sake. If the rebels appear, I’ll have Harry’s passport. I don’t want—no, I won’t allow—that your delicate wife and this dear little baby should stay here, only increasing the danger for all of us! We must send them to Boston or New York. Don’t talk about defending me! Who would hurt a harmless old woman? If the rebels come, I’ll hide behind Mrs. Fanny’s petticoats. I’ll be far safer without you in the house than with you.” She spoke partly because it made sense—but mostly because she wanted me and my family out of harm’s way. And though danger threatened, she herself was determined to remain in the land where her father was buried and where she was born. She lived backward, so to speak. She had seen the new generation, blessed them, and bid them farewell. She belonged to the past—to old days and memories.

While we debated sending our family north, news arrived: the British had evacuated Boston entirely. They had never dared attack Washington’s camp at Cambridge—though he lay there for months without powder, at our mercy—waiting until he secured ammunition and seized Dorchester Heights, which commanded the city. Then the whole British army and colony were forced into retreat. Yes, the King’s troops won at Bunker Hill—as surely as they defeated the French at Blenheim. Yet after that, their commanders seemed afraid to attack entrenched Continentals. Why, then, from July to March, hesitate against an almost defenseless enemy? Why delay at Long Island, when the Continental army was within our grasp? Why the astonishing timidity of Howe before Valley Forge—where starving, sick, ragged soldiers barely manned the lines, yet held them against a great, well-equipped army?

As the fortunes of the two sides rose and fell, so too did the tone of their supporters. When word reached us in the countryside of Boston’s evacuation, every Whig in the neighborhood bowed to Madam Esmond and urged her to surrender quickly. She no longer displayed her loyalty as openly as before—no longer flew her flag in defiance—but she never wavered. Each morning and evening, Hagan prayed for the Royal Family in our home. On Sundays, neighbors were welcome to attend service, where my mother served as clerk, and the prayer for the High Court of Parliament under our gracious and devout King was delivered with solemn conviction. Brave Hagan was a parson without a living—just as I was a militia colonel without a regiment. He had continued praying for King George in Williamsburg long after the Governor fled. But one Sunday, when he came to church to perform his duty, he found a corporal’s guard at the door. They told him the Committee of Safety had appointed another minister, and advised him to keep quiet. “Lead me before their chiefs,” he replied—our honest friend always loved grand words and dramatic gestures. So he was marched through the streets, followed by a crowd of white and black ruffians, to the Capitol. There he met Messrs. Henry and the new state officials, confronting the robbers, as he called them, in their den. Of course, he meant to deliver a heroic speech (like many men who would gladly be martyrs, if only they could be roasted before a crowd), but Mr. Henry refused him the chance. After making Hagan wait hours in an anteroom with negroes, the divine entered the magistrate’s chamber with unshaken dignity, beginning: “Sir, by what authority am I, a minister of the—” “Mr. Hagan,” interrupted the other, “I’m too busy to listen to speeches. As for King George, he has no more authority here than King Nebuchadnezzar. Remember that—and hold your tongue. Stick to King John and King Macbeth. If you’d like to send round benefit tickets, the entire Assembly will come to hear you. Have you ever seen Mr. Hagan on the stage when you were in London, General?” Saying this, Henry turned to General Lee, second-in-command to Washington, who had just arrived in Virginia. Shamed and red-faced, Hagan was hurried out of the room, nearly weeping. After that, we decided his services were better kept in the country, removed from the restless flock in the city.

The appointment of Virginians to the highest civil and military offices in the new government flattered and tempted many leaders who, otherwise, might have stayed loyal to the Crown. But even though we Loyalists were silenced, the Capitol was in Whig hands, and our so-called levies of loyal recruits were often little more than Falstaff’s troops—empty shells—we still maintained secret communication across the colony and beyond. Though we did not rise in open revolt, though many fled, and though some, under pressure from committees and justices, feigned Republicanism and cursed kings and nobles—we knew each other well. Depending on how favorable the tide turned, we hid our colors, revealed them, half showed them, or even pretended to abandon them altogether, shouting “Down with King George!” Our enslaved servants carried messages and tokens between homes. Countless covert plots stirred among those who could not afford open rebellion. After battle, the neutrals rushed to join the victors, cheering as loudly as the patriots. The runaways were never counted. Will anyone tell me the signers of the Declaration of Independence were not a minority—and that a minority won?

We knew that part of the defeated Massachusetts army was preparing a major southern expedition, and I, eager for action, made contact with the ex-Governor Martin of North Carolina. I planned to join him, along with several fellow Virginian officers—officers of a corps that lacked only privates. We did not make a secret of our departure from Castlewood. Congress’s affairs were not yet strong enough to persecute those of doubtful allegiance. Gentlemen’s houses remained open; in our southern way, we visited friends for months at a time. My wife and I, with our infant and a small retinue of servants, took leave of Madam Esmond on a visit to a neighboring plantation. From there we moved to another friend’s house, then another, until we reached Wilmington, North Carolina—the place where we expected to meet reinforcements.

Before our arrival, the Carolinian Royalists had already shown strength. Their clashes with the Whigs had been unfortunate. The Highlanders, fighting for King George, fared no better than they had when they fought against him in Scotland. We did not reach Wilmington until late May, by which time Admiral Parker’s squadron had arrived, carrying General Clinton and five British regiments, destined for a landing on Charleston.

General Clinton, whom I approached immediately, received us grimly—my “regiment” consisting of Lady Warrington, our infant she was nursing, and three black servants. But Captain Horner of the frigate Sphinx, who had served in Jamaica and known our beloved Governor well, heard that my wife was General Lambert’s daughter and welcomed her warmly, offering his finest cabin. Thus, we became refugees—like Lord Dunmore—having waved our flag, tucked it away, and slipped out the back door. From Wilmington, we sailed swiftly to Charleston. During the voyage and our delay in the river before the assault, I grew acquainted with Mr. Clinton, and our friendship deepened.

It was the King’s birthday when we appeared in the harbor. We declared it a glorious day to begin the expedition.

But it did not begin for several days, and I omit, intentionally, all descriptions of Penelope bidding farewell to Hector, setting forth on this campaign. First, Hector is perfectly well—though slightly afflicted with gout—and no rogue Pyrrhus has taken his widow. In times of war, such scenes of sorrow and separation occur every hour. I still see her gentle face above the ship’s bulwark as we descended into the boats, and the smile of the infant in her arms. How quaint these old tales sound! Captain Miles, lacking poetic taste, may have forgotten the verses in Mr. Pope’s Homer describing your parting from your heroic father—but your mother read them to you as a boy, and keeps the gorget I wore that day tucked away in her dressing box.

My second attempt at battle proved no more successful than my first. That evening, we returned to our ships thoroughly defeated. The reckless Lee—whom Clinton had faced at Boston—now met him at Charleston. Lee and the gallant garrison put up a brilliant and victorious resistance. The fort on Sullivan’s Island was a nut we could not crack. Our frigates’ fire failed to break its shell; the path to the assault was impassable—too deep for wading, as Sir Henry discovered, leading the charge himself. Death by shot, drowning, or cold—these I had faced before returning to my wife. Our frigate grounded briefly, struggled free, and was cannonaded by the enemy until clear.

Amid this misfortune, a small incident sparked a lasting bond between me and Sir Harry Clinton—a man I came to admire deeply throughout the war. Though opinions vary on his leadership, I dare not criticize one I respect so fully. His personal courage was undeniable—he was always eager to show it. Whether at Breed’s Hill, where he led the rallied troops to carry the Continental lines; here before Sullivan’s Fort; or later at Fort Washington, where he charged with standard in hand and entered the fort at the head of the storming column—Clinton was always foremost in battle. No soldier in the King’s service was more admirable.

We were wading toward the fort, aiming to force a column through a path our guns had cleared, when a shot struck a boat beside ours—so precisely that three-quarters of its crew were disabled, the officer steering knocked down, and the flagbearer fallen. I could not help exclaiming, “Bravo! Well aimed!” For no ninepins ever fell more helplessly than those poor men before the round shot. Then the General turned to me, saying grimly, “Sir, the enemy’s conduct seems to please you?” “I am pleased, sir,” I replied, “that my countrymen yonder fight as becomes our nation.” We struggled forward, still under fire from both small arms and artillery, until the water rose to our chests and deepened with each step. We were forced to return to our boats and pull away.

Afterward, Sir Henry visited Lady Warrington aboard the Sphinx. He was kind and witty, joking about the humble author of these memoirs, whom he described as a rebel at heart. I pray my children may never live through—or take part in—such revolutions as the one raging in France. Save a few, the players in such tragedies bear close scrutiny poorly. The leaders are often mere quacks; heroes, ignoble puppets; heroines, anything but pure. Victory does not always go to the brave. In our revolution, it did—once, miraculously—to the most deserving. But who truly knows his enemies now? His greatest triumphs were not in rare battles where he gained slight advantage—but over Congress, over hunger and disease, over lukewarm allies and smiling foes within his own ranks. When the war ended, and the great leaders began quarreling before the public—what accusations, counter-accusations, excuses! This fleet arrived too late; that regiment misunderstood orders; these cannonballs wouldn’t fit those guns—and so on. Here was a general who beat us with no shots, no powder, no money—and never thought of a convention. His courage never surrendered. Through doubt, darkness, danger, and tempest, I believe it was only the American leader’s indomitable spirit that remained steady.

Of course, our Charleston expedition was hailed as a great victory by the enemy, who learned—perhaps from their parents—to cry “victory” if a corporal’s guard was surprised, as loudly as if we had won a full-scale battle. Mr. Lee rushed back to New York, the conqueror of conquerors, proclaiming his glory. And none received him with greater delight than the Commander-in-Chief of the American Army. It was my dear Lee and my dear General—then, and always. I find it touching in the early history of our Revolution how simply the General-in-Chief regarded officers who had once served the Crown. Like the Mexicans, who stared in wonder at an armored Spanish horseman. And this flashy, boastful general—and another Continental commander, whose name and fate later became infamous—surely exploited the modesty of the Commander-in-Chief, advising, blustering, sneering, disobeying orders, daily adding obstacles to a path only Washington’s extraordinary endurance could navigate.

While we were away on our South Carolina campaign, the Fourth of July had passed. We and the thirteen United States were forever parted. My native Virginia had declared all men equally free, that all power rests in the people, who have the right to alter or abolish their government at will—and that hereditary rule is unnatural and absurd! Our General presented me with this document fresh from Williamsburg as we sailed north past the Virginia capes. Amid laughter and amusement, he pointed out the faith I was now bound to uphold from that date forward. There was no escape. I was a Virginian—my godfathers had sworn, in my name, that all men were free (including poor Gumbo), that monarchy was absurd, and that I had the right to change my government whenever I pleased. I thought of Madam Esmond at home—how she would react when asked to sign such articles. What would Hagan say? He tore them apart in a sermon—logical, passionate, but ultimately powerless. The U.S. Government ignored his words. When he argued that since all men were free, Gumbo, Sady, and Nathan certainly had a right to sit in Congress—“Tut, tut, my good Mr. Hagan,” my mother interjected, “let us hear no more of this nonsense. Leave such wickedness to the rebels!”

By mid-August, we stood before New York, where Mr. Howe had brought his army—the same force that had fled to Halifax after its disgraceful expulsion from Boston. The American Commander-in-Chief was there, and a great battle was inevitable. I faced it with a deep anxiety, knowing my dearest brother and his regiment were among the troops we would attack—and would surely overwhelm. Almost the entire American army crossed to a small island, where every officer on both sides knew they would be beaten and had no hope of escape. Two frigates, positioned to block their retreat across the East River to New York, could have destroyed every vessel they used to flee and forced them to surrender. They fought—hasty levies were crushed, generals captured, artillery seized, the remnants huddled in their entrenched camp. The victors were called back. The enemy was trapped in a corner, helpless. “They are at our mercy,” said the gentle General, “and ours tomorrow.” Not a single ship watched the American camp. Not a sentinel could see their movements. An entire army crossed under our very eyes in one night—without losing a single man. General Howe remained in command after this feat, completing his glories at Long Island and Breed’s5 Hill, and later at Philadelphia!

A spy had crossed during the night to warn us—only to fall upon a picket of Germans who couldn’t understand him. Their commander was drunk or asleep. By morning, when the message reached someone who could comprehend English, the entire Continental force had vanished across the East River—and the empire over thirteen colonies had slipped away.

My views on our chief were not uncommon among the army—though perhaps wisely kept silent by those under Howe’s direct command. Am I more unlucky than others? Or why do my careless remarks travel farther than my neighbors’? My rage at the waste of such a victory matched that of many officers. Why must my name be singled out as the worst of the grumblers? Personally, General Howe was brave, pleasant, and good-natured.

“So, Sir George,” he said, “you fault me as a military man because there was fog after the battle on Long Island, and your friends, the Continentals, escaped? Surely we took and killed enough of them. But you gentlemen amateurs are never satisfied!” And he turned his back, shrugged, and spoke to someone else. Amateur I might be—and he the most amiable of men. But if King George had said to him, “Never again serve me,” that agreeable Cassio would have been dismissed—deservedly.

It has often struck me—though I speak with humility before those who have worn the sword—that the entrenchments of Breed’s Hill served as a lasting shield for the Continental army throughout the entire American war. The toll exacted upon us from behind those lines was so great, and the enemy’s resolve so unyielding, that the British commanders henceforth held the Americans’ barricades in high regard. Indeed, even had they been firing from behind mere blankets, certain generals would hesitate to press forward. At White Plains, when Washington’s army was once again at the mercy of victory, we learned afterward that our own troops had paused before a barrier made not of stone or timber, but of cornstalks and straw. Another chance was given to us—and it lasted through an entire winter. During that time, the dwindling, disheartened forces of Congress lay starving and nearly unarmed within our grasp, yet the magnanimous General Howe left Valley Forge untouched. While his well-supplied, disciplined army feasted and gambled in Philadelphia, he allowed the American cause to endure, untouched by conquest.

And what of the celebrations? Triumphal arches rose in London; tournaments were staged in mock medieval splendor; ladies offered garlands and verses to this noble commander, proclaiming his laurels eternal! Why, then, have my fellow countrymen in America never raised statues to such a man? Among all their officers, none fought their battles more wisely, none helped them recover from defeat with greater skill, none ensured their losses were less costly. And when fortune finally turned, and strength prevailed, none showed more patience, compassion, or quiet dignity in helping the fallen rise again.

Ah, think back eighteen years—of the young warrior England sent across the sea, burning with ambition and fire. Picture him pacing endlessly around the enemy’s defenses, sleepless by night and day, consumed by fury and longing, eyes fixed on every shadow, scenting battle like a hound. He crept through midnight forests, scaled cliffs before dawn, waited until the foe revealed himself—then leapt upon him, grappled, and died still striking. That was Wolfe at Quebec. Now listen: here is Howe, smiling amid dancers in Philadelphia, while fiddles play and wine flows freely.

One of the grand schemes devised by our ministers and generals was to sever New England from the rest of the colonies by establishing a link between Canada and New York. Burgoyne was entrusted with this task, and he set out from Quebec with bold confidence, promising success. His march began in full military pomp—trumpets blared proclamations before him, summoning the colonists to remember England’s might and lay down arms. He led a formidable force: English regulars, German veterans, Indian warriors, and a brilliant artillery train. It was believed the people along his path would rally to the Crown. But the Continental resistance, though initially small, grew stronger. Washington’s army was weakened as troops were diverted to meet this northern threat. A detachment from New York was meant to ascend the Hudson, clear the way, and join Burgoyne at Albany. That was the moment to strike Washington’s diminished force—but fate intervened. Nor do I regret the war’s end. Looking back now, how clear the errors of the losing side appear!

From beginning to end, we arrived too late. Our reinforcements came too late. Our fleet appeared off Yorktown just after Cornwallis had surrendered. A route of escape opened for Burgoyne—but he chose retreat too late. I’ve heard defeated officers argue, years later, that a different wind could have saved America for us; that a storm spared the French fleet; that three times, but for darkness, Washington and his army were ours. Who hasn’t wondered, reading history, about what *might* have been?

I take down my old, tattered map-book and trace the battlefield. I marvel at the strange turns that decided the outcome. Setting aside talk of courage—both sides fought bravely—we held the better hand and still lost the game. Yet the contest stirred something deep in me. I felt its pulse.

My brother Hal, settled on his Virginia plantation, found perfect contentment in simple life. The company of neighbors, tending crops, fishing, hunting, playing cards—these were his joys. Happy Hal, beneath his wide porches, dogs at his feet, Will Wimbles living freely in his house, negroes fat and idle, his sharp little wife ruling over all, her husband obeying without question. She died, and he mourned briefly—then moved on. Happy, truly, though such a life would have driven me mad.

My income was fivefold his, my house in England large and stately, built of brick and stone. My wife—would I trade her for any other? My children—I accept Lady Warrington’s judgment. Yet with all these blessings, I fear I’ve been ungrateful. Hodge, my gatekeeper, shares his bread and bacon with a family as large as mine, and seems to enjoy his meal as much as I do—though Mrs. Molly prepares her best dishes, and Mr. Gumbo opens the finest bottle. Ah, sweetmeats no longer taste sweet to me, though they delight the nursery. Claret’s perfume grows stale with age.

Our parson has preached to me many times. I may not have listened at first—but now I understand. Do you remember, honest Joe? (He does—he’s repeated it as often as his sermons, and Lady Warrington pretends she’s never heard it.) That October evening when we scrambled up an embrasure at Fort Clinton, and a clubbed musket nearly ended my life—had not your sword cut through the rebel’s throat, I’d be gone. You wore red then—the uniform of the brave Sixty-third, under the gallant Sill, who fell beside you pierced by many wounds. You traded red for black and took the pulpit. Your sermons are sound and brief. We read the papers together over wine. Not two months ago, we read of Howe’s triumph on June 1st. We heard of Rawdon, who fought with us at Fort Clinton, joining the Duke of York. Now, the Duke is retreating before Pichegru, and my son Miles has captured Valenciennes. Ah, parson—would you not don your old Sixty-third coat again? (Though I doubt Mrs. Blake could fit the buttons.)

The boys played a play with my militia sword. Oh, that I were young again, Mr. Blake! That I had no gout in my toe! I’d saddle Rosinante and ride into the world once more, feel the blood quicken, and play life’s glorious game!

The last decisive move I witnessed was won gallantly by our side—though the Americans claimed the final rubber. We gained only the ground we stood on, and the guns, stores, and ships we destroyed. But our rescue attempt came too late to save Burgoyne’s doomed army.

After one of those delays that plagued our campaigns, an expedition sailed from New York in late September 1777. Had it advanced just two weeks earlier, it might have saved Burgoyne. But fate decreed otherwise. The delay wasn’t Sir Henry Clinton’s fault—he couldn’t leave New York undefended. It was the winds and weather that delayed reinforcements from England. The fleet brought letters from home—long, loving missives from Aunt Hetty and Grandfather, with news of the children. My wife’s heart ached for them. She said nothing, but I saw her plea in her eyes—her fears, her longing. “Why stay?” she seemed to say. “You have no duty here. Why risk your life, my happiness?”

I understood. We weren’t going into immediate danger. I told her Sir Henry would only accompany part of the way. I’d return with him, and Christmas, God willing, would see us reunited in England.

Three thousand men—including two weak regiments of Loyalists and New York Militia (among whom was my cousin, Captain Will Esmond)—embarked at New York. Our fleet sailed up the Hudson River, which, to my mind, rivals the Rhine in beauty. No fire greeted us from the steep cliffs known as the Palisades—strangely, the enemy was unaware of our movement.

We landed first on the eastern bank at Verplancks Point. The Continental troops withdrew after slight resistance. Their commander, the seasoned Putnam, assumed we were advancing toward the Eastern Highlands. He fell back to guard the passes, sending a small detachment forward as if pursued—believing the main force would follow.

Meanwhile, before dawn, two thousand men crossed to Stoney Point on the western shore, opposite Verplancks. There loomed the Dunderberg—a great hill, named by Dutch lords, rising sharply over the river. A stream ran at its base, separating it from the height where Fort Clinton stood—not named for our general, but for a respected New York gentleman, now commanding against us. Above Fort Clinton rose Fort Montgomery; behind them, Bear Hill. Across the river, Saint Antony’s Nose towered—named whimsically by the Dutch.

The assaults began almost simultaneously. Half our force, under Campbell, attacked Fort Montgomery. He fell before the ramparts. Sir Henry, ever seeking danger, led the rest. He hoped we’d fare better than at Sullivan Island.

A narrow path led up the Dunderberg—so tight that only three men could pass abreast. In silence, we climbed, amazed at each step that no one challenged us. The enemy had no watch there. We weren’t seen until descending the slope, where a small force rushed to oppose us. The gunfire spoiled surprise. But the fort was before us.

With no artillery, we had to assault. Silently, swiftly, the men climbed the hill under cannon fire. Orders forbade firing. Sir Henry took the colors of the Sixty-third and led the stormers upward. The incline was so steep that soldiers pushed each other over walls and through embrasures. There, Lieutenant Joseph Blake—father of the young Joseph Clinton Blake, who gazes fondly at a certain lady—saved the life of his unworthy patron by striking down a rebel aiming at him.

About a quarter of the garrison escaped. The rest were killed, wounded, or captured. Fort Montgomery was taken in similar fashion. That night, from the heights where the king’s flag flew, we watched a magnificent spectacle below. A boom and chain stretched from Fort Montgomery to Saint Antony’s Nose, protecting several American frigates and galleys. With the fort lost, the ships tried to flee upstream in darkness. But the wind turned against them. Escape was impossible. Crews abandoned ship, setting them ablaze with sails unfurled. We saw towering pyramids of flame reflected in the river, exploding in thunderous blasts before sinking beneath the water.

The next morning, a parlementaire arrived to inquire about wounded and prisoners. An officer handed me a note—my heart stopped. It was dated October 7, from General George Clinton’s headquarters. It read: “Colonel H. Warrington, of the Virginia line, hopes Sir George Warrington escaped unhurt in the assault of last evening, from which the Colonel himself was fortunate enough to retire without injury.”

Never did I pray more fervently. I thanked Heaven my brother lived—and vowed to withdraw from this fraternal war, entered only because duty called. I longed to see him before leaving. I requested, and received, a mission to General Clinton’s camp.

His headquarters lay miles upriver. A boat with a flag of truce carried me to the shore, where pickets met me. Soon, my brother stood before me. He had recently joined Clinton’s division, bearing orders from Philadelphia. He’d heard I’d been present at the attack.

We spent a short, joyful night together. Mr. Sady, always loyal to Hal, cooked a feast for both of us. Only one straw bed existed in our hut—Hal and I slept side by side, as we had in boyhood. We spoke of everything—past, present, future.

When I told him I planned to retire, his face lit with joy. “Praised be God!” he cried. “Oh, George—think what might have happened had we met in that fight two nights ago!” He turned pale at the thought.

He reassured me about our mother. Though a staunch Tory, the Chief had ordered her protection. “And Fanny,” he added proudly, “watches over her—she’s as good as a company!” Then, with enthusiasm: “Isn’t she clever? Isn’t she beautiful? Isn’t she kind?”—never waiting for an answer. “And to think I almost married Maria! Mercy, what an escape!”

He spoke of Hagan, who prayed daily for the King at Castlewood—though the doors were bolted, and no one heard. “Gracious powers! His wife is sixty, and oh, George—what she drinks!” But why dwell on faults? I’m glad she lived to toast King George long after his dominion was lost.

Morning came. My mission ended. My brother walked with me to the riverside, where my boat waited. We embraced. His hand lingered in mine as I stepped aboard.

“Shall I ever see thee again, dearest companion of my youth?” I asked myself. “Among cold Englishmen, can I find a friend like thee? When did you ever harbor a thought that wasn’t kind? When a desire, that you wouldn’t give up for me? How brave, how modest, how gentle, how strong—how simple, unselfish, humble—you who see others’ merit and shrink from your own!”

He stood on the shore until his figure faded. Tears blurred my vision.

Sir Henry’s victory, brilliant as it was, came too late. It could not prevent Burgoyne’s disaster at Saratoga, which followed soon after. Our advance was insufficient to relieve him. Secret messengers were sent—none reached him. One, carrying a letter from Sir Henry, fell into the hands of General Clinton’s troops, mistaken for British soldiers due to their red uniforms. The spy was discovered and executed.

Ten days after the forts fell, we learned of Saratoga’s ruin. We carried the grim news home. I feared my wife could not mourn. She had her children, her father, her sister to greet—and nightly prayers of thanksgiving that her husband returned alive.

Need I paint, dear readers, the joy of returning home, the warmth of reunion, and the quiet bliss that filled our house when all the children were once more gathered beneath their mother’s loving roof? It shone in her eyes, it trembled in her voice, and it found its truest expression on her knees in silent gratitude. Our home was spacious enough to hold us all, yet Aunt Hetty refused to stay. She confessed plainly that surrendering her role as mother to the elder children—those she had cared for nearly three years—was a wound too deep to bear so soon. She could not endure being near them while taking second place. So she and her father withdrew to a modest cottage at Bury St. Edmunds, not far from us, where they lived quietly, indulging her eldest nephew and niece with affectionate secrecy.

It was the year after our return that Mr. B., the Jamaican planter, passed away, leaving her half his fortune. Then, for the first time, I learned how deeply he had loved her during his time in the West Indies—how, though she had turned him down, he had honored her memory by bequeathing her wealth. Heaven only knows what part of Aunt Hetty’s inheritance Monsieur Miles has already consumed—the cost of his commission, his grand uniforms, his debts at the gaming tables, his little ventures in the Minories. Do you think, sirrah, I do not know the price of Pall Mall taverns, of petits soupers, or even of moderate play at the Cocoa-Tree? A gentleman cannot enjoy such pleasures on five hundred pounds a year—no matter how generously I allow him.

Aunt Hetty insists she will remain an old maid. “I vowed,” she declared, “never to marry until I found a man as good as my dear father. And I never did, Sir George. Not half as good. You may put that in your pipe and smoke it.”

And yet, when the General died—calm, aged, and ready to depart—it was my wife who wept most bitterly. “I weep,” she said softly, “because I feel I did not love him enough.” Hetty, meanwhile, remained outwardly composed, speaking of him as if he still walked among us. She recalled his jests, his gentle kindness to the children—then brightened like a young girl again—and sat contentedly gazing up at the stone in church that bore his name and virtues, never lying about him, for once.

I had long suspected that my brother Hal, whom Hetty had once adored in her youth, still held a place in her heart. When he came to visit us ten years ago, I told him of this early infatuation, hoping—though I confess it—that he might offer to replace Mrs. Fanny, who had passed on, and whose memory my wife, ever prone to self-reproach, felt she had mourned insufficiently. Hal arrived steeped in grief over his loss, swearing there was no woman like her in the world. Our beloved General, still living then, welcomed him back into the family fold as he had done in happier times. The women played the same melodies he’d heard as a boy at Oakhurst. Every heart softened with nostalgia, and Harry poured out his sorrow and praise for his late wife to Hetty, often speaking fondly of his dear Aunt Lambert, whose virtues delighted the faithful husband, whose thoughts, I believe, never strayed from her memory for more than three waking minutes a day.

General Hal journeyed to Paris as an American officer in his blue and yellow uniform—fashionable here thanks to Mr. Fox and others—and was well received at Versailles, though presented by Monsieur le Marquis de Lafayette to the Most Christian King and Queen, who did not favor the Marquis. I suspect a certain Marquise took a fancy to the Virginian General and would have married him willingly had he not resisted and fled back to England, to Warrington, and especially to Bury, where people listened patiently to his stories of his departed wife.

As for us, who had known the poor paragon, we were courteous but less fervent in our admiration, often puzzled when our children asked about Uncle Hal’s angelic wife.

The two Generals, myself, Captain Miles, and Parson Blake—knocked unconscious at Monmouth the year after I returned from America—used to reenact the battles of the Revolution over wine. The parson would cry, “By Jupiter, General!” (he substituted for Jupiter when he laid aside his military garb), “you are the Tory, and Sir George is the Whig! He always finds fault with our leaders, while you defend them endlessly. And last Sunday, when I prayed for the King, I heard you following me—loudly!”

“And so I do, Blake, with all my heart,” replied Hal. “I can’t forget I wore his coat.”

“Ah, if Wolfe had lived twenty years longer!” lamented Lambert.

“Ah, sir,” cried Hal, “you should hear the General talk about him!”

“What General?” I asked, just to tease him.

“My General,” said Hal, rising and filling a bumper. “His Excellency, General George Washington!”

“With all my heart,” I answered—but the parson looked displeased, as if the toast or the claret offended him.

Hal never tired of speaking of his General. It was on one such evening, warm with camaraderie, that he revealed how he had once fallen out with the very man he revered above all others. Their disagreement concerned the Marquis de Lafayette, the young French nobleman who had made such a mark in history—and who had so abruptly vanished from it.

Lafayette’s rank in the French service and his gallantry during the war should have secured Colonel Warrington’s promotion in the Continental army. Instead, a mere youth like M. de Lafayette arrived and was immediately elevated to Major-General by Congress. Hal, speaking freely as an old soldier, had expressed scorn for some of Congress’s appointments—appointments born of intrigue and ambition among officers hungry for rank. Mr. Warrington, perhaps emulating his now-famous friend from Mount Vernon, carried himself as a gentleman: he accepted pay, yes, but spent it on comforts and clothing for his men. Rank, he said, mattered not at all; he would serve equally well as colonel or general. He also voiced disdain for certain officers, particularly regarding the sudden elevation of the young Frenchman—this Marquis, as they called him—who, incidentally, was immensely favored by the Commander-in-Chief himself.

Few in the Continental army could speak French. Thus, Hal had a clearer view of the young Major-General than most, including the Commander-in-Chief. General Washington, good-naturedly, chided Hal for jealousy toward the beardless commander of Auvergne. He appreciated the youthful nobleman’s devotion and recognized political necessity in treating the Marquis kindly.

Yet behind the scenes, Washington was urgently advocating for Colonel Warrington’s promotion before Congress. At a time when winter gripped Valley Forge, where Washington commanded barely five or six thousand men—without fire, blankets, food, or ammunition—while facing Sir William Howe’s fully equipped and thrice-larger force—his troubles were immense. As if these hardships weren’t enough, he faced the cowardly distrust of Congress and rebellion within his own ranks. During the terrible winter of ’77, when a single blow from the British could have ended the war, despair reigned in the American camp—except in one unyielding heart.

My brother had a meeting with the Chief, which he later described to me, and which he could never recount without emotion. Washington had won no great triumphs like those of Arnold or Burgoyne—whose folly had brought victory to Gates and the northern army. Aside from minor skirmishes that proved his courage and vigilance, Washington had suffered defeat after defeat against a superior enemy. Congress distrusted him. Many officers hated him. Those disappointed in ambition, caught in corruption, or exposed for incompetence—all conspired against him. Gates became their leader. Gates, they believed, was the only genius fit to lead the war. And with a vanity he later admitted, he accepted the homage paid him.

To grasp the depth of Washington’s burdens, consider the “Conway Cabal.” An Irishman—a Chevalier of St. Louis and officer in the French army—arrived in America early in 1777 seeking employment. He was swiftly promoted to brigadier, but demanded immediate advancement to major-general.

Mr. Conway had allies in Congress who promised him swift promotion. Washington protested, arguing it was unjust to elevate the youngest brigadier to the highest rank. While the matter lingered, he received a letter from Conway to Gates, praising him: “Heaven must have been determined to save America, or a weak general and bad councillors would have ruined it.” Washington forwarded the letter to Conway without comment. Conway offered his resignation, which Congress refused, instead appointing him Inspector-General with the rank of Major-General.

“And it was at this time,” said Harry, passionate with regret and awe, “when the glorious Chief was burdened with troubles enough to drive ten thousand men mad—that I had to interfere with my jealousies about the Frenchman! I didn’t say much—just some nonsense to Greene and Cadwalader about getting frogs against the Frenchman. But I should have known the Chief’s trials, and that he had a better head than mine. I should have held my tongue.”

For a time, Washington said nothing, but Hal noticed a chill between them. Mrs. Washington, visiting camp, sensed something was wrong. Women, he said, have ways of uncovering secrets. “I might not have sought the cause,” Hal added, “for I am as proud as he is. And when the Chief is angry, it’s no pleasure to approach him.”

Indeed, my brother was subdued by his old friend, obeying him like a boy before a schoolmaster.

“At last,” Hal continued, “Mrs. Washington discovered the truth. ‘Speak to me after dinner, Colonel Hal,’ she said. ‘Come to the parade-ground before the dining-house, and I’ll tell you all.’ I left a dozen generals and brigadiers drinking around the General’s table and found her waiting. She told me it was my remark about the box of Marquises that had offended the General. ‘I wouldn’t have minded another,’ he said, ‘but I never thought Harry Warrington would oppose me.’”

That night, Hal waited to speak. He found Washington alone at his desk.

“Can your Excellency give me five minutes?” he asked, heart pounding.

“Yes, sir,” Washington replied, pointing to the chair. “Please sit.”

“It wasn’t always ‘Sir’ and ‘Colonel Warrington’ between us,” Hal said.

“The times are altered,” Washington answered calmly.

“Et nos mutamur in illis,” Hal quoted. “Times and men change.”

“You had business with me?” Washington asked.

“Am I speaking to the Commander-in-Chief or to my old friend?” Hal questioned.

The General looked at him gravely. “Well—to both, sir. Pray sit, Harry.”

“If to General Washington,” Hal began, “I tell his Excellency that I, and many officers, are not pleased to see a boy of twenty made major-general over us because he’s a Marquis and can’t speak English. If I speak to my old friend, I must say he has shown me little trust or friendship lately. I have no desire to sit at your table while others make impertinent remarks about your turning your back on me.”

“Which charge shall I take first, Harry?” Washington asked, turning his chair and crossing his legs.

“You’re jealous of the Marquis?” he guessed.

“Jealous, sir!” Hal exclaimed. “An aide-de-camp of Mr. Wolfe is not jealous of a Jack-a-dandy who was being whipped at school five years ago!”

“You yourself declined higher rank,” the Chief said, turning slightly red.

“But I never agreed to have a macaroni Marquis command me!” Hal shouted. “I will not carry the young gentleman’s orders. Since Congress and your Excellency choose to appoint generals from the nursery, I humbly request leave to resign and retire to my plantation.”

“Do, Harry,” Washington said gently, surprising him. “That is true friendship. Now that your old friend is in trouble, it’s the best time to leave.”

“Sir!” Hal gasped.

“Do as so many others are doing, Mr. Warrington,” Washington said. “Et tu, Brute, as the play says. Well, well, Harry—I did not think it of you. But at least, you are in fashion.”

“You asked which charge I should take first?” Hal reminded him.

“Oh, the Marquis’s appointment? I recommended it to Congress, no doubt. You and others disapprove.”

“I have spoken for myself, sir,” Hal said.

“If you take me in that tone, Colonel Warrington, I have nothing to answer!” the Chief rose sharply. “I presume I may recommend officers for promotion without your prior approval.”

“Being on that tone, sir,” Hal replied, “let me respectfully submit my resignation, based on the fact that Congress, at your recommendation, offers its highest commands to boys of twenty who barely know our language.” He stood and bowed.

“Great heavens, Harry!” Washington cried—beaten on the matter of the Marquis, unable to reply. “Can’t you believe that in this critical hour, there are reasons why special honor must be shown to the first distinguished Frenchman to join us?”

“No doubt, sir,” Hal said. “If you acknowledge that Monsieur de Lafayette’s merits have nothing to do with it.”

“I acknowledge or deny nothing!” the General snapped, stamping his foot. “Am I here to be catechised by you? Wait—listen, Harry. I speak to you as a man of the world—nay, as an old friend. This appointment humiliates you and others, you say? Be it so! Must we not bear humiliation, along with other burdens, for our country? It may be unjust that the Marquis commands you, just as it would be unfair if your Prince Ferdinand or Prince of Wales commanded veterans at home. But if appointing this young nobleman brings us twenty million allies, will you sulk because we honor him? It’s easy to sneer at him—though, believe me, the Marquis has more merit than you allow. It would be more generous, more polite, for Harry Warrington to welcome this stranger for the sake of our nation’s benefit—not mock his quirks, but aid him with your experience. That is what I expect of you—what I would do. But you choose to join my enemies, and when I am in distress, you say you will leave me. That is why I’ve been hurt. That is why I’ve been cold. I trusted you as a brother. Tell me, was I right? I relied on you, and you come and tell me you will resign. Be it so. Having entered this struggle by God’s will, I will see it through to the end. You are not the first, Mr. Warrington, to leave me on the way.”

He spoke with such tenderness, his face so full of sorrow, that Hal was seized with remorse and pity. He blurted out incoherent words about old times, vowing he would never leave him if he said the word.

“You never loved him, George,” Hal said, turning to me, “but I did beyond any mortal man. Though I’m not clever like you, I think my instinct was right. He has a greatness unmatched by any other.”

“I don’t say no, brother,” I replied.

“Greatness, pooh!” growled the parson, swirling his wine.

“We walked into Mrs. Washington’s tea-room arm-in-arm,” Hal continued. “She looked up kindly and saw we were reconciled. ‘Is it all over, Colonel Harry?’ she whispered. ‘I know he’s applied often about your promotion—’”

“I never will take it,” Hal said.

“And that,” he concluded, “is how I came to do penance with Lafayette the next winter.” (Hal imitated the Frenchman perfectly.) “‘I will go weez heem,’ I said. ‘I know the way to Quebec. When we’re not fighting Sir Guy, I can hear His Excellency the Major-General recite his lesson.’ There was no fight—we couldn’t raise an army for Canada. We returned to headquarters. And what disturbed the Frenchman most? The idea that people would laugh at him because his command had achieved nothing. And they did—almost to his face. How could one help it? If our Chief had a weakness, it was this Marquis.”

After their quarrel, they became closer than ever—if a man may be said to be friends with a sovereign prince, for Hal could not help seeing Washington as one. One night, after the others had retired, they talked of old days—the joyful hunts, the adventures before and after Braddock’s defeat, and that near-duel between us when we were boys. Washington laughed, saying he had never seen anyone look more deadly intent on killing than I did. “And to do Sir George justice,” he added, “I think he has hated me ever since.” Then he paused. “Ah! An open enemy I can face easily. It is the secret foe who causes doubt and anguish. Today, I have sat with men at my table who must pretend civility, shake hands with me, knowing they stab my reputation and seek to pull me down. You recently complained of being humiliated by a junior commanding you. What is your humiliation compared to mine? I must play the farce of welcome to traitors, endure Congress’s neglect, and watch men who insult me promoted in my own army. If I followed my own feelings, would I continue in command? You know my temper—whether as a private man I could endure such slights. But for the sacred cause, we must endure hardship, danger, calumny, and wrong. May God give us strength to do our duty!” Then he showed me the papers concerning Conway—whom Congress promoted despite the conspiracy—and how John Cadwalader sent the best ball he ever fired down the black throat of that fellow.

“And it was here,” Hal said, concluding, “as I watched the Chief speaking in the quiet of the camp, remembering how lonely he was, how vast his responsibility, how spies and traitors fed from his plate, and an enemy lay before him ready to crush him—then I thought: ‘Surely, this is the greatest man in the world. And what a wretch I am to fret over petty jealousies while he walks serenely under his immense burdens.’”

“We spoke of Wolfe just now,” I said. “Here, indeed, is a greater than Wolfe. To endure is greater than to dare. To wear down hostile fortune. To be daunted by no difficulty. To keep heart when all have lost it. To pass through intrigue untouched. To renounce ambition when victory is won—can any say this is not greatness? Or show another Englishman who has achieved so much?”

“I wonder, Sir George,” grumbled Parson Blake, “you didn’t take Washington’s side and wear the blue and buff yourself.”

“You and I thought scarlet suited our complexions, Joe Blake,” Sir George replied. “And my wife thinks there wouldn’t have been room for two such great men on one side.”

“Well, at any rate,” Lady Warrington interjected, “you were better than that odious, swearing, crazy General Lee, who was second in command! And I’m certain Mr. Washington never wrote poetry or tragedies like you can! What did the General say about George’s tragedies, Harry?”

Harry burst into laughter—Captain Miles joining in.

“Well!” he said, “it’s true Hagan read one at my house to the General, Mrs. Washington, and others—and they all fell sound asleep!”

“He never liked my husband,” Theo declared, tossing her head. “And it’s all the more magnanimous of Sir George to speak so well of him.”
